Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 1:

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾.

Since the first of the themes of this surah, the one with which it was revealed, is the matter of disputing with the Christians of Najran when they came as a delegation to Madinah, and the demonstration of the superiority of Islam over Christianity, it was therefore opened with the letters of the alphabet (ḥurūf al-tahajjī, the disjoined letters), which are symbolic of the challenge to those who deny this Book. The greatest share of denial of the Qur'an came from the polytheists among them, and then from the Arab Christians; for the Jews who settled in the lands of the Arabs and spoke their language were not counted among the people of the language, and eloquent speakers of Arabic were rare among them, such as Samaw'al. This verse and what follows it, up to His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 33], is a preface to that which caused the surah to be revealed, and an excellent introduction to it.

The discussion of the meanings of (Alif Lam Mim) has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

[Page 147]

﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾ ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what came before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ ﴿before, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 2–4].

The speech begins with the subject (musnad ilayhi) whose predicate (khabar) is a verb (fi'li), in order to strengthen the predicate and to draw attention to it.

The proper name is used to instil awe upon hearing it. Then it is followed by the sentence ﴿there is no god but Him﴾, as a parenthetical (mu'tarida) or circumstantial (haliyya) clause, refuting the polytheists and, especially, the Christians. It is followed by the two attributes ﴿the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ to negate confusion about the referent of this name, and to point to the reason He alone deserves divinity, and that others do not deserve it, because they are either not living or not self-subsisting. Idols have no life, and according to the Christians' belief, 'Isa (Jesus) has died, so he is now not self-subsisting, nor, during his life, was he self-subsisting in governing the world. How could he be, when he was harmed for God's sake, was denied, and hid from his enemies? The meaning of ﴿the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ has already been discussed in the commentary on the Verse of the Throne.

His saying ﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾ is a predicate of the Name of Majesty (Allah). The predicate here is used for reminding of favour (imtinan), or it is an allusion and a rebuke to the People of the Book who denied this. The predicate is expressed as a verb to strengthen the statement, or to indicate, along with that, exclusivity: that is, Allah, and no other, sent down to you the Book, refuting the saying of the polytheists that the Qur'an is from the speech of Satan, or from the methods of soothsaying, or that a human teaches it.

The doubling in (nazzala) is for transitivity (ta'diya), so it is equivalent to the hamza in (anzala). Doubling indicates strength of the verb in its manner or quantity in a verb that is transitive without doubling, because they have used some transitive verbs with doubling to indicate that, such as their saying: fasara and fassara, faraqa and farraqa, and kasara and kassara. They have also used intransitive verbs in the doubled form, without transitivity, to indicate the strength of the verb, as they said: mata and mawwata, and sàha and sayyaha. However, when doubling becomes for transitivity, I am not certain that it indicates the strengthening of the verb, unless it is said that the shift from transitivity by hamza to transitivity by doubling was intended for the known meaning of strengthening in doubling, so his saying

[Page 148]

﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾ is more important than his saying ﴿and He sent down the Torah﴾, to indicate the greatness of the matter of the sending down of the Qur'an. I have explained this fully in the first introduction of this tafsir. In al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari), here and in many other places, it is stated that (nazzala) indicates tanjim (gradual revelation), and that (anzala) indicates that the two books were sent down all at once. This has no connection with the meaning of strengthening claimed for the doubled verb, unless he means that (nazzala) is used in the sense that implies repetition, which is distribution (tawzi'). Abu Hayyan refuted this with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ [al-Furqan: 32], combining doubling with ﴿all at once﴾. I add that the Torah and the Gospel were sent down in parts, as is the case with everything revealed to the messengers during the period of their mission, and this is the truth, since it is not known that any book was sent down to a messenger all at once.

Al-Kitab (the Book) is the Qur'an. The (ba') in His saying ﴿in truth﴾ is for accompaniment (mulabasa), and the meaning of its accompanying the truth is that it includes the truth in all the meanings it contains. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended﴾ [al-Isra': 105].

The meaning of ﴿confirming what came before it﴾ is that it confirms the earlier books preceding it. What precedes is placed "before his hands" because it comes before him, as if it walks in front of him.

The Torah is the name of the book revealed to Musa (Moses), peace be upon him. It is a Hebrew name, originally "Tora", meaning "guidance". It seems that it is the name of the tablets on which were the Ten Words which were sent down to Musa, peace be upon him, on Mount Sinai (Tur), because they are the root of the Law that came in the books of Musa. So that name was applied to all the books of Musa. The Jews say "Sefer Tora". When this name entered Arabic, they added to it the definite article (lam al-ta'rif), which is added to adjectives and indefinite nouns to make them proper names by dominance, like al-'Aqaba. Among the people of linguistics and tafsir are those who attempted to derive it from an Arabic root, saying that it is derived from al-wary, which is kindling, in the form tif'ala or fawala. What led them to this were two matters: the first is the entry of the definite article into it, which does not enter foreign names. It was answered that there is no obstacle to its entry into arabized words, as they said: al-Iskandariyya. This answer is not correct, because al-Iskandariyya has an Arabic form, since it is a nisba (relative adjective) to Iskandar. The correct answer is that it was made obligatory to be definite because it is an arabization of a name with the meaning of a description, a proper name, so when they arabized it, they made the lam obligatory for that reason.

[Page 149]

The second: it is written in the Mushaf with ya' (in the orthography), and this they did not mention in the justification that it is Arabic. The reason it is written in that way is to indicate the Arabic pronunciation of imala (vowel inclination).

As for al-Injil (the Gospel), it is the name of the revelation that was revealed to 'Isa, peace be upon him, which his companions collected. It is an arabized noun. It is said to be from Greek (Rumiyya), and its origin is (ithanjeliyon), meaning "good news". So its meaning is that of a common noun (ism jins). For this reason they added the word for definiteness in the Greek language. When the Arabs arabized it, they added the definite article. al-Qurtubi reported from al-Tha'labi that the Gospel in Syriac, which is Aramaic, is (ankeliyun). Perhaps al-Tha'labi confused Greek with Syriac, because this word is not Syriac; rather, when the Christians of Iraq pronounced it, they thought it was Syriac. Or perhaps there is an error in the wording, and the correct form is Greek, and in Greek it is (ouwaneliyun), meaning the eloquent word.

Some people of linguistics and tafsir attempted to make it derived from al-najl, which is the water that comes out of the earth, but that is also far-fetched. The hamza of al-Injil is most commonly pronounced with a kasra, so that it follows the pattern of Arabic nouns, because ifi'il exists, though rarely, such as ibzim. It is sometimes pronounced with a fatha on the hamza, but that has no parallel in Arabic.

The phrase ﴿before﴾ (min qablu) is connected to ﴿He sent down﴾. The better view is that it is the first circumstantial (hal) of the Torah and the Gospel, and ﴿as guidance﴾ (huda) is the second circumstantial. The noun qablu has an implied, understood genitive complement, as its being built on a damma indicates, and the estimate is: "from before this time", which is the time of the Qur'an's revelation.

Placing ﴿min qablu﴾ before ﴿as guidance for mankind﴾ is for emphasis on it. As for mentioning this condition, it is so that it is not assumed that the guidance of the Torah and the Gospel continues after the revelation of the Qur'an. It also indicates that they were like preliminaries to the revelation of the Qur'an, which is the completion of Allah's purpose for mankind: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. So the guidance that preceded it is not complete.

As for ﴿mankind﴾ (lil-nas), its definiteness is either for a known reference (al-'ahd), namely the people who were addressed by the two books, or it is for conventional generality (al-istighraq al-'urfi): although the two books were addressed to known people, what they contain guides everyone who wishes to be guided. Many who were not included in the call of Musa and 'Isa, peace be upon them both, became Jewish or Christian. The people whom Muhammad ﷺ called are not included in the generality, because the Qur'an

[Page 150]

abrogated the rulings of the two books (naskh, abrogation). As for the view that the law of those before us (shar' man qablana) is law for us according to the majority of the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), that applies to what the Qur'an has related from them, not to what is found in the two books. Therefore, it is not correct to take generality in this sense; rather, it is in the sense we have mentioned.

Al-Furqan (the Criterion) is originally a verbal noun (masdar) of faraqa, like shukran, kufran, and buhtan. Then it was applied to that by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿And We did not send down upon Our servant on the Day of the Criterion﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], which is the Day of Badr. The Qur'an is also named by it. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]. The meaning of al-Furqan here is the Qur'an, because it distinguishes between truth and falsehood. In describing it with this, there is a preference of its guidance over the guidance of the Torah and the Gospel, because distinguishing between truth and falsehood is the greatest state of guidance, since it contains proof and removes doubt. The repetition of His saying ﴿and He sent down the Criterion﴾ [Al 'Imran: 4] after His saying ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth﴾ is for emphasis, and in order to connect the speech to His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 4] and the rest of the verse, that is, His signs in the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah – for them is a severe punishment. And Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution.﴾ This is a explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani), prepared for by His saying ﴿He has sent down to you the Book with truth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3], because the soul of the listener yearns to know the outcome of those who denied this revelation.

His saying ﴿those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾ includes the polytheists, the Jews and the Christians at one level, because all of them share in disbelief in the Qur'an, and this is what is meant here by "the signs of Allah"; for it is the only Book that may be described as a sign of Allah, since it is a miracle (mu'jizah). He expressed them by the relative pronoun for brevity, since the relative clause (silah) gathers them together, and it indicates the reason for the construction of the predicate, which is His saying ﴿for them is a severe punishment﴾.

His saying ﴿And Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾, because it is part of the completion of this resumptive sentence, as it comes in the manner of clarification of the severity of their punishment; for it is the punishment of One who is Mighty and Avenging, like His saying ﴿So We seized them with the seizure of One Mighty and Omnipotent﴾ [al-Qamar: 42].

Page 151
Al-'Aziz (the Exalted in Might) has already been discussed at His saying, Exalted be He, in Surah al-Baqarah ﴿Know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 209].
Al-intiqam (retribution) is punishment for transgression with anger; for this reason the one who hates is called naqim (resentful). In this attribute the word (dhu) is used, which indicates possession/ownership, to point out that His retribution is by choice, for the establishment of the interests of the servants, and He, exalted be He, is not driven to retribution by an impulse of nature or by rage.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 5:

﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah.﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) that serves as an explanation of the description of the Ever-Living, because the all-encompassing nature of knowledge demonstrates the perfection of life.

The word "shay'" (thing) is used here because it is among the general nouns.

His saying ﴿on earth or in heaven﴾ is intended to express the generality of the places of things. Thus, what is meant by "earth" here is the terrestrial globe with what it contains of seas, and what is meant by "heaven" is the category of heavens, namely the worlds distant from the earth. The mention begins with the earth so that there may be a gradual progression in the coordination toward what is farther in the ruling; for many people know much of the things of the earth, whereas no one knows some of the things of the heavens, let alone knows all of them.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 3, verse 6:**

﴿He is the One who forms you in the wombs however He wills.﴾ This is a second resumptive statement (isti'naf) that explains part of the meaning of al-qayyumiyya (the attribute of being the Self-Subsisting Sustainer of all). It is like a partial substitution (badal al-ba'd min al-kull), where a part is substituted for the whole. Among the aspects of al-qayyumiyya, the formation of human beings is singled out because it is one of the most wondrous manifestations of power. It also contains an allusion that refutes the Christians, who believed in the divinity of 'Isa because God formed him in an unusual manner. So God showed them that all the modes that occur to existing things are from the creation and formation of Allah, both the customary and the non-customary.

Here "kayfa" (كَيْفَ) does not carry the meaning of interrogation. Rather, it indicates the bare sense of kayfiyya (manner, mode), that is, a state (al-ha'la). It is used here in its original lexical sense. There is no doubt that "kayfa" (كَيْفَ) contains the root letters of kayfiyya and takkayyuf, which mean state and condition. Although its most common usage is as an interrogative noun, "kayfa" is not a verb, because it does not indicate time, and it is not a particle, because it contains a root from which derivation is possible. "Kayfa" may also come as a conditional noun when the superfluous "ma" (ما) is attached to it. In all these uses, it never ceases to indicate a state, and the verbal clause following it is always attached to it, except for the rare saying, "kayfa anta" (كَيْفَ أنْتَ). When it is interrogative, the clause after it is what is being asked about, so it functions as an object of the verb after it, and its fronting is obligatory because the interrogative has priority of position. When it is stripped of the interrogative sense, its place in i'rab (grammatical analysis) is determined by the governing elements of the sentence in which it occurs, like all other nouns.

As for the clause following it in that case, the more apparent view is that it is considered a genitive complement of which "kayfa" is the noun. "Kayfa" is regarded as one of the nouns that necessarily require an annexed complement. Some grammarians of Arabic have held that the fatha on "kayfa" is a fatha of construction (bina').

In my view, the more apparent position is that the fatha on "kayfa" (كَيْفَ) is a fatha of naṣb (accusative case), which became fixed on it because it is always connected to a verb. So it functions as an object of that verb, in the sense of a circumstantial accusative or something similar. Because this fatha is constantly attached to it, it resembles the fatha of construction.

Accordingly, "kayfa" in His words here, ﴿kayfa yashā'u﴾ (however He wills), is parsed as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of "yuṣawwirukum" (He forms you), since the implied meaning is: a manner of forming that He wills. This is what Ibn Hisham said regarding the words of Allah, Exalted is He, ﴿kayfa fa'ala rabbuka﴾ (how your Lord dealt) [al-Fajr: 6].

The author of al-Mughni (Ibn Hisham) allowed that it could be conditional, with the response omitted, the response being indicated by "yuṣawwirukum." But this is far-fetched, because it does not occur in the conditional form except when accompanied by "ma." As for people's saying, "kayfa shā'a fa'ala" (however He wished, He did), it is a grammatical error (laḥn). Likewise, the jazm (apocopation) of the verb after it has been considered an error by the majority of the leading grammarians of Arabic.

The definiteness of the two components indicates that the attribute of forming is restricted to Him, Exalted is He. This is a real restriction (qaṣr ḥaqiqi), because that is indeed the case in reality, since He is the one who brings about the causes of that formation. This is also an indication that refutes the Christians' confusion, since they imagined that the creation of 'Isa without the water of a father is proof that he is not a human being and that he is a god. They failed to realize that formation in the wombs, although its modes vary, does not depart from being a creation of what was non-existent. So how could that created being formed in the womb be a god?

﴿There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾
This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) confirming the preceding rulings. The meaning of "al-'Azīz al-Ḥakīm" (the Mighty, the Wise) has already been explained in His words, ﴿Know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 209]. The opening of the surah with these verses is an excellent introductory device (baraʿat istihlal), since they were revealed in the dispute with the Christians of Najran. For this reason, the restriction of divinity to Allah, Exalted is He, is repeated in this opening: in His words, ﴿Allah, there is no god but He﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 2], and His words, ﴿He is the One who forms you﴾, and His words, ﴿there is no god but He﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 2].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 7 (part 1 of 4)**

﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are definite (muhkamat), they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are ambiguous (mutashabihat).﴾

This is a third resumptive sentence (isti'naf), informing about one of God's affairs, and it is related to the purpose for which the discourse was brought: confirming His sending down the Qur'an and the two Books before it. This resumption reinforces the content of His words, ﴿He has sent down to you the Book with truth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3], and paves the way for His words, ﴿in it are verses that are definite﴾, because the verses were revealed in the context of disputing with the delegation of Najran, and they opened by refuting their belief in the divinity of the Messiah, by pointing to the true attributes of God. Here the discourse turns to removing their confusion regarding their claim that the texts of the Qur'an acknowledge the divinity of the Messiah, since in them he is described as "a spirit from God," that he gives life to the dead, that he is "the Word of God," and other such things. So they were told that what they clung to was a clinging based on confusion and misinterpretation.

In His words, ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book﴾, there is a restriction (qasr) of the attribute of sending down the Qur'an to God, Exalted is He, so that the sentence, along with being a confirmation and a preparation, is also a refutation of the words of the polytheists: ﴿It is only a human who teaches him﴾ [al-Nahl: 103], and their words: ﴿Tales of the ancients, which he had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening﴾ [al-Furqan: 5]. It is likewise like His words: ﴿The devils have not brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 210], ﴿It is not befitting for them, nor are they able to do so﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 211], ﴿Indeed, they are removed from hearing it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 212]. This is because they said: "It is the speech of a soothsayer," and "the speech of a poet," and they believed that the speech of soothsayers and poets was dictated by the rā'īs (plural: ar'iya', meaning the jinn who inspire them).

[p. 154]

Among the marvels of eloquence is that He mentioned in the restriction the verb "sent down" (anzala), which is specific to God, Exalted is He, even without the form of restriction, since "sending down" is synonymous with revelation (wahy) and does not occur except from God. This is unlike if He had said: "It is He who gave you the Book" (ataka).

The pronoun in "from it" (minhu) refers to the Qur'an. "Min-hu" is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and "verses that are definite" (ayatun muhkamat) is the subject (mubtada').

Ihkam (definiteness) originally means prevention. Jarir said:

*"Sons of Hanifa, restrain your foolish ones,*
*I fear for you that I will become angry."*

Ihkam was then used for perfecting and securing, because that prevents the intrusion of what contradicts the intended meaning; for this reason wisdom (hikmah) was called hikmah. This usage is either literal or a well-known metaphor.

In this verse, "definite" (muhkam) is applied, by way of metaphor, to what is clear in its indication, because clarity of indication prevents the intrusion of possibilities that would cause hesitation about the intended meaning.

"Ambiguous" (mutashabih) is applied here, by way of metaphor, to the obscurity of indication regarding the meaning, because the intrusion of possibility into the meanings of speech leads to the non-determination of one of the possibilities. This is like the similarity of essences in that one of them cannot be distinguished from another.

His words, ﴿the foundation of the Book﴾: the "mother" (umm) of a thing is its origin and that which gathers its many parts, from which its branches spread. From this, the head-covering that gathers the head is called "umm al-ra's," and that is the brain; the banner is called "the mother" because the army gathers around it; and a great city is called "the mother of the cities" (umm al-qura). The origin of this is that the mother, literally, is the one who gives birth, and she is the root of the offspring and the one who gathers the children in her care. Based on these two meanings, the name "mother" was applied to what we have mentioned, by way of eloquent comparison (tashbih baligh). Then this application spread until it equaled the literal meaning. This was discussed in naming al-Fatihah "the mother of the Qur'an."

"The Book" (al-kitab) is undoubtedly the Qur'an, because it is what is spoken of in His words, ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book﴾. Therefore, His words ﴿the foundation of the Book﴾ here are not like His words ﴿and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39].

His words ﴿and others that are ambiguous﴾: "mutashabihat" means the similar ones (mutamathilat), and similarity occurs in many attributes, so it is specified by what indicates the aspect of similarity. Sometimes its explanation is left out when the aspect of similarity is apparent, as in His words, ﴿Indeed, cattle have become confused for us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 70]. In this verse, the aspect of similarity is not mentioned.

[p. 155]

The verse has indicated that the verses of the Qur'an are of two kinds: definite and their opposites, which are called ambiguous. Then it explained that the definite ones are "the foundation of the Book," so we know that the ambiguous ones are the opposites of the definite ones. Then it followed this with His words: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation﴾, meaning, its interpretation that those like them have no means of reaching. So we know that the ambiguous ones are those whose intended meanings have not become clear, and we know that the attributes of definite and ambiguous refer to the wording of the verses.

By describing the definite verses as "the foundation of the Book," it is possible that the meaning of "mother" is origin or reference, and these two are close: that is, they are the origin of the Qur'an or its reference. Nothing suits these two meanings except the indicative function of the Qur'an, since the Qur'an was sent down for guidance and direction. So the definite verses are the foundations of belief and legislation, of manners and admonitions, and they were foundations for that because their indication is clear, such that they indicate meanings that do not admit of anything else, or admit of it only in a weak way that is not considered. Examples include His words: ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]; ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23]; ﴿God intends ease for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]; ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205]; ﴿As for one who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 40]; ﴿Then indeed, Paradise will be the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 41]. And through the clarity of their meanings, such that they are grasped by the understanding of most of those addressed by them, and they are qualified to be understood, they are the origin of the Qur'an to which reference is made in deriving the meanings of others from them, for clarification or for branching out.

The ambiguous ones are the opposite of the definite ones; they are those that indicate meanings which are similar in that each of them could be the one intended. The meaning of their similarity is that they are similar in the validity of directing one's intent toward them; that is, none of them is more preferable than another, or their meaning may be true in many contradictory forms or may be unsuitable for being the one intended, so the purpose from them is not made clear. This is the way I see the interpretation (tafsir) of the verse.

The scholars of Islam have differed regarding determining what is meant by the definite and the ambiguous, in several opinions, all of which return to determining the degree of clarity and obscurity.

From Ibn 'Abbas: the definite is what the legislations do not differ on, such as the oneness of God and the prohibition of abominations. This is what is contained in the three verses at the end of Surat al-An'am: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ [al-An'am: 151], and the verses in Surat al-Isra': ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. And the ambiguous is the unspecified generalities that were not explained, like the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs.

[p. 156]

From Ibn Mas'ud and also Ibn 'Abbas: the definite is what has not been abrogated (mansukh), and the ambiguous is the abrogated. This is far from being intended here, because it does not fit the two descriptions, nor the rest of the verse.

From al-Asamm: the definite is what its proof is clear, and the ambiguous is what requires reflection (tadabbur). Such as His words: ﴿And He who sent down from the sky water in measure, and We revived with it a dead land; thus you will be brought forth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 11]. Its first part is definite, and its last part is ambiguous.

The majority hold two positions. The first is that the definite is what its indication is clear, and the ambiguous is what God has kept knowledge of to Himself. This view is attributed to Malik, in a narration of Ashhab from the Jami' of al-'Utbiyya, and al-Khafaji attributed it to the Hanafiyya, and al-Shatibi inclined to it in al-Muwafaqat.

The second is that the definite is what is clear in its indication, and the ambiguous is what is obscure in it. This was the position of al-Fakhr (al-Razi). So the explicit text (nass) and the apparent meaning (zahir) are the definite, because of the clarity of their indication, even though the apparent meaning may admit a weak possibility. The general (mujmal) and the interpreted (mu'awwal) are the ambiguous, because they share obscurity of indication, even though one of them, namely the interpreted, indicates a less-preferred meaning which is opposed by a preferred meaning, and the general indicates a less-preferred meaning which is opposed by another less-preferred meaning. This method is attributed to the Shafi'iyya.

Al-Shatibi said: Ambiguity is of two kinds: real (haqiqi) and relative (idafi). The real is that for which there is no path to understanding its meaning, and this is what is intended by the verse. The relative is that whose meaning is unclear, because it needs consideration of another proof. So when the mujtahid (jurist) investigates the proofs of the Shari'ah, he finds in them what clarifies its meaning. Real ambiguity is very rare in the Shari'ah, and relative ambiguity is abundant.

This verse has indicated that the Qur'an contains both definite and ambiguous verses. Other verses have indicated that the whole Qur'an is definite, as He said: ﴿A Book whose verses have been made definite﴾ [Hud: 1], and He said: ﴿These are the verses of the wise Book﴾ [Yunus: 1]. What is meant is that it was made definite and perfected in its eloquence. Other verses have indicated that the whole Qur'an is ambiguous, as He said: ﴿God has sent down the best statement, a Book whose parts are similar (mutashabihan)﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. The meaning is that it is similar in its beauty, its eloquence, and its truthfulness, and this is the meaning of: ﴿And if it had been from other than God, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [al-Nisa': 82]. There is no contradiction among these verses, because the meanings of definiteness and ambiguity differ in their places, according to what the contexts require.

[p. 157]

The cause of the occurrence of ambiguous verses in the Qur'an is that it is a call, admonition, instruction, lasting legislation, and a miracle, and it was addressed to a people who had no previous experience with instruction and legislation. So it came in a style suited to combining these matters, according to the condition of those addressed, who were not accustomed to pedagogical styles or scholarly dictations; their habit was rather oratory and debate. The style of admonition and call is close to the style of oratory, and therefore it does not follow the style of books composed for knowledge, or of laws laid down for legislation. So the sciences intended by it were placed within the course of admonition and call, and likewise legislation was placed within it. You do not find the rulings of one type of transaction, such as sale, connected to one another; rather you find them distributed according to what the contexts of admonition and call required, so that their reception would be easy for the listeners, and they would become accustomed to the knowledge of what they had not been familiar with, in a style they were already familiar with. So the rulings were scattered, and some of them are joined to others by reflection. Moreover, the delivery of those rulings took place over a long period, exceeding twenty years, during which rulings were delivered to them in the measure that their needs called for and their capacity could bear. Some of its legislation consists of unchanging principles, and some of it consists of branches that vary according to their conditions. Therefore you find some of them general, absolute, or unspecified, and some specific, restricted, or explanatory. So if some mujtahids hold that the specification of some general texts by some particular circumstances is valid, for example, some of them may hold to the generality only in that case; like one who holds that a specific ruling coming after a general one abrogates it, and so needs to determine the date.

Furthermore, the sciences that the Qur'an addresses are among the higher sciences: they are sciences beyond nature (ma ba'd al-tabi'ah), the sciences of the levels of souls, the sciences of the social order ('umran), wisdom, and the sciences of rights.

Because the language that was established is too narrow to fulfill the ultimate aims of meanings in these sciences, and because the capacity of the understanding of most of those addressed to grasp them is limited, this caused ambiguity in the meanings of the verses that indicate them. The miraculousness of the Qur'an includes a miracle of arrangement (nazm) and a miracle of scientific content ('ilmi), and this is a noble branch of miraculousness that I explained in the tenth introduction of this commentary. When the Qur'an addressed some of the signs of the cosmos and its characteristics, among what it addressed, it brought them in a description that suits relating its condition as it is in reality. Perhaps the knowing of the true nature of its condition in reality was unknown to certain peoples, so they counted those verses that indicate it as ambiguous. But when those who came after them arrived, they knew that what those before them had counted as ambiguous was nothing but definite.

[p. 158]

This passage continues the commentary on the ends (maqasid) of the Qur'an and the reasons for the existence of the mutashabih (ambiguous verses). I translate it in full.

Furthermore, among the aims of the Qur'an are two other matters. The first is that it is a perpetual law (shari'a), and this requires opening the doors of its expressions to the varied deductions (istinbat) of those who derive rulings, so that the rulings of the earlier and later generations may be drawn from it. The second is the training of the bearers of this law and the scholars of this community in investigation (tanqib), inquiry (bahth), and the extraction of meanings from the intricate proofs, so that the strata of the community's scholars, in every age, will be fit to understand the Lawgiver's legislation and its purpose, and will be able to derive legal rulings. Had the legislation been formulated in a style easy to handle, they would have become accustomed to dwelling only on what lies before their eyes in a single reading. For this reason, the capacity of its expressions to accommodate the differing tendencies of the mujtahids has taken the place of the successive authors in writing the books of the sciences, in accordance with the differing ranks of the eras.

Once you know this, you know the root cause of the existence of what is called the mutashabih in the Qur'an. It remains for us to mention to you the degrees of ambiguity and the variation of their causes. By our inductive survey up to now, they are ten degrees.

The first: meanings that were intended to be deposited in the Qur'an and whose details were intended to remain general, either because humans are not capable of understanding them, even in part (if we accept the existence of the general (mujmal) that God alone has kept knowledge of, as will come, though we do not adopt it), or because some of them are not capable of grasping their true nature, so they were conveyed to them in a general way. Or because some of them, in a given age or circumstance, are not capable of understanding them in their full reality. Among this category are the conditions of the Resurrection and some matters of divine lordship, such as God coming in shadows of clouds, seeing (ru'ya), speech (kalam), and the like.

The second: meanings whose indication to the Muslims was intended, but whose details are necessarily general, while being capable of being interpreted as known meanings, but through interpretations. Examples are the opening letters of the surahs, and such verses as ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5] and ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ [al-Baqara: 29].

The third: lofty meanings whose true reality the language, established for the most common usage of its people, was too narrow to convey. These meanings were therefore expressed by the nearest expressions that bring their meanings closer to understanding. This is like most of the attributes of God, such as the Most Merciful (al-Rahman), the Compassionate (al-Ra'uf), the Supremely Great (al-Mutakabbir), and the Light of the heavens and the earth.

The fourth: meanings which human understanding fell short of in some periods, and which were deposited in the Qur'an so that their existence would be a Qur'anic miracle (mu'jiza) for the people of knowledge in ages when the perception of the miracle of the composition (nazm) may weaken. Examples are His saying ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place for it﴾ [Ya-Sin: 38], ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾ [al-Hijr: 22], ﴿He wraps the night over the day﴾ [al-Zumar: 5], ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass away as the clouds pass﴾ [al-Naml: 88], ﴿grows with the oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20], ﴿an olive tree neither of the east nor of the west﴾ [al-Nur: 35], ﴿And His Throne was upon the water﴾ [Hud: 7], ﴿Then He turned to the heaven and it was smoke﴾ [Fussilat: 11], and the mention of the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj.

The fifth: figurative expressions (majazat) and metonymies (kinayat) used in the language of the Arabs, except that their apparent meaning gives rise to senses that are not fitting to attribute to God, Exalted is He, since they indicate attributes contrary to the perfection of divinity. A group hesitated over their intended sense out of the desire to affirm God's transcendence. Examples are ﴿So indeed you are before Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48], ﴿And the heaven We built with hands﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47], and ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 27].

The sixth: words from the dialects of the Arabs that were not known to those among whom the Qur'an was revealed, namely the Quraysh and the Ansar, such as ﴿And fruit and pasture﴾ [Abasa: 31], and such as ﴿Or He seizes them with gradual wasting﴾ [al-Nahl: 47], ﴿Indeed Ibrahim was tender-hearted and forbearing﴾ [al-Tawba: 114], and ﴿nor any food except from the pus of the wound﴾ [al-Haqqa: 36].

The seventh: legal technical terms for which the Arabs had no knowledge of their particular meaning. Those that became well known among the Muslims took on their meaning and became a customary technical meaning (haqiqa 'urfiyya), like tayammum and zakat. Those that did not become well known remained ambiguous, like riba. 'Umar said: "The verses on riba were among the last of what was revealed, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) died without explaining them," and this was discussed earlier in Surat al-Baqara.

The eighth: Arabic stylistic forms that were hidden from some peoples, so they thought speech using them was ambiguous. Examples are the insertion of the particle "kaf" in His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11], and the figure of speech by association (mushakala) in His saying ﴿They seek to deceive God, but He is deceiving them﴾ [al-Nisa: 142].

So the listener knows that attributing "deceiving" (khadi') to the pronoun of the Majesty (God) is an attribution with a figurative meaning, required by the mushakala.

The ninth: verses that came in accordance with the customs of the Arabs, which the original addressees understood, but those who came after did not understand, and so they regarded them as ambiguous. Such is His saying ﴿So whoever performs the Hajj to the House or the 'umra, there is no sin upon him to circumambulate them both﴾ [al-Baqara: 158]. In the Muwatta', Ibn al-Zubayr said: "I said to 'A'isha, and I was then a young man who had not yet acquired understanding: 'I see no harm for anyone in not circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwa.' She said to him: 'It is not as you say. Rather, the Ansar used to assume ihram for Manat the Idol,'" etc.

From this is His saying ﴿God knew that you were betraying yourselves, so He accepted your repentance﴾ [al-Baqara: 187], and ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they ate, if they fear God and believe﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 93], the verse. The intended meaning there is what they drank of wine before its prohibition.

The tenth: weak understandings that counted much of what is not mutashabih as mutashabih, and that is the understanding of the Batiniyya and the understanding of the Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists), such as His saying ﴿On the day when a shin will be uncovered﴾ [al-Qalam: 42].

What is not mutashabih is that in which it is explicitly stated that we cannot reach knowledge of it, such as His saying ﴿Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 85], nor that in which it is explicitly stated that its time is unknown, such as His saying ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾ [al-A'raf: 187].

Nor is it mutashabih what indicates a meaning which conflicts with a construal of it by another, separate proof, because that falls under the principle of reconciling two conflicting proofs or preferring one over the other, such as His address to Iblis: ﴿And incite whomever you can among them with your voice﴾ [al-Isra': 64], the verse in Surat al-Isra', along with the verses that imply ﴿Indeed God is not in need of you, and He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ [al-Zumar: 7] and ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾ [al-Baqara: 205].

You have known from this that the criterion of ambiguity is the absence of correspondence (tawatu') between the meanings and the language, either because the language is too narrow for the meanings, or because the understandings are too narrow to use the language for the meaning, or because some of the language has been forgotten. It thus becomes clear to you that the categories of muhkam and mutashabih are attributes of the expressions in relation to the understanding of their meanings.

The pronoun referring back to the plural "verses" (ayat muhkamat), which is a plural pronoun, is used with the singular noun "umm" (mother), which does not denote parts, because the intended sense is that the class of the muhkam verses occupies within the Book the position of its "mother," that is, its origin and reference to which one returns in understanding the Book and its purposes. The meaning is: they are like a mother of the Book. It follows from this that every muhkam verse is a "mother" of the Book in what it comprises of meaning. This is like the saying of al-Nabigha, describing the Banu Asad:

"They are my coat of mail in which I have clothed myself,"

meaning their collectivity is like a coat of mail for me. It follows that each one of the Banu Asad is like a single ring of the coat of mail. From this sense is His saying: ﴿And make us an imam for the righteous﴾ [al-Furqan: 74].

The discussion of "ukhar" (others) was given earlier at His saying ﴿then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqara: 184].

* * *

﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that of it which is ambiguous, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation.﴾

This is a detailing of a generality implied by the preceding discourse. Since He divided the Book into muhkam and mutashabih, and that division was in terms of the indication of words upon meanings, the soul is eager to know how people receive the mutashabih. As for the muhkam, people receive it in one manner, so there is no need to detail it. He limited the detail to mentioning one of its categories: the state of ﴿those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, how they receive the ambiguous matters, because explaining this is the more important in the purpose for which the discourse is directed, namely uncovering the doubt of those whom the ambiguous matters deceived and who did not find the path to the true interpretation. The state of their counterparts, those who have no deviation in their hearts, is known by way of contrast. Then He will explicitly state, in general terms, the state of the guided in receiving the ambiguous passages of the Qur'an.

The hearts (qulub) are the seats of perception, namely the intellects, and this was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful﴾ [al-Baqara: 283] in Surat al-Baqara.

Zaygh (deviation) is inclination and turning away from the intended target: ﴿The sight did not swerve﴾ [al-Najm: 17]. It is said: "The sun deviated (zaghat al-shams)." Thus zaygh is more specific than mayl (inclination), because it is an inclination away from correctness and the intended aim.

Following (ittiba') here is a figurative expression for constant attachment and repetition, meaning they devote themselves to delving into the ambiguous, counting it. That attachment is likened to the attachment of a follower to the one he follows.

He mentioned the reason for the following, which is seeking discord and seeking to make them interpret it. Seeking its interpretation in itself is not blameworthy, as is shown by His saying ﴿And none knows its interpretation except God and those firm in knowledge﴾, as we will explain. The point of blame is only that they seek an interpretation for which they are not qualified, and so they interpret it in a way that suits their desires. This is the custom of the heretics (malahida) and people of desires, who deliberately lead people to follow them in order to multiply their numbers.

Since He described the people of this aim as having deviation in their hearts, we know that He blamed them for this aim. There is no doubt that every occupation with the ambiguous, when it leads to this aim, incurs some of this blame. Those who followed the ambiguous seeking discord and seeking its interpretation are the hypocrites, the zindiqs, and the polytheists. An example of the polytheists' interpretation is the story of al-'As ibn Wa'il, one of the polytheists, when Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, one of the Muslims, came to him seeking his wages. Al-'As said, mocking him: "Am I indeed to be resurrected after death (according to your belief)? Then I will pay you when I return to wealth and children." So al-'As imagined, or intended to create the impression, that resurrection after death is a return to this world, or he wanted to deceive the common polytheists in this so that it would be more effective in denying the report of resurrection, by observing that none of the dead returns. For this reason they used to say: ﴿Then bring our fathers, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Dukhan: 36].

An example of the zindiqs' interpretation is what Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Razim al-Ta'i al-Kufi related, saying: "I was in Mecca when al-Janabi, the leader of the Qaramita, was in Mecca, and they were killing the pilgrims, saying: 'Did not Muhammad of Mecca tell you: ﴿And whoever enters it is secure﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]? Then what security is there here?'" He said: "I said to him: 'This came in the form of a report, but the intended meaning is a command, that is, whoever enters it, grant him security,' like His saying ﴿And divorced women shall wait﴾ [al-Baqara: 228]." Those who resembled them in this are every group that makes the investigation of the ambiguous its habit, and that leads them to disputes and factionalism. And everyone who interprets the ambiguous according to his own desire, without evidence for his interpretation, relying on a proof or Arabic usage.

It is understood that the intended meaning is interpretation according to desire, or interpretation that induces discord, by the indication of His saying: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except God and those firm in knowledge say: We believe in it﴾, the verse, and as is understood from His saying "they follow" that they are concerned with this and are reckless about it. This is the criterion distinguishing the state of one who follows the ambiguous in order to cause doubt and unbelief, from the state of one who explains the ambiguous and interprets it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 7 (part 3 of 4):

When someone calls him to that. In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr: a man said to Ibn 'Abbas, "I find in the Qur'an things that contradict one another for me." He said, "What are they?" The man said: ﴿So there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101]. And he said: ﴿They will turn to one another, asking each other﴾ [al-Saffat: 27]. And he said: ﴿And they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [al-Nisa': 42]. And he said: ﴿They will say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ [al-An'am: 23].

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿So there will be no kinship between them﴾ refers to the first blast, and then at the second blast ﴿they will turn to one another, asking each other﴾. As for His words ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾, Allah forgives the sins of the people of sincerity (ikhlas), so the polytheists say, "Come, let us say: we were not polytheists." Then Allah seals their mouths, and their limbs speak of their deeds. At that point ﴿they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾.

Al-Bukhari also related, on the authority of 'A'isha, who said: The Messenger of Allah recited this verse up to His words ﴿those of understanding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269], and then said: "When you see those who follow what is ambiguous (mutashabih) of it, then they are the ones Allah has named, so beware of them."

What is intended by His words ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it﴾ is an allusion to the Christians of Najran, who obliged the Muslims to accept that the Qur'an testifies that God is the third of three, by the pronoun of the speaker that occurs in the Qur'an together with others, such as "We created," "We commanded," and "We decreed." They claimed that this pronoun refers to Him, to Jesus and to Mary. Without doubt, this, if it is truly what they said, is deception, since it is well known that this pronoun has two well-known usages: either to express plurality (al-tashrik) or to express majesty (al-ta'zim). They intended by this argument nothing but to deceive the common people.

* * *

﴿None knows its interpretation except Allah, and those firmly grounded in knowledge say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." And none will be reminded except those of understanding﴾.

This is a circumstantial clause (jumlat hal), meaning: while they have no capacity to interpret it, since its interpretation is not for the likes of them, as the proverb says: "This is not your nest, so slip away."

From here, the early generations (al-salaf) refrained from interpreting the ambiguous verses (al-mutashabihat) that do not refer back to legislation. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "What earth would carry me and what sky would shade me if I said about the Book of Allah something I do not know?"

In the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, a man came to Medina from Basra, called Subay' ibn Shurayk, or Ibn 'Asal al-Tamimi, and he began asking people about the ambiguous verses of the Qur'an and other things. 'Umar summoned him and beat him painfully, repeating this for several days. He said, "Enough, O Commander of the Faithful, for what I used to find in my head has gone." Then 'Umar sent him back to Basra and wrote to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that he should prevent the people from associating with him.

Among the early generations there were those who did interpret when doubt arose for some people, as Ibn 'Abbas did in what we mentioned just now.

Ibn al-'Arabi said, in al-'Awasim min al-Qawasim: "Among those who plot against Islam are the Batiniyya and the Zahiriyya." I say: As for the Batiniyya, they made most of the Qur'an ambiguous and interpreted it according to their own desires. As for the Zahiriyya, they multiplied the ambiguous verses and believed the cause of ambiguity to be real. The former entered into His words ﴿seeking its interpretation﴾, while the latter departed from His words ﴿None knows its interpretation except Allah, and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾, or ﴿None knows its interpretation except Allah﴾, and so they opposed both later and early generations. Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'Awasim: "The origin of the Zahiriyya is the Kharijites, who said, 'There is no judgment except for Allah,' meaning that they took the apparent sense of His words, ﴿The judgment is only for Allah﴾, and did not interpret it according to what is meant by judgment."

What is meant by "those firmly grounded in knowledge" (al-rasikhun fi al-'ilm) is those who have become established in the knowledge of the Book and in knowing its possible meanings, and for whom there are proofs that have guided them to the intent of Allah, such that doubts do not deceive them. In Arabic usage, rusukh means firmness and settledness in a place. One says "the foot became firmly rooted (rasakhat al-qadam)" when it remains steady while walking and does not waver. Rusukh was borrowed for the perfection of intellect and knowledge, such that doubts do not mislead it and errors do not usually reach it. This metaphor became so common that it became like a literal meaning. Thus "those firmly grounded in knowledge" are those who are steady in it, who know its subtleties; they discern the proper places of interpretation and know it.

Therefore His words "and those firmly grounded" are coordinated with the Name of Majesty (Allah). In this coordination there is great honour, like His words ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, the Shafi'is, Ibn Fawrak, Shaykh Ahmad al-Qurtubi, and Ibn 'Atiyya inclined to this interpretation. According to this, there is no verse in the Qur'an whose knowledge Allah has kept exclusively to Himself. This is supported by the fact that Allah attributed a virtue to those firmly grounded in knowledge and described them as firmly grounded, which indicates that they have a distinction in understanding the ambiguous. The clear verses (al-muhkam) are understood equally by everyone who understands speech, so in what is their firmness? Imam al-Haramayn narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said about this verse, "I am among those who know its interpretation."

It was said: the pause is at His words "except Allah," and the clause "those firmly grounded in knowledge" is a new, independent sentence. This is reported from the majority of the early generations, and it is the view of Ibn 'Umar, 'A'isha, Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy. Ashhab related it from Malik in the Jami' al-'Utbiyya, and 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, al-Farra' and the Hanafis said it, and Fakhr al-Din inclined to it.

The first view is supported by the description of them as firmly grounded in knowledge, since this is clear evidence that the judgment attributed to this group concerns knowledge and understanding of difficult matters, which is the interpretation of the ambiguous. Moreover, the original form of coordination is coordination of single words, not of clauses, so "those firmly grounded" is coordinated with the Name of Majesty, and they are included in knowing its interpretation. If "those firmly grounded" were the subject and the clause ﴿they say, "We believe in it"﴾ were the predicate, the content of this predicate would be something shared by all Muslims whose hearts are free from deviation, and so singling out "those firmly grounded" would serve no purpose. Ibn 'Atiyya said: calling them "firmly grounded" implies that they know more than the clear verses, which everyone knows equally, and firmness is nothing but knowledge of the varieties of speech by a prepared natural aptitude. What we mentioned, and what Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned, is nothing more than preferring one of the two interpretations, and it does not refute the other, since one may be described as firmly grounded when he distinguishes between what its interpretation can be straightened and what has no hope of interpretation.

In His words ﴿and none will be reminded except those of understanding﴾ there is an indication that those firmly grounded know the interpretation of the ambiguous.

The proponents of the second view, that of pausing at the Name of Majesty, argued: the apparent sense is that the clause "those firmly grounded" should be a new sentence, to serve as a counterpart to the clause ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, and the implied meaning is: "As for those firmly grounded in knowledge." Al-Taftazani answered that the counterpart does not have to be stated, but may be omitted when the context indicates it. They also argued with His words ﴿they say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord"﴾. Al-Fakhr said: If they knew its interpretation, this statement would have no benefit, since believing in what its meaning is clear is not something strange. We will answer this when we discuss this clause. Al-Fakhr also mentioned arguments that are not sound.

It is not hidden that the people of the first view do not affirm an ambiguity other than what its meaning is hidden from, and that the hiddenness of meaning varies. The people of the second view affirm an ambiguity whose knowledge Allah has kept to Himself, and this too varies, since some of it admits near interpretations, and that should not be counted as ambiguous according to their own terminology. Yet their practice of refraining from interpreting many verses whose interpretation is easy, such as ﴿So indeed You are before Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48], shows that they close the door of interpretation in the case of the ambiguous. Shaykh Ibn 'Atiyya said: the interpretation of what can be interpreted is not known, in full detail, except by Allah. Whoever among the skilled scholars says that those firmly grounded do not know the interpretation of the ambiguous means only this kind, and they feared that someone might think Allah described those firmly grounded as having perfect knowledge of interpretation.

On the basis of the difference over how the conjunction in His words ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾ is to be understood, a disagreement arose among the scholars of the community concerning the interpretation of what is ambiguous in the verses of the Qur'an and in the authentic reports from the Prophet (ﷺ).

One group held that one should believe in them, despite their vagueness and generality, and entrust the knowledge of the precise intended meaning to Allah, the Exalted. This was the method of our early scholars, before the doubts of the heretics (mulhidun) or of the ignorant learners appeared. This was in the era of the Companions and the Successors and part of the era of their successors. It is expressed as the method of the early generations (tariqat al-salaf), and they say: "The method of the early generations is safer," meaning more secure for them from interpreting in ways whose outcome is not known, which might lead to matters unfitting to the majesty of Allah the Exalted and not consistent with the laws He established for people. They also observed that the people of their time were content with their method and turned away from going deep into seeking interpretation.

The view of most of those who came after the era of the early generations was to interpret them with meanings drawn from the eloquent usages of Arabic speech: metaphor (majaz), figurative expression (isti'ara), and symbolic representation (tamthil). This was alongside the existence of a motive for interpretation, namely the thirst of scholars who had become accustomed to reflecting, examining, and understanding how to reconcile the evidence of the Qur'an and the Sunna. This approach is expressed as the method of the later generations (tariqat al-khalaf), and they say: "The method of the later generations is more knowledgeable," meaning more suitable to the rules of knowledge and stronger in achieving knowledge, for refuting the heretics, and for convincing those among students who seek the realities. They sometimes describe it as "more precise," meaning more firmly established, because it persuades people of all sorts of aims. These two descriptions appear in the words of the exegetes and the scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh). I have not been able to determine who first said them. Shaykh Ibn Taymiyya, in al-'Aqida al-Hamawiyya, addressed the rejection of these two descriptions without attributing them to any speaker. What is described as "safer" and "more knowledgeable" is the method itself, not its people, since the people of both methods are among the imams of knowledge and among those who were kept safe in their religion from trials.

Describing this method as "more knowledgeable" or "more precise" is no disparagement of the first method, because among the generations who followed the first method, there were those whose meanings were not hidden from them, due to their Arab taste and their Prophetic guidance, and there were those who did not give the search for them any part of their concern, like the common people. Therefore, leaving aside a detailed inquiry into them was necessarily safer for the general public, and detailing them afterwards was more knowledgeable for those who came later. Had they not interpreted them in that way, they would have opened up room for those eager to clarify them to doubt, or to unbelief, or to narrowness of heart in belief.

Know that interpretation (*ta'wil*) includes what is clear and evident. Diverting an ambiguous expression (*mutashabih*) from its apparent meaning to such an interpretation is equivalent to taking the expression in one of its two well-known meanings because that expression is frequently used in the meaning that is not the apparent one. This kind of *ta'wil* is deserving of not being called *ta'wil*. Neither of its two possible senses is stronger than the other, except that one of them precedes the other in lexical imposition (*al-wad'*), while the two senses are equal in usage. Priority in applying the expression to one of the two meanings does not require preferring that meaning, for many a metaphorical application of an expression comes to the mind more readily than its literal application. The statement of the scholars of legal theory (*'ilm al-usul*) that the literal meaning (*haqiqa*) is preferred over the metaphorical (*majaz*) is not acceptable in its generality.

Calling this type by the name *mutashabih* is not what is intended in the verse, and counting it among the *mutashabih* is rigidity.

Among *ta'wil* is that in which the apparent meaning of the expression is more widely known than the meaning of its interpretation, but contextual indicators (*qara'in*) or evidences (*adilla*) have required diverting the expression from the apparent sense of its meaning. This is deserving of being counted among the *mutashabih*.

Then, the interpretation of an expression of this kind may be made easy by a sound meaning that is likely to be what is intended, when the expression is taken in one of the usages that occur in eloquent speech, such as the hands and the eyes in His saying ﴿We built it with hands﴾ (51:47) and His saying ﴿Indeed, you are before Our eyes﴾ (52:48). Those who derive from such expressions that God has eyes whose reality is unknown, or that He has a hand unlike our hands, have increased the strength of the ambiguity.

Among it is that whose interpretation is considered a matter of possibility and conjecture, in that the diversion from the apparent sense is not definitively determined. As for taking it to mean what they have interpreted it as, this is in the manner of possibility and example. Of this kind is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful, established over the Throne﴾ (20:5), and His saying: ﴿Do they await only that God should come to them in canopies of cloud?﴾ (2:210). Such expressions are definitively required to be interpreted, and no one claims that what they have interpreted it as is what is meant by it. Rather, it is a possibility that follows from the possibility of interpretation. This type is the most intense locus of ambiguity and interpretation.

It has become clear to you from these interpretations that the composition of the verse came in the most eloquent form that could be used in a context that accommodates two groups of Muslim scholars across the various eras.

His saying ﴿They say, "We believe in it"﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to *al-rasikhun* (those firmly rooted in knowledge), meaning: they know its interpretation in this state. The meaning according to this reading allows that the saying is a metaphor for belief, because the nature of one who believes is to say what he believes; that is, they know its interpretation and no doubt about the occurrence of the ambiguous passages arises in their souls, such that they would say, "Why did the speech not come entirely clear?" and from this there would come to them doubt about its being from God. Therefore they say: ﴿Everything is from our Lord.﴾ It is also possible that the intended meaning is that they say it to others, i.e., those among the common Muslims who have not reached the rank of being firmly rooted and who have no capacity to grasp its interpretation, in order to teach them to stop at the limits of faith and to avoid aspiring to what is not attainable. This comes close to what the scholars of legal theory have said: a *mujtahid* (qualified jurist) is not obliged to explain the basis of his ruling to a layman who asks him about the source of the ruling, when the basis is obscure. By this, the answer is obtained to the argument of al-Fakhr (al-Razi) using this sentence to prefer pausing at the divine name (*ism al-jalala*).

According to the view of the earlier scholars, His saying "they say" is a predicate (*khabar*), and the meaning of His saying ﴿We believe in it﴾ is: we believe that it is from God, even if we do not understand its meaning.

His saying ﴿Everything is from our Lord﴾ means: everything, of the decisive (*muhkam*) and the ambiguous (*mutashabih*). According to both readings it is an explanation of the meaning of their saying ﴿We believe in it﴾, and for this reason the clause is separated. That is: each of the decisive and the ambiguous is sent down from God.

[Page 169]

The word "*'inda*" (with, from) is added to indicate that "*min*" here is for the true origin (*ibtida' haqiqi*) and not the figurative one. That is, it is sent down from the revelation of God, exalted is He, and His speech. It is not like His saying: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ (4:79).

The clause ﴿And none will be reminded except those of understanding﴾ is a concluding remark (*tadhyil*). It is not part of the speech of those firmly rooted, and it is presented as praise of them for their guidance to correct understanding.

*Al-albab* means the intellects. It was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾ (2:197) in Surat al-Baqarah.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 3, verses 8–9:**

﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, indeed You will gather the people for a Day about which there is no doubt. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise.﴾

This is a supplication that the Prophet (ﷺ) was taught as instruction for the Ummah. The situation described is one of lessons and a source of anxious fear about the bad end that comes to those ﴿in whose hearts is deviation﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 7]. They are nothing but among the rational members of mankind, with no difference between them and those firmly grounded in knowledge, in humanity, or in the soundness of their minds and perceptions. Their misguidance came only from being deprived of success (tawfiq), of divine kindness (lutf), and of the means of guidance.

It is known from the sequence of His statement ﴿He it is who sent down to you the Book﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 7] and the verses that follow, together with the statement ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate﴾, that among the purposes of describing the Book as containing a muhkam (clear, definitive verses) and a mutashabih (ambiguous verses) is to awaken the Ummah to this, so that it may be insightful in reflecting upon its Book. This is a warning against falling into misguidance, which the existence of ambiguous matters in their books caused many nations to fall into, and a warning to Muslims against following false glittering appearances, as some Arabs fell into apostasy and disobedience after the death of the Messenger (ﷺ), under the delusion that adherence to the religion was only for the sake of the Messenger's presence among them. For this reason Abu Bakr used to recite this verse in his prayer during the period of the apostasy of those Arabs who apostatized. In the Muwatta' (the approved collection of Imam Malik), on the authority of al-Sunabihi, he said: "I came to Medina during the caliphate of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and I prayed behind him the Maghrib prayer. He stood up for the third rak'ah, so I drew close to him until my garments nearly touched his garments. I heard him reciting Umm al-Qur'an (al-Fatiha) and this verse, ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate﴾, to the end of the verse."

Deviation of the heart arises from accidental conditions that come upon the intellect due to some defect in its nature, or from motives of companionship or desire, or from weakness of will. These turn the self away from the virtues with which it is adorned toward vices that were once present in the self, and the self repels them by what has become settled within it of the teachings of goodness, called guidance. The believer, the rational person, the wise person, and the refined person do not know at what hour the causes of misery will befall them. Likewise, the wretched person, the one who is absorbed in wrongdoing, and the obstinate one do not know at what hour the causes of abandoning what they are engaged in will surround them, whether through a change of disposition or character, or a change of companions. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight﴾ [Surah Al-An'am: 110]. For this reason, it is the Qur'an's habit to join praise with warning and good tidings with admonition.

His statement ﴿after You have guided us﴾ is a confirmation of the supplication through a gentle approach, since they attributed guidance to Allah the Exalted. This was an act of generosity from Him, and a generous person does not take back his gift. The Prophet (ﷺ) himself sought refuge from having something taken away after it had been given.

As for "إذْ" (idh): it is a noun denoting past time that is declinable (mutasarrif). Here it is used in a limited declinable way, because when a noun in the genitive follows it, it takes the meaning of a time adverb; and since it is not in the accusative case, there is in it a trace of declension, as in يَوْمَئِذٍ (yawma'idhin) and حِينَئِذٍ (hina'idhin). The meaning is: after the time of Your guiding us.

His statement ﴿and grant us from Yourself mercy﴾: they sought the effect of continuance upon guidance, which is mercy in this world and the Hereafter, and a barrier against the motives of deviation and evil. Mercy is attributed to Allah because facilitating its causes and arranging its preconditions is by the decree of Allah. For had Allah willed, a human being would be exposed to the descent of calamities and evils at every moment, since he is surrounded by many existents, living and non-living, against which he is extremely weak, were it not for Allah's kindness to him: by awakening his intellect to guard against misfortunes, by guiding him to avoid destructive evil acts, by inspiring him to what benefits him, and by making those dominant forces that surround him blind forces that cannot find their way to their target, and that encounter him only rarely. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah is Subtle with His servants﴾ [Surah Al-Shura: 19]. Among the clearest manifestations of kindness are states of necessity and seeking refuge. I had said the phrase: "Kindness in the moment of necessity."

The restriction (qasr) in His statement ﴿indeed You are the Bestower﴾ is for emphasis, due to the perfection of this attribute in Allah the Exalted, since the gifts of people, compared with what Allah bestows of goodness, are a thing of no account. In this sentence there is emphasis through "inna," through the nominal sentence, and through the method of restriction.

His statement ﴿Our Lord, indeed You will gather the people for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾: when seeking mercy, they called to mind the time when they would most need it, which is the Day when mercy will be the means of eternal success. So they followed their supplication with mention of this Day in a concise manner, as if they were saying: ﴿and grant us from Yourself mercy﴾, especially on the Day of the gathering of people. This is like Ibrahim's statement: ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day the reckoning is established﴾ [Surah Ibrahim: 41], in addition to the appropriateness of mentioning the Day of gathering after the mention of the conditions of the misguided and the guided, and of the scholars firmly grounded in knowledge.

The meaning of "لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ" (la rayba fihi, "about which there is no doubt"): it means it is worthy of occurring, so the intended sense is the negation of doubt concerning its occurrence. They negated it in the manner of negating the genus, because the doubts of the doubters are not taken into account. This is if you make "fihi" the predicate. You may also make it a qualifier of "rayb" and make the predicate omitted, in the manner of the "la" that negates the genus, so the estimated meaning would be: "with Us" or "for Us."

His statement ﴿indeed Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ is a reason for the negation of doubt, meaning: because Allah promised to gather people for Himself, He does not fail in that. The meaning is: indeed Allah does not fail in His news, and "al-mi'ad" (promise) here is a noun of place.
