This is a resumptive statement (istinaf) arising from the narration of what the believers asked for: the continuation of guidance, the request for mercy, and the hope of success on the Day of Resurrection. It describes the state of the disbelievers on that Day, following the Qur'an's usual practice of pairing good tidings with warning. The sequence, in which the believers' supplication is followed by a description of the polytheists' state, also hints that their supplication was answered.

By "those who disbelieved" (alladhina kafaru) is meant the polytheists, and this is a description that predominates over them in the Qur'anic usage. It has also been said that those who disbelieved in the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) are meant here, namely the Banu Qurayzah, the Banu al-Nadir, and the people of Najran. This view is supported by the fact that they were reminded of the state of Pharaoh rather than the state of 'Ad and Thamud, since the Jews and Christians were more closely acquainted with the reports about Pharaoh, just as the Arabs were more closely acquainted with the reports about 'Ad and Thamud. Also, the refutation of the Christians is among the most important aims of this surah. It is also permissible that what is meant is all disbelievers: the polytheists and the People of the Book, and the reminder of Pharaoh is because the threat against the Jews in this verse is more important.

The meaning of "tughni" (it will avail) is: it will recompense, suffice, and ward off. It is an intransitive verb which takes an object by means of "'an," as in the verse ﴿ما أغنى عني ماليه﴾ [al-Haqqah: 28] ("My wealth has not availed me").

Because this verb indicates recompense and warding off, it signals that there is something whose harm is to be averted and whose burden is to be relieved. For this reason they sometimes mention with this verb a second complement, and they connect the verb to it with the preposition "min" (from), as in this verse, so that "min" is for substitution and exchange, according to the view taken in al-Kashshaf. Ibn 'Atiyya took "min" to indicate the starting point (ibtida').

His saying "min Allah" (from God) means: from a matter attributed to God. This is because when this verb is connected a second time to a proper noun (ism dhat), what is intended is only the most distinctive condition for which it is known, or the purpose for which the statement is directed. So the meaning of a noun governing the name of Majesty (ism al-jalalah) is understood. The estimate here is "from the mercy of God," or "from His obedience," if "min" is for substitution, and this is how al-Kashshaf also estimated it, comparing it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وإن الظن لا يغني من الحق شيئا﴾ [al-Najm: 28] ("Surely conjecture avails nothing against the truth"). According to taking "min" as indicating the starting point, as Ibn 'Atiyya said, the estimate is "from the anger of God" or "from His punishment," meaning: an availing that starts from that, in the manner of their saying: "he rescued him from such-and-such," i.e., he separated him from it. It is not necessary that "min" with this verb, when it is transitive by means of "'an," be similar to the "min" that follows this verb when it is not transitive by means of "'an," since the meaning of the connection can differ with the difference in the context of the statement.

Most often, after the verb aghna (to avail), they use the word "shay'" (anything) together with mentioning the two complements, as in this verse, and without mentioning the two complements, as in the saying of Abu Sufyan on the day he embraced Islam: "I have known that if there had been with Him another god besides Him, it would have availed me something."

[Page 173]

His saying "shay'an" (anything) is in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object (mafʿul mutlaq), meaning: "some availing." Its indefiniteness is for belittlement, meaning: a weak availing, let alone availing for them. It cannot be a direct object because the meaning of the verb does not fit transitivity.

By this it has become clear how this verb is used in a remarkable way in their speech, and what was obscure in the wording of al-Kashshaf and what falls below it regarding the meaning of this construction has become clear to you.

The discussion of the occurrence of the word "shay'" has already passed at His saying: ﴿ولنبلونكم بشيء من الخوف﴾ [al-Baqarah: 155] ("We shall surely test you with something of fear"). He specified wealth and children among the most important things possessed by those who disbelieved, because availing comes through ransom with wealth, such as paying blood-money and fines, and it also comes through help and fighting. The one who defends a man most fittingly from among his clan is his sons, and the one who defends a tribe is its sons. Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

"I avenged 'Adi and al-Khatim, and I did not neglect
the guardianship of elders whom I was placed facing them."

The word "amwal" (wealth) means the acquisitions that are consumed, stored, and exchanged for other things. It is the plural of "mal," and the term "mal" in the speech of most of the Arabs predominated over camels. Zuhayr said:

"Healthy camels of wealth,
rising up toward Makhram."

The term came to predominate in the speech of people of agriculture and tilling over gardens and orchards. In the hadith: Abu Talhah was the most wealthy of the Ansar in Madinah in wealth, and the most beloved of his wealth to him was Bi'r Ha' (a garden). "Mal" is generally applied to dirhams and dinars, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to al-'Abbas: "Where is the wealth that is with Umm al-Fadl?"

The apparent meaning is that this is a threat of worldly punishment, because it was made to resemble, "like the practice of the people of Pharaoh," up to His saying: ﴿فأخذهم الله بذنوبهم﴾ [Al 'Imran: 11] ("So God seized them for their sins"). The norm for the one likened to is that it should be known. Also, because He conjoined to it the punishment of the Hereafter in His saying: ﴿وأولئك هم وقود النار﴾ ("And those are the fuel of the Fire").

The demonstrative in His saying "wa-ula'ika" (and those) is used to make them present as if they were pointed to, and to alert that they deserve what is coming in the predicate, which is His saying: ﴿هم وقود النار﴾ ("They are the fuel of the Fire"). This sentence is joined and not separated, because what is meant by the previous one is a threat in this world, and this one is a threat of the Hereafter, by the indication of His saying in the verse after this: ﴿ستغلبون وتحشرون إلى جهنم وبئس المهاد﴾ [Al 'Imran: 12] ("You will be overcome and gathered to Hell, and wretched is the resting place").

[Page 174]

"Waqud" with a fatha on the waw is what is kindled with, like "wadu'" (ablution water). Its counterpart has already passed at His saying: ﴿التي وقودها الناس والحجارة﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24] ("whose fuel is men and stones") in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying: ﴿كدأب آل فرعون﴾ ("like the practice of the people of Pharaoh"): the position of the particle of comparison "ka" is the position of a predicate for an omitted subject, which is indicated by the one likened to. The estimate is: "their practice in that is like the practice of the people of Pharaoh," meaning their habit and affair are like the affair of the people of Pharaoh.

"Da'b" (practice) originally means striving in work and repeating it. It seems that the root of its verb is transitive, which is why its verbal noun comes on the pattern "fa'l." Then it was applied to habit because habit comes from much work, so it became a widely used reality. Al-Nabigha said:

"Like your practice with a people
whom you have treated well."

That is, your habit. Then it was used with the meaning of affair, as in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Like your practice with Umm al-Huwayrith before her."

This is what is meant here in His saying: ﴿كدأب آل فرعون﴾, and the meaning is: their affair in that is like the affair of the people of Pharaoh, since there is no repeated habit in that. God has set this as an example for them as a lesson and admonition, because when they survey the nations that were struck by punishment, they find that all of them were alike in disbelief in God, in His messengers, and in His signs. Such a survey is sufficient admonition for the likes of the polytheists of the Arabs. It has become determined that what is likened to is the threat of extermination and punishment in this world, since the principle is that the condition of the one likened is more evident to the hearer than the condition of the one to which it is likened.

On this basis, the seizing in His saying: ﴿فأخذهم الله بذنوبهم﴾ is the seizing of retribution in this world, like His saying: ﴿أخذناهم بغتة فإذا هم مبلسون﴾ [al-An'am: 44] ("We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair") and ﴿فقطع دابر القوم الذين ظلموا﴾ [al-An'am: 45] ("So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off").

By "Al Pharaoh" (the people of Pharaoh) is meant Pharaoh and his household, because "al" (family) is applied to the people most closely specific to the one it is attributed to. The specificity here is specificity in following and conspiring in disbelief, as in His saying: ﴿أدخلوا آل فرعون أشد العذاب﴾ [Ghafir: 46] ("Cause the people of Pharaoh to enter the most severe punishment"). So the mention of "al" here has a particularity that the mention of "qawm" (people) does not have, since a man's people may oppose him, so the ruling concerning them does not indicate that he is equal to them in

[Page 175]

the ruling. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿ألا بعدا لعاد قوم هود﴾ [Hud: 60] ("Be gone, 'Ad, the people of Hud"), and similar verses in many places, and He said: ﴿أن ائت القوم الظالمين﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 10] ("Go to the wrongdoing people") and ﴿قوم فرعون﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 11] ("the people of Pharaoh").

His saying: "kaththabu" (they denied) is an explanation of their practice, a explanatory resumptive statement. The specification of the people of Pharaoh by mention, from among the rest of the nations, is because their destruction is known among the People of the Book, unlike the destruction of 'Ad and Thamud, which is more famous among the Arabs. Also, because Moses' challenge to them was with great signs, yet these availed them nothing against their error. And also because they were the nations closest in time to the era of the Prophet (ﷺ). So it is like the saying of Shu'ayb: ﴿وما قوم لوط منكم ببعيد﴾ [Hud: 89] ("The people of Lot are not far from you"), and like God's saying to the polytheists: ﴿وإنها لبسبيل مقيم﴾ [al-Hijr: 76] ("Indeed, it is on a road that remains"), and His saying: ﴿وإنهما لبإمام مبين﴾ [al-Hijr: 79] ("And they are indeed on a clear highway"), and His saying: ﴿وإنكم لتمرون عليهم مصبحين﴾ [al-Saffat: 137] ("And indeed you pass by them in the morning") and ﴿وبالليل أفلا تعقلون﴾ [al-Saffat: 138] ("and at night; will you not then understand?").

[Page 176]

This is an initiatory resumption (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic), which shifts from warning (*nidhara*) to threat (*tahdid*), and from setting forth the example of their predecessors' disbelief to setting forth the example of their own past circumstances, which indicates that their affair is heading toward collapse and that the affair of Islam will crush the solid mountains. In this threat the most emphatic and eloquent expression has been used, because the context calls for elaboration (*ithnab*) to increase admonition and reminder, by describing a day that was against them and that they know. The phrase "those who disbelieved" (*alladhina kafaru*) may refer to those mentioned in the words ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them at all against Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 10], in which case what was said there applies here. The shift from the pronoun *hum* ("them") to the explicit noun is to make this warning independent.

The apparent meaning is that the intended people are the polytheists specifically, and for this reason the explicit noun was repeated rather than using a pronoun, as indicated by the following words ﴿There has already been a sign for you﴾ up to ﴿you see them as twice their number with the eye of sight﴾, and this is something the polytheists witnessed on the day of Badr.

It has also been said that the intended people are specifically the Jews. They cited for this a cause of revelation (*sabab*) narrated by al-Wahidi in *Asbab al-Nuzul*: the Jews of Yathrib had made a treaty with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for a fixed period, but when the Muslims suffered the misfortune they suffered on the day of Uhud, they broke the covenant, and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf set off with sixty riders to Abu Sufyan in Makkah, and they said to them: "Our word shall be one." When they returned to Madinah, this verse was revealed.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "overcame Quraysh at Badr and returned to Madinah, he gathered the Jews and said to them: 'O assembly of Jews, beware of Allah's like of what befell Quraysh, and embrace Islam, for you know that I am a sent prophet.' They said: 'O Muhammad, do not let it deceive you that you met a people who were inexperienced in war, so you gained an opportunity against them. By Allah, if we fought you, you would know that we are the people.' So Allah revealed this verse." On the basis of these two narrations, the victory they were warned of is the conquest of Qurayza, al-Nadir and Khaybar. Also, the threat and warning encompass both groups in all circumstances.

The conjunction of ﴿and wretched is the resting place﴾ with ﴿you will be overcome﴾ is the conjunction of a performative statement (*insha'*) with a declarative statement (*khabar*).

Al-Jumhur read ﴿sa-tughlabun wa-tuhsharun﴾ with both verbs in the second-person (*ta' al-khitab*). Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read them with the third-person (*ya' al-ghayba*). Both are valid options in reporting speech addressed to someone, and the second-person is more common, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117], and He did not say "your Lord and their Lord."

The address in ﴿There has already been a sign for you﴾ is addressed to those who disbelieved, as is apparent, because the context is one of argument, so the warning and threat are followed by the establishment of proof. It is therefore part of what is spoken. It is also permissible that the address is to the Muslims, in which case it is a resumption arising from the phrase "you will be overcome," since perhaps the large number of those addressed among the polytheists or the Jews, or both, provokes the wonder of the listeners at their victory, so Allah reminded them of what happened on the day of Badr.

The two groups (*al-fi'atan*) are the Muslims and the polytheists on the day of Badr.

*Al-iltiqa'* means encounter (*al-liqa'*), and the form *ifti'al* in it is for intensification. *Al-liqa'* is one person coinciding with another in one place. The word *liqa'* is also used for coming out to fight, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing in battle, do not turn your backs to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 15], which will come. *Iltiqa'* is also used in this sense, as in the saying of Unayf ibn Zabban:

*When we met, the sword made clear between us, to a questioner about us whose question is persistent.*

This verse admits both meanings.

The phrase ﴿a group fighting in the way of Allah﴾ is an elaboration of the two groups, and it is in the nominative because it is the first element of a sentence in a resumption, in the detailed division that follows the general summary and collection.

*Al-fi'ah* is a group of people. Its discussion has already been mentioned in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿How often has a small company overcome a large company by the permission of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The address in *tarawnahum* ("you see them") is like the address in "there has already been for you."

The seeing here is visual, as indicated by "with the eye of sight" (*ra'y al-'ayn*).

It is apparent that the disbelievers saw the Muslims on the day of Badr at the time of the encounter and close fighting as twice their number, so terror entered their hearts and they were routed. This sight was made a sign for those who saw it, and they realised after the defeat that they had been mistaken in what they saw, so that this would be a greater regret for them. This sighting is different from the sighting mentioned in al-Anfal in the words ﴿and He makes you appear few in their eyes﴾ [al-Anfal: 44], for that one suitably occurred before the close fighting, so that the polytheists would underestimate the Muslims, and thus not take up their readiness for the encounter. When they met them, they saw them as twice their number, so terror and defeat entered them, and after the battle was uncovered they realised the Muslims' fewness. Thus the showing of fewness and the showing of greater number were both causes of victory for the Muslims by the wondrous handiwork of Allah the Exalted. It is also permissible that the Muslims saw the polytheists as twice the number of the believers, while the polytheists were three times their number, so Allah made them appear few in the eyes of the Muslims lest they lose heart, because they already knew that a Muslim overcomes two disbelievers; had they known that the polytheists were three times their number, they would have feared defeat. In this case the showing is the showing mentioned in Surat al-Anfal: ﴿and when He showed them to you, when you met, few in your eyes﴾ [al-Anfal: 44], and the pronoun of the third person in *mithlayhim* ("twice them") refers back to the Muslims by way of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), its original form being *tarawnahum mithlaykum* ("you see them as twice you"), as part of what is spoken.

Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read *tarawnahum* with the second-person *ta'* (*ta' al-khitab*). The rest read it with the third-person *ya'* (*ya' al-ghayba*), taking it as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of *wa-ukhra kafirah* or of *fi'atun tuqatilu fi sabili Allah*, meaning twice the number of those seen, if the seers are the polytheists, or twice the number of the seers, if the seers are the Muslims. This is because the pronoun of both has taken the third-person form, and both sightings occurred on the day of Badr, and each group knew its sighting and was challenged by this verse. On this reading, the shift from the expression "your group and their group" to the words ﴿a group fighting in the way of Allah and another disbelieving﴾ is for the purpose of making the third-person pronoun suitable for both groups, so the wording conveys two signs by distribution, through the method of *tawjih* (a reading that allows multiple valid directions of meaning).

*Ra'y al-'ayn* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) specifying the kind of seeing. Since the verb *ra'a* can refer to sight and to the heart, its attachment to *al-'ayn* is evidence that it is used as a verbal noun for the mental *ra'a*, especially as *ra'y* is a name for the intellect; the visual *ra'a* shares it in this, unlike *ru'yah*, which is specific to sight.

The clause ﴿and Allah supports with His help whom He wills﴾ is a concluding appendage (*tadhyil*), because that sighting, however it is interpreted, is a support for the Muslims. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when He showed them to you, when you met, few in your eyes, and He made you appear few in their eyes, that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾ [al-Anfal: 44].

[Page 176]

This is an initiatory resumption (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic), which shifts from warning (*nidhara*) to threat (*tahdid*), and from setting forth the example of their predecessors' disbelief to setting forth the example of their own past circumstances, which indicates that their affair is heading toward collapse and that the affair of Islam will crush the solid mountains. In this threat the most emphatic and eloquent expression has been used, because the context calls for elaboration (*ithnab*) to increase admonition and reminder, by describing a day that was against them and that they know. The phrase "those who disbelieved" (*alladhina kafaru*) may refer to those mentioned in the words ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them at all against Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 10], in which case what was said there applies here. The shift from the pronoun *hum* ("them") to the explicit noun is to make this warning independent.

The apparent meaning is that the intended people are the polytheists specifically, and for this reason the explicit noun was repeated rather than using a pronoun, as indicated by the following words ﴿There has already been a sign for you﴾ up to ﴿you see them as twice their number with the eye of sight﴾, and this is something the polytheists witnessed on the day of Badr.

It has also been said that the intended people are specifically the Jews. They cited for this a cause of revelation (*sabab*) narrated by al-Wahidi in *Asbab al-Nuzul*: the Jews of Yathrib had made a treaty with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for a fixed period, but when the Muslims suffered the misfortune they suffered on the day of Uhud, they broke the covenant, and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf set off with sixty riders to Abu Sufyan in Makkah, and they said to them: "Our word shall be one." When they returned to Madinah, this verse was revealed.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "overcame Quraysh at Badr and returned to Madinah, he gathered the Jews and said to them: 'O assembly of Jews, beware of Allah's like of what befell Quraysh, and embrace Islam, for you know that I am a sent prophet.' They said: 'O Muhammad, do not let it deceive you that you met a people who were inexperienced in war, so you gained an opportunity against them. By Allah, if we fought you, you would know that we are the people.' So Allah revealed this verse." On the basis of these two narrations, the victory they were warned of is the conquest of Qurayza, al-Nadir and Khaybar. Also, the threat and warning encompass both groups in all circumstances.

The conjunction of ﴿and wretched is the resting place﴾ with ﴿you will be overcome﴾ is the conjunction of a performative statement (*insha'*) with a declarative statement (*khabar*).

Al-Jumhur read ﴿sa-tughlabun wa-tuhsharun﴾ with both verbs in the second-person (*ta' al-khitab*). Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read them with the third-person (*ya' al-ghayba*). Both are valid options in reporting speech addressed to someone, and the second-person is more common, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117], and He did not say "your Lord and their Lord."

The address in ﴿There has already been a sign for you﴾ is addressed to those who disbelieved, as is apparent, because the context is one of argument, so the warning and threat are followed by the establishment of proof. It is therefore part of what is spoken. It is also permissible that the address is to the Muslims, in which case it is a resumption arising from the phrase "you will be overcome," since perhaps the large number of those addressed among the polytheists or the Jews, or both, provokes the wonder of the listeners at their victory, so Allah reminded them of what happened on the day of Badr.

The two groups (*al-fi'atan*) are the Muslims and the polytheists on the day of Badr.

*Al-iltiqa'* means encounter (*al-liqa'*), and the form *ifti'al* in it is for intensification. *Al-liqa'* is one person coinciding with another in one place. The word *liqa'* is also used for coming out to fight, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing in battle, do not turn your backs to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 15], which will come. *Iltiqa'* is also used in this sense, as in the saying of Unayf ibn Zabban:

*When we met, the sword made clear between us, to a questioner about us whose question is persistent.*

This verse admits both meanings.

The phrase ﴿a group fighting in the way of Allah﴾ is an elaboration of the two groups, and it is in the nominative because it is the first element of a sentence in a resumption, in the detailed division that follows the general summary and collection.

*Al-fi'ah* is a group of people. Its discussion has already been mentioned in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿How often has a small company overcome a large company by the permission of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The address in *tarawnahum* ("you see them") is like the address in "there has already been for you."

The seeing here is visual, as indicated by "with the eye of sight" (*ra'y al-'ayn*).

It is apparent that the disbelievers saw the Muslims on the day of Badr at the time of the encounter and close fighting as twice their number, so terror entered their hearts and they were routed. This sight was made a sign for those who saw it, and they realised after the defeat that they had been mistaken in what they saw, so that this would be a greater regret for them. This sighting is different from the sighting mentioned in al-Anfal in the words ﴿and He makes you appear few in their eyes﴾ [al-Anfal: 44], for that one suitably occurred before the close fighting, so that the polytheists would underestimate the Muslims, and thus not take up their readiness for the encounter. When they met them, they saw them as twice their number, so terror and defeat entered them, and after the battle was uncovered they realised the Muslims' fewness. Thus the showing of fewness and the showing of greater number were both causes of victory for the Muslims by the wondrous handiwork of Allah the Exalted. It is also permissible that the Muslims saw the polytheists as twice the number of the believers, while the polytheists were three times their number, so Allah made them appear few in the eyes of the Muslims lest they lose heart, because they already knew that a Muslim overcomes two disbelievers; had they known that the polytheists were three times their number, they would have feared defeat. In this case the showing is the showing mentioned in Surat al-Anfal: ﴿and when He showed them to you, when you met, few in your eyes﴾ [al-Anfal: 44], and the pronoun of the third person in *mithlayhim* ("twice them") refers back to the Muslims by way of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), its original form being *tarawnahum mithlaykum* ("you see them as twice you"), as part of what is spoken.

Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read *tarawnahum* with the second-person *ta'* (*ta' al-khitab*). The rest read it with the third-person *ya'* (*ya' al-ghayba*), taking it as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of *wa-ukhra kafirah* or of *fi'atun tuqatilu fi sabili Allah*, meaning twice the number of those seen, if the seers are the polytheists, or twice the number of the seers, if the seers are the Muslims. This is because the pronoun of both has taken the third-person form, and both sightings occurred on the day of Badr, and each group knew its sighting and was challenged by this verse. On this reading, the shift from the expression "your group and their group" to the words ﴿a group fighting in the way of Allah and another disbelieving﴾ is for the purpose of making the third-person pronoun suitable for both groups, so the wording conveys two signs by distribution, through the method of *tawjih* (a reading that allows multiple valid directions of meaning).

*Ra'y al-'ayn* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) specifying the kind of seeing. Since the verb *ra'a* can refer to sight and to the heart, its attachment to *al-'ayn* is evidence that it is used as a verbal noun for the mental *ra'a*, especially as *ra'y* is a name for the intellect; the visual *ra'a* shares it in this, unlike *ru'yah*, which is specific to sight.

The clause ﴿and Allah supports with His help whom He wills﴾ is a concluding appendage (*tadhyil*), because that sighting, however it is interpreted, is a support for the Muslims. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when He showed them to you, when you met, few in your eyes, and He made you appear few in their eyes, that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾ [al-Anfal: 44].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 14 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires: women, sons, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, and tilled land. That is the enjoyment of the worldly life, but with Allah is the excellent return.﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) arising from His words: ﴿Neither their wealth nor their children will avail them at all﴾ [Al 'Imran: 10]. The attribution of wealth and children to the pronoun "them" indicates that these are known to the Muslims. Its purpose is to admonish the Muslims not to be deceived by the state of those who disbelieve, lest the adornment of the world impress them and distract them from striving for what brings success in the Hereafter. Warning against ends requires warning against beginnings. This admonition and discipline were introduced by explaining how this condition enters the souls, so that they would be on the utmost guard against it, because what settles in the soul flows into it along with the breaths.

[p. 179]

Tazyin (adornment, beautification) is making a thing zayn, meaning good (husn). It is the embellishment of a thing that needs embellishment and the removal of what befalls it of ugliness or disfigurement. For this reason the barber is called muzayyin (one who adorns).

Imru' al-Qays said:

"War, at its first beginning, is a young girl who advances with her adornment to every ignorant one."

Thus zina (adornment) is what there is in a thing of attractions which make observers desire to acquire it. God, exalted, said: ﴿You desire the adornment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Kahf: 28]. The word zayn is rarely used in the speech of the Arabs despite its goodness and lightness. 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a said:

"My beloved resolved, at dawn, to part, so may God clothe that face with adornment."

In the hadith of Sunan Abi Dawud: Abu Barza al-Aslami entered upon 'Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad, who had sent for him to ask him about the hadith of the Pool. When Abu Barza entered, 'Ubayd Allah said to his companions: "This Muhammadi of yours is a stout fellow." Abu Barza said: "I did not think that I would remain among a people who reproach me for companionship with Muhammad." 'Ubayd Allah said: "Indeed, companionship with Muhammad is an adornment for you, not a blemish."

Ash-shahawat is the plural of shahwa (desire). The root of shahwa is the verbal noun of shahiya, like radiya, and the form shahwa is on the pattern of the single instance (marra). Most often the verbal noun of shahiya is used in this pattern. Here ash-shahawat is applied to the things desired, as an intensification in the strength of the description. Linking the adornment to "love" runs contrary to the apparent requirement, because what is adorned for people is the desires themselves, that is, the desired things, not their love. When they are adorned for them, they love them, since love arises from finding something pleasing, and love is not what is adorned. This is a concision that dispenses with saying "the desires are adorned for people so they love them." The commentators have been silent about the reason for composing the sentence with this linkage.

In my view, there are two possibilities. Either ﴿love of desires﴾ is a verbal noun standing in place of an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), specifying the type of adornment, meaning: adornment was made attractive to them with the adornment of love, which is the most intense adornment. The absolute object is made to stand in place of the subject (na'ib 'an al-fa'il). The original sentence would be: "The desires were adorned for people as love," then it was altered and attached to the substitute for the subject, and was made to substitute for the subject, just as it was made an object in His words: ﴿So he said: Indeed I have loved the love of good, remembering my Lord﴾ [Sad: 32]. Or "love" is a verbal noun in the sense of the object, meaning the beloved desires, that is, the desires which are loved. Or "adorned" is used as a metonymy (kinaya), intending its necessary consequence, which is the soul's inclination toward what is pleasing in the adorned thing while concealing what is harmful in it. This is expressed by the term adornment, meaning the beautifying of what is not purely good. The desires of people contain matters that are agreeable and acceptable, but in many of them there may be harms, the gravest of which is that they distract from many perfections. For this reason they are like an adorned thing whose defects are covered by embellishments. In this way, there is no problem in linking "adorned" to "love."

The agent of the adornment is omitted because it is hidden from the general understanding of the addressees. What indicates instincts and natural dispositions, when its agent is unknown in common usage, the custom is to attribute its verbs to the passive, as in the expressions: "He was concerned with such-and-such" (u'niya bi-kadhā) and "He was compelled to such-and-such" (ud-turra ila kadhā), especially when the intended meaning is the metonymy for the necessary consequence of adornment, which is overlooking the faults in the adorned thing, because the agent no longer remains intended in any state. The adorned thing in reality is the human perception that loves the desires, and that is a natural matter which God placed in the order of creation. God, exalted, said: ﴿We subjected them to them, so some of them are their mounts and some of them they eat﴾ [Ya Sin: 72].

When adornment reverted to an affect in the natural disposition, its agent in truth is the Creator of these natural dispositions. So the one who adorns is God, through His creation, not through His call. The like of this is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. If we turn to the near and immediate causes, the one who adorns is the soul's inclination toward the desired thing, or the enticement of those who call to the enjoyment of desires, from close friends and companions. It is narrated from al-Hasan: the one who adorns is Satan. It seems that he understood adornment in the sense of enticement and encouragement through whispering toward blameworthy desires and corruption, and he restricted it to this. This is far-fetched, because the adornment of these desires in themselves may accord with the aspect of permissibility and obedience. Satan's enticement does not necessarily accompany them except when he makes them means to the unlawful. In a hadith: They said: "O Messenger of God, does one of us fulfill his desire and have a reward in it?" He said: "Do you see that if he placed it in the unlawful, would he have a burden of sin? Likewise, when he places it in the lawful, he has a reward."

The context of the verse is the preference of lofty matters and righteous deeds over desires whose kinds are mixed with lawful and unlawful elements, and which are exposed to passing away. Perfection lies in purifying the soul so that it may attain the sacred ranks and obtain the great everlasting bliss, as His words indicate: ﴿That is the enjoyment of the worldly life, but with Allah is the excellent return.﴾

[p. 180]

The explanation of the desires by ﴿women and sons﴾ and what follows them is an explanation through the foundations of human desires, which gather many desired things and which do not differ according to nations, eras, or regions. Inclination toward women is rooted in the natural disposition, which God established for the wisdom of the survival of the species, through the drive to seek procreation, since the woman is the locus of procreation. Man's inclination toward her was placed in his nature so that the survival of the species would not need an effort that may be followed by weariness. In a hadith: "I have left after me no trial more harmful to men than the trial of women." He did not mention men, because women's inclination toward men is weaker in nature, and love from them toward men arises only through familiarity and kindness.

The love of children is also natural, for God placed in parents, both fathers and mothers, an emotional feeling that makes them sense that the child is a piece of themselves. This is so that it would be a motive to preserve the child, who is the future generation, and through his survival the species survives. Thus this is the survival of the species by protecting it from the dissolution written for it. In the child there is also a preservation of the species from the dissolution that befalls it through aggression against its weak members, for a person comes to weakness after strength, so his child becomes a defender of him against the aggression of whoever attacks him. Just as the parent defended his son in the son's weakness, so the son defends the parent in the parent's weakness.

﴿Gold and silver﴾ are two desires because of the beauty of their appearance and what is made from them of ornaments for men and women. Their coinage, the dinars and dirhams, is a desire for what God placed in souls from ancient ages, the love of money by which the exchange of things needed is made.

Qanatir is the plural of qintar, which is what weighs one hundred ritl. Its origin is an arabicized word said to derive from the Roman, the Eastern Latin, as al-Naqqash transmitted from al-Kalbi, and this is the correct view, for its origin in Latin is (kintal), which is one hundred ritl. Ibn Sida said: it is arabicized from the Syriac. What is in the Kashshaf in the surah of al-Nisa' that qintar is derived from qantartu al-shay' (I raised the thing) is far-fetched. The qintar was among the Arabs a weight and a measure of wealth, which some of the wealthy would reach: that is, when a man's wealth reaches one hundred ritl of silver. They say: qantara al-rajul (the man became a qintar-holder) when his wealth reached a qintar, which is twelve thousand dinars, meaning what equals a qintar of silver. It is also said that it is the measure of one hundred thousand dinars of gold.

[p. 182]

What is intended here by ﴿al-muqantara﴾ (heaped up) is multiplied and abundant accumulation, because the derivation of an adjective from the name of the thing described, when the owner of the name is well known for a quality, indicates through that derivation an intensification in what is obtained by it, as in the expressions: laylun alyal (a very dark night), zillun zalil (deep shade), dahiya dahyā' (a great calamity), shi'run sha'ir (a truly poetic verse), ibilun mu'abbala (camels gathered in herds), and alafun mu'allafa (thousands in combination).

Horses have been loved and desired in past ages and after them, and what human beings have invented of various kinds of vehicles by land, sea, and air has not made them forget this. Even the advanced nations today, despite the trains running by steam and electricity on iron tracks, and the great ships propelled by steam engines, and the small automobiles driven by wheels moved by the heat of refined petroleum, and the aircraft in the air, which humans did not reach in a past era, all of this has not made people independent of riding horses, drawing carriages with stallions, and taking care of racing between horses.

He mentioned horses because the souls of the people of luxury are habituated to love of riding them. Imru' al-Qays said:

"As if I had never ridden a steed for pleasure."

As for ﴿branded﴾ (al-musawwama), the most apparent of what has been said about it is that it means grazing (ra'iya). It is derived from sawm, which is grazing, and one says: asama al-mashiya (he let the livestock graze) when he pastured them in the pasture. The form fa''ala here is for intensification, meaning those which are left in pastures for long periods. This happens only because their owners are wealthy and have many pastures, so their horses are honored in meadows and gardens. In a hadith mentioning horses: "He lengthened their grazing in a meadow or a garden."

It is also said: al-musawwama is from al-sumah, with a damma on the sin, which is the mark, meaning a sign made of wool or the like. They make this for them as a distinction for their nobility and the goodness of their trial in war. Al-'Attabi said:

"Had it not been for them, I would have branded my young horse, and in the Merciful there is a sufficiency for the weak."

He means: I made for him the brand of war-horses, that is, its sign. The derivation of simah and sumah has already been discussed at His words: ﴿You recognize them by their mark﴾ [al-Baqara: 273] in surah al-Baqara.

Cattle are an adornment for the people of the wool-tents. God, exalted, said: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home and when you drive them out to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl: 6], and in them are great benefits, to which His words point: ﴿And the cattle, He created them for you; in them is warmth﴾ [al-Nahl: 5] and what follows, in surah al-Nahl. The desires of city dwellers may not be closely tied to strong attachment to cattle, but they love to see them and take pleasure in them in general.

[p. 183]

Al-harth (tilled land): its root is the verbal noun of haratha al-ard (he plowed the land), when he split it with an implement in order to sow or plant in it. This verbal noun was applied to what is tilled, so it came to be applied to gardens, orchards, and fields of crops. It has been mentioned at His words: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 223] in surah al-Baqara, and at His words: ﴿nor irrigates the tilth﴾ [al-Baqara: 71] therein.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿That is the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾ refers to everything mentioned before. He used the singular form of the second-person pronoun (kaf al-khitab) because the address is to the Prophet ﷺ or to an unspecified addressee. Moreover, the sign of the single addressee is the most common when it accompanies demonstratives, to express distance. The distance here is figurative, meaning elevation and preciousness.

Al-mata' (enjoyment) indicates scarcity, and it is that which is enjoyed for a period of time.

And ﴿with Allah is the best place of return﴾ means that the reward of Allah is better than all of that. Al-ma'ab (the place of return, destination): it is here a verbal noun, of the form mafal derived from āba yaūbu (to return), and its original form was ma'wab; the vowel of the waw was transferred to the hamza, and the waw was changed into an alif. What is meant by it is the final outcome in this world and the Hereafter.

[Page 184]

This is a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani), arising from His saying ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14], which implies that the discourse is aimed at restraining these desires. He opened the resumption with the word "Say" (qul) to draw attention to what is to be said. The one addressed by "Say" is the Prophet (ﷺ). The interrogative form is used for presentation, to arouse the listeners' souls to receive what will be related to them, like His saying: ﴿Shall I direct you to a commerce that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ [al-Saff: 10], and so on.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far, and Ruways from Ya'qub read ﴿a-unabbi'ukum﴾ with the second hamza softened to a waw. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Rawh from Ya'qub, and Khalaf read it with both hamzas made clear.

The clause ﴿For those who fear God, with their Lord are gardens﴾ is a new resumed sentence, and it is what is being announced. It is also permissible for ﴿for those who fear God﴾ to be connected to the word ﴿better﴾, with ﴿gardens﴾ being a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "for them", or a predicate of an omitted subject. The pleasures that correspond to the desires of this world are omitted in the mention of the bliss of the Hereafter, because the pleasure of sons and the pleasure of wealth are absent there, since one is free from them. Likewise the pleasure of horses and livestock, since there are no beasts in Paradise. What remains corresponds to women and tillage, namely the gardens and the spouses, because by them the bliss and companionship are complete. To these is added God's approval, which is denied to one who makes his share the pleasures of this world and turns away from the Hereafter. The meaning of "purified" (mutahhara) is free from what afflicts the women of mankind, of what souls find repugnant; so the purity here is physical, not moral.

"Approval from God" is coordinated with what He has prepared for those who fear Him with God, because His approval is greater than that material bliss, since the approval of God is a spiritual nearness. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And approval from God is greater﴾ [al-Tawba: 72].

The majority read ﴿ridwan﴾ with a kasra on the ra'; Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with a damma on the ra'. Both are dialectal forms.

He made the name of God explicit in His saying ﴿and approval from God﴾, rather than saying "and approval from Him", that is, from their Lord, because the explicit name of God carries an indication of the greatness of that approval.

The clause ﴿and God is Seeing of the servants﴾ is a parenthetical insertion explaining the promise: that is, He is Knowing of those who fear Him and of the degrees of their piety, so He will reward them. Because "Seeing" (basir) includes the meaning of "Knowing" ('alim), it is followed by the preposition ba' (bi-). The explicit name of God in ﴿and God is Seeing of the servants﴾ is for the purpose of making the clause stand independently, so that it serves as a proverb.

His saying ﴿Those who say﴾ is an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to ﴿for those who fear God﴾. He described them with piety and with turning to God, the Exalted, in seeking forgiveness. The meaning of "saying" here is speech that corresponds to reality in its report, and flows from the intensity of desire in supplication, in their words ﴿So forgive us our sins﴾ and so on. Such speech flows in this way only when the supplicant strives through the means of answer and watches for it through its causes, which piety guides him to; so one is not rewarded with this reward if he says it with his mouth and does not act for it.

His saying ﴿the patient and the truthful﴾ and the verse that follows are attributes of ﴿those who fear God﴾, or attributes of ﴿those who say﴾; the first is more apparent. Here He mentioned the foundations of the virtues of the attributes of the religious: patience, which is the basis of performing acts of obedience and abstaining from sins; truthfulness, which is the basis of uprightness and of spreading trust among the members of the community; devotion (qunut), which is constancy in acts of worship at their times and perfecting them, and is a worship both of the soul and of the body; and spending, which is the foundation of sustaining the community by meeting the needs of the needy, and is a financial act of nearness, while wealth is a sibling of the soul. He added seeking forgiveness at the pre-dawn hours, which is supplication and prayer containing it in the last part of the night. The saḥar is the last sixth of the night, because worship in it is more sincere, owing to the stillness of souls at that time, and because it indicates its doer's concern for the matter of his Hereafter. So these truthful ones chose for it the end of the night, because it is the time when hearts are clear and free from preoccupations.

This is a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani), arising from His saying ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14], which implies that the discourse is aimed at restraining these desires. He opened the resumption with the word "Say" (qul) to draw attention to what is to be said. The one addressed by "Say" is the Prophet (ﷺ). The interrogative form is used for presentation, to arouse the listeners' souls to receive what will be related to them, like His saying: ﴿Shall I direct you to a commerce that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ [al-Saff: 10], and so on.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far, and Ruways from Ya'qub read ﴿a-unabbi'ukum﴾ with the second hamza softened to a waw. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Rawh from Ya'qub, and Khalaf read it with both hamzas made clear.

The clause ﴿For those who fear God, with their Lord are gardens﴾ is a new resumed sentence, and it is what is being announced. It is also permissible for ﴿for those who fear God﴾ to be connected to the word ﴿better﴾, with ﴿gardens﴾ being a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "for them", or a predicate of an omitted subject. The pleasures that correspond to the desires of this world are omitted in the mention of the bliss of the Hereafter, because the pleasure of sons and the pleasure of wealth are absent there, since one is free from them. Likewise the pleasure of horses and livestock, since there are no beasts in Paradise. What remains corresponds to women and tillage, namely the gardens and the spouses, because by them the bliss and companionship are complete. To these is added God's approval, which is denied to one who makes his share the pleasures of this world and turns away from the Hereafter. The meaning of "purified" (mutahhara) is free from what afflicts the women of mankind, of what souls find repugnant; so the purity here is physical, not moral.

"Approval from God" is coordinated with what He has prepared for those who fear Him with God, because His approval is greater than that material bliss, since the approval of God is a spiritual nearness. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And approval from God is greater﴾ [al-Tawba: 72].

The majority read ﴿ridwan﴾ with a kasra on the ra'; Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with a damma on the ra'. Both are dialectal forms.

He made the name of God explicit in His saying ﴿and approval from God﴾, rather than saying "and approval from Him", that is, from their Lord, because the explicit name of God carries an indication of the greatness of that approval.

The clause ﴿and God is Seeing of the servants﴾ is a parenthetical insertion explaining the promise: that is, He is Knowing of those who fear Him and of the degrees of their piety, so He will reward them. Because "Seeing" (basir) includes the meaning of "Knowing" ('alim), it is followed by the preposition ba' (bi-). The explicit name of God in ﴿and God is Seeing of the servants﴾ is for the purpose of making the clause stand independently, so that it serves as a proverb.

His saying ﴿Those who say﴾ is an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to ﴿for those who fear God﴾. He described them with piety and with turning to God, the Exalted, in seeking forgiveness. The meaning of "saying" here is speech that corresponds to reality in its report, and flows from the intensity of desire in supplication, in their words ﴿So forgive us our sins﴾ and so on. Such speech flows in this way only when the supplicant strives through the means of answer and watches for it through its causes, which piety guides him to; so one is not rewarded with this reward if he says it with his mouth and does not act for it.

His saying ﴿the patient and the truthful﴾ and the verse that follows are attributes of ﴿those who fear God﴾, or attributes of ﴿those who say﴾; the first is more apparent.
