﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those of knowledge, standing in justice. There is no god but He, the Almighty, the Wise.﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf, a new sentence that introduces a topic) and a preface to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. This is because the foundation of Islam is the Oneness of Allah (tawhid), the proclamation of this Oneness, and its purification from the taints of polytheism (shirk). It also contains an allusion to the polytheists, the Christians and the Jews, even though they differ in degrees of shirk. It also contains a kind of "return of the last to the first" (radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr), because it confirms what the surah opened with, His saying: ﴿Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ [Al 'Imran: 2], and ﴿He has sent down to you the Book with truth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3].

Shahada (witnessing) in its real sense is a statement by which the report of one informant is affirmed, and by which the report of another may be denied, as was explained earlier at His saying: ﴿And call to witness two witnesses from among your men﴾ [Al Baqara: 282] in Surat al-Baqara. Since its usual function is to affirm or deny rights, it is a context in which the informant's concern and firmness about it are expected. Therefore it has been used figuratively for a report that ought not to be doubted. He said: ﴿And Allah testifies that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1]. This is a figurative usage (majaz mursal) with a relation of necessary connection ('alaqat al-talazum). Thus, the witnessing of Allah is His establishing His Oneness through the proofs He set up for it; the witnessing of the angels is their affirming it among themselves and some of them conveying it to the messengers; and the witnessing of those of knowledge is their affirming it through arguments and evidences.

So the use of shahada for these reports is figurative, by a relation of necessity (ʻalaqat al-luzum), or by likening a report to a report or an informant to an informant. You may also take "shahida" to mean "made clear and established the proofs." Here the establishing of proofs for His Oneness, from the bringing into existence of creatures and the setting up of rational proofs, is likened to a witness's testimony that confirms a claim, in clarification and disclosure, by way of metaphor in the derived form (isti'ara tab'iyya). The angels made this clear by what they brought down of revelation to the messengers and by the praises they uttered, and those of knowledge made it clear by the arguments they established against the atheists (mulhidun). You may also take the witnessing of Allah to mean indication and the setting up of proofs, and the witnessing of the angels and those of knowledge to have another meaning, namely affirmation (iqrar), or take it in two senses: the affirmation of the angels and the argumentation of those of knowledge. Then you would base this on the use of "shahida" in figurative meanings, like His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56]; or on the use of "shahida" in a more general figurative sense, namely manifestation (al-izhar), so that the setting up of proofs, affirmation and argumentation are instances of that general meaning, based on the generality of the metaphor.

[p. 187]

The phrase ﴿standing in justice﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in His saying ﴿but He﴾, meaning: He bears witness to His Oneness and to His standing by justice. It may also be a circumstantial clause from the name of majesty (ism al-jalala) in His saying ﴿Allah bears witness﴾. In that case it is a confirmatory circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida) for the content of "shahida," because this testimony is itself a standing in justice, and the one who testifies to it is standing in justice. He said: ﴿Be steadfast in justice, witnesses for Allah﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 8]. Ibn Hisham, in the fourth chapter (of Mughni al-Labib), claimed that its being a confirmatory circumstantial clause is a mistake, and he justified this with something that is itself a mistake. Shaykh Muhammad al-Rassa' mentioned that a discussion took place on the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of such a circumstantial clause in Surat al-Saff, in the lesson of his teacher Muhammad ibn 'Uqab.

Qiyam (standing) here means perseverance and constancy (al-muwazaba), as in His saying: ﴿Is then He who is standing over every soul in what it has earned [like others]?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33], and His saying: ﴿that people may maintain justice﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. You say: "The ruler stands (qa'im) with the interests of the nation," just as you say: "He watches over (sahir) it." From this is His saying: ﴿and the establishment of prayer﴾ [al-Anbiya': 73], and the verse of Ayman ibn Khuraym al-Ansari:

"Ghazala has set up the market of striking swords for the people of the two Iraqs for a full year, a tight-knit year."

In all of this it is an image (tamthil).

Qist means justice, and it is an abbreviation of qistas, with a damma on the qaf. Al-Bukhari related from Mujahid that he said: "Qistas means justice in Roman (Greek/Latin)." This word is established in the Roman languages, and it comes from Latin. Qist and qistas are also used for the balance, because it is an instrument of justice. He said: ﴿And weigh with an even balance﴾ [al-Isra': 35], and He said: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Anbiya': 47]. Allah has established justice in the formation of the worlds according to their orders, in the determination of the continuation of species, in placing in the souls of existent beings the causes of resistance (al-mudafa'a), and in what He legislated for mankind of laws in belief and action, to repel the oppression of some of them against others and their oppression of themselves. He is therefore the one who stands by justice, glory be to Him, and human justice is borrowed from imitation of His justice.

His saying ﴿there is no god but He﴾ is an exaltation (tamjid) and an affirmation (tasdiq). It arises from the testimony of all existent beings to Him in this, so it is an instruction in the affirmation of Him in this respect, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who have believed, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56], meaning: following the example of Allah and His angels. Moreover, it conveys together with that the emphasis of the preceding sentence, and it prepares for His description of Himself as the Almighty, the Wise.

[Page 188]

**"Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam"** (Q. 3:19). Most of the Qur'an reciters read *inna al-dina* with a kasra on the hamza of *inna*. In that case it is a fresh, independent sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a newly started statement), given to explain the excellence of this religion in the most comprehensive and concise terms.

This begins the first of the themes for which this surah was revealed: the debate with the Christians of Najran. This new sentence fits the opening of the surah, which mentions the revelation of the Qur'an, the Torah and the Gospel, then singles out the Qur'an and presents it as superior, since its guidance surpasses the guidance of the earlier scriptures, for it is the *Furqan* (the criterion that distinguishes truth from falsehood). That is the foundation of the upright religion. Since the preceding discourse contained an allusion to the Jews and Christians who denied the Qur'an, and a refutation of the statement of the Najran delegation when the Messenger ﷺ asked them to accept Islam and they said, "We submitted before you," he told them, "You have lied," it was fitting to proclaim Islam, the religion brought by the Qur'an, after that. Al-Wahidi and Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated that when the delegation of Najran entered the Prophet's Mosque, al-Sayyid and al-Aqib spoke. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them, "Submit (aslima)." They said, "We have already submitted before you." He said, "You have lied. What prevents you from Islam is your claim that Allah has a son and your worship of the cross." For this reason, the verse was followed by the statement: **"Those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them"** (Q. 3:19).

Know that the sentences of eloquent speech are never free of connection, even when some of them are independent. The absence of connection is tolerated only in casual conversation and abrupt transitions.

The emphasis of the statement with *inna* confirms what it contains of the restriction (*hasr*, exclusivity) of the true nature of religion with Allah to Islam, that is, to the complete religion.

Al-Kisa'i read *anna al-dina* with a fatha on the hamza of *anna*, making it a substitution (*badal*, apposition) for **"that there is no god but He"** (Q. 3:18). The meaning is: Allah bore witness that the religion with Allah is Islam.

The primary meaning of *din* (religion) is recompense. It then became a customary technical term for the totality of beliefs and practices conveyed by a messenger from Allah, who promises those who act upon them bliss and threatens those who turn away from them with punishment. Then it was applied to what resembles that, namely what some leaders of people devise from their own minds and which a group of people then adopt. The term *din* was used because the follower of a religion expects a reward from it, either quickly

[Page 189]

or later. Thus, every people of a religion expects a reward from the Lord of that religion. The polytheists hope for the help, intercession and approval of their gods, and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah." Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud, "Hubal is supreme!" And on the day of the conquest of Mecca, when al-Abbas said to him, "Has the time not come for you to testify that there is no god but Allah?", he said, "I have known that if there had been another god with Him, it would have benefited me in some way." The people of the divine religions expect the complete reward in this world and the Hereafter. The first divine religion was true, and by it humanity was guided. Then false religions appeared and imitated the true ones. Allah the Exalted said, teaching His Messenger, **"For you is your religion, and for me is my religion"** (Q. 109:6), and He said, **"He could not have taken his brother within the religion of the king"** (Q. 12:76).

The scholars have defined the true religion as a divine ordinance that leads people of sound intellect, by their praiseworthy free choice, to good, both inwardly and outwardly.

*Al-Islam* (submission) has become a proper name by predominance for the totality of the religion brought by Muhammad ﷺ, just as the term *al-iman* (faith) is also applied to it. For this reason, the followers of this religion have been called *al-Muslimun* (the submitters) and *al-Mu'minun* (the believers). The meaning intended here is the former. It is a name taken from the verbal noun of *aslama*, when one submits and does not resist, submitting out of acknowledgment of the truth and not out of incapacity. This title is more appropriate for applying to this religion than the title *iman*, because Islam is the clear manifestation of following the Messenger in what he brought of truth and of abandoning every obstacle that stands between a person and that. Faith, by contrast, is an inward belief. For this reason Allah the Exalted said, **"He named you Muslims"** (Q. 22:78), and He said, **"Say: I have submitted my face to Allah, and so have those who follow me"** (Q. 3:20). Also, because Islam is only possible on the basis of belief, since the act is the effect of perception, whereas the reverse is not the case: belief can exist together with arrogance.

Sometimes *Islam* is applied specifically to actions and *iman* to belief. This usage suits the situation in which the two are separated in reality, as in Allah's words, addressing a people who had submitted hesitantly: **"Say: You have not believed, but say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts"** (Q. 49:14). It also suits the separation in the description of the reality when teaching the true meanings of the legal or linguistic terms, as occurred in the Hadith of Jibril concerning the explanation of the meanings of *iman*, *Islam* and *ihsan*.

The definite article in *al-din* is the generic definite article (*ta'rif al-jins*), since the sense of a specific referent (*'ahd khariji*) cannot be sustained here. The definition of *al-Islam* is a proper-name definition by predominance, because Islam became a name by predominance for the Muhammadan religion.

So the statement **"Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam"** is a construction of restriction (*sigha hasr*). In the language, it requires restricting the subject, which is *al-din*, to the predicate, which is *al-Islam*, according to the rule of restriction by defining both parts of the sentence. That is, there is no religion except Islam. This restriction has been emphasized by the particle of emphasis.

[Page 190]

The phrase **"with Allah"** is a qualifier of the religion. The meaning of "with" (*'indiyya*) here is the "with" of consideration and attention, not the "with" of knowledge. So it conveys that the true religion is Islam. This is a restriction of the subject with regard to a certain qualification within it, not with regard to all its aspects. It is similar to the verse of al-Khansa':

*When weeping over a slain man is deemed ugly,*
*I see your weeping as beautiful and good.*

She restricted the goodness to her weeping by the rule that the restricted element is the one with the definite article, which here is *al-hasan* (the good). This restriction is by way of qualification, to the time when weeping over the slain is ugly. This means restricting the goodness of her weeping to that time, so that her weeping over Sakhr has an added distinction beyond the customary weeping over the slain. Although the author of *al-Mutawwal* denied that the poem contains any restriction at all.

Since true religions have come which Allah commanded, the restriction must be interpreted in one of two ways. Either it refers to the fact that the true religion with Allah, at the time of the announcement, is Islam, because a report is considered in relation to the time of its announcement, since all reports are realities in the present. Without doubt, at the time of the announcement there is no true religion except Islam, since the remaining divine religions have been affected by the mixing of falsehood with truth, which has corrupted the totality of the religion. Or it refers to perfection with Allah, so that the restriction applies to all times and ages, since there is no religion more perfect than this one. The religions that preceded it did not reach the full aim intended for humanity in the welfare of its affairs. Rather, each religion that passed was limited to the measure of need of a particular nation in a particular era. This second meaning is the better of the two interpretations of the verse, because its implication is more general, and its expression of the essential quality of the religion of Islam, in comparison with the rest of the divine religions, is more complete.

This is because Allah's purpose in directing the laws and sending the messengers is not merely the striking of the ears with expressions of legislation, or the savouring of the subtleties of its structures. Rather, Allah's purpose in what He legislated for people is that they act according to the teachings of His messengers and books. Since the purpose of this is action, Allah made the laws suitable to the capacities of those addressed by them and in accordance with the measure of their intellects' acceptance and their capabilities, so that they could act upon them with constancy and regularity. Therefore, the aim of religiosity is that this religious teaching become a habit and custom for its adherents. Since souls cannot submit to what does not agree with their perceptions, it is necessary to take into account the condition of the addressees in all religions, so that nations can act upon the teachings of their laws with regularity and persistence.

In the earliest ages of civilization, human communities were in states of attachment to simple customs and traditions, which gradually came together according to the demands of their needs. The motives that caused those customs to coalesce were not widespread, because they were limited to what benefits the individual in preserving his life and warding off pain from himself, and then to preserving the life of those whom he sees as closely connected to him and improving their condition. By this, the system of the individual came together, then the system of the family, then the system of the clan. These interlinked systems are of similar forms, since all of them do not go beyond preserving life through food and self-defence, and warding off pain through clothing, shelter and marriage, and through victory for the family and the tribe, since honour lies in them. Then came the mutual cooperation of individuals in these matters, by preparing the means, which is exchange and dealing. The thinking of people did not go beyond this condition, and no group had awareness of what was happening among another group, let alone thinking of adopting from another group what it did. This was the condition of contentment with living, lack of ambition, and the absence of motives. When the above conditions were in place, people considered themselves to be in the height of happiness.

The distance between communities in their homelands, together with the difficulty of communication and the dangers and hardships that arose in it, prevented them from encountering what would necessitate nations borrowing from one another and one of them becoming aware of the manners of another. Thus the factor that diverted cooperation in intellectual civilization came to be the combination of two barriers: the absence of motive, and the closing of the channels of chance encounters. The exception was what happened through the visit of a visitor, or intermingling during a seasonal migration or a fair. Yet even if that occurred, forgetfulness would quickly overtake it, and it would become like something that has passed into the past tense.

How, then, can one expect from peoples in this condition that a summoner calls them to a reform beyond the circles of their perceptions and the near scope of their intellectual conceptions? Did they not, when a reformer of this kind came to them, put on the skin of the leopard, and feel the burning of the coal from the evil of obedience? For this reason, in ancient ages, the wisdom of Allah the Exalted did not require the legislation of a comprehensive law suitable for all of humanity. Rather, laws used to come to specific peoples. In the Hadith of Muslim, concerning the description of the presentation of the nations for reckoning, the Messenger of Allah said: "The prophet will come with his group, and the prophet with a man or two men, and the prophet with no one with him." In the narration of al-Bukhari: "So the prophet and the two prophets would pass by with their groups..." etc. The truth remained in the midst of all this shared among the nations, so that in every nation you find some rectitude and some portion, while part of the truth remained hidden and was not made manifest by clarification.

Then humanity began to get to know one another through conquests and migrations, and nations that were close in their dwelling places fought one another. Thus the nations acquired a share of civilization, their customs drew closer, and their knowledge and civilization expanded. Among the divine laws were the law of Abraham, peace be upon him, and others besides it, such as the law of Hammurabi in Iraq, the law of the Brahmins, and the law of the Egyptians, which Allah the Exalted mentioned in His words: **"He could not have taken his brother within the religion of the king"** (Q. 12:76).

Then there followed a great divine law, which is the law of Moses, peace be upon him. Its adherents mixed with many nations in their journey in the wilderness and after it. Alongside it, or following it, came laws such as the law of Zoroaster among the Persians, the law of Confucius in China, and the law of Solon in Greece.

In all these ages, none of the laws was universal in its call. The greatest of these laws, the Mosaic law, called only the children of Israel, and did not call the other nations that it passed by and mixed with and intermarried with. Likewise, Christianity came limited to calling the children of Israel, until Saint Paul called people to it, about thirty years after Christ.

[Page 193]

...until, in the fourth century after Christ, there came about a mixing and blending of the kinds of humanity in their characters and customs, through two causes: one compulsory and one voluntary.

As for the compulsory cause, nations were thrown against one another. The people of the East turned toward the West, and the people of the West toward the East, through the great conquests between the Persians and the Romans, who were at that time the two poles of the world, along with whatever nations belonged to each of their realms. The war was a back-and-forth struggle between the two sides and continued for a long time.

As for the voluntary cause, it is what that mingling left behind of observing characters and customs that were admired in the eyes of those who saw them, so they borrowed them, and things that were considered ugly in their eyes, so they avoided them. In both cases a new awakening arose, diverse civilizations were founded, and minds became prepared to accept strong changes. Thus all the nations became prepared to accept teachings foreign to their customs and conditions. The nations became equal and close to one another to this degree, even though they differed in civilization and sciences, a difference that perhaps included something that made some of them more ready to accept the sound teachings, while it set back others from that because of the self-admiration that had entered them regarding the extent of their knowledge, or their devotion and attachment to their civilization.

Then the appointed and determined term arrived for the coming of the true, final, and universal Law (sharia).

God made the religion of Islam manifest at a time suitable for its appearance, and He chose that its appearance would be among a people who had no precedent of authority, and who were not at that time possessors of dominion over any part of the earth. Rather, they were a people whom God had preserved from most of the vulgarities of human communities, so that they would be closer to accepting the truth. He made this religion manifest through a man from among them, who was neither a man of learning, nor of the state, nor of the descendants of kings, nor had he acquired prior experience through emigration or mixing with others. This was so that the emergence of this clear truth and sound knowledge from one such as him would be a sign that it is a revelation from God, which He breathed into His servants.

Then He made the foundations of this religion distant from the blameworthy customs of the nations, even of the nation in which it appeared, and in agreement with the truth even if its enemies had preceded to it. Its principles were founded upon the natural disposition (fitra), meaning that it looks only at what is good according to sound reason, not captive to customs or to doctrines. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So set your face toward the religion as a people inclined to truth, the natural disposition of God upon which He created mankind. There is no alteration in the creation of God. That is the upright religion, but most of mankind do not know.﴾ [al-Rum: 30]

Shaykh Abu 'Ali Ibn Sina (Avicenna) said: "The fitra is that a person imagines himself to have come into the world all at once, while he is rational, having heard no opinion, having adopted no doctrine, and having not mixed with any nation; but he has witnessed sensible things. Then he presents things to his mind one by one. If it is possible for him to doubt something, then the fitra does not testify to it; and if it is not possible for him to doubt it, then the fitra requires it. Not everything that the fitra requires is true; rather, what is true of it is that which the fitra of the faculty called intellect (reason) testifies to, before the illusion (wahm) overtakes it."

Included in the fitra are the ancient ethical norms agreed upon by all the wise of mankind, by which their souls have been trained, provided they bring them perfection and do not lead to corruption. These are the principles of the rules for preserving lineage and honor in particular. By this principle, the principle of the fitra, Islam became a religion suitable for all nations in all ages.

Then this principle appeared in nine manifestations, serving it and preparing all people to accept it.

The first manifestation: the reform of belief by bringing the mind to a conviction that is not tainted by doubt, deception, illusions, or superstitions. Then by making its belief founded upon submission to one Great Being, and upon acknowledging that this One is characterized by the perfect attributes of perfection that make submission to Him a matter of free choice; then so that those perfections become the aspiration of the believer's gaze to adorn himself with them; then by bringing all people to purify their beliefs, so that the principle of moral conduct becomes unified among them: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we not worship except God and not associate anything with Him and not take one another as lords instead of God."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 64]

The reform of belief was the most important thing Islam began with and the thing it addressed most, because the reform of thought is the beginning of every reform; and because there is no hope of righteousness for a people whose minds are smeared with misguided beliefs, and whose souls are degraded by the effects of those agitating beliefs, fearing what is nothing and hoping for what is nothing. When belief is sound, the rest can become sound, because a person is a human by his spirit, not by his body.

Then from this Islamic belief arose: dignity of the self, originality of opinion, freedom of the intellect, and equality of people in everything other than virtues.

Islam has expounded upon the articles of belief to an extent that no other religion resembles. Indeed, you see that in many of the true religions, you find little explanation of the attributes of the Creator.

The second manifestation: its combining the reform of souls through purification (tazkiya) with the reform of the system of life through legislation. Whereas most religions did not touch upon the system of life at all, and some of them, even if they touched upon it, did not give it its due; rather, most of their concern was directed toward admonitions and acts of worship.

The Qur'an combined the two benefits in more than one verse. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do.﴾ [al-Nahl: 97]

The third manifestation: its specialty in establishing proof, disputing with the addressees through various kinds of argumentation, and explaining its rulings, through encouragement and warning. This is a consideration of the varying ranks of the souls of those addressed. Among them is the wise scholar who is convinced only by proof and evidence; among them is the stubborn one who desists only through disputation and rhetoric; among them is the ascetic who is accustomed to desire what is with God; and among them is the stubborn, obstinate one, whom only shocking and forceful admonitions turn away from his contention.

The fourth manifestation: that it came with a general call to all of mankind, and this is something that was never preceded in any religion before it. In the Qur'an: ﴿Say, "O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of God to you all."﴾ [al-A'raf: 158] And in the authentic hadith: "I have been given five things that no one before me was given," and he mentioned: "A prophet used to be sent to his own people specifically, but I have been sent to mankind generally." God, may He be exalted, mentioned all the messengers and said that He sent them to their peoples.

As for the disagreement over whether Noah was a messenger to all the people of the earth, it is based on the fact that after the Flood, the people of the earth were restricted to the followers of Noah, according to those who say the Flood covered the whole earth. Do you not see His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had certainly sent Noah to his people﴾ [Hud: 25]? And whatever the possibility that the inhabitants of the earth in the time of Noah were only those gathered by the homeland of Noah, the generality of his call is achieved, though not intended.

The fourth manifestation: permanence. No messenger among the messengers claimed that his law was everlasting. Rather, there is no messenger or book except that you find in it good news of a messenger who will come after him.

The fifth manifestation: minimizing the derivation of details in the rulings. Rather, it brings their principles, and the derivation is left to the deductions of the jurists (mujtahidun). Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi has explained this in his commentary on God's saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An'am: 38], so that the rulings are suitable for every age.

The sixth manifestation: that the purpose of the precepts of the religions is the possibility of acting upon them. In the principles of ethics, sound upbringing is that which reaches souls by preventing them from thoughts of evil, because evils, once they seep into souls, become impossible or difficult to uproot from them. The laws used to compel people to follow their precepts directly, so Islam came to lead people to good by two methods: a direct method, and the method of blocking the means that lead to corruption. Most of the rulings of Islam are of this kind, and I think they are among what is meant by the ambiguous matters in the hadith: "Indeed the lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are ambiguous matters that many people do not know."

The seventh manifestation: compassion toward people, even in leading them to their benefits by limiting legislation to the place of benefit, while seeking to present that legislation in a gentle form. In the Qur'an: ﴿God intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. And in the hadith: "I have been sent with the tolerant, easy monotheism (al-hanifiyya al-samha), and no one will overburden this religion except that it will overcome him." The previous laws used to compel following with severity, so they were not suitable for lasting, because they took into account the state of the harshness of nations in particular eras, and they were not those suited to what the destiny of mankind has come to, of gentleness of disposition and elevation of understanding.

The eighth manifestation: the combination of the Law with authority in Islam, and this is among its distinctive features. For there is no meaning to legislation except establishing a law for the nation, and what is the value of a law that is not protected by power and government? By the combination of government with the Law it became possible to generalize the Law and to unite the nation in action and order.

The ninth manifestation: the clarity of the principles of the religion, such that what definitive rulings of the Law can be deduced is repeated in the Qur'an, so that the Law is safeguarded from false interpretations and distortions that befell the people of the earlier scriptures. This becomes clearer when explaining His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then say, "I have submitted myself entirely to God, and so have those who follow me."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20]

* * *

﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of animosity among themselves. And whoever disbelieves in the signs of God – indeed, God is swift in reckoning.﴾ The phrase ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion in the sight of God is Islam﴾, to inform about the state of the People of the Scripture regarding their poor reception of the religion of Islam, and their poor understanding of their own religion.

This informing was delivered in a manner that signals the arrival of a question, since the expression of restriction (hasr) was used to explain the cause of their disagreement, as though their disagreement were a matter known to the listener. This is a wondrous style in informing about their condition, an informing that includes an explanation of its cause and the refutation of other causes that may appear, along with highlighting the contrast between the state of the religion they were upon that day of disagreement and the soundness of Islam from that.

For His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion in the sight of God is Islam﴾ indicates that other religions had not reached the level of perfection and suitability for generality and permanence before alteration, let alone what befell them of alteration and bad interpretation until the coming of Islam. This is so that the listeners may know that what the People of the Scripture are upon has not attained the most perfect purpose of God from creation, and that alteration and disagreement have occurred in it, and that the cause of this disagreement is rebellion (baghy) after knowledge had come to them. Along with an alert that the reason for the invalidity of what they were upon that day is their disagreement and alteration. Among what they altered were the signs indicating the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). In this there is also an alert that Islam is far from the kinds of distortion into which they fell, as was mentioned in the ninth manifestation. For this reason our scholars have censured the distant interpretations that no clear indication called for.

The verse came in a wondrous arrangement that contains several meanings. Among them: a warning against disagreement in religion, that is, in its principles, and the obligation to seek meanings that do not contradict the objective of the religion, taking a lesson from what befell the People of the Scripture of disagreement.

Among its purposes is to alert that the disagreement of the People of the Scripture arose although the means of knowing the truth were present; hence it is an indirect rebuke that they misunderstood the religion.

Another purpose is to point out that the disagreement that occurred among the People of the Scripture is of two kinds. The first is the disagreement of each community with the other concerning the validity of its religion, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the Jews say, "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians say, "The Jews are not upon anything," while they recite the Scripture﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113]. The second is the disagreement of each of the two communities among themselves and their splitting into sects with conflicting tendencies, as in the hadith: "The Jews split into seventy-one sects," warning the Muslims against what they did.

Another purpose is that their disagreement arose from the aggression of some of them against others.

Another purpose is that they unanimously opposed Islam and turned away from it out of aggression and envy, although its truthfulness was evident to their scholars and rabbis, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize it as they recognize their own sons. And indeed, a party of them conceal the truth while they know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146]. ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters﴾ [al-Baqarah: 147]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could turn you back to disbelief after your belief, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109]. That is, they turned away from Islam and insisted on remaining upon their religion, and they wished that they could return you to polytheism or to following their religion, out of envy at the guidance that has come to you, after the truth had become clear to them.

So that the structure of the verse would allow these meanings, the object of the disagreement is omitted in His saying: ﴿And the People of the Scripture did not differ﴾, so that it includes every disagreement among them: the disagreement of some of them with others within the same religion, the disagreement of the adherents of each religion with the adherents of the other religion, and the disagreement of all of them with the Muslims concerning the validity of the religion.

The object of knowledge is also omitted in His saying: ﴿after knowledge had come to them﴾ for the same reason.

"Baghyan" (out of transgression) is placed right after His saying: ﴿after knowledge had come to them﴾ so that it may be governed by both the verb "ikhtalafa" (differed) and the noun "al-'ilm" (knowledge).

"Baynahum" (among themselves) is placed after all that could be attached to it, so that it may be governed by the verb "ikhtalafa," the verb "jaahum" (came to them), the noun "al-'ilm," and the word "baghyan."

From this you learn that the meaning of this verse is broader than the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after the clear evidence had come to them, out of mutual transgression among themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided except after the clear proof had come to them﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 4] in Surat al-Bayyinah, as we have mentioned in those two places, due to the difference of the contexts.

Thus the disagreement of those who were given the Scripture includes their disagreement among themselves, that is, the disagreement of the adherents of each religious community about the affairs of their religion. This is what the form "ikhtalafa" suggests, such as the disagreement of the Jews after Moses on many occasions, and their disagreement after Solomon into two kingdoms: the kingdom of Israel and the kingdom of Judah, and how each kingdom came to have a religious practice that differed from that of the other. Likewise is the disagreement of the Christians concerning the matter of the Messiah and concerning the rituals of the religion. Here His saying "baynahum" (among themselves) is a circumstantial element (hal) for "baghyan": that is, transgression spreading among them, with each group transgressing against the other.

It also includes their disagreement among themselves regarding the matter of Islam, since one of them said, "It is true," another group said, "He is sent to the Ummiyyin (the unlettered)," and a group disbelieved and a group became hypocrites. This aspect is more fitting with His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾. In this case, His saying "baynahum" is a qualifier of "baghyan": that is, a transgression occurring among them.

The coming of knowledge is the revelation that their messengers and prophets brought, because the word "jaa" (came) indicates knowledge received from Allah the Exalted. That is, the knowledge that came to them was supposed to restrain them from disagreeing about its meaning, but they did wrong and so acted contrary to Allah's purpose in sending guidance.

"Baghyan" is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). The governing element of the object of purpose is the verb that is left free to govern what follows the exception particle. The exception here is from omitted times and causes. The estimated sense is: they did not differ except at a time after knowledge had come to them, and it was not except out of transgression among themselves. You may also take "baghyan" as accusative as a circumstantial element (hal) from "alladhina utu al-kitab" (those given the Scripture). Although the governing element is a verb negated in form, the restrictive exception (istithna' mufarragh) places it in the sense of an affirmative, so the circumstantial element comes after it, meaning that those who disagreed were transgressing. Thus the verbal noun is interpreted as a participle. It is also permissible to take it as an object of purpose of "ikhtalafa" in view of it having become affirmative, as we have established.

The verse also hints that this disagreement and transgression amount to disbelief, because it led them to undermine the foundations of their religions and to deny the religion of Islam. For this reason He follows it with His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah﴾, etc.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ is an indirect threat, because the swift in reckoning begins with the reckoning of whoever disbelieves in His signs. The "reckoning" here is a metonymy for recompense, like His saying: ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 113].

In mentioning these blameworthy conditions among the conditions of the People of the Scripture, there is a warning to the Muslims not to fall into the same as what those fell into. And the Muslims, although they have differed in many matters, their disagreement has been only a scholarly, subsidiary (far'i) disagreement, and they have not differed in a way that undermines the foundations of their religion; rather, the ultimate goal of all of it is reaching the truth of the religion and serving the objectives of the Shari'ah. The Children of Israel worshipped the calf while the Messenger was among them, and they worshipped the gods of the nations more than once; the Christians worshipped Mary and the Messiah, violated the foundations of monotheism, and claimed the indwelling of the Creator in the created. As for the Muslims, when one of the Sufis among them said a statement that suggests indwelling, their scholars ruled for his execution.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 20 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if they argue with you, say: "I have submitted myself entirely to God, and so have those who follow me." And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered: "Have you submitted?" If they submit, then they have been guided. But if they turn away, then your duty is only to convey the message. And God is Seeing of [His] servants.﴾

This is a branch (tafri') from His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam. And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. Islam is a religion they have rejected, and their disagreement about their religions leads them to dispute with the Messenger, to justify what they hold of religion, and [to claim] that they are not at a lower standing than what the religion of Islam brought.

The word al-muhajjah (argument, dispute) is a form of mufa'alah (reciprocal action), and its verb has come only in the mufa'alah pattern. The meaning of al-muhajjah is contention (al-mukhasamah), and the verb hajja is used most often in the sense of contending in falsehood, as in His saying: ﴿And his people argued with him﴾ [al-An'am: 80]. It was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258] in Surat al-Baqarah.

So the meaning is: if they dispute with you with the contentiousness of obstinacy, then say: "I have submitted myself entirely to God."

The plural pronoun in His saying ﴿if they argue with you﴾ refers to something not mentioned in the discourse but known from the context, namely the context of the revelation of the surah, that is, the case of the delegation of Najran, for they were the ones who were concerned with arguing at that time. As for the polytheists, the distance between them and the Prophet ﷺ had grown after the Hijrah, so their argument ceased. As for the Jews, they feigned peace with the Muslims in Medina.

God had instructed His Messenger to answer their disputation with His saying: ﴿I have submitted myself entirely to God.﴾ The word "face" (wajh) is used for the self, as in His saying: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88], meaning His Essence.

[Page 201]

The commentators have three approaches regarding the intended meaning of this saying.

The first: it is a disengagement and withdrawal from disputation, meaning: "I acknowledge that I have no power to make you understand any further." That is, I have brought the utmost of what is within my capacity of proof, and you have not been convinced. Since that did not convince you, there is no benefit in adding more theoretical proofs. Your disputation with me is therefore nothing but obstinacy and denial of self-evident and necessary truths, and bewilderment. It is more fitting that I refrain from further addition. Al-Razi said: When the one who is right is tested by a stubborn wrongdoer, he says: "As for me, I am submissive to the truth." Al-Qurtubi also inclined to this interpretation.

On this approach, the function of ending the disputation with the sentence ﴿I have submitted myself entirely to God and so have those who follow me﴾ and His saying ﴿Have you submitted?﴾ is, instead of saying "So turn away from them and say: peace," a kind of integration (idmaj), since within the cutting off of the disputation he integrated a renewed call to Islam, by showing the difference between the two religions.

The purpose of this is eagerness for their guidance and the giving of a valid excuse to them. On this approach, His saying ﴿And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered: "Have you submitted?"﴾ falls outside the subject of the argument; it is only a repetition of the call, meaning: leave off disputing with them, but do not leave off calling them.

The argument referred to is not specifically what was mentioned in the preceding verses. Rather, what is meant is what passed between the Messenger and the delegation of Najran of arguments known to them. Some of it was alluded to in the preceding verses, and some of it was left unmentioned.

The second approach: His saying ﴿So say: "I have submitted myself"﴾ is a summary of the proof and an inducement for them to accept it. In its explanation there are aspects that all return to the view that this is an argument for the truth of Islam. The best of these is what Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: the Jews, Christians and polytheists were all in agreement on the rightness of the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, apart from additions that their laws had introduced. Just as God commanded His Messenger to follow the religion of Abraham in His saying ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾ [al-Nahl: 123], so He commanded him here to dispute with people in the same manner as the words of Abraham. Abraham said: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 79], and Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, said: ﴿I have submitted myself entirely to God﴾. That is: I have said what God said, and you acknowledge the reality of that. So how can you deny that I am upon the truth? He said: This is from the mode of holding them to their own commitments (ilzamat), and it falls under His saying: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl: 125].

[Page 202]

The third approach is what al-Razi said, and its summary, together with its explanation, is that this is connected to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. That is: if they dispute with you about the claim that the religion with God is Islam, then say: "I, by Islam, have submitted my face to God, so I do not turn toward the worship of anyone other than Him, like you do. So the religion with which I was sent is the religion with God," that is, it is the true religion, and what you are upon is not a religion with God.

On the first two approaches, the commentators regarded His saying ﴿And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered: "Have you submitted?"﴾ as falling outside the argument, since it has no connection to the claim that Islam is the religion of Abraham. It would mean a renewed call to Islam by way of a question used for urging (tahdid), like His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91], that is: say to those people: "Will you submit?"

In my view, since a conditional clause implies futurity, the meaning of the verb ﴿they argue﴾ is continuation of the argument. That is: if the delegation of Najran continues in their disputation, then say to them a decisive word that distinguishes between your religion with which you were sent and what they adhere to. So the meaning of ﴿I have submitted myself entirely to God﴾ is: I have made my worship purely for Him, and I do not direct my face to anything else. The intended meaning is that this is the essence of the religion of Islam, and it is shown that it is the pure religion, and that they do not find their religiosity to be described in this way.

His saying ﴿And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered: "Have you submitted?"﴾ is coordinated with the conditional clause that is a consequence of what precedes it. So the coordinated clause falls within the consequence. The structure of the discourse would then be: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the signs of God, then indeed God is swift in account﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. Then say to those who disbelieved in the signs of God, those who were given the Scripture and the unlettered: ﴿Have you submitted?﴾. That is: repeat your call to them to Islam.

The interrogative is used to express impatience and urging, as in His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91]. The past tense was used in His saying ﴿Have you submitted?﴾ instead of saying "Will you submit?", contrary to what the apparent form requires, to alert to the fact that he hopes for the realization of their submission, so that it is as if it has already occurred in the past.

Know that His saying ﴿I have submitted myself entirely to God﴾ is a comprehensive phrase gathering the meanings of the essence of Islam and its foundations. It was cast to people so that they might reflect on its inner meanings, so that those who are astray may be guided and the Muslims may increase in certainty about their religion. For we know that the coming of His saying ﴿I have submitted myself entirely to God﴾ after His saying ﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19] and His saying ﴿if they argue with you﴾, and its being followed by His saying ﴿Have you submitted?﴾, indicates that the purpose of it is to state the comprehensive meanings of Islam, so that

[Page 203]

the argument becomes easy and the discussion is shortened, and so that the skeptics can easily present themselves to this reality, in order to know what they are upon of religious practice. This phrase makes clear that this religion is an expression of the reality of its name. Its name is Islam, which conveys a known meaning in their language that goes back to surrender and submission. Its object has been omitted and the verb has been treated as intransitive. It is understood that the object was omitted because the meaning of the agent indicates it. It is as if one were saying: "I have surrendered myself," that is: I have surrendered my soul. So here it made explicit this omitted object of the name Islam, lest there be ambiguity in it or an interpretation that does not match what is intended. It expressed it by His saying "my face" (wajhi), that is, my self. This is because it is evident that the word "face" here cannot be understood as the well-known part of the body, and understanding it that way would not convey what is meant. Rather, the clear meaning is that "face" refers to the whole essence, as in His saying: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88].

The submission of the self to God means its surrender for His sake and its becoming His possession, such that all of the self's actions are for the pleasure of God. Under this are many meanings that comprise Islam. We confine them to ten.

The first meaning: complete servitude to God Most High, which is by not worshipping other than God. This is a nullification of polytheism, for the one who associates partners with God has not surrendered his self, but has surrendered only part of it.

The second meaning: sincerity of action for God Most High, so that one does not seek anything other than God in his action. He does not show off, nor does he flatter in matters that do not please God, and he does not give precedence to the pleasure of anyone other than God over the pleasure of God.

The third: sincerity of speech for God Most High, so that he does not say what God does not approve, and no speech issues from him except in what God has permitted to be said. In this meaning come frankness, enjoining good and forbidding evil according to one's capacity and knowledge, and undertaking argument to support the purpose of God Most High. This is a quality that distinguishes Islam, and by this meaning hypocrisy and flattery are dispelled. God Most High said, regarding His Messenger: ﴿And I am not of those who pretend﴾ [Sad: 86].

The fourth: that he be striving to learn what God Most High intends from people, in order to arrange his actions according to it. This is achieved by listening to the call of the messengers who inform that they are sent from God, and receiving it with reflection on the evidence of its truthfulness, and distinguishing between it and false claims, without a readiness to deny it, nor obstinacy in receiving the call, nor turning away from it through the impulse of desire. This is the attainment of certainty (al-ifham), such that his knowledge of what God intends from creation becomes his sought-after goal.

[Page 204]

The fifth: carrying out what God has commanded and avoiding what He has forbidden through the tongues of the truthful messengers, and preserving the following of that without alteration or distortion, and that he defend it against anyone who wishes to change it.

The sixth: that he not set up for himself a judgment alongside God in what He has judged, so he does not undertake to arbitrarily accept some of what God has commanded and reject some of it. As God Most High has related: ﴿And when they are called to God and His Messenger to judge between them, behold, a party of them turn away﴾ [al-Nur: 48] ﴿But if the right is theirs, they come to him willingly﴾ [al-Nur: 49]. God has described the Muslims by His saying: ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when God and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice about their affair﴾ [al-Ahzab: 36]. The disbelievers turned away from belief in resurrection because they had not seen a dead person raised.

The seventh: that he be seeking the intent of God in what is unclear to him, and in need of applying it according to God's intent, by seeking to attach it to its perfect analogues, analogizing it to what is known to be God's intent, as God Most High said: ﴿If they had referred it to the Messenger and to those of authority among them, those who would draw correct conclusions from it would have known it﴾ [al-Nisa': 83]. For this reason the scholars of Islam included the ruling of jurisprudence (tafaqquh) in religion and independent reasoning (ijtihad) under the piety commanded in His saying: ﴿So fear God as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16].

The eighth: turning away from blameworthy desire in religion, and from speaking about it without authority: ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from God?﴾ [al-Qasas: 50].

The ninth: that the dealings of individuals of the community with one another, and of its groups, and its dealings with nations, be conducted in accordance with God Most High's intent in those dealings.

The tenth: belief in what is unseen to us, of what God has informed us: of His attributes, of divine decree and predestination, and that God is the absolute Disposer.

His saying ﴿And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered: "Have you submitted?"﴾ is a negation of their being characterized by this meaning. As for the polytheists, their far remove from it is clearly evident. As for the Christians, they have made Jesus a god, and made Mary a consort of God Most High. This is the foundation for the invalidity of their having submitted their faces

[Page 205]

Part 2 of 2 of the commentary begins mid-argument, so I translate it as it stands.

For Allah. For they worshipped others alongside Allah, and they courted the ruling nations and the kings, so they founded the religion according to what pleases them and what wins them favour with them.

As for the Jews, although they did not associate partners with Allah, they have nonetheless violated the foundations of piety. They ridiculed the prophets, killed some of them, mocked the call to goodness towards Allah, altered the rulings out of pursuit of their desires, denied the messengers, and killed the rabbis (aḥbār). So how could these people have submitted to Allah? The greatest refutation of this is their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) without considering the proofs of his truthfulness.

Then, His saying: ﴿But if they submit, then they are guided﴾ means: if they commit themselves to descending to the realisation of the meaning of ﴿I have submitted my face to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137], then ﴿they are guided﴾, and nothing remains except that they follow you to receive what you convey to them from Allah, for that is the first meaning of submitting one's face to Allah. But if they turn away and refuse your saying to them, "Have you submitted?", then no blame for their aversion falls upon you: ﴿Your duty is only to deliver the message﴾. So His saying ﴿Your duty is only to deliver the message﴾ takes the place of the response to the conditional, and in meaning it is the cause of the response. Its placement in the position of the response is a wonderful brevity, meaning: do not grieve, and do not suppose that their failure to be guided, and your disappointment in obtaining their submission, was due to any shortcoming on your part, since you were sent only to convey the message, not to bring about the guidance of those to whom it is conveyed.

His saying: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of the servants﴾ means: He is fully aware of them, so He is the one who will recompense them, and He knows that you have conveyed what you were commanded.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read "ittaba'anī" (ittabaʿanī) with the first-person ya' (yāʾ al-mutakallim) affirmed when joined (waṣl) but not when pausing (waqf). Ya'qub read it affirmed in both states, while the rest read it without the ya', both in joining and in pausing.

[Page 206]

It is a resumptive statement (istinaf) explaining some of the conditions of the Jews, which contradict "submitting one's face to God." The intended referents of these relative clauses are specifically the Jews, and they are known for these attributes in many places in the Qur'an. The occasion (munasabah) is that the argument with the Christians was ongoing, and they were all placed together in the same context as His saying: ﴿And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered, "Have you submitted?"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 20].

In these relative clauses, the present-tense verbs were used to convey the immediacy of this terrible condition, not to indicate repetition (tajaddud). For although repetition is possible in His saying "yakfurun" (they disbelieve), it is not possible in His saying "wa yaqtulun" (and they kill), because they killed the prophets and those who command justice in a past time. The intended referents of these relative clauses are the Jews of the Prophetic age, because they are the ones He threatened with a painful punishment. He attributed the responsibility of their ancestors to them because they hold that what their ancestors did was correct. Their ancestors killed Zakariyya (Zechariah) because he tried to save his son Yahya (John) from being killed; they killed Yahya because of his belief in 'Isa (Jesus); they killed the prophet Irmiya (Jeremiah) in Egypt; they killed the prophet Hizqil (Ezekiel) because he rebuked them for their evil deeds. They also claimed that they had killed 'Isa, peace be upon him, so this killing is counted against them by their own admission, even though they were lying about it. Manasha ibn Hizqil, king of Israel, killed the prophet Ashya' (Isaiah): he sawed him in two with a saw because he forbade him from wrongdoing, in the sight and hearing of the Children of Israel, and they did not protect him. So this killing is counted against them. And how many they killed of those who command justice! All these crimes are counted against them, because they were pleased with them and insisted upon their occurrence.

His saying "bi-ghayri haqq" (without right) is a stationary adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqarr) in the position of a confirmatory circumstantial qualifier (hal mu'akkidah) for the content of the clause "yaqtulun al-nabiyyin" (they kill the prophets), since the killing of prophets is never except without right. It has no implied restrictive meaning (mafhum), because it is evident that the intention is not restriction or exclusion; for no prophet is killed rightfully. So mentioning a qualifier of this kind raises no difficulty. The difficulty arises only with a qualifier that falls within the scope of negation, when the intention is not for the negation to apply to it, such as His saying: ﴿They do not ask people persistently﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273], and His saying: ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it, and do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41]. This has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The purpose of this circumstantial qualifier is to increase the ugliness of their action.

Since His saying "wa yaqtulunal-ladhina ya'murun bil-qist" (and they kill those who command justice) indicates the reason for the construction of the statement, namely that they killed them only because they commanded justice, meaning rightness, the statement suffices in conveying the enormity, and so it does not need an additional intensification of condemnation.

[Page 207]

The reading of the majority of the Ten Readers is "yaqtulun" for the second verb like the first, with a sukun on the qaf. Hamzah alone read it as "wa yuqatilun," with a fatha on the qaf followed by an alif, in the form of mufa'alah, which is an intensification of killing.

The fa' in ﴿fa-bashshirhum﴾ (so give them good tidings) is the fa' of the response (jawab) used in the sense of a conditional, and it entered upon the predicate of "inna" (indeed), because the subject of "inna," which is a relative pronoun, contains the meaning of a condition. This indicates that the intention is not specific people, but that whoever has this attribute, his recompense is that he should know that he has a painful punishment. He used "bashshirhum" (give them good tidings) in the sense of "andhirhum" (warn them), as sarcasm (tahakkum).

The essential meaning of tabshir (giving good tidings) is informing someone of something that shows the joy of the one informed (with a fatha on the ba'). Here it is used in the opposite of its literal sense, since what is intended is informing them of the occurrence of punishment, which causes the grief of those informed. This use in the opposite sense is counted by the scholars of rhetoric (ulama' al-bayan) as a metaphor (isti'arah), and they call it sarcastic (tahakkumiyyah), because likening an opposite to its opposite is not accepted by anyone's mind except in the sense of sarcasm or witty irony (tamlih), just as 'Amr ibn Kulthum applied the name of guests to enemies, and applied hospitality (qira) to the killing of enemies, in his saying:

"You have come to us in the position of guests, so we hastened the hospitality before you could insult us.
We hosted you, and we hastened your hospitality before dawn, a crushing blow."

Al-Sakkaki said: This happens through abstracting the resemblance of opposition and attaching it to the resemblance of correspondence.

The demonstrative noun was used in His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become void﴾ because they were distinguished by these actions, which are indicated by the relative clauses, in the most complete distinction, and to draw attention to the fact that they are deserving of what He will report about them after the demonstrative noun.

The demonstrative noun is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿those whose deeds have become void﴾. It has been said that it is the predicate of "inna," and the clause ﴿fa-bashshirhum bi-'adhabin alim﴾ (so give them good tidings of a painful punishment) is a separate sentence. This is the view following the school of Sibawayh, because he prohibits the entry of the fa' into the predicate absolutely.

The voiding of deeds (habt al-a'mal) is the removal of their beneficial effects, such as reward and bliss in the Hereafter, and a good life in this world. The use of habt (voiding) for this is an allegory (tamthil) for the condition of camels that suffer from habt, which is a swelling in their bellies from excessive eating, which becomes the cause of their death, while they ate what they ate for the enjoyment of it.

[Page 208]

It was previously mentioned at His saying: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning here is that the Jews, since they were religious and hoped from their good deeds to benefit from them in the Hereafter by being saved from punishment, and to benefit in this world through the effects of God's pleasure upon His righteous servants, then when they disbelieved in the signs of God, denied the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, and approved of those who killed the prophets and those who command justice, they had apostatized from their religion, and so they deserved the painful punishment. For this reason, it was begun with it in His saying: ﴿so give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾. Therefore, their deeds are necessarily voided, so they do not benefit from their reward in the Hereafter, nor from their good effects in this world. The meaning of ﴿and they have no helpers﴾ is that they have no one who will rescue them from the punishment with which they were warned.

The particle "min" (from/any), which indicates the explicit generality, was used so that no way of interpretation (ta'wil) would be left for them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 23–25:

﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book being invited to the Book of Allah, that it may judge between them, and then a faction of them turns away while they are refusing?﴾ ﴿That is because they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days," and what they used to fabricate has deluded them in their religion.﴾ ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt, and every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged?﴾

This is an initial, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) expressing wonder at the state of the Jews in the extremity of their misguidance. The interrogative in His words "Have you not seen" (alam tara) is for affirmation and wonder. It is customary in such usage for the interrogative to enter upon a negation of the verb, while the intended meaning is that the listener acknowledge the act, so that the affirmation of its negation spurs the addressee to confess it, on the basis that he would not be content to be among those who are ignorant of it. This was discussed earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The seeing (ru'yah) is visual, as evidenced by its being followed by the preposition "ila" (to), which is the one that the verb of looking takes. The author of al-Kashshaf permitted, in His words: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, purchasing error﴾ [al-Nisa': 44] in Surat al-Nisa', that the seeing be mental (qalbiyyah), with "ila" entering upon the first object, to emphasize the connection of knowledge to the known and its figurative arrival at it, so that it is like His words: ﴿Have you not seen the one who argued with Abraham﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258].

Those spoken of are identified by the relative construction rather than by their title, namely the Jews, because the relative clause adds to the wonder at their state; for their being in possession of some knowledge of the Book, little or much, is by nature something that should restrain them from what He reports about them. Moreover, this clause also weakens their supposed knowledge.

"The Book" is the Torah, so the definite article is for prior reference (al-'ahd), which is the apparent reading; it has also been said that it is for the genus (al-jins).

By "those who were given it" are meant the Jews; it has also been said that the Christians are intended, namely the people of Najran.

Al-nasib (portion) means share and lot, and it was discussed earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿For them is a portion of what they earned﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

The indefiniteness of "nasiban" is for kind (naw'iyyah), not for magnification, because the context is one of contempt for them; it is possible that the tanwin is for diminution.

"Min" is partitive (lil-tab'id), as is apparent from the word "nasib," so "al-Kitab" refers to the class of books, and the "nasib" is their book, and the meaning is: they were given part of their book, by way of insinuation that they know of their book only a meagre share. It is also permissible for "min" to be explanatory (lil-bayan), and the meaning is: they were given a share of the shares of perfection, namely the Book that was given to them.

The clause ﴿being invited to the Book of Allah﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because it is the locus of wonder; this is with respect to what is conjoined to it, namely His words, "then a faction of them turns away," for that is the wonderful thing, not the mere fact of their being invited to the Book of Allah. If you make "tara" mental, then the clause "yud'awna" is in the position of the second object, and you know how remote this is.

"The Book of Allah" is the Qur'an, as in His words: ﴿A party of those who were given the Book threw the Book of Allah behind their backs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101]. It is therefore other than the "Book" meant in His words "min al-Kitab," as the change of expression indicates. The meaning is: they are invited to follow the Qur'an and to reflect on its meanings, so that it may judge between them, and they refuse. It is also permissible that "Kitab Allah" be the very same as what is meant by "al-Kitab," and that the wording was changed for variety and to draw attention to the one being invited to; that is, they are invited to their own Book so that they may reflect upon it and thereby know its good tidings of a Messenger who will come after, and its allusion to his attributes.

It is related concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse that: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the study-house (midras) of the Jews and invited them to Islam. Nu'aym ibn 'Amr and al-Harith ibn Zayd said to him: 'Upon what religion are you?' He said: 'Upon the religion of Abraham.' They said: 'Abraham was a Jew.' He said to them: 'Between us and you is the Torah, so come to it.' But the two refused."

His words, "Then a faction of them turns away": "thumma" (then) is the conjunction for the clause "yatawalla fariq" over the clause "yud'awna," so the conjoined element here has the status of a single noun, and "thumma" indicates that their turning away is continuous over many periods of time far removed from the time of the invitation, that is, they do not refrain, so they turn away, then they turn away again; for a person may turn away out of anger, or because of the great shock of an unexpected matter, then his right judgment returns to him, he reconsiders himself, and he returns. It is known that their turning away immediately upon the invitation, without delay, is obtained from the implication of the address.

Thus the entry of "thumma" is to indicate delay in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), for they might turn away immediately after the invitation; but the intent is to express wonder at their state, how they turn away after being given the Book and conveying it. So when they are invited to their own Book, they turn away. The use of the present tense in His words "yatawallawna" indicates renewal, as in the verse of Ja'far ibn 'Ulbah al-Harithi:

"None removes the distress except the son of a free woman, who sees the surges of death and then visits them."

"Tawalli" is a metaphor for aversion and refusal, and its original sense is turning away from and departing from a place.

His words, "while they are refusing" (wa-hum mu'ridun), form a circumstantial clause emphasizing the clause "a faction turns away," since turning away is refusal. And since it is a circumstantial clause, it does not carry a sense of permanence and stability, so it indicates the renewal of their refusal, which is also conveyed by the present tense in His words "thumma yatawalla fariqun minhum."

His words, "That is because they said, 'The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days'": the demonstrative refers to their turning away and refusal, and the "ba'" is causal: that is, they did what they did because of their claim that they are secure from punishment except for a few numbered days, so their concern for following the truth vanished, since their belief in being saved from the punishment of Allah in every case emboldened them to commit this kind of refusal. This belief, along with its falsehood, also indicates the baseness of their religious aspiration, so they did not compete in purifying the souls. He expressed the belief by saying, indicating that this belief has no proof behind it and that it is a fabricated, deceptive claim; and this doctrine is the doctrine of the Jews, as was mentioned earlier in al-Baqarah.

His words, "and what they used to fabricate has deluded them in their religion": that is, what they had invented about the religion and inserted into it. For this reason "fi" is used, which indicates figurative containment. Among what they used to fabricate is their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80]; and they also used to claim that Allah promised Ya'qub that He would not punish his descendants.

Allah, Exalted is He, has informed of the corruptions of this delusion and fabrication, which cast them into perpetual error, because opposition that does not arise from delusion can be abandoned, with hope, whereas one who is deluded is not expected to abandon it. The Muslims have been afflicted with much delusion in the branches of their religion, and with fabrications from the fabricated reports, which have returned to the aims of the religion and the foundations of the Shari'ah by nullifying them; the detail of this belongs to another place.

His words, "So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt," are a consequence of His words "and what they used to fabricate has deluded them in their religion." That is: if this was delusion, then what will be their state or their recompense when We gather them and pay them their full recompense? The interrogative here is used figuratively for wonder and for the expression of severity.
