Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 23–25:

﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book being invited to the Book of Allah, that it may judge between them, and then a faction of them turns away while they are refusing?﴾ ﴿That is because they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days," and what they used to fabricate has deluded them in their religion.﴾ ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt, and every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged?﴾

This is an initial, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) expressing wonder at the state of the Jews in the extremity of their misguidance. The interrogative in His words "Have you not seen" (alam tara) is for affirmation and wonder. It is customary in such usage for the interrogative to enter upon a negation of the verb, while the intended meaning is that the listener acknowledge the act, so that the affirmation of its negation spurs the addressee to confess it, on the basis that he would not be content to be among those who are ignorant of it. This was discussed earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The seeing (ru'yah) is visual, as evidenced by its being followed by the preposition "ila" (to), which is the one that the verb of looking takes. The author of al-Kashshaf permitted, in His words: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, purchasing error﴾ [al-Nisa': 44] in Surat al-Nisa', that the seeing be mental (qalbiyyah), with "ila" entering upon the first object, to emphasize the connection of knowledge to the known and its figurative arrival at it, so that it is like His words: ﴿Have you not seen the one who argued with Abraham﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258].

Those spoken of are identified by the relative construction rather than by their title, namely the Jews, because the relative clause adds to the wonder at their state; for their being in possession of some knowledge of the Book, little or much, is by nature something that should restrain them from what He reports about them. Moreover, this clause also weakens their supposed knowledge.

"The Book" is the Torah, so the definite article is for prior reference (al-'ahd), which is the apparent reading; it has also been said that it is for the genus (al-jins).

By "those who were given it" are meant the Jews; it has also been said that the Christians are intended, namely the people of Najran.

Al-nasib (portion) means share and lot, and it was discussed earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿For them is a portion of what they earned﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

The indefiniteness of "nasiban" is for kind (naw'iyyah), not for magnification, because the context is one of contempt for them; it is possible that the tanwin is for diminution.

"Min" is partitive (lil-tab'id), as is apparent from the word "nasib," so "al-Kitab" refers to the class of books, and the "nasib" is their book, and the meaning is: they were given part of their book, by way of insinuation that they know of their book only a meagre share. It is also permissible for "min" to be explanatory (lil-bayan), and the meaning is: they were given a share of the shares of perfection, namely the Book that was given to them.

The clause ﴿being invited to the Book of Allah﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because it is the locus of wonder; this is with respect to what is conjoined to it, namely His words, "then a faction of them turns away," for that is the wonderful thing, not the mere fact of their being invited to the Book of Allah. If you make "tara" mental, then the clause "yud'awna" is in the position of the second object, and you know how remote this is.

"The Book of Allah" is the Qur'an, as in His words: ﴿A party of those who were given the Book threw the Book of Allah behind their backs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101]. It is therefore other than the "Book" meant in His words "min al-Kitab," as the change of expression indicates. The meaning is: they are invited to follow the Qur'an and to reflect on its meanings, so that it may judge between them, and they refuse. It is also permissible that "Kitab Allah" be the very same as what is meant by "al-Kitab," and that the wording was changed for variety and to draw attention to the one being invited to; that is, they are invited to their own Book so that they may reflect upon it and thereby know its good tidings of a Messenger who will come after, and its allusion to his attributes.

It is related concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse that: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the study-house (midras) of the Jews and invited them to Islam. Nu'aym ibn 'Amr and al-Harith ibn Zayd said to him: 'Upon what religion are you?' He said: 'Upon the religion of Abraham.' They said: 'Abraham was a Jew.' He said to them: 'Between us and you is the Torah, so come to it.' But the two refused."

His words, "Then a faction of them turns away": "thumma" (then) is the conjunction for the clause "yatawalla fariq" over the clause "yud'awna," so the conjoined element here has the status of a single noun, and "thumma" indicates that their turning away is continuous over many periods of time far removed from the time of the invitation, that is, they do not refrain, so they turn away, then they turn away again; for a person may turn away out of anger, or because of the great shock of an unexpected matter, then his right judgment returns to him, he reconsiders himself, and he returns. It is known that their turning away immediately upon the invitation, without delay, is obtained from the implication of the address.

Thus the entry of "thumma" is to indicate delay in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), for they might turn away immediately after the invitation; but the intent is to express wonder at their state, how they turn away after being given the Book and conveying it. So when they are invited to their own Book, they turn away. The use of the present tense in His words "yatawallawna" indicates renewal, as in the verse of Ja'far ibn 'Ulbah al-Harithi:

"None removes the distress except the son of a free woman, who sees the surges of death and then visits them."

"Tawalli" is a metaphor for aversion and refusal, and its original sense is turning away from and departing from a place.

His words, "while they are refusing" (wa-hum mu'ridun), form a circumstantial clause emphasizing the clause "a faction turns away," since turning away is refusal. And since it is a circumstantial clause, it does not carry a sense of permanence and stability, so it indicates the renewal of their refusal, which is also conveyed by the present tense in His words "thumma yatawalla fariqun minhum."

His words, "That is because they said, 'The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days'": the demonstrative refers to their turning away and refusal, and the "ba'" is causal: that is, they did what they did because of their claim that they are secure from punishment except for a few numbered days, so their concern for following the truth vanished, since their belief in being saved from the punishment of Allah in every case emboldened them to commit this kind of refusal. This belief, along with its falsehood, also indicates the baseness of their religious aspiration, so they did not compete in purifying the souls. He expressed the belief by saying, indicating that this belief has no proof behind it and that it is a fabricated, deceptive claim; and this doctrine is the doctrine of the Jews, as was mentioned earlier in al-Baqarah.

His words, "and what they used to fabricate has deluded them in their religion": that is, what they had invented about the religion and inserted into it. For this reason "fi" is used, which indicates figurative containment. Among what they used to fabricate is their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80]; and they also used to claim that Allah promised Ya'qub that He would not punish his descendants.

Allah, Exalted is He, has informed of the corruptions of this delusion and fabrication, which cast them into perpetual error, because opposition that does not arise from delusion can be abandoned, with hope, whereas one who is deluded is not expected to abandon it. The Muslims have been afflicted with much delusion in the branches of their religion, and with fabrications from the fabricated reports, which have returned to the aims of the religion and the foundations of the Shari'ah by nullifying them; the detail of this belongs to another place.

[Page 212]

﴿Say: O Allah, Master of the Kingdom, You give the kingdom to whom You will, and You take the kingdom away from whom You will. You exalt whom You will, and You abase whom You will. In Your hand is all good. Indeed, You are over all things Competent.﴾ ﴿You cause the night to enter into the day and You cause the day to enter into the night. You bring the living out of the dead and You bring the dead out of the living. And You provide for whom You will without account.﴾

This is a new, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i). Its purpose is to make an oblique allusion to the People of the Book, that their aversion is nothing but envy at the removal of prophethood from them and the ending of sovereignty from them. It threatens them and establishes the proof against them that it is no wonder that prophethood should pass from the Children of Israel to the Arabs. It also hints that the Islamic law is a law that goes together with authority and dominion.

"Allahumma" in the speech of the Arabs is specific to addressing Allah, the Exalted, in supplication, and its meaning is "O Allah." Since the particle of address was frequently omitted with it, the grammarians said that the mim (م) is a substitute (ʿiwad) for the particle of address. They mean that the attachment of the mim to the name of Allah in this word, since it occurs only when supplication is intended, made it independent of the particle of address by way of abbreviation. It is not meant that the mim indicates address. The apparent view is that the mim is a sign of tanwin in the language from which the word "Allahumma" was borrowed, whether Hebrew or Qahtani, and that its original form was "Lahum," a synonym of "Ilah" (god).

What indicates that the Arabs pronounced it in this form outside of address is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Like a supplication from Abu Rabah, which the Great Allahum hears."

And that they pronounced it in this way also with address, as in the saying of Abu Khirash al-Hudhali:

"Indeed, when some calamity befalls me, I say: O Allahumma, O Allahumma."

And they often say "Ya Allah." The majority of grammarians said that the mim is a substitute for the omitted particle of address, that this substitution is not analogical, and that what occurs contrary to this is an anomaly. Al-Farra' claimed that "Allahumma" is contracted from the name of majesty and a clause whose original was "Ya Allah umma," meaning "Turn toward us with good." All of this is far-fetched and has no evidence.

[Page 213]

The "Malik" (owner, master) is the one specially entitled to dispose of a thing with all the dispositions that are applied to its like, of the things that are intended for it, such as their essences, their benefits and their fruits, as he wills. This may be by sole possession, which is the most common, or by a broad or narrow partnership.

And "al-mulk" (kingdom) with a damma on the mim and a sukun on the lam is a type of "al-milk" (possession), with a kasra on the mim. So "al-milk" with a kasra is the genus, and "al-mulk" with a damma is a species of it, and it is the highest of its kinds. Its meaning is disposing over a great community or a numerous nation with the disposition of managing affairs, establishing rights, guarding interests, repelling aggression from them, and directing them to what is good for them, by means of desire and fear. Consider His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They said: How can he have kingship over us?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:247] in Surat al-Baqarah. Some of this was already mentioned at His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Fatihah 1:4]. So the meaning of "Malik al-Mulk" is that He is the one who disposes of the species of kingdom (with a damma) as He wills, such that "al-mulk" here means this species.

The definite article in the first "al-mulk" is for comprehensiveness of the genus, i.e., every kingdom that exists in the world. Since kingdom is a quiddity among the quiddities, the meaning of Allah being "Malik al-Mulk" is that He is the one who owns the direction of kingdom, that is, its giving, distribution, expansion and restriction. Thus it is, in meaning, an implied construction with an omitted genitive.

The definite article in the second and third "al-mulk" is for the genus, not for comprehensiveness of any group or portion of the genus of kingdom. The basis for distinguishing the extent of the genus is the contextual indicators. That is why the attribute of "Malik al-Mulk" is explained by His saying: ﴿You give the kingdom to whom You will, and You take the kingdom away from whom You will.﴾ Its giving and taking away are predicated of it by gradation: affirmation and negation, abundance and scarcity.

"An-nazʿ" (taking away), literally, is the removal of a body from its place, such as removing a garment or drawing water from a well. It is used figuratively for the removal of attributes and meanings, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾ [al-A'raf 7:43], by likening the firmly established meaning to an entity attached to a place, and likening its removal to pulling out. From this is His saying here: "You take the kingdom away," i.e., You remove the quality of kingship from whom You will.

His saying: ﴿In Your hand is all good﴾ is a figure of speech for disposal over the matter, because the one who disposes of something exercises his strongest disposal by placing something in his hand, even if it is not something that is placed in the hand. ʿAntara ibn al-Akhras al-Maʿni al-Taʾi said:

"There is no good in your two hands that I hope for, and apart from your turning away there is only great calamity."

This is counted among the mutashabih (ambiguous verses, whose meaning is not immediately clear), because it involves the attribution of a hand to the Divine Name. But it is not ambiguous, because the intended meaning of its use in Arabic speech is clear. Restricting "good" in the disposal of Allah, the Exalted, is sufficiency, like His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl 16:81], meaning and from the cold.

Good is inherently and primarily what is required, while evil is required only incidentally. Al-Jalal al-Dawani said in his commentary on the preface of Hayakil al-Nur: "Good is specified here because the context is the context of Muslims hoping for good from Allah, and it is known that their good is evil for their opponents, as it has been said:

'The calamities of one people are the benefits of another.'"

That is, good is required by the essence, and evil is decreed incidentally and proceeds by consequence, since some of what includes many goods necessarily entails a small evil. If those many goods were abandoned because of that small evil, abandoning them would itself be a great evil. So when that good proceeded, that evil necessarily followed.

The literal meaning of "tulij" is "you cause to enter." It is here a metaphor for the succession of the light of day and the darkness of night, as if one of them enters into the other. Because the length of day exceeds the length of night, and the reverse, in the days and seasons, except the days of equinox, which in reality are a few moments. Then one of them increases, but the increase is not perceived at its beginning, so only the scholars know it. Apparently, it is two days in every half of a solar year. Ibn ʿArafa said: "Some of them used to say: The Qur'an contains words that the common people understand, words that the elite understand, and what both groups understand. This verse is one of them, for the entering (iyla') includes the days that only the elite understand and the seasons that all common people perceive."

In this there is a symbol of what occurred in the world of darkness of ignorance and polytheism after people had been upon a sound religion like the religion of Musa, and of what happened with the appearance of Islam in the abolition of misguidance. For this reason it begins with His saying: ﴿You cause the night to enter into the day﴾, so that it ends with His saying: ﴿and You cause the day to enter into the night.﴾ This is analogous to the allusion I explained in His saying: ﴿You give the kingdom to whom You will﴾, and so on. What indicates this symbolism is the opening of the speech with His saying: ﴿O Allah, Master of the Kingdom﴾, and so on.

The bringing out of the living from the dead is like the emergence of an animal from the embryonic lump (mudgha) and from the yolk of an egg, and the bringing out of the dead from the living is the reverse of all of that. An explanation of this will come at His saying:

[Page 214]

﴿And who brings the living out of the dead?﴾ [Yunus 10:31] in Surat Yunus. This is a symbol of the emergence of guidance and kingship among an unlettered nation, and the emergence of the misguidance of disbelief among the People of the Two Books, and the removal of kingship from them after it had been the emblem of their forebears, as indicated by the opening of the speech with His saying: ﴿O Allah, Master of the Kingdom﴾, and so on.

Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from ʿAsim, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read "al-mayyit" with a shadda on the ya. Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir, Abu ʿAmr, Abu Bakr from ʿAsim and Ya'qub read it with a sukun on the ya. These are two valid readings of the word "al-mayyit."

His saying: ﴿and You provide for whom You will without account﴾ serves as a concluding summation of all of that.

Provision (rizq) is what a person benefits from. It is applied to food and fruits, as in His saying: ﴿She found with her provision﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:37], and His saying: ﴿So let him bring you provision from it﴾ [al-Kahf 18:19]. It is also applied to something more general that is benefited from, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They call therein for abundant fruit and drink﴾ [Sad 38:51]. ﴿And with them are women limiting their glances, equal in age﴾ [Sad 38:52]. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Sad 38:54]. And His saying: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Say: Allah﴾ [Saba' 34:24]. For this reason, dirhams and dinars are called provision, because with them is exchanged what is provision. In this there is an indication of good news for the Muslims of the treasures of the Persian and Byzantine domains and others, which were hidden for them.

They mean that the attachment of the mim to the name of Allah in this word, since it occurs only when supplication is intended, made it independent of the particle of address by way of abbreviation. The apparent view is that the mim is a sign of tanwin in the language from which the word "Allahumma" was borrowed, whether Hebrew or Qahtani, and that its original form was "Lahum," a synonym of "Ilah" (god).

What indicates that the Arabs pronounced it in this form outside of address is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Like a supplication from Abu Rabah, which the Great Allahum hears."

And that they pronounced it in this way also with address, as in the saying of Abu Khirash al-Hudhali:

"Indeed, when some calamity befalls me, I say: O Allahumma, O Allahumma."

And they often say "Ya Allah." The majority of grammarians said that the mim is a substitute for the omitted particle of address, that this substitution is not analogical, and that what occurs contrary to this is an anomaly. Al-Farra' claimed that "Allahumma" is contracted from the name of majesty and a clause whose original was "Ya Allah umma," meaning "Turn toward us with good." All of this is far-fetched and has no evidence.

[Page 213]

The "Malik" (owner, master) is the one specially entitled to dispose of a thing with all the dispositions that are applied to its like, of the things that are intended for it, such as their essences, their benefits and their fruits, as he wills. This may be by sole possession, which is the most common, or by a broad or narrow partnership.

And "al-mulk" (kingdom) with a damma on the mim and a sukun on the lam is a type of "al-milk" (possession), with a kasra on the mim. So "al-milk" with a kasra is the genus, and "al-mulk" with a damma is a species of it, and it is the highest of its kinds. Its meaning is disposing over a great community or a numerous nation with the disposition of managing affairs, establishing rights, guarding interests, repelling aggression from them, and directing them to what is good for them, by means of desire and fear. Consider His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They said: How can he have kingship over us?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:247] in Surat al-Baqarah. Some of this was already mentioned at His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Fatihah 1:4]. So the meaning of "Malik al-Mulk" is that He is the one who disposes of the species of kingdom (with a damma) as He wills, such that "al-mulk" here means this species.

The definite article in the first "al-mulk" is for comprehensiveness of the genus, i.e., every kingdom that exists in the world. Since kingdom is a quiddity among the quiddities, the meaning of Allah being "Malik al-Mulk" is that He is the one who owns the direction of kingdom, that is, its giving, distribution, expansion and restriction. Thus it is, in meaning, an implied construction with an omitted genitive.

The definite article in the second and third "al-mulk" is for the genus, not for comprehensiveness of any group or portion of the genus of kingdom. The basis for distinguishing the extent of the genus is the contextual indicators. That is why the attribute of "Malik al-Mulk" is explained by His saying: ﴿You give the kingdom to whom You will, and You take the kingdom away from whom You will.﴾ Its giving and taking away are predicated of it by gradation: affirmation and negation, abundance and scarcity.

"An-nazʿ" (taking away), literally, is the removal of a body from its place, such as removing a garment or drawing water from a well. It is used figuratively for the removal of attributes and meanings, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾ [al-A'raf 7:43], by likening the firmly established meaning to an entity attached to a place, and likening its removal to pulling out. From this is His saying here: "You take the kingdom away," i.e., You remove the quality of kingship from whom You will.

His saying: ﴿In Your hand is all good﴾ is a figure of speech for disposal over the matter, because the one who disposes of something exercises his strongest disposal by placing something in his hand, even if it is not something that is placed in the hand. ʿAntara ibn al-Akhras al-Maʿni al-Taʾi said:

"There is no good in your two hands that I hope for, and apart from your turning away there is only great calamity."

This is counted among the mutashabih (ambiguous verses, whose meaning is not immediately clear), because it involves the attribution of a hand to the Divine Name. But it is not ambiguous, because the intended meaning of its use in Arabic speech is clear. Restricting "good" in the disposal of Allah, the Exalted, is sufficiency, like His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl 16:81], meaning and from the cold.

Good is inherently and primarily what is required, while evil is required only incidentally. Al-Jalal al-Dawani said in his commentary on the preface of Hayakil al-Nur: "Good is specified here because the context is the context of Muslims hoping for good from Allah, and it is known that their good is evil for their opponents, as it has been said:

'The calamities of one people are the benefits of another.'"

That is, good is required by the essence, and evil is decreed incidentally and proceeds by consequence, since some of what includes many goods necessarily entails a small evil. If those many goods were abandoned because of that small evil, abandoning them would itself be a great evil. So when that good proceeded, that evil necessarily followed.

The literal meaning of "tulij" is "you cause to enter." It is here a metaphor for the succession of the light of day and the darkness of night, as if one of them enters into the other. Because the length of day exceeds the length of night, and the reverse, in the days and seasons, except the days of equinox, which in reality are a few moments. Then one of them increases, but the increase is not perceived at its beginning, so only the scholars know it. Apparently, it is two days in every half of a solar year. Ibn ʿArafa said: "Some of them used to say: The Qur'an contains words that the common people understand, words that the elite understand, and what both groups understand. This verse is one of them, for the entering (iyla') includes the days that only the elite understand and the seasons that all common people perceive."

In this there is a symbol of what occurred in the world of darkness of ignorance and polytheism after people had been upon a sound religion like the religion of Musa, and of what happened with the appearance of Islam in the abolition of misguidance. For this reason it begins with His saying: ﴿You cause the night to enter into the day﴾, so that it ends with His saying: ﴿and You cause the day to enter into the night.﴾ This is analogous to the allusion I explained in His saying: ﴿You give the kingdom to whom You will﴾, and so on. What indicates this symbolism is the opening of the speech with His saying: ﴿O Allah, Master of the Kingdom﴾, and so on.

The bringing out of the living from the dead is like the emergence of an animal from the embryonic lump (mudgha) and from the yolk of an egg, and the bringing out of the dead from the living is the reverse of all of that. An explanation of this will come at His saying:

[Page 214]

﴿And who brings the living out of the dead?﴾ [Yunus 10:31] in Surat Yunus. This is a symbol of the emergence of guidance and kingship among an unlettered nation, and the emergence of the misguidance of disbelief among the People of the Two Books, and the removal of kingship from them after it had been the emblem of their forebears, as indicated by the opening of the speech with His saying: ﴿O Allah, Master of the Kingdom﴾, and so on.

Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from ʿAsim, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read "al-mayyit" with a shadda on the ya. Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir, Abu ʿAmr, Abu Bakr from ʿAsim and Ya'qub read it with a sukun on the ya. These are two valid readings of the word "al-mayyit."

His saying: ﴿and You provide for whom You will without account﴾ serves as a concluding summation of all of that.

Provision (rizq) is what a person benefits from. It is applied to food and fruits, as in His saying: ﴿She found with her provision﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:37], and His saying: ﴿So let him bring you provision from it﴾ [al-Kahf 18:19]. It is also applied to something more general that is benefited from, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They call therein for abundant fruit and drink﴾ [Sad 38:51]. ﴿And with them are women limiting their glances, equal in age﴾ [Sad 38:52]. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Sad 38:54]. And His saying: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Say: Allah﴾ [Saba' 34:24]. For this reason, dirhams and dinars are called provision, because with them is exchanged what is provision. In this there is an indication of good news for the Muslims of the treasures of the Persian and Byzantine domains and others, which were hidden for them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 28 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Whoever does that has nothing to do with Allah, unless you are protecting yourselves against them in some way. And Allah warns you about Himself, and to Allah is the final return.﴾ This is a resumption (istinaf) that follows the verses before it, which contained the enmity of the polytheists toward Islam and its people, the envy of the Jews toward them, and their turning away from it, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth will not avail them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 10] up to here.

The connection is that this verse is like a conclusion drawn from what preceded it: after Allah had made clear to the believers the transgression and aversion of those who opposed them, He forbade them to take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. For their taking them as allies, after the others had belittled their religion and mocked their wisdom in following it, would amount to weakness in the religion and an endorsement of the aggressors.

The term "disbelief" (kufr) came to be used in the terminology of the Qur'an for polytheism, and "the disbelievers" and "those who disbelieved" for the polytheists. Perhaps the prohibition on taking allies is tied to the disbelievers here in this sense because the polytheists were the ones who had ties of kinship, lineage, affection and financial dealings with the emigrants, so they were liable to be allied with one another. Every listener knows that whoever resembles the polytheists in their stance toward Islam, the believers' allegiance to him is like their allegiance to the polytheists. It may also be that by "the disbelievers" is meant all opponents in religion, similar to the meaning in His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah, then Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19]. For all of this, it has been said that the verse was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a, who was among the most excellent emigrants and sincere believers, except that he misinterpreted, and wrote a letter to the Quraysh informing them of the Prophet's (ﷺ) preparation for the conquest of Makkah. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning Asma', the daughter of Abu Bakr, when she asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about being dutiful to her mother and maintaining ties with her, that is, before her mother came to Madinah desiring (Islam); for it is established in the Sahih that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to her: "Keep ties with your mother." It has also been said that it was revealed concerning a group of the Ansar who were allied with Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Abu Rafi' ibn Abi al-Huqayq, two Jews of Yathrib. It has been said that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who are those who allied with the Jews, since they are disbelievers of their kind. It has been said that it was revealed concerning 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, who had an alliance with the Jews; when the Day of the Confederates came, "'Ubada said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'I have with me five hundred men from the Jews, and I wish that they go out with me so that I may gain support through them against the enemy.'" It has been said that it was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir when the polytheists seized him and tortured him severely, so he said what they wanted from him, and they left him alone; he complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said to him: "How do you find your heart?" He said: "Content with faith." He said: "If they return, then return."

His saying: ﴿instead of the believers﴾ — the "min" (from) here is to emphasize the adverbial sense.

The meaning is: "distancing themselves from the believers," that is, in allegiance. This is a restriction of the prohibition on the surface, so the forbidden thing becomes taking the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers, that is, the believer's allegiance to the disbelievers which contradicts his allegiance to the believers. This occurs when allegiance to the disbelievers involves harm to the believers. The basic principle of qualifiers is that they serve to exclude, and this is supported by His saying after it: ﴿Whoever does that has nothing to do with Allah﴾, for it is a negation of the connection of whoever does that with Allah, the Exalted, in all circumstances. The Arabs say (you are
page 217
from me and I am from you) to express intense connection, as if one of them were a part of the other or originated from him; and in separation and severance they say: "You are not from me and I am not from you." Al-Nabigha said:
"Indeed I am not from you, and you are not from me."
His saying "in anything" is an explicit statement of the generality of the negation in all circumstances, to remove the possibility of interpreting it as a negation of connection only in most circumstances. So the meaning is that the one who does that is cut off from belonging to Allah. This indicates that the prohibition here is a kind of disbelief, namely the state in which the hypocrites were, and they used to think they could pass it off upon the believers, so Allah exposed them. For this reason it has been said that this verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites. Among what indicates this is that it is parallel to the other verse: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do you wish to give Allah a clear authority against yourselves?﴾ [An-Nisa: 144] ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire﴾ [An-Nisa: 145].

It has been said that there is no implied meaning (mafhum) in His saying "instead of the believers," because many verses indicate the prohibition on allegiance to disbelievers absolutely, such as His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies; they are allies of one another﴾ [Al-Ma'ida: 51], and His saying: (﴿O you who believe, do not take those who have taken your religion as mockery and play, from among those given the Scripture before you, nor the disbelievers, as allies﴾ [Al-Ma'ida: 57]). To this view al-Fakhr (al-Razi) inclined.

The demonstrative in His saying "that" refers to what was mentioned, namely the content of His saying: "as allies instead of the believers."

The verse is a prohibition on allegiance to disbelievers instead of believers, either by way of the qualifier or absolutely. Allegiance may be outward and inward, or outward only, and it has various states, each followed by rulings. From this I have derived eight states:

The first state: that a Muslim takes a group or faction of disbelief as allies for himself in his inner affairs, inclining toward their disbelief and opposing the people of Islam. This state is disbelief, and it is the state of the hypocrites. In the hadith of 'Itban ibn Malik: "A speaker said in the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Where is Malik ibn al-Dukhshun?' Another said: 'That is a hypocrite who does not love Allah and His Messenger.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Do not say that. Did you not hear him say: There is no god but Allah, seeking by it the face of Allah?' The speaker said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best; we see his face and his counsel directed toward the hypocrites.'" So this man made siding with the hypocrites a sign of hypocrisy, were it not for the Messenger's testimony to Malik's faith, that is, in his heart together with his outward profession by the testimony that there is no god but Allah.

The second state: relying on groups of disbelief and supporting them for the sake of kinship and affection, without inclining toward their religion, at a time when the disbelievers openly show enmity to the Muslims, mock them and harm them, as was the case of most of the disbelievers' conditions at the rise of Islam, while not severing affection for the Muslims. This state does not make its bearer a disbeliever, but committing it is a grave sin, because its bearer is likely to ally with them against the harm of Islam. Moreover, it is obligatory to show zeal for Islam and jealousy on its behalf, as al-'Attabi said:
"You love my enemy, then you claim that I am your friend; indeed, the opinion of you is far from sound."
In a similar context was revealed His saying: (﴿O you who believe, do not take those who have taken your religion as mockery and play, from among those given the Scripture before you, nor the disbelievers, as allies﴾ [Al-Ma'ida: 57]). Ibn 'Atiyya said: The disbelievers of Quraysh were among the mockers, and in a similar context came His saying: ﴿Allah only forbids you from those who fought you over religion and expelled you from your homes﴾ [Al-Mumtahana: 9], and His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not take an intimate circle from other than yourselves; they will not spare you corruption﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118]. These were revealed concerning a people who had between them and the Jews a neighborly bond and alliance in the Jahiliyya, and they continued it in Islam, so they felt at ease with them and inclined to them; among them were the companions of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Abu Rafi' ibn Abi al-Huqayq, and these two used to harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The third state: likewise, but without the factions of disbelief openly displaying hatred of the Muslims or harming them, as was the case with the Christians of the Arabs at the rise of Islam. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe are those who say, "We are Christians"﴾ [Al-Ma'ida: 82]. Similarly was the condition of Abyssinia, for they protected the believers and sheltered them. Al-Fakhr said: This is an intermediate position; it does not necessitate disbelief, but it is forbidden, since it may lead to approving of what they hold and to their schemes against the Muslims being overlooked.

The fourth state: allying with a faction of the disbelievers for the purpose of harming a specific group of Muslims, such as seeking victory through the disbelievers over a group of Muslims. The rulings on this state vary. Malik said concerning the spy who spies for the disbelievers against the Muslims: he is left to the judgment of the Imam, and this is correct, because the purpose of espionage differs: one may do it out of delusion, another out of greed, it may be a single lapse, or it may be a habit and custom for him. Ibn al-Qasim said: That is zandaqa (heresy) with no repentance for it, meaning he is not asked to repent and is killed like the zindiq, who is one who shows Islam and conceals disbelief, once he is discovered. Ibn Wahb said: it is apostasy and he is asked to repent. These are two views weak from the standpoint of analysis.

Al-Mu'tamid Ibn 'Abbad, ruler of Seville, sought the help of the Jalaliqa against the Lamtuni Murabitun. It is said that the jurists of al-Andalus issued a fatwa to the Commander of the Muslims 'Ali ibn Yusuf ibn Tashfin declaring Ibn 'Abbad a disbeliever, and this was the cause of his imprisonment; he did not kill him, and it is not reported that he asked him to repent.

The fifth state: that the believers take a faction of the disbelievers as allies for the purpose of supporting the Muslims against their enemies, at a time when those disbelievers show love for the Muslims and offer them support. The scholars have differed on its ruling. In the Mudawwana, Ibn al-Qasim said: one does not seek help from polytheists in fighting, because of his peace be upon him saying to a disbeliever who followed him on the day he went out to Badr: "Return, for I will never seek help from a polytheist." Abu al-Faraj and 'Abd al-Malik ibn Habib narrated that Malik said: there is no harm in seeking their help when there is need. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: the hadith "I will never seek help from a polytheist" is disputed in its chain. A group said it is abrogated. 'Iyad said: some of our scholars understood it to refer to a specific time, and these argued from the expedition of Safwan ibn Umayya with the Prophet (ﷺ) at Hunayn and at the battle of al-Ta'if, while he was not a Muslim at that time. They also argued that when the Prophet (ﷺ) learned that Abu Sufyan was gathering armies for the Day of Uhud, he said to the Banu al-Nadir of the Jews: "We and you are people of the Book, and the people of the Book have a right to support against the people of the Book; so either you fight with us, or you lend us weapons." Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, al-Layth and al-Awza'i adopted this view. Among our companions some said: we do not request help from them, and if they ask our permission we do not grant it, because permission is like a request; but if they go out with us of their own accord, we do not prevent them. Ibn Rushd, in al-Bayan from the Book of Jihad, reported that this view aimed to reconcile the statement of Ibn al-Qasim with the narration of Abu al-Faraj. Ibn Rushd reported from al-Tahawi, from Abu Hanifa, that he permitted seeking help from the People of the Book but not from polytheists. Ibn Rushd said: this has no basis. And from Asbagh, a total prohibition without interpretation.

**[Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on 3:28, part 2 of 2]**

The sixth case: a Muslim takes one particular disbeliever as a close friend (wali), either for good companionship or because of kinship, or because of some excellence in him or the like, provided that this does not harm the Muslims. This is not prohibited. God the Exalted said about the two parents: ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, and accompany them in this world with kindness﴾ [Luqman: 15]. Asma' asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission to be dutiful to her mother and to maintain ties with her, although she was a disbeliever, and he said to her: "Maintain ties with your mother." In this sense God the Exalted revealed: ﴿God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being kind to them and dealing justly with them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 8]. It was said that it was revealed about the mother of Asma'. It was also said that it was revealed about groups of the polytheists of Mecca, namely Kinana, Khuza'a, Muzayna, and the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, who wished for the victory of the Muslims over the people of Mecca. It is related from Malik that it is permissible to offer condolences to a disbeliever for the death of one of his relatives. The Prophet (ﷺ) was pleased with al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi, because of the affection he showed for the Prophet and his frequent visits to him. He benefited them on the day of al-Ta'if when he turned away the Banu Zuhra, who numbered three hundred horsemen, from fighting the Muslims, and he withdrew with them, as was mentioned in God's saying: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the worldly life may impress you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204], and so on.

The seventh case: the case of worldly transactions, such as trade, covenants, and reconciliations. Their rulings differ according to circumstances, and their details are found in jurisprudence (fiqh).

The eighth case: the case of outwardly showing allegiance to them in order to avoid harm. This is the case referred to by God the Exalted's saying: ﴿except when you fear them, taking precaution﴾.

The exception in ﴿except when you fear them﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), arising from the sentence ﴿then he has nothing to do with God﴾, because taking precaution (ittiqa') is not something contained in the demonstrative noun (of the prohibition), but it resembles wilaya in dealing (with them).

Ittiqa' means avoiding what is disliked. Its being transitive with the preposition "min" is either because ittiqa' means concealment, so it takes "min" just as the verb "tasattara" (to conceal oneself) does, or because the verb is implicitly containing the meaning of "takhafu" (you fear).

As for "tuqatan" (taqiyya/precaution), the majority recited it with a dammah on the first letter, a fatha on the qaf, and an alif after it. It is the verbal noun of ittiqa'. Its original form was "wuqyatun," and the waw, which is the first radical of the root, was dropped in conformity with the verb "ittaqa," whose waw had been changed to ta' so that it could be assimilated into the ta' of the ifti'al pattern. Then they made the noun of the verbal noun follow it, as in al-tujah, al-tukla, al-tu'da, and al-tukhamah, since there is no reason for changing the fa' into ta' in a form like "tuqatan" except this. The form "turath" is an anomaly. What supports this meaning is al-Jawhari's statement: "Their saying tujahaka (in front of you) was formed on the basis of their saying ittajaha lahum ra'yun (an opinion turned toward them)." In Lisan al-'Arab, under "tukhamah," it is said: "because they assumed the ta' to be original due to frequent usage." What also supports this is the pairing of these nouns with their verbs in such verses as this one, and in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, fear God as He should be feared﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102]. Ya'qub recited it with a fatha on the ta' at the beginning, a kasra on the qaf, and a shaddah on the ya' with a fatha, in the pattern fa'ilah.

The purpose of emphasizing with the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) here is to indicate that the condition is definitely a condition of taqiyya. This taqiyya is like the state of the weak among the believers who could find no way to emigrate, of whom God the Exalted said: ﴿except one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith﴾ [al-Nahl: 106]. It is also like the state that the Muslims of al-Andalus faced when the Christians forced them to disbelieve, so they outwardly showed it until some groups of them were able to flee, and some groups asked the disbelievers' permission to emigrate to the lands of Islam, and the enemy allowed them. Likewise, taqiyya must not be permanent, because if it is prolonged, disbelief enters into the descendants.

His saying: ﴿and God warns you of Himself﴾ is a warning against opposition and against laxity in claiming taqiyya, and against its continuation or prolongation.

The accusative of "nafsahu" (Himself) is by removal of the preposition, and its original form was "and God warns you of His self." This removal is the origin of the accusative of the two nouns in the chapter of warning, as in their saying: "iyyaka al-asad" (beware of the lion), whose original form was "uhadhdhiruka min al-asad" (I warn you against the lion). Here the warning has been made to be from God's very self, that is, His essence, so that it is more general in all circumstances, because if it had said "God warns you of His anger," it would have been understood that God has a pleasure which does not harm one who deliberately opposes His commands. When the Arabs want to generalize the states of the essence, they attach the judgment to the essence, as in their saying: "Had it not been for so-and-so, so-and-so would have perished," and in God's saying: ﴿And had it not been for believing men﴾ [al-Fath: 25], up to His saying: ﴿We would have punished those of them who disbelieved with a painful punishment﴾ [al-Fath: 25]. Of this kind is the conditioning of "law la" (had it not been for) on absolute existence, which permitted the omission of the predicate after "law la."

The discussion of the validity of applying "nafs" (self) as a noun in construct with God the Exalted will come in the chapter of al-Ma'idah, at His saying: ﴿You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Yours﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116].

This is an excuse, an admonition, and a threat of punishment for disobeying what God has forbidden them.

[p. 222]

The "maṣir" (final return) means the return, and it is intended here as the resurrection after death. Those who affirm the resurrection know that it can only be to God. Thus the placement of "to God" in His saying "and to God" is merely for emphasis. This is an implicit threat, which reinforces the explicit threat that came before it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 29:

﴿Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it. And He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth. And Allah is over all things competent.﴾

A transition from the general warning to one of the kinds of its detailing, which is making the one being warned aware of Allah's knowledge of what they conceal of the matter.

Here he mentions "breasts" (ṣudūr), while what is meant is the inner selves and consciences, in keeping with the familiar usage of the language in attributing psychological thoughts to the breast and the heart, because psychological emotions, the fluctuations of reflection, and the intentions of souls are all felt as movements in the breasts.

He added "or reveal it," thereby conveying the generality of knowledge, as a teaching for them about the vastness of Allah the Exalted's knowledge, because the context of affirming the attributes of Allah the Exalted calls for clarification.

The clause ﴿And He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth﴾ is conjoined to the conditional clause, so it is governed by the verb of "Say" (qul), and it is not conjoined to the response of the condition. This is because Allah's knowledge of what is in the heavens and what is on the earth is established absolutely, not conditioned upon their concealing or revealing what is in their souls, and the generality contained in the clause makes it in the force of a concluding statement (tadhyīl).

His saying: ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾ is an announcement that, along with knowledge, He possesses power over all things. This is of the nature of a threat, since the one who threatens cannot be prevented from carrying out his warning except by one of two things: ignorance of the criminal's crime, or inability to act against him. So when He informed them of the generality of His knowledge and the generality of His power, they knew that Allah would not let them escape His punishment.

The manifest mention of the name Allah instead of a pronoun, so that He did not say "and He is over all things competent," is so that the clause stands independently and functions like a proverb, and the clause has the meaning of a concluding statement (tadhyīl). The address is to the believers, following His saying "Let not the believers take the disbelievers," the verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 30:

Page 223
﴿On the Day every soul will find whatever good it has done present, and whatever evil it has done, it will wish that between itself and that (evil) there were a long distance. And Allah warns you of Himself, and Allah is Kind to His servants.﴾
This is a resumptive sentence (jumla mustaानifa). The original arrangement of the statement in it is: "Every soul will wish that between itself and whatever evil it has done there were a long distance, on the Day it finds whatever good it has done present." So its adverbial phrase (zarf) has been placed before its governing verb, in a well-known Arabic usage concerning time-nouns when the time is the intended focus of the utterance, in fulfilment of the requirement of concision (ijaz) with an elegant composition. This is because when a time-noun is the most important element in the purpose for which the speech is directed, and at the same time it is a container (zarf) for something of its related circumstances, it is brought in the accusative as an adverb of time, and the meaning of some of what occurs in it is formulated in the form of a verb governing that adverb. Or the original arrangement is: "On the Day of Presentation, there will be presented to every soul what it did of good and what it did of evil, so on that Day it will wish that between itself and what it did of evil there were a long distance, that is, a delayed time, and that it had not been presented on that Day." In this case the pronoun in His words "and between it" (wa baynahu) refers to "what it did of evil", and the structure has been transposed, making "tawaddu" the governing verb of "yawma" so that its being an adverb suffices instead of its being the subject. Or the original arrangement may be: "On the Day every soul finds whatever good and whatever evil it has done present, it wishes that between itself and that Day there were a long distance," so that the pronoun in "baynahu" refers back to "yawma", i.e., it wishes that it (the Day) had been delayed and had not come, like His words: ﴿My Lord, if only You would delay me to a near term so that I might give charity﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10]. This transposition is of the kind of the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"And a day upon the back of the dune, she made herself unattainable to me, and swore an oath that would not be dissolved."

For his intended meaning is what occurred on the day, but he made the concern lie with the day itself, since it is its container. Such (usage) occurs in the Qur'an more than once, and this is common in sentences separated from one another without a conjunction, because the adverb and the prepositional phrase resemble connectives; so a separated sentence that is introduced by one of them gains a kind of connection with what precedes it, as in this verse, and His exalted words: ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35], and the like. This is the best of the possibilities in the composition of this verse, and al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) pointed to it.

Page 224
It has been said that it is in the accusative governed by "udhkur" (remember). It has also been said that it is related to the word "al-masir" (the return), but there is distance in this because of the long separation. It has been said that it is related to His words "wa yuhadhdhirukum" (and He warns you), and this is far-fetched, because the warning has been present since the revelation of the verse, and it is not good to make the governing element of the adverb the verse preceding this one, because the speech does not fit together in the fullest sense.

According to the first possibility, His words "tawaddu" (she wishes) are the beginning of the resumption; according to the other possibilities, it is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) relating to His words: ﴿and what it did of evil﴾.

As for His words: ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾, it may be a repetition of the first warning for added emphasis, like the words of Labid:

"They contended over a flowing shade whose shadow flies, like the smoke of a kindled fire whose flames are lit."

"Mashmula ghulithat bi-nabit 'arnaj, ka-dukhan nar sati'in asnamuha"
["A wine-like (smoke) covered with a growth of 'arnaj, like the smoke of a blazing fire whose humps rise."]

It may also be that the first is a warning against allying with the disbelievers, and the second a warning against finding on the Day of Resurrection the evil they did presented before them.

The address is to the believers, and for this reason He called the admonition a warning, because the one being warned is not already caught up in the danger; for warning is a distancing from falling into (harm), not a rescue after falling into it. He concluded it here with His words "and Allah is Kind to His servants" to remind that this warning is for the benefit of those being warned.

The definite article in "al-'ibad" (the servants) is for generalization (istighraq), because Allah's compassion encompasses all people, both their Muslims and their disbelievers: ﴿And if Allah were to take people to account for what they earned, He would not leave upon it (the earth) a single creature﴾ [Fatir: 45]; ﴿Allah is Gentle with His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 19]. His threat to them is only for bringing about their good, and its execution after the purpose has passed is only for the truthfulness of His words and the coherence of His wisdom, glorified is He. You may also take "al" as a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning "His servants," in which case it is good news for the believers.

[Page 225]

This is a transition from warning to encouragement, as is the Qur'an's habit. The connection is that the preceding warning ended with His words: ﴿And Allah is Compassionate toward His servants﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:207], and compassion (ra'fah) entails that the one shown compassion loves the one who shows it. So making Allah's love the condition (fi'l li-l-shart) in the context of conditioning the command to follow the Messenger on it is based either on the premise that compassion entails love, or on the premise that Allah's love is something certain on the part of the addressees. Thus the conditioning on it is a conditioning on a realized condition (shart muhaqqaq). Then another condition is ordered upon the consequent, namely His words ﴿Allah will love you﴾, because it too is something the addressees certainly desire, since the address is to the believers, and the believer's ultimate aim is to obtain Allah's pleasure with him and His love for him.

Love (mahabbah) is an inner emotional response (infi'al nafsani) that arises upon perceiving the goodness of something, whether from its essential attributes, from a benefit it confers, or from a belief that it loves what is good and brings good to its recipient. When this emotional response occurs, it is followed by an inclination and attraction toward the thing whose excellences are perceived. The one affected becomes a lover (muhibb), and the one whose excellences are perceived becomes a beloved (mahbub). The attributes that caused this emotion are regarded as beauty (jamal) in the eyes of the lover. When this emotion grows strong, it becomes a psychological agitation, which is called ishq (passionate love) for essences and infatuation (iftinan) with other things.

The perception of goodness that necessitates love is drawn from the senses in perceiving the essential beauties known as jamal, and is also drawn from reflection on perfections that are inferred by reason, which are called fadilah (virtue). For this reason, believers love Allah, Exalted is He, and love the Prophet (ﷺ), out of exalting perfections and believing that both call them to good. People love the earlier people of virtue such as the prophets, the wise, and the virtuous, and they love the bearers of good among the present who they have not met nor seen.

Beauty and virtue return to the soul's perception of what suits it: of shapes, melodies, sensible things, and qualities. This suitability is sensory due to the natural affinity of the temperament, like the suitability of coolness in summer and warmth in winter, of softness for smooth skin and roughness for one with an itch, or it is toward the attainment of benefits, like the suitability of kindness and relief. It is intellectual (fikriyyah) for the sake of beneficial ends, like the suitability of medicine for the sick, of fatigue for one who picks fruit, and of sleeplessness for one who reflects on knowledge. It also occurs for the sake of familiarity, and it occurs for the sake of pure belief, as when people accept that knowledge is a virtue. Within these two categories falls the love of peoples for their customs without reflecting on their soundness. It may also have an unknown cause, like the suitability of regular shapes to souls and the suitability of delicate colors.

[Page 226]

In all of this, you can clarify further by means of their opposites, such as corrupt shapes, hideous sounds, and repulsive colors, always or in some circumstances, like the red color that the feverish person sees.

The philosophers were unable to clarify the cause of the suitability of some of what is described as beauty to souls: such as the essence being beautiful or ugly in form, and the square or the circle being pleasing to the soul while a distorted shape is ugly. Along with acknowledging that people differ in some of what is described as beauty and ugliness, as Abu al-Tayyib said:

*People are of many kinds, lovers of many kinds.*

And that some people prefer in garments what another does not accept, and find in colors what another finds ugly. Despite all this, what is observed is that in most circumstances people with sound tastes do not differ.

As for the earlier thinkers, Socrates said: the cause of beauty is love of benefit. Plato said: (Beauty is a divine, eternal matter, existing in the world of intellect, not subject to change, which souls enjoyed before their descent into bodies. When they descended into bodies, whenever they saw something resembling what they had known in the intellectual worlds, which is the world of forms (*'alam al-mithal*), they inclined toward it, because it was familiar to them from before their descent.) The naturalists (*al-tabi'iyyun*) held that beauty is something that arises in us from sensory perception through the senses. I have seen in the book *Jami' Asrar al-Tibb* by the physician 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zuhr al-Qurtubi: (Sensual passion is nothing but the soul's inclination toward the thing it finds beautiful and pleasurable. That is because the psychic spirit (*al-ruh al-nafsani*), whose seat is the brain, is close to the visual light that surrounds the eye and is connected to the back of the brain, which is memory. When the eye looks at the beautiful thing, the visual light contracts and quivers. By that contraction and quivering it connects with the psychic spirit, which receives it well, and then deposits it in memory, and this causes love. It also participates with the animal spirit (*al-ruh al-hayawani*), whose seat is the heart, through its connection with its actions in the whole body, and then there is thought, anxiety, and sleeplessness.)

[Page 227]

The truth is that the origin of the perception of beauty may be from what is suitable, and from nervous impression, and this also returns to what is suitable, such as the feverish person's impression by red color. It may also come from familiarity and habit through frequent practice, and this too returns to what is suitable, as Ibn al-Rumi said:

*The aims which youth fulfilled there made the homelands beloved to men.*
*When they remember their homelands, the memories of youth there remind them, so they yearn for that.*

It may also arise from anticipating good and benefit, and this returns to what is suitable. It may arise from belief in perfection and virtue, and this returns to what is familiar, which returns to practice, because of anticipating good from the possessor of perfection and virtue.

Beyond all of this there is something of beauty and love that cannot be explained: the approval of good essences and the disapproval of unpleasant things. We see a child who has no familiarity with anything recoil from things that we see as unpleasant.

The earlier thinkers differed as to whether love and beauty are restricted to sensible things. Those who restricted them to sensible things did not establish any love except material love. Those who did not restrict them to sensible things established symbolic love (*al-mahabbah al-ramziyyah*), meaning love related to non-sensible existents, like the servant's love for Allah, Exalted is He. This is the truth, and among the earlier thinkers Plato held it, and among the Muslims al-Ghazali and Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi). This love has been attributed to Plato, and it is called Platonic love (*mahabbah aflatuniyyah*), because he investigated it and explained it. We hear the attributes of famous men, such as the messengers, people of goodness, those who benefited people, and those who possessed praiseworthy qualities like knowledge, generosity, and justice, and we find within ourselves an inclination to mention them. Then that inclination grows until it becomes love from us toward them, even though we have not met them. Do you not see that engaging with the books of hadith and the biography (*sirah*) strengthens the love of the one who engages in them for the Messenger (ﷺ)? Likewise the attributes of the Creator, Exalted is He: since they are all perfections and beneficence toward us and reform of our corruption, believing in them produced in us veneration (*ijlal*) for the one they describe, and then that veneration grows until it becomes love. In a hadith: "Whoever has three qualities will find the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger become dearer to him than anything else; that he loves a person only for the sake of Allah; and that he hates to return to disbelief as he hates to be thrown into the Fire." So these three were of the category of love, and for this reason the finding of the sweetness of faith (*wijdan halawat al-iman*) was attached to them, meaning finding it beautiful in the eyes of the one who believes in it.

[Page 228]

Those of the first opinion see the attachment of love to the essence of Allah in this verse and similar verses as metaphorical (*majaz*), by likening the desire for His pleasure to love. Those of the second opinion see it as literal (*haqiqah*), and this is the correct view.

Among the effects of love is seeking closeness to the beloved, connecting with him, and avoiding separation from him. Among its effects is loving what pleases him and gladdens him, and avoiding what angers him. Thus the attachment of the obligation to follow the Messenger to the love of Allah, Exalted is He, is because the Messenger called to what Allah commands and to devoting the direction of worship to Him alone, and that is the perfection of love.

As for the use of the word love in His words ﴿Allah will love you﴾, it is undoubtedly a metaphor, by which is meant the necessary consequence of love, which is approval, the bestowal of benefit, and similar manifestations of Allah that He, Glorified is He, knows. These two are what is expressed by His words ﴿Allah will love you and forgive you your sins﴾, for that is an indication of love. In the Qur'an: ﴿The Jews and the Christians said: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." Say: "Why then does He punish you for your sins?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:18].

The attachment of Allah's love for them to ﴿follow me﴾, which is conditioned on His words ﴿if you love Allah﴾, produces from it a conditional syllogism of the conjunctive type (*qiyas shartiy iqtirani*). It indicates that the alleged love, if it is not accompanied by following the Messenger, is false love, because the lover obeys the one he loves, and because committing what the beloved dislikes is an angering of him and an association with his enemy. Abu al-Tayyib said:

*Shall I love him while in loving him there is blame? Indeed the blame in him comes from his enemies.*

Thus it is known that love of the enemy does not combine with love. Al-'Itabi said:

*You wish for my enemy, then you claim that I am your friend. Foolishness is not far from you.*

The phrase ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is in the force of a concluding phrase (*tadhyil*), like the earlier phrase ﴿And Allah is powerful over everything﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:29]. No object was mentioned for the two attributes, so that people would strive to obtain the means of forgiveness and mercy.

**Surah 3, verse 32:**

﴿Say: "Obey Allah and the Messenger." But if they turn away, then indeed Allah does not love the disbelievers.﴾ This is a return to the admonition (*al-mawʿiẓa*, exhortation) in a purely summary manner, as a conclusion (*fadhlaka*, a summing-up) to the discourse, and out of eagerness for a response. He began the admonition first with an introduction, which is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will not avail them against Allah at all﴾ [Al 'Imran: 10]. Then he proceeded with the admonition by His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 12], to the end of the verse, and this is intimidation (*tarhīb*). Then he mentioned its counterpart in encouragement (*targhīb*) by His saying: ﴿Shall I inform you of something better than that?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 15], to the end of the verse. Then he confirmed what the Muslims hold by His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18], to the end of the verse, and on this there is much detail. Then he came by way of argumentation (*al-mujādala*) with His saying: ﴿And if they argue with you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20], to the end of the verse. Then (he came) with intimidation without explicit proof, but by allusion (*al-īmāʾ*) to the proof, and this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21]. Then by way of threat and indirect warning, by His saying: ﴿Say: "O Allah, Owner of sovereignty"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26], and the verses that follow. Then he commanded disassociation (*al-qaṭīʿa*) in His saying: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28]. Then he moved to the method of encouragement in His saying: ﴿Say: "If you should love Allah"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31], up to His saying: ﴿the disbelievers﴾. And he concluded by mentioning the non-love of the disbelievers, as a response (*radd*) of the second half (*ʿajuz*) to the first half (*ṣadr*) previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth will not avail them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 10], to the end of the verse, so that the negation of love would apply to all disbelievers, and be a negation concerning these specific disbelievers.

[p. 229]

[Page 230]

This is a transition from the introductory matters concerning the occasion of revelation of the surah to the intermediate introduction and the main purpose, in the manner of what is called *takhallus* (a smooth transition from one theme to another). It is a transition to the argument with the delegation of Najran, which we mentioned at the beginning of the surah. Here it begins with the mention of Adam and Noah, who are the fathers of mankind, or one of them, and the mention of Abraham, who is the father of those addressed and favoured in the discourse.

As for Adam, he is the father of mankind by the agreement of all nations, except for a few deviants from the atheistic currents that emerged in Europe and invented the theory of the descent of the species of animals from one another. That theory is a failed one.

"Adam" is the name of the father of mankind according to all the followers of the religions. It is his proper name, which he himself assigned by inspiration from Allah, the Exalted, just as the origin of language was established. There is no doubt that among the first things he and his spouse needed was for one of them to express to the other. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that Allah named him by this name before his departure from the Garden of Eden. It is not permissible that his name be derived from *al-udmah* (the brownish complexion), which is a specific colour, because naming that colour *udmah* is specific to the speech of the Arabs. Rather, the Arabs may have assigned the name of that colour, taking it from the description of the colour of Adam, the father of mankind.

[Page 230]

The Book of Genesis in the Book of the Covenant among the Jews contains what implies that Adam appeared on earth at a time corresponding to the year 3942, that is, three thousand, nine hundred and forty-two years before the birth of Jesus, and that he lived nine hundred and thirty years. Thus his death would be in the year 3012, that is, three thousand and twelve years before the birth of this Jesus. This is what the historians who follow the fixing of years have accepted. However, it is assumed among the verifiers who consider the evidences of human civilisation that this dating is not to be relied upon, and that Adam's existence is much more ancient, in periods far more distant than what the Book of Genesis specifies.

As for Noah, the Torah says that he is the son of Lamech, whom the Arabs call Lamak, son of Methuselah, son of Enoch (who is Idris according to the Arabs), son of Jared (with a *ta'* at its beginning), son of Mahalalel (with a *mim* that is fatha, then a *ha'* that is sakin, then a *lam* that is fatha), son of Kenan, son of Enosh, son of Seth, son of Adam. Based on this, and on the years of their lifespans, he was born in the year 2886 before the birth of Jesus, and died in the year 1936 before the birth of Jesus. What was said about the dating of Adam's existence applies to it as well.

At the time of Noah, the Flood befell the whole earth, and Allah saved him, his sons and their wives in the Ark. Thus he became a second father of mankind. Some people claim that the Flood did not cover the whole earth. The historians of China adopted this view and asserted that the Flood did not reach their region. According to them, Noah is not a second father of mankind. According to the view of the majority, all of mankind goes back to Noah's three sons: Shem, Ham and Japheth. He is the first messenger whom Allah sent to people, according to the authentic hadith. Noah lived nine hundred and fifty years according to the Torah, and this is the apparent meaning of His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years﴾. In the Torah, the Flood occurred when Noah was six hundred years old, and that after the Flood Noah became a farmer, planted the vine and made wine.

Al-Alusi (Ibn 'Ali al-Alusi) mentioned his description without a chain of transmission, saying: Noah had a fine face, a long head, large eyes, thick upper arms, a full thigh, a large navel, a tall stature, a massive build, and a long beard. It is said that his burial place is in Iraq, in the regions of Kufa; it is said at the foot of Mount Lebanon; and it is said in the city of Karak. The mention of the Flood will come in Surat al-A'raf and in Surat al-'Ankabut, and the mention of his law (shari'ah) will come in Surat al-Shura and in Surat Nuh.

[Page 231]

*Al-al* (the household) means the lineage or kin. The family of Abraham are his sons, his grandson and his descendants, and the intention is to favour a group among them. The family of Abraham included the prophets from his lineage, such as Moses and those before him and after him, and such as Muhammad (ﷺ), and Isma'il, Hanzalah ibn Safwan, and Khalid ibn Sinan.

As for the family of 'Imran, they are Mary and Jesus. Mary is the daughter of 'Imran son of Matan, so the exegetes named him, and he was among the rabbis of the Jews and their righteous ones. His original name in Hebrew is 'Imram, with a *mim* at its end. He is the father of Mary. The exegetes said that he was from the offspring of Solomon son of David, but this is an error; the truth is that he is from the offspring of Aaron, the brother of Moses, as will come shortly. In the books of the Christians, his name is said to be Joachim, so perhaps he had two names, and there are many like this. The 'Imran here is not the father of Moses and Aaron, since the intention here is to introduce the mention of Mary and her son Jesus, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said﴾.

The discussion concerning the possible meanings of *al* was already presented at His saying: ﴿And when We rescued you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Baqarah: 49] in Surat al-Baqarah. However, *al* here is definitely to be understood as the kin and relatives of the man.

The meaning of the choosing of these people over the worlds is either the choosing of the group as a whole over others, or the choosing of each excellent person among them over the people of his time.

His saying: ﴿offspring, some of them from others﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the family of Abraham and the family of 'Imran. The word *dhurriyyah* (offspring) was already explained at His saying: ﴿He said: and of my offspring?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124] in Surat al-Baqarah. Here the word "some" (*ba'd*) has been stated in a general form, because the purpose is to show the intensity of connection among this offspring. The *min* here expresses connection, not partition; that is, between this offspring there is the connection of kinship, so each part of them is connected to the other part, as was mentioned in His saying: ﴿then he is not of Allah in anything﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28].

The purpose of mentioning these people is to remind the Jews and Christians of the close affiliation of their prophets to the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). It was not fitting for them to make the requirement of kinship a cause of enmity and division. From here the position of His saying becomes clear: ﴿and Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾, meaning: He hears the statements of some of you about others of this offspring, such as the saying of the Jews about Jesus and his mother, and their denial, and the denial of the Jews and Christians of Muhammad (ﷺ).
