In the books of the Christians, his name is said to be Joachim, so perhaps he had two names, and there are many like this. The 'Imran here is not the father of Moses and Aaron, since the intention here is to introduce the mention of Mary and her son Jesus, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said﴾.

The discussion concerning the possible meanings of *al* was already presented at His saying: ﴿And when We rescued you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Baqarah: 49] in Surat al-Baqarah. However, *al* here is definitely to be understood as the kin and relatives of the man.

The meaning of the choosing of these people over the worlds is either the choosing of the group as a whole over others, or the choosing of each excellent person among them over the people of his time.

His saying: ﴿offspring, some of them from others﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the family of Abraham and the family of 'Imran. The word *dhurriyyah* (offspring) was already explained at His saying: ﴿He said: and of my offspring?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124] in Surat al-Baqarah. Here the word "some" (*ba'd*) has been stated in a general form, because the purpose is to show the intensity of connection among this offspring. The *min* here expresses connection, not partition; that is, between this offspring there is the connection of kinship, so each part of them is connected to the other part, as was mentioned in His saying: ﴿then he is not of Allah in anything﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28].

The purpose of mentioning these people is to remind the Jews and Christians of the close affiliation of their prophets to the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). It was not fitting for them to make the requirement of kinship a cause of enmity and division. From here the position of His saying becomes clear: ﴿and Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾, meaning: He hears the statements of some of you about others of this offspring, such as the saying of the Jews about Jesus and his mother, and their denial, and the denial of the Jews and Christians of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿When the wife of ʿImrān said: "My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as a dedicated offering, so accept it from me. Indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing."﴾ ﴿And when she had given birth to it, she said: "My Lord, I have given birth to a female," and God knew best what she had given birth to, "and the male is not like the female. I have named her Maryam, and I seek refuge for her in You and for her offspring from Satan, the accursed."﴾

The discussion of the position of *idh* (when) in such contexts has already been given under the tafsir of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I will place a khalifah (successor) on earth"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. Its position here is more clearly one in which it is not dependent on any governing verb (ʿāmil). It serves merely to draw attention to the report. For this reason Abu ʿUbayda said: "*idh* here is superfluous (zāʾidah)." It is also permissible for it to be dependent on an elided *udhkur* ("remember"). It is not permissible for it to depend on *iṣṭafā* ("chose"), because that refers specifically to the excellence of the family of ʿImrān and has no connection to the excellence of Adam, Noah and the family of Abraham.

The wife of ʿImrān was Ḥannah, daughter of Fāqūdhā. It is said that her husband died and left her pregnant, so she vowed the child in her womb as *muḥarraran* (dedicated), that is, set apart for service to the Bayt al-Maqdis (the Temple in Jerusalem). They used to make such vows when the newborn would be a male. The use of the word *muḥarrar* in this sense is an expression of honour, because when the child was devoted to the service of the Bayt al-Maqdis, it was as though it had been freed from the captivity of this world and its bonds, into the freedom of worshipping God, exalted is He. It is said that she thought it was a male, so the vow she made was unrestricted as to sex, and they would only say: "If it comes out a male, then it is dedicated." The pronoun in His saying ﴿when she had given birth to it﴾ is feminine, and it refers back to ﴿what is in my womb﴾, taking into account that what was revealed to be a female was what it referred to.

Her saying ﴿I have given birth to a female﴾ is a statement (khabar) used in the sense of an exhortation (inshāʾ al-tahdhīr), since it is evident that the one addressed is knowing of everything.

The emphasis of the statement with *inna* is in accordance with the basic principle of the declarative form (*aṣl al-khabariyyah*), to affirm that the child was a female. Since its occurrence contradicted what she had expected, she was in a state where she doubted that it was a female and addressed herself in the manner of emphasis. Therefore she emphasised it. Then, when she used this statement in the sense of an imperative (*inshāʾ*), she used it in its entirety by way of a compound, sent (*al-majāz al-murakkab al-mursal*) figure. It is known that a compound figure is a figure in its whole, not in its parts and individual words. This construction, with the particularities it contains, depicts the meanings contained in her speech in her own language: namely, dismay and dislike at giving birth to a female, her attempt to deceive herself into accepting this decree, then her confirming it to herself and calming herself with it, and then her moving on to lament over it. For this reason she placed in the report of her speech particularities of Arabic that express many meanings she intended in her intimate address in her own language.

The pronoun in ﴿I have given birth to a female﴾ is feminine in accordance with what is indicated by the necessary state (*al-ḥāl al-lāzimah*) in her words *unthā* ("a female"), since without that state the speech would not convey a meaning. Therefore the pronoun was made feminine in accordance with that state.

His saying ﴿and God knew best what she had given birth to﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*jumlah iʿtirāḍiyyah*). The majority of readers read *waḍaʿat* with a sukūn on the *tāʾ*, so the pronoun refers to the wife of ʿImrān, and then it is part of the speech of God, exalted is He, not of her quoted speech. The meaning intended is that God knows better than she does the preciousness of what she gave birth to, and that she is better than the male in general which she had asked for. So the statement informs the people of the Qur'an that she was mistaken, and teaches that whoever entrusts his affair to God should not presume to question His management.

Ibn ʿĀmir, Abu Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim, and Yaʿqūb read *waḍaʿtu* with a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ*, taking it as the pronoun of the speaker, the wife of ʿImrān. Then the sentence belongs to her quoted speech. On this reading, the divine name (*ism al-jalālah*) is a shift (*iltifāt*) from address (*khiṭāb*) to third person (*ghaybah*), and it serves as a verbal indicator that the statement is used in the sense of lament (*taḥassur*).

The sentence ﴿and the male is not like the female﴾ is a statement used in the sense of lament, because what she intended, that the child be a male so that she could dedicate it to the service of the Bayt al-Maqdis, had been lost.

The definiteness of *al-dhakar* ("the male") is the definiteness of the genus (*taʿrīf al-jins*), because of what is firmly fixed in people's souls regarding the desire for male offspring. That is, the genus of the male is not equal to the genus of the female.

It is also said that the definiteness in ﴿and the male is not like the female﴾ is the definiteness of a known referent (*taʿrīf al-ʿahd*) for what was known to her. The sentence ﴿and the male is not﴾ completes the parenthetical clause that begins with His saying ﴿and God knew best what she had given birth to﴾. The meaning is: the male which she desired is not equal to the female which she was given, had she known the high rank of this female. Those who take this view consider the negation of resemblance to be on its ordinary basis, namely the negation of the resemblance of the inferior to the superior. This view was favoured by the author of al-Kashshāf, and the author of al-Miftāḥ followed him. The first view is more evident.

The negation of resemblance between the male and the female is used in such contexts to convey the meaning of preference (*tafḍīl*). This is found in the Arabs' saying: "Such-and-such is not equal to such-and-such," "such-and-such is not like such-and-such," and "he is not like such-and-such," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ [al-Zumar: 9], and His saying: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other of the women﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 32], and the words of al-Samawʾal:

*fa-laysa sawāʾan ʿālimun wa-jahūlu*
So a knowing man and an ignorant one are not equal.

And their saying: "Pasture, and it is not like saʿdān (a thistle); water, and it is not like ṣadā." For this reason they do not deliberately make the thing being compared, in such a construction, weaker than the thing it is compared to, since then no effect of the comparison would remain. Therefore it was said here: ﴿and the male is not like the female﴾, and if it had been said: "and the female is not like the male," the intended meaning would still have been understood. But the male was placed first here because it is what is hoped for and desired, so it is the first to come to the speaker's tongue. The negation may also come in the sense that the negated thing compared is weaker than the thing it is compared to, as al-Ḥarīrī said in the fourth maqāmah: "I rose before the saddling of the mounts, not with the rising of the crow," and he said in the eleventh: "You laughed at the time of the burial, not with your laughter at the hour of the dance," and in the fourteenth: "I stood for God, not like ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd." He brought all of these in the same pattern as in this verse.

His saying ﴿And indeed I have named her Maryam﴾: the apparent meaning is that she intended to name her after the most excellent prophetess among the Children of Israel, namely Maryam, the sister of Moses and Aaron. What permitted her to do so was that her father was namesake of the father of Maryam, the sister of Moses.

The emphasis was repeated in ﴿And indeed I have named her﴾ and ﴿And indeed I seek refuge for her in You﴾ for emphasis, because the state of her dislike indicates that she would turn away from her, so she would not occupy herself with her. It is as though she emphasised this statement to show her contentment with what God had decreed. For this reason she moved on to supplicating for her, which indicates contentment and love. She also emphasised the sentence ﴿I seek refuge﴾ even though it is used in the sense of supplication (*inshāʾ al-duʿāʾ*), because the statement is used in the sense of an imperative in its entirety, in the state it was in when it was a declarative, as we have already mentioned regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I have given birth to a female﴾, and like the saying of Abu Bakr: "Indeed I have appointed ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb as your successor."

[Page 235]

﴿So her Lord accepted her with a good acceptance and caused her to grow in a good growth.﴾

This is a consequence of the supplication, indicating the swiftness of the response. The pronouns in the accusative refer to Maryam. The meaning of "accepted her" is that He accepted her dedication to the service of Bayt al-Maqdis (the Temple in Jerusalem). That is, God established Maryam in the station of one devoted wholly to God, and such a thing had not been legislated before.

As for His words ﴿with a good acceptance﴾, the particle "bi" here is for emphasis (ta'kid). The underlying structure of the sentence is: "So He accepted her with a good acceptance (qabulan hasanan)." The "bi" was added to the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq, the cognate object) so that it would function like an instrument of accepting, making it seem like a second thing. This shows special care for her in this acceptance. This acceptance was made known by a revelation from God to Zakariyya that Zakariyya should be her guardian, and that he, the greatest of their rabbis, should undertake her upbringing. He was also revealed to establish her afterward in service to the mosque. Such a thing had not been done for women before her. All of this is an irhas (a prophetic foreshadowing sign) that a messenger would come from her, abrogating (nasikh) many rulings of the Torah, because women's service to the Holy Mosque was not legislated.

The meaning of ﴿and caused her to grow in a good growth﴾ is that He brought her into being in a righteous way. This refers to her character and purity of inner self. Her coming into being and her youth were likened to the growth of tender plants through the figure of metaphor (isti'arah). "Nabatan" is an absolute object of "anbata" (caused to grow), and it is the verbal noun of "nabata" (grew). It was used in the form of "anbata" for lightness of expression.

* * *

﴿And Zakariyya became her guardian.﴾

This is counted among Maryam's virtues, because it is one of the things that increases her excellence, since the one who raises a child imparts his character and righteousness to the one he raises.

Zakariyya was a Israelite priest named Zakariyya, from the descendants of Abiya ibn Bakir ibn Binyamin, from the priests of the Jews. Prophethood came to him in old age. He was the second prophet of the Children of Israel named Zakariyya. He was married to a woman from the descendants of Harun named (Elizabeth) (al-Isabat), and his wife was a relative of Maryam, as in the Gospel of Luke. It was said that she was Maryam's sister, but the correct view is that she was her maternal aunt, or from the kin of her mother. When Maryam was born, her father had died, so a group of the rabbis of the Children of Israel disputed over her guardianship, eager for the guardianship of the daughter of their great rabbi,

[Page 236]

and they cast lots over it, as will come. The lot fell to Zakariyya. The apparent view is that the guardianship of her was given to the rabbis because she was dedicated to the service of the mosque, so she had to be raised in a manner suitable for that.

The majority of readers recited: "wa kafala-ha Zakariyya" (with a light fa'), meaning he undertook her guardianship. Hamzah, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited: "wa kaffala-ha" (with a doubled fa'), meaning that God made Zakariyya her guardian. The majority recited "Zakariyya" with a hamza at the end, extended (mamdud) and with the hamza in the nominative. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, and Khalaf recited it without the hamza (maqsur). Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited it with a hamza at the end and with the hamza in the accusative.

* * *

﴿Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab (prayer niche), he found provision with her. He said, "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said, "It is from God. Indeed, God provides for whom He wills without reckoning."﴾

His words ﴿Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab he found provision with her﴾ indicate an omitted statement, meaning: Maryam was constantly devoted to the service of Bayt al-Maqdis, and she would worship in a place that she took as a mihrab for herself. Zakariyya would look after her worship, and as a mark of honor for her he saw that with her were fruits out of their season.

The word "kullama" (whenever) is composed of "kull" (every), which is a noun indicating the generality of what it is added to, and "ma" (the temporal ma), with its clause implied as a verbal noun. The meaning is: at every time of Zakariyya's entering upon her, he found provision with her.

"Kull" is in the accusative by substitution for the adverbial object (al-maf'ul fihi), and this was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿Whenever they were provided with fruit from it, they said, "This is what we were provided with before"﴾ (al-Baqarah: 25) in Surah al-Baqarah.

So the clause ﴿he found provision with her﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) of Zakariyya in His words ﴿And Zakariyya became her guardian﴾.

[Page 237]

You may also make the clause ﴿he found provision with her﴾ a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause ﴿And Zakariyya became her guardian﴾.

The mihrab is a structure that a person builds to be alone in for his worship and prayer. It is most often made in a high place reached by a ladder or stairs, and it is other than the mosque. It has been applied to other things in several senses, by way of likeness or extension, such as the saying of 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a:

A doll beside a monk, a priest, they had fashioned it
in the altar of the mihrab.

He meant the altar of the church, because a mihrab does not have an altar in it. It has also been said that the mihrab is derived from "harb" (war), because the worshipper is, as it were, fighting Satan in it, so they made that place an instrument for fighting Satan.

Then the term mihrab came to be applied among Muslims to a place shaped like a half dome, about a man's height and a half, placed in the direction of the qiblah for the imam to stand in for prayer. This is a later (muwallad) usage. The first mihrab in Islam was the mihrab of the Messenger's mosque (ﷺ), made in the caliphate of al-Walid ibn 'Abd al-Malik, during the governorship of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz over Medina. The definite article in "al-mihrab" is the definite article of the genus, and it is known that what is meant is a mihrab that Maryam made for worship.

"Anna" (from where) is an interrogative about place, meaning: from where is this for you? For this reason, the answer to her question was her saying: "from God."

Zakariyya's question to Maryam about the provision was because it was out of its season and time of such things. It was said that it was grapes in the winter season. The word "rizq" (provision) was mentioned earlier at His words: ﴿and You provide for whom You will without reckoning﴾ (Al 'Imran: 27).

The clause ﴿Indeed, God provides for whom He wills﴾ is part of Maryam's reported speech.

The word "hisab" (reckoning) in His words ﴿without reckoning﴾ (Al 'Imran: 27) carries the sense of limitation (hasr), because reckoning requires confining the counted thing so that it neither exceeds nor falls short. So the meaning is: God provides for whomever He wills with a provision whose measure is not known, because it is left to God's bounty.

Here, at that place, before he departed. The sight of extraordinary events, together with Maryam's words, "Indeed Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning" (Ali 'Imran 3:37), had prompted him to supplicate. Wisdom is the lost property of the believer, and people of pure souls take lesson from what they see and hear. Therefore he resorted to supplication for a child, seeking one out of its time, although he had been grieved by the lack of offspring, as Allah related of him in Surat Maryam. Moreover, he was at that time in a place where a divine outpouring was witnessed. People of goodness have always sought out places where good has occurred, and likewise favourable times, for these are only like good persons in that they are the locations of the manifestations of Allah's good pleasure.

He asked for a "good offspring" because it is from them that the good of this world and the Hereafter is hoped for, through the arising of beneficial good effects. Witnessing extraordinary events empowered Zakariyya to supplicate for what is among the extraordinary or among the improbable, because he regarded himself as not far from Allah's care, especially in a time or place of outpouring. Thus his supplication for this is not considered a transgression of the bounds of courtesy toward Allah, in line with what al-Qarafi established in al-Furuq (the Differences) between what is permissible in supplication and what is not. "Samia'" (All-Hearing) here means "mujib" (the One who responds).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 39–41:**

"Know that the leadership of peoples
has a long ascent to its goal.

This quality was placed among the qualities of perfection as a comfort to Zakariyya and to lighten his loneliness at the ending of his lineage after Yahya.

Its purpose is to learn the possibility of a child, because when he asked for a son, the means for that had already been prepared. So his words "how can I have a boy" are only a seeking to know the manner of that, in a way that would confirm the good news for him. It is not doubt about the truth of the promise. It is like the saying of Ibrahim: ﴿لِيَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِي﴾ ("that my heart may be at rest") [al-Baqara: 260]. He was answered that possible things are within Allah's power, even if their occurrence is rare by custom.

This wonder entails gratitude for this favour, so it is a metonymy for gratitude. There is also an allusion in it that the child should be from his barren wife, without being commanded to marry another woman. This is an honour for Zakariyya's wife.

The original would be "and I have reached old age", and its benefit is to show that old age had firmly taken hold of him, as if it sought him until it reached him, like the Almighty's words: ﴿أيْنَما تَكُونُوا يُدْرِكُكُمُ المَوْتُ﴾ ("Wherever you are, death will overtake you") [al-Nisa: 78].

Since it is a quality specific to females, it was not made feminine, like their saying ha'id (menstruating), nafis (in postpartum bleeding), and muridi' (nursing). But it takes the feminine form outside the pattern of the active participle, such as their saying "'aqra" as an invocation against a woman, and in the hadith: "'aqra halqa" (barren and sterile). Perhaps this creation occurred because Zakariyya, before his decrepitude, had an extra strength by which the seed did not settle in the womb; when he became decrepit, that strength became balanced and became like the common course. Or it was among the circumstances in his wife's womb. For this reason he expressed this creation by the sentence ﴿يَفْعَلُ ما يَشاءُ﴾ ("does what He wills"), meaning that it is a creation which Allah decreed, and He brought into being its causes. For this reason he did not say here "creates what He wills", as He said regarding the creation of Jesus.

His words ﴿قالَ رَبِّ اجْعَلْ لِيَ آيَةً﴾ ("He said: My Lord, appoint a sign for me") mean he wanted a sign of the time when what he had been given good news of would occur, and whether it was near or far. So "āya" is the sign indicating the beginning of his wife's pregnancy. It is reported from al-Suddi and al-Rabi': "a sign that the address that came to him was from Allah, the Exalted", and this is what is in the Gospel of Luke. But in my view there is an issue here, because prophets are not confused about an address that comes to them from Allah, and they know it with necessary knowledge.

[p. 243]

His words ﴿آيَتُكَ ألّا تُكَلِّمَ النّاسَ ثَلاثَةَ أيّامٍ إلّا رَمْزًا﴾ ("Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gestures") mean that Allah made the impediment of his tongue from speech a sign of the time in which his wife would conceive. This is because Allah diverted the strength that was in the nerves of speech, which are connected to the brain, to the nerves of reproduction, by a wondrous wisdom, close to what is mentioned about the loss of some sensation in one who eats al-baladhur, due to the strength of thought. Or He commanded him to refrain from speaking with the people, to help the strength turn from speech to procreation; that is, when the three days were completed, that would be the sign of the beginning of the pregnancy. Al-Rabi' said: Allah made this a punishment for him because of his hesitation about the truth of what the angel had told him. This is explicitly stated in the Gospel of Luke. So on this view the answer is of the type of "the method of the wise", because he asked for a sign and was given something other than it.

His words ﴿واذْكُرْ رَبَّكَ كَثِيرًا وسَبِّحْ بِالعَشِيِّ والإبْكارِ﴾ ("Remember your Lord much, and glorify Him in the evening and the morning") are a command to give thanks. The remembrance intended is remembrance in the heart and through prayer, if the power of speech had been taken from him; or it is oral remembrance, if he had only been forbidden from it. The exception in His words "except by gestures" is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati').

Perhaps this creation occurred because Zakariyya, before his decrepitude, had an extra strength by which the seed did not settle in the womb; when he became decrepit, that strength became balanced and became like the common course. Or it was among the circumstances in his wife's womb. For this reason he expressed this creation by the sentence ﴿يَفْعَلُ ما يَشاءُ﴾ ("does what He wills"), meaning that it is a creation which Allah decreed, and He brought into being its causes. For this reason he did not say here "creates what He wills", as He said regarding the creation of Jesus.

His words ﴿قالَ رَبِّ اجْعَلْ لِيَ آيَةً﴾ ("He said: My Lord, appoint a sign for me") mean he wanted a sign of the time when what he had been given good news of would occur, and whether it was near or far. So "āya" is the sign indicating the beginning of his wife's pregnancy. It is reported from al-Suddi and al-Rabi': "a sign that the address that came to him was from Allah, the Exalted", and this is what is in the Gospel of Luke. [p. 243]

His words ﴿آيَتُكَ ألّا تُكَلِّمَ النّاسَ ثَلاثَةَ أيّامٍ إلّا رَمْزًا﴾ ("Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gestures") mean that Allah made the impediment of his tongue from speech a sign of the time in which his wife would conceive. Or He commanded him to refrain from speaking with the people, to help the strength turn from speech to procreation; that is, when the three days were completed, that would be the sign of the beginning of the pregnancy. So on this view the answer is of the type of "the method of the wise", because he asked for a sign and was given something other than it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 39–41:**

﴿Then the angels called to him as he stood praying in the sanctuary: "Allah gives you good news of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah, and a noble leader, chaste, and a prophet among the righteous."﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a son when old age has overtaken me and my wife is barren?" He said: "Thus Allah does what He wills."﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, appoint a sign for me." He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gestures. Remember your Lord much, and glorify Him in the evening and the morning."﴾

The "fa" (ف) in His words ﴿فَنادَتْهُ المَلائِكَةُ﴾ ("Then the angels called to him") indicates immediate sequence (ta'qib), meaning that his supplication was answered at once.

[p. 239]

His words ﴿وهُوَ قائِمٌ﴾ ("while he stood") form a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya). The purpose of mentioning it is to show how quickly he was answered, since his supplication was made during his prayer.

The implication of the Almighty's words ﴿هُنالِكَ﴾ ("there") [Al 'Imran: 38], and the fact that ﴿فَنادَتْهُ﴾ follows as a consequence of it, is that the sanctuary (mihrab) was the sanctuary of Maryam.

The majority of readers recite ﴿فَنادَتْهُ﴾ with the feminine ta' marbuta, since "the angels" is a plural noun. Attributing the verb to a plural subject permits the feminine form, by treating it as a group, i.e. a company of angels called to him. It is also possible that the one who called to him was a single angel, namely Jibril (Gabriel). This has been explicitly stated in the Gospel of Luke (Injil Luqa). In that case, attributing the calling to "the angels" is of the type of attributing the act of one to his tribe, as in the saying: "The tribe of Bakr killed Kulayb."

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recite ﴿فَناداهُ المَلائِكَةُ﴾ (with the masculine verb), considering the caller to be one of the angels, namely Jibril.

The majority recite ﴿أنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ with a fath on the hamza of "anna", as being in the position of a genitive after a deleted preposition (bi), meaning: "the angels called to him that Allah gives you good news of Yahya."

Ibn 'Amir and Hamza recite ﴿إنَّ﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, as direct speech (hikaya). In both readings, emphasis with "anna" (whether fathah or kasrah) confirms the report, because since it is unusual, the one being informed is treated as one who is doubtful and seeking assurance.

The meaning of ﴿يُبَشِّرُكَ بِيَحْيى﴾ ("gives you good news of Yahya") is: gives you good news of a child who will be named Yahya. From the presence of the preposition "bi" before it, it is known that "Yahya" is a proper name and not a verb. This is mentioned in Surat Maryam: ﴿إنّا نُبَشِّرُكَ بِغُلامٍ اسْمُهُ يَحْيى﴾ ("We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya") [Maryam: 7].

Yahya is an arabicised form of "Yuhanna" in Hebrew (John), so it is undoubtedly a foreign (ajami) name. The Arabs pronounced it in the pattern of the imperfect of "hayiya". It is diptote (ghayr munsarif), either because of its foreignness ('ujma) or because of the pattern of a verb (wazn al-fi'l). Yahya was killed in his middle age, peace be upon him, by order of Herod (Hirudus), a short time before the raising of the Messiah.

To his good news of a son was added good news of his goodness, as Zakariyya had hoped. So it was said to him: ﴿مُصَدِّقًا بِكَلِمَةٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ ("confirming a word from Allah"). Here "muşaddiqan" is a circumstantial state (hal) of Yahya, meaning one of perfect guidance who does not hesitate about a word that comes from Allah. This report was stated in summary to Zakariyya so that he would know that a great event would take place in which his son would confirm a messenger who would come, namely Jesus, peace be upon them both.

[p. 240]

Jesus was described as "a word from Allah" because he was created by the mere command of divine creation, expressed by the word "Be" (kun), meaning that his coming into being was unusual. This will come in His words: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يُبَشِّرُكِ بِكَلِمَةٍ مِنهُ اسْمُهُ المَسِيحُ عِيسى ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ ("Allah gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Maryam") [Al 'Imran: 45]. On this view, "the word" is an indication of the coming of Jesus, peace be upon him.

There is no doubt that confirming a messenger, and knowing that he is truthful without hesitation, is a great guidance from Allah, since it indicates a swift reflection that recognises the truth. Yahya attained this quality among the earlier ones, and Khadija and Abu Bakr among the later ones. The Almighty said: ﴿وَالَّذِي جَاءَ بِالصِّدْقِ وَصَدَّقَ بِهِ﴾ ("And he who brought the truth and confirmed it") [al-Zumar: 33].

It has also been said that "the word" here means the Torah (al-Tawrat), and it was called "a word" because the word (kalima) is applied to speech in general, and the word here is the Torah.

"Al-sayyid" is on the pattern fay'il from sada yasudu, when a person surpasses his people in praiseworthy qualities, until they put him before themselves and acknowledge his excellence. Leadership (al-su'dud) among the Arabs in the Jahiliyya depended on being sufficient for the important affairs of the tribe, giving to it, and exhausting oneself for the comfort of the people. Al-Hudhali said:

"Know that the leadership of peoples
has a long ascent to its goal.

Do you hope to lead while you are not troubled?
How can one at ease and stingy lead?"

Among them, leadership depended on qualities whose source is pleasing the people in the noblest manner: its foundation is generosity, restraining harm, bearing great burdens, and its root is sound judgement and eloquence of tongue.

In the terminology of the Shari'a, "al-sayyid" is one who works to reform the condition of people in both their worldly and their otherworldly life. In a hadith: "I am the master (sayyid) of the children of Adam, and I say it without boasting." And in another: "Verily this son of mine is a master (sayyid)," referring to al-Hasan ibn 'Ali. Al-Hasan combined the qualities of Shari'i leadership, and it suffices as evidence that he renounced his right to the caliphate in order to unite the word of the community and to reconcile between its people.

In the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyya, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, he said: "I have not seen anyone more of a sayyid than Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan." It was said to him: "And Abu Bakr and 'Umar?" He said: "They are better than Mu'awiya, and Mu'awiya is more of a sayyid than they." Ibn 'Atiyya said: he pointed out that Abu Bakr and 'Umar, in the matter of reform and establishing rights, were on a level where they were better than Mu'awiya in that respect, but with their adherence to the path and their lack of concern for the people's pleasure, many qualities of leadership were lacking in them.

[p. 241]

Mu'awiya excelled in the qualities of leadership, which consist of striving to please the people in the noblest manner, and he did not fall into what is forbidden.

Allah described Yahya as a "sayyid" because from his youth he attained religious leadership, so he grew up respected by all his people. The Almighty said: ﴿وآتَيْناهُ الحُكْمَ صَبِيًّا وحَنانًا مِن لَدُنّا وزَكاةً﴾ ("And We gave him judgement while still a boy, and tenderness from Us, and purity") [Maryam: 12]. It has also been said that "sayyid" here means both forbearing and pious. This was said by Qatada, al-Dahhak, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima. It has been said that it means forbearing only; this was said by Ibn Jubayr. It has been said that "sayyid" here means noble; this was said by Jabir ibn Zayd. It has been said that "sayyid" here means learned; this was said by Ibn al-Musayyib and also Qatada.

The conjunction of "sayyidan" with "muşaddiqan", and the conjunction of "haşuran" and what follows it with it, indicates that the intended meaning is other than knowledge and piety, though other meanings are possible. "Haşur" is on the pattern fa'ul in the sense of maf'ul, like rasul. It means one who abstains from intercourse with women.

Mentioning this quality among the qualities of praise is either praise of him, because this quality entails distance from forbidden desires by nature itself, and perhaps this was to safeguard his innocence from accusations that the people of slander attach to some ascetics. The Jews in his time were in the greatest slander and fabrication. Or the intention in mentioning this quality is not praise of him, because those who were superior to Yahya among the prophets and messengers were fully capable of intercourse with women. It is therefore determined that the mention of this quality for Yahya is an announcement to Zakariyya that Allah granted him a son in answer to his supplication, when he said: ﴿فَهَبْ لِي مِن لَدُنْكَ ولِيًّا يَرِثُنِي﴾ ("so grant me from Yourself an heir who will inherit from me") [Maryam: 5], and that He had fulfilled His intention regarding the cutting off of Zakariyya's line, for a wisdom He knew. This is a demonstration of Zakariyya's honour before Allah, the Exalted.

This quality was placed among the qualities of perfection as a comfort to Zakariyya and to lighten his loneliness at the ending of his lineage after Yahya.

His words ﴿أنّى يَكُونُ لِي غُلامٌ﴾ ("how can I have a boy") are an interrogative meant to express wonder. Its purpose is to learn the possibility of a child, because when he asked for a son, the means for that had already been prepared. So his words "how can I have a boy" are only a seeking to know the manner of that, in a way that would confirm the good news for him. It is not doubt about the truth of the promise. It is like the saying of Ibrahim: ﴿لِيَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِي﴾ ("that my heart may be at rest") [al-Baqara: 260]. He was answered that possible things are within Allah's power, even if their occurrence is rare by custom.

"Anna" here means "how", or it means "where", since the two meanings which are the cause of the connection, namely old age and barrenness, prevent it from operating in either sense. This wonder entails gratitude for this favour, so it is a metonymy for gratitude. There is also an allusion in it that the child should be from his barren wife, without being commanded to marry another woman. This is an honour for Zakariyya's wife.

His words ﴿وقَدْ بَلَغَنِيَ الكِبَرُ﴾ ("and old age has overtaken me") come in the form of inversion (qalb). The original would be "and I have reached old age", and its benefit is to show that old age had firmly taken hold of him, as if it sought him until it reached him, like the Almighty's words: ﴿أيْنَما تَكُونُوا يُدْرِكُكُمُ المَوْتُ﴾ ("Wherever you are, death will overtake you") [al-Nisa: 78].

"Al-'aqir" is the woman who does not bear children; she "cut" (qata'a) her womb, i.e. she severed it. Since it is a quality specific to females, it was not made feminine, like their saying ha'id (menstruating), nafis (in postpartum bleeding), and muridi' (nursing). But it takes the feminine form outside the pattern of the active participle, such as their saying "'aqra" as an invocation against a woman, and in the hadith: "'aqra halqa" (barren and sterile). Likewise "nufasa'" (postpartum woman).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 42–44:

﴿And when the angels said: "O Mary, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate yourself, and bow with those who bow."﴾ ﴿That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you, and you were not with them when they cast their pens, [to see] which of them would take charge of Mary, nor were you with them when they disputed.﴾

This is coordinated with the clause ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35]. It is a transition from mention of Mary's mother to mention of Mary itself.

(Maryam) is a Hebrew proper name, and in Hebrew it is pronounced with a kasra on the mim. It is an ancient name; the sister of Musa (peace be upon him) was named with it. The books of the Christians do not mention the name of Mary's father, the mother of 'Isa, nor her birth; rather they begin abruptly with the statement that a virgin in the town of Nazareth, betrothed to Yusuf the carpenter, had conceived without a husband.

The Arabs use the name Maryam for a woman who behaves like a man and frequently sits with men, as Ru'bah said:

"I said to a zir whose maryam did not reach him."

Al-Zir (with a kasra on the zay) is one who frequently visits women. In the Kashshaf it is said: "Maryam in their language, that is the language of the Hebrews, means 'the worshipper.'"

The verb (asṭafāki) is repeated because the first choosing (iṣṭifā') is essential, namely making her free of defects and pure, while the second carries the meaning of preference over others. Therefore the first is not followed by a complement, whereas the second is followed by one. "The women of the worlds" means the women of her own time, or the women of all times. The angels' speaking to her and the choosing indicate her prophethood, and prophethood may belong to women, though messengerhood does not.

The repetition of the vocative in the angels' words ﴿O Mary, be devoutly obedient﴾ is intended to express admiration for her state, because the first address was sufficient to attain the purpose of drawing her attention to hear the angels' speech. So the second address is used merely as an alert, from which one moves to its implication, which is to honour this state and admire it. A parallel is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"She said, when the saddle had tilted with us both together: 'You have hamstrung my camel, O Imru' al-Qays, so dismount!'"

Here it is used as an alert, from which one moves to a rebuke.

Qunut is constancy in worship; it was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And stand before Allah devoutly obedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238] in Surat al-Baqarah.

He placed prostration first because it is more inclusive of gratitude, and the context here is one of gratitude.

His saying ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾ is a permission for her to pray in congregation. This is a distinction granted to her among the women of the Children of Israel, displaying the meaning of her elevation above the rest of the women. For this reason the masculine plural sign was used in "those who bow" (al-raki'in).

This address is a preface to the address that follows, which is ﴿O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 45], intended to put her at ease with the news that follows. Since its outcome would bring her grief and evil talk among people, it was preceded by what brings her joy and assures her that she is under Allah's care. Thus she would certainly know that Allah is making a way out for her and that He will not disgrace her.

His saying ﴿and you were not with them﴾ is an indication that their books were silent about some of this; otherwise He would have said, "You did not recite their books," as in ﴿and you did not recite any book before it﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48]. That is, you inform them about their conditions as if you were present among them.

His saying ﴿when they cast their pens﴾ refers to the pens with which they wrote the Torah. They used to draw lots with them in difficult matters, by writing on them the names of those casting lots or the names of the things being drawn for. People resort to lots when there is nothing to tip the truth toward one side. The people of the pre-Islamic age used to seek division by arrows (al-azlam), and the Jews made drawing lots with the pens with which they wrote the Torah in their schools, hoping that its blessing would guide them to what is good. This is not part of the emblems of Islam; in Islam, drawing lots is applied only in cases of distinguishing equal rights from all sides, and its details are in jurisprudence. The verse indicates that they disputed over the guardianship of Mary when her mother Hannah gave birth to her, since she was an orphan, as was mentioned earlier. Thus this favour conveys the information that Zakariyya's guardianship of Mary came after the drawing of lots, and it contains an alert to their rivalry over her guardianship.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 42–44:

﴿And when the angels said: "O Mary, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate yourself, and bow with those who bow."﴾ ﴿That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you, and you were not with them when they cast their pens, [to see] which of them would take charge of Mary, nor were you with them when they disputed.﴾

This is coordinated with the clause ﴿When the wife of 'Imran said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35]. It is a transition from mention of Mary's mother to mention of Mary itself.

(Maryam) is a Hebrew proper name, and in Hebrew it is pronounced with a kasra on the mim. It is an ancient name; the sister of Musa (peace be upon him) was named with it. The books of the Christians do not mention the name of Mary's father, the mother of 'Isa, nor her birth; rather they begin abruptly with the statement that a virgin in the town of Nazareth, betrothed to Yusuf the carpenter, had conceived without a husband.

The Arabs use the name Maryam for a woman who behaves like a man and frequently sits with men, as Ru'bah said:

"I said to a zir whose maryam did not reach him."

Al-Zir (with a kasra on the zay) is one who frequently visits women. In the Kashshaf it is said: "Maryam in their language, that is the language of the Hebrews, means 'the worshipper.'"

The verb (asṭafāki) is repeated because the first choosing (iṣṭifā') is essential, namely making her free of defects and pure, while the second carries the meaning of preference over others. Therefore the first is not followed by a complement, whereas the second is followed by one. "The women of the worlds" means the women of her own time, or the women of all times. The angels' speaking to her and the choosing indicate her prophethood, and prophethood may belong to women, though messengerhood does not.

The repetition of the vocative in the angels' words ﴿O Mary, be devoutly obedient﴾ is intended to express admiration for her state, because the first address was sufficient to attain the purpose of drawing her attention to hear the angels' speech. So the second address is used merely as an alert, from which one moves to its implication, which is to honour this state and admire it. A parallel is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"She said, when the saddle had tilted with us both together: 'You have hamstrung my camel, O Imru' al-Qays, so dismount!'"

Here it is used as an alert, from which one moves to a rebuke.

Qunut is constancy in worship; it was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And stand before Allah devoutly obedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238] in Surat al-Baqarah.

He placed prostration first because it is more inclusive of gratitude, and the context here is one of gratitude.

His saying ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾ is a permission for her to pray in congregation. This is a distinction granted to her among the women of the Children of Israel, displaying the meaning of her elevation above the rest of the women. For this reason the masculine plural sign was used in "those who bow" (al-raki'in).

This address is a preface to the address that follows, which is ﴿O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 45], intended to put her at ease with the news that follows. Since its outcome would bring her grief and evil talk among people, it was preceded by what brings her joy and assures her that she is under Allah's care. Thus she would certainly know that Allah is making a way out for her and that He will not disgrace her.

His saying ﴿and you were not with them﴾ is an indication that their books were silent about some of this; otherwise He would have said, "You did not recite their books," as in ﴿and you did not recite any book before it﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48]. That is, you inform them about their conditions as if you were present among them.

His saying ﴿when they cast their pens﴾ refers to the pens with which they wrote the Torah. They used to draw lots with them in difficult matters, by writing on them the names of those casting lots or the names of the things being drawn for. People resort to lots when there is nothing to tip the truth toward one side. The people of the pre-Islamic age used to seek division by arrows (al-azlam), and the Jews made drawing lots with the pens with which they wrote the Torah in their schools, hoping that its blessing would guide them to what is good. This is not part of the emblems of Islam; in Islam, drawing lots is applied only in cases of distinguishing equal rights from all sides, and its details are in jurisprudence. The verse indicates that they disputed over the guardianship of Mary when her mother Hannah gave birth to her, since she was an orphan, as was mentioned earlier. Thus this favour conveys the information that Zakariyya's guardianship of Mary came after the drawing of lots, and it contains an alert to their rivalry over her guardianship.

[p. 245]

It is a *badal ishtimal* (substitute of inclusion, a type of appositive substitution) for the clause ﴿And when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah has chosen you"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 42]. Its purpose is repetition, to complete what was said after the intervening clauses. Because it is a substitute, it is not joined by a conjunction to the first "إذْ قالَتِ" (when [they] said). The discussion of "يُبَشِّرُكِ" (gives you good news) has already been given.

The word "كَلِمَةٌ" (word) is intended here in the sense of the Word of Creation, which is the instantaneous effect of power (*ta'alluq al-qudrah al-tanjizi*), as in the hadith on the creation of man, in his saying: "He is commanded with four words: to write his provision, his term..." etc.

The description of 'Isa as "a word" means a particular word, different from what is customary in the formation of the embryo, that is, without the usual causes.

[p. 246]

His saying "مِنهُ" (from Him): "مِن" here is for the figurative origin (*ibtida' al-majazi*), meaning without the intermediary of the usual causes of procreation. This is shown by His saying: "when He decrees a matter."

His saying ﴿whose name is the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam﴾ expresses the proper name, the epithet (laqab) and the descriptive by "name," because each of the three has an effect in distinguishing the one named. As for the epithet and the proper name, this is evident. As for the descriptive that indicates lineage, it is because the listeners were accustomed to mentioning the father's name when naming persons for identification, and this is the common practice. The mother is mentioned in lineage either because the father is unknown, as in the saying of some: "Ziyad son of Sumayya," before he was attached to Abu Sufyan in the time of Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan; or because the mother has great distinction, as in their saying: "'Amr son of Hind," who was 'Amr ibn al-Mundhir, king of the Arabs.

"Al-Masih" (the Messiah) is a Hebrew word meaning "the anointed," and it was transferred into Arabic through its predominance as a designation of 'Isa. Some of the Arabs who had become Christians named some of their sons 'Abd al-Masih. Its original form is "مَسِّيِّحْ" (*massiyyah*) with a fatha on the mim, then an unpointed sin with kasra and shadda, then a yaa with kasra and shadda, then an unpointed ha' with sukun. Some Arabs pronounced it on the pattern of "سِكِّينٌ" (*sikkin*).

The meaning of "masih" is "anointed with the oil of anointing," which is the scented oil that Allah commanded Musa to take in order to pour it on the head of his brother Harun when he appointed him priest for the Children of Israel. The priests of the Children of Israel used to anoint with its like whomever they made king over them, from the time of King Saul. So "masih" came to mean "king" among them. In the first book of the Second Book of Samuel, of the Old Testament books, David said to the one who had brought him the crown of King Saul, known among the Arabs as Talut: "How were you not afraid to stretch out your hand to destroy the anointed of the LORD?"

It is possible that 'Isa was named with this description as they name someone "king." It is also possible that it was a title given to him by the Jews in mockery, since they accused him of trying to become king over Israel. Then the use of this description became predominant among them, and it became well known afterward. Therefore he was named by it in the Qur'an.

"Wajih" means one who has *wajaha*, which is: precedence over peers, and honour among the people. It is a descriptive derived from "wajh" (face) of a person, which is the most excellent of his visible organs and the most comprehensive of his means of perception and direction of actions. The word "wajh" was therefore applied to the beginning of a thing by the common usage of metaphor, so one says "wajh al-nahar" (the face of the day) for the beginning of the day. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And a group of the People of the Book said: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72]. Al-Rabi' ibn Ziyad al-'Absi said:

"Whoever is pleased by the killing of Malik,
let him come to our women with the face of the day."

And al-A'sha said:

"And there appeared to them the face of the evenings, bright."

They also say: "huwa wajh al-qawm," meaning he is the chief of the people and their foremost. From this noun was derived the verb "wajuha" with a damma on the jim, like "karuma," so "wajih" came from it as an adjective of quality (*sifah mushabbahah*). Thus "wajih al-nas" means the one honoured among them and whose word is accepted by them. Allah the Exalted said, describing Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And he was honoured with Allah.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69].

"Al-mahd" is something like a box of wood with no lid, in which a bed is prepared for the child during the period of nursing, and in which he is placed to protect him from falling.

His speech was restricted to two states: the state of being in the cradle, and the state of being a *kahl* (a man of middle age), although he would speak between these two states. This is because these two states have a particular distinction of honour from Allah. As for his speaking to people in the cradle, it is because it was a departure from the normal habit, as a *irhas* (a prelude or sign) to his prophethood. As for his speaking to them as a *kahl*, it means his calling people to the Law. So "al-takallum" (speaking) is used in its literal sense and its implicit sense, according to the specific context that determines the two meanings, which is what is connected to the verb through the two prepositional phrases.

[p. 247]

"Wa min al-salihin" (and of the righteous) is conjoined to it. The prepositional phrase is a settled adverbial in the position of a circumstantial state (*hal*).

"Al-salihun" are those whose attribute is righteousness, which does not leave them. Righteousness is the uprightness of deeds and the purity of the soul. Ibrahim said: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ [al-Saffat: 100].

A *kahl* is one who has entered the decade of forties, and he is the one who has left the age of youth. The feminine is "shahlah" with a shin, and one does not say "kahlah," just as one does not say "shahl" for a man. However, the Arabs in ancient times named a man "Shahl," such as Shahl ibn Shayban, known as al-Findu al-Zimani, and this indicates that the descriptive "kahl" became obsolete. 'Isa, peace be upon him, was about thirty-some years old when he was sent as a prophet.

His saying "wajihan" is a *hal* (state) from "kalimah" (word) in terms of what it refers to. "Wa min al-muqarrabin" is conjoined to the *hal*. "Yukallimu" is a clause conjoined to the single *hal*, because a clause that has a place in the grammatical structure has the ruling of a single word.

His saying "fi al-mahd" is a *hal* from the pronoun in "yukallimu." "Kahlan" is conjoined to the place of the prepositional phrase, because the two (the prepositional phrase and the adverbial phrase) are in the position of a *hal*, so it is conjoined to them with the accusative case. "Min al-salihin" is conjoined to "wa min al-muqarrabin."

**Page 249**

Her words "My Lord" form a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'tarida*, a clause inserted between other statements) within her own speech, placed between the speech of the angels.

The vocative here expresses lamentation (*tahassur*), not direct address, because the one who spoke to her was the angel, while she had turned toward God.

The interrogative in her words ﴿How can I have a son?﴾ expresses denial and astonishment. Accordingly, she received two answers. The first, ﴿Thus God creates what He wills﴾, removes her denial. The second, ﴿when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾, removes her astonishment.

The clause ﴿He said: Thus God creates...﴾ is the answer to her question and is not joined by a conjunction, because it follows the style of dialogue, as was mentioned earlier in God's words ﴿They said: "Will You place therein...?"﴾ (al-Baqarah: 30), and what follows it in Surat al-Baqarah. The one who addressed her was God Most High, by way of revelation.

The demonstrative in "Thus" (*kadhalika*) refers to the meaning of what was mentioned in God's words ﴿God gives you good news of a word from Him﴾ (Al 'Imran: 45), up to His words "and in maturity." That is, God creates what He wills in the same manner as that mentioned creation.

Placing the name of God (*ism al-jalala*) before the verb in ﴿God creates﴾ serves to affirm the strength of the ruling and the certainty of the statement.

The creation of Jesus by God is expressed with the verb "creates" (*yakhluqu*), because it is the bringing into existence of a being outside the customary causes used to bring about its like. It is therefore an unprecedented creation, not arising from the causes by which people are produced. Hence the verb "creates" has a fixed and specific place here. When a craftsman makes something from customary materials by customary workmanship, he does not say "I created" but "I made."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 48–49:**

﴿And He will teach him the Book, the wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel﴾ ﴿and [make him] a messenger to the Children of Israel: "I have certainly come to you with a sign from your Lord. I will create for you from clay the form of a bird, then breathe into it, and it will be a bird by the permission of Allah. I will heal the blind and the leper, and I will bring the dead to life by the permission of Allah. And I will inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses. Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers."﴾

The clause "and He will teach him" (wa-yu'allimuhu) is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the clause "and he will speak to the people in the cradle" (Q. 3:46), after the end of the parenthetical digression (i'tiraد).

Nafi' and 'Asim read *wa-yu'allimuhu* with the *ya'* (third person), meaning "Allah will teach him." The rest read it with the *nun* of majesty (nun al-'azamah), as a shift in grammatical person (iltifat).

"The Book" here refers to the well-known Book. The coordination of the Torah serves as a preparation for the coordination of the Gospel. It is also possible that "the Book" means "writing" (al-kitabah). The discussion of the Torah and the Gospel has already been made at the beginning of the surah.

*Wa-rasulan* (and [as] a messenger) is coordinated with the clause *yu'allimuhu*. This is because a circumstantial clause (jumlat al-hal), by virtue of having a place in grammatical structure (dhat mahall min al-i'rab), is in the sense of a single word (fi quwwat al-mufrad). Therefore *rasulan* is put in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (hal). The one in circumstance (sahib al-hal) is the phrase *bi-kalimah* ("with a word"), so it is part of the speech of the angels.

The opening of the hamzah of *anni* ("that I") in *anni qad ji'tukum* ("that I have certainly come to you") is due to the implied preposition bi- (the particle of attachment) after *rasulan*, meaning "a messenger with this statement," because the description *rasulan*, in that it implies being sent with a speech, is the beginning of a speech after the end of the speech of the angels.

The meaning of *ji'tukum* ("I have come to you") is "I have been sent to you from Allah." A parallel is His saying: ﴿And when 'Isa came with clear proofs, he said, "I have certainly come to you with wisdom."﴾ (Q. 43:63).

His saying *bi-ayah* ("with a sign") is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in *ji'tukum*, because the intended point is the information that he is a messenger, not that he came with a sign. He likened the command of Allah to him to convey a message to the coming of a messenger from one people to others. For this reason the prophet is called a messenger (rasul).

The *ba'* in *bi-ayah* indicates accompaniment (mulabasah), meaning "accompanied by the signs that indicate my truthfulness in this mission," expressed by the verb "came." The prepositional phrase is related to *ji'tukum* as an adverbial of mere attachment (zarf laghw). It is also possible that it is a settled adverbial (zarf mustaqirr) in the place of a circumstantial clause from *ji'tukum*, because the meaning of *ji'tukum* is "I have been sent to you," so it does not need anything to which it is attached.

His saying *inni akhluqu* ("I create"), with the hamzah of *inni* in the kasrah, is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) explaining the sign. This is the reading of Nafi' and Abu Ja'far. The rest read the hamzah of *anni* with the fatha, as a substitute (badal) for *anni qad ji'tukum*.

The basic meaning of *al-khalq* is determining a thing by a measure. From it comes the "creating" of leather, which is its determining according to what is intended to be cut from it before the piece is cut. Zuhayr said:

*"Indeed you cut what you have shaped, while some people shape but do not cut."*

He means the determining of the leather before cutting it, and cutting is *al-fary*. It is also used figuratively, well known, or as a shared term (mushtarak), for origination and innovation without a model or imitation, and for creation according to a model, which determines and measures. Allah said: ﴿And We created you, then We gave you form﴾ (Q. 7:11). Thus it is the origination of a thing and bringing it into existence. The word *al-khalq* is used here in its literal sense, meaning "I determine for you from clay the form of a bird." It does not mean the creating of a living animal, as is shown by His saying *fa-anfukh fihi* ("then I breathe into it").

The discussion of the word *al-tayr* ("bird") has already been made at His saying: ﴿So take four of the birds﴾ (Q. 2:260), in Surah al-Baqarah. The *kaf* in *ka-hay'ati al-tayr* ("like the form of a bird") means "like," and it is an attribute of an implied noun indicated by *akhluqu*, meaning "something determined, like the form of a bird." The majority read *al-tayr*, which is a collective noun (ism jam') that is generally used for the plural and sometimes for the singular. Abu Ja'far read *al-ta'ir*.

[p. 251]

The pronoun in the genitive after *fi* in *fa-anfukh fihi* refers back to that implied noun, which the *kaf* indicates.

Nafi' alone read *fa-yakunu ta'iran* ("so it becomes a bird") in the singular. The rest read *fa-yakunu tayran* in the form of the collective noun. The reading of Nafi' takes into account the singularity of the pronoun, and the reading of the rest takes into account the meaning. He made the determining his own, and attributed to Allah the bringing about of life in it. *Al-hay'ah* means the form and the manner, meaning "I shape from clay a form like the form of a bird." All read *ka-hay'ati* with a silent *ya'* after which is an open hamzah.

He added *bi-idhni Allah* ("by the permission of Allah") to show servitude and to negate the suspicion of partnership in the creating of beings.

*Al-akmah* means the blind, or the one who was born blind.

*Al-abras* is one afflicted with the disease of *al-baras* (leprosy-like skin disease). It is a skin disease with varied manifestations, some mild and some severe. Its symptoms are white patches, very intensely white, appearing on the skin. If they are sunken into the skin, it is *al-baras*; if they are level with the surface of the skin, it is *al-bahaq*. Then it spreads over the skin, and sometimes it covers the whole skin until it becomes white, and sometimes it remains distinct from the color of the skin.

Its causes are unknown. It may come by heredity. It is not contagious. It has been observed that infection with it increases among those who neglect cleanliness or live in filthy places. The Hebrews and the Greeks use the word *baras* for another disease, which is among the beginnings of leprosy (judham), so they used to consider it a bad omen when its symptoms appeared on one of them. As for the Arabs, their kings did not speak to the leper except from behind a screen, as occurred in the story of al-Harith ibn Hilliza the poet with the king 'Amr ibn Hind. As for the Hebrews, they were stricter in this. The Torah paid great attention to the rulings concerning the leper, explained them at length, and repeated them many times. It appears from them that it is a disease that descends through the air and clings to the walls of houses. The revelation described it to Musa so that he could teach it to the priests (kahanah) from the Children of Israel and teach them the method of treating it. Among their rulings was that the afflicted person is isolated from the people and placed in a special place. Its detailed rulings are in the Book of Leviticus. For this reason, the miracle of the Messiah in healing the leper was the most important of miracles in usefulness to them, both religiously and worldly.

The raising of the dead is also a miracle of the Messiah, like the breathing of the spirit into the bird formed from clay. When he brought a dead person to life, he would speak to him, then he would return to death. It is recorded in the Gospels that he raised a girl who had died, bringing her back to life immediately after her death. It occurs in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 17, that 'Isa ascended the mountain with Butrus (Peter), Ya'qub (James), and Yuhanna (John), his brother, and there appeared to them Musa and Iliya' (Elijah), speaking with them. All of this was by the permission of Allah for him to do it.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses﴾ is that he informs them of their conditions which no one knows. He tells them what they ate in their houses, and what they have stored in them. The purpose is that all these conjunctions (mutaʻatifat) be of the kind of miracles, by the indication of his saying *unabbi'ukum* ("I inform you"), because informing occurs in hidden matters.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers﴾ makes all these things signs calling to belief in him, meaning "if you want to believe," in contrast to when your habit is obstinacy. The address is directed from him to the Children of Israel, for they rushed to reject his call with denial and insult.

The Qur'an's mention of these miracles is an allusion (ta'rid) to the Christians, who made of them a proof of the divinity of 'Isa, on the basis that these deeds do not fall within human capability, so whoever is able to do them is the god. This is a sophistical argument (sufsata'i), whose exposure Allah pointed out by His saying "with a sign from your Lord" and His saying "by the permission of Allah," twice. The people of biography (ahl al-siyar) have related that the Christians of Najran argued with these deeds before the Prophet (ﷺ).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 48–49:**

﴿And He will teach him the Book, the wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel﴾ ﴿and [make him] a messenger to the Children of Israel: "I have certainly come to you with a sign from your Lord. I will create for you from clay the form of a bird, then breathe into it, and it will be a bird by the permission of Allah. I will heal the blind and the leper, and I will bring the dead to life by the permission of Allah. And I will inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses. Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers."﴾

The clause "and He will teach him" (wa-yu'allimuhu) is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the clause "and he will speak to the people in the cradle" (Q. 3:46), after the end of the parenthetical digression (i'tiraد).

Nafi' and 'Asim read *wa-yu'allimuhu* with the *ya'* (third person), meaning "Allah will teach him." The rest read it with the *nun* of majesty (nun al-'azamah), as a shift in grammatical person (iltifat).

"The Book" here refers to the well-known Book. The coordination of the Torah serves as a preparation for the coordination of the Gospel. It is also possible that "the Book" means "writing" (al-kitabah). The discussion of the Torah and the Gospel has already been made at the beginning of the surah.

*Wa-rasulan* (and [as] a messenger) is coordinated with the clause *yu'allimuhu*. This is because a circumstantial clause (jumlat al-hal), by virtue of having a place in grammatical structure (dhat mahall min al-i'rab), is in the sense of a single word (fi quwwat al-mufrad). Therefore *rasulan* is put in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (hal). The one in circumstance (sahib al-hal) is the phrase *bi-kalimah* ("with a word"), so it is part of the speech of the angels.

The opening of the hamzah of *anni* ("that I") in *anni qad ji'tukum* ("that I have certainly come to you") is due to the implied preposition bi- (the particle of attachment) after *rasulan*, meaning "a messenger with this statement," because the description *rasulan*, in that it implies being sent with a speech, is the beginning of a speech after the end of the speech of the angels.

The meaning of *ji'tukum* ("I have come to you") is "I have been sent to you from Allah." A parallel is His saying: ﴿And when 'Isa came with clear proofs, he said, "I have certainly come to you with wisdom."﴾ (Q. 43:63).

His saying *bi-ayah* ("with a sign") is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in *ji'tukum*, because the intended point is the information that he is a messenger, not that he came with a sign. He likened the command of Allah to him to convey a message to the coming of a messenger from one people to others. For this reason the prophet is called a messenger (rasul).

The *ba'* in *bi-ayah* indicates accompaniment (mulabasah), meaning "accompanied by the signs that indicate my truthfulness in this mission," expressed by the verb "came." The prepositional phrase is related to *ji'tukum* as an adverbial of mere attachment (zarf laghw). It is also possible that it is a settled adverbial (zarf mustaqirr) in the place of a circumstantial clause from *ji'tukum*, because the meaning of *ji'tukum* is "I have been sent to you," so it does not need anything to which it is attached.

His saying *inni akhluqu* ("I create"), with the hamzah of *inni* in the kasrah, is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) explaining the sign. This is the reading of Nafi' and Abu Ja'far. The rest read the hamzah of *anni* with the fatha, as a substitute (badal) for *anni qad ji'tukum*.

The basic meaning of *al-khalq* is determining a thing by a measure. From it comes the "creating" of leather, which is its determining according to what is intended to be cut from it before the piece is cut. Zuhayr said:

*"Indeed you cut what you have shaped, while some people shape but do not cut."*

He means the determining of the leather before cutting it, and cutting is *al-fary*. It is also used figuratively, well known, or as a shared term (mushtarak), for origination and innovation without a model or imitation, and for creation according to a model, which determines and measures. Allah said: ﴿And We created you, then We gave you form﴾ (Q. 7:11). Thus it is the origination of a thing and bringing it into existence. The word *al-khalq* is used here in its literal sense, meaning "I determine for you from clay the form of a bird." It does not mean the creating of a living animal, as is shown by His saying *fa-anfukh fihi* ("then I breathe into it").

The discussion of the word *al-tayr* ("bird") has already been made at His saying: ﴿So take four of the birds﴾ (Q. 2:260), in Surah al-Baqarah. The *kaf* in *ka-hay'ati al-tayr* ("like the form of a bird") means "like," and it is an attribute of an implied noun indicated by *akhluqu*, meaning "something determined, like the form of a bird." The majority read *al-tayr*, which is a collective noun (ism jam') that is generally used for the plural and sometimes for the singular. Abu Ja'far read *al-ta'ir*.

[p. 251]

The pronoun in the genitive after *fi* in *fa-anfukh fihi* refers back to that implied noun, which the *kaf* indicates.

Nafi' alone read *fa-yakunu ta'iran* ("so it becomes a bird") in the singular. The rest read *fa-yakunu tayran* in the form of the collective noun. The reading of Nafi' takes into account the singularity of the pronoun, and the reading of the rest takes into account the meaning. He made the determining his own, and attributed to Allah the bringing about of life in it. *Al-hay'ah* means the form and the manner, meaning "I shape from clay a form like the form of a bird." All read *ka-hay'ati* with a silent *ya'* after which is an open hamzah.

He added *bi-idhni Allah* ("by the permission of Allah") to show servitude and to negate the suspicion of partnership in the creating of beings.

*Al-akmah* means the blind, or the one who was born blind.

*Al-abras* is one afflicted with the disease of *al-baras* (leprosy-like skin disease). It is a skin disease with varied manifestations, some mild and some severe. Its symptoms are white patches, very intensely white, appearing on the skin. If they are sunken into the skin, it is *al-baras*; if they are level with the surface of the skin, it is *al-bahaq*. Then it spreads over the skin, and sometimes it covers the whole skin until it becomes white, and sometimes it remains distinct from the color of the skin.

Its causes are unknown. It may come by heredity. It is not contagious. It has been observed that infection with it increases among those who neglect cleanliness or live in filthy places. The Hebrews and the Greeks use the word *baras* for another disease, which is among the beginnings of leprosy (judham), so they used to consider it a bad omen when its symptoms appeared on one of them. As for the Arabs, their kings did not speak to the leper except from behind a screen, as occurred in the story of al-Harith ibn Hilliza the poet with the king 'Amr ibn Hind. As for the Hebrews, they were stricter in this. The Torah paid great attention to the rulings concerning the leper, explained them at length, and repeated them many times. It appears from them that it is a disease that descends through the air and clings to the walls of houses. The revelation described it to Musa so that he could teach it to the priests (kahanah) from the Children of Israel and teach them the method of treating it. Among their rulings was that the afflicted person is isolated from the people and placed in a special place. Its detailed rulings are in the Book of Leviticus. [Page 253]

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "bi-āyah" (with a sign), on the basis that His saying "bi-āyah" is a stationary adverbial phrase (ẓarf mustaqarr) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), as has already been mentioned. Or it is coordinated with the clause "jiʾtukum" (I have come to you), so the verb "jiʾtukum" is understood after the conjunction "wāw", and "muṣaddiqan" (confirming) is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in the understood verb. It is not coordinated with His saying "wa-rasūlan" (and a messenger), because "rasūlan" is part of the speech of the angels, whereas "muṣaddiqan" is part of the speech of ʿĪsā, as shown by his saying "limā bayna yadayya" (what is before me).

*Muṣaddiq* (one who confirms) is one who informs of the truthfulness of another. The lām was placed before the object for emphasis, to indicate a confirmation that is affirmed and established, that is, a confirmation free from any doubt or any attribution of error. The confirmation was made to govern the Torah as its object in preparation for His saying: ﴿and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾.

The meaning of "mā bayna yadayya" (what is before me) is what came before me, because the one who precedes walks before the one who comes after; so it is here a figure for the state of precedence. Even though there was a long span of time between the revelation of the Torah and his coming, the practice of it continued up to his coming, so it is as though it had not preceded him by a long time. The expression "bayna yadayʾ kadhā" is also used in the sense of what is witnessed and present, as has been mentioned in His saying ﴿He knows what is before them﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying "wa-li-uḥilla" (and to make lawful) is coordinated with "rasūlan" and what follows it of circumstantial qualifiers, because the circumstantial qualifier resembles the cause, since it is a restriction on its governing element. When the restriction carries the sense of causation, it resembles the object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi) and resembles the genitive governed by the lām of causation, so it is valid to coordinate with it a genitive governed by the lām of causation. It is also permissible that it be coordinated with His saying "bi-āyatin min rabbikum" (with a sign from your Lord), so that it is connected to the verb "jiʾtukum". He followed with it His saying "muṣaddiqan limā bayna yadayya", to draw attention to the fact that abrogation (naskh) does not contradict confirmation, because abrogation is the informing of a change in a ruling.

The Sharia of ʿĪsā was confined to reviving the rulings of the Torah and what they had abandoned of them. In this he was like others among the prophets of the Children of Israel, and in making lawful some of what God had forbidden to them, out of consideration for their circumstances at different times; and by this he was a messenger. It has been said that he made lawful for them fats, the flesh of camels, some fish, and some birds that had been forbidden before, and that he made the Sabbath lawful for them. I have not come across anything of that in the Gospel. The apparent meaning of this is that he did not forbid them what had been made lawful for them. So what is said, that he forbade them divorce, is a fabrication against him; he only warned them against it and explained to them its evil consequences, and he forbade marrying a divorced woman. To this are added what no call is free of: admonition, exhortations, and encouragements.

﴿And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, so fear God and obey me.﴾ ﴿Indeed, God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.﴾

It is an emphasis of His first saying: ﴿that I have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:49]. It was coordinated with "wāw" only because it was intended to be among the earlier statements, and the emphasis is achieved merely by the prior mention of its content. Thus this sentence has two aspects that make it like two sentences, and so that the consequence "so fear God and obey me" may be built upon it.

Ḥafṣ (sic: the majority of readers, al-Jumhūr) read His saying "wa-aṭīʿūni" (and obey me) by omitting the first-person yāʾ both in continuous recitation and in pause, while Yaʿqūb read it with the yāʾ retained in both.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him﴾: "inna" is with a kasra on the hamza without doubt, and it occupies the position of a causal explanation for the command to piety and obedience, as is its manner when it occurs merely for emphasis, like the saying of Bashshār:

*Go early, my two companions, before the midday heat; indeed that success lies in going early.*

For this reason He said "my Lord and your Lord"; so He, being their Lord, deserves piety, and being the Lord of ʿĪsā and the One who sent him, His piety requires obedience to His messenger.

His saying "fa-ʿbudūhu" (so worship Him) is a consequence built upon lordship. He made the saying "Indeed God is my Lord" a causal explanation, and then a principle from which the consequence is derived.

His saying: ﴿This is a straight path﴾: the demonstrative refers to all that he said, meaning that it is the clear truth. So He likened it to a straight path, along which the one who travels does not go astray and does not become confused.
