﴿So when Jesus sensed their disbelief, he said, "Who are my helpers in the cause of Allah?" The disciples said, "We are the helpers of Allah. We believe in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, we believe in what You have sent down and follow the Messenger, so write us down among the witnesses."﴾

The conditional "lamma" (when) implies omitted clauses, and their estimated form is: "Jesus was born, and he spoke to the people in the cradle with what the angels had informed Mary, and he spoke to the people about the message. He showed them the promised signs and called them to affirm him and obey him, but they disbelieved him. So when he sensed their disbelief, he said..." until the end of the verse. That is, he sensed disbelief from a group among those he had addressed with his call in His saying "and obey me" (Ali 'Imran 3:50), meaning he heard their denial of him and was informed of their plotting against him. "Minhum" (from them) is connected to "ahassa" (sensed). The pronoun in "minhum" refers to something known from the context, which is explained by the description "disbelief."

Seeking help to make the call to Allah manifest is one of the stances of the messengers. Allah reported about Noah: ﴿So he called upon his Lord, "I am overcome, so help [me]."﴾ [al-Qamar: 10]. Moses said: ﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family﴾ [Ta-Ha: 29]. The Prophet (ﷺ) also presented himself to the tribes of the Arabs so that they would help him until he conveyed the call of his Lord.

His saying "Who are my helpers in the cause of Allah?" was perhaps said in the assembly of the Children of Israel, for the purpose of conveying the call and cutting off excuses. Help includes proclaiming the religion and calling to it. The description "my helpers" is joined with "ila" (to/in the cause of) either by the grammatical device of "tadmin" (inclusion of meaning), where the attribute "helpers" implies the sense of joining, meaning: those who join their help to me in addition to Allah's help to me, which He promised me. For the obtaining of help necessarily requires obtaining its cause, as is Allah's way. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿If you help Allah, He will help you﴾ [Muhammad: 7]. This is like His saying: ﴿And do not consume their property in addition to your own property﴾ [al-Nisa: 2], meaning, those who join them. In this case the prepositional phrase is an idle adverbial clause (zarf laghw). Or it is taken as a circumstantial state (hal) of the first-person pronoun, meaning: while I am going to Allah, that is, to convey His law. In that case the prepositional phrase is a stable adverbial clause (zarf mustaqirr). On both views, the state that the prepositional phrase requires is one of the conditions of Jesus (peace be upon him). For this reason the disciples did not use a similar construction in their saying: ﴿We are the helpers of Allah﴾.

"Al-Hawariyyun" (the disciples) is a title for the companions of Jesus (peace be upon him), those who believed in him and stayed close to him. It is a word arabized from Nabataean, and its singular is "hawari." This is stated in al-Itqan (al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an) on the authority of Ibn Hatim, on the authority of al-Dahhak. However, he claimed that its meaning is "launderer," that is, a washer of clothes. Arabic linguists explained it as the one who is among the closest of those to whom he is attached and of his kin.

The term became dominant for the companions of Jesus. In a hadith the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every prophet has a hawari, and my hawari is al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam." Commentators and philologists have multiplied speculations about its derivation and the variations of its meaning, but all of that is forcing words with the letters ha', waw and ra' into meanings, and nothing from it is sound.

The disciples were twelve men, and they are: Simon Peter, his brother Andrew, John son of Zebedee, and his brother James. All of these were fishermen; Matthew the tax collector; Thomas and Philip; Bartholomew; James son of Alphaeus; Lebbaeus; Simon the Canaanite (al-Qanawi); and Judas Iscariot.

The disciples' answer indicated that they knew that the help for Jesus was not for his own essence, but rather it was help for the religion of Allah. There is nothing in their saying "We are the helpers of Allah" that conveys exclusivity, because verbal annexation (idafa lafziyya) does not convey definiteness, so neither of the two parts became definite. But the disciples hastened to this assignment.

Individuals from the Jews who were scattered also believed alongside the disciples, such as those whose sick ones the Messiah healed. Among the women who believed in him was his mother (peace be upon her), Mary Magdalene, the mother of John, the mother-in-law of Simon, Joanna the wife of Chuza, the steward of Herod, Susanna, and other women. But women are not called upon for help.

His saying "Our Lord, we believe" is part of the speech of the disciples, and they built upon that the supplication that Allah make them among the witnesses, that is, among those who testified for the messengers of Allah to their conveying and their truthfulness. This indicates that they had received from Jesus, in what he taught them, the virtues of one who bears witness to the truthfulness of the messengers.

Help includes proclaiming the religion and calling to it. The description "my helpers" is joined with "ila" (to/in the cause of) either by the grammatical device of "tadmin" (inclusion of meaning), where the attribute "helpers" implies the sense of joining, meaning: those who join their help to me in addition to Allah's help to me, which He promised me. For the obtaining of help necessarily requires obtaining its cause, as is Allah's way. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿If you help Allah, He will help you﴾ [Muhammad: 7]. This is like His saying: ﴿And do not consume their property in addition to your own property﴾ [al-Nisa: 2], meaning, those who join them. In this case the prepositional phrase is an idle adverbial clause (zarf laghw). Or it is taken as a circumstantial state (hal) of the first-person pronoun, meaning: while I am going to Allah, that is, to convey His law. In that case the prepositional phrase is a stable adverbial clause (zarf mustaqirr). On both views, the state that the prepositional phrase requires is one of the conditions of Jesus (peace be upon him). For this reason the disciples did not use a similar construction in their saying: ﴿We are the helpers of Allah﴾.

"Al-Hawariyyun" (the disciples) is a title for the companions of Jesus (peace be upon him), those who believed in him and stayed close to him. It is a word arabized from Nabataean, and its singular is "hawari." This is stated in al-Itqan (al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an) on the authority of Ibn Hatim, on the authority of al-Dahhak. However, he claimed that its meaning is "launderer," that is, a washer of clothes. Arabic linguists explained it as the one who is among the closest of those to whom he is attached and of his kin.

The term became dominant for the companions of Jesus. In a hadith the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every prophet has a hawari, and my hawari is al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam." Commentators and philologists have multiplied speculations about its derivation and the variations of its meaning, but all of that is forcing words with the letters ha', waw and ra' into meanings, and nothing from it is sound.

The disciples were twelve men, and they are: Simon Peter, his brother Andrew, John son of Zebedee, and his brother James. All of these were fishermen; Matthew the tax collector; Thomas and Philip; Bartholomew; James son of Alphaeus; Lebbaeus; Simon the Canaanite (al-Qanawi); and Judas Iscariot.

The disciples' answer indicated that they knew that the help for Jesus was not for his own essence, but rather it was help for the religion of Allah. There is nothing in their saying "We are the helpers of Allah" that conveys exclusivity, because verbal annexation (idafa lafziyya) does not convey definiteness, so neither of the two parts became definite. But the disciples hastened to this assignment.

Individuals from the Jews who were scattered also believed alongside the disciples, such as those whose sick ones the Messiah healed. Among the women who believed in him was his mother (peace be upon her), Mary Magdalene, the mother of John, the mother-in-law of Simon, Joanna the wife of Chuza, the steward of Herod, Susanna, and other women. But women are not called upon for help.

His saying "Our Lord, we believe" is part of the speech of the disciples, and they built upon that the supplication that Allah make them among the witnesses, that is, among those who testified for the messengers of Allah to their conveying and their truthfulness. This indicates that they had received from Jesus, in what he taught them, the virtues of one who bears witness to the truthfulness of the messengers.

[Page 255]

[Page 256]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 54:

﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed, and Allah is the best of schemers﴾.

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿When Jesus perceived disbelief from them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52], for he perceived from them disbelief, and he perceived from them treachery and scheming.

The pronoun in "makarū" (they schemed) refers back to what the pronoun in "minhum" (from them) refers to, namely the Jews. This is clarified by the words of the Exalted in Surah al-Saff: ﴿The disciples said, "We are the helpers of Allah." So a group of the Children of Israel believed, and a group disbelieved﴾ [al-Saff: 14]. Makr (scheming) is an act intended to harm someone in a manner concealed from him, or the disguising of an act of harm in the appearance of benefit. What is meant here is the Jews' plotting to seize the Messiah and their effort with the rulers to enable them to kill him. Allah's scheming against them is a figurative expression for Allah's thwarting of their endeavours at the very moment they thought their endeavours had succeeded, and it is here a case of mushakalah (correspondence of terms). It is permissible to apply the word makr to the act of Allah without mushakalah, as in His words: ﴿Do they feel secure from the scheming of Allah?﴾ in Surah al-A'raf. Some of our teachers call such a usage a "mushakalah taqdiriyyah" (presumed correspondence).

As for ﴿and Allah is the best of schemers﴾ [al-Anfal: 30], its meaning is: the most powerful of them when it comes to countering their scheming by abandoning them.

It is also possible that the meaning of "the best of schemers" is this: the respite (imla') and gradual leading-on (istidraj) which He ordains for the wicked, the tyrants and the hypocrites, which resembles scheming in that its outward appearance is good while its outcome is evil, is in fact pure good, producing nothing but general welfare. Even if it harms one person or several persons, it is from this aspect free of the ugliness found in scheming. For this reason Allah's acts are exalted above being described as ugly or shameful, because they are not accompanied by the circumstances that make some human acts ugly, such as indicating foolishness of opinion, evil intention, cowardice, weakness, greed, or the like. That is, if there is ugliness in scheming, then Allah's scheming is pure good; and you may, in this sense, take "khayr" (best) as a comparative and also as a non-comparative.

[p. 257 continues]

It is a resumption (istinaf). "Idh" is an adverbial particle that is either not dependent on anything, or dependent on an omitted element, meaning: "Remember when God said..." As mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I am placing upon the earth a khalifa (successor)"﴾ [al-Baqara: 30]. This is a narration of the event of the raising of the Messiah and his concealment from the sight of his enemies. In His address, God first informed him of this as a comfort to him, since what he desired of guiding his people had not been accomplished, while knowing that he loved to meet God,

[p. 258]

and as good news to him that God would make His religion prevail, because the greatest concern of the Messenger is guidance and conveying the Law. Therefore He said to him: ﴿And making those who followed you superior to those who disbelieved﴾. The call (al-nida') in it is for comfort. In a hadith, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No prophet is taken (in death) until he is given the choice."

His words ﴿Indeed I am causing you to die (mutawaffika)﴾: the apparent meaning is "Indeed I am causing you to die." This is the meaning of this verb in the contexts where it is used, because the basic sense of the verb tawaffa is that he took something completely and received it in full. One says: "God took him (tawaffahu Allah)," meaning He decreed his death. One says: "The Angel of Death took him (tawaffahu malak al-mawt)," meaning he carried out God's will concerning his death. The verb tawaffi is also applied to sleep figuratively, by the relation of resemblance, as in His words: ﴿And it is He who takes you in death by night﴾ [al-An'am: 60], and His words: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep. Then He withholds those for which He has decreed death and releases the others until a specified term﴾ [al-Zumar: 42]. That is: as for the one that has not died the known death, He causes it to die in its sleep a death resembling complete death, as in His words: ﴿And it is He who takes you in death by night﴾ [al-An'am: 60]. Then He said: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him in death﴾ [al-An'am: 61]. So all of this is causing death in reality, and only custom and usage distinguish between them. For this reason He explained it by saying: ﴿Then He withholds those for which He has decreed death and releases the others until a specified term﴾ [al-Zumar: 42]. The discourse is thus perfectly coherent, though its arrangement has been obscured for some minds.

Clearer than this verse is the verse of al-Ma'ida: ﴿So when You took me in death (tawaffaytani), You were the Watcher over them﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 117], because it indicates that he underwent the known death that prevents a person from knowing what happens on earth. To interpret it as sleep with reference to Jesus has no meaning, since if He intended to raise him, it does not necessarily follow that he would sleep. Moreover, sleep in that case would be a means to the raising, so it would not be fitting to emphasize mentioning it while leaving out mention of the purpose. Therefore, the claim that it means raising him away from this world is an invention of a new meaning for "wafat" in the language without evidence. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb ibn Munabbih said that it is a death of dying, and this is the apparent position of Malik in the Jami' al-'Utbiyya. Malik said: "Jesus died at the age of thirty-one." Ibn Rushd said in al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil: "It is possible that his saying 'he died at the age of thirty-three' is meant literally and not figuratively."

Al-Rabi' said: it is a death of sleep, in which God raised him during his sleep. Al-Hasan and a group said: its meaning is "Indeed I am taking you (qabidu-ka) from the earth and delivering you (mukhallisu-ka) in heaven." It was also said: "Mutawaffika" means "accepting your deed." What led them to interpret the meaning of wafat is what has come in the authentic hadiths: "that Jesus will descend at the end of the duration of the world." This implies that he has a special life, more specific than the life of the spirits of the rest of the prophets, which is a life

[p. 259]

more specific than the life of the other spirits. The life of spirits varies, as indicated by the hadith: "The souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds." They related that the interpretation of the meaning in this verse is more preferable than the interpretation of the hadith concerning the meaning of his life and his descent. Some of them interpreted the meaning of wafat and made him alive with his first life, while others kept wafat in its apparent sense and made his life a second life. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "God caused him to die for three hours and raised him during them, then revived him with Himself in heaven." Some said: "He died for seven hours." Ibn 'Abbas and Malik refrained from specifying how this was. They were indeed guided and rightly directed. It is possible that his life is like the life of the rest of the prophets, and that his descent, if it is taken in its apparent sense, is a resurrection of him before the appointed time of resurrection, in a particular manner. The descent has been expressed with the wording: "God will send Jesus, and he will kill the Dajjal," narrated by Muslim from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar. He will not die after that, but will pass from there to the Hereafter.

It has also been said in its interpretation that the conjunction of ﴿and raising you to Me﴾ is in inverted order, since the wa (and) does not indicate chronological sequence. The meaning would be: "Indeed I am raising you to Me, then causing you to die after that." There is nothing in the speech indicating that he will die at the end of time, except that in the hadith of Abu Hurayra in the Sunan of Abu Dawud: "He (Jesus) will remain forty years, then he will die, and the Muslims will pray over him." The correct approach is to take His words ﴿Indeed I am causing you to die﴾ in their literal sense, which is the apparent meaning, and to interpret the reports whose apparent meaning indicates that he is alive as meaning a life of honour with God, like the life of the martyrs but stronger. And if his descent is taken in its apparent sense without interpretation, then that serves in place of resurrection. The saying in Abu Hurayra's hadith, "then he will die, and the Muslims will pray over him," is an addition (mudraj) from Abu Hurayra, since no one else among those who narrated the hadith of Jesus's descent narrated it, and they are a group of the Companions. The reports differ and are not explicit. The Qur'an, in enumerating his virtues, does not mention that he will descend at the end of time.

The purification (al-tat-hir) in His words ﴿and purifying you from those who disbelieved﴾ is figurative (majaz), in the sense of protection and exemption, because the purity of Jesus is itself complete. But if his enemies had been given power over him, that would have been a humiliation to him.

The object of "disbelieved" (kafaru) is omitted because it is clear: "those who disbelieved in you," and they are the Jews. The Jews did not disbelieve in God, but disbelieved in the mission of Jesus, since Jesus was not sent to anyone other than them. So his purification is not understood as purification from the polytheists, by the indication of the context.

[p. 260]

The superiority in His words ﴿above those who disbelieved﴾ means dominance and victory, and it is a worldly superiority, as shown by His words ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾.

By "those who followed him" are meant the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) and whoever followed him after them, until his law was abrogated (nusikhat, naskh) by the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The clause ﴿Then to Me is your return﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿and making those who followed you superior to those who disbelieved﴾, since the content of both clauses concerns God's recompense for the followers of Jesus and the disbelievers in him. "Thumma" (then) here indicates a graded remoteness (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because the recompense that occurs at the people's return to God on the Day of Resurrection, together with the judgment between the two groups regarding what they disagreed about, is greater in rank and more important than making the followers of Jesus superior to the disbelievers in this world.

It is apparent that this clause is among what God addressed to Jesus, and that the pronoun in "your return" (marji'ukum) and what accompanies it of second-person pronouns refers to Jesus, those who followed him, and those who disbelieved in him.

It is also possible that it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, in which case "thumma" indicates a transition from one purpose to another, in addition to graded and temporal remoteness.

The noun "al-marji'" is a mimi verbal noun meaning "return." The literal meaning of return is not appropriate here, so it is determined that it is a figurative return. It may mean the resurrection for reckoning after death, and its use in this sense is frequent in the Qur'an, both in this word and in its synonym, such as "al-masir" (destiny). It may also mean the end of God's respite for them in a term He willed, so that His will takes effect on them in this world.

It is permissible to combine the two meanings by using the word in both its figurative senses, and this suits the combining of the two punishments in His words ﴿So I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter﴾. On both interpretations, the explanation of God's judgment between them concerning what they differ about applies.

His words ﴿As for those who disbelieved, I will punish them﴾ up to His words ﴿and We will pay them their rewards in full﴾ are a detailed explanation of what was summarized in His words ﴿I will judge between you concerning that over which you differ﴾.

His words ﴿So I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter﴾: the intended purpose of this threat is the punishment of the Hereafter, because it falls within the scope of the detailed explanation of the pronouns in His words ﴿I will judge between you concerning that over which you differ﴾, and that only occurs in the Hereafter. So the mention of the punishment of this world here is an embedding (idmaj). If this is among what God addressed to Jesus, then it is used in its plain meaning. If it is a statement from God in the Qur'an addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, it is valid that it also intends an allusion to the polytheists in their wronging of Muhammad (ﷺ) out of arrogance and envy. The explanation of attributing love to God was already given under His words ﴿Say: If you should love God﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 31] in this surah.

The clause ﴿and they will have no helpers﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil) for the clause ﴿I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter﴾, meaning: they will not find helpers who will support them in their punishment, which God has decreed.

Know that His words ﴿So I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter﴾ are a particular case, and do not necessitate the continuation of the two punishments. As for the punishment of this world, it proceeds according to the order of worldly conditions: with strength and weakness, and without permanence. So the meaning of the absence of helpers for them in it is the absence of helpers during the period God decreed for their punishment in this world. This varies, and the Jews have found helpers at some times, such as the story of Esther in the past and the question of Palestine in this age.

As for the punishment of the Hereafter, it is unrestricted here, but restricted in many verses to perpetuity, as He said: ﴿and they will never leave the Fire﴾ [al-Baqara: 167].

The clause ﴿and God does not love the wrongdoers﴾ is a concluding clause for the whole detailed explanation. It is thus a second concluding clause for ﴿So I will punish them with a severe punishment﴾ in its explicit meaning, meaning: "I will punish them because they are wrongdoers, and God does not love wrongdoers." It is also a concluding clause for ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ to its end, by the implication of its meaning, because the absence of God's love for wrongdoers necessitates that He loves those who believed and did righteous deeds, and therefore He gives them their reward in full.

The meaning of their being wrongdoers is that they wronged themselves by their disbelief. The Christians wronged God by diminishing Him through affirming a son for Him, and they wronged Jesus by attributing to him sonship to God, the Exalted. The Jews wronged him by denying him and harming him.

[p. 261]

The punishment of this world is the loss of sovereignty, the imposition of humiliation, poverty, and the poll tax (jizya), dispersion across the lands, and their living as dependents of other people. The punishment of the Hereafter is Hell. The meaning of ﴿and they will have no helpers﴾ is that they will not find a helper who repels this from them, and even if they attempt it, they will not succeed.

He attributed ﴿and We will pay them﴾ to the "nun of majesty" (nun al-'azama), to draw attention to the greatness of the object of this agent, since a great one gives a great reward. The estimated meaning is: "We will pay them their rewards in this world and the Hereafter," as shown by its counterpart in their opposites in His words ﴿So I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter﴾. The payment of rewards in this world appears in many matters: among them God's pleasure with them, His blessings with them, a good life, and good remembrance. The clause ﴿and God does not love wrongdoers﴾ is a concluding clause, and in it is an implicit omission: meaning, "and He loves those who believed and did righteous deeds."

If it is a statement from God in the Qur'an addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, it is valid that it also intends an allusion to the polytheists in their wronging of Muhammad (ﷺ) out of arrogance and envy. The explanation of attributing love to God was already given under His words ﴿Say: If you should love God﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 31] in this surah.

The clause ﴿and they will have no helpers﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil) for the clause ﴿I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter﴾, meaning: they will not find helpers who will support them in their punishment, which God has decreed.

Know that His words ﴿So I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter﴾ are a particular case, and do not necessitate the continuation of the two punishments. As for the punishment of this world, it proceeds according to the order of worldly conditions: with strength and weakness, and without permanence. So the meaning of the absence of helpers for them in it is the absence of helpers during the period God decreed for their punishment in this world. This varies, and the Jews have found helpers at some times, such as the story of Esther in the past and the question of Palestine in this age.

As for the punishment of the Hereafter, it is unrestricted here, but restricted in many verses to perpetuity, as He said: ﴿and they will never leave the Fire﴾ [al-Baqara: 167].

The clause ﴿and God does not love the wrongdoers﴾ is a concluding clause for the whole detailed explanation. It is thus a second concluding clause for ﴿So I will punish them with a severe punishment﴾ in its explicit meaning, meaning: "I will punish them because they are wrongdoers, and God does not love wrongdoers." It is also a concluding clause for ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ to its end, by the implication of its meaning, because the absence of God's love for wrongdoers necessitates that He loves those who believed and did righteous deeds, and therefore He gives them their reward in full.

The meaning of their being wrongdoers is that they wronged themselves by their disbelief. The Christians wronged God by diminishing Him through affirming a son for Him, and they wronged Jesus by attributing to him sonship to God, the Exalted. The Jews wronged him by denying him and harming him.

[p. 261]

The punishment of this world is the loss of sovereignty, the imposition of humiliation, poverty, and the poll tax (jizya), dispersion across the lands, and their living as dependents of other people. The punishment of the Hereafter is Hell. The meaning of ﴿and they will have no helpers﴾ is that they will not find a helper who repels this from them, and even if they attempt it, they will not succeed.

He attributed ﴿and We will pay them﴾ to the "nun of majesty" (nun al-'azama), to draw attention to the greatness of the object of this agent, since a great one gives a great reward. The estimated meaning is: "We will pay them their rewards in this world and the Hereafter," as shown by its counterpart in their opposites in His words ﴿So I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter﴾. The payment of rewards in this world appears in many matters: among them God's pleasure with them, His blessings with them, a good life, and good remembrance. The clause ﴿and God does not love wrongdoers﴾ is a concluding clause, and in it is an implicit omission: meaning, "and He loves those who believed and did righteous deeds."

Ḥafṣ from 'Āṣim and Ruways from Ya'qub read ﴿fa-nuwaffīhim﴾ with the nun, while the majority read it with the nun ("fa-nuwaffihim"). Ḥafṣ from 'Āṣim, and Ruways from Ya'qub, read "fa-yuwaffīhim" with the yā' of the third person, as a shift of person (iltifat).

[p. 257 continues]

It is a resumption (istinaf). "Idh" is an adverbial particle that is either not dependent on anything, or dependent on an omitted element, meaning: "Remember when God said..." As mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I am placing upon the earth a khalifa (successor)"﴾ [al-Baqara: 30]. This is a narration of the event of the raising of the Messiah and his concealment from the sight of his enemies. In His address, God first informed him of this as a comfort to him, since what he desired of guiding his people had not been accomplished, while knowing that he loved to meet God,

[p. 258]

and as good news to him that God would make His religion prevail, because the greatest concern of the Messenger is guidance and conveying the Law. Therefore He said to him: ﴿And making those who followed you superior to those who disbelieved﴾. The call (al-nida') in it is for comfort. In a hadith, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No prophet is taken (in death) until he is given the choice."

His words ﴿Indeed I am causing you to die (mutawaffika)﴾: the apparent meaning is "Indeed I am causing you to die." This is the meaning of this verb in the contexts where it is used, because the basic sense of the verb tawaffa is that he took something completely and received it in full. One says: "God took him (tawaffahu Allah)," meaning He decreed his death. One says: "The Angel of Death took him (tawaffahu malak al-mawt)," meaning he carried out God's will concerning his death. The verb tawaffi is also applied to sleep figuratively, by the relation of resemblance, as in His words: ﴿And it is He who takes you in death by night﴾ [al-An'am: 60], and His words: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep. Then He withholds those for which He has decreed death and releases the others until a specified term﴾ [al-Zumar: 42]. That is: as for the one that has not died the known death, He causes it to die in its sleep a death resembling complete death, as in His words: ﴿And it is He who takes you in death by night﴾ [al-An'am: 60]. Then He said: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him in death﴾ [al-An'am: 61]. So all of this is causing death in reality, and only custom and usage distinguish between them. For this reason He explained it by saying: ﴿Then He withholds those for which He has decreed death and releases the others until a specified term﴾ [al-Zumar: 42]. The discourse is thus perfectly coherent, though its arrangement has been obscured for some minds.

Clearer than this verse is the verse of al-Ma'ida: ﴿So when You took me in death (tawaffaytani), You were the Watcher over them﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 117], because it indicates that he underwent the known death that prevents a person from knowing what happens on earth. To interpret it as sleep with reference to Jesus has no meaning, since if He intended to raise him, it does not necessarily follow that he would sleep. Moreover, sleep in that case would be a means to the raising, so it would not be fitting to emphasize mentioning it while leaving out mention of the purpose. Therefore, the claim that it means raising him away from this world is an invention of a new meaning for "wafat" in the language without evidence. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb ibn Munabbih said that it is a death of dying, and this is the apparent position of Malik in the Jami' al-'Utbiyya. Malik said: "Jesus died at the age of thirty-one." Ibn Rushd said in al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil: "It is possible that his saying 'he died at the age of thirty-three' is meant literally and not figuratively."

Al-Rabi' said: it is a death of sleep, in which God raised him during his sleep. Al-Hasan and a group said: its meaning is "Indeed I am taking you (qabidu-ka) from the earth and delivering you (mukhallisu-ka) in heaven." It was also said: "Mutawaffika" means "accepting your deed." What led them to interpret the meaning of wafat is what has come in the authentic hadiths: "that Jesus will descend at the end of the duration of the world." This implies that he has a special life, more specific than the life of the spirits of the rest of the prophets, which is a life

[p. 259]

more specific than the life of the other spirits. The life of spirits varies, as indicated by the hadith: "The souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds." They related that the interpretation of the meaning in this verse is more preferable than the interpretation of the hadith concerning the meaning of his life and his descent. Some of them interpreted the meaning of wafat and made him alive with his first life, while others kept wafat in its apparent sense and made his life a second life. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "God caused him to die for three hours and raised him during them, then revived him with Himself in heaven." Some said: "He died for seven hours." Ibn 'Abbas and Malik refrained from specifying how this was. They were indeed guided and rightly directed. It is possible that his life is like the life of the rest of the prophets, and that his descent, if it is taken in its apparent sense, is a resurrection of him before the appointed time of resurrection, in a particular manner. The descent has been expressed with the wording: "God will send Jesus, and he will kill the Dajjal," narrated by Muslim from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar. He will not die after that, but will pass from there to the Hereafter.

It has also been said in its interpretation that the conjunction of ﴿and raising you to Me﴾ is in inverted order, since the wa (and) does not indicate chronological sequence. The meaning would be: "Indeed I am raising you to Me, then causing you to die after that." There is nothing in the speech indicating that he will die at the end of time, except that in the hadith of Abu Hurayra in the Sunan of Abu Dawud: "He (Jesus) will remain forty years, then he will die, and the Muslims will pray over him." The correct approach is to take His words ﴿Indeed I am causing you to die﴾ in their literal sense, which is the apparent meaning, and to interpret the reports whose apparent meaning indicates that he is alive as meaning a life of honour with God, like the life of the martyrs but stronger. And if his descent is taken in its apparent sense without interpretation, then that serves in place of resurrection. The saying in Abu Hurayra's hadith, "then he will die, and the Muslims will pray over him," is an addition (mudraj) from Abu Hurayra, since no one else among those who narrated the hadith of Jesus's descent narrated it, and they are a group of the Companions. The reports differ and are not explicit. The Qur'an, in enumerating his virtues, does not mention that he will descend at the end of time.

The purification (al-tat-hir) in His words ﴿and purifying you from those who disbelieved﴾ is figurative (majaz), in the sense of protection and exemption, because the purity of Jesus is itself complete. But if his enemies had been given power over him, that would have been a humiliation to him.

The object of "disbelieved" (kafaru) is omitted because it is clear: "those who disbelieved in you," and they are the Jews. The Jews did not disbelieve in God, but disbelieved in the mission of Jesus, since Jesus was not sent to anyone other than them. So his purification is not understood as purification from the polytheists, by the indication of the context.

[p. 260]

The superiority in His words ﴿above those who disbelieved﴾ means dominance and victory, and it is a worldly superiority, as shown by His words ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾.

By "those who followed him" are meant the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) and whoever followed him after them, until his law was abrogated (nusikhat, naskh) by the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The clause ﴿Then to Me is your return﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿and making those who followed you superior to those who disbelieved﴾, since the content of both clauses concerns God's recompense for the followers of Jesus and the disbelievers in him. "Thumma" (then) here indicates a graded remoteness (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because the recompense that occurs at the people's return to God on the Day of Resurrection, together with the judgment between the two groups regarding what they disagreed about, is greater in rank and more important than making the followers of Jesus superior to the disbelievers in this world.

It is apparent that this clause is among what God addressed to Jesus, and that the pronoun in "your return" (marji'ukum) and what accompanies it of second-person pronouns refers to Jesus, those who followed him, and those who disbelieved in him.

It is also possible that it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, in which case "thumma" indicates a transition from one purpose to another, in addition to graded and temporal remoteness.

The noun "al-marji'" is a mimi verbal noun meaning "return." The literal meaning of return is not appropriate here, so it is determined that it is a figurative return. It may mean the resurrection for reckoning after death, and its use in this sense is frequent in the Qur'an, both in this word and in its synonym, such as "al-masir" (destiny). It may also mean the end of God's respite for them in a term He willed, so that His will takes effect on them in this world.

This is a closing statement (tadhyil). The phrase "al-Ayat wal-Dhikr" is more general than what is recited here, and the demonstrative "dhalika" refers to the preceding speech, from His saying, ﴿When the angels said: O Maryam, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 45]. The demonstrative is masculine singular to agree with the referent understood as "the speech" or "the matter mentioned."

The clause "natluhu" ("We recite it") is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the demonstrative, in the manner of ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72]. This is a eloquent Arabic usage, although some grammarians disputed the validity of a circumstantial clause coming from a demonstrative.

His saying "min al-Ayat" ("from the signs") is the predicate (khabar) of "dhalika," meaning that the recitation of that to you is among the signs of your truthfulness in your claim of prophethood, for you did not know that. It is also a reminder and an admonition for people. This is better than making "natluhu" the predicate of the subject, and there are other considerations. "Al-Hakim" is in the sense of "al-Muhkam" (the perfected/firm), or it is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), meaning that the Wise one is its knower or its reciter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 59–60:

Page 263
﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before God is like the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was.﴾ ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani): it clarifies what arose among the Christians of misconceptions about Jesus being "a word from God," for they went astray through their assumption that he was not purely human (al-nasut). This is the beginning of refuting the Christian doctrine of deifying Jesus (ta'lih), and of answering their objections against Islam, and it is the most decisive proof by way of argumentum ad hominem (tariq al-ilzam). For they affirmed the divinity of Jesus on the ground that he was created by a word from God and had no father; so they said, "He is the son of God." God therefore showed them that Adam is more deserving of being claimed to have this status. If Adam was not God, though he was created without two parents, then Jesus is more deserving of being a created being than Adam.

The point of comparison is that both were created without a father, and Adam has the added feature of being created without a mother too. For this reason it was necessary to mention the aspect of resemblance with His words, "He created him from dust," i.e., He created him without father or mother, but by the word "Be," while showing that he is stronger in the thing compared to, as is generally the case. His saying "before God" (ʿinda Allah) means that his relation to God does not exceed that of Adam in being an unusual creation for you, because they made his wondrous creation a ground for the Messiah having a special relation with God, namely sonship. Ibn 'Atiyya said: by His words "before God" God intended the actual state of affairs (nafs al-amr al-waqi').

The pronoun in "khalaqahu" refers to Adam, not to Jesus, since everyone knows that Jesus was not created from dust; so the locus of the comparison is His saying, "Then He said to him, 'Be,' and he was."

The clause "khalaqahu" and what is conjoined to it explains the clause "like the likeness of Adam."

"Thumma" (then) indicates a rank-based delay (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), for His forming him by the command "Be" is higher in rank than creating him from dust, and it is prior in existence. The formation indicated by "Be" is His formation of him in the intended attribute; for this reason He did not say "He formed him from dust," nor "He said to him 'Be' from dust, then gave him life," but rather said "He created him, then said to him, 'Be.'" The saying "Be" is an expression of the connection of power to his formation as a living being possessing a soul, so that the hearers may know that formation is not the work of a hand, nor carving with a tool, but by will, the connection of power, and the subjugation of the beings which have an effect in bringing about the intended thing, until they come together and move toward the manifestation of the formed thing; and all of that results from the direction of the will toward immediate execution. By that word, Adam too was a word from God, but he was not described as such, because there was no need for that at his time.

He said "fa-yakunu" (and he was) and did not say "fa-kana" (and he became), in order to bring before the mind the image of his coming into being; the present tense in such a context is not to be understood except in this sense, like His words: "God is He who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds" [Fatir: 9]. To understand it otherwise here has no basis.

His words "The truth is from your Lord" is the predicate of an omitted subject: i.e., this is the truth. "From your Lord" is a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to "the truth." The address in "so do not be among the doubters" is to the Prophet ﷺ, while the intended meaning is an indirect allusion to others; those indirectly addressed here are the Christians, the doubters who disputed about divinity because of the certainty that Jesus had no father.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 61:

﴿Then whoever argues with you concerning it, after the knowledge has come to you, say: "Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves; then let us invoke earnestly and lay the curse of Allah upon the liars."﴾

This is a consequence of His saying: ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters﴾ [Al 'Imran: 60], as it implies that the delegation of Najran are doubters regarding what Allah has made clear to them in these verses. That is: if they persist in their disputation with you, in arrogance regarding this truth or regarding the matter of 'Isa, then call them to mubahala (mutual invocation of curse). For their insistence upon their belief after this clarification is pure arrogance, "after the knowledge has come to you," and you have explained it to them. Nothing clearer than what you have argued with them remains, so you know that they dispute with you only out of arrogance and lack of certainty. Therefore call them to mubahala (mutual cursing) in the manner described here.

"Ta'alaw" (تعالوا) is a verb-noun (ism fi'l) used to demand coming. Originally it is an imperative from ta'ala (تعالى), which means to seek height. So it was originally an order to ascend to a high place, honoring the one addressed; then it spread until it became used for any command to come or to be present, and the grammatical features of the verb-noun applied to it, so it is built on a final fatha. As for the verse of Abu Firas al-Hamdani:

"O neighbor, fate has not dealt justly between us; come (ta'ali), let me share my worries with you, come (ta'ali)"

they have made a grammatical error in it.

The meaning of ﴿Come, let us call our sons and your sons﴾ is: come and call your sons, and we call our sons, and so on to the end. The intended part is His saying: ﴿then let us invoke earnestly﴾ to the end.

"Thumma" (ثم) here indicates a sequence of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi).

Ibtihal (الابتهال) is derived from bahl (البهل), which is supplication with cursing, and it is applied to striving in supplication in general, because one who invokes a curse strives in his supplication. In the verse the first meaning is intended.

The meaning of ﴿we lay the curse of Allah﴾ is: we invoke the infliction of the curse of Allah upon the liars. This call to mubahala is a compulsion for them to either acknowledge the truth or desist. The exegetes and the historians narrate that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the delegation of Najran to mutual cursing, al-'Aqib said to them: "We will not curse him. By Allah, if he is a prophet and curses us, we will never prosper, nor will our descendants after us." So they did not respond to mubahala and turned to reconciliation, as will come.

This mubahala was perhaps among the methods of arbitration among the Christians, so the Prophet (ﷺ) invited them to it to establish the proof against them.

He mentioned sons and women in the mutual cursing only because, when their arrogance regarding the truth and love of worldly life became evident, it was known that one with such a character would hold his family and women dearer than the truth, as Shu'ayb said: ﴿Is my clan more dear to you than Allah?﴾ [Hud: 92], and that he fears the hardship of life and the loss of family, and does not fear the punishment of the Hereafter.

The apparent meaning of the first-person plural pronoun is that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ) and those Muslims with him, and those who attend for this purpose, and the sons of the delegation's members and their women who were with them.

The women here are, without doubt, the wives. This is a well-known usage among the Arabs when the word "nisa'" (women) is annexed to one or more persons, unlike when it occurs unannexed. Allah says: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other of women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 32], and He says: "and the women of the believers," and al-Nabigha says:

"Lest my leadership be taken, and my women (niswati) not remain free until they die."

"Al-anfus" (the selves) means our selves, the speakers, and your selves, the addressees, that is, ourselves and yourselves. As for the sons, it is possible that the intended meaning is their young men, and it is possible that it includes the children; the purpose is that the effects of the mutual cursing return upon them.

Ibtihal is an itifal form derived from bahl, which means cursing. It is said: "bahalahu Allah," meaning "cursed him," and the curse is bahlah and buhlah, with a damma or a fatha. Then ibtihal was used figuratively, in a well-known manner, for supplication in general. Al-A'sha said:

"Do not sit, though you have consumed her as firewood, seeking refuge from her evil one day, and supplicating."

This is the intended meaning here, as evidenced by his consequently stating: ﴿so we lay the curse of Allah upon the liars﴾.

This is a call to fairness that none issues except one confident that he is upon the truth. This mubahala did not take place, because the Christians of Najran did not respond to it. Abu Nu'aym narrated in al-Dala'il that the Prophet (ﷺ) prepared 'Ali, Fatimah, Hasan and Husayn to accompany him for the mubahala. They did not mention the bringing of his wives or the bringing of some of the Muslims in it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 62–63:

﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative. There is no god except Allah. And indeed, Allah is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, then indeed Allah is Knowing of the corrupters.﴾

The sentence ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative﴾ and what is conjoined to it with the particle waw is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) to explain what the phrase "the liars" (al-kadhibin) required, because they denied that 'Isa was a servant of Allah and claimed that he was overcome. Therefore, affirming that he is a servant is the truth.

The demonstrative (ism al-isharah) refers to what was mentioned of the denial of divinity from 'Isa.

صفحة ٢٦٧
The pronoun in His saying "lahuwa al-qasas" is a pronoun of separation (ḍamir al-fasl), and the lam of commencement (lam al-ibtida') entered upon it to add the emphasis that the pronoun of separation conveys, because the lam alone conveys the emphasis of the predicate, while the pronoun of separation conveys restriction (qasr), i.e., this is the narrative, not what the books of the Christians and their beliefs relate.
And al-qasas, with a fatha on the qaf and the ṣad, is a noun for what is related. One says: qassa al-khabar qaṣṣan, when he reported it. Qaṣṣ is more specific than reporting, for qaṣṣ is reporting of a report that has length and detail. The event that ought to be reported is called qiṣṣah with a kasra on the qaf, i.e., something related (maqṣūṣah), that is, of what the storytellers (quṣṣāṣ) relate. And the one who stands to narrate the reports of past people to people is called qaṣṣāṣ with a fatha on the qaf. So al-qasas is a noun for what is related. God the Exalted said: ﴿We relate to you the best of narratives﴾ [Yusuf: 3]. It was said: it is a noun of verbal action (ism al-masdar) and not a verbal noun (masdar). Whoever among the lexicographers has said on his tongue that it is a masdar, that is a laxity from the laxity of the earlier scholars. So al-qaṣṣ, with assimilation (idgham), is a masdar, and al-qasas, unassimilated, is a noun of verbal action and a noun for the narrated report.

His saying: "There is no god except Allah" is an affirmation of the truth of this narrative. The redundant "min" entered after the negative particle to explicitly indicate the intention of negating the genus, so that the sentence indicates monotheism and the denial of a partner clearly and by direct (muṭābaqah) indication, and so that it is not meant as negating unity from other than Allah, which would give the false impression that there might be two gods or more in some other direction. Although this ultimately leads to the denial of a partner, it does so by implication (iltizam).

His saying: "And indeed, Allah is the Exalted in Might, the Wise" contains what is in His saying "Indeed, this is the true narrative," so it adds emphasis to the report about God the Exalted through might and wisdom. The intended meaning is to nullify the divinity of the Messiah according to the belief of the addressees from the Christians, for they claim that the Jews killed him, and that is humiliation and incapacity, which do not agree with divinity. How could one be a god while not mighty, and subject to judgment? It is also a nullification of his divinity according to our belief, because he was in need of being rescued from the hands of the wrongdoers.

The sentence ﴿But if they turn away, then indeed Allah is Knowing of the corrupters﴾ is conjoined to His saying "Say: Come," and this is a recording against them, since they recoiled from the mubahalah. Thereby it is known that they intended obstinacy and did not seek the truth. It is narrated that when they refused the mubahalah, the Prophet ﷺ said to them: "If you refuse, then embrace Islam." They refused. He said: "If you refuse, then pay the jizyah from a position of submission." They refused. He said to them: "Then I will throw back to you [the covenant] on equal terms," i.e., I will abandon the covenant between us. They said: "We have no power to fight the Arabs, but we will make peace with you on condition that you do not raid us, nor frighten us, nor turn us back from our religion, in return for our paying you every year two thousand red garments: a thousand in Safar and a thousand in Rajab, and thirty iron coats of mail." They asked him to send with them a trustworthy man to judge between them. He said: "I will surely send with you a trustworthy man, truly trustworthy." So he sent with them Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, may Allah be pleased with him. I have not found what prompted them to request a trustworthy man, nor the length of time Abu 'Ubaydah remained among them.

﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we worship none but Allah and associate nothing with Him, and that some of us do not take others as lords besides Allah. But if they turn away, then say: Bear witness that we are Muslims.﴾

A return to the argument, after it had been cut off by the call to mubahalah (a mutual invocation in which the parties call down God's curse upon the liar). What prompted this return was concern for their faith, and it alludes to some deviation by the People of the Two Scriptures from the reality of "submitting one's face to Allah" (islam al-wajh lillah), as its explanation has already passed. In this disputation an argument is presented from which they cannot find any refuge: their summons to single out Allah for worship and to renounce the belief in associating others with Him in divinity. Thus the clause "Say: O People of the Scripture" stands in the position of an emphasis for the clause ﴿Say: Come, let us call our sons﴾ (3:61). This is because the implication of the first is an argument against them through the weakness of their confidence in the correctness of their belief, while the implication of this one is an argument against them through the soundness of the creed of Islam. For this reason this clause is not joined by a conjunction. By "the People of the Scripture" is meant here the Christians, because they are the ones who took a created being as lord and worshipped him alongside Allah.

"Come" (taʿalaw) is used here to request gathering around a equitable word, and this is a figurative expression: the word upon which people gather is made like a place at which the gathering is intended. The discussion of "taʿalaw" has passed shortly before.

"Word" (kalimah) is used here for a concise statement, as in His saying: ﴿No! It is but a word he utters﴾ (23:100).

[Page 269]

"Equitable" (sawāʾ) is here a verbal noun of istiwāʾ (equality). It has been said to mean justice, and it has been said to mean a moderate matter with no excess in it. Both may derive from their saying: "a place that is sawāʾ," "siwan," and "sawan," meaning intermediate. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So he saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ (37:55). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it means that about which all people are equal, for taking some of them as lords of others does not occur in a state of equality, and this is a good view. In any case, sawāʾ is not feminine, and it is applied as an attribute to "word" (kalimah), which is feminine, because describing with a verbal noun or a noun of verbal noun does not require agreement.

"That we not worship" (allā naʿbuda) is a substitute (badal) for "word" (kalimah). A group of scholars said that it is a substitute for "equitable" (sawāʾ). Ibn Hisham rejected this in the second type of the sixth aspect of the rules of grammatical parsing (qawāʿid al-iʿrāb) in his Mughni al-Labib, and al-Damamini and others objected to him.

The truth is that it is rejected from the standpoint of observing the technical convention, not from the standpoint of meaning; for "equitable" (sawāʾ) is an attribute of "word" (kalimah), and if "that we not worship" were made a substitute for "equitable," it would become in effect an attribute of "word," and it would not be proper to describe "word" with it.

The pronoun in "between us" (baynanā) refers to something known from the context, namely the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims. For this reason there followed it: ﴿then say: Bear witness that we are Muslims﴾.

From His saying "that we not worship none but Allah" to the end, there is derived an allusion to all those who worshipped the Messiah.

As for His saying "But if they turn away": the conditional particle "in" (in) is used in this condition, because turning away after the establishment of this argument and the proofs preceding it is rare in occurrence. The context contains what is suitable for uprooting the occurrence of this condition, so the verb of the condition has become, by its nature, something rare in occurrence and supposed. This is among the uses of the conditional "in." So if that happens from them, they have come to a state in which their submission is to be despaired of, so turn away from them, and hold fast to your own submission, and have them bear witness that you are upon your submission. The meaning of this calling to witness is recording against them, lest they display the Muslims' withdrawal from pursuing the argument with them in the guise of incapacity and submission to the correctness of what the People of the Scripture hold. This is the meaning of calling them to witness: "that we are Muslims."

[Page 270]

﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you dispute about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him? Will you not then use your reason?﴾ ﴿Here you are, you who argued about what you had knowledge of, but why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of? And Allah knows, while you do not know.﴾

This is a fresh resumptive sentence (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a new sentence beginning a new topic) that shifts from calling them to the word of truth that unites the essence of religion, to rebuking them for their false disputation with the Muslims concerning the religion of Abraham. Each group among them claimed to be upon his religion, aiming to conclude that whoever opposes their religion cannot be upon the religion of Abraham, as the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) claimed. Thus, the disputation is a branch of the opposition in claims. This disputation proceeds by way of *qiyas al-musawat fi al-nafy* (analogy of equality in negation), or their disputation with the Prophet regarding his claim that he was upon the religion of Abraham. It is a disputation by which they intended to refute the equivalence of his religion with the religion of Abraham, also by way of *qiyas al-musawat fi al-nafy*.

This sentence may be part of what the Messenger was commanded to say in the verse ﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, come to a word [common to us and you]﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:64], meaning: say to them, "O People of the Scripture, why do you dispute..." It may also be that the resumption is from the speech of Allah the Exalted, following His command to the Messenger to say "come," so that it is a direct address to the People of the Scripture. In that case, the first sentence is considered part of the Messenger's speech and this one is not, because the first concerns the matters of the call (*da'wah*), while this one concerns the methods of disputation and refuting their claims, which belong to the second level of the call. All of this is equal in its attribution to Allah.

The occasion for shifting from the previous speech to this one arose from His saying: ﴿But if they turn away, then say: Bear witness that we are Muslims﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:64]. This is because it became widely known, in what was revealed of the Qur'an in Mecca and after it, that the Islam brought by Muhammad (peace be upon him) goes back to the *hanifiyyah*, the religion of Abraham, as has been established previously in Surat al-Baqarah, and as in Surat al-Naḥl: ﴿Then We revealed to you: Follow the religion of Abraham, a *hanif*﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:123]. It will also come that Abraham was a *hanif* and a Muslim. This was publicized and proclaimed among the polytheists in Mecca, among the Jews in Medina, and among the Christians in the delegation of Najran. It is known that the polytheists in Mecca claimed that they were the heirs of the law of Abraham and custodians (*sadanah*) of his House, and the People of the Scripture had claimed that they were upon the religion of Abraham. It is not clear to me whether this was an old claim from them, or whether they became aware of it from the call of Muhammad (ﷺ) and so awakened to imitate him in that, or whether they said it in order to confound the Messenger when he argued with them that his religion is the truth and that the religion with Allah is Islam. So they forced him to one of two options: either the addition to the religion of Abraham does not take one out of following him, in which case it is a shared obligation for Judaism and Christianity alike; or it does take one out of the religion of Abraham, in which case Islam cannot be a follower of the religion of Abraham.

I think that their claim to be upon the religion of Abraham was adopted in order that each of the two groups might spread its call to its religion among the Arabs, especially Christianity, since its missionaries tried to spread it among the Arabs and found nothing that would be accepted by them except saying: "It is the religion of Abraham." For this reason, it was followed by some Arab tribes. There are reports about the occasions of revelation that stir these possibilities. It is narrated that "the delegation of Najran said to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he called them to follow his religion: 'Upon what religion are you?' He said: 'Upon the religion of Abraham.' They said: 'You have added to it what was not in it.'" According to this narration, the People of the Scripture addressed here are specifically the Christians, as in the address before it. It is also narrated that the Jews and the Christians of Najran disputed in Medina in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and each group claimed that it alone was upon the religion of Abraham, so the address is to all the People of the Scripture, both Jews and Christians.

Perhaps the difference in the addressees is what calls for the repetition of the address.

His saying ﴿when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾ according to the first narration is a prohibition of their statement "you have added to it what is not from it," and its intended purpose is to refute that Islam is the religion of Abraham. The detail of this prohibition is: you have no means of knowing the religion of Abraham, so from where do you know that Islam added to what came from Abraham's religion? You have no basis for acting in matters of religion except the Torah and the Gospel, and both were revealed after Abraham. So how can it be known what the law of Abraham was, so that what was added to it could be known? The mention of the Torah in this context is because it is the root of the Gospel. According to the second narration, it is a negation of the claim of each of the two groups that it is upon the religion of Abraham: the religion of the Jews is the Torah, and the religion of the Christians is the Gospel, and both were revealed after Abraham, so how could they be a law for him? Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: meaning, it is not stated in either of these two books that it agrees with the law of Abraham. So the mention of the Torah and the Gospel in this sense is *nashr ba'd al-laff* (distribution after folding): since the People of the Scripture includes both groups, the mention of the Torah refutes the claim of the Jews, and the mention of the Gospel refutes the claim of the Christians. The mention of the Torah and the Gospel here aims to include both groups in the charge of error, even though the primary intended addressees, from the start, are the Christians with whom the discourse is concerned.

In my view, the clearest arrangement of the argument is what results from the totality of His saying ﴿when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾, His saying ﴿why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of﴾, and His saying ﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾. Thereby, their claim that they are upon the religion of Abraham is refuted, and their claim that Islam is not upon the religion of Abraham is refuted, and it is established against them that Islam is upon the religion of Abraham. This is because His saying ﴿when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾ indicates that their knowledge of the religion is confined to these two, and both were revealed after Abraham, so it is not possible that they are the very scrolls of Abraham.

His saying ﴿why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of﴾ refutes their statement that Islam added to the religion of Abraham, and does not indicate that they are upon the religion of Abraham, because the Torah and the Gospel do not state this explicitly. This is the distinction between the attribution of Islam to Abraham and the attribution of Judaism and Christianity to him. They say: how can it be claimed that Islam is the religion of Abraham when the Qur'an was revealed after Abraham, just as the Torah and the Gospel were revealed after him?

His saying "And Allah knows" indicates that Allah informed in the Qur'an that He sent Muhammad with Islam, the religion of Abraham, and He is more knowing of that than you. He had not previously bestowed upon you a similar favor in the Torah and the Gospel, so you do not know this. When Islam came and informed of this, you wanted to claim this distinction, and you awakened to it out of envy for this blessing. Thus the proof was established against them, and they had no excuse to say that the coming of the Torah and the Gospel after Abraham is a shared obligation for us and for you, since the Qur'an was revealed after Abraham. Had the proof not been arranged in the manner we have mentioned, it would have been a shared obligation.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿why do you argue﴾ is intended to alert them to an error.

[Page 271 continues below]

[Page 273]

In this argument against them, He left aside refuting the contradiction between the addition in the religion brought by Muhammad (ﷺ) over the religion brought by Abraham, and the description of Islam as the religion of Abraham. This is because they did not have the soundness of reasoning to distinguish between the addition of branches and the unity of roots. The equality of the two religions is regarded in terms of the unity of their roots, which we will explain when interpreting His saying: ﴿And if they argue with you, say: I have submitted myself to Allah﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:20], and at His saying: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:67]. Thus, in the argument, it suffices to refute their basis in their saying "you have added to it what is not in it," in the manner of prohibition, and then with His saying: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a *hanif*, a Muslim﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:67] in the manner of assertion, based on the principle that the objector's interruption is sufficient to counter the claim of the one who argues by proof.

His saying ﴿Here you are, you who argued﴾ has had its parallel discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Then you, these are the ones who kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:85] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Ibn Kathir and the majority read "*hā antum*" with the *alif* of *hā* retained and the hamza of *antum* lightened. Qalun, Abu ʿAmr, and Yaʿqub read it with the *alif* retained and the hamza of "*antum*" softened (*tashīl*). Warsh read it with the *alif* of "*hā*" deleted, the hamza of "*antum*" softened, and also replaced by an *alif* with extension (*madd*). Qunbul read it with the hamza lightened without an *alif*.

The interrogative "*mā*" occurs after the particle of causation *lām*, so what is asked about is the cause of the disputation. Thus the referent of "*mā*" is an unknown cause among the causes, meaning the cause of the disputation is unknown, because it is not of the kind that can be known, since it has no existence, and therefore it is not known. So the question about it is a figurative expression for its non-existence. This is close to the meaning of the reproachful interrogative, but is not identical to it.

The *alif* of the interrogative "*mā*" is deleted, as is the usual practice when it is preceded by a preposition, as in ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ [al-Naba' 78:1], and in the verse of Ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

"Why do you say the spear weighs upon my shoulder?"

When the letters written in the form of *yā'* in the prepositions are followed by one of those prepositions, "*mā*" is written with an *alif* in the form of *alif*, because "*mā*" has become a single letter and so resembles part of a word, and therefore the *alifs* are written like those in the middle of words.

His saying "*fi Ibrahim*" means "in some aspect of his affairs," and it is evident that what is meant here is his religion. This is an instance of attributing a ruling to the essence, where the intended meaning is a state of the essence that is determined by the context, as was explained previously in interpreting His saying: ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:173] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The "*ha*" in "*ha antum*" is for alerting attention. The original sentence is "*antum hajajtum*" (you argued). Such a construction occurs in contexts of wonder, rebuke, alerting, and the like. For this reason, it is often emphasized by a demonstrative after it, so one says "*ha anā*," "*ha antum ulā'*," or "*hā'ulā'*."

"*Hajajtum*" is the predicate of "*antum*." You may also take the clause "*hajajtum*" as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) which is the locus of wonder, in view of what is conjoined to it, namely His saying: "*falima tuhājjūna*" (why do you argue), because the interrogative there is reproachful, so its meaning is: "*fa-lā tuhājjūna*" (so do not argue).

The explanation of a similar construction will come in His saying: ﴿Here you are, you love them﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:119].

His saying ﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾ is a completion of the proof, meaning: the Qur'an, which is from Allah, has established that it is the religion of Abraham, and you were not guided to that because you do not know.

This is like His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Or do they say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes were Jews or Christians? Say: Are you more knowing, or is Allah?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:140].

[Page 270]

﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you dispute about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him? Will you not then use your reason?﴾ ﴿Here you are, you who argued about what you had knowledge of, but why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of? And Allah knows, while you do not know.﴾
