Thus, the disputation is a branch of the opposition in claims. This disputation proceeds by way of *qiyas al-musawat fi al-nafy* (analogy of equality in negation), or their disputation with the Prophet regarding his claim that he was upon the religion of Abraham. It is a disputation by which they intended to refute the equivalence of his religion with the religion of Abraham, also by way of *qiyas al-musawat fi al-nafy*.

This sentence may be part of what the Messenger was commanded to say in the verse ﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, come to a word [common to us and you]﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:64], meaning: say to them, "O People of the Scripture, why do you dispute..." It may also be that the resumption is from the speech of Allah the Exalted, following His command to the Messenger to say "come," so that it is a direct address to the People of the Scripture. In that case, the first sentence is considered part of the Messenger's speech and this one is not, because the first concerns the matters of the call (*da'wah*), while this one concerns the methods of disputation and refuting their claims, which belong to the second level of the call. All of this is equal in its attribution to Allah.

The occasion for shifting from the previous speech to this one arose from His saying: ﴿But if they turn away, then say: Bear witness that we are Muslims﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:64]. This is because it became widely known, in what was revealed of the Qur'an in Mecca and after it, that the Islam brought by Muhammad (peace be upon him) goes back to the *hanifiyyah*, the religion of Abraham, as has been established previously in Surat al-Baqarah, and as in Surat al-Naḥl: ﴿Then We revealed to you: Follow the religion of Abraham, a *hanif*﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:123]. It will also come that Abraham was a *hanif* and a Muslim. This was publicized and proclaimed among the polytheists in Mecca, among the Jews in Medina, and among the Christians in the delegation of Najran. It is known that the polytheists in Mecca claimed that they were the heirs of the law of Abraham and custodians (*sadanah*) of his House, and the People of the Scripture had claimed that they were upon the religion of Abraham. It is not clear to me whether this was an old claim from them, or whether they became aware of it from the call of Muhammad (ﷺ) and so awakened to imitate him in that, or whether they said it in order to confound the Messenger when he argued with them that his religion is the truth and that the religion with Allah is Islam. So they forced him to one of two options: either the addition to the religion of Abraham does not take one out of following him, in which case it is a shared obligation for Judaism and Christianity alike; or it does take one out of the religion of Abraham, in which case Islam cannot be a follower of the religion of Abraham.

I think that their claim to be upon the religion of Abraham was adopted in order that each of the two groups might spread its call to its religion among the Arabs, especially Christianity, since its missionaries tried to spread it among the Arabs and found nothing that would be accepted by them except saying: "It is the religion of Abraham." For this reason, it was followed by some Arab tribes. There are reports about the occasions of revelation that stir these possibilities. It is narrated that "the delegation of Najran said to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he called them to follow his religion: 'Upon what religion are you?' He said: 'Upon the religion of Abraham.' They said: 'You have added to it what was not in it.'" According to this narration, the People of the Scripture addressed here are specifically the Christians, as in the address before it. It is also narrated that the Jews and the Christians of Najran disputed in Medina in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and each group claimed that it alone was upon the religion of Abraham, so the address is to all the People of the Scripture, both Jews and Christians.

Perhaps the difference in the addressees is what calls for the repetition of the address.

His saying ﴿when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾ according to the first narration is a prohibition of their statement "you have added to it what is not from it," and its intended purpose is to refute that Islam is the religion of Abraham. The detail of this prohibition is: you have no means of knowing the religion of Abraham, so from where do you know that Islam added to what came from Abraham's religion? You have no basis for acting in matters of religion except the Torah and the Gospel, and both were revealed after Abraham. So how can it be known what the law of Abraham was, so that what was added to it could be known? The mention of the Torah in this context is because it is the root of the Gospel. According to the second narration, it is a negation of the claim of each of the two groups that it is upon the religion of Abraham: the religion of the Jews is the Torah, and the religion of the Christians is the Gospel, and both were revealed after Abraham, so how could they be a law for him? Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: meaning, it is not stated in either of these two books that it agrees with the law of Abraham. So the mention of the Torah and the Gospel in this sense is *nashr ba'd al-laff* (distribution after folding): since the People of the Scripture includes both groups, the mention of the Torah refutes the claim of the Jews, and the mention of the Gospel refutes the claim of the Christians. The mention of the Torah and the Gospel here aims to include both groups in the charge of error, even though the primary intended addressees, from the start, are the Christians with whom the discourse is concerned.

In my view, the clearest arrangement of the argument is what results from the totality of His saying ﴿when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾, His saying ﴿why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of﴾, and His saying ﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾. Thereby, their claim that they are upon the religion of Abraham is refuted, and their claim that Islam is not upon the religion of Abraham is refuted, and it is established against them that Islam is upon the religion of Abraham. This is because His saying ﴿when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾ indicates that their knowledge of the religion is confined to these two, and both were revealed after Abraham, so it is not possible that they are the very scrolls of Abraham.

His saying ﴿why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of﴾ refutes their statement that Islam added to the religion of Abraham, and does not indicate that they are upon the religion of Abraham, because the Torah and the Gospel do not state this explicitly. This is the distinction between the attribution of Islam to Abraham and the attribution of Judaism and Christianity to him. They say: how can it be claimed that Islam is the religion of Abraham when the Qur'an was revealed after Abraham, just as the Torah and the Gospel were revealed after him?

His saying "And Allah knows" indicates that Allah informed in the Qur'an that He sent Muhammad with Islam, the religion of Abraham, and He is more knowing of that than you. He had not previously bestowed upon you a similar favor in the Torah and the Gospel, so you do not know this. When Islam came and informed of this, you wanted to claim this distinction, and you awakened to it out of envy for this blessing. Thus the proof was established against them, and they had no excuse to say that the coming of the Torah and the Gospel after Abraham is a shared obligation for us and for you, since the Qur'an was revealed after Abraham. Had the proof not been arranged in the manner we have mentioned, it would have been a shared obligation.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿why do you argue﴾ is intended to alert them to an error.

[Page 271 continues below]

[Page 273]

In this argument against them, He left aside refuting the contradiction between the addition in the religion brought by Muhammad (ﷺ) over the religion brought by Abraham, and the description of Islam as the religion of Abraham. This is because they did not have the soundness of reasoning to distinguish between the addition of branches and the unity of roots. The equality of the two religions is regarded in terms of the unity of their roots, which we will explain when interpreting His saying: ﴿And if they argue with you, say: I have submitted myself to Allah﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:20], and at His saying: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:67]. Thus, in the argument, it suffices to refute their basis in their saying "you have added to it what is not in it," in the manner of prohibition, and then with His saying: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a *hanif*, a Muslim﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:67] in the manner of assertion, based on the principle that the objector's interruption is sufficient to counter the claim of the one who argues by proof.

His saying ﴿Here you are, you who argued﴾ has had its parallel discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Then you, these are the ones who kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:85] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Ibn Kathir and the majority read "*hā antum*" with the *alif* of *hā* retained and the hamza of *antum* lightened. Qalun, Abu ʿAmr, and Yaʿqub read it with the *alif* retained and the hamza of "*antum*" softened (*tashīl*). Warsh read it with the *alif* of "*hā*" deleted, the hamza of "*antum*" softened, and also replaced by an *alif* with extension (*madd*). Qunbul read it with the hamza lightened without an *alif*.

The interrogative "*mā*" occurs after the particle of causation *lām*, so what is asked about is the cause of the disputation. Thus the referent of "*mā*" is an unknown cause among the causes, meaning the cause of the disputation is unknown, because it is not of the kind that can be known, since it has no existence, and therefore it is not known. So the question about it is a figurative expression for its non-existence. This is close to the meaning of the reproachful interrogative, but is not identical to it.

The *alif* of the interrogative "*mā*" is deleted, as is the usual practice when it is preceded by a preposition, as in ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ [al-Naba' 78:1], and in the verse of Ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

"Why do you say the spear weighs upon my shoulder?"

When the letters written in the form of *yā'* in the prepositions are followed by one of those prepositions, "*mā*" is written with an *alif* in the form of *alif*, because "*mā*" has become a single letter and so resembles part of a word, and therefore the *alifs* are written like those in the middle of words.

His saying "*fi Ibrahim*" means "in some aspect of his affairs," and it is evident that what is meant here is his religion. This is an instance of attributing a ruling to the essence, where the intended meaning is a state of the essence that is determined by the context, as was explained previously in interpreting His saying: ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:173] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The "*ha*" in "*ha antum*" is for alerting attention. The original sentence is "*antum hajajtum*" (you argued). Such a construction occurs in contexts of wonder, rebuke, alerting, and the like. For this reason, it is often emphasized by a demonstrative after it, so one says "*ha anā*," "*ha antum ulā'*," or "*hā'ulā'*."

"*Hajajtum*" is the predicate of "*antum*." You may also take the clause "*hajajtum*" as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) which is the locus of wonder, in view of what is conjoined to it, namely His saying: "*falima tuhājjūna*" (why do you argue), because the interrogative there is reproachful, so its meaning is: "*fa-lā tuhājjūna*" (so do not argue).

The explanation of a similar construction will come in His saying: ﴿Here you are, you love them﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:119].

His saying ﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾ is a completion of the proof, meaning: the Qur'an, which is from Allah, has established that it is the religion of Abraham, and you were not guided to that because you do not know.

This is like His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Or do they say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes were Jews or Christians? Say: Are you more knowing, or is Allah?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:140].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 67:

﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a ḥanīf (one who turns away from falsehood to pure monotheism), a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾

This is a conclusion drawn from the argument, since it has become clear from the preceding proof that Judaism and Christianity are other than the ḥanīfiyyah, and that Musa (Moses) and 'Isa (Jesus), peace be upon them both, did not declare that they were upon the ḥanifiyyah. Hence it follows that Abraham was not upon the state of Judaism or Christianity, since this was not transmitted from Musa or 'Isa, peace be upon them both. Its basis is the absence of any claim to that in their books. How can Judaism or Christianity be part of the ḥanifiyyah when they are devoid of the obligation of the Pilgrimage (ḥajj), while Islam has come with mention of its obligation for whoever is able to undertake it?

What supports this is what Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned in his tafsir on the words of God Most High in this surah: ﴿We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are Muslims﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 84], from 'Ikrimah, who said: "When this verse was revealed, the people of the religions said, 'We became Muslims before you, and we are the Muslims.' So God said to him: 'Argue with them, O Muhammad,' and God revealed: ﴿And for God, upon mankind, is the pilgrimage to the House﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 97], and the Muslims performed the Pilgrimage while the disbelievers stayed back." [p. 275] Then God completed this with His words: "and he was not of the polytheists," thereby nullifying the claims of the three groups.

The ḥanīf was discussed earlier, at His words: ﴿Say: Rather, the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 135], in Surah al-Baqarah.

His words: ﴿but he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ express a correction (istidrak) after negating the opposite, restricting Abraham's state to what agrees with the foundations of Islam. For this reason he clarified "ḥanīf" with the word "Muslim," because they knew the meaning of the ḥanifiyyah but did not believe in Islam. So He informed them that Islam is the ḥanifiyyah. He then said, "and he was not of the polytheists," negating for Abraham agreement with Judaism, agreement with Christianity, and agreement with the polytheists, and that he was a Muslim, so his agreement with Islam is established. It has been mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah in several places that Abraham asked to be a Muslim, that God commanded him to be a Muslim, that he was a ḥanīf, and that the Islam brought by Muhammad (ﷺ) is the same Islam brought by Abraham: ﴿They say, "Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided." Say: Rather, the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 135]. All of this leaves no doubt that Islam is the Islam of Abraham.

I have already explained, a little earlier, at His words: ﴿So if they argue with you, say: I have submitted my face to God﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 20], the principles included under the meaning of ﴿I have submitted my face to God﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 20]. Let us apply them to the meaning of Abraham's words: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 79]. Abraham brought tawhid (monotheism) and declared it openly, leaving no path for shirk (polytheism) into the hearts of the heedless. He established a sanctuary, which is the Ka'bah, the first House placed for mankind, and he made its Pilgrimage obligatory upon mankind, in connection with its purpose. He declared his complete servitude to God Most High with His words: ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him, except that my Lord wills something﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 80]. He made his speech and action sincerely for God Most High, saying: ﴿And how should I fear what you associate, while you do not fear that you associate with God that for which He has not sent down to you any authority?﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 81]. He sought guidance with His words: ﴿Our Lord, and make us Muslims to You﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 128], ﴿and show us our rites and accept our repentance﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 128]. He smashed the idols with his own hand: ﴿So he reduced them to fragments﴾ [Surah al-Anbiya': 58]. He manifested devotion to God with His words: ﴿He who created me, and He guides me﴾ [Surah al-Shu'ara': 78], ﴿and He who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ [Surah al-Shu'ara': 79], ﴿and when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾ [Surah al-Shu'ara': 80], ﴿and He who causes me to die and then gives me life﴾ [Surah al-Shu'ara': 81]. He undertook argument for the oneness of God and His attributes: ﴿Abraham said, "Indeed, God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west"﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 258], and ﴿That was Our argument which We gave to Abraham against his people﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 83]. His people argued with him.

[p. 276] His words ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ are conjoined so that the polytheists of the Arabs would despair of being upon the religion of Abraham, and so that no one would imagine that the restriction (qaṣr) derived from His words ﴿but he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim﴾ is a restriction relative to (qaṣr idafi, a restriction limited to a specific counterpart) Judaism and Christianity, since the Arabs used to claim that they were upon the religion of Abraham, but they were polytheists.

**[Page 277]**

It is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) arising from the negation of Judaism and Christianity from Abraham. Neither the Jews, nor the Christians, nor the polytheists are the closest of people to him. This indicates that they used to say: "We are closer to your religion."

"*Awlā*" is an elative form (*ism tafḍīl*), meaning more intensely *walā*, that is, nearer, derived from *waliya* when one becomes a *walī* (close ally). It takes the preposition *bi-* because it implies the sense of connection: the people most specially connected to Abraham and nearest to him. Some exegetes took "*awlā*" here to mean "more deserving" (*ajdar*), so they had to posit an omitted noun before "*bi-Ibrāhīm*," meaning "by the religion of Abraham."

Those who followed Abraham are those who followed him during his lifetime, such as Lot, Ishmael and Isaac. No account is taken of those who tried to follow the *ḥanīfiyya* (the pure monotheism of Abraham) but did not reach it, such as Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt, his father Abū al-Ṣalt, and Abū Qays Ṣirma ibn Abī Anas of the Banū al-Najjār. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt almost became Muslim," though he did not live to see Islam, so the meaning is that he almost became a *ḥanīf*.

In the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of al-Bukhārī: Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl went out to Syria seeking the religion. He met a learned man of the Jews and asked him about his religion. He said: "I want to be upon your religion." The Jew said: "You will not be upon our religion until you take your share of the wrath of God." Zayd said: "I only flee from the wrath of God, and I will never bear any of the wrath of God, while I am able. Can you guide me to a religion that does not include this?" He said: "I know of none except that you be a *ḥanīf*." He said: "And what is the *ḥanīf*?" He said: "The religion of Abraham; he was neither a Jew nor a Christian, and he worshipped none but God." So he left him and met a learned man of the Christians, and debated with him like the debate with the Jew, except that the Christian said: "You must take your share of the curse of God." So he left him, and they had agreed upon the religion of Abraham for him. He then kept raising his hands to the sky and said: "O God, bear witness that I am upon the religion of Abraham." This was a wish from him that did not coincide with reality.

In the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of al-Bukhārī, from Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr, she said: "I saw Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl before Islam, leaning his back against the Kaʿba, and he was saying: 'O assembly of Quraysh, none of you is upon the religion of Abraham except me.'" In it also: "The Prophet (ﷺ) met Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl at the lower part of Baldaḥ before revelation came to the Prophet (ﷺ). A food-spread (*sufra*) was presented to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Zayd ibn ʿAmr refused to eat from it, and said: 'I do not eat what you slaughter on your idols (*anṣāb*), and I eat only what the name of God has been mentioned over.'" This was a misconception on his part that the Prophet (ﷺ) acted as Quraysh acted. Zayd used to criticise Quraysh for their slaughter, saying: "God created the sheep, sent down water for it from the sky, and caused to grow for it from the earth, then you slaughter it for other than the name of God."

The demonstrative in His saying "*wa-hādhā al-Nabiyy*" ("and this Prophet") is used figuratively for one who is well known by a description among those addressed, as in his saying in the Hadith: "The moth and these creatures (*dawābb*) began to fall into the fire." Here the demonstrative is used to evoke the creatures known for falling into fire when it is kindled. The Prophet was not present before the addressees at that time of the verse, nor was the demonstrative intended to refer to his person. It is also possible that the demonstrative is used with the sense of presence of speech, in view of the Prophet being the one who utters this speech. It is like the saying of the poet:

*You were saved, and this (one) you carry is free.*

That is: and the one whom you carry is the speaker. The noun that comes after the demonstrative, in apposition to it, is what specifies what the demonstrative refers to. "The Prophet" is conjoined to "those who followed Abraham" for the sake of emphasis on him, and there is in this an indication that his following of Abraham (peace be upon him) is not a general following. Thus Islam's being of the *ḥanīfiyya* is that it agrees with it in its foundations.

By "those who believed" (*alladhīna āmanū*) is meant the Muslims. The intended meaning is the title-sense, for the description "those who believed" became a title for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), which is why their address in the Qur'an is frequent with "O you who believe."

The reason why this Prophet and those who believed are the closest of people to Abraham, like those who followed him, is that they have adopted the principles of his law, recognised his station, and were for him a truthful tongue, constantly mentioning him. These are more deserving of him than those who ascribed themselves to him but violated the principles of his law, namely the polytheists; and than those who ascribed themselves to him and forgot the remembrance of his law, namely the Jews and Christians. From this meaning is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying, when he asked about the Jews' fast on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ and they said: "It is a day on which God delivered Moses," he said: "We are more deserving of Moses than they are," and he fasted it and commanded the Muslims to fast it.

His saying: "*wa-Allāhu walīyu al-mu'minīn*" ("and God is the Protector of the believers") is a *tadhyīl* (concluding statement), meaning: these are the closest of people to Abraham, and God is the Protector of Abraham, of those who followed him, of this Prophet, and of those who believed. This is because the *tadhyīl* certainly includes what it concludes, and then includes other things as a completion, like a general statement upon a particular cause. In His saying "*wa-Allāhu walīyu al-mu'minīn*," after His saying "*mā kāna Ibrāhīmu yahūdiyyan*" ("Abraham was neither a Jew") [Āl ʿImrān: 67], there is an allusion that those who are not of Abraham's religion are not believers.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 69:**

﴿A group of the People of the Book wish they could lead you astray, but they lead astray none except themselves, and they do not perceive.﴾

It is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh point) whose connection is His saying: ﴿So if they turn away, then say, "Bear witness that we are Muslims"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 64] and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham﴾ [Al 'Imran: 68], and so on. The intended "People of the Book" here are specifically the Jews. For this reason He described them as ﴿a group of the People of the Book﴾, lest it be supposed that they are the People of the Book with whom the argument was held in the preceding verses.

The intended "group" is a company of them from Qurayza, al-Nadir and Qaynuqa', who invited 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman to return to polytheism (*shirk*).

The clause ﴿they wish they could lead you astray﴾ explains the content of the clause "they wish" (*wadda*) by way of summary and detail. The *law* (*lau*) here is a conditional particle used metaphorically to express a wish (*tamanni*), because wishing is one of the implications of the counterfactual conditional (*al-shart al-imtina'i*). The apodosis of the condition is omitted, and it is indicated by the verb *wadda* ("they wish"); its estimated form is: "If they led you astray, their desired outcome would be achieved." The truth is that the expression of a wish is an incidental meaning of *law* (in its counterfactual use) in certain contexts, not one of its original meanings. A parallel to this has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 96], in the surah of al-Baqarah.

[p. 279]

His saying ﴿they wish they could lead you astray﴾ means: they wished for your misguidance. It may be understood in two ways: that they wished to make them astray in the view of the People of the Book, i.e., to cause them to waver (*yudhabdhibuhum*); or that the intended meaning is actual misguidance, although the People of the Book's wish was that they would make them Jews. On both interpretations, His saying ﴿but they lead astray none except themselves﴾ may mean: when they lead people astray, they themselves have also become astray, because leading astray is itself a form of straying. It may also mean: they had been astray from before, by their contentment with remaining upon a religion that has been abrogated (*dinun mansukh*; *naskh* being the abrogation of a ruling or a religion by a later one). His saying ﴿and they do not perceive﴾ suits both possibilities, because knowledge of both states is subtle.

This is a turn to address the Jews. The interrogative is one of denunciation. "Verses" (āyāt) means the miracles, and for this reason He said, "while you witness [them]." Repeating their address with "O People of the Book" a second time is for the purpose of rebuke and of recording their falsehood against them. Confounding the truth with falsehood (talbīs al-ḥaqq bil-bāṭil) refers to their distorting their religion with what they introduced into it of fabrications, superstitions, and false interpretations, to the point that trust in all of it was lost. Concealing the truth may be taken to mean their concealing the confirmation of Muhammad (ﷺ), and it may also be taken to mean their concealing what is in the Torah of rulings, which they caused to die out and replaced with the deeds of their rabbis and the traces of their interpretations, while they know it and do not act upon it.

[p. 280]

This is coordinated with ﴿they desired (ودّت)...﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 69]. The first group sought to lead [the believers] astray openly, while this group sought it through deception. It has been said that this refers to a group of Jews, among them Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik ibn al-Sayf, and others from the Jews of Khaybar, whom conceit in their religion led astray, so they imagined that they were a model for the people. When open opposition failed them through obstinacy, they devised another scheme for the plot. They said to a group of their followers: "Believe in Muhammad at the beginning of the day, showing that you have affirmed him, then disbelieve at the end of the day, so that it appears that you disbelieved in him with insight and experience. Then the Muslims will say: 'Nothing turned these people away from us except what was revealed to them of the truth of this religion, and that it is not the religion promised in the earlier Books.'" So they did this.

His saying ﴿upon those who believed﴾ may be from the wording of the reported speech itself, meaning that the Jews said: "Believe in what has been sent down upon the followers of Muhammad," and God, exalted is He, changed it to ﴿upon those who believed﴾ to honour the sincerity of their faith. It may also be from the reporter's own words, meaning that the Jews applied this description to the followers of Muhammad, since it had become a designation for them through dominance. ﴿The beginning of the day (وجه النهار)﴾ means its first part, and this was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿honoured in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 45].

His saying ﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 73] is part of the speech of this group of the People of the Book. By it they intended a precaution (ihtiras), lest the believers suppose from their saying ﴿Believe in what has been sent down upon those who believed at the beginning of the day﴾ that it was true faith. The meaning is: "Do not believe with true faith ﴿except in one who follows your religion﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 73]; as for Muhammad, do not believe in him, for he has not followed your religion." This is thus a justification for the prohibition.

This is an excuse against the obligation they were under, since their Books had given good news of the coming of a messenger who would come after Moses (muqaffin). They imagined that he would come only with the law of the Torah, and they erred regarding the lack of benefit in his coming with what is in the Torah, because that would be obtaining what is already obtained (tahsil al-hasil), and the act of God is exalted above such a thing. So the messenger who comes after Moses could only be one who abrogates (naskh) part of the law of the Torah. Thus their combining between the statement ﴿Believe in what has been sent down upon those who believed﴾ and the statement ﴿And do not believe﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 73] is like ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾ [al-Anfal: 17].

His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 73] is an interjected statement (kalam mu'taridh). The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was commanded to say it to them. It is an allusion (kinaya) to the improbability of their being guided, and that God had not guided them, because the guidance of others, that is, the attempt by others to guide people, does not achieve the desired result unless God decrees it. The restriction (qasr) here is real (haqiqi): what God has not decreed is only the appearance of guidance and not guidance, and this is the counterpart of their saying ﴿Believe in what has been sent down﴾ and ﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 73], since they intended the appearance of faith and it was not faith.

[p. 281] In this answer there is also a demonstration of independence from their following.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 73–74:**

﴿أنْ يُؤْتى أحَدٌ مِثْلَ ما أُوتِيتُمْ أوْ يُحاجُّوكم عِنْدَ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ .

The placement of this verse after what precedes it was problematic, both in terms of the structure of the discourse and in determining which group its meaning refers to. Al-Qurtubi said it is the most difficult verse in this surah. Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned eight interpretations, which go back to two fundamental possibilities.

The first possibility is that it completes the dialogue of a group of the People of the Book among themselves, and that the sentence ﴿قُلْ إنَّ الهُدى هُدى اللَّهِ﴾ ("Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God") is a parenthetical interjection within that dialogue. Under this possibility come several interpretations, of which we will mention two clear ones. The first is that they intended to give a reason for their statement ﴿ولا تُؤْمِنُوا إلّا لِمَن تَبِعَ دِينَكُمْ﴾ ("And do not believe except in one who follows your religion"). The context of the speech requires that they meant the impossibility of abrogating (naskh) the law of the Torah, and the impossibility of sending a messenger after Moses. An explanatory lam (the lam of purpose) is understood before the verbal particle ''an'' (أنْ), and this deletion is common. Then either a negative particle is understood after ''an'', as the context indicates and as the word ''aḥad'' (أحَدٌ) requires, since it is meant to denote the inclusion of every individual. That word is not used with the sense of universal inclusion except in a negative context, or in something that carries the meaning of negation, such as a rhetorical interrogative of denial. When ''aḥad'' is used in an affirmative statement, it means the attribute of oneness, and that is not appropriate in this verse.

So the sense of the sentence is: "Lest anyone be given what you have been given." The deletion of the negative particle after the lam of purpose, whether expressed or understood, is frequent in speech, and an example is the words of God, Exalted: ﴿يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكم أنْ تَضِلُّوا﴾ ("God makes clear to you, lest you go astray") [al-Nisa: 176], meaning: lest you go astray.

The meaning is that their aim in this statement was to firm up their own souls in adherence to the religion of Judaism, because the Jews do not permit the abrogation of God's rulings and imagine that abrogation implies a change of divine will (al-bada').

[Page 282]

The second possibility is that they meant to deny that anyone could be given prophethood as the prophets of the Children of Israel were given it. In that case the statement is a rhetorical interrogative of denial from which the interrogative particle has been omitted, as the context indicates. The reading of Ibn Kathir supports this: ﴿أنْ يُؤْتى أحَدٌ﴾ with two hamzas.

As for His words ﴿أوْ يُحاجُّوكم عِنْدَ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ ("or that they should argue with you before your Lord"), the particle ''aw'' (أوْ) here is used for division, like the words ﴿ولا تُطِعْ مِنهم آثِمًا أوْ كَفُورًا﴾ ("Do not obey any of them who is sinful or ungrateful") [al-Insan: 24]. What follows ''aw'' is coordinated with the negation, or with the rhetorical interrogative of denial, according to the two different estimates. The meaning is: "And they should not argue with you before your Lord," or "And how could they argue with you before your Lord?", i.e., they have no proof against you before God.

The plural waw in ﴿يُحاجُّوكم﴾ ("they argue with you") is a pronoun referring back to ''aḥad'' (أحَدٌ), because of its generality in a negative or denying context.

The benefit of the interjection in the midst of their speech is that it immediately states what indicates their misguidance, because God deprived them of success.

The second possibility is that the sentence is among what the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say to them, as a continuation of his statement ﴿إنَّ الهُدى هُدى اللَّهِ﴾.

According to this view, the speech is a refutation of their statements ﴿آمِنُوا بِالَّذِي أُنْزِلَ عَلى الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وجْهَ النَّهارِ﴾ ("Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe, at the beginning of the day") [Al 'Imran: 72] and ﴿ولا تُؤْمِنُوا إلّا لِمَن تَبِعَ دِينَكُمْ﴾, in the manner of the inverted interlacing (al-laff wa al-nashr al-ma'kus), so that His words ﴿أنْ يُؤْتى أحَدٌ مِثْلَ ما أُوتِيتُمْ﴾ are a nullification of their statement ﴿ولا تُؤْمِنُوا إلّا لِمَن تَبِعَ دِينَكُمْ﴾, meaning: you said that out of envy that anyone should be given what you were given. His words ﴿أوْ يُحاجُّوكُمْ﴾ are a refutation of their statement ﴿آمِنُوا بِالَّذِي أُنْزِلَ عَلى الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وجْهَ النَّهارِ واكْفُرُوا آخِرَهُ﴾ ("Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end") [Al 'Imran: 72], in the manner of mockery (al-tahakkum), meaning: your purpose is to disclaim responsibility for arguing with you, that is, for those who believe arguing with you before God on the Day of Resurrection. You combined belief in what the Muslims believe with the intention that, when they achieve success on the Day of Resurrection, they cannot argue against you before God that you are disbelievers; and if success is yours, you have taken the prudent course by not renouncing the religion of Judaism. According to this, the plural waw in His words ﴿أوْ يُحاجُّوكُمْ﴾ refers back to ﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72]. This possibility is more suitable in its arrangement with the words of God, Exalted: ﴿قُلْ إنَّ الفَضْلَ بِيَدِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God"), so that every statement of theirs that is reported has a response taught to the Prophet: the response to their statement ﴿آمِنُوا بِالَّذِي أُنْزِلَ عَلى الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72] and so on is His words ﴿قُلْ إنَّ الهُدى هُدى اللَّهِ﴾, and the response to their statement ﴿ولا تُؤْمِنُوا﴾ and so on is His words ﴿قُلْ إنَّ الفَضْلَ بِيَدِ اللَّهِ﴾ and so on.

[Page 283]

This is the core of the possibilities. We will not lengthen the discussion by covering them all, since that is not our purpose in this tafsir.

The word ''aḥad'' (أحَدٌ) is an indefinite noun whose usage is predominantly in negative contexts. Its meaning is "a person" or "a human being." It is counted among the nouns that occur only within the scope of negation, so that it conveys generality, like ''arīb'' (عَرِيبٌ) and ''diyār'' (دِيارٌ) and similar words, though it rarely occurs in an affirmative context. Its hamza is substituted from a waw, and its origin is ''waḥad'' (وَحَدَ), meaning "one," and it also occurs as an attributive adjective meaning "one."

The majority of readers recite ﴿أنْ يُؤْتى أحَدٌ﴾ with a single hamza, which is part of the particle ''an'' (أنْ). Ibn Kathir recited it with two open hamzas: the first is the hamza of interrogation, and the second is part of the particle ''an'', and he eased the second hamza.

* * *

﴿قُلْ إنَّ الفَضْلَ بِيَدِ اللَّهِ يُؤْتِيهِ مَن يَشاءُ واللَّهُ واسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ ("Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills, and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing") ﴿يَخْتَصُّ بِرَحْمَتِهِ مَن يَشاءُ واللَّهُ ذُو الفَضْلِ العَظِيمِ﴾ ("He specifies for His mercy whom He wills, and God is the Lord of great bounty").

This is an additional reminder to them and a refutation of their claim that Muhammad (ﷺ) could not be a messenger from God. It is also a reminder to them to cast off envy of the blessings of God, Exalted. That is, just as God gave the message to Moses, He also gave it to Muhammad (ﷺ). This is like His words, Exalted: ﴿أمْ يَحْسُدُونَ النّاسَ عَلى ما آتاهُمُ اللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِ فَقَدْ آتَيْنا آلَ إبْراهِيمَ الكِتابَ والحِكْمَةَ﴾ ("Or do they envy the people for what God has given them of His bounty? We had already given the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom") [al-Nisa: 54].

The emphasis of the statement with ''inna'' (إنَّ) is because they are treated as one who denies that bounty is in the hand of God, and as one who supposes that bounty follows their own desires. The sentence ﴿واللَّهُ واسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ is coordinated with the sentence ﴿إنَّ الفَضْلَ بِيَدِ اللَّهِ﴾, and nothing is hidden from Him of who is worthy of receiving His bounty.

''Wāsi'' (واسِعٌ) is the active participle of one characterized by ''si'a'' (سِعَة), that is, "expansiveness."

The real meaning of expansiveness is the extension of the space of a container, whether a place or a vessel, extended enough to hold what that container contains without crowding or overlapping among the parts of what is contained. One says: "a wide land," "a wide vessel," "a wide garment." The term and its derivatives are also used for something's fulfilling the work its kind does without hardship. One says: "So-and-so is wide of means," "wide of chest," "wide in giving," "wide of character." It thus indicates the great intensity or abundance of what is ascribed to it, described by it, or related to it, of things and meanings. This usage became common until it became a second meaning.

''Wāsi'' is among the attributes of God and His Most Beautiful Names, and it is undoubtedly used in its figurative sense, since the literal sense is impossible with respect to Him, Exalted. The meaning of this Name is the non-finitude of the objects of relation of His attributes that have objects of relation. So He is All-Encompassing in knowledge, All-Encompassing in mercy, All-Encompassing in giving. The expansiveness of His attributes, Exalted, is that there is no limit to their objects of relation. He is the most deserving of all existents of the description "All-Encompassing," because He is the absolutely All-Encompassing.

The ascription of the attribute ''wāsi'' to His Name, Exalted, is also figurative, because He is the one whose attributes are all-encompassing. For this reason, after this attribute, or what has the same meaning as the verb of expansiveness, there is mention of what specifies the aspect of expansiveness by a specifier, such as His words: ﴿وسِعَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ عِلْمًا﴾ ("He encompasses all things in knowledge") [Ta-Ha: 98], and ﴿رَبَّنا وسِعْتَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ رَحْمَةً وعِلْمًا﴾ ("Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge") [Ghafir: 7]. So His being described in this verse as ''wāsi'' is the expansiveness of bounty, because it comes as a concluding remark (tadhyil) to His words: ﴿ذَلِكَ فَضْلُ اللَّهِ يُؤْتِيهِ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ ("That is the bounty of God; He gives it to whom He wills").

I think that describing God with the attribute ''wāsi'' in Arabic is one of the innovations of the Qur'an.

His word ''ʿalīm'' (عَلِيمٌ) is a second attribute, indicating the strength of His knowledge, that is, the abundance of the objects of relation of His attribute of knowledge, Exalted.

His description as ''ʿalīm'' here is to convey that He knows who is qualified to be given His bounty. What indicates His knowledge of this is the manifestation of the effects of His will and power, which proceed in accordance with His knowledge, whenever what God has deposited of excellences in some of His creatures becomes apparent to people. God, Exalted, said: ﴿اللَّهُ أعْلَمُ حَيْثُ يَجْعَلُ رِسالَتَهُ﴾ ("God knows best where He places His message") [al-An'am: 124].

The sentence ﴿يَخْتَصُّ بِرَحْمَتِهِ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ ("He specifies for His mercy whom He wills") is a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull) for the sentence ﴿إنَّ الفَضْلَ بِيَدِ اللَّهِ يُؤْتِيهِ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ ("Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills"), since His mercy is part of what is His bounty.

The sentence ﴿واللَّهُ ذُو الفَضْلِ العَظِيمِ﴾ ("God is the Lord of great bounty") is a concluding remark (tadhyil), and the explanation of its counterpart has already been given at His words, Exalted: ﴿واللَّهُ يَخْتَصُّ بِرَحْمَتِهِ مَن يَشاءُ واللَّهُ ذُو الفَضْلِ العَظِيمِ﴾ ("God specifies for His mercy whom He wills, and God is the Lord of great bounty") [al-Baqarah: 105] in Surat al-Baqarah.

We had already given the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom") [al-Nisa: 54].

The emphasis of the statement with ''inna'' (إنَّ) is because they are treated as one who denies that bounty is in the hand of God, and as one who supposes that bounty follows their own desires. The sentence ﴿واللَّهُ واسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ is coordinated with the sentence ﴿إنَّ الفَضْلَ بِيَدِ اللَّهِ﴾, and nothing is hidden from Him of who is worthy of receiving His bounty.

''Wāsi'' (واسِعٌ) is the active participle of one characterized by ''si'a'' (سِعَة), that is, "expansiveness."

The real meaning of expansiveness is the extension of the space of a container, whether a place or a vessel, extended enough to hold what that container contains without crowding or overlapping among the parts of what is contained. One says: "a wide land," "a wide vessel," "a wide garment." The term and its derivatives are also used for something's fulfilling the work its kind does without hardship. One says: "So-and-so is wide of means," "wide of chest," "wide in giving," "wide of character." It thus indicates the great intensity or abundance of what is ascribed to it, described by it, or related to it, of things and meanings. This usage became common until it became a second meaning.

''Wāsi'' is among the attributes of God and His Most Beautiful Names, and it is undoubtedly used in its figurative sense, since the literal sense is impossible with respect to Him, Exalted. The meaning of this Name is the non-finitude of the objects of relation of His attributes that have objects of relation. So He is All-Encompassing in knowledge, All-Encompassing in mercy, All-Encompassing in giving. The expansiveness of His attributes, Exalted, is that there is no limit to their objects of relation. He is the most deserving of all existents of the description "All-Encompassing," because He is the absolutely All-Encompassing.

The ascription of the attribute ''wāsi'' to His Name, Exalted, is also figurative, because He is the one whose attributes are all-encompassing. For this reason, after this attribute, or what has the same meaning as the verb of expansiveness, there is mention of what specifies the aspect of expansiveness by a specifier, such as His words: ﴿وسِعَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ عِلْمًا﴾ ("He encompasses all things in knowledge") [Ta-Ha: 98], and ﴿رَبَّنا وسِعْتَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ رَحْمَةً وعِلْمًا﴾ ("Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge") [Ghafir: 7]. So His being described in this verse as ''wāsi'' is the expansiveness of bounty, because it comes as a concluding remark (tadhyil) to His words: ﴿ذَلِكَ فَضْلُ اللَّهِ يُؤْتِيهِ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ ("That is the bounty of God; He gives it to whom He wills").

I think that describing God with the attribute ''wāsi'' in Arabic is one of the innovations of the Qur'an.

His word ''ʿalīm'' (عَلِيمٌ) is a second attribute, indicating the strength of His knowledge, that is, the abundance of the objects of relation of His attribute of knowledge, Exalted.

His description as ''ʿalīm'' here is to convey that He knows who is qualified to be given His bounty. What indicates His knowledge of this is the manifestation of the effects of His will and power, which proceed in accordance with His knowledge, whenever what God has deposited of excellences in some of His creatures becomes apparent to people. God, Exalted, said: ﴿اللَّهُ أعْلَمُ حَيْثُ يَجْعَلُ رِسالَتَهُ﴾ ("God knows best where He places His message") [al-An'am: 124].

The sentence ﴿يَخْتَصُّ بِرَحْمَتِهِ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ ("He specifies for His mercy whom He wills") is a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull) for the sentence ﴿إنَّ الفَضْلَ بِيَدِ اللَّهِ يُؤْتِيهِ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ ("Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills"), since His mercy is part of what is His bounty.

The sentence ﴿واللَّهُ ذُو الفَضْلِ العَظِيمِ﴾ ("God is the Lord of great bounty") is a concluding remark (tadhyil), and the explanation of its counterpart has already been given at His words, Exalted: ﴿واللَّهُ يَخْتَصُّ بِرَحْمَتِهِ مَن يَشاءُ واللَّهُ ذُو الفَضْلِ العَظِيمِ﴾ ("God specifies for His mercy whom He wills, and God is the Lord of great bounty") [al-Baqarah: 105] in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 285]

**Qur'an 3:75–76:** "Among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you; and among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you unless you keep standing over him. That is because they say, 'There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered.' And they speak falsehood about God, while they know. Rather, whoever fulfils his covenant and is mindful of God—indeed, God loves those who are mindful."

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with his saying, "And a group of the People of the Book said" [Al ʿImran: 72], or with his saying, "A group of the People of the Book wish they could mislead you" [Al ʿImran: 69]. It is the coordination of one account upon another account. The connection is the explanation of the inner dispositions of the Jews in their dealings with the Muslims, which arise from their envy, and of their deviation from the religion of Abraham, despite their claim that they are the people most entitled to it. In this verse He relates the treachery of one faction among them.

God mentions here two factions among the People of the Book: a faction that renders trust faithfully, abstaining from treachery, and a faction that does not render trust, making excuses to permit betrayal in their religion. It is said that from the first faction was ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, and from the second Finḥāṣ ibn ʿAzūrāʾ, and both were from the Jews of Yathrib.

The purpose of the verse is to censure the second faction, since, in their belief, their religion permits betrayal. He said, "That is because they say, 'There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered.'" Therefore the true aim is His saying, "And among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you," and so forth, and for this reason He lengthened the discourse on it. He placed before it His saying, "Among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar," out of fairness to the rights of this faction, because fairness is what Islam is known for. Although in their belief their religion permits them to betray others, the censure is directed at them, and the expression of this statement applies to all of them, both the trustworthy and the treacherous, because the trustworthy one then has no merit except that he gave up a right which his religion permits him to take, so he rose above that, as one who is exceedingly scrupulous in manliness rises above some permissible things.

The fronting of the predicate (musnad) in His saying, "Among the People of the Book," in both places, serves to express wonder at the content of the predicate's relation to the subject: in the first, it expresses wonder at the strength of trustworthiness despite the possibility of betrayal and the existence of an excuse for it in the custom of their religion; in the second, it expresses wonder that treachery should be a trait of a follower of one of the books of God. The wonder increases at His saying, "That is because they say," which lends the predicate a further wondrous state.

[Page 286]

The verb "tamanhu" is transitive with the preposition *bi* (with), although its like is usually transitive with *ʿalā* (over), as in His saying, "Shall I entrust you with him?" [Yusuf: 64]. This is because it is made to imply the meaning of "you deal with him with a qintar," so that it includes trust by deposit and trust by transaction in the sense of seeking trust. It is also said that the *bā'* here has the sense of *ʿalā*, as in the line of Abu Dharr or ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas:

"Is there a lord whose head the foxes urinate upon?"

But this is a remote interpretation, because the *bā'* in the line denotes place (ẓarfiyya), as in His saying, Exalted is He: "In the valley of Mecca" [al-Fath: 24].

The majority read *yu'addihi ilayka* with a kasra on the *hā'* of *yu'addihi*, according to the original rule for pronominal suffixes.

Abu ʿAmr, Ḥamza, Abu Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim, and Abu Jaʿfar read it with the *hā'* of the pronoun in *yu'addihi* sukūn-ed. Al-Zajjāj said: "This sukūn that is narrated from these readers is a clear error, because the *hā'* should not be jussive, and if it is not jussive, it is not permissible to make it kasra in connected speech." Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmitted this, and its meaning is that the jussive of the response does not appear on the *hā'* of the pronoun but on the last letter of the verb, and it is not permissible to make it sukūn in connected speech, as is the case in most of the verses in which they made the *hā'* sukūn. It is also said that this is the treating of connected speech as pause (wuqūf), which is rare. Al-Zajjāj said: "As for Abu ʿAmr, I think he was doing *ikhtilās* of the kasra, and those who transmitted it from him made an error." But al-Zajjāj's statement is rejected, because he considered the well-known, analogical usage, whereas language is broader than that, and the Qur'an is a proof. Hishām, on the authority of Ibn ʿĀmir, and Yaʿqūb read it with *ikhtilās* of the kasra.

Al-Qurṭubī related from al-Farrāʾ that some Arabs make the *hā'* jussive when the letter before it is vowelled, saying *ḍarabtuh* as they make the *mīm* of *antum* and *qumtum* sukūn, though its original is ḍammah; this is like what the rajaz poet said:

"When he saw that there was neither leaving him alone nor satiety, he inclined to the sand-hill's broom-bush and lay down."

Qinṭār was already mentioned earlier in His saying, Exalted is He: "And the heaped-up hoards of gold and silver" [Al ʿImran: 14].

Dinar is a name for minted gold whose weight is seventy-two grains of medium barley. It is an arabicized form of *dīnār* from Roman (Byzantine) usage.

The qintar and the dinar have been made two examples of abundance and scarcity. The intended meaning, what the context implies, is the rendering of trust in what is less than a qintar, and the occurrence of treachery in what is more than a dinar.

[Page 287]

His saying, "unless you keep standing over him," uses "standing" here in the sense of persistence and constancy, like His saying: "standing in justice" [Al ʿImran: 18], meaning that he does only what is just.

"Standing" is construed with the particle *ʿalā* because standing here is a metaphor for insistence and repeated pressing; construing it with a particle of elevation is an indicator and a reinforcement (tajrīd) of the metaphor.

The *mā* in His saying, "unless you keep standing over him," is a verbal (maṣdarī) particle, after which the verb takes the sense of a verbal noun. It is common to presume with it a noun of time that is obligatorily elided, indicated by the context of the speech; in that case one says that *mā* is a temporal verbal particle (ẓarfiyya maṣdariyya). The temporal sense is not its primary meaning, nor does it substitute for the adverb; rather it is derived from the position of *mā* within a context that indicates time. This occurs frequently when *mā* enters upon a verb from the root *dāma* (to last) and its synonyms.

The *mā* in this verse is similarly so. The meaning is: he will not return it to you except during the period of your continued standing over him, that is, your insistence upon him. The true meaning of *dawām* is the continuation of an act, and here it is a metaphor for the length of a period, because the literal meaning is impossible in the presence of the particle of exception, since when life ends, insistence does not occur after death.

The exception in His saying, "unless you keep standing over him," may be an exception from an unstated (mufarragh) construction, from times indicated by the position of *mā*; the sense being: he will not return it to you at all times except a time during which you remain standing over him. In that case what follows *illā* is in the accusative as an adverb of time. It may also be an exception from verbal nouns indicated by the meaning of the verbal *mā*; in that case what follows it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), since the verbal noun may occur as a state.

The prepositional phrase is placed before its governing element in His saying, "over him, standing," for emphasis of the meaning of the prepositional phrase. In fronting it there is the sense of insistence, that is: if your standing over him does not exist, he will not return your trust to you.

The reference in His saying, "That is because they say," is to the ruling mentioned, namely, "If you entrust him with a dinar, he will not return it to you." It is pointed to only for full attention in distinguishing it, since it is specific to this astonishing matter.

The *bā'* is causal, meaning: that is caused by statements they fabricated. He expressed this by "saying," because saying issues from belief; therefore it takes its place, and it is applied to supposition in various places in Arabic speech.

By "the unlettered" they meant those who were not of the People of the Book in former times. The meaning of "unlettered" was already explained in Surat al-Baqara.

[Page 288]

The particle *fī* here indicates cause (taʿlīl). Since causation does not attach to essences, it is necessary to posit a genitive-governed noun elided after the particle *fī*, and the sense is: "regarding the treatment of the unlettered."

The meaning of "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered" is: there is no sin or wrongdoing upon us in consuming their rights. The attaching of the ruling to "the unlettered," meaning their persons, intends their most appropriate situation with respect to the purpose for which the speech was delivered.

Thus *sabīl* here means the path of accountability. Then the word *sabīl* became in Arabic speech a well-known metaphor for accountability; God, Exalted is He, said: "There is no blame upon the good-doers" [al-Tawba: 91], and He said: "The blame is only upon those who ask your permission" [al-Tawba: 93]. The Arabs sometimes expressed it by "the road," as Ḥumayd ibn Thawr said:

"Would I, if I beguile my soul with a sarḥa tree of the sarḥ trees, find that a road is open against me?"

Their intention in this was to belittle the Muslims and to boast of what they had been given of knowledge of reading and writing before them. Or they meant by "the unlettered" those ignorant of the Torah, that is, a metonymy for their not being followers of the religion of Moses, peace be upon him.

Whichever is the case, this indicates a strange character trait in them: their contempt for the rights of those who oppose them in religion, and their permitting themselves to wrong them, while believing that the ignorant or unlettered one deserves to have his right rejected. The apparent reason that emboldened them to this was their misunderstanding of the Torah, for the Torah mentioned rulings that distinguished between the Israelite and others regarding rights, but that concerned solidarity and association within the community. In the Book of Deuteronomy, chapter 15, it is written: "At the end of every seven years you shall make a release. Every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbour; you shall exact it of the foreigner, but whatever is yours with your brother you shall release." And in chapter 23 of it: "You shall not lend upon interest to your brother, interest on money or interest on food, but to the foreigner you may lend upon interest." But there is a great difference between rights and solidarity, for the prohibition of usury was intended for the sake of solidarity, and solidarity is not obligatory with those outside the single religious community. It is related from Ibn al-Kalbī that the Jews said: "All the wealth was ours; what is in the hands of the Arabs of it is ours, and they wronged us and seized it, so there is no sin upon us in taking our wealth from them." These two blameworthy traits, which God related of the Jews, have been exhibited by many Muslims, so some of them declared lawful the rights of the protected people (ahl al-dhimma), interpreting them as having become people of war, when there is no war or fighting.

[Page 289]

God, Exalted is He, has refuted them in this claim, saying: "And they speak falsehood about God." The exegetes said: they claimed that they had found that in their book. It is related from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr that when the words of God, Exalted is He, "Among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him..." down to "while they know" [al-Baqara: 75] were revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said: "The enemies of God have lied. There is nothing from the days of ignorance that is not under these two feet of mine, except trust, for it is to be rendered to the pious and the wicked alike."

His saying, "while they know," is a circumstantial clause, meaning that they deliberately lie, either because they knew that what they analogized from their book was not valid analogy in it, or because false interpretation is equivalent to knowledge of falsehood, since a weak doubt is like a covenant.

*Balā* is a particle of response, specific to nullifying a negation. Here it nullifies their statement: "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered."

*Balā* is not restricted to answering a negated interrogative; rather it is used to answer with the intention of nullification. Most of its occurrences are in answer to a negated interrogative. In the response a general ruling is given to include the intended meaning and other meanings, for the sake of completeness of meaning and brevity of expression. So He said: "Whoever fulfils his covenant," that is, he does not betray, because trust is a covenant; "and is mindful of his Lord," so he does not violate the right of another; "then God loves those who are mindful," that is, those described by piety. The intended meaning is the negation of God's love from the opposite of what was mentioned, by the indication of the context.

[Page 285]
