In the Book of Deuteronomy, chapter 15, it is written: "At the end of every seven years you shall make a release. Every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbour; you shall exact it of the foreigner, but whatever is yours with your brother you shall release." And in chapter 23 of it: "You shall not lend upon interest to your brother, interest on money or interest on food, but to the foreigner you may lend upon interest." But there is a great difference between rights and solidarity, for the prohibition of usury was intended for the sake of solidarity, and solidarity is not obligatory with those outside the single religious community. It is related from Ibn al-Kalbī that the Jews said: "All the wealth was ours; what is in the hands of the Arabs of it is ours, and they wronged us and seized it, so there is no sin upon us in taking our wealth from them." These two blameworthy traits, which God related of the Jews, have been exhibited by many Muslims, so some of them declared lawful the rights of the protected people (ahl al-dhimma), interpreting them as having become people of war, when there is no war or fighting.

[Page 289]

God, Exalted is He, has refuted them in this claim, saying: "And they speak falsehood about God." The exegetes said: they claimed that they had found that in their book. It is related from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr that when the words of God, Exalted is He, "Among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him..." down to "while they know" [al-Baqara: 75] were revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said: "The enemies of God have lied. There is nothing from the days of ignorance that is not under these two feet of mine, except trust, for it is to be rendered to the pious and the wicked alike."

His saying, "while they know," is a circumstantial clause, meaning that they deliberately lie, either because they knew that what they analogized from their book was not valid analogy in it, or because false interpretation is equivalent to knowledge of falsehood, since a weak doubt is like a covenant.

*Balā* is a particle of response, specific to nullifying a negation. Here it nullifies their statement: "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered."

*Balā* is not restricted to answering a negated interrogative; rather it is used to answer with the intention of nullification. Most of its occurrences are in answer to a negated interrogative. In the response a general ruling is given to include the intended meaning and other meanings, for the sake of completeness of meaning and brevity of expression. So He said: "Whoever fulfils his covenant," that is, he does not betray, because trust is a covenant; "and is mindful of his Lord," so he does not violate the right of another; "then God loves those who are mindful," that is, those described by piety. The intended meaning is the negation of God's love from the opposite of what was mentioned, by the indication of the context.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (*al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*) on Surah 3, verse 77:

﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price, those will have no share in the Hereafter. Allah will not speak to them, nor will He look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that breaking trust (*khiyanat al-amanah*) amounts to nullifying the covenant and the alliance that existed between them, and between the Muslims and the Quraysh. This statement is a new sentence (*isti'naf*) whose purpose is to mention the trait that gathers together the scattered vices of the People of the Book among the Jews. It was prompted by His words ﴿A party of the People of the Book wish to mislead you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 69] and what follows it.

Similar descriptions have been applied to the Jews in scattered form in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿And fulfil My covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40]; ﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41]; ﴿for him there is no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]; and ﴿Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 174] (p. 290). Thus we know that they are the ones intended here. We have already explained there the reason their religion is called "the covenant" and "the pledge" in several places, because Musa (Moses) made a covenant with them to act upon it, and we have explained the meanings of these descriptions and reports.

The meaning of ﴿Allah will not speak to them, nor will He look at them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is His anger toward them, since the negation of speech has become a common metaphor (*kinaya*) for anger, and the use of "looking" has become common for regard and care, while the negation of looking signifies displeasure. So the looking that is negated here is a specific kind of looking. Both of these metaphors also permit the literal meaning to be intended as well.

His words ﴿nor will He purify them﴾ mean that He will not cleanse them from their sins, and they will not desist from their wrongdoing. For whoever has reached such a degree of weakness in religious commitment that he sells the covenant of Allah and His oaths for a small price has reached the utmost extreme of audacity against Allah, so how can any righteousness be hoped for from him after that? It is also possible that the meaning is "nor will He increase them," that is, He will not multiply their portions of good.

In the placing of this threat right after the relative clause, which is ﴿who sell the covenant of Allah﴾ and so on, there is an indication that whoever resembles them in these traits is subject to the same fate as they are. Some of the early generations (*al-salaf*) thought that this verse was revealed concerning whoever swears a false oath, and each one thought it was revealed concerning the case of a wicked oath he knew about. In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Abu Wa'il, on the authority of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears an oath of perjury (*yamin sabr*) by which he seizes the property of a Muslim man will meet Allah while He is angry with him." Then Allah revealed, as confirmation of this, ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths﴾ and so on. Then al-Ash'ath ibn Qays entered and said: "What is Abu 'Abd al-Rahman telling you?" We said: "Such and such." He said: "It was revealed concerning me. I had a well in the land of a cousin of mine, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'Your evidence, or his oath.' I said: 'Then he will swear.' The Messenger of Allah said: 'Whoever swears an oath of perjury...'" and the hadith continues.

In al-Bukhari, on the authority of 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa: a man displayed a commodity in the market and swore, "By Allah, I was offered for it what I was not offered," in order to deceive a Muslim man into it. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾ and so on.

Also in it, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he recited this verse concerning a case in which an oath was required to settle a claim.

[Page 291]

﴿And indeed, among them is a party who twist their tongues with the Book, so that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book. And they say, "It is from Allah," but it is not from Allah. And they speak falsehood about Allah while they know.﴾

That is, among the Jews there is a group that makes the Muslims imagine that certain things are from what came in the Torah, when they are not. This is either in making excuses for some of their blameworthy deeds, like their saying, ﴿There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75], or in confusing the Muslims so that they doubt what the Qur'an has stated that differs from this, or in introducing doubt into them concerning some of what the Qur'an has revealed. So al-layy (twisting) is general, but it is specified by His saying, ﴿so that you may think it is from the Book﴾ and His saying, ﴿And they say, "It is from Allah," but it is not from Allah.﴾

Al-layy in its original sense is turning, that is, the turning of a non-rigid body away from the direction in which it extends. From this comes the twisting of a rope, and the turning of a horse's bridle to steer it in a direction other than its line of travel. From it also comes the twisting of the neck, and the turning of the head meaning a sidelong glance or aversion. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿They twisted their heads﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 5].

Al-layy in this verse may literally mean distorting the tongue by shifting from one letter of the alphabet to another letter close to it, so that the word gives the listener's ear the sound of another word. This is like what Allah related about them in their saying "Ra'ina" (Do not say "Ra'ina" [Al Baqara: 104]), and in the hadith about their saying in greeting to the Prophet (ﷺ), "As-sam 'alayka" (death upon you), that is, "al-mawt" or "as-salam" with a kasra on the sin, "upon you." This layy resembles al-ishmam (a slight rounding of the lips toward a vowel without fully pronouncing it) and al-ikhtilas (rapid, clipped articulation of a vowel). From it is also imalah (inclining the alif toward the ya'). Words change through tarqiq (thinning) and tafkhim (thickening) and through differences in the attributes of letters. The apparent meaning is that the Book is the Torah. Perhaps when they read some of the Torah in Arabic, they pronounced some of its words' letters in an intermediate manner (bayna bayn), to give the Muslims a meaning other than the intended one. They had skill and practice in this.

Close to this is what al-Mubarrad mentioned in al-Kamil, that one of the Azariqa (a Kharijite sect) repeated the verse of Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a in the assembly of Ibn 'Abbas:

She saw a man: as for when the sun confronts him, he becomes bright (yadha), and as for in the evening, he becomes thin (yakhsar).

[Page 292]

So he began to say yahza (he is disgraced) instead of yadha, and he began to say yakhsar with a sin, yakhsar (he loses), to distort the meaning, because he was angry at Ibn 'Abbas's attentiveness to listening to his poetry. In riddles and puzzles there is something of this, such as their saying: "Indeed, for al-lahi (the playful one) there is a god above him," and someone says it in the presence of people, not fully pronouncing the kasra of al-lahi, which the listener takes to be lillah (for Allah), so he thinks he has committed disbelief. Or perhaps they used to read what was not from the Torah with the manners or melodies with which they read the Torah, to make the listeners imagine that they were reading the Torah.

It is also possible that al-layy here is a metaphor for turning the meaning toward another meaning, as in their saying: "lawa al-hujjah" (he twisted the argument), meaning he presented it in other than its proper form. It is the distortion of words from their places, through false interpretations, corrupt analogies, and fabricated fabrications, and they attribute that to Allah. Whatever the case, this layy is intended by them to deceive the Muslims for a purpose, as Ibn Suriya did in concealing the ruling on stoning the adulterer in the Torah, and his saying: "We blacken his face" (nuhammim wajhahu).

The addressee in "tahsabuhu" (so that you may think it) is the Muslims, not the Prophet (ﷺ), or it is he and the Muslims in the assumption of the Jews.

The present tense was used in these verbs, "yalwuna" and "yaqulun," to indicate the renewal of that and that it is their habit.

The repetition of "the Book" twice in the verse, and the name of Allah also twice, is for the purpose of emphasizing the two names, and that leads to emphasis on the report related to them and to those connected with them. Al-Marzuqi said in his commentary on al-Hamasa, in the chapter on literature, at the saying of Yahya ibn Ziyad:

When I saw the whiteness of gray appear at the parting of my head, I said to the gray hair, "Welcome!"

The proper form would have been, "I said to it, 'Welcome!'" But they often repeat proper names and common nouns, and the purpose of repetition is glorification. I say: from this is the saying of the poet:

I do not see death overtaking death, anything that overcame death, the rich and the poor alike.

The detailed explanation of this has already passed in Surat al-Baqara: ﴿And fear Allah; and Allah teaches you; and Allah is Knower of all things﴾ [Al Baqara: 282].

[Page 293]

The well-known reading of "yalwuna" is with a fatha on the ya' (taḥtiyyah), a sukun on the lam, and a light (takhfif) on the waw, present tense of lawa. Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned that Abu Ja'far read it "yulawwuna," with a damma, then a fatha, then a shaddah on the waw, present tense of lawwa on the pattern of fa''ala, for intensity. But I have not seen this reading attributed to Abu Ja'far in the books of readings.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 79–80:

﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Book, the judgment and the prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be worshippers of me rather than of Allah." Rather, [he would say], "Be people of the Lord (rabbaniyyin), by what you have been teaching of the Book and by what you have been studying."﴾ ﴿Nor would he command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would he command you to disbelieve after you have submitted [to Allah]?﴾.

This is an interjection and a digression (i'tiraḍ wa istiṭrad). When He mentioned the twisting of their tongues with the Torah by the Jews, which is a kind of distortion (taḥrif), He digressed to mention the distortion found among the Christians, because of the resemblance in distortion: the Christians claim about the Messiah that he commanded them to worship him. So "human being" (bashar) here refers to Jesus, peace be upon him, and the purpose is to exonerate Jesus from having said that, as a refutation of the Christians. This returns to the theme in His words ﴿Say: O People of the Book, come to a word that is equitable﴾ [Al 'Imran: 64] up to His words ﴿that we are Muslims﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52].

In the Kashshaf it is said: it was revealed because a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, we greet you as some of us greet one another; shall we not prostrate to you?" He said: "It is not fitting that prostration be made to anyone other than Allah, but honour your Prophet and recognise the rights of those who deserve them." I say: 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated it from al-Hasan. So, on the assumption that it is an acceptable hadith, the connection of mentioning this verse here is that it is intended to refute all these beliefs together. And it occurs in Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi, from the narration of al-Kalbi, from Ibn 'Abbas: that Abu Rafi' the Jew and the leader (al-Sayyid) of the Christians of Najran said: "O Muhammad, do you want us to worship you?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "God forbid that anyone be worshipped other than Allah," and this verse was revealed.

His words ﴿It is not for a human being﴾ are a negation of anyone's entitlement to that statement, and the lam in it denotes entitlement (al-istihqaq). The original form of this construction in speech is "such-and-such was not one who does such-and-such," but when emphasis in negation was intended, he turned away from negating the verb to negating the verbal noun denoting the category, and made the negation of the category attached to the person through the negation of entitlement, since there is no way to predicate one noun of another except through some particle. So the construction becomes: "It is not for him to do such-and-such," and it is also said: "It is not for him to do such-and-such," and similarly in affirmation, as in His words ﴿Indeed, for you there is that you will not hunger therein, nor be bare﴾ [Ta-Ha: 118].

So the meaning of the verse is: the statement ﴿Be worshippers of me﴾ is not due to any human being whatsoever. This lam is the origin of the lam of denial (lam al-juhud), as in ﴿And Allah would not punish them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33]. All the constructions of the lam of denial are of the type of inverting this construction for the purpose of emphasising the negation, such that it is negated that the existence of the subject was made for the sake of doing such-and-such; that is, he is free of it by his very creation. For this reason it is called juhud (denial).

What is apparently negated in this verse is the giving of judgment and prophethood, but it is known that the true target of the negation is the conjoined clause in His words ﴿then he should say to the people, "Be worshippers of me"﴾, i.e., it is not for him to say "Be worshippers of me" when Allah has given him the Book, etc.

''Ibad'' is the plural of ''abd'' like ''abid''. Ibn 'Atiyya said: what I have inferred regarding the word ''ibad'' is that it is the plural of ''abd'' in which no contempt is intended, whereas ''abid'' carries contempt; for this reason He said ﴿O My servants﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 56]. The Arabs named groups of Arabs who settled in al-Hira and entered under the rule of Kisra as "al-'Ibad," and it was said that this was because they had become Christians, so they were called "al-'Ibad." Its plural as ''abid'' differs, as in their saying "they are the slaves of the stick" (abid al-'asa). Hamza ibn al-Muttalib said: "Are you anything but slaves of my father?" From this is His words ﴿Your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46], because it is compassionate and informs of their weakness, and that He, the Exalted, is not unjust to them despite that. Since the word ''ibad'' implies obedience, it was not used here; for this reason it was used with ease in His words ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]. This kind of consideration is pursued along the paths of wonders in the eloquence of the Qur'an according to the sound Arabic manner, end of quote.

His words ﴿beside Allah﴾ are a restriction intended to shame the statement that they should be servants of the speaker, on the basis that this implies they had departed from servitude to Allah, the Exalted, to servitude of a human being, because the reality of servitude does not accept division among objects of worship. When the Christians made Jesus their lord and made him the son of Allah, it followed that they had cast off the servitude of Allah, so their saying "we are servants of Allah and servants of Jesus" carries no weight. For this reason their statement was made to imply that Jesus commanded them to be his servants beside Allah, and the meaning is that the one who commands people to be his servants is one who commands them to turn away from the worship of Allah.

"But be rabbaniyyin": that is, "but he would say: be attributed to the Lord," who is Allah, the Exalted, because attribution to a thing occurs only for greater specific belonging of the attributed to the one to whom it is attributed. The meaning is that they should be sincere to Allah alone, to the exclusion of others.

Al-rabbani is a relative adjective (nisba) to al-Rabb not by regular analogy, as one says al-lihyani for one with a large beard, and al-sha'rani for one with abundant hair.

His words ﴿by what you have been teaching of the Book﴾ mean: because your knowledge of the Book is of such a nature that it should restrain you from associating partners in worship, for the benefit of knowledge is action.

The majority read ﴿tu'allimuna﴾ (you teach) with a fatha on the ta', sukun on the 'ayn and fatha on the lam, as the present of 'alima. 'Amir, Hamza, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a damma, then fatha, then a doubled kasra on the lam, as the present of 'allama (the doubled form).

Tadrusuna means taqra'una, i.e., reading with repetition and reiteration, because the root d-r-s in Arabic usage revolves around the meanings of being effaced through repeated action performed upon similar things. From it is the saying: "the wind effaced the traces of the house" when it wore it away and obliterated it, so it is "dāris"; one says "a dāris dwelling," and "a dāris road," meaning the worn-away one not clearly visible; and "a dāris garment," worn out. They also said: "darasa al-kitab" when one reads it slowly for memorisation or for reflection. In the hadith: "No group gathers in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it among themselves, except that tranquillity descends upon them," etc. — narrated by al-Tirmidhi — he conjoined tadarus (studying together) with recitation, from which it is known that dirasa is more specific than qira'a. They named the house where the Jews recited "midras," as in the hadith: "The Prophet ﷺ went out with a group of his companions until he came to the midras of the Jews, and he recited the Qur'an to them and invited them," etc. The root d-r-s implies mastery over the object, so the study of a book became a metaphor for understanding and mastering it; for this reason in this verse He conjoined "and by what you have been studying" to "by what you have been teaching of the Book."

Its verb is of the pattern nasara, and its verbal noun in most of its meanings is "dars." The verbal noun of darasa in the sense of reading comes on the original pattern as "darsan," and from it the teaching of knowledge is called "dars." It also comes on the pattern fi'ala as "dirasa," a form indicating the working upon an action, like kitaba and qira'a, by analogy with the verbal nouns of crafts like tijara (trade) and khiyata (tailoring).

In His words ﴿Nor would he command you﴾ there is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person.

The majority read ya'murukum with a damma (ya'muruku-m), on the basis of beginning a new sentence. This is the original case when the negation particle is repeated: when it came after a negated verb, and then its negation was annulled by "lakin" (but), it became necessary to repeat the negation particle. The meaning on this reading is clear: it is not for a human being to say to people "be..." etc., nor does he command you to take the angels as lords. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, Ya'qub and Khalaf read it with a fatha, conjoined to "an yaqula," with "la" being superfluous for emphasising the negation in His words ﴿It is not for a human being﴾, and not governing "an" — because governing would make the meaning: "it is not fitting for a human who was given the Book that he not command you to take..." whereas the intended meaning is the reverse, since what is intended here is that it is not fitting for him to command. Therefore, in the parsing of this reading, they were compelled to make "la" superfluous to emphasise the negation, not a new negation. Al-Duri, from Abu 'Amr, read it with the damma being slightly reduced toward sukun.

Perhaps the intention of His words ﴿nor would he command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾ is this: when they exaggerated in exalting some of the prophets and angels, they fashioned images of the prophets, such as Yahya and Maryam, and worshipped them, and they fashioned images of angels, and the making of images combined with excessive exaltation of the image and worship before it is a kind of idolatry.

Ibn 'Arafa said: if it is said that the negation of commanding is more general than the prohibition, why was it not said "nor would he forbid you"? The answer is that this is with regard to their claim and their attributing it to the messengers. I say: perhaps the expression "la ya'murukum" is by way of mushakala (matching) with His words ﴿then he should say to the people﴾, because they claimed that the Messiah said: "I am the son of Allah," so when it was negated that he would say that, there was negated what is similar to it, namely that he would command them to take the angels as lords. Or because, since they claimed to adhere to the religion, all their conditions were taken to have come from him. Or because the Messiah did not forbid them from that in reality, since this is something that would not occur to the mind that a religious community would engage in it, so the refutation was restricted to the community. Moreover, their prophets did not command them to it, and for this reason he followed it with the interrogative of denunciation and the time clause conveying extra denunciation of their committing this condition, namely His words "Would he command you to disbelieve after you have submitted [to Allah]?"

Thus there are two reasons for denouncing that what they were upon could be pleasing to their prophets: it is disbelief, and they do not accept disbelief. So it was not right for those who follow them to be involved in disbelief after they had come out of it.

The address in His words ﴿nor would he command you﴾ is a shift from the third-person manner in His words ﴿then he should say to the people, "Be worshippers of me beside Allah"﴾. So those directly addressed are those who claimed that Jesus said to them: "Be worshippers of me beside Allah."

The meaning of ﴿that you are Muslims﴾ implies that they were Muslims, and the address is to the Christians, and their religion is not described as submission (islam). It was said: islam here means faith (iman), i.e., not associating partners, by the indicator of His words "with disbelief." It was also said: the address is to the Muslims, based on the apparent sense of His words "after you are Muslims," because the Jews and Christians are not described in the Qur'an as Muslims. It is this which emboldened those who said that the verse was revealed concerning a man's statement to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "shall we not prostrate to you?" But I do not think, even if it were sound, that the verse intends that; for if that were intended it would have said "then he would command people to prostrate to him," and it would not have turned to the command to be servants of him beside Allah, nor to the command to take the angels and prophets as lords.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 79–80:

﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Book, the judgment and the prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be worshippers of me rather than of Allah." Rather, [he would say], "Be people of the Lord (rabbaniyyin), by what you have been teaching of the Book and by what you have been studying."﴾ ﴿Nor would he command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would he command you to disbelieve after you have submitted [to Allah]?﴾.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "God forbid that anyone be worshipped other than Allah," and this verse was revealed.

His words ﴿It is not for a human being﴾ are a negation of anyone's entitlement to that statement, and the lam in it denotes entitlement (al-istihqaq). The original form of this construction in speech is "such-and-such was not one who does such-and-such," but when emphasis in negation was intended, he turned away from negating the verb to negating the verbal noun denoting the category, and made the negation of the category attached to the person through the negation of entitlement, since there is no way to predicate one noun of another except through some particle. So the meaning of the verse is: the statement ﴿Be worshippers of me﴾ is not due to any human being whatsoever. For this reason it is called juhud (denial).

What is apparently negated in this verse is the giving of judgment and prophethood, but it is known that the true target of the negation is the conjoined clause in His words ﴿then he should say to the people, "Be worshippers of me"﴾, i.e., it is not for him to say "Be worshippers of me" when Allah has given him the Book, etc.

''Ibad'' is the plural of ''abd'' like ''abid''. Ibn 'Atiyya said: what I have inferred regarding the word ''ibad'' is that it is the plural of ''abd'' in which no contempt is intended, whereas ''abid'' carries contempt; for this reason He said ﴿O My servants﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 56]. The Arabs named groups of Arabs who settled in al-Hira and entered under the rule of Kisra as "al-'Ibad," and it was said that this was because they had become Christians, so they were called "al-'Ibad." Its plural as ''abid'' differs, as in their saying "they are the slaves of the stick" (abid al-'asa). Hamza ibn al-Muttalib said: "Are you anything but slaves of my father?" From this is His words ﴿Your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46], because it is compassionate and informs of their weakness, and that He, the Exalted, is not unjust to them despite that. Since the word ''ibad'' implies obedience, it was not used here; for this reason it was used with ease in His words ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]. This kind of consideration is pursued along the paths of wonders in the eloquence of the Qur'an according to the sound Arabic manner, end of quote.

His words ﴿beside Allah﴾ are a restriction intended to shame the statement that they should be servants of the speaker, on the basis that this implies they had departed from servitude to Allah, the Exalted, to servitude of a human being, because the reality of servitude does not accept division among objects of worship. When the Christians made Jesus their lord and made him the son of Allah, it followed that they had cast off the servitude of Allah, so their saying "we are servants of Allah and servants of Jesus" carries no weight. For this reason their statement was made to imply that Jesus commanded them to be his servants beside Allah, and the meaning is that the one who commands people to be his servants is one who commands them to turn away from the worship of Allah.

"But be rabbaniyyin": that is, "but he would say: be attributed to the Lord," who is Allah, the Exalted, because attribution to a thing occurs only for greater specific belonging of the attributed to the one to whom it is attributed. The meaning is that they should be sincere to Allah alone, to the exclusion of others.

Al-rabbani is a relative adjective (nisba) to al-Rabb not by regular analogy, as one says al-lihyani for one with a large beard, and al-sha'rani for one with abundant hair.

His words ﴿by what you have been teaching of the Book﴾ mean: because your knowledge of the Book is of such a nature that it should restrain you from associating partners in worship, for the benefit of knowledge is action.

The majority read ﴿tu'allimuna﴾ (you teach) with a fatha on the ta', sukun on the 'ayn and fatha on the lam, as the present of 'alima. 'Amir, Hamza, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a damma, then fatha, then a doubled kasra on the lam, as the present of 'allama (the doubled form).

Tadrusuna means taqra'una, i.e., reading with repetition and reiteration, because the root d-r-s in Arabic usage revolves around the meanings of being effaced through repeated action performed upon similar things. From it is the saying: "the wind effaced the traces of the house" when it wore it away and obliterated it, so it is "dāris"; one says "a dāris dwelling," and "a dāris road," meaning the worn-away one not clearly visible; and "a dāris garment," worn out. They also said: "darasa al-kitab" when one reads it slowly for memorisation or for reflection. In the hadith: "No group gathers in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it among themselves, except that tranquillity descends upon them," etc. — narrated by al-Tirmidhi — he conjoined tadarus (studying together) with recitation, from which it is known that dirasa is more specific than qira'a. They named the house where the Jews recited "midras," as in the hadith: "The Prophet ﷺ went out with a group of his companions until he came to the midras of the Jews, and he recited the Qur'an to them and invited them," etc. The root d-r-s implies mastery over the object, so the study of a book became a metaphor for understanding and mastering it; for this reason in this verse He conjoined "and by what you have been studying" to "by what you have been teaching of the Book."

Its verb is of the pattern nasara, and its verbal noun in most of its meanings is "dars." The verbal noun of darasa in the sense of reading comes on the original pattern as "darsan," and from it the teaching of knowledge is called "dars." It also comes on the pattern fi'ala as "dirasa," a form indicating the working upon an action, like kitaba and qira'a, by analogy with the verbal nouns of crafts like tijara (trade) and khiyata (tailoring).

In His words ﴿Nor would he command you﴾ there is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person.

The majority read ya'murukum with a damma (ya'muruku-m), on the basis of beginning a new sentence. This is the original case when the negation particle is repeated: when it came after a negated verb, and then its negation was annulled by "lakin" (but), it became necessary to repeat the negation particle. The meaning on this reading is clear: it is not for a human being to say to people "be..." etc., nor does he command you to take the angels as lords. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, Ya'qub and Khalaf read it with a fatha, conjoined to "an yaqula," with "la" being superfluous for emphasising the negation in His words ﴿It is not for a human being﴾, and not governing "an" — because governing would make the meaning: "it is not fitting for a human who was given the Book that he not command you to take..." whereas the intended meaning is the reverse, since what is intended here is that it is not fitting for him to command. Therefore, in the parsing of this reading, they were compelled to make "la" superfluous to emphasise the negation, not a new negation. Al-Duri, from Abu 'Amr, read it with the damma being slightly reduced toward sukun.

Perhaps the intention of His words ﴿nor would he command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾ is this: when they exaggerated in exalting some of the prophets and angels, they fashioned images of the prophets, such as Yahya and Maryam, and worshipped them, and they fashioned images of angels, and the making of images combined with excessive exaltation of the image and worship before it is a kind of idolatry.

Ibn 'Arafa said: if it is said that the negation of commanding is more general than the prohibition, why was it not said "nor would he forbid you"? The answer is that this is with regard to their claim and their attributing it to the messengers. I say: perhaps the expression "la ya'murukum" is by way of mushakala (matching) with His words ﴿then he should say to the people﴾, because they claimed that the Messiah said: "I am the son of Allah," so when it was negated that he would say that, there was negated what is similar to it, namely that he would command them to take the angels as lords. Or because, since they claimed to adhere to the religion, all their conditions were taken to have come from him. Or because the Messiah did not forbid them from that in reality, since this is something that would not occur to the mind that a religious community would engage in it, so the refutation was restricted to the community. Moreover, their prophets did not command them to it, and for this reason he followed it with the interrogative of denunciation and the time clause conveying extra denunciation of their committing this condition, namely His words "Would he command you to disbelieve after you have submitted [to Allah]?"

Thus there are two reasons for denouncing that what they were upon could be pleasing to their prophets: it is disbelief, and they do not accept disbelief. So it was not right for those who follow them to be involved in disbelief after they had come out of it.

The address in His words ﴿nor would he command you﴾ is a shift from the third-person manner in His words ﴿then he should say to the people, "Be worshippers of me beside Allah"﴾. So those directly addressed are those who claimed that Jesus said to them: "Be worshippers of me beside Allah."

The meaning of ﴿that you are Muslims﴾ implies that they were Muslims, and the address is to the Christians, and their religion is not described as submission (islam). It was said: islam here means faith (iman), i.e., not associating partners, by the indicator of His words "with disbelief." It was also said: the address is to the Muslims, based on the apparent sense of His words "after you are Muslims," because the Jews and Christians are not described in the Qur'an as Muslims. It is this which emboldened those who said that the verse was revealed concerning a man's statement to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "shall we not prostrate to you?" But I do not think, even if it were sound, that the verse intends that; for if that were intended it would have said "then he would command people to prostrate to him," and it would not have turned to the command to be servants of him beside Allah, nor to the command to take the angels and prophets as lords.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 81–82:

﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and you must support him." He said: "Do you affirm and accept My covenant on that condition?" They said: "We affirm it." He said: "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses."﴾ ﴿Whoever turns away after that, those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾

He connected ﴿And when Allah took﴾ to ﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels﴾ [Al 'Imran: 80]. That is: the Prophets did not command you to anything of what you have invented about them, when they had commanded you otherwise, and you neglected it, at the time when Allah took their covenant so that they would convey it to you. So what is connected (ma'tuf) is the temporal clause (zarf) of ﴿idh﴾ and what is attached to it.

[Page 298]

It is also permissible that ﴿idh﴾ be connected to the phrase ﴿Do you affirm﴾ placed before it. It is also valid that ﴿idh﴾ be taken to mean "time" and not as a temporal adverb (zarf). The implied meaning is: "Remember when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets." The purpose is then the narration of that time and what occurred in it, and ﴿He said: Do you affirm﴾ becomes a coordinated clause with the conjunction omitted, as is the case in dialogue sentences, and likewise His saying ﴿They said: We affirm﴾.

It is also valid that the sentence ﴿He said: Do you affirm﴾ and what follows it be an explanation (bayan) of the sentence ﴿Allah took the covenant of the Prophets﴾, in view of what the verb ﴿Allah took the covenant of the Prophets﴾ implies: that the Prophets gave a covenant to Allah. So He said: "Do you affirm?" They said: "We affirm," and so on. And His saying ﴿Whatever I have given you﴾ up to His saying ﴿and you must support him﴾ is the wording of the covenant.

This covenant was taken by Allah from all the Prophets, in which they were informed that a Messenger would come confirming what was with them, and would command them to believe in him and support him. The purpose of that is to inform their nations of it, so that the covenant would be preserved among all generations. The evidence is His saying ﴿Whoever turns away after that﴾ and so on, since it is not permissible for the Prophets to turn away or to be defiantly disobedient. Rather, the intended ones are their nations, as in His saying ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. The evidence is also His saying ﴿He said: Then bear witness﴾, meaning: over your nations. To this goes what is reported in the Qur'an of the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a Messenger from themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]. And in the Book of Deuteronomy there is the saying of Musa, peace be upon him: "The LORD said to me: I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren, like you, and I will put My words in his mouth, and he will speak to them all that I command him." The brethren of the Children of Israel are the children of Isma'il. Had the intended one been an Israelite prophet, it would have said "I will raise up for them a prophet from among them," as in the translation of the Torah, which has some obscurity. Perhaps the original text is more correct than this translation.

The glad tidings in the books of the Prophets of the Children of Israel and in the Gospel are numerous. In Matthew there is the saying of the Messiah: "And many false prophets will arise and will mislead many. But he who endures, that is, remains to the end, he will be saved. And this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come." In the Gospel of John there is the saying of the Messiah: "And I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Comforter, to be with you forever. But the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord will send in My name, He will teach you all things and will remind you of all that I have told you. And when the Comforter comes, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, He will bear witness of Me," and so on.

[Page 299]

In the taking of the covenant from the Prophets there is additional honoring of the Message of Muhammad (ﷺ). This meaning is the apparent meaning of the verse, and it was the interpretation of the critical scholars among the early exegetes (salaf), including 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus, and al-Suddi.

Among the scholars, some considered it unlikely that taking the covenant from the Prophets was literal, in view of His saying ﴿whoever turns away after that, those are the defiantly disobedient﴾. They supposed that "whoever turns away" necessarily refers to the addressed Prophets, but you will know that this is not so. So they interpreted the verse as meaning that the covenant was taken from their nations, and they took various approaches to interpretation. Some made the annexation of "covenant" to "the Prophets" an annexation resembling the annexation of a verbal noun (masdar) to its agent, meaning: Allah took from the nations the covenant of their prophets. Others assumed an omitted annexed noun, meaning: the nations of the Prophets, or the sons of the Prophets. To this view the statement of Mujahid and al-Rabi' inclines. They argued from the recitation of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud of this verse: "And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book, what I have given you of the Book," without the words "of the Prophets." Mujahid went further and said: the recitation of Ubayy is the Qur'an, and the word "the Prophets" is a scribal error. Ibn 'Atiyya and others refuted this by the consensus of the Companions and the Muslim community upon the Codex of 'Uthman.

As for His saying ﴿what I have given you﴾: Ibn Kathir... [note: the text here reads] — the majority (al-jumhur) read ﴿lamma﴾ with a fatha on the lam and a light mim. So the lam is a preparatory lam (lam mutawwi'a) for the oath, and also because taking a covenant is in the sense of an oath. ﴿Ma﴾ is a relative pronoun serving as the subject (mubtada'), ﴿ataynakum﴾ is its relative clause, and the omitted returning pronoun in the accusative case follows the usual pattern in such constructions. ﴿Min kitab﴾ ("of a Book") is an explanation (bayan) of the relative pronoun and its clause. ﴿Thumma ja'akum﴾ ("then there came to you") is coordinated with ﴿ataynakum﴾, meaning: what We gave you, and then there came to you after it a Messenger. The lam in ﴿latu'minunna﴾ ("you must believe") is the lam of the answer to the oath, and the answer took the place of the predicate of the subject, as is well known. The pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ refers to the Messenger, and what would refer back to ﴿ma ataynakum﴾ was omitted because it is clear.

Hamzah recited it with a kasra on the lam of ﴿lamma﴾, so the lam is causal (lam al-ta'lil), connected to His saying ﴿latu'minunna bihi﴾, meaning: in gratitude for what I have given you, and because I have sent to you a Messenger confirming what you were upon of religion. The action following the lam of the oath does not harm what precedes it. So the covenant was taken from them unconditionally, and then He gave the reason for the answer to the oath: that it is from gratitude for the blessing of giving and confirmation. It is not valid, in terms of meaning, to link ﴿what I have given you﴾ with the omitted verb of the oath, because gratitude is the reason for the answer, not for the taking of the covenant.

The lam of ﴿latu'minunna﴾ is the lam of the answer to the oath according to the first reading, and a preparatory lam for the oath according to the second.

[Page 300]

Nafi' and Abu Ja'far recited ﴿ataynakum﴾ with the "we" of majesty (nun al-'azama), while the rest recited ﴿ataytukum﴾ with the first-person singular (ta' al-mutakallim).

The sentence ﴿He said: Do you affirm﴾ is an inclusive substitute (badal ishtimal) of the sentence ﴿Allah took the covenant of the Prophets﴾.

The word "affirm" (iqrar) here is used in the sense of confirming by fulfilling what was taken in the covenant.

Al-Isr, with a kasra on the hamza, means a firm, strongly sealed covenant. Its derivation is from al-isar, with a kasra on the hamza, which is what is tied and fastened with it. The discussion of its literal and figurative meaning has already been presented in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, do not place upon us a burden (isran)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286] in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying ﴿then bear witness﴾: if it is a witness against themselves, then it means securing and confirming. Likewise His saying ﴿and I am with you among the witnesses﴾, like His saying ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]. If it is a witness against their nations regarding the conveying of that covenant, then the meaning is: bear witness against your nations of that, and Allah is a witness over all, just as the Prophets bore witness against the nations.

His saying ﴿whoever turns away after that﴾, that is: whoever of those against whom you have borne witness turns away, and they are the nations. For this reason He did not say "whoever turns away after that among you," as He said in the verse in which the Children of Israel are addressed in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿whoever disbelieves after that among you has surely strayed from the right way﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 12].

The aspect of restriction (hasr) in His saying ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ is that it is for emphasis, because their disobedience in this state is the most severe disobedience, so other forms of disobedience are treated as though they were non-existent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 83:

﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah, while to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they will be returned?﴾

This is a continuation of the reminder of what the Prophets were upon.

The interrogative is for reproach and warning.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "tabghun" with the second-person ta' (of address) directed at the People of the Book, in keeping with the mode of address in His words just before: ﴿And He would not command you to take the angels﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 80]. Abu 'Amr, Hafs and Ya'qub read it with the third-person ya' (of absence). This is an iltifat (shift) from address to absence, turning away from addressing them toward addressing the Muslims, expressing wonder at the People of the Book.

All of this is a continuation of the mention of the states of the successors of those nations, how they followed other than what the covenant had been taken from them to uphold. The interrogative here is then for wonder.

"The religion of Allah" is Islam, according to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 19]. Its attribution to Allah is for its honour over other religions, or because the others had by that time been abrogated (nusikha) by what is the religion of Allah.

The meaning of "tabghun" is "you seek." It is said: baghā al-amr yabghīhi bughā'an (with a damma on the ba' and with a long vowel, and it may be shortened), and al-bughya (with a damma or kasra on the ba', and a ha' at its end) is said to be a verbal noun and is said to be a noun. It is also said ibtagha in the sense of baghā. It is designated for seeking, and it takes one object. The regular verbal noun would be al-baghy, but al-baghy has only been heard in the sense of transgression and injustice, and that verb is intransitive. Perhaps they intended to distinguish between seeking and transgression, so they let the regular verbal noun of baghā meaning "sought" die out and reserved it for baghā meaning "transgressed and wronged." He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿The way [of blame] is only against those who wrong people and transgress in the earth without right﴾ [al-Shura: 42]. It is also said tabaghgha in the sense of ibtagha.

The clause "wa lahu aslama" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the name of Allah, and the explanation of the meaning of submission to Allah has already preceded at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to Allah﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 20].

The meaning of ﴿willingly and unwillingly﴾ is that among the rational beings there are those who submitted by choice, because the truth became manifest to them, and among them are those who submitted by nature and innate disposition, like the angels. Or, submission "unwillingly" is submission after refusal, meaning the proofs and signs compelled him. Or it is the submission of the disbelievers at death and seeing the evil end. Or it is compulsion to Islam before the revelation of ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ [al-Baqara: 256].

Al-karh with a fatha on the kaf is compulsion, and al-kurh with a damma on the kaf is that which is disliked.

The meaning of "wa ilayhi turja'un" is that He returns you to Himself. The verb raja'a in its transitive form is here in the passive, because its agent is known, i.e., Allah returns you after death and at the Resurrection. The relevance of mentioning this, following the reproach and warning, is that the Lord from whose judgment there is no escape, it is not permissible for the intelligent person to turn away from a religion He has commanded him to follow, and it is his duty to surrender himself to Him by choice before he surrenders himself by compulsion.

His saying "wa ilayhi turja'un" has indicated the intended meaning of "wa karhan."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "turja'un" with the ta' of address, and Hafs read it with the ya' of absence.

[Page 302]

﴿Say: "We believe in Allah, and in what has been revealed to us, and in what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting."﴾ The addressee of the imperative "Say" is the Prophet (ﷺ), so that he would say this in the hearing of the people: its Muslims and its disbelievers. For this reason, in this verse His saying ﴿and what was revealed to us﴾ came, i.e., "what was revealed to me for your conveyance." He made the sending down to the Messenger and the community [equal] because of their sharing in the obligation to act upon what has been revealed. The verb "revealed" is here followed by the preposition ʿalā (upon) on the basis that sending down implies height, so the arrival of the thing sent down is an arrival of elevation. In the verse of Surah al-Baqarah it is followed by ilā (to), on the basis that sending down includes arrival, and it governs ilā. The sentence is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) and a resumptive statement (istiʾnāf): to instruct the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims in a comprehensive statement of the meaning of Islam so that they persist in it and proclaim it to the nations, arising from His saying ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾ [Al ʿImran: 83].

The meaning of ﴿we make no distinction between any of them﴾ is that we do not oppose the prophets, and the love of our Prophet does not lead us to hate them. This is an indirect allusion (taʿrīḍ) to the Jews and Christians. The conjunct is elided, and its implied meaning is "we make no distinction between one and another." The parallel of this verse has already appeared in Surah al-Baqarah. This verse is the emblem of Islam, and Allah the Exalted said ﴿and you believe in the Book, all of it﴾ [Al ʿImran: 119].

Here ended the debate with the Christians of Najran.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 85:

﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers.﴾

It is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 83], and what lies between them is an interjection (i'tiradh), as you know. This is a despairing of the People of the Book from salvation in the Hereafter, and a refutation of their saying: "We are upon the creed of Ibrahim, so we will be saved in every case." The meaning is: whoever seeks other than Islam after the coming of Islam.

All readers recited it with the clear pronunciation (idhhar) of the two ghayn letters, in the word man yabtaghi and in the word ghayra. Al-Susi, from Abu 'Amr, narrated the assimilation (idgham) of one of them into the other, and this is the major assimilation (al-idgham al-kabir).

This is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new sentence opening a fresh topic), which suits what precedes it in praise of the nobility of Islam.

﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief, and had testified that the Messenger is true, and the clear proofs had come to them? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

"Kayf" (كَيْفَ) is an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari, a question used to reject something), and the intended meaning is to deny that they could attain a particular guidance. This guidance is either:
- the guidance that arises from Allah's care for the servant and His gentleness towards him, whose attribution to Allah is evident; or
- the guidance that arises from applying the evidences and drawing conclusions from them, whose attribution to Allah is because He is the originator of the causes and their effects.

It is also permissible for the interrogative to be used to express improbability (istibad, regarding something as unlikely), since they had believed and known what was in the Books of Allah, then they disbelieved after that concerning their prophets, when the Jews worshipped idols more than once and the Christians worshipped the Messiah. They had testified that Muhammad was truthful because the signs of truthfulness were established; then they were stubborn and cast doubt upon people. The signs came to them, but they did not take heed. So there is no hope of their guidance after these conditions. Guidance flows only to one who is fair and prepared to perceive the signs, not to the people who wronged themselves.

It was said that it was revealed concerning the Jews specifically. It was also said that it was revealed concerning a group of Arabs who had embraced Islam, then disbelieved and joined Quraysh, then regretted and sent word to their Muslim kinsmen asking them whether there was any repentance for them, and so it was revealed. Among them were al-Harith ibn Suwayd, Abu 'Amir al-Rahib, and Tu'aymah ibn Ubayriq.

His saying "wa-shahidu" (وَشَهِدُوا) is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon "imanihim", meaning "and their testimony", because the noun resembling the verb in derivation (al-ism al-shabih bi-l-fi'l, a noun that resembles a verb in form and function) may fittingly be coordinated with a verb, and a verb may be coordinated with it.

[Page 304]

﴿Those—their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾ ﴿Except those who repent after that and make amends; indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

The demonstrative (al-ishara) is for alerting the listener that they deserve what follows the demonstrative in terms of the judgment against them. The meaning of "the curse of Allah, and of the angels" up to His words "all together" has been explained in Surat al-Baqarah. The meaning of ﴿except those who repent and make amends﴾ [al-Baqarah: 160] was also explained earlier in Surat al-Baqarah, and the meaning of ﴿indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is a metaphor (kinaya) for His forgiveness of them. It is said that it was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Suwayd al-Ansari, from the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, who apostatized and joined Quraysh. It is also said that he joined the Christians of Syria. Then he wrote to his people asking them whether there was any repentance for him. They asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed, so he embraced Islam again and returned to Madinah. His saying ﴿indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is a reason (illa) for an omitted statement, whose implied meaning is: Allah forgives them, because He is Forgiving and Merciful.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief, their repentance will never be accepted, and they are the astray.﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:90]

Qatada, 'Ata' and al-Hasan said: this verse was revealed concerning the Jews. On this view, the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is used with the meaning of lam al-'ahd (the lam of prior reference, indicating a known group). Thus the Jews, after believing in Musa, disbelieved in 'Isa, and increased in disbelief by disbelieving in Muhammad (ﷺ).

It was also said that the verse means both the Jews and the Christians. As you know, the Jews are as described. The Christians believed in 'Isa, then disbelieved, worshipped him and made him a god, and then increased in disbelief by disbelieving in Muhammad (ﷺ).

As for the interpretation of ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾, it may be a metaphor (kinayah) meaning that they will not repent, so that their repentance is not accepted, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿nor will any intercession be accepted from it﴾ [al-Baqara 2:48], meaning there is no intercession for it, so it is not accepted. This is like the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"Over a faded road whose landmark cannot be followed"

meaning there is no landmark for it. This is because it is known from the (other) textual evidence that repentance is accepted. Its indication is the restriction (hasr) intended for emphasis in His saying, ﴿and they are the astray﴾.

Or God forbade His Prophet from being deceived by what they display of Islam as hypocrisy [Page 305], so the meaning of non-acceptance is that their belief is not accepted as true. Or it is an informing that disbelief has become firmly settled in their hearts, so that it has become their nature from which they do not turn; thus when they show repentance, they are liars. The non-acceptance then means that one is not reassured about them, and their secrets are left to God, exalted is He.

Some Jews had embraced Islam before the revelation of the verse, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam, so there is no difficulty in that, and some of them embraced Islam after the revelation of the verse.

It was also said that the intended people are those Muslims who apostatised and died in disbelief. On this view, increasing (in disbelief) means persisting and not desisting. The discussion of the meaning of ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ is as already mentioned. On this view, His saying ﴿indeed, those who disbelieve and die﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:91] is a verbal emphasis (tawkid lafzi) by means of a synonym, and it serves as the basis for the consequence stated in His saying ﴿never will there be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:91].

In any case, the interpretation of the verse is necessary, because its apparent meaning is contradicted by the decisive evidences that the Islam of a disbeliever is accepted, even if disbelief recurred from him, and that the repentance of sinners is accepted, even if it is later broken, according to the most correct opinions. A verse like this one will come in Surat al-Nisa', namely His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief, God would not forgive them, nor would He guide them to a way﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:137].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 91:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers — never will be accepted from any one of them the earth filled with gold, even if he were to ransom himself with it. For those is a painful punishment, and they will have no helpers.﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) explaining the condition of the disbelievers who died upon their disbelief. It arises from the ruling concerning a group of disbelievers whose disbelief was repeated until it became firmly established in them and became their habit. If the intended meaning of those who "increased in disbelief" in the preceding verse is those who died upon disbelief, then this verse serves as an verbal emphasis (tawkid lafzi) of the first, repeated so that his statement ﴿never will be accepted from any one of them the earth filled with gold﴾ may be built upon it. In either case, the relative pronoun here is intended in its generality, like the definite article with the particle of comprehensiveness (lam al-istighraq).

The fa' in his statement ﴿fa-lan yuqbala﴾ indicates that the relative clause is treated like a conditional noun (ism al-shart), to show that the relative clause is the cause of the non-acceptance of repentance. For this reason the predicate of the relative clause is not joined by fa' in the preceding sentence: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved after their belief and then increased in disbelief — their repentance will never be accepted﴾ [Al 'Imran: 90], because if they did that and did not die as disbelievers, their repentance would be accepted. Unlike those who die upon disbelief, the cause of the non-acceptance of repentance from them is explicitly stated. Accordingly, the sentence ﴿fa-lan yuqbala min ahadihim﴾ through its end is in the position of the predicate of inna, and the sentence ﴿ulaika lahum 'adhabun alim﴾ is a resumptive statement of explanatory type (isti'naf bayani) arising from the report that no ransom will be accepted from any one of them. It is also possible that the sentence ﴿fa-lan yuqbala min ahadihim﴾ through its end is an interposed clause between the subject of inna and its predicate, joined by fa', like the one in his saying the Exalted: ﴿That, so taste it; and that for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire﴾ [al-Anfal: 14], and then the sentence ﴿ulaika lahum 'adhabun alim﴾ is the predicate of inna.

The meaning of ﴿fa-lan yuqbala min ahadihim mil'u al-ardi dhahaban﴾ is: nothing by which they might ransom themselves will be accepted from them in the Hereafter, since it is evident that the intended meaning is not the negation of the acceptance of ransom in this world, because they are described as having died while they were disbelievers. The mil' (with a kasra on the mim) is that which fills a vessel, and "the filling of the earth" in their speech is a metaphor for the unattainable abundance, because the earth cannot be filled by any of the existing things, and this is like their saying "the number of the sands of al-Dahna'" and "the number of the pebbles." This quantity is specified by "gold" (dhahaban) because of the rarity of gold, the competition of people for its possession, and the eagerness of the one who offers it to meet his need. Al-Hariri said:

"And the swiftness of his stride accompanied the success of endeavours."

His saying ﴿wa-law ifta da bihi﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the waw is the waw of circumstance, i.e., it will not be accepted from them even in the state of supposing that they ransom themselves with it. The particle law is conditional and the omission of its answer is due to the indication of what precedes it. This usage is common in Arabic speech, and because of its frequency many grammarians said: the conditional particles law and in in such a context are stripped of the meaning of condition, and are intended only for emphasis; they named them "connective" (wasliyyatan), i.e., that they are merely for connection and linking in a context of emphasis. They also disagreed about the i'rab of the clause occurring in this position, and about the waw joined to it. The verifiers hold that it is the waw of circumstance, and to this al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Jinni and al-Marzuqi inclined. Among the grammarians there are those who made the waw conjunctive, upon an omitted condition that is the opposite of the stated condition, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Be steadfast in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 135]. Among the grammarians there are those who made the waw one of resumption, which al-Radi mentioned while refuting it; and it does not deserve refutation, for the explanatory resumption has a place with this waw.

Moreover, the positions of this waw indicate that the condition following it is a hypothetical condition, the furthest thing that might be expected to negate the ruling before it, so the speaker mentions it to intend the establishment of the ruling in all circumstances, like the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'di Karib:

"Beauty is not a cloak; so know, even if you are wrapped in a mantle."

For this reason the grammarians' custom is to posit before it a condition that is the contradiction of the condition following it, so they say in such a saying as "wa-in ruddita burdan" — "if you are not wrapped in a mantle, but even if you are wrapped in a mantle." Likewise the saying of al-Nabigha:

"I will muzzle my dog lest its barking disturb you, and even if I were pasturing Musahhilan and Hamiran."

Because of this, a problem arose concerning this verse: what follows "law" in it is the very same as what precedes it, since the ransoming is the very same as the giving of the earth filled with gold, so it is not sound to posit "if he does not ransom himself with it, but even if he ransoms himself with it." For this reason the exegetes needed interpretations of this verse. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Never will be accepted from any one of them the earth filled with gold, which he spends in this world, even if he ransoms himself with it in the Hereafter," i.e., nothing will ransom them from the punishment. This view is remote, for it is not conceivable that there is a ransoming in the Hereafter such that one should be exaggerated about it. Some people said: the waw is superfluous. Al-Zamakhshari in the Kashshaf said: it is understood according to the meaning, as if it were said: "Never will a ransom be accepted from any one of them, even if he ransoms himself with the earth filled with gold," meaning that the expression "the earth filled" is equivalent in force to the expression "ransom," and after that it was abbreviated to the pronoun. He said: it is also possible to posit the word "like" (mithl) before the genitive pronoun, i.e., "even if he ransoms himself with its like," i.e., even if he increased it twofold, as in His saying: ﴿And if those who did wrong had all that is in the earth and the like of it with it, they would surely ransom themselves with it﴾ [al-Zumar: 47].

In my view, the position of this conditional in the verse follows a usage that the people of Arabic grammar overlooked mentioning, namely: that the conditional occurs as an explanatory resumption, an answer to a question, realized or presumed, which the speaker imagines from the addressee and intends to posit. It does not then require that its condition be the limit of the ruling mentioned before it; rather it may be so, and it may be that the question is merely an expression of wonder at the ruling, so it occurs by repeating what the ruling contained, as an affirmation upon the speaker, in the manner of their saying: "Know what you are saying," and the speaker answers by repeating the question, confirming it for him and signalling that he spoke with clear evidence. Yes, the usual case is that the question concerns the limit, as in the saying of Ru'ba, and it is one of the witnesses for this:

"The cousins said, 'O Salma, even if he be poor and destitute,' she said, 'even if.'"

And sometimes the question is omitted and the answer remains, as in the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

"Do not hold me to the words of the slanderers, when I have not sinned, even if the sayings about me multiply."

And sometimes the question is mentioned without the answer, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah? Say: "Even though they own nothing and do not understand?"﴾ [al-Zumar: 43]. For if the answer from the polytheists were mentioned, they would have answered by affirming that.

So His saying ﴿wa-law ifta da bihi﴾ is the answer to the question of one wondering at the ruling, which is His saying ﴿fa-lan yuqbala min ahadihim﴾, as if he said, "even if he ransomed himself with it," and it was answered by affirming that, in the manner of the verse of Ka'b. Thus the import of this conditional is then merely emphasis.

It is also possible that the conditional is a conjunction upon an omitted element indicated by "ifta da" (ransomed himself): i.e., never will be accepted from any one of them the earth filled with gold as a pledge, even if he gave it as a ransom, because among the customs of the Arabs is that one who is owed a right may give a pledge in it until settlement or pardon occurs, and likewise in debts. When they agreed upon a reconciliation, the tribes would give hostages from among themselves, as al-Harith said:

"Remember the alliance of Dhu al-Majaz, in which covenants and guarantors were arranged."

And it occurred in the hadith of Abu Rafi' the Jew that Muhammad ibn Maslama said to Abu Rafi': "We will pledge to you the weapons and the armour."

The sentence ﴿ulaika lahum 'adhabun alim﴾ is a summation of the meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved after their belief﴾ [Al 'Imran: 90], the two verses.

His saying ﴿wa-ma lahum min nasirin﴾ is a completion of the negation of the states of help from them, for the one held for something may give a ransom of wealth, or may be guaranteed by one whose guarantee is trusted, or may be interceded for by one whose word is heeded; and each of the guarantor and the intercessor is a helper.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 92:

Page 5
﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love. And whatever you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.﴾
It is an resumptive clause (isti'naf) that came interposed between the clause ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91], and the clause ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93].

Opening the discourse by explaining some of the means of righteousness (birr) is an indication that the laws of Islam revolve around the axis of righteousness, and that righteousness is a great inner meaning, whose reality is not impaired except by what leads to the breaking of one of the foundations of inner uprightness. So the purpose of this verse comprises two matters: the first is exhortation to spending and affirming that it is among righteousness; the second is affirming the righteousness of which spending is one of the characteristics.

The reason for this verse's position right after its predecessor is that when the previous verse explained that the greatest of what those who disbelieve spend will not be accepted from any of them, this verse explained what benefits the people of faith from giving wealth, and that it brings its giver to the rank of righteousness. Between the two extremes there are many degrees, which the discerning know from this contrast. The address is to the believers, because they are the intended audience of every address in which no preceding element specifies its intended audience.

Righteousness is the perfection of good and its comprehensiveness within its kind, since good may be magnified in quality, in quantity, or in both together. Thus the giving of one's soul in support of the religion is magnified in quality by facing a numerous enemy with a small number; likewise rescuing a drowning person amid the terror of the sea, where multiplicity is not conceivable in such a case; and feeding the hungry is magnified by multiplicity; and spending is magnified in both respects together. And the reward for an act of good, when it reaches the perfection and comprehensiveness of reward, is also righteousness.

Page 6
Al-Nawwas ibn Sim'an narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Righteousness is good character, and sin is that which stirs in the soul and you dislike that people should become aware of it." Related by Muslim.
The contrasting of righteousness with sin indicates that righteousness is the opposite of sin. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 177].

Spending has been made the end (ghayah) of the non-attainment of righteousness, from the very wealth that is loved. The implication of the end is that the attainment of righteousness does not occur without it. This suggests that before spending there are intermediate inner stages on the path leading to righteousness, and those are all the characteristics of righteousness, which remain untraversed; and that righteousness is not attained except by its final point, which is spending from what is beloved. Thus there appears for "hatta" here a rhetorical position that nothing else could fill: for if it were said "except that you spend of what you love," the hearer would suppose that spending from the beloved alone brings about the attainment of righteousness, and the indication of the stages and degrees that "hatta" implies would be lost.

"Tunalu" is derived from "nawal," which is obtaining something given.

The definite article in "al-birr" is the definite article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), because this genus is composed of many acts, among them the specific spending; without it, this reality is not realized.

Infaq (spending): giving wealth, sustenance, and clothing.

What is referred to by "ma" in His saying ﴿of what you love﴾ is wealth: that is, precious wealth dear to the soul. The indefiniteness here is justified by the presence of "tunfiqu," since spending is not applied except to the giving of wealth; so "min" here is only partitive. As for one who permitted that "min" be explanatory, he has erred, because the explanatory "min" must be preceded by an indefinite term.

Beloved wealth varies according to the circumstances of those who give charity, their desires, and the abundance of their riches. Spending from it, i.e., giving charity, is an indication of generosity for the sake of Allah the Exalted, and in that is a purification of the soul from what remains in it of stinginess. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul, it is those who are the successful﴾ [al-Hashr: 9]. In this there is great benefit for the community, for its wealthy give to its poor from the choice wealth their souls aspire to, so the bonds of brotherhood are strengthened and the life of all becomes pleasant.

Malik related in the Muwatta', from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "Abu Talha was the wealthiest of the Ansar in Madinah, and the most beloved of his properties to him was Bi'r Ha', and it faced the mosque, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to enter it and drink from its pleasant water. When the saying of Allah the Exalted ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love﴾ was revealed, Abu Talha came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, indeed Allah said: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love﴾, and indeed the most beloved of my properties is Bi'r Ha', and it is a charity for Allah, and I hope for its righteousness and its store with Allah. So place it, O Messenger of Allah, wherever Allah shows you.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Bakh! That is profitable wealth, that is profitable wealth. I have heard what you said, and I think you should give it to the nearest relatives.' He said: 'I will do so, O Messenger of Allah.' So he gave it to Hassan ibn Thabit and Ubayy ibn Ka'b."
Allah has explained the characteristics of righteousness in His saying ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets, and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask, and for freeing captives; and [who] establishes prayer and gives zakah; and [who] fulfills his promise when he has promised; and the patient in poverty and hardship and during battle﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Allah has joined it with piety in His saying ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2], thus contrasting righteousness with sin, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Sim'an mentioned just above.

A small thing may be precious according to the condition of its owner, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who find not but their effort﴾ [al-Tawbah: 79].
