His saying ﴿indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾ is meant in its literal sense, i.e., He is aware of the measure of the effect of what He has encouraged, and it is also meant as a metaphor (kinayah) for the reward for it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 93–95:

﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel had forbidden to himself before the Torah was revealed. Say: "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿Whoever fabricates a lie against God after that, they are the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿Say: "God has spoken the truth, so follow the religion of Abraham, a upright monotheist (ḥanīf), and he was not one of the polytheists."﴾

This is connected to the preceding verses in His saying, ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾ [Al 'Imran: 67], and between them there are digressions and shifts across different modes of address.

This is a partial argument, following the principal arguments, that the religion of Judaism has nothing to do with the ḥanīfiyya (the upright monotheistic faith of Abraham). The food that was forbidden by the text of the Torah was not forbidden in the ḥanīfiyya. For this reason, the Children of Israel before the Torah were under the law of Abraham, so the only food forbidden to them was food that Jacob had forbidden to himself. The argument is evident, and the connection is confirmed by His saying at its end, ﴿Say: "God has spoken the truth, so follow the religion of Abraham, a upright monotheist."﴾

It is possible that the Jews, despite this, criticised Islam, claiming that it was not based on the law of Abraham, since it permitted Muslims to eat what was forbidden to the Jews. This would be either out of ignorance of the history of their legislation, or out of misguidance by their rabbis towards their common people, to repel them from Islam, because nations in their simplicity cling to what is familiar, consider it akin to truths, and make it a measure for acceptance and criticism. So He made clear to them that this is not something to be considered when examining the rest of the religions. It is enough for you that a great religion, namely the religion of Abraham, and a group of prophets from his sons and descendants, did not forbid that.

[p. 9]
The definite article in "al-ṭa'ām" (the food) is the article of the genus (ta'rīf al-jins).
"Kull" (all) is used to make the generality explicit.

The Qur'an has argued against them with this ruling, because it is the clearest indication in the Torah of the occurrence of abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by a later one). The Torah mentions in the Book of Genesis what indicates that Jacob forbade to himself the eating of the sciatic nerve that is on the thigh. It has also been said that he forbade to himself the flesh and milk of camels. It was said that this was by way of a vow (nadhr). It was also said that physicians forbade him to eat what contained the sciatic nerve, because he was afflicted with sciatica. A ḥadīth also states that Jacob was in the desert and his health was not sound from eating the meat that contained the sciatic nerve. As for what Jacob forbade to himself of food: the apparent meaning of the verse is that this was not by any revelation from God to him, but from his own initiative. Some of it he intended as a means of drawing near to God by depriving himself of some desired good things, and this is part of the struggle against the self (jihād al-nafs), one of the stations of the ascetics. The prohibition on himself was by vow or by resolve. There is no proof in this that prophets may exercise independent reasoning (ijtihād) in legislation, because this was an exercise in regard to himself concerning what was permitted to him, and he did not impose it on anyone else. Perhaps the sons of Jacob followed their father in what he forbade to himself, and so it persisted among them.

His saying ﴿before the Torah was revealed﴾ is an explicit statement of the point on which the refutation rests, since the intent is to alert them to what they had forgotten, so they were treated as one ignorant of the fact that Jacob lived before Moses. Al-'Isam said: His saying ﴿before the Torah was revealed﴾ is connected to His saying "lawful" (ḥillan), so that it does not become void of benefit. But this is not useful, because when it came after the exception from His saying "lawful," and it became clear from the exception that the speech concerns the time of Jacob, the mention of the qualifier became superfluous, were it not for treating them as ignorant, and for the purpose of openly exposing their error and implicitly mocking their stupidity.

His saying ﴿Say: "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful."﴾ means: in your claim that the matter is not as we have stated, or: if you are truthful in everything that preceded, namely your saying that Abraham was upon the religion of Judaism. It is a command to demonstrate their inability, since it is known that they will not bring it when they argue for truthfulness.

The fā' in His saying "fa-'tū" (so bring) is the fā' of consequence.

[p. 10]
His saying ﴿if you are truthful﴾ is a conditional clause whose answer has been omitted, because the consequence stated before it indicates it. The implied meaning is: "If you are truthful, then bring the Torah."
His saying ﴿Whoever fabricates a lie against God after that, they are the wrongdoers﴾ is the conclusion of the exposure of their lying, meaning: whoever persists in lying against God. That is, "whoever among you fabricates after We have made the Torah a decisive judgment between us," since they have no pretext they could claim as a basis for their invention. The fabrication is attributed to God because it concerns the religion of God.

The fā' is for consequence following the command.

Al-iftirā' means lying, and it is a synonym of al-ikhtilāq (invention). Al-iftirā' is derived from al-fary, which is cutting leather into pieces to be prepared, such as when a sandal is shaped, or a mat or a waterskin is made. The form "iftara" is an iftiʿāl form from "fara," perhaps to convey intensification of the cutting, as one says "iftarā al-jild" (he cut up the hide), as if he struggled intensely in cutting it, or cut it in a manner of corruption, and this is the most common usage of "iftarā." They used the name "iftirā'" for reporting something as having happened when it had not happened, in the sense of lying. It seems its origin was a metaphor and an allusion to lying, and this became widespread until it became a synonym for lying. A parallel is the use of the name "ikhtilāq" for lying. So iftirā' is synonymous with kadhib (lying), and its being followed here by "al-kadhib" is an emphasis on iftirā', and parallels to this pairing occur in many verses.

Thus "al-kadhib" is in the accusative as an absolute object emphasising its verb. The lām in "al-kadhib" is the lām of the genus, so it is like His saying ﴿fabricated a lie against God, or is there madness in him?﴾

Al-kadhib is a report that contradicts what is the case in reality, without regard to whether the report agrees with the belief of the one who reports it or differs from his belief. But if a report combines contradicting reality and contradicting the belief of the reporter, that is blameworthy and reprehensible. If he believes its occurrence due to a doubt or a poor reflection, it is blameworthy, but the reporter is not despised for it. In the usage of the Arabs, the term kadhib most commonly refers to what is blameworthy.

Then He declared that what is required on the side of truthfulness is the report of God, the Exalted, to certify that they will not bring the Torah, and this is like His saying ﴿and they will never wish for it, ever﴾. After He finished exposing their lying with a decisive proof, He said ﴿Say: "God has spoken the truth"﴾, which is an implicit reference to their lying, because the truthfulness of one of two contradictory reports necessitates the falsehood of the other. So it is used in its literal and its implicative meaning.

The consequence in His saying ﴿so follow the religion of Abraham, a upright monotheist﴾ is a consequence of "God has spoken the truth," because following what the truthful one commands is deliverance from danger.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 96 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds.﴾ ﴿In it are clear signs: the Station of Ibrahim (Abraham). And whoever enters it is safe.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97].

This statement stands in the position of a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the command in His words ﴿Follow the creed of Ibrahim, a man of pure faith﴾ [Al 'Imran: 95], because this House, whose status is highlighted, was a station of Ibrahim. So the virtues of this House establish the excellence of the law of its builder in the common understanding of people. Thus this argument is rhetorical (khitabi). It is also an informative statement about the excellence and sanctity of the Ka'bah in past time.

The fact that this statement is a causal explanation is indicated by the position of *inna* (indeed) at its beginning. The emphasis with *inna* here is merely for the purpose of giving importance (al-ihtimam), and not to refute the denial of a denier or the doubt of a doubter.

Among the characteristics of *inna* when it occurs in speech merely for the purpose of giving importance is that it takes the place of the conjunctive *fa'* (of consequence, *fa' al-tafri'*) and conveys causation and connection, as in *Dala'il al-I'jaz* (by 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani).

Because this function of conveying connection is present, the conjunction (*'atf*) is dispensed with, since *inna* signals connection. The explanation of the causal aspect is that this House, when it was the first House established for guidance and for the proclamation of the Oneness of Allah, to be a visible sign perceived by the senses, indicating the meaning of unity and the negation of associating partners with Allah, it comprised the evidences of the *hanifiyyah* (pure monotheism). When the honor of priority was established for it, and the lasting sanctity through the passage of ages, in contrast to other religious edifices that came into existence after it, while it still stands, this was a divine indication that it is in the place of Allah's special care. Thus it indicates that the religion which accompanied its establishment is the religion desired by Allah. This returns to the meaning of His words ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19].

This causal explanation is rhetorical, proceeding by the method of customary implication (al-luzum al-'urfi).

Al-Wahidi said, on the authority of Mujahid: The Muslims and the Jews boasted, and the Jews said: "The Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) is better and greater than the Ka'bah, because it is the place of migration of the prophets and it is in the holy land." And the Muslims said: "Rather, the Ka'bah is better." So Allah revealed this verse.

*Awwal* is a term for the one who precedes in a certain action. When it is added to a noun denoting a genus, it means the first of that genus which is attributed to it, in the matter being spoken of.

*Al-bayt* is a structure that shelters one person or a group. It may be a dwelling (bayt sukna), a house of prayer (bayt salah), or a meeting place (bayt nadwah). It may be built of stone, or of cloth woven from hair or wool, or it may be of leather, in which case it is called a *qubbah* (tent dome). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And He made for you from the hides of cattle houses﴾ [al-Nahl: 80].

The meaning of *wudi'a* (was placed) is "was founded and established," and from it the place is called *mawdi'* (a location). The original meaning of *wad'* (placing) is "setting down," the opposite of "raising." Since the raised thing is far from reach, the placed thing is near to reach. So the word *wad'* was applied to the meaning of bringing something near to the one who reaches for it, and preparing it for benefit.

*Al-nas* (the people) was discussed previously in the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8] in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Bakkah* is the name of Makkah. It is a dialectal form in which the letter *mim* is replaced by *ba'* in many words that have been counted among synonyms, such as *lazib* for *lazim* (necessary), and *arbad* and *armad* (meaning "ashen in color"). In the *al-'Utbiyyah* report of Ibn al-Qasim, from Malik, it is stated that *Bakkah* with *ba'* is the name of the place of the House, and that *Makkah* with *mim* is the name of the rest of the site. So the *ba'* of the preposition here indicates locative containment of the place of the House specifically, not the whole town in which the House is located. My own view is that *Bakkah* is a name meaning "the town," which Ibrahim (Abraham) gave as a designation for the place he chose for the settlement of his son, intending that it become a town. Its origin is therefore from the Chaldean language, the language of Ibrahim. Do you not see that they named the city of Ba'albak, meaning "the town of Ba'l," and Ba'l was the deity of the Chaldeans? And among the miraculous aspects of the Qur'an is this word when mentioning that it was the first House. So observe also the first name. This is supported by His words ﴿Lord of this city﴾ [al-Naml: 91] and His words ﴿My Lord, make this city secure﴾ [Ibrahim: 35]. It has also been said that *Bakkah* is derived from *al-bakk*, which means crowding, but I do not think that this meaning was intended by the one who coined the name.

The naming of the House by its proper name, the Ka'bah, which had become predominant, was avoided, and instead it was described by a relative clause, "the one at Bakkah." This is because this descriptive clause became more famous for identifying it to the listeners, since at that time there was no other house of worship in Makkah besides it. This contrasts with the name al-Ka'bah, which was applied to the church that the Abyssinians built in San'a for the Christian religion, and they called it "al-Ka'bah al-Yamaniyyah" (the Yemeni Ka'bah).

The intended meaning is to establish the priority of the Ka'bah in existence over other houses of the same type. The apparent meaning of the verse is that the Ka'bah is the first of the houses built on earth. On this apparent meaning Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and a group held firm, saying: "It is the first building." They also said that it had been built since the time of Adam, peace be upon him, then it was effaced, and Ibrahim renewed it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Stories have been transmitted regarding this whose chains of transmission are weak, so I have left them aside." They also claimed that it used to be called *al-Diraah* (on the pattern of *Ghurab*). But the researchers and the majority of the scholars did not adopt this apparent meaning, and they interpreted the verse otherwise.

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "There were many houses before the House." There is no doubt that the Ka'bah was built by Ibrahim, and the mention of this has been repeated in the Qur'an. Had it been built by prophets before him, the mention of that would have been increased to add to the honoring of its status. And if that is so, then it cannot be that the first building erected on earth was in the time of Ibrahim, because before Ibrahim there were nations and ages in which building existed. The most famous of that is the Tower of Babel, built after the Flood; and what the Egyptians built before the time of Ibrahim; and what the Chaldeans built in the land of Ibrahim before his migration to Egypt. Among that is the house of their idols, and that was before Hajar came to it, whom the king of Egypt gave to him as a gift. The Qur'an has also related about them: ﴿They said, "Build for him a building and throw him into the blazing fire"﴾ [al-Saffat: 97]. So the interpretation of the verse is determined in a clear manner. Scholars have followed various approaches to it, and they all return to interpreting either the word "first," or the word "house," or the verb "was placed," or "people," or the structure of the verse. What I see in interpretation is that the Qur'an is a book of religion and guidance. Therefore the purpose of the speech is not to record the earliest points of history, but the earliest causes of guidance. So the priority in the verse is on its proper footing, and the House is likewise. The meaning is that it is the first House of true worship established for proclaiming monotheism, by the context and by the indication of His words ﴿was placed for mankind﴾, which implies that it was from the placing of one who places for the benefit of people, for if it had been a house of dwelling, it would have said "the people placed it." And by the indication of the two states that follow, namely His words ﴿blessed and a guidance for the worlds﴾. This is an interpretation regarding the meaning of "house." And if it was the first house of true worship, it was the first center of guidance, so every guidance was derived from it. There is no escape for any people who were upon guidance from acknowledging it and its virtue. This requires following the creed founded upon the foundations of the creed of its builder. And this is what is implied by the consequence of His words ﴿Follow the creed of Ibrahim, a man of pure faith﴾ [Al 'Imran: 95].

'Ali ibn Abi Talib also interpreted the verse. It was narrated from him that a man asked him: "Is it the first house?" He said: "No. There were houses before it. But it is the first house placed for mankind, blessed and a guidance." So he made ﴿blessed and a guidance﴾ two states of the pronoun in ﴿was placed﴾, not of the relative pronoun. This is an interpretation regarding the structure of the verse which the mind does not reach except with the meaning that it is the first house among the houses of guidance, as we have said. And his intention is not that the verb "was placed" is the predicate, because the predicate is determined to be His words ﴿the one at Bakkah﴾, as indicated by the entry of the particle *lam* upon it.

And on the authority of Mujahid: The Jews said: "The Bayt al-Maqdis is better than the Ka'bah, because it is the place of migration of the prophets." The Muslims said: "The Ka'bah." So Allah revealed this verse. This is an interpretation which takes "first" to mean first of two things, not first of all houses in general.

It has also been said: he intended by "the first" the most honored, as a metaphor.

In my view, it is permissible that the intended "people" be the known people, namely the People of the Book: I mean the Jews, the Christians, and the Muslims. All of them acknowledge the origin of the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. So the first place of worship, by the consensus of all of them, is the Ka'bah. Therefore they are obliged to acknowledge that it is more excellent than what is other than it among their houses of worship.

[p. 15]

The priority was only a cause of preference because places of worship do not differ in excellence in terms of worship, since in that respect they are equal. Rather, they differ by what accompanies that, such as the length of time during which worship has been performed in them, their attribution to their builder, and the goodness of the intention in that. Allah the Exalted said about the Mosque of Quba': ﴿A mosque founded on piety from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it﴾ [al-Tawbah: 108].

The Ka'bah has combined all these excellences, so it was the earliest of the houses of true worship. It precedes the Bayt al-Maqdis by nine centuries. For Ibrahim built the Ka'bah around the year 1900 BC, and Sulayman (Solomon) built the Bayt al-Maqdis in the year 1000 BC. The Ka'bah was built by Ibrahim with his own hand, so it was built by the hand of a messenger. As for the Bayt al-Maqdis, its laborers built it for Sulayman by his command. And it was related in Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah: 'Which mosque was placed first?' He said: 'The Sacred Mosque.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'The Farthest Mosque.' I said: 'How long was between them?' He said: 'Forty years.'" The scholars found this problematic, since between Ibrahim and Sulayman there were centuries, so how could it be forty years? Some answered that it is possible that Ibrahim built a mosque at the site of the Bayt al-Maqdis, then it was effaced, and Sulayman renewed it.

I say: There is no doubt that the Bayt al-Maqdis was built by Sulayman, as is the explicit text of the Jewish book, and the Qur'an alluded to it in His words ﴿They made for him whatever he willed of sanctuaries﴾ [Saba': 13], and so on. The apparent meaning is that when Ibrahim passed through the lands of Syria, and Allah promised him that He would give that land as an inheritance to his offspring, Allah designated for him the place where his descendants would later build the greatest mosque. So he established there a small mosque in thanks to Allah the Exalted, and he placed it upon the rock which was made an altar for sacrifice. This is the rock upon which Sulayman later built the mosque. When the people of that land were polytheists at that time, that structure was effaced, until Allah guided Sulayman to establish the Farthest Mosque upon it. This is among the knowledge which the books of the Jews neglected. It is established in the Book of Genesis that Ibrahim built altars in places through which he passed in the land of the Canaanites, because Allah informed him that He would give that land to his offspring. So the apparent meaning is that he also built an altar at the site of the mosque of Jerusalem.

[p. 16]

*Mubarak* is a passive participle from *barraka al-shay'*, meaning he made a blessing for it, and blessing is an increase in good. That is, blessing was placed in it by the decree of Allah the Exalted, since He decreed that whoever enters it would be rewarded and would attain good in proportion to his intention. He also decreed for its neighbors and the inhabitants of its land that they would be blessed with increased reward and a comfortable state. He commanded that its interior be made secure, and He decreed this among the people, and all of that was a blessing. The meaning of blessing will come up again at His words ﴿And this is a Book which We have sent down, blessed, confirming what is before it﴾ [al-An'am: 92] in Surat al-An'am.

He described it with the verbal noun in His words *wa-huda* (and a guidance), for emphasis, because it is the cause of guidance.

It was made a guidance for all the worlds, because its fame and the people's hearing of it would lead them to inquire about the reason for its establishment, namely that it is for the Oneness of Allah and the purification of souls from the filth of polytheism. So the one seeking guidance is guided by that, and the skeptic is restrained.

And among the blessing of its essence is that its stones were placed in its construction by the hand of Ibrahim, the hand of Isma'il, and then the hand of Muhammad (ﷺ), especially the Black Stone.

*Mubarakan wa-huda* is in the accusative as states (hal) from the predicate, which is the relative pronoun.

[Page 17]

The clause ﴿In it are clear signs﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:97] is a resumed statement of praise for this House, for the virtues and distinctions surrounding it. The style is changed for emphasis. For this reason the clause is not made a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) coordinated with the two circumstantial phrases before it, because ﴿blessed and a guidance﴾ are inherent attributes of it, and they are concomitant circumstances (ḥālān muqārinān), whereas the signs are accidents that occurred at different times. Or it is a third circumstance, and it was not joined with "wa" (and) because it is a clause while what precedes it consists of single words. It was also to avoid the supposition that the "wa" in it is the "wa" of circumstance, so that its form would follow a form other than the more eloquent form for such cases, namely not being connected with "wa", as Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qāhir established. Had it been connected with the conjunctive "wa", it would have been confused with the circumstantial "wa", and so it would be disliked in hearing. This is therefore a case of disjunction (qaṭʿ) to remove ambiguity. Or we may say it is a circumstance, and it was not coordinated with the other circumstances because it is a clause, so it dispensed with a conjunctive link by means of the pronoun.

Describing the signs as "clear" (bayyināt) is because they are manifest in the knowledge of those addressed. The sum of these signs is what God facilitated for the inhabitants of the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram) and its visitors of the paths of good, and what He repelled from them of harms, in a state upon which all the Arabs agreed, and by which they restrained themselves and their desires, despite their eagerness to satisfy their souls. The greatest of them is security, which the souls of all the Arabs had settled upon in the Jāhiliyya (the Age of Ignorance), despite their not being religious. A man would meet the killer of his father in the Ḥaram and would not be harmed by him. The submission of such people among the various tribes, who differ in lineages, customs and religions, is a sign that God established this in their souls. Likewise is the safety of its game animals, despite the Arabs' passion for hunting. Among them is what spread among the Arabs regarding the destruction of anyone who intended it with evil. The withdrawal of the Abyssinians from it after they had taken possession of all of Yemen and Tihama is nothing but one of the signs of God concerning it. Among them is the gushing forth of water in it for Ishmael when he was on the brink of death. And among them is God's ransoming him with a great sacrifice when his father Abraham, peace be upon him, intended to sacrifice him. Among them is what spread among the Arabs, and they inherited its report from father to grandfather, concerning the descent of the Black Stone from heaven onto Abū Qubays in Abraham's sight, and perhaps it is a meteoritic stone. Among them is the facilitation of provision for its inhabitants despite the barrenness of its land and the brackishness of its water.

As for His saying, "the station of Abraham" (maqām Ibrāhīm): the origin of "maqām" is that it is a noun of place from "qiyām" (standing). "Qiyām" is used in its common meaning, which is the opposite of sitting, and it is used in the specific sense of standing for prayer and supplication. According to the second meaning, the nominative "maqām" is the predicate of an omitted pronoun referring back to ﴿the one at Bakka﴾, meaning: it is the station of Abraham, i.e., the House that is at Bakka. The omission of the subject here is of the kind named by the scholars of ʿilm al-maʿānī (the science of meaning), following the terminology of al-Sakkākī, "omission for customary usage", which occurs in the nominative when praising, blaming or expressing compassion, after the attributes preceding it applied to the subject clarify what is meant by it, as in the verse of Abū al-Ṭamḥān al-Qaynī:

Indeed the sons of Lām ibn ʿAmr are a noble stock
that rose above a steep height whose ascents cannot be reached.
Stars of a sky, whenever one star sets,
another star appears to which its stars return.

This is the preferred reading of the position of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿the station of Abraham﴾ [3:97].

The Sacred Mosque has been described as ﴿the station of Abraham﴾ [3:97], meaning the place of his standing for prayer and circumambulation. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer﴾ [2:125]. This is supported by the saying of Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl:

I seek refuge in what Abraham sought refuge in,
facing the Kaʿba while standing.

According to the first meaning, what is intended is the stone in which there is the trace of the feet of Abraham, peace be upon him, in the rock upon which he ascended to raise the walls of the Kaʿba. This is how al-Zajjāj interpreted it, and al-Zamakhsharī followed him in that. Al-Zamakhsharī answered the objection that the plural (signs) is being explained by the singular: this singular is in effect equal to a group of signs, because the trace of the foot in the rock is a sign, its sinking into it up to the ankles is a sign, and the softening of some of the rock and not the rest is a sign. I say: it is indeed plural signs, because it indicates the prophethood of Abraham through a miracle granted to him, and the knowledge and power of God, and the survival of that trace while many traces have vanished over the length of centuries is also a sign.

As for His saying, "And whoever enters it is safe" (wa man dakhalahu kāna āminan), it is coordinated with the House's virtues and merits, namely the security within it in general, and a favour (imtinān) reminding of what was established in past ages. It is therefore grammatically a declarative statement, used in the sense of a favour, for security within it had been established and become constant. This favour is like God's favouring people by creating for them hearing and sight, which is not nullified by someone born blind or whom something has befallen that removed some of that.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: This is a report about what was, and it contains no establishment of a legal ruling. It is only an admonition to multiple signs and blessings: God, glory be to Him, had turned hearts away from intending to oppose it, and turned hands away from harming it. This was related from al-Ḥasan. If it is a report, it is a report about what passed before the coming of the law of Islam, when they had no restraining force in the Jāhiliyya. It is not refuted by what happened in it of disruption of security in fighting between al-Ḥajjāj and Ibn al-Zubayr, and in the strife of the Qarāmiṭa. We have mentioned that in the commentary on His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and others are ambiguous﴾ [3:7], at the beginning of this sūra.

Some scholars understood His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And whoever enters it is safe﴾ [3:97], as a report used in the sense of a command to make its interior secure from being harmed. This was related from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs and al-Shaʿbī.

Those who went to this meaning differed about how this command is to be acted upon. A group said: This is a ruling that was abrogated (nusikha), meaning that it was abrogated by the evidences which indicate that the Sacred Precinct does not protect a disobedient person. Al-Bukhārī related from Abū Shurayḥ al-Kaʿbī that he said to ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, while he was sending expeditions to Mecca, that is, to fight Ibn al-Zubayr: "Permit me, O Amir, to relate to you a saying which the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, uttered on the day after the Conquest. My ears heard it, my heart retained it, and my eyes saw him when he spoke it: 'He praised God and extolled Him, then said: Indeed Mecca was made sacred by God and not made sacred by people. It is not lawful for a man who believes in God and the Last Day to shed blood in it, nor to cut down a tree in it. If anyone seeks a concession to fight in it on account of the Messenger of God, say to him: Indeed God permitted His Messenger, but He did not permit you. He only permitted me to fight in it for an hour of the day, and today its sanctity has returned as it was yesterday. Let the one present convey it to the one absent.'" He said: Then ʿAmr said to me: "I know this better than you, O Abū Shurayḥ. The Sacred Precinct does not protect a disobedient person, nor a fugitive with blood guilt, nor a fugitive with a crime (kharba)." Al-Kharba, with a fatḥa on the kh and a sukūn on the r, means a crime or calamity that falls upon people. And it is established that "the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, ordered that Ibn Khaṭal be killed while he was clinging to the curtains of the Kaʿba on the day of the Conquest."

Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī said: Whoever commits a crime inside the Sacred Precinct or outside it, then takes refuge in the Sacred Precinct, the prescribed punishment (ḥadd) is carried out against him in the Precinct and retaliation (qiṣāṣ) is taken from him.

Abū Ḥanīfa and his four companions said: Retaliation is not exacted in the Sacred Precinct from one who has taken refuge in it from outside, as long as he remains in it. However, he is not to be sold to, eaten with, or sat with until he leaves the Sacred Precinct. They related this from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, and those we mentioned along with them just now.

In Aḥkām Ibn al-Faras it is said that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar said: Whoever fears being tricked (into harm) is not secure, and it is not permissible to harm him by refusing to speak with him.

Another group said: It is an established, unabrogated ruling. Some of them said: His saying ﴿and whoever enters it﴾ [3:97] implies that he committed what requires punishment outside the Sacred Precinct, so if he commits a crime within it, retaliation is exacted from him. This is the view of the majority. Perhaps their basis is His saying ﴿and sacred things are subject to retaliation﴾ [2:194], or they relied on evidences from analogy. A deviant opinion said: The prescribed punishment is not carried out in the Sacred Precinct even if the offender committed the crime within it. These people extended their evidence (to its logical end).

We have touched on this at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you in it﴾ [2:191].

Al-Zajjāj made the clause ﴿And whoever enters it is safe﴾ [3:97] a second sign among the clear signs, so it is an explanation of "signs" (āyāt). Al-Zamakhsharī followed him and said: It is permissible to apply the plural form to the dual, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [66:4]. A clause may explain a singular noun because this clause has the meaning of a singular noun, since the estimated sense is: "the station of Abraham and the security of whoever enters it." He did not compare this with what is used in Arabic speech so that this view would be brought closer. In my view, a parallel to it is the saying of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥillizah:

Who among us has, in His presence, three signs of good
in all of which there is judgment?
A sign: the striking of Shāriq al-Shaqīqa, when
the Maʿadd came, each clan with its banner.

Then he said:

Then Ḥujr, I mean the son of Umm Qaṭām,
and he has a green Persian (garment).

Then he said:

And we loosened the shackle of Imru' al-Qays from him
after his imprisonment and hardship had lasted long.

So he made "And we loosened" the fourth sign, by agreement of the commentators, since the estimated sense is: "and we loosened the shackle of Imru' al-Qays."

Al-Zamakhsharī also allowed that "signs" (āyāt) may remain in the sense of the plural, and it has been explained by two signs, while the third is omitted, like the saying of Jarīr:

Ḥanīfa were in three parts, and one third of them
were slaves, and a third were their clients.

That is, he did not mention the third part.

[Page 21]

This is a weak parallel, because Jarīr's verse has its third part shown, for they are the core, whereas in the case of the verse the rest of the signs are not known. It is also permissible for us to make His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And for God, from the people, is the pilgrimage to the House﴾ [3:97] and what follows, to include the third of the clear signs.

This is a ruling, and the verse follows it with a reminder of God's favour. Because the ruling honours the status of the House, its conjunction with the preceding clause is fitting. The implied sense is: blessed, a guidance, and its pilgrimage obligatory. So it is a conjunction to the circumstantial states (al-ahwal).

Hajj (pilgrimage) was discussed earlier, at God's words ﴿The pilgrimage is in well-known months﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], in Surah al-Baqarah. It has two vowel forms, with the ḥāʾ pronounced with a fatḥa or a kasra. In all its occurrences in the Qur'an it was not read with a kasra on the ḥāʾ except in this verse. Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, and Abū Jaʿfar read it with a kasra.

It is likely that this verse is the one by which the hajj was made obligatory on the Muslims, and our scholars have cited it as evidence for the obligation of hajj. The hajj performed by the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims before its revelation was therefore an act of drawing closer to God and a continuation of the ḥanīfiyya (the primordial monotheistic faith of Abraham). It is established that "the Prophet (ﷺ) performed hajj twice in Mecca before the Hijra and stood with the people (at ʿArafa)." As for the obligation of hajj in the Islamic law, there is no evidence that it was established except by this verse. The scholars of Islam have unanimously agreed to cite it as evidence for the obligation of hajj. Thus, what took place of hajj before its revelation, after the mission, is considered only a tahannuth (a devotional practice of seeking purity) and an act of drawing closer to God. It is also established that it was revealed in the third year after the Hijra, following the Battle of Uhud, so the hajj was made obligatory at that time.

Al-Qurṭubī mentioned the disagreement over the time when hajj became obligatory, in three opinions. It was said: the fifth year; it was said: the seventh year; and it was said: the ninth year. He did not attribute the opinions to their proponents, except that he mentioned from Ibn Hishām, from Abū ʿUbayd al-Wāqidī, that it was made obligatory in the year of the Trench (al-Khandaq), after the departure of the confederates (al-Aḥzāb), and their departure was at the end of the fifth year. Ibn Isḥāq said: "The idolaters were in charge of that pilgrimage."

In the Muqaddimāt of Ibn Rushd there is something implying that al-Shāfiʿī said: the hajj became obligatory in the ninth year. More apparent than these opinions is a fourth opinion, on which the jurists have unanimously agreed: the evidence for the obligation of hajj is God's words ﴿And due to God from the people is the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to make his way to it﴾. Al-Shāfiʿī cited it as evidence that its obligation is "with latitude" (ʿalā al-tarākhī, meaning it may be delayed without sin within a lifetime). Thus, its obligation upon the Muslims was established in the third year, and from that day the Muslims were prevented from performing this obligation until God opened Mecca, and the hajj of the ninth year took place.

In this verse there are two forms of obligation: the lām of entitlement (lām al-istiḥqāq), and the particle ʿalā, which indicates that a right is established upon the one to whom it is attached. It was difficult, or impossible, for the Muslims to perform the hajj immediately after its revelation, because the idolaters would not permit them to do so. Perhaps the wisdom of making hajj obligatory at that time was that the Muslims should be ready to perform it whenever they became able to, and that the proof should be established against the idolaters that they were preventing this worship, barring access to the Sacred Mosque, and preventing the mosques of God from having His name mentioned in them.

God's words ﴿for whoever is able to make his way to it﴾ are a substitution (badal) for "the people," to restrict the condition of the obligation. Al-Kisā'ī permitted that it be the subject (fāʿil) of ḥajj. This was rejected on the grounds that the sentence would become: "For God, over all people, is the obligation that the able among them perform hajj," and there is no sense in imposing on all people an act performed by some of them. The truth is that this rejection is not valid, because the Arabs vary their speech, relying on the listener's knowledge that the imposition on the people is a general imposition which the subject of ḥajj clarifies. It is not like your saying: "He was able to fast," or "He was able to carry the load." The meaning of "he was able to make his way (istaṭāʿa sabīlan)" is "he found a way and was enabled to it," and the sense of the sentence depends on its ends. The word sabīl (way) here is a metaphor for that by which the responsible person is enabled to perform hajj.

Concerning the interpretation of sabīl in God's words ﴿for whoever is able to make his way to it﴾, the scholars have given opinions whose wording differs but whose purposes are one. The dispute among them over it should not remain recorded in the books of tafsīr and others. The way for one near to the Sacred House is very easy, while the way for one far away is the mount and provisions. For this reason Mālik said: "The sabīl is capability, and people are according to their strength, their travel, and their endurance."

There is disagreement concerning one who has no provisions but can earn a living on his way. Mālik said: if that does not disgrace him, then let him travel and earn along the road. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Shaʿbī, and ʿIkrima said the same. From Mālik there is a dislike of travelling by sea for hajj, except for one who finds no other way, like the people of al-Andalus. He argued that God said ﴿They will come to you on foot and on every lean camel﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 27], and I did not find any mention of the sea. Shaykh Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is a comfort from Mālik, and the verse is not one that requires the cancellation of sea travel." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Some people of my community were shown to me as warriors in the way of God, riding the back of this sea." And is not jihad an act of worship like hajj? Mālik disliked sea travel for women because it exposes them. All of this applies when safety is the more likely outcome; otherwise casting oneself into destruction is not permitted. The state of sea travel today is safer than land travel, except in incidental circumstances in wars when they include the seas.

The apparent meaning of God's words ﴿for whoever is able to make his way to it﴾ is that the address of hajj and the ability belong to the person in his own action, not in the action of another. For this reason Mālik said: "Proxy performance of hajj during life for an excuse is not valid. The one who is unable has the obligation of hajj waived for him, and he saw in it nothing except that a man may bequeath that someone perform the voluntary hajj on his behalf after his death, if the man bequeaths it after his death." Al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, and Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh said: "If he has a prevention from hajj due to an excuse, and he has someone who obeys him, were he to order him to perform hajj on his behalf, or he has wealth with which he can hire someone to perform hajj on his behalf, he becomes capable in general, and hajj becomes obligatory upon him." They argued with the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās: "A woman from Khathʿam asked the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of the Farewell Pilgrimage, saying: 'The obligation of God upon His servants regarding hajj has reached my father, an old man who cannot stay on the mount. Would it suffice if I performed hajj on his behalf?' He said: 'Yes, perform hajj on his behalf. Tell me: if your father had a debt, would you pay it?' She said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then God's debt is more deserving to be paid.'" The Mālikīs answered this by saying that the hadith does not indicate obligation; rather, he answered her with what urges obedience to her father and obedience to her Lord.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Sufyān al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfa, and Ibn al-Mubārak said: "Only a proxy is valid, other than a proxy of obedience (i.e., one who performs hajj on behalf of another does not discharge it unless it is in a manner other than obedience)."

The apparent meaning of the verse is that when ability is established, hajj becomes obligatory upon the able person immediately (ʿalā al-fawr, i.e., without delay). This falls under the question of whether a command requires immediacy (iqtiḍāʾ al-amr al-fawr) or does not require it. The scholars of Islam have differed over whether hajj is obligatory immediately or with latitude. The Baghdādī Mālikīs, Ibn al-Qaṣṣār, Ismāʿīl ibn Ḥammād, and others, held that it is immediate, and they interpreted this from Mālik's statement. This is the correct view in the school of Abū Ḥanīfa, and it is the view of Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and Dāwūd al-Ẓāhirī. Most scholars held that it is with latitude, and this is the correct view of the school of Mālik, and the narration of Ibn Nāfiʿ and Ashhab from him. It is also the view of al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Yūsuf. Al-Shāfiʿī argued that hajj was made obligatory years before the Prophet's (ﷺ) hajj; had it been immediate, he would not have delayed it, and had he delayed it for an excuse, he would have explained it, since he was an exemplar for the people. A group said: when a person reaches sixty, it becomes obligatory on him to perform hajj immediately, if he is able, for fear of death. Ibn Khuwayz Mandād related this from Ibn al-Qāsim.

The meaning of immediacy (al-fawr) is that the responsible person performs it in the hajj season that comes first, upon the completion of the condition of ability.

As for God's words ﴿and whoever disbelieves, then God is free of need of the worlds﴾, its apparent meaning is that it is the counterpart of His words ﴿for whoever is able to make his way to it﴾. So the intended meaning of "whoever disbelieves" is one who does not perform hajj while being able. For this reason a group of the verifying scholars said: the mention of him as a disbeliever here is an intensifying of the seriousness of abandoning hajj, and the intended meaning is disbelief of blessing (kufr al-niʿma). It is also permissible that what is intended is a condemnation of his conduct, that it is like the conduct of one who does not believe in God, His messengers, and the excellence of His sanctuary. Some said: the intended meaning is "whoever disbelieves in the obligation of hajj." Others said, according to its apparent meaning: abandoning hajj while having the capacity for it is disbelief. This is attributed to al-Ḥasan. A group of the exegetes did not hold that the conjunction is for contrast, and they made it an independent sentence, like a concluding remark (tadhyīl), showing by it God's indifference to whoever disbelieves in Him.

In my view, it is permissible that the intended meaning of "whoever disbelieves" is whoever disbelieves in Islam. This is an allusion to the idolaters of Mecca: that their hajj is not counted in God's sight, and that God only wants the believers in Him and those who affirm His oneness to perform hajj.

In God's words ﴿free of need of the worlds﴾ there is a symbol of the removal of the guardianship of the Sanctuary from their hands. Because when He made hajj obligatory, while they were barring access to it, He informed us that He is free of need of the people, so He is not made powerless by whoever bars people from His intended purpose, may He be exalted.

[Page 26 of the original]

The beginning of a new speech, in which he returns to disputing with the People of the Book and admonishing them. It is connected to His saying, ﴿Say: "God has spoken the truth"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 95], and so on.

The Messenger, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him, was commanded to openly denounce the People of the Book, after first laying down the proofs of the soundness of this religion. For this reason the speech opens with the verb (قُلْ) (say), to emphasise what is to be said, and the words spoken begin with the vocative يا أهْلَ الكِتابِ (O People of the Book), to put them on notice. By "the signs of God" is meant either the Qur'an or the evidences of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ. Disbelief (kufr) on these two readings has its legal (shar'i) meaning, which is clear. Or it means the signs of the excellence of the Sacred Mosque over other places, and on this reading kufr has its linguistic (lughawi) meaning. The interrogative form is a rebuke.

The clause ﴿God is witness over what you do﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), because the People of the Book are certain of God's all-encompassing knowledge, and that nothing is hidden from Him. Therefore their denial of His signs while holding that certainty is a more severe denial. For this reason it is not correct to take ﴿God is witness﴾ as a mere statement, unless they are treated as if they were ignorant.

His saying ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, why do you bar from the way of God those who believe"﴾ is a second rebuke and denunciation of their disputing, because they mislead the believers, after He had denounced their error within themselves. It is disjoined without a conjunction (fa-faṣl), to indicate that it is independent in its purpose; had it been conjoined, the conjunction would have been valid.

[Page 27 of the original]

The verb ṣadda (to bar, turn away) is used both intransitively and transitively: one says ṣaddahu ʿan kadhā, fa-ṣadda ʿanhu. Its intransitive form means "to turn away", and its transitive form means "to make the one who is barred turn away", i.e. to turn him aside. One says aṣuddahu ʿan kadhā, and this is clear.

"The way of God" is a figurative usage (majāz) for the statements and proofs that lead to the true religion. By "barring from the way of God" is meant either attempting to turn the believers back to disbelief by casting doubt upon them; this meaning meets the sense of disbelief in His saying ﴿why do you disbelieve in the signs of God﴾ in both of its aspects, which go back to the legal meaning. Or it means barring people from the Hajj, that is, barring their followers from pilgrimage to the Ka'bah, and encouraging them to make pilgrimage to Jerusalem by preferring it over the Ka'bah; this meets disbelief in its earlier linguistic meaning. It may also be an allusion to their denial of the qibla, in their saying ﴿What turned them from their qibla, which they had been facing?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142], since the intent of that was to bar the believers from facing the Ka'bah.

His saying تَبْغُونَها عِوَجًا (you seek it crooked) means: you seek the way crooked. He made its pronoun feminine because the way (sabīl) can be masculine or feminine; God says ﴿Say: this is my way﴾ [Yusuf: 108]. Al-baghy means seeking, i.e. you seek. ʿIwaj, with a kasra on the ʿayn and a fatḥa on the wāw, is the opposite of straightness; it is the noun of the verb ʿawija (like firiḥa), and its verbal noun (maṣdar) is ʿawaj (like faraḥ). Usage has generally restricted the verbal noun to crookedness in perceptible things, such as a wall or a spear-shaft, and restricted the noun-of-the-verbal-noun form (ism al-maṣdar) to crookedness that is not seen, such as the unevenness of the ground or a surface, and to abstract matters such as religion.

The meaning of تَبْغُونَها عِوَجًا may be that ʿiwaj remains in its verbal-noun sense, so that ʿiwaj is the object of tabghūnahā; the object pronoun in tabghūnahā is then governed by the omission of a preposition (nazʿ al-khāfid), as they say shakartuka and bi'tuka kadhā, meaning shakartu laka and bi'tu laka. The implied sense is: "and you seek for it crookedness", i.e. you seek to attribute crookedness to it, and you portray it as false and transient. It may also be that ʿiwaj is a description of the way, by way of describing with a verbal noun for emphasis, meaning: you seek it crooked, extremely crooked. In that case the pronoun in tabghūnahā is the object of tabghūn, and ʿiwaj is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of that pronoun, meaning: you desire it bent, i.e. you seek a crooked way, which is the way of polytheism (shirk).

[Page 28 of the original]

The meaning is: you bar from the straight way and you desire the crooked way. In the pronoun of tabghūnahā there is an ambiguity (istikhdām), because the way of God from which they bar is Islam, and the way they desire is the religion they hold after its abrogation (naskh) and distortion (taḥrīf).

His saying ﴿while you are witnesses﴾ is also a circumstantial clause, balancing the circumstantial clause before it, ﴿God is witness over what you do﴾. Its meaning: while you know that it is the way of God. In this speech He has referred them to what is in their hearts, which only God knows, because that is the aim of piercing their hearts and making them turn in blame upon themselves. For this reason He follows it with His saying ﴿God is not heedless of what you do﴾, which is a threat, warning, and reminder, since they know that God knows what the breasts conceal. It has the same meaning as His saying in their earlier admonition, ﴿God is witness over what you do﴾, except that this is harsher in rebuke, because it nullifies the belief that He, glorified is He, is heedless, since their condition was that of one who holds that belief.

﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you to disbelief after your belief.﴾ ﴿And how can you disbelieve while the verses of Allah are recited to you and His Messenger is among you? And whoever holds fast to Allah has been guided to a straight path.﴾

Address to the believers, warning them against the plotting of the People of the Book and the evil of their attempts to deceive the believers. Allah has favoured the believers by addressing them directly, without an intermediary, unlike His address to the People of the Book when He said, ﴿Say, O People of the Scripture﴾ [Al 'Imran: 99], and He did not say, "Say, O you who have believed."

Al-farīq (the faction) is a group of people. Here it refers to a faction of the Jews, namely Shas ibn Qays and his companions, or it may mean Shas alone, and he is called a faction just as Abu Sufyan was called "people" in His saying, ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173]. The context of the verse indicates that it was revealed concerning an incident that occurred, and that its revelation had a cause.

The cause of the revelation of this verse: the Aws and the Khazraj in the pre-Islamic era had abandoned one another and fought until they were nearly annihilated. There were wars between them, the last of which was the Day of Bu'ath, which ended three years before the Hijra. When they united upon Islam, those grudges were removed from between them, and they became a strength for Islam. This grieved the Jews of Yathrib, so Shas ibn Qays, a Jew and an elder among them, sat with the Aws and the Khazraj, or sent someone to sit with them, reminding them of the wars of Bu'ath. They were on the verge of fighting one another. Each faction called out, "O (for) the Aws!" and "O (for) the Khazraj!" and they took up their weapons. The Prophet ﷺ came, entered between them and said: "Do you call to the jahiliyya while I am among you?" In another narration: "With the call of the jahiliyya?" That is, "Do you call with the call of the jahiliyya?" He then recited this verse, and before he had finished, they had cast down their weapons and embraced one another. Jabir ibn 'Abdullah said: "No dawn was more hateful to us than the rising of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but when Allah reconciled us, no person was dearer to us than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. I never saw a day more ugly or more terrifying at first, and better in its outcome, than that day."

The basic meaning of radd (return) is to turn or to bring back. Allah the Exalted says, ﴿And among you is he who is returned to the most decrepit age﴾ [al-Nahl: 70]. Here it is used metaphorically (isti'āra) for a change of state after association, so it conveys the meaning of "making," as in the words of the poet, cited by the lexicographers:

"So he turned their black hair white, and turned their white faces black."

The phrase kāfirīn is its second object. His saying ﴿after your belief﴾ is an emphasis on what His saying ﴿they will return you﴾ already conveys. The purpose of this explicit statement is to clarify the loss of a great blessing which they would have forfeited had they disbelieved.

His saying ﴿And how can you disbelieve?﴾ is an interrogative (istifhām) used to express disapproval (istib'ād), disapproving of their disbelief and negating it, as in the words of Jarir:

"How (can there be) satire, when there still come to me, from the family of Lam, messages in absentia?"

The clause ﴿while the verses of Allah are recited to you﴾ is circumstantial (ḥāl), and it is the locus of the disapproval and negation, because both the recitation of the verses of Allah and the presence of the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, among them are a restraint preventing them from disbelief. And what a restraint! The "verses" here are the Qur'an and its admonitions.

The locative expression in His saying ﴿and His Messenger is among you﴾ is literal, and it indicates a great honour and a magnificent favour: the presence of this great Messenger among them. This is the distinction which his Companions, the addressees, attained, and through it the meaning of his saying ﷺ becomes clear, as narrated by al-Tirmidhi from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "Do not revile my Companions. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you were to spend the equivalent of Uhud in gold, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor even half of it." Nasīf is half a mudd.

The verse indicates the great status of the Companions, and that they had two restraints against falling into error: hearing the Qur'an, and witnessing the light of the Messenger, peace be upon him. His presence was a safeguard from their going astray. Qatada said: "As for the Messenger, he has passed on to the mercy of Allah; as for the Book, it remains upon the face of the earth forever."

His saying ﴿And whoever holds fast to Allah has been guided to a straight path﴾ means: whoever adheres to the religion will not be feared to go astray. Here i'tiṣām (holding fast) is a metaphor (isti'āra) for adherence.

In this there is an indication of adherence to the Book of Allah and His religion for all Muslims who did not witness the life of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 102–103 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah as He should be feared, and do not die except as Muslims.﴾ ﴿And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. And remember the favour of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favour, brothers. And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it. Thus Allah makes clear to you His signs that you may be guided.﴾

[Page 30]

He moved from warning the addressees against being deceived by the whisperings of some of the People of the Book to urging them towards perfect taqwa (God-consciousness), because in that there is an increase of their goodness and a firmness of their faith. This is an address to the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), and it extends to all who come after them.

This verse is a great foundation among the foundations of Islamic ethics. Taqwa has already been explained at the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. Its essence is carrying out the command and avoiding what is forbidden, in outward deeds and in inner intentions. The due taqwa (ḥaqq al-taqwā) is that there be no shortcoming in it, and no pretence of what is not from one's own deeds. This is the meaning of His, exalted is He, words ﴿so fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16], because istiṭāʿah (ability) is power, and taqwa is within people's capacity. Accordingly, there is no contradiction between the two verses, and no abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one). It has been said that this verse is abrogated by His, exalted is He, words ﴿so fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16], because this verse indicated complete taqwa, as Ibn Mas'ud explained it: that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, that He is thanked and not denied, and that He is remembered and not forgotten. And they related that when this verse was revealed they said, "O Messenger of Allah, who can attain this?" So He, exalted is He, revealed His words ﴿so fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16], and this abrogated it. This view is based on the assumption that the command in both verses is obligatory, and on a difference in the meaning of the two taqwās. The truth is that this is clarification (bayān), not abrogation, as the scholars who investigated the matter have verified. at evening, by which al-'ulya' is turned aside (?)

at Kharazá, when will you have warmth from it?"

﴿Let there be among you a community (ummah) who invite to good, enjoin what is right (al-ma'ruf), and forbid what is wrong (al-munkar). It is they who are the successful.﴾ ﴿Do not be like those who divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them. For them there is a great punishment.﴾

This is a consequence (mufarra') of the preceding discourse. When Allah showed them the blessing of being transferred from two states of wretchedness and abomination to two states of bliss and perfection, and they had tasted both states, the hardship and then the sweetness, having drunk the cup of time to its dregs, they were worthy of striving with all their resolve to rescue others from the evil in which they were to the good in which they themselves were, so that people might become one good community. Human nature includes love of sharing good. Thus you find that a child, when he sees something that pleases him, calls out to those around him so they may see it with him.

For this reason this statement was fitting to be joined with the particle fa' (so). Had it been joined with it, it would have been an acceptable Arabic style. However, it was departed from joining with fa', to draw attention to the fact that the content of this statement

[Page 37]

is intended for its own sake, such that even if the preceding discourse had not come before it, it would still be fitting for it to be commanded. Therefore it is not mentioned for the sake of being a consequence of, or a follower of, something else.

In it, by way of the good antithesis in the division, there is a kind of rhetorical oratory. For He denounced the People of the Book for their disbelief and for their barring people from faith, saying: ﴿Say: O People of the Book, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah, when Allah is witness over what you do?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 98] ﴿Say: O People of the Book, why do you bar from the way of Allah?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 99], and so on.

He countered this by commanding the believers to faith and to calling others to it, when He said: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah as He should be feared﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102], and His saying ﴿Let there be among you a community who invite to good﴾, and so on.

If enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong was not known among them before the revelation of this verse, then the command is to legislate obligation. If it was already established among them, as His saying indicates: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for people, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110], then the command is to emphasize what they were already doing and its obligation. In it there is additionally the command to call to good. The obligation had already been established before, by other verses such as ﴿and enjoining one another to truth and enjoining one another to patience﴾ [al-'Asr: 3], or by prophetic commands. So the command here is also to emphasize the obligation, indicating its continuity and steadfastness, like ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 136].

The word ummah (community) means a group or a party, as in His saying: ﴿Every time a community enters, it curses its sister﴾ [al-A'raf: 38].

The origin of ummah in the speech of the Arabs is a party of people who aim at one purpose, whether by lineage, homeland, religion, or a combination of these. What unites them is specified by an annexation or a description, as when they say: "the ummah of the Arabs," "the ummah of Ghassan," and "the ummah of the Christians."

If the addressees of the pronoun in ﴿among you﴾ are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, as is the apparent meaning of the preceding addresses, then (min) may be explanatory (bayaniyyah), with the explanatory element placed before what it explains. The referent of ummah would then be the Companions themselves, who are the people of the first era of Muslims. The meaning would be: "Let you be a community who invite to good." This community, whose members have this description, has been commanded to form from their totality the community described as inviting to good. The aim is to bring about this attribute, because what is obligatory upon them is to adopt this disposition. When they adopt it, the required community comes into being. It is the best of communities, and it is the people of the virtuous city which the wise sought long ago. The verse thus came with this command in this eloquent and concise style.

In this there is also the figure of tajrid (abstraction): another community is abstracted from the addressees, for the sake of emphasizing this ruling, as one says: "For so-and-so, among his sons, there are helpers." The intended meaning is: "Let you be commanders of good and forbidders of evil, until you become a community with this description." This is the most apparent reading. Thus all the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ are addressed with the command to be callers to good. Indeed, they are those who received the Shari'ah directly from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so they are the most entitled of people to convey it, and the most knowledgeable of its occasions and circumstances. The saying of the Prophet ﷺ on many occasions supports this: "Let the one present convey to the one absent. Have I not conveyed?" To this interpretation al-Zajjaj and several other exegetes inclined, as Ibn 'Atiyya reported.

It is also permissible, on the basis that the pronoun is an address to the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ, that (min) be partitive (tab'idiyyah), and that ummah means a group or a faction. The meaning would be: "Let some of you be a group who invite to good." The obligation would then fall on a group of the Companions. Ibn 'Atiyya said, quoting al-Dahhak and al-Tabari: He commanded the believers that there should be from among them a group with this attribute. They are the special Companions of the Messenger and the special narrators.

I say: On this reading the ruling of obligation is established for every generation after them by way of analogy, lest guidance become inoperative. Among people there are those who cannot call to good or enjoin what is right or forbid what is wrong. Allah says: ﴿Why should not a group from every section of them go forth, that they may gain understanding in religion and warn their people?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122], and so on.

If the address by the pronoun is to all believers, following the fact that the one addressed by "O you who have believed" is also them, then (min) is necessarily partitive, and ummah means a party. This is because not all believers are commanded to call to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. Rather, the obligation is a collective obligation (fard al-kifayah, a duty that is fulfilled when a sufficient number perform it). Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Tabari, and those who followed them held this view. On this view the commanded party is an unspecified group, and the intent is that this act, which has been imposed upon the community, be carried out.

Moreover, this reading does not prevent (min) from being explanatory, meaning that they themselves are the community. What is meant by their calling to good, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong is the establishing of this among them, and that they should not be free of it according to need and the capacity to carry it out. This would follow the common Arab practice of describing a tribe by the attributes prevalent among it and dominant over its individuals, as when they say: "Bahilah are miserly," and "'Udhrah are lovers."

On these readings the same considerations apply to His saying ﴿and do not be like those who divided﴾, as will come.

Calling to good varies. Some of it is evident and is performed by every Muslim. Some of it requires knowledge and is performed by those who possess it. This is what is called collective obligation: if some people perform it, it suffices and relieves the rest. The group who perform it are determined by the availability among them of the conditions for performing that act, such as strength with weapons in war, swimming in rescuing the drowning, and knowledge of the matters of religion in enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. Likewise, the number sufficient to perform the act is determined, such as an army being at least half the size of the enemy's army. Since the command requires an object, the one commanded in collective obligation is the group among whom the conditions are present, or the totality of the people of the city or tribe, to carry it out. When a sufficient number of those among whom the conditions are present perform it, the obligation is lifted from the rest. If they do not perform it, the sin falls upon the city or tribe, because all of them stayed silent and the righteous ones were negligent in performing it while also remaining silent. Then, if some of them perform it, only those who perform it are rewarded.

It was also said that good is intended to include all goods, of which enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong are among them. Then the conjunction is of the particular to the general, for the sake of emphasizing it.

What is meant here is what is accepted by people of intellect and in the Shari'ah, namely truth and righteousness, because these are accepted when external obstacles are absent.

Aversion is a necessary consequence of denial, because munkar in the original language means ignorance, and from it comes the naming of what is unfamiliar as nakirah (unknown). What is meant here is falsehood and corruption, because these are disliked by natural disposition when external obstacles are absent.

Among the exegetes, some have specified that (min) in His saying ﴿Let there be among you a community﴾ is explanatory,

[Page 41]

and interpreted the statement by positing that the explanatory element is placed before what it explains, so the meaning becomes: "Let there be a community which is you," i.e., "Let you be a community who call." This is an attempt to harmonize the meaning of this verse with His saying ﴿You are the best community brought forth for people, enjoining what is right﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]. However, the equivalence of the meanings of the two verses is not necessarily established, since it is possible that by "best community" is meant this very community, which undertook enjoining what is right, as we will explain there.

There is no doubt that commanding and forbidding are among the kinds of speech and utterance. Therefore what is required of the responsible person is to make clear what is right and to command it, and to make clear what is wrong and to forbid it. As for what occurred in the hadith, "Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; if he cannot, then with his heart," that is the level of changing, and changing may be by hand, or by the heart, meaning wishing for change. Since determining the capacity to undertake this collective obligation of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong depends on levels of knowledge of what is right and wrong, and levels of ability to change and to make people understand this, the leaders of the Muslims saw fit to appoint officials to investigate

[Page 42]

...of the *munkar* and specifying the manner of carrying out its alteration. They called this office *ḥisba* (the office of supervising public conduct and enforcing what is right). 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb assigned this office to Umm al-Shifā'. The most famous holder of it in the 'Abbasid state was Ibn 'Ā'isha, who was a man firm in the truth. In the Maghrib this office is called *wilāyat al-sūq* (the office of the market). In Qurṭuba, the office was held by the Imam Muḥammad ibn Khālid ibn Martanīl al-Qurṭubī, known as al-Ashajj, one of the companions of Ibn al-Qāsim, who died in the year 220 [AH]. In the Ḥafṣid state, the office of *ḥisba* was among the distinguished offices, and it was sometimes joined to the judiciary, as was the case in Tunis after the Ḥafṣid state.

The sentence ﴿And those are the successful﴾ is conjoined to the descriptions of a community, which are contained in the clauses ﴿they call to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong﴾. The estimated sense is: "and they are successful," because success, being a consequence of those three attributes, was made as if it were an attribute of them. It is also permissible to make the sentence ﴿And those are the successful﴾ a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "a community," with the *wāw* being the *wāw* of circumstance.

The intended meaning is the good news of complete success, if they do this. The apparent expectation was that this sentence be separated from what precedes it without a conjunction, like the separation of the sentence ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 5]. But this one is conjoined, or came as a circumstantial clause, because its content is a recompense for the sentences that precede it, so it is more fitting that it be attached to them.

The meaning of this sentence is the restriction of the attribute of success to them. This is either a restriction relative to those who do not do this while being able to, or a restriction intended for emphasis, because in this context the success of others is not considered, and this is the meaning of intending to indicate the sense of perfection.

His saying ﴿And do not be like those who divided﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿and let there be among you a community﴾, and it refers back to His earlier saying ﴿and do not be divided﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 103], because it depicts the condition of division in its most hideous forms, which were known to them from reading about the conditions of the Jews. It also contains an indication that abandoning enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong leads to division and disagreement, since disputes and discords multiply and the community is split apart by that, with a severe splitting.

[Page 43]

The one addressed by it follows the two possibilities mentioned regarding the one addressed in His saying ﴿and let there be among you a community﴾. Yet there is doubt as to whether the ruling of this verse covers all Muslims, either by the wording or by *laḥn al-khiṭāb* (the implicit indication of an address), because what is forbidden is the condition resembling the condition of those who divided and disagreed.

By ﴿those who divided and disagreed﴾ is meant, regarding the foundations of religion, the Jews and Christians, after the clear proofs had come to them that prevent disagreement and division. Division is mentioned before disagreement to signal that disagreement is the cause of division. This is one of the implications arising from the arrangement of speech and the mention of things together with their concomitants. The reverse of this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and fear God, and God teaches you﴾ [al-Baqara: 282].

It also contains an indication that the blameworthy disagreement, which leads to division, is disagreement regarding the foundations of the religion, which leads to one part of the community declaring another to be unbeliever or sinful, not disagreement in the derivative matters based on the differing interests of the community in different regions and eras, which is what is expressed by *ijtihād* (independent juristic reasoning). When we trace the history of the Islamic schools of thought, we find no division that arose among Muslims except from disagreement in creed and foundations, and not from disagreement in *ijtihād* regarding the branches of the Sharia.

The *bayyināt* (clear proofs) are the indications which contain protection from falling into disagreement, if they were granted understandings.

His saying ﴿And those, for them is a great punishment﴾ is the counterpart of His saying regarding the other group ﴿And those are the successful﴾. So what is said about it is what is said about its counterpart, and this is a recompense for division and disagreement and for their neglect in avoiding its causes.
