In the Ḥafṣid state, the office of *ḥisba* was among the distinguished offices, and it was sometimes joined to the judiciary, as was the case in Tunis after the Ḥafṣid state.

The sentence ﴿And those are the successful﴾ is conjoined to the descriptions of a community, which are contained in the clauses ﴿they call to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong﴾. The estimated sense is: "and they are successful," because success, being a consequence of those three attributes, was made as if it were an attribute of them. It is also permissible to make the sentence ﴿And those are the successful﴾ a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "a community," with the *wāw* being the *wāw* of circumstance.

The intended meaning is the good news of complete success, if they do this. The apparent expectation was that this sentence be separated from what precedes it without a conjunction, like the separation of the sentence ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 5]. But this one is conjoined, or came as a circumstantial clause, because its content is a recompense for the sentences that precede it, so it is more fitting that it be attached to them.

The meaning of this sentence is the restriction of the attribute of success to them. This is either a restriction relative to those who do not do this while being able to, or a restriction intended for emphasis, because in this context the success of others is not considered, and this is the meaning of intending to indicate the sense of perfection.

His saying ﴿And do not be like those who divided﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿and let there be among you a community﴾, and it refers back to His earlier saying ﴿and do not be divided﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 103], because it depicts the condition of division in its most hideous forms, which were known to them from reading about the conditions of the Jews. It also contains an indication that abandoning enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong leads to division and disagreement, since disputes and discords multiply and the community is split apart by that, with a severe splitting.

[Page 43]

The one addressed by it follows the two possibilities mentioned regarding the one addressed in His saying ﴿and let there be among you a community﴾. Yet there is doubt as to whether the ruling of this verse covers all Muslims, either by the wording or by *laḥn al-khiṭāb* (the implicit indication of an address), because what is forbidden is the condition resembling the condition of those who divided and disagreed.

By ﴿those who divided and disagreed﴾ is meant, regarding the foundations of religion, the Jews and Christians, after the clear proofs had come to them that prevent disagreement and division. Division is mentioned before disagreement to signal that disagreement is the cause of division. This is one of the implications arising from the arrangement of speech and the mention of things together with their concomitants. The reverse of this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and fear God, and God teaches you﴾ [al-Baqara: 282].

It also contains an indication that the blameworthy disagreement, which leads to division, is disagreement regarding the foundations of the religion, which leads to one part of the community declaring another to be unbeliever or sinful, not disagreement in the derivative matters based on the differing interests of the community in different regions and eras, which is what is expressed by *ijtihād* (independent juristic reasoning). When we trace the history of the Islamic schools of thought, we find no division that arose among Muslims except from disagreement in creed and foundations, and not from disagreement in *ijtihād* regarding the branches of the Sharia.

The *bayyināt* (clear proofs) are the indications which contain protection from falling into disagreement, if they were granted understandings.

His saying ﴿And those, for them is a great punishment﴾ is the counterpart of His saying regarding the other group ﴿And those are the successful﴾. So what is said about it is what is said about its counterpart, and this is a recompense for division and disagreement and for their neglect in avoiding its causes.

[p. 44]

It is permissible for ﴿The Day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾ to be in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), dependent on a meaning in His words ﴿for them is a painful punishment﴾ (Q. 3:105) such as "existing" or "being established." That is: a punishment will be theirs on the day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black. This is the common usage when time-nouns are attached to clauses. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as the direct object of a deleted verb, "remember" (udhkur), with the clause ﴿some faces turn white﴾ serving as a qualifier of "day," with the sense: on it some faces turn white and on it some faces turn black.

Defining this day by the occurrence of white and black faces in it conveys its gravity and arouses interest in what follows regarding the detailed account of the people with white faces and the people with black faces, as a warning to one group and an encouragement to the other. The more evident view is that the hearers already knew, from earlier verses revealed before this one, that faces would turn white and black on that day. Such verses include His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against God, their faces blackened﴾ (Q. 39:60), and His words ﴿Faces that Day will be bright﴾ (Q. 80:38), ﴿laughing, joyful﴾ (Q. 80:39), ﴿and faces that Day will have dust upon them﴾ (Q. 80:40), ﴿darkness will cover them﴾ (Q. 80:41).

The whiteness and blackness are literal whiteness and blackness, by which believers and disbelievers will be marked on the Day of Resurrection. They are a specific whiteness and blackness, because this belongs to the conditions of the Hereafter, so there is no reason to divert them from their literal meaning.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?"﴾ are a detailed explanation of the preceding general statement. It is arranged in the inverted order of enumeration (nashr al-maʿkūs), and it is concise, since the original wording would be: "As for those whose faces turn black, they are the disbelievers, who are told, 'Did you disbelieve…?'" to the end of the verse. "As for those whose faces turn white, they are the believers, and in the mercy of God they will abide forever."

When describing the day, the mention of whiteness is placed first, since whiteness is the emblem of the people of bliss. This honors that day by showing that it is the day on which the mercy and favor of God become manifest. It is also because God's mercy precedes His wrath. And because mentioning the mark of the people of bliss right after the threat of punishment to others is a source of regret for them, as the hearer knows that they will have a great punishment on a day in which there is great bliss. Then, in the detailed account, the mark of the people of punishment is mentioned first, to hasten their distress.

[p. 45]

His words ﴿Did you disbelieve…?﴾ are the object of a deleted verb of speech, which is omitted in the same way in speech because it is evident, since a question is not issued except by one who asks. That speech is the response of ʾammā (as for). For this reason the particle fa- (then) does not enter before ﴿Did you disbelieve…?﴾, to show that it is not the response, and that the response has been deleted entirely.

The speaker of this speech is unknown, since nothing preceding indicates him. It is possible that this is said to them by the people of the gathering (al-Maḥshar), namely those who knew them in the world as believers and then saw them bearing the mark of disbelief. This is as reported in the hadith of the Basin (al-Ḥawḍ): "There will come to me people whom I recognize, then they will be driven away from me, and I will say: 'My companions!' And it will be said: 'You do not know what they innovated after you.'" The one asking would be their predecessor from among their people or their messenger, so the question is literal, while it also implies astonishment.

It is also possible that it is addressed to them by God, Exalted is He, in which case the question is figurative, meaning denial and rebuke. Then, if by "those whose faces turn black" the People of the Book are meant, the meaning of their disbelief after their belief is their altering the law of their prophets and concealing what they concealed of it, or their disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ after their belief in Moses and Jesus, as already mentioned in His words ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved after their belief﴾ (Q. 3:90). This is the clear interpretation, and the context and wording of the speech require it, since it is directed toward the warning to those people.

Some interpretations were made by Muslims, and they fell into what the Qur'an warned them against, so they divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them. Concerning them the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Do not return after me as disbelievers, striking one another's necks." These are like the apostates (ahl al-ridda, those who abandoned Islam) who died in that state. Here the meaning of disbelief after belief is evident. In accordance with this meaning, Mālik ibn Anas interpreted the verse, as transmitted from him by Ibn al-Qāsim, in the third of the questions in the book of the apostates and those who wage war from al-ʿUtbiyya. He said: "There is no verse in the Book of God more severe for the people of disagreement than the people of desires, than this verse: ﴿The Day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾." Mālik said: "This is only for the people of the qibla (Muslims)." He meant that it does not apply to those among the nations before us who divided and differed, as evidenced by His words ﴿Did you disbelieve after your belief?﴾. Abū Ghassān Mālik al-Harawī transmitted it from Mālik, from Ibn ʿUmar. Something similar is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās.

On this interpretation, the meaning is those who innovated after their belief into disbelief, either by apostasy or by abominable statements that lead to disbelief and the abrogation of the law. Examples are the Ghurābiyya among the Shīʿa, who said that prophethood belonged to ʿAlī, and the extremist Ismāʿīliyya, followers of Ḥamza ibn ʿAlī, and followers of al-Ḥākim al-ʿUbaydī. This is distinguished from one whose statement does not reach disbelief either explicitly or by clear necessary implication, such as the Khawārij and the Qadariyya, as is detailed in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh) and theology (kalām) concerning the ruling on those who interpret (al-mutaʾawwilīn) and on one who interprets their statement into bad necessary consequences.

Tasting the punishment (dhawq al-ʿadhāb) is a metaphor for perceiving it. It is a well-known metaphor whose relational link (ʿalāqa) is restriction (taqyīd).

تَذْيِيلاتٌ (*tadhyilat*, concluding appended statements). The demonstrative in His words ﴿تِلْكَ﴾ ("These") refers to a portion of the earlier verses of the Qur'an in this surah, as His words ﴿نَتْلُوها عَلَيْكَ بِالحَقِّ﴾ ("We recite them to you in truth") require.

And *al-tilawa* (recitation) is a term for relating speech with the intention of conveying it in its exact wording. It is like *al-qira'a* (reading), except that *qira'a* is specific to relating written speech. Accordingly, the group of verses intended by the demonstrative may be the verses beginning with His words ﴿إنَّ مَثَلَ عِيسى عِنْدَ اللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ آدَمَ﴾ ("Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before Allah is like the likeness of Adam") [Al 'Imran: 59] up to this point. This is because what precedes it ended with a concluding statement close to this one, namely His words ﴿ذَلِكَ نَتْلُوهُ عَلَيْكَ مِنَ الآياتِ والذِّكْرِ الحَكِيمِ﴾ ("That which We recite to you of the signs and the wise reminder") [Al 'Imran: 58]. Thus each concluding statement stands independently with the group of sentences it follows.

This group of the Qur'an was singled out for the demonstrative because it contains the proofs that establish the soundness of the creed of Islam and that refute the claims of the three groups: the Jews, the Christians, and the polytheists. Examples include His words ﴿إنَّ مَثَلَ عِيسى عِنْدَ اللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ آدَمَ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]; His words ﴿وما مِن إلَهٍ إلّا إلَهٌ واحِدٌ﴾ ("There is no god except One God") [al-Ma'ida: 73] and the verse continues; His words ﴿فَلِمَ تُحاجُّونَ فِيما لَيْسَ لَكم بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾ ("Why do you argue about that of which you have no knowledge?") [Al 'Imran: 66] and the verse continues; His words ﴿إنَّ أوْلى النّاسِ بِإبْراهِيمَ لَلَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوهُ﴾ ("Indeed, the most worthy of Abraham among people are those who followed him") [Al 'Imran: 68] and the verse continues; His words ﴿ما كانَ لِبَشَرٍ أنْ يُؤْتِيَهُ اللَّهُ الكِتابَ والحُكْمَ والنُّبُوَّةَ﴾ ("It is not for a human that Allah should give him the Book, the wisdom, and prophethood") [Al 'Imran: 79] and the verse continues; His words ﴿وإذْ أخَذَ اللَّهُ مِيثاقَ النَّبِيئِينَ﴾ ("And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets") [Al 'Imran: 81] and the verse continues; His words ﴿فَأْتُوا بِالتَّوْراةِ فاتْلُوها﴾ ("Bring the Torah and recite it") [Al 'Imran: 93]; and His words ﴿إنَّ أوَّلَ بَيْتٍ وُضِعَ لِلنّاسِ لَلَّذِي بِبَكَّةَ مُبارَكًا﴾ ("Indeed, the first house established for people is that at Bakkah, blessed") [Al 'Imran: 96]; along with what lies between these of parables, admonitions, and proofs.

The *ba'* in His words ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾ is for *mula¬abasa* (accompaniment), namely the accompaniment of the report to the thing reported. That is, *bi-l-haqq* means in accordance with what is actually the case and the reality. These verses thus clarified the creeds of the People of the Book and detailed their conditions in this world and the Hereafter.

Part of the truth is that each of the two groups deserves what it is treated with, as justice from Allah. For this reason He said ﴿وما اللَّهُ يُرِيدُ ظُلْمًا لِلْعالَمِينَ﴾ ("And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds"), meaning He does not intend to wrong people. Even if He willed that, He would do it, but He promised not to wrong anyone, and so His promise is true. There is no proof in the verse for the Mu'tazila (the rationalist theological school) that it is impossible for Allah to intend injustice, since there is no disagreement between us and the Mu'tazila over the absence of its occurrence. The disagreement is only over whether it is possible or impossible.

The predicate (*musnad*) was put in verbal form to convey the strengthening of the ruling, which is the negation of the intention of injustice toward the worlds from Allah, the Exalted. The indefiniteness of ﴿ظُلْمًا﴾ in the context of negation indicates the negation of the whole category of injustice from being the object of Allah's intention. Thus everything that counts as injustice in the realm of sound minds is negated from being what Allah intends.

His words ﴿ولِلَّهِ ما في السَّماواتِ وما في الأرْضِ﴾ ("And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth") are coordinated with the concluding statement. Since whatever is in the heavens and on the earth belongs to Him, He intends their well-being, and He has no need to harm them except as recompense for their deeds. So He does not intend their wronging. And to Him all matters are returned, so the reward of the good-doer and the punishment of the wrongdoer are not lost to Him.

The repetition of the name of Majesty (Allah) three times in the three sentences after the first, without using a pronoun, is intended to make each sentence independent in its meaning, not dependent on the others, so that it is suitable to be cited as a proverb, to be recalled by souls, and to be preserved by ears.

So He does not intend their wronging. And to Him all matters are returned, so the reward of the good-doer and the punishment of the wrongdoer are not lost to Him.

The repetition of the name of Majesty (Allah) three times in the three sentences after the first, without using a pronoun, is intended to make each sentence independent in its meaning, not dependent on the others, so that it is suitable to be cited as a proverb, to be recalled by souls, and to be preserved by ears.
