Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 110 (part 1 of 2):

﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and believing in Allah.﴾

This stands in the position of a reason (ta'lil) for their being commanded to call to good and for what follows. His saying ﴿enjoining what is right﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in "you were." It thus indicates the reason for their being the best nation, and it follows that whatever their excellence consists in is fitting to be made obligatory upon them, if it was not already obligatory before, and that its obligation be emphasized for them, if it had already been made obligatory upon them before.

The address in His saying "you were" is either to the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ). This is reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn 'Abbas. 'Umar said: "This applies to our first generation and not to our last." The annexation of "best" (khayr) to "nation" (ummah) is an annexation of an attribute to the thing described: that is, "you were a nation, the best nation brought forth for mankind." Thus, by "nation" is meant a community, the people of the Prophetic era, like a generation (qarn). This is a well-known usage, and from it is His saying ﴿and after a nation [of time] he remembered﴾ [Yusuf: 45], meaning after a long period, like the duration of a full age. There is no doubt that the Companions were the most excellent of the generations that have appeared in the world, because their Messenger is the most excellent of the messengers, and because the guidance they followed is not matched by the guidance of the companions of the earlier messengers. If you take the nation as including its Messenger, then the Companions are the best nation among the nations with their messenger. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The best of generations is my generation." The excellence belongs to the whole over the whole. And if the nation is taken as excluding the Messenger, then likewise the Companions are the best of the nations that passed away without their messengers, and this is a preference for the guidance by which they were guided, which is the guidance of their Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) and his law (shari'ah).

Or the address with the pronoun of "you were" is to all Muslims in every generation in which they have appeared. The meaning of their being preferred by enjoining what is right, although it is among the collective obligations (fard al-kifayah) that not all members of the nation perform, is that no Muslim is free of carrying out what he is able to do of this matter, according to the extent of his knowledge and the limit of his capacity. So, from changing the wrong among the household and children up to changing it among all the people of the land. Or because the existence of groups that undertake this matter within the whole nation is a greater virtue for the whole nation, since these groups are part of it, just as a tribe used to take pride in the praiseworthy qualities of its groups. In this there is a guarantee from Allah the Exalted that this will not cease among the Muslims, God willing.

The verb "kana" (was) indicates the existence of what is predicated of it in a past time, without indicating continuity or discontinuity. Allah the Exalted said ﴿And Allah has ever been Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa': 96], meaning "and He still is." So the meaning of ﴿you were the best nation﴾ is that you existed in the state of being the best of all nations. That is, this excellence was attained for you by the attainment of its causes and means, and because they were characterized by faith, by calling to Islam, by establishing it in its proper form, and by defending it against deficiency and neglect. This is so because, since that was made part of their duty and each one did what he was able to do, it became established that they carried it out. Or it became evident from them that they were resolved to comply with it whenever an occasion calling for it arose. Thus it is established that they are, in general, the best nation, and so it was reported about them. This is when we explain the command in His saying earlier ﴿And let there be [arising] from you a nation calling to good, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran: 104], and what follows it of the prohibition in His saying ﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾ [Al 'Imran: 105], as not being something already present among them before.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "You were the best nation, described by those attributes in the past, doing them either of your own accord, out of eagerness to establish the religion, and out of approval and divine success in coinciding with His pleasure and will; or out of an earlier obligation derived from other verses, such as His saying ﴿and enjoin one another to truth﴾ [al-'Asr: 3]." In that case, when He commanded them in that matter in an absolute manner, He praised them for not having neglected it before. This is when we base it on the command in His saying ﴿And let there be [arising] from you a nation﴾ [Al 'Imran: 104] being an affirmation of what they were already doing and an informing that it is obligatory, or an emphasis of its obligation, in the ways I mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿And let there be [arising] from you a nation﴾ [Al 'Imran: 104].

[Page 50]

Among the confusion (hayrah) into which a group of exegetes (mufassirun) have resorted is making the report about the addressees, that they were in past time the best nation, to mean that they were so in the knowledge and decree of Allah the Exalted, or that this status was established in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or making "kana" mean "became."

By "nation" (ummah) is meant the totality of all nations, according to what is well known in the annexation of the elative (af'al al-tafdil) to an indefinite noun: it is for the genus and therefore conveys comprehensiveness (istighraq).

His saying ﴿brought forth for mankind﴾: "brought forth" (ikhraj) is used figuratively for bringing into existence and manifesting, as in His saying ﴿So he brought forth for them a calf, a body that lowed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88], meaning he manifested, by his fashioning, a calf, a body.

The meaning is: "You were the best of the nations that came into existence in the world." The agent of "brought forth" is known, and it is Allah, the Originator of nations, and the one who drives them toward that by which they differ in excellence. By "mankind" (al-nas) is meant all human beings from the beginning of creation.

The clause ﴿enjoining what is right﴾ is a circumstantial clause with the meaning of a reason, since what it signifies is not one of the perceptible qualities such that it would describe the state of the excellence while accompanying it. Rather, it is one of the inward good deeds, suitable for giving a reason, not for describing. It is also possible that it is a new sentence explaining that they are the best nation. It is also possible that it is a second predicate of "kana," but this is weak because it would defeat the intention of giving a reason. "Right" (ma'ruf) and "wrong" (munkar) have already been explained shortly before.

He placed ﴿enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾ before ﴿and believing in Allah﴾ only because these two are the more important in this context, which is set forth to honor the excellence of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, derived from His saying ﴿And let there be [arising] from you a nation calling to good, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran: 104]. The concern that is the cause of the precedence varies with the situations of speech, and one does not look to what is in the reality of the matter, because their faith was established and confirmed before.

He mentioned faith in Allah among the states by which they deserved preference over the nations because each of those states that make them superior has an effect in preferring them over some groups. Faith was intended for preference over the polytheists, who used to boast that they were the people of the sanctuary of Allah and the keepers of His House. Allah has rejected that explicitly in His saying ﴿Have you made the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintenance of al-Masjid al-Haram equal to [the deeds of] one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in the cause of Allah? They are not equal in the sight of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 19]. The mention of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong was intended for preference over the People of the Book, who neglected that among themselves, and of whom He said ﴿They did not prohibit one another from wrongdoing they committed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 79].

If you say: If the aspect of preference over the nations is enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and believing in Allah, then some groups of the righteous among the nations before us have shared this excellence with us. For they believed in Allah according to their laws, enjoined what is right, and forbade what is wrong. It would be impossible for the nations to leave off enjoining what is right, because zeal for the religion is a matter fixed in the souls of the sincere among its followers. I say: It has not been established that the righteous of the earlier nations used to commit themselves to enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, either because it was not obligatory upon them, or because they were lax in using dissimulation (taqiyyah). Here is Harun in the time of Musa: the Children of Israel worshipped the calf in his sight and hearing, and he did not change it. Allah related the dialogue of Musa with him in His saying ﴿[Musa] said, "O Harun, what prevented you when you saw them going astray? That you would not follow me? Have you then disobeyed my order?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 92-93] ﴿[Harun] said, "O son of my mother, do not seize [me] by my beard or by my head. Indeed, I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word.'"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 94]. As for His saying ﴿Among the People of the Scripture is a community standing [in obedience]; they recite the verses of Allah during periods of the night while prostrating﴾ [Al 'Imran: 113], and ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, and enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran: 114], and the rest of the verse, these are a small group of the People of the Scripture, who entered Islam, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam. They were a small group among their people, and so they were not the main body of the nation.

It has become widespread among the scholars to cite this verse as evidence for the authority of consensus (ijma') (the consensus of the scholars as a source of law) and its immunity from error, on the basis that the definite article in "right" and "wrong" is for comprehensiveness. So if the nation agrees upon a ruling, it is not permissible that what they agreed upon be wrong, and it must be right. This is because the group commanded to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong is among them, and it is not permissible for them to remain silent about a wrong that occurs, or about a right that is left aside. This argument, if it is intended to establish the authority of consensus in the sense of the established legal text (shar' mutawatir) known as part of the religion by necessity, is a sound argument, because the right and wrong in this category are self-evident and necessary. But if it is intended as an argument for the authority of consensuses formed by independent reasoning (ijtihad), and this is what those who cite the verse intend, then their citing it for that is sophistry (sufsata'i), because wrong is not considered wrong except after its ruling has been established by the law, and the way to establish its ruling is consensus. So if they agreed upon something wrong in the sight of Allah by their error, it would not be wrong until a group among them forbade it, because their independent reasoning is the extent of their ability.

* * *

﴿If the People of the Scripture had believed, it would have been better for them. Among them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors.﴾

This is joined to His saying ﴿You were the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾, because that preference has overwhelmed the People of the Scripture, including the Jews and others, so this conjunction alerts them that they can attain this excellence too, along with an implicit reproach to them for hesitating in following Islam. Mukhayriq had hesitated for a time and then embraced Islam, and likewise the delegation of Najran hesitated over the matter of Islam.

The People of the Scripture include the Jews and the Christians, but the primary intended group here is the Jews, because they were mixed with the Muslims in Medina, and the Prophet (ﷺ) had invited them to Islam and visited their house of study (midras), and because a small number of them had embraced Islam. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If ten Jews had believed in me, all the Jews would have believed in me."

The object of "believed" is not mentioned here, because what is meant is: if they had been characterized by faith, which is the title of the religion of Islam, and from which the designation of "those who" (alladhina) is derived.

[Page 53]

...they became Muslims, as a name, through dominance, and this is like their saying "aslama" (he became a Muslim), "sabi'a" (he converted from one religion to another), "ashraka" (he became a polytheist), and "alhada" (he became a heretic), without mentioning the complements of these verbs. This is because what is meant is that he took on these attributes, which became known as labels for well-known religions. So the verb is treated as intransitive (lazim). More obvious than these are: "tahawwada" (he became a Jew), "tanassara" (he became a Christian), "tazandaqa" (he became a Zindiq), and "tahannafa" (he became a Hanif). The indication for this meaning is clear: the believing of the People of the Book is placed within the condition of the impossibility (the counterfactual "law" particle), although their belief in God is well known and no one denies it. In the Kashshaf it occurs that what is meant is: "if they believed with complete belief," but this is an obvious strain, and the context does not call for it. The most sound interpretation of why faith would be better for them is so that their souls may go in every direction, between hope and apprehension. When he reported about the People of the Book that faith is impossible for them, according to the requirement of placing their belief within the scope of the counterfactual condition, it became necessary that what is meant is those who remain with the description of the People of the Book. This is a description that does not remain with them after they adopt Islam as their religion. It might be imagined that the description "People of the Book" includes those who were of them before that, even if they entered Islam. So the precautionary qualification (ihtiras) was brought with His saying ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors﴾, meaning: among them are those who believed in the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and so the title "believer" applies to him, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, whose name was Husayn, and who was from Banu Qaynuqa', and his brother, and his paternal aunt Khalida, and Sa'ya or Sin'a ibn Ghurayd ibn Adiya al-Taymawi, who was the nephew of al-Samaw'al ibn Adiya, and Tha'laba ibn Sa'ya, and Asad ibn Sa'ya al-Qurazi, and Asad ibn Ubayd al-Qurazi, and Mukhayriq from Banu al-Nadir or from Banu Qaynuqa', and like Ashama al-Najashi, for he believed in his heart, and in place of openly performing the acts of Islam he gave support to the Muslims and protected them in his land, until the religion of God prevailed. God accepted this from him. For this reason the Messenger of God (ﷺ) reported about him that he was a believer, and he prayed over him when he was informed of his death. It is possible that the meaning is: among the People of the Book is a group who are mindful of God in their religion, so they are close to faith in Muhammad (ﷺ). These are like those who remained hesitant about faith without harming the Muslims, such as the Christians of Najran and the Christians of Abyssinia, and like Mukhayriq the Jew before he became Muslim, according to the disagreement about his Islam, for he bequeathed his property to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). So what is meant by their belief is the sincerity of belief in God and in their religion. And a group among them are defiant of their religion, distorting it, hostile to the people of good, as God the Exalted said: ﴿and they kill those who enjoin justice among people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21], like those who poisoned the sheep for the Messenger of God on the day of Khaybar, and those who tried to drop a rock on him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 111:

﴿They will not harm you except for some insult. And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you; then they will not be helped.﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) arising from His words ﴿and most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110], because the report about most of them being non-believers implies their hostility towards the believers. By its nature, this would cause fear to enter the hearts of the Muslims about their might. This applies specifically to the Jews, for they were spread around Madinah, in Khaybar, al-Nadir, Qaynuqa' and Qurayzah. They were people of cunning, strength, wealth, equipment and numbers, while the Muslims at that time were few. So Allah reassured the Muslims that they do not fear the might of the People of the Book, nor do they fear their harm, but only their hurtful words.

As for the Christians, there is no contact between them and the Muslims such that they would be feared. Al-adha (الأذى, insult) is light pain, which does not reach the level of harm (al-darr), which is pain. It has been said that it is harm by speech, so it would be like the saying of Ishaq ibn Khalaf:

I fear the harshness of an uncle or the coarseness of a brother, and I used to guard myself from the hurt of words.

The meaning of ﴿they will turn their backs to you﴾ is that they will flee in defeat.

His words ﴿then they will not be helped﴾ are a precaution, meaning: they will turn their backs in the manner of defeated people, not in the manner of those who turn aside to fight or who withdraw to a company (of their own), or who are reflecting on the matter. In departing from making it coordinated with the answer clause to making it coordinated with both the conditional clause and its answer together, there is an indication that this is their habit and their way, if they fight you; and likewise in their fighting others.

Page 55

And "thumma" (then) indicates the sequence of reports, showing a distance in rank (tarakhi al-rutbah). The meaning of distance in rank is that the rank of what it coordinates is greater than the rank of what it is coordinated with, regarding the purpose for which the speech is directed. This is other than figurative distance (al-tarakhi al-majazi), because figurative distance is when something that is not actually later than the coordinated element is likened to something later than it.

All of this is a threat to them that they will fight the Muslims and that they will be routed, and an incitement for the Muslims to fight them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 112:

﴿They were struck with humiliation wherever they were found, except under a rope from Allah and a rope from the people; and they returned with anger from Allah, and they were struck with poverty.﴾

The pronoun in ﴿عَلَيْهِمُ﴾ refers back to ﴿وأكْثَرُهُمُ الفاسِقُونَ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110], which is undoubtedly specific to the Jews. It serves as an explanation of ﴿ثُمَّ لا يُنْصَرُونَ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 111].

The sentence is explanatory (bayaniyyah), mentioning a severe state of their wretchedness in this world.

The meaning of "striking humiliation" (darb al-dhillah) is its attachment to them and its encompassing of them. In it there is a metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah wa tab'iyyah): humiliation, which is an abstract matter, is likened to a dome or tent that covers them, and its attachment and firmness are likened to the pitching of a dome and the tightening of its ropes. A similar usage has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

"Thuqifu" originally means they were captured in war: ﴿فَإمّا تَثْقَفَنَّهم في الحَرْبِ﴾ [al-Anfal: 57]. This root indicates gaining firm control over a thing and dealing with it forcefully, and from it captivity is called thiqaf. The thiqaf is a tool like a clamp by which the hollow shafts of spear-shafts are broken. Al-Nabighah said:

"Gripped by the thiqaf upon the hollow shafts."

The meaning here is: wherever they are found or come upon, that is, they are only encountered as those under subjection. It likens the state of their encounter outside of war to the state of taking a prisoner, due to the severity of their humiliation.

Page 56
His words ﴿إلّا بِحَبْلٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ وحَبْلٍ مِنَ النّاسِ﴾: "rope" (habl) is used metaphorically for a covenant. What relates to this has already been mentioned at His words ﴿فَقَدِ اسْتَمْسَكَ بِالعُرْوَةِ الوُثْقى﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256] in Surah al-Baqarah. The "covenant of Allah" is His protection (dhimmah), and the "covenant of the people" is their alliance and their support. The exception is from the general class of circumstances, and these circumstances are indicated by the ba' of accompaniment (li-al-musahabah). The implied meaning is: humiliation was struck upon them, with them being in every state, except being in a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people. So the sense is: they went off in humiliation, except with a rope from Allah.

The meaning is that they are not spared from humiliation except when they are bound by a covenant from Allah, that is, the protection of Islam, or when they seek support from tribes of great might. As for themselves, they have no victory. This is among the proofs of prophethood, for the Jews were honored in Yathrib, Khaybar, al-Nadir and Qurayzah, then they became abased, and humiliation enveloped them in all the regions of the world.

﴿وباءُوا بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾: that is, they returned; it is a metaphor, in the sense of "they became," since there is no returning here.

Maskanah is extreme poverty, derived from the name miskin, which means a poor person. Perhaps its derivation is from sukun (stillness), a figurative stillness, applied to lack of means in livelihood. The intended sense of "striking poverty upon them" is its decreeing for them, and it is an announcement of an unseen matter, because the Jews being addressed were afflicted with poverty when their dwellings were seized in Khaybar, al-Nadir, Qaynuqa' and Qurayzah, and then after that by their expulsion in the time of 'Umar.

* * *
﴿ذَلِكَ بِأنَّهم كانُوا يَكْفُرُونَ بِآياتِ اللَّهِ ويَقْتُلُونَ الأنْبِئاءَ بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ ذَلِكَ بِما عَصَوْا وكانُوا يَعْتَدُونَ﴾
[That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress.]

The demonstrative "that" refers to the striking of humiliation derived from ﴿ضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الذِّلَّةُ﴾. The meaning of ﴿يَكْفُرُونَ بِآياتِ اللَّهِ ويَقْتُلُونَ الأنْبِئاءَ﴾ was discussed at His words ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ يَكْفُرُونَ بِآياتِ اللَّهِ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21] at the beginning of this surah.

Page 57
His words ﴿ذَلِكَ بِما عَصَوْا وكانُوا يَعْتَدُونَ﴾ may refer to their disbelief and their killing of the prophets without right, so the ba' is a "cause of a cause." It may also be a second reference to the striking of humiliation and poverty, in which case it is a second cause. The "ma" is masdariyyah, meaning "because of their disobedience and transgression." This is an exposition (nashr) following the order of the enfolding (laff): their disbelief in the signs has as its cause disobedience, and their killing of the prophets has as its cause transgression.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 113–114:

﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Scripture is an upright community who recite the verses of Allah during the hours of the night, and they prostrate themselves.﴾ ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds. And those are among the righteous.﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) intended to be fair to a group of the People of the Scripture, after the judgment passed on most of them in a comprehensive form, as a confirmation of what His saying ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110] conveyed. The pronoun in His saying "they are not" refers to the People of the Scripture just mentioned, namely the Jews, and this sentence serves, relative to what follows it, as a preparation (tamhid).

"Sawa'" (equal, alike) is a noun meaning "the similar," and its origin is a verbal noun derived from "taswiyah" (equalization).

The clause ﴿among the People of the Scripture is an upright community﴾ and so on explains the vagueness of ﴿they are not alike﴾. The use of the explicit noun in place of a pronoun is for the sake of drawing attention to this community. Here "ummah" (community) means "group" (fariq).

Applying the name "People of the Scripture" to them is a metaphor (majaz) based on what they were, as in His saying Exalted is He ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [An-Nisa': 2], because they had become Muslims.

He deviated from saying "among them is an upright community" to saying ﴿among the People of the Scripture﴾ so that this praise would include the righteous among the Jews and the righteous among the Christians, and not be restricted to the righteous Jews. For the righteous Jews before the mission of 'Isa were adhering to their religion and steadfast upon it, and among them were those who believed in 'Isa and followed him. Likewise, the righteous Christians before the mission of Muhammad ﷺ were steadfast upon the law of 'Isa, and many of them were people of night prayer in the monasteries and hermitages, and they became Muslims after the Muhammadan mission.

"Ummah" means group and community.

The meaning of "upright" (qa'imah) is that it is a figurative expression for acting upon their religion in the true manner, as one says "a standing market" (suq qa'imah) and "an established law" (shari'ah qa'imah).

"Ana'" (hours): its original form is "a'na'" with two hamzas, on the pattern of "af'al," and it is the plural of "in'" (with a kasrah on the hamzah and a fathah on the nun, as a maqsur form). It is also said "ana" with a fathah on the hamzah. Allah says ﴿not waiting for its ripeness (ghayra nazirina inahu)﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 53], meaning not waiting for its appointed time.

The clause ﴿while they prostrate﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning they perform night prayer at night by reciting their Book, and their recitation of the Book is restricted to the state of their prostration. This style is more eloquent and clearer than saying "they perform tahajjud," because it conveys the image of their action.

The meaning of ﴿they hasten to good deeds﴾ is that they hasten toward them, i.e., they eagerly desire to increase in them. "Musara'ah" (hastening) is used figuratively for increasing in the act and being prompt to it, likening the increasing and the earnest care to a swift pace in order to reach the desired goal. "Fi" here denotes figurative containment, and it is an imaginative (takhyiliyyah) usage that indicates the comparison of good deeds to a path along which travelers journey, and these people have the merit of speed in traversing it. You may also take the whole composition of His saying ﴿and they hasten in good deeds﴾ as an image of the state of their eagerness and zeal for performing good deeds, by the state of a traveler who desires to reach his destination and hastens in his journey. Its parallel will come at His saying ﴿Let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 41] in Surah Al-'Uqud.

The demonstrative "those" (ula'ika) refers to the upright community described by those attributes. The placement of the demonstrative serves to draw attention to the fact that they deserved the description mentioned after the demonstrative because of the attributes that preceded the demonstrative.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 113–114:

﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Scripture is an upright community who recite the verses of Allah during the hours of the night, and they prostrate themselves.﴾ ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds. And those are among the righteous.﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) intended to be fair to a group of the People of the Scripture, after the judgment passed on most of them in a comprehensive form, as a confirmation of what His saying ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110] conveyed. The pronoun in His saying "they are not" refers to the People of the Scripture just mentioned, namely the Jews, and this sentence serves, relative to what follows it, as a preparation (tamhid).

"Sawa'" (equal, alike) is a noun meaning "the similar," and its origin is a verbal noun derived from "taswiyah" (equalization).

The clause ﴿among the People of the Scripture is an upright community﴾ and so on explains the vagueness of ﴿they are not alike﴾. The use of the explicit noun in place of a pronoun is for the sake of drawing attention to this community. Here "ummah" (community) means "group" (fariq).

Applying the name "People of the Scripture" to them is a metaphor (majaz) based on what they were, as in His saying Exalted is He ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [An-Nisa': 2], because they had become Muslims.

He deviated from saying "among them is an upright community" to saying ﴿among the People of the Scripture﴾ so that this praise would include the righteous among the Jews and the righteous among the Christians, and not be restricted to the righteous Jews. For the righteous Jews before the mission of 'Isa were adhering to their religion and steadfast upon it, and among them were those who believed in 'Isa and followed him. Likewise, the righteous Christians before the mission of Muhammad ﷺ were steadfast upon the law of 'Isa, and many of them were people of night prayer in the monasteries and hermitages, and they became Muslims after the Muhammadan mission.

"Ummah" means group and community.

The meaning of "upright" (qa'imah) is that it is a figurative expression for acting upon their religion in the true manner, as one says "a standing market" (suq qa'imah) and "an established law" (shari'ah qa'imah).

"Ana'" (hours): its original form is "a'na'" with two hamzas, on the pattern of "af'al," and it is the plural of "in'" (with a kasrah on the hamzah and a fathah on the nun, as a maqsur form). It is also said "ana" with a fathah on the hamzah. Allah says ﴿not waiting for its ripeness (ghayra nazirina inahu)﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 53], meaning not waiting for its appointed time.

The clause ﴿while they prostrate﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning they perform night prayer at night by reciting their Book, and their recitation of the Book is restricted to the state of their prostration. This style is more eloquent and clearer than saying "they perform tahajjud," because it conveys the image of their action.

The meaning of ﴿they hasten to good deeds﴾ is that they hasten toward them, i.e., they eagerly desire to increase in them. "Musara'ah" (hastening) is used figuratively for increasing in the act and being prompt to it, likening the increasing and the earnest care to a swift pace in order to reach the desired goal. "Fi" here denotes figurative containment, and it is an imaginative (takhyiliyyah) usage that indicates the comparison of good deeds to a path along which travelers journey, and these people have the merit of speed in traversing it. You may also take the whole composition of His saying ﴿and they hasten in good deeds﴾ as an image of the state of their eagerness and zeal for performing good deeds, by the state of a traveler who desires to reach his destination and hastens in his journey. Its parallel will come at His saying ﴿Let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 41] in Surah Al-'Uqud.

The demonstrative "those" (ula'ika) refers to the upright community described by those attributes. The placement of the demonstrative serves to draw attention to the fact that they deserved the description mentioned after the demonstrative because of the attributes that preceded the demonstrative.

**Page 59**

**Tadhyil** (a concluding phrase that sums up what precedes it) for the sentences that open with His words ﴿Among the People of the Book is a community standing [upright]﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:113], up to His words ﴿among the righteous﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:114]. The majority of readers recite ﴿tafʿalū﴾ with the second-person ta', so it is a promise addressed to those present. From this it is understood that the righteous who came before them are like them, by the indication of the context of favour and by its occurring right after mention of them. It is as if it were said: "Whatever good you do, and they do." It is also permissible that it be an iltifat (a shift in address) to the People of the Book. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ and Khalaf recited it with the ya' of the third person, referring back to ﴿a community standing [upright]﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:113].

**Kufr** (ingratitude, denial) is the opposite of **shukr** (gratitude). That is, it is the denial that a bestowed blessing has reached one. ʿAntarah said:

*"I was informed that ʿAmr is not thankful for my blessing,*
*and ingratitude is a corruption for the soul of the benefactor."*

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Be grateful to Me and do not be ungrateful to Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:152]. The original use of shukr and kufr is that each is transitive to one object, and its object is the blessing, as in the line of verse. It may also be that their object is the benefactor, by way of extension in dropping the preposition, since the original is "I thanked him" and "I was ungrateful to him." Al-Nābighah said:

*"I thanked you for the blessing..."*

The verse ﴿Be grateful to Me and do not be ungrateful to Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:152] combines both usages. Here ﴿tukfarūhu﴾ has been made transitive to two objects: the first is the deputy of the subject, because the verb has been given the meaning of deprivation. The pronoun in the accusative refers back to **khayr** (good), with the interpretation of "good" as "the recompense of doing good," in the manner of **istikhdam** (a figure in which a pronoun refers to a different sense of the word it stands for). Kufr is used here for withholding the recompense of doing good, by likening doing good to a blessing, as though the doer of good had bestowed a blessing upon God, exalted is He, like His words ﴿If you lend Allah a goodly loan﴾ [al-Taghābun 64:17]. The comparison term is omitted and is indicated by what belongs to it in customary usage, which is kufr. Moreover, in the context there is an explicit metaphor (**istiʿārah**), like ﴿they break the covenant of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:27]. God has bestowed favour upon us by making our obedience to Him like a blessing bestowed upon Him, exalted is He, and by making its reward gratitude (shukr), and the withholding of its reward ingratitude (kufr), and then negating it. He named Himself al-Shakūr (the Appreciative).

Here the verb **kufrān** (ingratitude) has been made transitive to the blessing, according to its original transitivity.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 116:

Page 60
﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve—neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah. And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

This is an initial resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf ibtidaʾi), marking a transition to the mention of the threat against the polytheists, occasioned by the mention of the promise to those among the People of the Book who believed.

The conjunction of "children" here is because provision (ghana') in common usage is by means of wealth and offspring: a person repels harm from himself by wealth, through ransom or the like, and children defend their father by support. The discussion of a similar case has already preceded in the opening of this surah.

He repeated the negative particle with the conjoined term in His saying ﴿nor their children﴾ to emphasize the non-availing of their children for them, to dispel the presumption of what is customary, that children do not refrain from defending their fathers.

The phrase "from Allah" (min Allah) is connected to the verb "will avail" (lan tughniya), in the sense of min al-ibtidaiyyah (the "min" of origin), meaning: any availing that proceeds from the side of Allah by pardoning their disbelief.

The word "shay'an" (anything) is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of the verb "will avail": that is, "any part of availing." The indefiniteness of "shay'an" indicates minimization.

The clause ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿will not avail them their wealth nor their children﴾. The clause is brought in coordinated, contrary to the usual practice in such cases of being without conjunction, in order that the clause be the object of emphasis by the particle "inna," so that there are completed for its confirmation of meaning five proofs: the emphasis by inna; the placement of the demonstrative pronoun; the informing about them that they are "companions of the Fire"; the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl); and the descriptor "abiding eternally."

[Page 61]

﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life is like the likeness of a wind in which is a freezing cold, which strikes the tilth of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys it. God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾

This is a resumptive explanatory discourse (istinaf bayani), because His saying ﴿Their wealth will never avail them at all﴾ [Al 'Imran: 116] raises the question of a questioner about their spending wealth on good works, such as relieving the distressed and paying blood-money (diyat) to settle killings.

He struck for their works connected with wealth a similitude (mathal). He likened the form of their spending, whose outward appearance is impressive and whose end is disappointing, when disbelief nullifies it, to the form of a crop that a cold wind struck and destroyed. This is the likening of the intelligible to the sensible. Since the comparison is an analogy (tamthil), it did not intend that each part of what is compared to correspond to the parts of their spending, so the text says ﴿like the likeness of a wind﴾ and did not say "like the likeness of the tilth of a people."

The discussion of wind has already been given at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-sirr (ṣirr): an intense cold that kills every crop or leaf over which it blows, leaving it as if burned. The Arabs did not use ṣirr to denote a violent cold wind; ṣirr is only the name of cold. As for ṣarṣar, it is a violent wind, and it may be cold. The meaning of the verse is clear without interpretation (ta'wil). Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, permitted that ṣirr here be a name for a cold wind and made it synonymous with ṣarṣar. Later writers accepted this, but it is not mentioned in Asas al-Balagha, nor does al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) mention it.

His saying ﴿in which is ṣirr﴾ conveys the intensity of the coldness of this wind, as if the very nature of ṣirr were enclosed within it, and it carries it to the tilth.

Al-harth (tilth) here is a verbal noun in the sense of a passive participle: that is, maḥrath qawm, meaning a cultivated land; the intended sense is that it struck the crop of a tilth. The discussion of the meanings of harth has already been given at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and the cattle and the tilth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14] at the beginning of the surah.

[Page 62]

His saying ﴿who wronged themselves﴾ is an interweaving (idmaj) within the course of the analogy, which gives the analogy a tone of severity and disfigurement. It is not part of the form of the thing likened. Eloquent speakers sometimes mention with the thing used as the comparison attributes that they intend only for embellishment or denigration, as in the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

Cracked by a cool water (of a spring) that is sweet and clear, at Abtah in the morning, and it is mixed,
The winds disperse the debris from it, and the white clouds of the rain pour upon it.

He thus attached to the water, which is part of the thing used as the comparison, attributes that have no effect on the comparison.

Those who hear it know that the punishment of peoples who wronged themselves is extremely severe. So He mentioned their description as those who wronged themselves, to remind the listeners of this as a form of admonition. His saying ﴿The likeness of what they spend﴾ came without a conjunction to what precedes it, because it serves as an explanation of His saying ﴿Their wealth will never avail them at all﴾ [Al 'Imran: 116].

His saying ﴿God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾: the pronouns in it refer back to those who disbelieved. The meaning is that God did not wrong them when He did not accept their expenditures; rather, they caused this themselves, since they did not believe, because God made faith a condition for the acceptance of works. When He informed them of this and warned them, His punishment afterwards was not an injustice to them. This contains an announcement (iydhan) that God does not break His promise, and that He negates injustice from Himself.

[Page 63]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 118:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take as intimates (bitana) those other than your own, who will not spare you corruption. They love that you suffer. Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their chests conceal is greater. We have certainly made the signs clear to you, if you use your reason.﴾

Now that God has fully exposed the inner intentions of those among the People of the Book who surround the Muslims, the warning about a group of them has come, together with the caution against being deceived by them and the prohibition against confiding in them with affection. These are the hypocrites (al-munafiqun), and the verse is given to inform about them through His saying ﴿And when they meet you, they say, "We believe"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119], and so on. Most of them were Jews, not those among the Aws and Khazraj who were polytheists. This is the place of the conclusion (al-istintaj) in the art of rhetoric (sina'at al-khitabah, the art of persuasive speech), after the premises (tamhidat) and persuasive arguments (iqna'at) have been mentioned. Its proper placement is as an independent resumption (al-istinaf al-ibtida'i), as it is here.

The word bitana, with a kasra on the ba', originally means the inside of a garment, and its plural is bata'in. In the Qur'an, ﴿its linings (bata'inuha) of brocade﴾ [al-Rahman: 54]. The outer surface of a garment is called the zhiharah, with a kasra on the zha'. Bitana also refers to the garment worn beneath another garment, which is called the shi'ar, while the one above it is called the dithar. In a hadith: «The Ansar are the shi'ar, and the people are the dithar.» Then the word bitana was applied to a man's close friend and confidant, who is privy to his affairs, by analogy with the lining of a garment in its closeness to its wearer.

The meaning of their taking them as bitana is that they used to be allied with them and loved them before Islam. When some of the Ansar embraced Islam, the affection remained between them and those who had been their allies among the Jews. Then some of the Jews displayed Islam, and some of them remained upon their religion.

His saying ﴿min dunikum﴾ may be understood in two ways. It is possible that min is extra (za'idah) and dun is a noun of place meaning "around you", and this is the more apparent interpretation, like His saying, exalted is He, in a similar context: ﴿And they did not take, besides God and His Messenger and the believers, any intimate (wali-jah)﴾ [al-Tawbah: 16]. It is also possible that min is partitive (lil-tab'id) and dun means "other than", like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among us are some other than that﴾ [al-Jinn: 11], meaning "other than those of your religion". The listeners already knew that the prohibition against taking them as bitana applied to those who used to deceive the believers into thinking they were from among them, and their hidden traits required a warning against admitting them into one's inner circle.

The clause ﴿who will not spare you corruption (la ya'lunakum khabalan)﴾ is a qualifier of bitana in the first interpretation. This qualification is not one of the apparent attributes that specify an indefinite noun from others that share its characteristics. Rather, it becomes evident through the appearance of its effects to those who discern. So God forbade the Muslims from taking as bitana those whose condition and manner are such, and He entrusted them to discerning the states and actions. His saying ﴿they love that you suffer (wadda ma 'anittum)﴾ and His saying ﴿hatred has already appeared (qad badat al-bagda')﴾ are also two clauses in the position of qualifiers, following the method of omitting the conjunction between qualifiers. His saying ﴿We have certainly made the signs clear to you, if you use your reason﴾ points to this.

[Page 64]

That is: We have certainly made clear to you the marks of their enmity through those qualities, if you use your reason, so that you may discern those qualities, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern (lil-mutawassimin)﴾ [al-Hijr: 75]. In the second interpretation, ﴿min dunikum﴾ is made a qualifier, and the clauses following it are independent resumptions in the position of a reason (ta'lil) for the prohibition against taking as bitana someone from outside our religious community. These traits belong to them, so they are suitable both as descriptions and as a cause for the prohibition. This is because enmity arising from difference of religion is a deeply rooted enmity, especially the enmity of a people who see this religion as having nullified their religion and removed their share of worldly standing, as we will explain.

The meaning of ﴿they will not spare you corruption (la ya'lunakum khabalan)﴾ is that they do not fall short in causing you corruption. The verb al-alw means to fall short or to leave off, and its verb is (ala ya'lu). They may expand the use of this verb so that it takes two objects, because they imply in it the sense of withholding in what the object desires. So they say: "la a'lu-ka jahdan" (I will not withhold effort from you), just as they say: "la adakhiru-ka nusḥan" (I will not withhold sincere counsel from you). It appears that this usage became common until the implied sense was forgotten, so it also took objects indicating evil just as it takes objects indicating good. Thus He said here ﴿will not spare you corruption﴾, meaning they do not fall short in causing you harm. It does not mean that they do not withhold from you, because corruption is not desired nor sought.

It is possible that this verse uses the expression as sarcasm (tahakkum) toward the bitana, because the nature of a bitana is to strive for the good of the one they are close to. Since these people were the opposite of that, He expressed their striving with harm, using the verb that is normally used for striving for good.

Khabal means disorder and corruption of a matter, and from it is called the corruption of the mind (fasad al-'aql) khabal, as well as the corruption of the limbs.

His saying ﴿they love that you suffer (wadda ma 'anittum)﴾: al-wudd means love, and al-'anat means severe exhaustion. That is, they desired what would cause you hardship. Here, ma is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), not temporal, so the verb 'anittum, once it takes on the meaning of a verbal noun, loses its indication of past time.

The meaning of ﴿hatred has already appeared from their mouths (qad badat al-bagda' min afwahihim)﴾ is that it became evident from slips of their speech, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will surely know them by the tone of their speech﴾ [Muhammad: 30]. So He expressed the hatred (al-bagda') by its indications.

[Page 65]

His saying ﴿and what their chests conceal is greater (wa ma tukhfi suduruhum akbar)﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal).

The signs (al-ayat) in His saying ﴿We have certainly made the signs clear to you﴾ means the indications of the ill intentions of this bitana, as He said: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern﴾ [al-Hijr: 75]. The Qur'an has never ceased to educate this nation in using reflection, inference, and recognizing causes from their effects in all its affairs, in legislation and in dealings, so that it would produce a nation of knowledge and discernment. Because these verses are verses of insight and discernment (firasah wa tawassum), He said ﴿if you use your reason (in kuntum ta'qilun)﴾ and did not say "if you know" or "if you understand", because reason (al-'aql) is more general than knowledge ('ilm) and understanding (fiqh).

His saying ﴿We have certainly made the signs clear to you﴾ is an independent resumption.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 119:

﴿Here you are, you love them, but they do not love you.﴾

This is an initial resumptive statement (isti'naf ibtida'i), intended to contrast the character of the two groups. The believers love the People of the Book, while the People of the Book hate them, and "every vessel drips what is in it." The rule is that love brings forth love, except when aims and dispositions differ.

The construction ﴿ha antum ula'i﴾ ("here you are") and its like, such as "ha ana" (here I am), has already occurred in His words in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Then you are those who kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85]. Since the wondering (ta'ajjub) in the verse is from the combination of the two states mentioned before ﴿here you are, you love them﴾, the wonder is at the believers' love for them while they hate the believers. After the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) in this construction, no clause is mentioned except that the purpose is to express wonder at the content of that clause.

The clause ﴿but they do not love you﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlat hal) from the nominative pronoun in ﴿you love them﴾, because the locus of wonder is the combination of the two states.

There is nothing of blame in this wondering; it is merely an awakening (iqaz). For this reason He follows it with His words ﴿and you believe in the Book, all of it﴾, for it serves as an excuse for the believers in their inner affection for the People of the Book, after the believers' faith. For when the believers believed in all the messengers of God and their books, they attributed to the People of the Book a guidance whose time had passed, and they introduced distortion into it. This is in contrast to the People of the Book, who look upon the Muslims with an eye of contempt and error, and with following what is not true. These two outlooks, ours and theirs, are the root of the Muslims' tolerance despite their strength, and of the rigidity of the two groups of People of the Book despite their weakness.

* * *

﴿And you believe in the Book, all of it; and when they meet you they say, "We believe," but when they are alone they bite the tips of their fingers at you out of rage. Say: "Die in your rage."﴾

The clause ﴿and you believe﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you love them﴾, just as the clause ﴿when they meet you﴾ is coordinated with ﴿but they do not love you﴾, and all of them are circumstances distributed over the pronouns of address and the pronouns of absence.

The definite article in "al-Kitab" (the Book) is for the genus, and it is emphasized by the singular form, observing its wording. By this is meant a group of hypocritical Jews, the most famous of whom was Zayd ibn al-Sitit al-Qaynuqa'i.

Al-'add (biting) is gripping a thing with the teeth. Biting the fingertips is a metonymy (kinaya) for intense rage and regret, even though it is not an actual physical biting of fingers; rather it is used as a metonym for its usual concomitant, for when a person's inner state is agitated by emotion, actions issue from him that correspond to that emotion. Sometimes these actions help in relieving the emotion, such as killing one's enemy, and in its opposite, kissing one whom one loves. Sometimes they are confined to the person himself, through which he relieves part of his emotion, such as a child thrashing on the ground when angry, a man striking himself in anger, biting his fingers from rage, striking his tooth from remorse, slapping palm against palm from grief, and similar things such as moaning and crying out. These are kinds of signs of distress: some are innate, like crying out, and some are customary, which people know and which spread among them, so that they come to do them without reflection. Al-Harith ibn Zalim al-Murri said:

"Then there came base, humble folk who bite, from rage, the heads of their thumbs."

His words ﴿ʿalaykum﴾ ("at you") with ʿala here indicate cause (ta'lil), and the pronoun in the genitive refers to the Muslims. It is the attachment of a judgment to the essence through the assumption of a specific state, meaning: because of your coming together and the disappearance of hatred, as Shas ibn Qays the Jew did, concerning whom the words of God were revealed: ﴿O you who believe, if you obey a party of those who were given the Book, they will return you to disbelief after your faith﴾ [Al 'Imran: 100]. A parallel to this attachment is the poet's saying:

"You will surely gnaw your teeth in remorse, whenever you recall one day some of my qualities."

﴿From rage﴾: min here indicates cause. Rage (al-ghayz) is intense anger accompanied by the desire for revenge.

His words ﴿Say: "Die in your rage"﴾ are a statement not addressed to specific listeners, for it is a supplication against those who bite their fingertips from rage, and they do so when they are alone. Thus it cannot be imagined that they are addressed directly with a supplication by name. Rather, it is a statement intended to be heard by everyone who knows in himself the quality of rage against the Muslims. It is close to the kind of address intended to cover every addressee, like ﴿If only you could see when the criminals hang their heads﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12].

The supplication against them "to die of rage" in its literal sense is a request for their death because of their rage; it is a metonymy for the constancy of rage in them throughout their lives, whether long or short, and that is a metonymy for the continuation of the cause of their rage, which is the good condition of the Muslims, the order of their affairs, and the increase of their good. In this supplication there is both a prayer that the pain of rage remain with them and a hastening of their death through it. Each of the two meanings metonymically intended is meant here. The metonymy by rage and by envy for the perfection of the one who is angered or envied is well known, and the Arabs say: "So-and-so is envied (muhassad)," meaning he is in a state of blessing and perfection.

* * *

﴿Indeed, God knows what is in the breasts.﴾

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to His words ﴿they bite the tips of their fingers at you out of rage﴾, and what lies between them is like a parenthetical interjection, meaning: God is aware of them, and He informs you of their inner secrets.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 120:

Page 68
﴿If good touches you, it grieves them; but if evil befalls you, they rejoice at it.﴾
Allah increased the disclosure of what is in their breasts by His saying ﴿If good touches you, it grieves them﴾, meaning: if good befalls you. Al-mass (al-massu) is al-isabah (reaching, befalling). Neither of the two words is restricted to good or to evil; so the use of one of them for good and the other for evil is variation of expression (tafannun). It was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Like one whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Here, al-hasanah and al-sayyi'ah refer to an event or a state which is good or bad for its possessor; they do not mean here the technical sense in the Sharia (al-istilah al-shar'i).

* * *
﴿But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their scheming will not harm you at all. Indeed, Allah is encompassing of what they do.﴾
Allah guided the believers to the manner of receiving the enemy's harm: that they receive it with patience and caution. He expressed caution by taqwa (mindfulness), meaning guarding against their scheming and deception. His saying ﴿their scheming will not harm you at all﴾ means that by this all harm is negated, because He had established at the beginning of the verses that they would not harm the believers except with a minor injury (adha). So harm is a light injury, and when the greatest harm, which requires strenuous resistance in repelling it—fighting, guarding, and spending—is negated, the negation of what remains of harm is easy, and that is achieved by patience over injury and paying little attention to it, together with caution lest they use that injury as a means to reach great harm. And in the hadith: "No one is more patient over harm than Allah: they attribute a rival to Him while He provides for them."

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read ﻻ ﻳَﻀِﺮْﻛﻢ (la yadirkum) with a kasra on the dad and sukun on the ra, from darra-hu yadirru-hu, meaning adarra-hu (harmed him). Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read it with a damma on the dad and a shadda on the ra, from darra-hu yadurru-hu. The damma is an itba' damma, following the vowel of the 'ayn when idgham occurs, to avoid the meeting of two sukuns: the sukun of jazm and the sukun of idgham. In such a form, with a damma on the 'ayn in the present tense, Arabic permits three forms: damma, following the vowel of the 'ayn; fatha, for its lightness; and kasra, which is the original form for avoiding the meeting of two sukuns. Only the damma is read in the mutawatir (widely transmitted) reading.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 3, Verses 121–122:**

﴿And [mention] when you set out early from your family to settle the believers at their positions for battle, and Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ ﴿When two groups among you were about to lose heart, though Allah was their ally. And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾

The presence of the conjunction (wa) in His saying ﴿وإذْ غَدَوْتَ (wa-idh ghadawta, "And when you set out")﴾ prevents attaching the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) to any of the preceding verbs, such as ﴿ودُّوا ما عَنِتُّمْ (they wish that you suffer)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118] or ﴿يَفْرَحُوا بِها (they rejoice in it)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 120]. Accordingly, it comes as its counterparts came at the beginnings of verses and Qur'anic narratives. It is a conjunction of one sentence to another and of one narrative to another, and this is a abrupt transition (intiqal iqtidabi). The estimated meaning is: "And mention when you set out early..." It is also not possible to attach the adverbial phrase to a verb that follows it, because His saying ﴿تُبَوِّئُ (tubawwi'u, "settling")﴾ cannot be the starting point of the topic, and His saying ﴿هَمَّتْ (hammat, "were about to")﴾ cannot serve to attach ﴿إذْ غَدَوْتَ (idh ghadawta)﴾, because it is the object of another ﴿إذْ (idh)﴾.

The reason for mentioning this event right after what preceded it is that it is among the clearest manifestations of the scheming of those who oppose the religion and of the hypocrites. Since the condition of the hypocrites and the people of Yathrib was one, and their inner nature was the same, and they acted according to what the Jews plotted, Allah gathered the plots of both groups by mentioning the Battle of Uhud. The revelation of this surah came right after the Battle of Uhud, as has already been mentioned. These verses refer to the Battle of Uhud, which took place in Shawwal of the third year after the Hijra, when the polytheists of Makkah and those with them from their allies descended upon the slope of Mount Uhud, around Madinah, to avenge what they had suffered at the Battle of Badr of defeat. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) consulted his Companions about what they should do. Among them was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the chief of the hypocrites. The majority advised remaining fortified within Madinah, so that if the polytheists entered the city, they would fight them in the houses and fortresses and defeat them, and if they retreated, they would retreat in failure. A group advised going out, and they were eager for jihad and urged the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) insistently. So the Prophet (ﷺ) adopted the opinion of those who advised going out. He put on his armor, but then some hesitation appeared among the Muslims about going out, so they returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "It is not fitting for a Prophet to put on his armor and then take it off until Allah judges between him and his enemy."

He went out with the Muslims to Mount Uhud, with the mountain behind them, and he arranged them for battle. The battle resulted in a slight defeat that befell the Muslims because of the scheme of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the chief of the hypocrites, when he and a third of the army withdrew. The number of the Muslim army was seven hundred, and the number of the army of the people of Makkah was three thousand. The clans of Banu Salamah and Banu Harithah among the Muslims were about to withdraw, but then Allah protected them. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿إذْ هَمَّتْ طائِفَتانِ مِنكم أنْ تَفْشَلا واللَّهُ ولِيُّهُما (When two groups among you were about to lose heart, though Allah was their ally)﴾, that is, their supporter against that satanic concern, which, had it become a resolve, would have been the cause of their misery. Because of Allah's care for them, He absolved them of acting upon what they had intended.

In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, he said: "We are the two groups: Banu Harithah and Banu Salamah. And concerning us was revealed ﴿إذْ هَمَّتْ طائِفَتانِ مِنكم أنْ تَفْشَلا (When two groups among you were about to lose heart)﴾. And I would not be pleased that it had not been revealed, since Allah says ﴿واللَّهُ ولِيُّهُما (though Allah was their ally)﴾."

The outcome of the event revealed the inferiority of the Muslims, as seventy of them were killed, while about twenty-odd of the polytheists were killed. Abu Sufyan said on that day: "Exalted is Hubal! A day for a day of Badr, and war is in turns (sijal)." Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with him, was killed, and Hind bint 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, the wife of Abu Sufyan, mutilated him, as she split open his belly and cut off a piece of his liver to eat it, out of the rancor that she held in her heart against him, because he had killed her father 'Utbah at the Battle of Badr. Afterward she embraced Islam and her Islam was good. The face of the Prophet (ﷺ) was wounded that day, and his front tooth (ruba'iyyah) was broken.

Al-ghuduww (going out) means departing at the time of early morning (al-ghada).

The ﴿مِن (min)﴾ in His saying ﴿مِن أهْلِكَ (min ahlika, "from your family")﴾ is for the starting point (ibtida'iyyah).

Al-ahl (family) here means the spouse. The speech implies an omitted noun, indicated by the verb ﴿غَدَوْتَ (ghadawta)﴾, meaning: "from the house of your family," and it was the house of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.

﴿تُبَوِّئُ (tubawwi'u)﴾ means to make [them] a place of settlement (mabaa'), that is, a place of return (ba'w).

Al-ba'w means return, and here it means the abode, because one returns to it. ﴿المُؤْمِنِينَ (al-mu'minin)﴾ is in the accusative as the first object of ﴿تُبَوِّئُ (tubawwi'u)﴾, and ﴿مَقاعِدَ (maqa'ida)﴾ is the second object, treating the verb tubawwi'u as analogous to tu'ti ("gives"). Al-maqa'id is the plural of maq'ad, which is the place of sitting (al-qu'ud), that is, sitting on the ground. Sitting is the opposite of standing and rising. The attachment of maqa'id to the noun "fighting" (al-qital) is an indication that it is applied to the places suitable for fighting, where the army is stationed and does not move from them, because they are suitable for its movements. So maqa'id is used here for places of stationing, either as a metaphor (kinayah) or as a general metonymic figure (majaz mursal) by the relation of generality. This usage became common in speech, until it came to equal the place of rest and the location, and from it is His saying ﴿فِي مَقْعَدِ صِدْقٍ (in a seat of truthful sincerity)﴾ [Al-Qamar: 55].

Know that the word maqa'id was subject to criticism from al-Sharif al-Radi, when he said in a lament for Abu Ishaq al-Sabi:

"It is hard for me that I see you, while the sitting places of the visitors have emptied from your two sides."

Ibn al-Athir mentioned in al-Mathal al-sa'ir that Ibn Sinan said: "His use of this word in this place is correct, except that it agrees with what is disliked to mention, especially since he attached it to those to whom its attachment may be borne, namely the visitors (al-'awwad). If it had stood alone, the matter would have been easy." Ibn al-Athir said: "This word has come in the Qur'an and came in an acceptable manner, namely His saying ﴿وإذْ غَدَوْتَ مِن أهْلِكَ تُبَوِّئُ المُؤْمِنِينَ مَقاعِدَ لِلْقِتالِ (And [mention] when you set out early from your family to settle the believers at their positions for battle)﴾. Do you not see that in this verse it is not attached to anything whose attachment would be ugly?"

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 3, verses 123–125:**

﴿And God had already given you victory at Badr, when you were weak. So be mindful of God, that you may be grateful.﴾ ﴿When you said to the believers: "Is it not enough for you that your Lord should reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?"﴾ ﴿Yes. If you are steadfast and mindful of God, and they come upon you immediately, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels, marked out.﴾

When the battle of Uhud had ended without a victory for the Muslims, God followed its mention by reminding them of the victory He had granted them at Badr, the victory He had decreed for them on that day. It was a great victory, for it was the triumph of a small company over a large army with abundant equipment. The dead among the polytheists that day were the chiefs of Quraysh and the leaders of polytheism, and it suffices to mention Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. For this reason God said: ﴿while you were weak﴾, that is, feeble. Dhull (humiliation, abasement) is the opposite of 'izz (honour, might), and it means weakness and frailty. This carries an implicit suggestion that the defeat at Uhud does not blunt the Muslims' resolve, because they have become mighty again, and war is a matter of alternating fortunes (sijal).

His saying ﴿So be mindful of God, that you may be grateful﴾ is an interjection (i'tiraD) between the clause ﴿And God had already given you victory at Badr﴾ and the element that depends on its verb, namely ﴿when you said to the believers﴾. The fa' here is for consequence (tafri'), and according to the sounder view the fa' may occur within an interjected clause, contrary to those grammarians who forbade this. When He reminded them of that great favour, He reminded them that it was a cause of gratitude, so He commanded them to be grateful by constant adherence to taqwa (God-consciousness), in keeping with the wording of His saying: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [Ibrahim: 7].

Part of gratitude for that victory is that they remain firm in fighting the enemy, obey the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that the defeat of the day of Uhud not dull their resolve.

The temporal clause ﴿when you said to the believers﴾ is adverbial of time and depends on (nasarakum), because the promise of His support through the angels and the believers was made on the day of Badr, not on the day of Uhud. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun).

This time was singled out for mention because it was the moment when this miracle and this blessing became manifest, so it was fitting to remind them of it and to remind them of the favour.

The meaning is: when you were promising the believers the aid of God through the angels, the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying this to them was only on the basis of a promise that God had revealed to him, that he should say it.

[p. 73]

The interrogative in ﴿Is it not enough for you﴾ is an interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqriri), and the affirmative interrogative often occurs with a negation, as we explained earlier at His saying ﴿Have you not seen those who left their homes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 243] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The negative particle here is (lan), which indicates emphasis of negation, to convey that on the day of Badr they were, because of their small number and weakness, despite the large number and might of their enemy, like people who despair that this number of angels would suffice. So the affirmative interrogative was placed upon that, so that it would serve as a prompt for whoever harboured despair about the sufficiency of that number of angels, that he should state what was in his soul. The intended meaning of this is its implication, and this is an affirmation that this number is sufficient.

Because the interrogative is not literal, its answer came from the questioner with (bala), since it is something about which there can be no dispute, as will come in His saying ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "God is witness between me and you"﴾ [al-An'am: 19] in Surah al-An'am. So (bala) served to nullify the negation and to affirm that this number was sufficient, and it is part of the Prophet's (ﷺ) statement to the believers.

In Surah al-Anfal, when mentioning the battle of Badr, it was reported that God promised them reinforcement with angels numbering one thousand, in His saying: ﴿When you sought help from your Lord and He answered you: "I will reinforce you with a thousand angels following one another"﴾ [al-Anfal: 9]. Here He mentions that God promised them three thousand, then raised this to five thousand. The way to reconcile the two verses is that God promised them one thousand angels and encouraged them with the prospect of more by His saying (murdifina), meaning "following one another," that is, followed by another number. His speech here indicates that they were still apprehensive about the large number of the enemy, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: ﴿Is it not enough for you that your Lord should reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?﴾ God intended by this to increase their steadfastness, then He added two thousand more if they were steadfast and mindful of God. The majority of exegetes explained it in this way, and this is what the context requires. It is established that the angels descended on the day of Badr to support the believers, and some of the Companions saw a group of them, and some of them witnessed the traces of their killing of men among the polytheists.

[p. 74]

He described the angels as (munzilin), "sent down," to indicate that they descend to the earth at the place of fighting, out of care for the Muslims, as God said: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾ [al-Hijr: 8].

The majority read (munzilin) with a sukun on the nun and a light zay, and anzala and nazzala have the same meaning.

The pronouns, the nominative and the genitive, in His saying ﴿and they come upon you immediately﴾ refer to the angels who were the subject of the discourse, as is the apparent sense, and a group of exegetes interpreted it this way.

Accordingly, the placement of His saying (wa-ya'tukum) is in the position of a promise, so in meaning it is conjoined to ﴿your Lord will reinforce you﴾, and its proper place would have been after it. However, it was placed before the element it is conjoined to, in order to hasten reassurance to the hearts of the believers. Thus its placement is an instance of placing the conjoined element before the element it is conjoined to. If this placement is permissible in the conjunction of single words, as in the verse of Sannan ibn 'Abbad al-Yashkuri:

"Then I complained to my neighbours, and its dweller is a grave at Sinjar, or a grave on Qahad."

Ibn Jinni said in his commentary on the verses of al-Hamasa: the conjoined element was placed before the element it is conjoined to, and what makes it acceptable is the strength of the connection between the verb and its subject. That is: the governing element, which is the verb, takes its portion of precedence, and there is no regard for the fact that the element conjoined to is delayed after the one it is conjoined to. If you said, "I struck and Zayd 'Amr," it would be weaker, because the connection of the object to the verb is not as strong as that of the subject to it. But if you said, "I passed by, and Zayd by 'Amr," it would not be permitted, because you did not place the governing element, which is the preposition (ba'), before the conjunctive particle. Among the placing of the object before is the statement of Zayd:

"You have combined backbiting, slander and gossip, three traits from which you will not desist."

And another's statement:

"God curse Hind of the Indians, along with her husband, the long-acting one."

It is not permissible to say, "You combined backbiting and slander with an insult," in the same way. As for his saying:

"Upon you and the peace of God."

this is among those whose derivation is close to that of Sibawayh, but the scholars did not accept this verse except on the assumption of the placement in it, and al-Marzuqi agreed with them on this. Their statements do not imply that the placement of the conjoined element in cases where its placement is acceptable is specific to necessity in poetry. Therefore we have derived this aspect for the verse, and it is of the conjunction of clauses (ataf al-jumal), since the conjunction of clauses is broader than the conjunction of single words, because it is a formal conjunction.

It occurs in Mughni al-Labib, under the letter waw, that placing its conjoined element before the element it is conjoined to is a matter of necessity, and Ibn al-Sayyid preceded him in this in his commentary on the verses of al-Jumal, and al-Taftazani in his commentary on al-Miftah, as al-Damamini cited from him in Tuhfat al-Gharib.

A group of exegetes took the pronouns of the third person in His saying ﴿and they come upon you immediately﴾ to refer to a group of polytheists, about whom news reached the Muslims that they would reinforce the enemy army on the day of Badr, namely Kurz ibn Jabir al-Muharibi and those with him. This troubled the Muslims and they feared, so God revealed ﴿When you said to the believers: "Is it not enough for you?"﴾, and so on, and this is the view adopted by al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) and those who followed him. In that case, the referent of the two pronouns is not mentioned in the text, but it is known to the people who were present at Badr. Then (wa-ya'tukum) would be conjoined to the conditional: that is, "if you are steadfast and mindful of God, and Kurz and his companions come upon you to aid the polytheists against you, your Lord will reinforce you with more than a thousand, and from three thousand up to five thousand." They said: news of the defeat of the polytheists at Badr reached Kurz and his companions, so he turned away from reinforcing them, and God did not reinforce them with angels, that is, with angels beyond the thousand. It was also said: He did not reinforce them with any angels at all, but the reports testify against this.

Some of the earlier exegetes, such as Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak and al-Zuhri, held that the speech reported in His saying ﴿When you said to the believers﴾ was uttered on the day of Uhud. They said: God promised them reinforcement with angels on condition that they remain steadfast, but when they did not remain steadfast and rushed to seize the spoils, God did not reinforce them, not even with a single angel. According to this interpretation, ﴿When you said to the believers﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿and when you set out early in the morning﴾, and then it is necessary that the clause (wa-ya'tukum) be placed before the clause it is conjoined to, for the reason mentioned earlier of securing the speed of victory. The grammatical analysis (i'rab) of (wa-ya'tukum), in accordance with the two possibilities we mentioned just above, stands.

The meaning of ﴿immediately﴾ is swift haste, for (fawr) is hastening to an action. The attribution of (fawr) to the pronoun of those who come serves to indicate the intensity of the fawr's specificity to them, that is, the intensity of their being characterized by it, to the point that it becomes known as "their fawr." Of this type is the saying: "He went out from his fawr," meaning immediately. (Min) here indicates the starting point.

"For you" (lakum) is connected to "good news." The purpose of stating it explicitly, though it is clear that the good news is directed to them, is to show Allah's honoring of them, by giving them good news for their sake, as in the explicit statement of this in His saying ﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ [Al-Sharh: 1].

"Bushra" is a noun for the verbal noun of bashsharа, like "ruj'a" (return). Bushra is news of the occurrence of something beneficial and joyful for the one informed. When Allah promised them victory, they were certain of it, so explaining its cause, which is the reinforcement by the angels, was a reassurance to their souls, because souls incline toward familiar forms.

They are used here metaphorically for the soul's certainty about the occurrence of a matter, likening firm knowledge to the steadiness of the soul, that is, the absence of its agitation. This was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿but that my heart may be at rest﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 260] in Surah al-Baqarah.

He surveyed the conditions of defeat: a group was killed, so a part of the disbelievers was cut off; a group was subdued and turned back frustrated; a group was granted favor by Allah through Islam, so they embraced Islam; and a group was punished by death upon disbelief after that, or was punished in this world with humiliation, degradation, captivity, and the favor granted to them on the day of the Conquest after their city was taken. The "or" (aw) between these verbs is for division.

This cutting off and subduing had already occurred on the day of Badr, about two years before the revelation of this verse. The expression of them in the present tense is to evoke the astonishing condition of that clear and unrivaled victory.
