That is, victory was achieved purely by Allah's grace upon the Muslims. This is part of the meaning of His saying ﴿So you did not kill them, but Allah killed them; and you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾ [Al-Anfal: 17].

It is also permissible that the clause be understood as a metonymy (kinaya) for turning the Prophet, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, away from preoccupation with what Allah did to those who disbelieved: cutting off a part of them, subduing them, relenting toward them, or punishing them. This is like the excuse for the non-victory of the Muslims at Uhud.

Perhaps the Prophet ﷺ wished to annihilate all the polytheists on the day of Badr when he saw the requirement for that, which was the descent of the angels to destroy them. So Allah reminded him that He had not decreed their total extermination, but made retribution against them of various kinds: He took vengeance on a group by cutting off a part of them, and on the rest by subduing them, which is grief over their dead, the loss of their leaders, and the disruption of their affairs. In the Sahih of Muslim, from Anas ibn Malik: "The Prophet ﷺ had his face wounded and his lower incisor broken on the day of Uhud, and the Muslims came to wipe the blood from the face of their Prophet. So the verse was revealed. Its meaning is: do not regard their prosperity as unlikely. There is no doubt that his saying "so this verse was revealed" must be interpreted as meaning: the Prophet ﷺ was reminded by this verse, since it is evident that what they mentioned is not suitable to be a cause for the Prophet's marveling at their prosperity or regarding it as unlikely, and he did not claim for himself any thing or deed, so that it could be said "You have no say in the matter."

Al-Tirmidhi related: "The Prophet ﷺ supplicated against four of the polytheists, naming individuals, and so this verse was revealed forbidding him from that, and then they embraced Islam." And it is reported that "when his face was wounded on the day of Uhud, his Companions said to him: 'Would that you supplicated against them.' He said: 'I was not sent as a curser, but I was sent as a caller and a mercy. O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know.'" Page 83

If you say: Why did He not gather the punishments in a continuous sequence, saying ﴿that He may cut off a part of those who disbelieve, or disgrace them so that they turn back frustrated﴾, or He turns to them, or He punishes them? I say: the rule of gathering similar items was observed first, and the gathering of opposites second, by joining "cutting off" and "disgracing", then joining "turning in repentance" and "punishment", in the manner in which Abu al-Tayyib answered the criticism of his saying about Sayf al-Dawla:

You stood, and there is no doubt in death for the one who stands, as if you were in the sheath of destruction while he is sleeping.
The heroes pass by you wounded and grieved, while your face is bright and your smile is cheerful.

For he placed first, of his two descriptions, the comparison of his being in the sheath of destruction, for the sake of the fitting relation to death, and he delayed the circumstantial clause "and your face is bright", for the sake of contrast with his saying "wounded and grieved", in a story mentioned in the books of literature.

The preposition lam is the lam of ownership, and the kaf of address is for a specific person, namely the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.

This sentence functions as a proverb, being composed in a concise construction from which some words are omitted. I have not found, in what I have memorized outside the Qur'an, that it was used among the Arabs; perhaps it is one of the Qur'an's own innovations. Close to it is His saying ﴿And I have no power for you against Allah in anything﴾ [al-Mumtahina: 4], and something close to it will come in His later saying ﴿They say: Is there anything of the affair for us?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154] and ﴿They say: If there had been anything of the affair for us, we would not have been killed here﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]. If their speech is being quoted in its exact wording, this shows that this phrase was in use among the Arabs; if it is a report of its meaning, then not.

His saying ﴿for they are wrongdoers﴾ indicates that they deserve punishment more, and that turning to them in mercy, if it occurs, is a bounty from Allah, exalted is He.

Among them are those who made ﴿or He turns to them﴾ a conjunction with His saying "the matter" (al-amr) or with His saying "anything" (shay'), as the conjunction of a verb with a pure noun, with the hidden "an" permitted, meaning: you have no part in their affair or in their repentance; or: you have no part in the matter, [anything] or a turning to them.

Page 83

You stood, and there is no doubt in death for the one who stands, as if you were in the sheath of destruction while he is sleeping.
The heroes pass by you wounded and grieved, while your face is bright and your smile is cheerful.

For he placed first, of his two descriptions, the comparison of his being in the sheath of destruction, for the sake of the fitting relation to death, and he delayed the circumstantial clause "and your face is bright", for the sake of contrast with his saying "wounded and grieved", in a story mentioned in the books of literature.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 126–128 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And Allah made it not except as good news for you, and that your hearts might be reassured by it. And victory is not except from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿That He might cut off a part of those who disbelieved, or subdue them, so that they turn back frustrated.﴾ ﴿You have no say in the matter; whether He relents toward them or punishes them, for indeed they are wrongdoers.﴾

It is permissible that the clause ﴿And Allah made it not except as good news﴾ be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the Name of Majesty (Allah) in His saying ﴿And Allah had already helped you at Badr﴾ [Al-'Imran: 123]. The meaning is: "Allah had already helped you at Badr when you said to the believers what Allah had promised you, while the state was that Allah had not made that promise except as good news for you. Otherwise, He had promised you victory, as in His saying, ﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾ [Al-Anfal: 7], and so on."

It is also permissible that the waw be a conjunction of narration (ʿatf al-ikhbar) upon the reminder and the expression of favor. The mention of the Name of Majesty in place of the pronoun serves to emphasize this care from Allah toward them. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims.

The pronoun of object in His saying "made it" (jaʿalahu) refers either to the reinforcement (al-imdad) derived from ﴿He will reinforce you﴾ or to the promise derived from His saying ﴿if you are patient and mindful of Allah﴾ [Al-'Imran: 125], and so on.

The exception is "exclusive-incomplete" (mufarragh). "Good news" (bushra) is the second object of "made" (jaʿala), meaning: Allah did not make the reinforcement and the promise of it except that it is good news, i.e., He made it good news, and did not make it anything other than that.

"For you" (lakum) is connected to "good news." The purpose of stating it explicitly, though it is clear that the good news is directed to them, is to show Allah's honoring of them, by giving them good news for their sake, as in the explicit statement of this in His saying ﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ [Al-Sharh: 1].

"Bushra" is a noun for the verbal noun of bashsharа, like "ruj'a" (return). Bushra is news of the occurrence of something beneficial and joyful for the one informed. When Allah promised them victory, they were certain of it, so explaining its cause, which is the reinforcement by the angels, was a reassurance to their souls, because souls incline toward familiar forms.

"Tamʾana" and "tuma'nina" mean calm and the absence of agitation. They are used here metaphorically for the soul's certainty about the occurrence of a matter, likening firm knowledge to the steadiness of the soul, that is, the absence of its agitation. This was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿but that my heart may be at rest﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 260] in Surah al-Baqarah.

"And that your hearts might be reassured" (wa li-tatma'inna) is conjoined to "good news," so it falls within the scope of the exception, making it an exception from causes (istithna' min ʿilal), meaning: Allah did not make it for the sake of anything except for the sake of your hearts being reassured by it.

The clause ﴿And victory is not except from Allah﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil), meaning: every victory is from Allah, not from the angels. The two descriptions ﴿the Mighty, the Wise﴾ are mentioned here because they are most suitable for mention in this context: the Mighty grants victory to whom He wills, and the Wise knows who deserves His victory and how it is given.

His saying ﴿That He might cut off a part﴾ is connected to "victory" in the sense that it is a cause for some circumstances of the victory, meaning: that He might cut off, on the day of Badr, a part of the polytheists.

"Ṭaraf" (a part, with a fatha on the ra') may mean a direction, and it is specifically applied to the direction which is the end of a place. Abu Tammam said:

*They were the protected center, then calamities joined them until they became an edge.*

Thus it is a metaphor for a group of polytheists, like His saying ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its edges?﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 41]. It may also mean the extremity of a body part, such as the hands, feet, or head, and then it is metaphorically applied here to the nobles of the polytheists, meaning: that He might cut off from the body of polytheism its most important limbs, that is, to uproot the chieftains of those who disbelieved. The indefiniteness of "ṭaraf" is for magnification. It is said: "He is among the edges of the Arabs," meaning among their nobles and the people of their households.

The meaning of ﴿or subdue them﴾ is: to strike them with grief and sorrow. The root of "kabata" is "kabada" with a dal, when one is struck in his liver (kabid). Similar expressions are: "ṣudira" when one is struck in his chest, "kuliya" when one is struck in his kidney, "mutina" when one is struck in his spine, and "ruʾiya" when one is struck in his lung. The dal was changed to a ta', and sometimes the ta' is changed to a dal, as in their saying "sabada ra'sahu" and "sabata ra'sahu," meaning he shaved his head. The Arabs imagine grief and sadness as residing in the liver, and anger as residing in the chest and the organs of breathing. Abu al-Tayyib praised Sayf al-Dawla at the time of his departure from Antioch:

*To subdue an envier and to show an enemy, as if your farewell and departure were both.*

He surveyed the conditions of defeat: a group was killed, so a part of the disbelievers was cut off; a group was subdued and turned back frustrated; a group was granted favor by Allah through Islam, so they embraced Islam; and a group was punished by death upon disbelief after that, or was punished in this world with humiliation, degradation, captivity, and the favor granted to them on the day of the Conquest after their city was taken. The "or" (aw) between these verbs is for division.

This cutting off and subduing had already occurred on the day of Badr, about two years before the revelation of this verse. The expression of them in the present tense is to evoke the astonishing condition of that clear and unrivaled victory.

The clause ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾ is a parenthetical clause (iʿtiraḍ) between the coordinated items. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ. It may be understood according to the literal meaning of its wording, so that the meaning is a negation that the Prophet had any influence in the occurrence of victory on the day of Badr through his fighting the disbelievers with his army of Muslims, since the Muslims were few on every side of the battle. That is, victory was achieved purely by Allah's grace upon the Muslims. This is part of the meaning of His saying ﴿So you did not kill them, but Allah killed them; and you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾ [Al-Anfal: 17].

The word "amr" in ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾ means affair or matter, and the definite article in it is for a known reference, meaning: of the matter you know, which is victory.

It is also permissible that the clause be understood as a metonymy (kinaya) for turning the Prophet, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, away from preoccupation with what Allah did to those who disbelieved: cutting off a part of them, subduing them, relenting toward them, or punishing them. That is, this is entrusted to Us; We bring it about when We will, and We delay it when We will, according to what Our wisdom requires. This is like the excuse for the non-victory of the Muslims at Uhud.

So the word "amr" means the affair of the polytheists. The definiteness in it is a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning: you have no concern for their affair. This is a reminder of what the Prophet ﷺ experienced on the day of Badr of fear that the polytheists would prevail over him, and of his urgent supplication for victory. Perhaps the Prophet ﷺ wished to annihilate all the polytheists on the day of Badr when he saw the requirement for that, which was the descent of the angels to destroy them. So Allah reminded him that He had not decreed their total extermination, but made retribution against them of various kinds: He took vengeance on a group by cutting off a part of them, and on the rest by subduing them, which is grief over their dead, the loss of their leaders, and the disruption of their affairs. He spared a group so that He might relent toward them and guide them, so that they would become a strength for the Muslims and believe after that. These are those from the people of Makkah who embraced Islam before the Conquest, and on the day of the Conquest, such as Abu Sufyan, al-Harith ibn Hisham (brother of Abu Jahl), 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl, Safwan ibn Umayya, and Khalid ibn al-Walid. And He punished a group with the punishment of this world, by captivity or by killing, such as Ibn Khatal and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. Therefore it was said to him: ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾.

This clause was placed between the coordinated items to make clear that the matter in question which revolves among these four conditions of the polytheists is not in the Prophet's hands. Rather, it is entrusted to Allah, who knows best what they will come to.

The placing of this clause before His saying ﴿or He relents toward them﴾ is a comfort for the Prophet ﷺ, since it first mentions what indicates retribution against them for its sake, then follows with what indicates pardoning them, then follows with what indicates their punishment. So in some of these conditions there is satisfaction for him on the side of his being victorious, and in others there is satisfaction for him on the side of their submission to him. For this purpose, the discourse returns to the remaining punishments of the polytheists with His saying ﴿or He punishes them﴾.

Since the reminder of the day of Badr occurred in the course of the reference to the battle of Uhud, it is as if this division contains an allusion to what may serve as an explanation of the wisdom of the defeat that afflicted the Muslims on the day of Uhud. For sparing many of the polytheists, who were not struck by death that day, meant the storing up of a great group of them for Islam later on, after their fear of the Muslims had arisen from the battle of Badr, even though they reckoned a reckoning for the Muslims by what they witnessed of their bravery on the day of Uhud, even though they did not win.

[p. 80]

It is not sound that His saying ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾ be connected to the conditions of the day of Uhud, because the context of the discourse rejects it, and the condition of the polytheists on the day of Uhud does not suit His saying ﴿That He might cut off a part of those who disbelieved﴾ down to His saying ﴿frustrated﴾.

In the Sahih of Muslim, from Anas ibn Malik: "The Prophet ﷺ had his face wounded and his lower incisor broken on the day of Uhud, and the Muslims came to wipe the blood from the face of their Prophet. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'How will a people prosper who did this to their Prophet while he calls them to their Lord?'" That is, while he calls them to goodness with their Lord. So the verse was revealed. Its meaning is: do not regard their prosperity as unlikely. There is no doubt that his saying "so this verse was revealed" must be interpreted as meaning: the Prophet ﷺ was reminded by this verse, since it is evident that what they mentioned is not suitable to be a cause for the Prophet's marveling at their prosperity or regarding it as unlikely, and he did not claim for himself any thing or deed, so that it could be said "You have no say in the matter."

Al-Tirmidhi related: "The Prophet ﷺ supplicated against four of the polytheists, naming individuals, and so this verse was revealed forbidding him from that, and then they embraced Islam." And it was said: he intended to supplicate, or he asked Allah to supplicate against them for their annihilation, and he was forbidden.

What refutes these views is what is in the Sahih of Muslim from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "It is as if I am looking at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ narrating a prophet of the prophets whom his people struck, while he wiped the blood from his face and said: 'My Lord, forgive my people, for they do not know.'"

And it is reported that "when his face was wounded on the day of Uhud, his Companions said to him: 'Would that you supplicated against them.' He said: 'I was not sent as a curser, but I was sent as a caller and a mercy. O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know.'" And it is established from his character ﷺ that he would never take revenge for himself.

Some scholars went to an extreme, saying that His saying ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾ abrogated (naskh) what the Prophet ﷺ used to supplicate in his qunut (the supplication in prayer) against Ri'l, Dhakwan, 'Usayya, and Lihyan, who killed the Companions at the well of Ma'una. Their evidence for this is what is in al-Bukhari, that the Prophet ﷺ continued to supplicate against them until Allah revealed ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is entirely a weak statement, and this is not one of the places of abrogation (naskh). How can it be correct that it was revealed to abrogate that, when it lies between the causes of the victory that took place on the day of Badr?"

The interpretation of what is in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, that the Prophet stopped supplicating against the polytheists after the revelation of this verse, out of taking the fullest courtesy (adab), is that when Allah informed him in this matter that Allah knows best what contains the benefit of Islam and the calamity of disbelief, he left supplicating against them, perhaps they would embrace Islam. And since we consider his ﷺ supplication against tribes of the polytheists in the qunut as a legislated ruling established by ijtihad (independent reasoning) in a place of permissibility, because the basic principle of supplicating against an enemy is permissible, his abandoning it after the revelation of this verse is of the type of abrogation by analogy (naskh bi-l-qiyas). It abrogated the ruling of permissibility, which is the equality of doing and not doing, by establishing the ruling of the preferability of doing it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 129:

﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Page 84

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) following His words ﴿or He will turn to them in forgiveness or punish them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 128], indicating that these two states are a division among the polytheists. Since this could prompt the desire to know why one group is singled out over another, or why the punishment is generalized, He concluded it by referring the matter to the comprehensive totality of the Divine absolute sovereignty (hadrat al-iṭlāq al-ilahiyya), because the secrets of why each individual is assigned what is determined for him are hidden secrets that none knows except Allah, the Exalted. And each is facilitated for that for which Allah created him.

If the discussion of the Battle of Uhud were not incomplete, since it will resume at God's words ﴿Many ways have passed before you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 137] up to His words ﴿rejoicing in a favour from God﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 171], we would say that His words ﴿O you who believe, do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled﴾ are an abrupt introduction of legislation. However, it is necessary to consider it a digression within the discussion of the Battle of Uhud, although the link between its placement in this context has not become clear. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "I do not know of any transmitted reason for this." Al-Fakhr [al-Razi] said: "Some people said: when God guided the believers to what was best for them in matters of religion and jihad, He followed that with what falls under commands and prohibitions, so He said ﴿O you who believe, do not consume usury﴾, and so it has no connection with what came before it."

Al-Qaffal said: "When the polytheists spent on their armies from wealth they had gathered through usury, it was feared that this might lead the Muslims to engage in usury." This is a far-fetched connection. Ibn 'Arafa said: "When God mentioned the threat against the disbelievers, He followed it by explaining that the threat does not apply only to them but also includes the disobedient, and He mentioned one form of disobedience, which is consuming usury." This is weaker than what came before it. In my view, from the very beginning, there is no need to insist on a consistent connection, since the period of the revelation of the surah is capable of containing events during which a Qur'an is revealed, and so it becomes part of that surah, as I explained in the eighth introduction. Thus this verse was revealed right after what came before it and was written here, and there is no connection between them, since it is appended to the discussion.

It may be asked why the prohibition of usury is repeated in this surah after what preceded it in the verses of Surat al-Baqara, which is more comprehensive than what is in this surah. The answer is that it appears this verse was revealed before the verse of Surat al-Baqara, so this one served as a preparation for that one, and the prohibition in it did not reach the full extent of what is in Surat al-Baqara. It has been narrated that the verse of al-Baqara was revealed after God had forbidden usury, and that the Thaqif tribe said: "How are we forbidden from usury when it is like trade?" The description of usury as ﴿doubled and redoubled﴾ is a prohibition of excessive usury, and it remained silent about what is less than that, which does not reach the level of doubling. Then the verse in Surat al-Baqara was revealed. It is also possible that some Muslims lent money to one another at interest after the Battle of Uhud, so the prohibition of usury was revealed during the period of the account of that battle.

The discussion of the meaning of consuming usury and the meaning of usury, and the reason for its prohibition, has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqara. His words ﴿doubled and redoubled﴾ are a circumstantial phrase describing usury. ''Adaf'' (multiples) is the plural of ''di'f'' (with a kasra on the dad), which is an equivalent in quantity when a thing and its like are mutually dependent. You do not say, "I have the di'f of your dirham," since the principal is not with you; rather, it is good to say, "I have two dirhams." You only say, "I have a dirham and its di'f," when the principal dirham is with you, and you say, "You have a dirham and its di'f if you do such-and-such."

The word ''di'f'' is applied to a single item when it is not defined with the article "al-," as in ''di'fihi'' (its double). When the plural is intended, it is expressed in the plural form, as here. When ''al-di'f'' is defined with the article, both the sense of a specific reference and the sense of the category are valid, as in God's words ﴿Those will have a recompense of double for what they did﴾ [Saba': 37], since the recompense is multiples, as it came in the hadith: "up to seven hundred times."

His words ''mudā'afa'' (redoubled) are an attribute of ''adaf'' (multiples), meaning they are multiples that undergo doubling. This is because when they lent money to someone until a term, they lent it with an increase, and whenever the debtor was unable to pay at the term or wished to delay, they added a similar increase, so the double becomes a double and increases, and so on. This fits the case in which they gather the debt doubled by a similar amount until the term, and when it is extended to a second term, they add an amount equal to all of that. Thus the multiples arise from the beginning of the loan for the first term, and their doubling occurs in the subsequent terms. It also fits the case in which they lend at usury less than the amount of the debt, and it grows with the extension of terms, until the debt becomes multiples and the multiples become multiples. If the phrase is the first case, then the circumstantial phrase serves to describe the actual situation and does not yield an implied meaning (mafhum), because the condition for deriving an implied meaning from restrictions is that the restricting phrase was not uttered merely to describe the actual situation. If it is the second case, then the circumstantial phrase is intended to denounce and to express the intention of this corrupt outcome. Since most debtors' need continues for long periods, falling into this outcome was habitual, and in that case the circumstantial phrase does not yield an implied meaning, since its purpose is not restriction but denunciation. Therefore the prohibition in this verse is not limited to usury that reaches many multiples, so that someone could say: "If usury is less than double the principal, it is not forbidden." This circumstance is not the target of the prohibition on consuming usury, so that someone would imagine that if it is less than double it is not forbidden. It appears that this is the first verse revealed on the prohibition of usury, and the verse of al-Baqara came after it, because the form of this verse suits the beginning of legislation, while the form of the verse of al-Baqara indicates that the ruling had already been established. That is why it mentioned in that verse the punishment for persisting in consuming usury, and mentioned the delusion of those who thought usury was like trading, and it was said in it: ﴿Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has passed﴾ [al-Baqara: 275], as we have mentioned just now. Thus the implied meaning of the restriction is nullified in every case.

The wisdom behind the prohibition of usury is the intention of the Sharia to lead the community to console its wealthy toward its needy one in a temporary, incidental need through a loan. It is thus a rank below charity, and it is a kind of consolation, except that consolation includes what is obligatory, like zakat, and includes what is recommended, like charity and lending. If a person volunteers for it, it becomes forbidden for him to seek a return for it, and likewise for all acts of kindness. This is because the custom that prevailed among past nations, especially the Arabs, was that a person would not borrow except out of dire necessity for his life, and therefore the community's right was to console him. Consolation appears to be a communal obligation (fard kifaya) upon those capable of it, so it is different from the case of one who comes seeking a transaction for profit, like buyers and sellers, or those who lend to one another, given the clear distinction in custom between dealing and borrowing. However, the Sharia distinguished these kinds of transactions from one another by their essential realities, not by differences in the circumstances of the contracting parties. Therefore it did not permit the owner of money to invest it by way of usury in a loan, even if the borrower was not in need, but rather was seeking abundance and enrichment by moving the money he borrowed into ways of profit and trade and the like. It did permit the owner of money to invest by way of partnership, trade and salam-contracts, even if the profit in those was greater than the amount of usury, as a distinction among the legal kinds of transactions.

It is possible that the purpose of the Sharia in prohibiting usury is to keep Muslims away from indolence in investing wealth, and to compel them to partnership and cooperation in worldly affairs. Thus the prohibition of usury, even if small, along with permitting the profit of trade and partnerships, even if large, is a realization of this purpose.

The Muslims spent long centuries during which they did not see themselves as needing to deal in usury, and their wealth at that time was not less than the wealth of the rest of the nations of the world, at times when the supremacy of the world was in their hands, or at times when they were independent in managing their affairs. But when the supremacy of the world came into the hands of non-Islamic nations, and Muslims became linked to others in trade and dealings, and the market of world wealth was organized according to the rules of laws that do not shy away from usury in transactions and do not know the methods of consoling Muslims, the Muslims were astonished, and today they ask themselves, while the prohibition of usury in the verse is explicit, and there is nothing permitting what God has forbidden. There is no escape from this except that Islamic states enact financial laws built on the principles of the Sharia regarding banks, sales, contracts of transactions composed of capital and the labour of workers, transfers of debts, their offsetting and their sale. This requires employing the views of the scholars of the Sharia and studying among them in a council that includes a group from every sect, as God the Exalted commanded.

The mention of usury and usurious sales has already been made when interpreting God's words ﴿Those who consume usury will not stand except as one stands whom Satan has driven mad by touch﴾ [al-Baqara: 275] and the five verses that follow in Surat al-Baqara.

[p. 88]
His words ﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ are a warning and an admonition against the Fire and what leads one into it, by stating that it has been readied for the disbelievers. Its preparation for the disbelievers is God's justice and His wisdom, because arranging things according to their like is one of the greatest manifestations of wisdom. Those who associated with God His creatures have deserved being deprived of His mercies, and Muslims do not accept partnership with the disbelievers, because true Islam requires hatred of what arises from disbelief. This is a clear allusion to the threat against taking usury.

Opposite to this admonition is the encouragement that comes in God's words ﴿and a Garden whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-fearing﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 133], and taqwa (God-consciousness) is the highest rank of faith.

If the discussion of the Battle of Uhud were not incomplete, since it will resume at God's words ﴿Many ways have passed before you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 137] up to His words ﴿rejoicing in a favour from God﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 171], we would say that His words ﴿O you who believe, do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled﴾ are an abrupt introduction of legislation. However, it is necessary to consider it a digression within the discussion of the Battle of Uhud, although the link between its placement in this context has not become clear. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "I do not know of any transmitted reason for this." Al-Fakhr [al-Razi] said: "Some people said: when God guided the believers to what was best for them in matters of religion and jihad, He followed that with what falls under commands and prohibitions, so He said ﴿O you who believe, do not consume usury﴾, and so it has no connection with what came before it."

Al-Qaffal said: "When the polytheists spent on their armies from wealth they had gathered through usury, it was feared that this might lead the Muslims to engage in usury." This is a far-fetched connection. Ibn 'Arafa said: "When God mentioned the threat against the disbelievers, He followed it by explaining that the threat does not apply only to them but also includes the disobedient, and He mentioned one form of disobedience, which is consuming usury." This is weaker than what came before it. In my view, from the very beginning, there is no need to insist on a consistent connection, since the period of the revelation of the surah is capable of containing events during which a Qur'an is revealed, and so it becomes part of that surah, as I explained in the eighth introduction. Thus this verse was revealed right after what came before it and was written here, and there is no connection between them, since it is appended to the discussion.

It may be asked why the prohibition of usury is repeated in this surah after what preceded it in the verses of Surat al-Baqara, which is more comprehensive than what is in this surah. The answer is that it appears this verse was revealed before the verse of Surat al-Baqara, so this one served as a preparation for that one, and the prohibition in it did not reach the full extent of what is in Surat al-Baqara. It has been narrated that the verse of al-Baqara was revealed after God had forbidden usury, and that the Thaqif tribe said: "How are we forbidden from usury when it is like trade?" The description of usury as ﴿doubled and redoubled﴾ is a prohibition of excessive usury, and it remained silent about what is less than that, which does not reach the level of doubling. Then the verse in Surat al-Baqara was revealed. It is also possible that some Muslims lent money to one another at interest after the Battle of Uhud, so the prohibition of usury was revealed during the period of the account of that battle.

The discussion of the meaning of consuming usury and the meaning of usury, and the reason for its prohibition, has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqara. His words ﴿doubled and redoubled﴾ are a circumstantial phrase describing usury. ''Adaf'' (multiples) is the plural of ''di'f'' (with a kasra on the dad), which is an equivalent in quantity when a thing and its like are mutually dependent. You do not say, "I have the di'f of your dirham," since the principal is not with you; rather, it is good to say, "I have two dirhams." You only say, "I have a dirham and its di'f," when the principal dirham is with you, and you say, "You have a dirham and its di'f if you do such-and-such."

The word ''di'f'' is applied to a single item when it is not defined with the article "al-," as in ''di'fihi'' (its double). When the plural is intended, it is expressed in the plural form, as here. When ''al-di'f'' is defined with the article, both the sense of a specific reference and the sense of the category are valid, as in God's words ﴿Those will have a recompense of double for what they did﴾ [Saba': 37], since the recompense is multiples, as it came in the hadith: "up to seven hundred times."

His words ''mudā'afa'' (redoubled) are an attribute of ''adaf'' (multiples), meaning they are multiples that undergo doubling. This is because when they lent money to someone until a term, they lent it with an increase, and whenever the debtor was unable to pay at the term or wished to delay, they added a similar increase, so the double becomes a double and increases, and so on. This fits the case in which they gather the debt doubled by a similar amount until the term, and when it is extended to a second term, they add an amount equal to all of that. Thus the multiples arise from the beginning of the loan for the first term, and their doubling occurs in the subsequent terms. It also fits the case in which they lend at usury less than the amount of the debt, and it grows with the extension of terms, until the debt becomes multiples and the multiples become multiples. If the phrase is the first case, then the circumstantial phrase serves to describe the actual situation and does not yield an implied meaning (mafhum), because the condition for deriving an implied meaning from restrictions is that the restricting phrase was not uttered merely to describe the actual situation. If it is the second case, then the circumstantial phrase is intended to denounce and to express the intention of this corrupt outcome. Since most debtors' need continues for long periods, falling into this outcome was habitual, and in that case the circumstantial phrase does not yield an implied meaning, since its purpose is not restriction but denunciation. Therefore the prohibition in this verse is not limited to usury that reaches many multiples, so that someone could say: "If usury is less than double the principal, it is not forbidden." This circumstance is not the target of the prohibition on consuming usury, so that someone would imagine that if it is less than double it is not forbidden. It appears that this is the first verse revealed on the prohibition of usury, and the verse of al-Baqara came after it, because the form of this verse suits the beginning of legislation, while the form of the verse of al-Baqara indicates that the ruling had already been established. That is why it mentioned in that verse the punishment for persisting in consuming usury, and mentioned the delusion of those who thought usury was like trading, and it was said in it: ﴿Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has passed﴾ [al-Baqara: 275], as we have mentioned just now. Thus the implied meaning of the restriction is nullified in every case.

The wisdom behind the prohibition of usury is the intention of the Sharia to lead the community to console its wealthy toward its needy one in a temporary, incidental need through a loan. It is thus a rank below charity, and it is a kind of consolation, except that consolation includes what is obligatory, like zakat, and includes what is recommended, like charity and lending. If a person volunteers for it, it becomes forbidden for him to seek a return for it, and likewise for all acts of kindness. This is because the custom that prevailed among past nations, especially the Arabs, was that a person would not borrow except out of dire necessity for his life, and therefore the community's right was to console him. Consolation appears to be a communal obligation (fard kifaya) upon those capable of it, so it is different from the case of one who comes seeking a transaction for profit, like buyers and sellers, or those who lend to one another, given the clear distinction in custom between dealing and borrowing. However, the Sharia distinguished these kinds of transactions from one another by their essential realities, not by differences in the circumstances of the contracting parties. Therefore it did not permit the owner of money to invest it by way of usury in a loan, even if the borrower was not in need, but rather was seeking abundance and enrichment by moving the money he borrowed into ways of profit and trade and the like. It did permit the owner of money to invest by way of partnership, trade and salam-contracts, even if the profit in those was greater than the amount of usury, as a distinction among the legal kinds of transactions.

It is possible that the purpose of the Sharia in prohibiting usury is to keep Muslims away from indolence in investing wealth, and to compel them to partnership and cooperation in worldly affairs. Thus the prohibition of usury, even if small, along with permitting the profit of trade and partnerships, even if large, is a realization of this purpose.

The Muslims spent long centuries during which they did not see themselves as needing to deal in usury, and their wealth at that time was not less than the wealth of the rest of the nations of the world, at times when the supremacy of the world was in their hands, or at times when they were independent in managing their affairs. But when the supremacy of the world came into the hands of non-Islamic nations, and Muslims became linked to others in trade and dealings, and the market of world wealth was organized according to the rules of laws that do not shy away from usury in transactions and do not know the methods of consoling Muslims, the Muslims were astonished, and today they ask themselves, while the prohibition of usury in the verse is explicit, and there is nothing permitting what God has forbidden. There is no escape from this except that Islamic states enact financial laws built on the principles of the Sharia regarding banks, sales, contracts of transactions composed of capital and the labour of workers, transfers of debts, their offsetting and their sale. This requires employing the views of the scholars of the Sharia and studying among them in a council that includes a group from every sect, as God the Exalted commanded.

The mention of usury and usurious sales has already been made when interpreting God's words ﴿Those who consume usury will not stand except as one stands whom Satan has driven mad by touch﴾ [al-Baqara: 275] and the five verses that follow in Surat al-Baqara.
