Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read (*sari'u*) without a conjunctive *waw*.

The clause *sari'u* ("hasten") stands in the position of an explanation (*bayan*), or of an inclusive substitute (*badal al-ishtimal*, a substitute that includes what it replaces), for the clause ﴿And obey Allah and the Messenger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 132]. This is because obedience to Allah and the Messenger is a hastening towards forgiveness and Paradise, and for this reason it is disjoined (from the preceding clause). Since the command to hasten towards forgiveness and Paradise ultimately amounts to a command to perform righteous deeds, it is permissible to join this clause to the clause commanding obedience. For this reason the rest of the ten readers read *wa-sari'u* with the conjunction. This verse also indicates that disjoining some clauses is permissible when viewed from two perspectives.

The speed from which *sari'u* is derived is used metaphorically for eagerness, competition and promptness in performing the acts of obedience that are the cause of forgiveness and Paradise. It is also possible that the speed is literal, namely the speed of going out to jihad when a call to mobilise is made, as in his words in the hadith: "And when you are called to go forth, then go forth."

[Page 89]

Hastening, under all interpretations, relates to the causes of forgiveness and the causes of entering Paradise. Therefore, attaching it to forgiveness and Paradise themselves is an instance of attaching rulings to essences, with the intention of their states, when it becomes clear that attaching it to the essence yields no benefit.

The form *mufa'alah* (*sari'u*, from *sara'a*) is used, stripped of the meaning of the act occurring from two sides, with the aim of intensifying the request for speed. The Arabs use a form that in its lexical structure denotes repetition of the act, while they intend emphasis and intensification rather than repetition. A parallel is the dual in their saying *labbayka wa-sa'daykа* ("at your service, again and again"), and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾ [al-Mulk: 4].

The indefiniteness of *maghfirah* ("forgiveness") and its connection to the phrase *min Rabbikum* ("from your Lord"), where the construct form would have been possible, saying *ila maghfirati Rabbikum*, is intended to indicate magnification. The description of Paradise as having a breadth equal to the heavens and the earth is in the manner of an eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*, a simile in which the particle of comparison is omitted), as evidenced by the explicit use of the particle of comparison in its parallel in the verse of Surah al-Hadid. In Arabic usage, *'ard* ("breadth") is used for what is opposite to length, but this is not the intended meaning here. It is also used for expansiveness, because a broad thing is, by common usage, a wide thing, unlike a long thing that is not broad, which is narrow. This is like the saying of al-'Udayl:

*And between me and the reach of al-Hajjaj's hand there lies a wide carpet woven by the hands of ewes.*

The mention of the heavens and the earth follows the Arab manner of depicting extreme vastness. The intended meaning is not the literal breadth of the heavens and the earth, so as to agree with the view of the majority of our scholars that Paradise is now created and that it is in the heaven. It has also been said that its breadth is literal, and that it is now created, but that it is greater than the heavens, and that it is above the heavens, beneath the Throne. It has been narrated: "The Throne is the ceiling of Paradise." As for those who say that Paradise has not yet been created and will be created on the Day of Resurrection, this is the view of the Mu'tazilah (a theological school) and some of Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni community), including Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti al-Andalusi al-Zahiri. According to them it is permissible that its breadth be like the breadth of the heavens and the earth, by being created in the expanse of space that the heavens and the earth once filled, or in an expanse of space greater than that. The evidences of the Book and the Sunnah are clear that Paradise is created. [This is also shown] in the lengthy hadith of a dream seen by the Prophet ﷺ, in which he said:

[Page 90]

"Jibril and Mika'il said to him: 'Raise your head.' So he raised it, and behold, above him was something like a cloud. They said: 'This is your abode.' He said: I said: 'Let me enter my abode.' They said: 'There remains for you a lifespan that you have not completed. If you had completed it, you would have come to your abode.'"

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 134:

﴿It has been prepared for the God-conscious﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133], ﴿those who spend in ease and in hardship, who restrain their anger and pardon people; and Allah loves the good-doers﴾.

He followed the description of Paradise with mention of its people, because that increases the honour of Paradise. Sensible people have always sought out good neighbourhood, as Abu Tammam said:

مَن مَبْلَغٌ أفَناءَ يَعْرُبَ كُلِّها أنِّي بَنَيْتُ الجارَ قَبْلَ المَنزِلِ

"Who will convey to all the scattered branches of Ya'rub that I built the neighbour before the dwelling?"

The clause ﴿أُعِدَّتْ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133] is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), because mention of Paradise right after mention of the Fire, which is described as "prepared for the disbelievers," stirs in the hearers' souls a desire to learn who it is that it has been prepared for. If by "the God-conscious" is meant those in whom taqwa (God-consciousness) is found in its most perfect form, then its being prepared for them means that they are its people by Allah's bounty, those who never enter the Fire at all by Allah's justice. This corresponds to His words ﴿and guard yourselves against the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 131]. And the sinful believers who did not repent have taken a share of both abodes, since their state resembles the state of the two groups, by Allah's justice and bounty. The closer one draws to either of them, the greater the share of it one takes. If by "the God-conscious" is meant those who are God-conscious in general, then the preparation for them is by way of their being destined in the end to be among its people.

He has attached to the God-conscious qualities of praise and honour. These are not the sum total of taqwa, but their gathering in one place indicates that the subject so described has perfected what makes up taqwa. These are the resisting of avarice that is obeyed and of desire that is followed.

The first quality: spending in ease and in hardship. Spending (infaq) has been mentioned more than once before; it means charity, giving wealth, weapons and equipment in the way of Allah. Al-sarra' is on the pattern fa'la'," a noun for the verbal noun of sarrahu sarran wa surura, "it gladdened him." Al-darra' is from darrahu, meaning in the two states of being characterised by joy and sorrow. The juxtaposition of the two here seems to be because ease contains a distraction from thinking about the affairs of others, and hardship contains a distraction and a lack of resentment. So constancy in spending in both of these states indicates that love of benefiting others through wealth, which is dear to the soul, has become a disposition for them, which no barrier prevents them from. This arises only from a pure soul.

The second quality: restraining anger (al-kazimin al-ghayz). Kazm al-ghayz means holding it back and concealing it so that it does not appear. It is taken from kazama al-qirbah, when one fills a waterskin and closes its mouth. Al-Mubarrad said: it is an image of holding back while full. There is no doubt that the most powerful of the faculties in its effect on the soul is the angry faculty, which craves to show the marks of anger. When one is able to hold back its manifestations while full of it, this indicates a firm resolve in the soul and the subjugation of the will to desire. This is among the greatest powers of noble character.

The third quality: pardoning people for what they have done to harm them. It completes the quality of restraining anger, as a safeguard. For restraining anger may be followed by regret, so that one seeks retribution against the one who angered him, in the name of right. When they are described as pardoning those who have harmed them, this indicates that restraining anger is a trait rooted in them and constant with them. When these qualities gather in a soul, whatever lies below them becomes easy for it.

With their totality, the perfection of ihsan (excellence in conduct) is gathered. For this reason Allah concluded their mention with His words ﴿and Allah loves the good-doers﴾, because it implies that, since they possess these qualities, they are good-doers, and Allah loves the good-doers.

Page 91

[p. 92]

If it is a conjunction to another group, then they are not the complete God-conscious (muttaqun), but rather a group of the God-conscious who mixed good deeds with other, bad ones. If it is a conjunction of attributes, then it is another elaboration on the condition of the God-conscious, by mentioning first their state of perfection and then, after it, their state of making amends for their shortcomings.

Al-fahisha (gross immorality) is the deed that exceeds the limit in corruption. For this reason it is used in plural form in His saying: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and the gross immoralities﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. Its derivation is from fahuka, meaning he spoke an ugly word, as in the saying of 'A'isha: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was neither obscene nor did he use obscene speech." Or it means he did an ugly deed, and from this comes: ﴿Say: Indeed Allah does not command immorality﴾ [al-A'raf: 28].

There is no doubt that the definite article here is the article of the genus, meaning they committed gross immoralities. The "wronging of themselves" is the major sins, and its conjunction here with the gross immoralities is like the conjunction of the gross immoralities with it in His saying: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and the gross immoralities﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. It has been said: the gross immorality is a major act of disobedience, and wronging oneself is a major sin without qualification. It has also been said: the gross immorality is a major sin that extends to others, and wronging oneself is a major sin confined to the self. And it has been said: the gross immorality is fornication, but this is an explanation by way of example.

The remembrance in His saying ﴿they remembered Allah﴾ is remembrance of the heart, which is remembrance of what is owed to Allah by His servant and what He has enjoined upon him. From it follows the seeking of forgiveness, whereas remembrance by the tongue alone does not result in that. The meaning of remembering Allah here is remembering His command, His prohibition, His promise and His threat.

Al-istighfar (seeking forgiveness) is asking for forgiveness, that is, asking for a covering over the sins, and it is a metaphor for not being held to account for the sin. For this reason it is construed with the sin by means of the lam that indicates cause, as here, and in His saying: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Ghafir: 55]. Since the request to be pardoned from being held to account for a sin proceeds only from remorse, and an intention to cease from the sin and not return to it, istighfar in the language of the Lawgiver came to mean repentance (tawbah, turning back to God in repentance). For how could one ask pardon for a sin when he is persisting in it, or resolved to return to it? And if he asked for that in such a state, he would be doing a greater wrong than the sin itself. Therefore istighfar is counted here as a level among the levels of God-consciousness. Istighfar is not merely the statement "I ask Allah's forgiveness" with the tongue while the speaker is still entangled in sins. It is reported from Rabi'a al-'Adawiyya that she said: "Our istighfar needs istighfar." But there is exaggeration in her words, for seeking forgiveness by speech is commanded in the religion, because it is a means to remembering the sin and a device for ceasing from it.

The clause ﴿And who forgives sins except Allah﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the clause "so they sought forgiveness" and the clause "and they did not persist in what they had done."

The interrogative is used in the sense of negation, as indicated by the exception that follows it. The purpose is to affirm their hastening to seek forgiveness from Allah immediately after the sin, and it is an allusion to the polytheists who took their idols as intercessors for them with Allah, and to the Christians in their claim that 'Isa (Jesus) removed the sins of the children of Adam by the tragedy of his crucifixion.

His saying "and they did not persist" completes the two pillars of repentance, because His saying ﴿so they sought forgiveness for their sins﴾ points to remorse, and His saying "and they did not persist" is an explicit statement of the negation of persistence. These are the two pillars of repentance. In a hadith: "Remorse is repentance." As for making amends for what was neglected because of the sin, that occurs only when it is possible, and there is detail when it is impossible or difficult, and how one takes the utmost of what is possible of making amends.

His saying ﴿and they did not persist in what they had done﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the nominative pronoun in "remembered," meaning: they remembered Allah in a state of not persisting. Al-israr (persistence) is remaining upon the sin, and its negation is the meaning of al-iqla' (ceasing from it). His saying "and they know" is a second circumstantial clause, and the object of "they know" is omitted because it is evident from the context, meaning: they know the evil of their deed, the greatness of the Lord's anger, the obligation of turning to Him in repentance, and that He graciously accepts repentance, erasing by it the sins that had occurred.

From His saying ﴿they remembered Allah and sought forgiveness﴾, and His saying "and they did not persist," and His saying ﴿and they know﴾, there is assembled the three pillars from which the meaning of repentance is composed, in the words of Abu Hamid al-Ghazali in the Book of Repentance from Ihya' Ulum al-Din (The Revival of the Religious Sciences), when he said: "It is knowledge, state and act."

Knowledge is the awareness of the harm of sins and that they are a veil between the servant and his Lord. When this is known with certainty, there arises from this awareness a pain in the heart due to the loss of what it loves, namely nearness to its Lord and His pleasure with it. This pain is called remorse. When this pain overcomes the heart, there is produced in the heart a state called will and intention toward an act that relates to the present, the past and the future. Its relation to the present is abandoning the sin (al-iqla'), its relation to the future is the resolve to abandon the sin in the future (negation of persistence), and its relation to the past is making amends for what has been lost.

So His saying ﴿they remembered Allah﴾ is an indication of the heart's being affected. His saying "and they did not persist" is an indication of the act, which is ceasing and negating the resolve to return. His saying "and they know" is an indication of the knowledge that stirs the soul's emotion. He has arranged these pillars in the verse according to the degree of their relation to the goal: remembrance of Allah occurs after the sin and so prompts repentance, and for this reason He arranged the seeking of forgiveness upon it with the particle fa' (so). As for knowledge that it is a sin, it is present before the act of disobedience occurs, and without it the deed would not be disobedience. Therefore it is mentioned after the remembrance and the negation of persistence, and also because a circumstantial clause does not indicate that its content follows the occurrence of the content of what precedes it in reports and attributes.

Furthermore, the pillars of persistence, which is continuing in the sin as it has been explained, its negation means ceasing out of fear of Allah the Exalted. It does not indicate that one is resolved not to return to it. But outwardly, he does not revert to a sin over whose act he has repented. And if by persistence is meant holding the belief that one will return to the sin, then its negation is sincere repentance, and this entails the occurrence of ceasing along with it, since being entangled in sin does not combine with a resolve not to return to it, for he is already entangled in it from now on.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 136:

Page 95
﴿Those—their reward is forgiveness from their Lord, and gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; and excellent is the reward of the workers.﴾.
It is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) concerning repentance, with the correctness of their deed: [consisting of] seeking forgiveness, and God's acceptance of them.

The demonstrative (ism al-ishara) was brought in to convey that those indicated have become deserving of the ruling that follows the demonstrative, because of those attributes for which they merited being pointed to.

This reward, which is forgiveness, is a promise from God Most High, a detailing from Him: in that He made abandoning sins a cause for the forgiveness of what had preceded of them. As for the gardens, they came to them solely on account of the forgiveness; had they been held to account for their past sins, they would not have deserved the gardens. So the whole matter is a bounty from Him, Most High.

His saying ﴿and excellent is the reward of the workers﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil) to the construction of praise for the reward. The object of praise is omitted, its estimated form being "He" (huwa). The conjunction "wa" is for coordination with the clause ﴿Their reward is forgiveness﴾, so it is coordination of a performative (insha') clause upon a declarative (ikhbar) clause, which is common and eloquent in speech. The reward was named "ajr" (wage) because it was in accordance with a promise to the worker for what he had done. The definiteness of "al-'amilin" is for the known (al-'ahd), i.e., "and excellent is the reward of the workers" — this reward — and this is an exaltation of it and of the deed for which it is recompense, meaning: if the categories of workers have wages, as is customary, then this is an excellent wage for a worker.

Initial resumptive statement (isti'naf ibtida'i): a preface to returning to the discussion of the Day of Uhud. What lies between them is a digression (istitrad), as you have learned above. This is the introduction to the consolation and good news that follow. This introduction opens with a historical fact: the lesson to be drawn from the circumstances of the earlier nations.

[Page 96]

The particle qad, which indicates emphasis on the statement, is used by treating them as those who deny it, because of the visible breaking of their hearts as a result of the defeat they suffered at the hands of the polytheists. Yet they were fighting to support God's religion, and they had already tasted the sweetness of victory at Badr. So God made clear to them that He has made the custom of this world such that conditions in it alternate, in turns and rotation. He reminded them of the circumstances of the earlier nations, saying: ﴿Ways (sunan) have passed before you﴾. God is able to grant them victory, but wisdom required this so that those Muslims who came after them would not be deceived and assume that victory was their ally.

The meaning of khalat is "passed away and perished," as in His saying: ﴿Messengers have passed before him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 144].

Sunan is the plural of sunnah (with a dammah on the sin). Sunnah means a course of conduct, or a disposition that consistently accompanies the performance of an action in accordance with its pattern. Labid said:

*From a group whose fathers set a way for them, and for every people there is a way and its leader.*

Khalid al-Hudhali addressed Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali, saying:

*So do not despair over a way whose originator you are; the first to be content with a way is the one who follows it.*

The lexicographers have disagreed over whether sunnah is a fixed noun not derived from a verb, or a verbal noun (masdar) of sanna. The verb sanna with the meaning of establishing a sunnah is not found in Arabic speech. In the Kashshaf, on His saying ﴿the sunnah of God concerning those who passed away before﴾ [al-Ahzab: 38] in Surat al-Ahzab, it says: "sunnata Allah" is a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun, like their saying turaban and jandalan. Perhaps what he means is that it is a fixed noun set in place of a verbal noun, just as turaban and jandalan are set in place of tabban and suhqan in the accusative of the absolute object, which is characteristic of verbal nouns, and the meaning is "dust for him and gravel for him," that is, he was pelted with dust and stoned with gravel. It appears that this is the preference of the author of the Qamus, because in the entry on sanna he mentions nothing that implies that sunnah is a verbal noun, nor does he cite it after the verb sanna, nor does he mention a verbal noun for the verb sanna. On this view, the verb sanna is derived from sunnah in the manner that verbs are derived from fixed nouns, and this is a rare kind of derivation. What is commonly current on the tongues of the exegetes and interpreters is that sunnah is a verbal noun of sanna, though they do not mention a regular verbal noun for sanna.

[Page 97]

In the Qur'an, sunnah is used very frequently in this sense: ﴿So you will not find any change in the sunnah of God﴾ [Fatir: 43]. The exegetes explained the "sunan" here as the sunan of God concerning past nations.

The meaning is: conditions of nations have passed before you, proceeding in one uniform way, which is God's habit in creation, namely that the power and arrogance of the wrongdoers over the weak is a thing that passes away, and the final outcome belongs to the God-fearing who are in the right. For this reason He said: ﴿So travel through the earth and see what was the end of those who denied﴾, that is, those who denied the messengers of their Lord. The purpose of looking at their traces is to attain certainty of what has reached you of their reports, or to inquire about the causes of their destruction, and how they were people of strength, and how they oppressed the weak, so that God uprooted them. This is so that the hearts of the believers may be reassured by witnessing with their own eyes what the one who informs about them has reported, for direct sight has a wondrous meaning. The believers had received reports of the deniers, among whom were 'Ad, Thamud, the People of the Thicket and the People of the Rass. All of them were in the lands of the Arabs, who could witness their traces, and many of them had seen these in their journeys.

The verse indicates the importance of the science of history, because in it lies the benefit of travelling through the earth, which is knowing the reports of the ancients and the causes of the righteousness and corruption of nations. Ibn 'Arafa said: travelling through the earth is both physical and conceptual. The conceptual kind is looking into books of history, such that the one who looks acquires knowledge of the conditions of nations and what approaches knowledge. Sometimes through this one gains knowledge that cannot be gained by physically travelling through the earth, because of human weakness and limitation.

God commanded travel through the earth rather than only reading books because among the addressees there were those who were unlettered, and because direct observation benefits the one who has not read by giving knowledge, and benefits the one who has read history or had it recounted to him by giving him a confirmed understanding.

This is an explanation for mankind, and a guidance and an admonition for those who are mindful of God.

A concluding statement (tadhyil) that encompasses the addressees present and those who come after them of the generations. The reference of "this" (al-isharah) is either to what preceded, taking the referent as "the mentioned matter" (ta'wil al-madhkur), or to something present in the mind at the time of reciting the verse, which is the Qur'an.

Al-bayan (clarification): making things clear and uncovering the realities that have occurred. Al-huda (guidance): direction toward what is good for people in the present and the future. Al-maw'izah (admonition): warning and causing fear.

If you take the reference to be the content of His words, ﴿Indeed, there have passed before you precedents (sunan)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 137] and what follows, then it is a clarification of what they overlooked: that there is no necessary connection between victory and a good outcome, nor between defeat and a bad outcome. It is guidance for them, so that they may derive effects from their causes, for the true cause of success is righteousness and uprightness. It is also an admonition for them, so that they beware of corruption and do not become deluded as 'Ad became deluded when they said, ﴿Who is stronger than us in power?﴾ [Fussilat: 15].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 139:

﴿So do not weaken, nor grieve, for you will be the superior ones if you are believers.﴾ His saying, ﴿Do not weaken, nor grieve﴾, is a prohibition addressed to the Muslims against the causes of failure (al-fashal). The word *al-wahn* (وهن) means weakness. Its original sense is weakness of the self, as in the body in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened (wahana) within me﴾ [Maryam: 4], and the rope in the verse of Zuhayr:

*So the rope became weak (wahiran) from them, worn out.*

Here it is used figuratively (majaz) for the slackening of resolve, the weakening of will, the turning of hope into despair, of courage into cowardice, and of certainty into doubt; for this reason they were forbidden from it. As for *al-huzn* (حزن), it is intense regret that reaches the point of dejection and brokenness. *Al-wahn* and *al-huzn* are two states of the soul that arise from the belief in failure and calamity, and from them follows submission and abandoning resistance. Therefore, the prohibition against weakness and grief is in reality a prohibition against their cause, which is the belief itself, just as one is forbidden from forgetting, or as one says, in a phrase like "I shall not see so-and-so in such-and-such a place," meaning "do not leave him to settle there." For this reason, He placed before this prohibition His saying, ﴿Indeed, ways (sunan) have passed before you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 137], and so on. He followed it with His saying, ﴿and you are the superior ones if you are believers﴾.

As for His saying, ﴿and you are the superior ones if you are believers﴾, the *waw* is for coordination (al-'atf), and this is good news to them of future victory. The "superiority" (al-'uluww) here is figurative, meaning superiority of rank.

Page 99

The conditional phrasing in His saying, ﴿if you are believers﴾, is intended to stir their zeal for faith, since God already knows that they are believers. However, when weakness and grief appeared upon them because of the defeat, they were in the position of one whose certainty has weakened, so it was said to them: "if you recognize faith in yourselves." The conditional particle *in* (إنْ), whose nature is that its condition is not realized, was used to complete this purpose.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 140–141 (part 1 of 2):

﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the people; and these days We alternate among the people.﴾

It is a consolation for what befell the Muslims on the Day of Uhud of defeat, that this is not strange in war, since no army is spared from being defeated in some of the positions of war, and it has already preceded that the enemy was victorious. The word "mass" (al-massu) here means "to afflict," as in His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Hardship and adversity touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. The word "qarh" (wound), with a fatha on the qaf, is the dialect of the Quraysh and means a wound; with a damma it is the dialect of others. The majority [of reciters] read it with a fatha on the qaf, while Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr (on the authority of 'Asim), and Khalaf read it with a damma on the qaf. Here it is used in other than its literal sense; rather, it is a metaphor for the defeat that befell them, since defeat is likened to a breach and a breaking, so it is likened here to a wound when it strikes the body. It cannot be meant literally, because the wounds that afflict an army are not regarded when victory accompanies them. There is no doubt that the consolation concerns the defeat that befell them.

"The people" (al-qawm) are the polytheists of Makkah and those with them.

The meaning is: if you were defeated on the Day of Uhud, then the polytheists were defeated on the Day of Badr, and you were even (kafaffan). For this reason He followed it with His saying ﴿and these days We alternate among the people﴾. The expression of what afflicted the Muslims in the present tense, "yamsaskum," is because it is close to the time of the present; and the expression of what afflicted the polytheists in the past tense is because it is distant, since it occurred on the Day of Badr.

His saying ﴿for a similar wound has touched the people﴾ is not, in meaning, the answer of the conditional; rather, it is an indication of it, which dispenses with it by way of brevity. The meaning is: if a wound touches you, then do not grieve, or do not weaken (wa-la tahinu), and here is doubt about God's promise to support His religion, since a similar wound has touched the people, ﴿so you were not defeated, but you were even, and that, relative to the scarcity of the believers, is a manifest victory.﴾ This comparison with what afflicted the enemy on the Day of Badr makes it necessary that the speech be a consolation, not an announcement of punishment, as a group of exegetes has said. Heraclius asked Abu Sufyan, and Heraclius said: "Thus are the messengers tried, and the final outcome is theirs."

His saying ﴿and these days We alternate among the people﴾: the waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), and the reference by "tilka" (those) is to what will be mentioned after it, so the reference here serves the position of the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n) for the purpose of emphasizing the report. This report is figuratively used as a rationale for the omitted answer, indicated by the clause ﴿for a similar wound has touched the people﴾.

"Al-ayyam" (the days) may be the plural of "yawm" meaning the day of the battle, as in their saying: "the Day of Badr," "the Day of Bu'ath," "the Day of al-Sha'thamayn," and from it "the days of the Arabs." It may also be used for time, as in the saying of Tarafah:

"The days diminish not, and time is exhausted."

That is, the eras.

"Al-mudawalah" (alternation) — its conjugation is unusual, since it is the verbal noun of "dawala," when a person makes a thing a dynasty (dawlah) for one and a dynasty for another, i.e., each of them obliges it until it becomes known through it. From it comes "dala yadulu dawlan," meaning it became famous, because constancy entails fame with a thing. So "tadawul" is originally a reciprocal form from "dala," and this occurs in things and in speech; it is said: "a circulated speech" (kalam mudawal). Then they used "dawaltu al-shay'" figuratively, when you make others circulate it. The indicator of this usage is your saying: "among them." The agent in this usage has no share in the act, but has a share in the causing. Close to it is their saying: "idtarartuhu ila kadha," i.e., I made him compelled to such-and-such, although the origin of "idtarra" is that it is the reflexive of "darrahu."

"Al-nas" (the people) means all of mankind, because this is among the cosmic customs (sunan kawniyyah), so it is not restricted to the people being spoken of.

* * *

﴿And that God may know those who believe, and take martyrs from among you — and God does not love the wrongdoers. And that God may purify those who believe, and destroy the disbelievers.﴾

It is a conjunction upon the clause ﴿and these days We alternate among the people﴾, so the content of this is a second reason for the omitted answer of the conditional, indicated by His saying ﴿for a similar wound has touched the people﴾. God's knowledge that they are believers is established before the wound touched them.

If by "those who believe" is meant here the meaning of "those who believe" with firm and complete faith, then the meaning becomes: God's knowledge of the firmness of their faith comes about after the wound touches them, and this is a meaning that is not correct. Therefore the exegetes differed about what is meant by this rationale, according to the divergence of their schools regarding the attribute of knowledge. It has been established in the principles of religion that the philosophers said: God knows universals entirely, i.e., the realities of things as they are, with a knowledge like the knowledge discussed in philosophy, since that knowledge is an attribute of perfection; and that He knows particulars of substances and accidents with a knowledge in a universal manner. The meaning of that is that He knows them insofar as they are not related to a time. An example: that He knows that the moon is a body that exists at the time of its creation, and that its attribute will be such and such, and that its luminous accidents acquired from the sun, and its eclipse, and its course over such and such a period. As for its occurrence in its time when its creation takes place, and similarly the occurrence of its accidents, these are not known to God, the Exalted. They said: because if God knew particulars at the time of their occurrence in their times, His knowledge would necessarily change, and that would entail the change of the Eternal, or the ignorance of the Knower. An example: if He knows eternally that the moon will eclipse at such and such an hour, then when it eclipses in fact, either that knowledge ceases, so the prior knowledge changes, and from this follows the change of the essence described by it from one attribute to another, and this entails origination, since the origination of an attribute entails the origination of the thing described; or that the first knowledge does not cease, and then the knowledge becomes ignorance, because God knew only that the moon would eclipse in the future, while the moon has now actually eclipsed. For this reason they said: God's knowledge is not temporal. The Muslims all said: God knows universals and particulars before their occurrence and at their occurrence. They answered the doubt of the philosophers by saying that knowledge is an attribute of the category of relation (idafah), i.e., a relation between the knower and the known, and relations are considered (i'tibariyyat), and considerations are non-existent (adamiyyat); or it is of the category of an attribute with relation, i.e., an existential attribute that has a connection, i.e., a relation between it and its known object. If knowledge is a relation, then its change does not entail the change of its subject, who is the knower. They illustrated this with the Eternal, who is described as being before the originated thing, with it, and after it, without any change in the essence of the Eternal. If knowledge is an attribute with a relation, i.e., with a connection, then change affects its connection, and the attribute does not change, let alone the subject. So God's knowledge that the moon will eclipse, and His knowledge that it is now eclipsing, and His knowledge that it was eclipsing yesterday, is one knowledge whose subject does not change, even though the attribute changes or its object changes in both respects. However, the early scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah and the Mu'tazilah refused to explicitly affirm a change in the connection, and for this reason there is no mention in their speech of two connections of divine knowledge, one eternal and the other originated, as they mentioned that regarding will and power, considering that the attribute of knowledge does not go beyond the essence of the knower in a perceptible way. For this reason their predecessors said: God knows from eternity that the moon will eclipse in this year of ours, in such and such a land, at such and such an hour; so when the moon eclipses, God likewise knows that it has eclipsed by that first knowledge, because that knowledge is composed of the act not having occurred in eternity, and of its occurring at its time in what continues to be. They said: this is not analogized to our knowledge when we know that the moon will eclipse according to calculation, and then when it eclipses we know that its eclipse has been realized by a new knowledge, because our need for a renewed knowledge arises only from the occurrence of heedlessness regarding the first.

Some of the Mu'tazilah, such as Jahm ibn Safwan and Hisham ibn al-Hakam, said: God is eternally knowing of universals and realities, but His knowledge of particulars, individuals, and states is acquired after their origination, because this knowledge belongs to the category of judgments (tasdiqat), and it entails the absence of prior knowledge.

Abu al-Husayn al-Basri of the Mu'tazilah, refuting the early scholars, said: it is not permissible that God's knowledge that the moon will eclipse be the very same knowledge as His knowledge after that that it has eclipsed, for three reasons. The first: the difference between them in reality, since the reality of its being going to occur is other than the reality of its having occurred; so knowledge of one of them differs from knowledge of the other, because the difference of the two objects requires the difference of the knower regarding them. The second: the difference between them in the condition, since the condition of knowing that a thing will occur is its non-occurrence, and the condition of knowing that it has occurred is its occurrence; so if the two knowledges were one thing, their conditions would not differ. The third: it is possible to know that it has occurred while being ignorant that it will occur, and vice versa, and what is not known is other than what is known (Abu al-Husayn expressed it thus, i.e., the unknown matter is different from the known matter). For this reason Abu al-Husayn affirmed the necessity of change occurring in God's knowledge of changing things, and that His essence necessitates His being characterized as knowing the known things that will occur, on condition of their occurrence, so knowledge arises that they have come into existence when they exist, and ceases when they cease, and another knowledge is attained. This is precisely the doctrine of Jahm and Hisham. It was refuted on the ground that it would follow that God, the Exalted, is not knowing in eternity of the states of events, and this is attributing ignorance to Him. 'Abd al-Hakim answered this in the margin of al-Mawaqif, saying that Abu al-Husayn held that God knows in eternity that the originated thing will occur in such and such a description, so there is no ignorance in it; and that His not witnessing events before their origination is not ignorance, since they are non-existent in reality; rather, if He knew them witnessingly at the time of their non-existence, that knowledge would be the ignorance, because witnessing the non-existent contradicts reality. So the changing, originated knowledge is the witnessing knowledge.

The conclusion is that there are two knowledges: one eternal, which is the knowledge conditioned by the conditions, and the other originated, which is the knowledge attained when the conditions are met. The unrestricted affirmation of an originated connection to God's knowledge of events is not from our scholars or the scholars of the Mu'tazilah. Shaykh 'Abd al-Hakim mentioned this in the Khaqaniyyah Treatise, which he composed to verify the knowledge of God, the Exalted, without attributing it to any speaker; rather, he expressed it with "it is said" (qila). I have seen that al-Taftazani followed this in the margin of al-Kashshaf on this verse, so perhaps Shaykh al-Hakim forgot to attribute it.

The interpretation of the verse according to the differing schools: as for those who refused to apply the notion of origination to the connection of knowledge, they said regarding His saying ﴿and that God may know those who believe﴾: He applied "knowledge" to its concomitant, which is the establishment of the known object, i.e., its distinction, by way of metonymy (kinayah), since it is like establishing a thing by proof.

This is like the saying of Iyas ibn Qabisah al-Ta'i:

"I came forward while the spear swayed between us, that I might know which of them is the coward and which the brave."

That is, that the coward and the brave might become manifest; so the "knowing" was applied and what is necessitated by it was intended.

Some of them made His saying ﴿so that God may know﴾ a figurative expression (tamthil), meaning that the act is like the act of one who wants to know. Al-Zamakhshari inclined to this in al-Kashshaf. Others said: the cause is the connection of God's knowledge to the event that occurs, and this connection is itself something new. That is, "so that God may know those who believed" as existent. This was said by al-Baydawi and al-Taftazani in his gloss on al-Kashshaf. If what is meant by His saying "those who believed" is its apparent sense, that is, "so that He may know whoever has the attribute of belief," then interpretation (ta'wil) is required in this verse. This is not because of the necessity that God's knowledge become new, but because God's knowledge of the believers among the people of Uhud was already present before the wound touched them. Al-Zajjaj said: he meant the knowledge on which the reward is based, which is their steadfastness in belief and their not wavering in the time of hardship. Al-Taftazani pointed out that the interpretation of the author of al-Kashshaf, that this comes in the mode of figurative expression, looks at the fact that knowledge of the believers was already present beforehand, not to avoid the necessity of new knowledge.

His saying ﴿and take martyrs from among you﴾ is joined to the preceding cause. The killing on that day, which is the reason for taking the slain as martyrs, is made a cause among the causes of the defeat, because the great number of the slain is what brought about the defeat.

The martyrs (shuhada') are those who were killed on the day of Uhud. He expressed the decree of martyrdom by "taking" because martyrdom is a virtue from God and an approach to His pleasure. For this reason it is contrasted with His saying ﴿and God does not love the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the disbelievers. So it is on the side of the disbelievers. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 140–141 (part 1 of 2):

﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the people; and these days We alternate among the people.﴾

It is a consolation for what befell the Muslims on the Day of Uhud of defeat, that this is not strange in war, since no army is spared from being defeated in some of the positions of war, and it has already preceded that the enemy was victorious. The word "mass" (al-massu) here means "to afflict," as in His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Hardship and adversity touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. The word "qarh" (wound), with a fatha on the qaf, is the dialect of the Quraysh and means a wound; with a damma it is the dialect of others. The majority [of reciters] read it with a fatha on the qaf, while Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr (on the authority of 'Asim), and Khalaf read it with a damma on the qaf. Here it is used in other than its literal sense; rather, it is a metaphor for the defeat that befell them, since defeat is likened to a breach and a breaking, so it is likened here to a wound when it strikes the body. It cannot be meant literally, because the wounds that afflict an army are not regarded when victory accompanies them. There is no doubt that the consolation concerns the defeat that befell them.

"The people" (al-qawm) are the polytheists of Makkah and those with them.

The meaning is: if you were defeated on the Day of Uhud, then the polytheists were defeated on the Day of Badr, and you were even (kafaffan). For this reason He followed it with His saying ﴿and these days We alternate among the people﴾. The expression of what afflicted the Muslims in the present tense, "yamsaskum," is because it is close to the time of the present; and the expression of what afflicted the polytheists in the past tense is because it is distant, since it occurred on the Day of Badr.

His saying ﴿for a similar wound has touched the people﴾ is not, in meaning, the answer of the conditional; rather, it is an indication of it, which dispenses with it by way of brevity. The meaning is: if a wound touches you, then do not grieve, or do not weaken (wa-la tahinu), and here is doubt about God's promise to support His religion, since a similar wound has touched the people, ﴿so you were not defeated, but you were even, and that, relative to the scarcity of the believers, is a manifest victory.﴾ This comparison with what afflicted the enemy on the Day of Badr makes it necessary that the speech be a consolation, not an announcement of punishment, as a group of exegetes has said. Heraclius asked Abu Sufyan, and Heraclius said: "Thus are the messengers tried, and the final outcome is theirs."

His saying ﴿and these days We alternate among the people﴾: the waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), and the reference by "tilka" (those) is to what will be mentioned after it, so the reference here serves the position of the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n) for the purpose of emphasizing the report. This report is figuratively used as a rationale for the omitted answer, indicated by the clause ﴿for a similar wound has touched the people﴾.

"Al-ayyam" (the days) may be the plural of "yawm" meaning the day of the battle, as in their saying: "the Day of Badr," "the Day of Bu'ath," "the Day of al-Sha'thamayn," and from it "the days of the Arabs." It may also be used for time, as in the saying of Tarafah:

"The days diminish not, and time is exhausted."

That is, the eras.

"Al-mudawalah" (alternation) — its conjugation is unusual, since it is the verbal noun of "dawala," when a person makes a thing a dynasty (dawlah) for one and a dynasty for another, i.e., each of them obliges it until it becomes known through it. From it comes "dala yadulu dawlan," meaning it became famous, because constancy entails fame with a thing. So "tadawul" is originally a reciprocal form from "dala," and this occurs in things and in speech; it is said: "a circulated speech" (kalam mudawal). Then they used "dawaltu al-shay'" figuratively, when you make others circulate it. The indicator of this usage is your saying: "among them." The agent in this usage has no share in the act, but has a share in the causing. Close to it is their saying: "idtarartuhu ila kadha," i.e., I made him compelled to such-and-such, although the origin of "idtarra" is that it is the reflexive of "darrahu."

"Al-nas" (the people) means all of mankind, because this is among the cosmic customs (sunan kawniyyah), so it is not restricted to the people being spoken of.

* * *

﴿And that God may know those who believe, and take martyrs from among you — and God does not love the wrongdoers. And that God may purify those who believe, and destroy the disbelievers.﴾

It is a conjunction upon the clause ﴿and these days We alternate among the people﴾, so the content of this is a second reason for the omitted answer of the conditional, indicated by His saying ﴿for a similar wound has touched the people﴾. God's knowledge that they are believers is established before the wound touched them.

If by "those who believe" is meant here the meaning of "those who believe" with firm and complete faith, then the meaning becomes: God's knowledge of the firmness of their faith comes about after the wound touches them, and this is a meaning that is not correct. Therefore the exegetes differed about what is meant by this rationale, according to the divergence of their schools regarding the attribute of knowledge. It has been established in the principles of religion that the philosophers said: God knows universals entirely, i.e., the realities of things as they are, with a knowledge like the knowledge discussed in philosophy, since that knowledge is an attribute of perfection; and that He knows particulars of substances and accidents with a knowledge in a universal manner. The meaning of that is that He knows them insofar as they are not related to a time. An example: that He knows that the moon is a body that exists at the time of its creation, and that its attribute will be such and such, and that its luminous accidents acquired from the sun, and its eclipse, and its course over such and such a period. As for its occurrence in its time when its creation takes place, and similarly the occurrence of its accidents, these are not known to God, the Exalted. They said: because if God knew particulars at the time of their occurrence in their times, His knowledge would necessarily change, and that would entail the change of the Eternal, or the ignorance of the Knower. An example: if He knows eternally that the moon will eclipse at such and such an hour, then when it eclipses in fact, either that knowledge ceases, so the prior knowledge changes, and from this follows the change of the essence described by it from one attribute to another, and this entails origination, since the origination of an attribute entails the origination of the thing described; or that the first knowledge does not cease, and then the knowledge becomes ignorance, because God knew only that the moon would eclipse in the future, while the moon has now actually eclipsed. For this reason they said: God's knowledge is not temporal. The Muslims all said: God knows universals and particulars before their occurrence and at their occurrence. They answered the doubt of the philosophers by saying that knowledge is an attribute of the category of relation (idafah), i.e., a relation between the knower and the known, and relations are considered (i'tibariyyat), and considerations are non-existent (adamiyyat); or it is of the category of an attribute with relation, i.e., an existential attribute that has a connection, i.e., a relation between it and its known object. If knowledge is a relation, then its change does not entail the change of its subject, who is the knower. They illustrated this with the Eternal, who is described as being before the originated thing, with it, and after it, without any change in the essence of the Eternal. If knowledge is an attribute with a relation, i.e., with a connection, then change affects its connection, and the attribute does not change, let alone the subject. So God's knowledge that the moon will eclipse, and His knowledge that it is now eclipsing, and His knowledge that it was eclipsing yesterday, is one knowledge whose subject does not change, even though the attribute changes or its object changes in both respects. However, the early scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah and the Mu'tazilah refused to explicitly affirm a change in the connection, and for this reason there is no mention in their speech of two connections of divine knowledge, one eternal and the other originated, as they mentioned that regarding will and power, considering that the attribute of knowledge does not go beyond the essence of the knower in a perceptible way. For this reason their predecessors said: God knows from eternity that the moon will eclipse in this year of ours, in such and such a land, at such and such an hour; so when the moon eclipses, God likewise knows that it has eclipsed by that first knowledge, because that knowledge is composed of the act not having occurred in eternity, and of its occurring at its time in what continues to be. They said: this is not analogized to our knowledge when we know that the moon will eclipse according to calculation, and then when it eclipses we know that its eclipse has been realized by a new knowledge, because our need for a renewed knowledge arises only from the occurrence of heedlessness regarding the first.

Some of the Mu'tazilah, such as Jahm ibn Safwan and Hisham ibn al-Hakam, said: God is eternally knowing of universals and realities, but His knowledge of particulars, individuals, and states is acquired after their origination, because this knowledge belongs to the category of judgments (tasdiqat), and it entails the absence of prior knowledge.

Abu al-Husayn al-Basri of the Mu'tazilah, refuting the early scholars, said: it is not permissible that God's knowledge that the moon will eclipse be the very same knowledge as His knowledge after that that it has eclipsed, for three reasons. The first: the difference between them in reality, since the reality of its being going to occur is other than the reality of its having occurred; so knowledge of one of them differs from knowledge of the other, because the difference of the two objects requires the difference of the knower regarding them. The second: the difference between them in the condition, since the condition of knowing that a thing will occur is its non-occurrence, and the condition of knowing that it has occurred is its occurrence; so if the two knowledges were one thing, their conditions would not differ. The third: it is possible to know that it has occurred while being ignorant that it will occur, and vice versa, and what is not known is other than what is known (Abu al-Husayn expressed it thus, i.e., the unknown matter is different from the known matter). For this reason Abu al-Husayn affirmed the necessity of change occurring in God's knowledge of changing things, and that His essence necessitates His being characterized as knowing the known things that will occur, on condition of their occurrence, so knowledge arises that they have come into existence when they exist, and ceases when they cease, and another knowledge is attained. This is precisely the doctrine of Jahm and Hisham. It was refuted on the ground that it would follow that God, the Exalted, is not knowing in eternity of the states of events, and this is attributing ignorance to Him. 'Abd al-Hakim answered this in the margin of al-Mawaqif, saying that Abu al-Husayn held that God knows in eternity that the originated thing will occur in such and such a description, so there is no ignorance in it; and that His not witnessing events before their origination is not ignorance, since they are non-existent in reality; rather, if He knew them witnessingly at the time of their non-existence, that knowledge would be the ignorance, because witnessing the non-existent contradicts reality. So the changing, originated knowledge is the witnessing knowledge.

The conclusion is that there are two knowledges: one eternal, which is the knowledge conditioned by the conditions, and the other originated, which is the knowledge attained when the conditions are met. The unrestricted affirmation of an originated connection to God's knowledge of events is not from our scholars or the scholars of the Mu'tazilah. Shaykh 'Abd al-Hakim mentioned this in the Khaqaniyyah Treatise, which he composed to verify the knowledge of God, the Exalted, without attributing it to any speaker; rather, he expressed it with "it is said" (qila). I have seen that al-Taftazani followed this in the margin of al-Kashshaf on this verse, so perhaps Shaykh al-Hakim forgot to attribute it.

The interpretation of the verse according to the differing schools: as for those who refused to apply the notion of origination to the connection of knowledge, they said regarding His saying ﴿and that God may know those who believe﴾: He applied "knowledge" to its concomitant, which is the establishment of the known object, i.e., its distinction, by way of metonymy (kinayah), since it is like establishing a thing by proof.

This is like the saying of Iyas ibn Qabisah al-Ta'i:

"I came forward while the spear swayed between us, that I might know which of them is the coward and which the brave."

That is, that the coward and the brave might become manifest; so the "knowing" was applied and what is necessitated by it was intended.

Some of them made His saying ﴿so that God may know﴾ a figurative expression (tamthil), meaning that the act is like the act of one who wants to know. Al-Zamakhshari inclined to this in al-Kashshaf. Others said: the cause is the connection of God's knowledge to the event that occurs, and this connection is itself something new. That is, "so that God may know those who believed" as existent. This was said by al-Baydawi and al-Taftazani in his gloss on al-Kashshaf. If what is meant by His saying "those who believed" is its apparent sense, that is, "so that He may know whoever has the attribute of belief," then interpretation (ta'wil) is required in this verse. This is not because of the necessity that God's knowledge become new, but because God's knowledge of the believers among the people of Uhud was already present before the wound touched them. For this reason it is contrasted with His saying ﴿and God does not love the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the disbelievers. So it is on the side of the disbelievers. That is: your slain are in Paradise, and their slain are in the Fire. This is like His saying ﴿Say: Do you await for us except one of the two best outcomes?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 52].

It is a virtue on the side of the believers and a calamity on the side of the disbelievers. "The coward's love of life led him to piety,
and the brave man's love of life led him to war.
The two intentions differ though the act is one,
until we see this man's kindness as a sin to us."
