As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124]. ﴿As for those in whose hearts is disease, it has added defilement to their defilement﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125]. And He said: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it increases the wrongdoers only in loss﴾ [al-Isra': 82]. This is from the wondrous decree of God, exalted is He.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 142:

﴿Or did you suppose that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet made evident those of you who strove, and made evident the patient?﴾

Here *am* (أم) is *munqati'ah* (disjunctive, introducing a new topic), with the meaning of *bal* (بل, "rather") of transition, because this speech moves from one theme to another. When *am* is used as disjunctive, it indicates that what follows it is a question, due to its constant association with the interrogative. Al-Zamakhshari and the verifiers said: it never separates from indicating the interrogative after it. Others said: that is the usual case, but it may separate from it, and they cited as evidence for its separation from the interrogative examples that admit of interpretation.

So His saying ﴿Or did you suppose...﴾ is a conjunction with the sentence ﴿and do not be weak﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139]. When the harm of the wound touched them, they grieved, and weakness overcame them, since they did not witness the same victory they had witnessed on the day of Badr. Allah clarified that there is no reason for weakness, given the causes already mentioned. Then He clarified to them here that entering Paradise, which is what they desire, is not attained unless they give up their souls in supporting the religion. So if they supposed that entering Paradise is attained without that, they were mistaken.

[p. 106]

The interrogative implied after *am* is used for rebuke and prohibition. For this reason *am* came to indicate rebuke: that is, do not suppose that you will enter Paradise without striving and enduring the consequences of striving.

Some exegetes assumed for *am* here a deleted counterpart (*mu'adil*) and made it conjunctive. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) transmitted from Abu Muslim al-Isfahani that he said: the custom of the Arabs is to use this kind of interrogative for emphasis, because when He said ﴿and do not be weak, and do not grieve﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139], it was as if He said: "Do you know that this is as you are commanded, or do you suppose that you will enter Paradise?"

The clause ﴿while Allah has not yet made evident...﴾ and so on is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and it is the target of the denial. That is: do not suppose that you will enter Paradise at a time when Allah has not made evident those who strove.

*Lamma* (لما) is a negative particle, a sister of *lam* (لم), except that it is more emphatic in negation than *lam*. This is because *lam* negates the statement of the speaker "so-and-so did," while *lamma* negates his statement "so-and-so has done"; this was said by Sibawayh, just as he said that *la* (لا) negates *yaf'alu* (he does), *lan* (لن) negates *sa-yaf'alu* (he will do), *ma* (ما) negates *laqad fa'ala* (he has indeed done), and *la* (لا) negates *huwa yaf'alu* (he is doing). So *lamma* indicates that the negation continues with it up to the time of speaking, unlike *lam*. From this indication another indication is derived: it signals that what is negated by it is expected to become established in the future, because it stands in place of your saying: "the negation has continued until now." Al-Zamakhshari went this way here, saying: *lamma* has the meaning of *lam*, except that there is in it a kind of expectation. He said, regarding His saying ﴿and faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14] in Surat al-Hujurat: in it is an indication that the Bedouins believed afterward.

The discussion of Allah's knowledge has preceded just before this verse.

By the state of the negation of Allah's knowledge of those who strove and those who are patient is meant a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the state of the negation of striving and patience in them. Because when Allah knows something, that known thing is certain to occur. Just as He used knowledge of Allah as a metonymy for certainty in His saying ﴿and that Allah might make evident those who believed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140], so He used the negation of knowledge as a metonymy for the negation of occurrence. The condition of the metonymy is fulfilled here, namely the permissibility of intending the implied meaning together with the literal meaning, since it is permissible to intend the negation of Allah's knowledge of their striving together with intending the negation of their striving.

[p. 107]

It is not affected by what al-Taftazani raised, which he answered by saying that the metonymy in negation is built upon the metonymy in affirmation. That is a forced argument, since the nature of constructions is that their meaning and implications are independent.

He followed this negation with His saying ﴿and make evident the patient﴾, conjoined with the particle of accompaniment *wa* (واو المعية), so it has the sense of the object of accompaniment (*maf'ul ma'ahu*), to arrange the conditions together, one with another. The meaning becomes: "Do you suppose that you will enter Paradise while Allah has not known your striving, together with not knowing your patience?" That is: "Did you suppose that you would enter Paradise while the two knowledges have not been gathered?"

Striving requires patience, because patience is the cause of success in striving and the attractor of victory. Ali was asked about courage, and he said: "An hour of patience." Zufar ibn al-Harith al-Kilabi, excusing the victory of their enemies over them, said:

*We gave them a cup, and they gave us its like, but they were more patient in facing death.*

The weakness of the archers' patience and their haste toward booty caused the defeat of the Muslims on the day of Uhud. In striving, the patience of the one overcome against the one who overcomes is required, so that he does not weaken and does not surrender.

﴿Wa-laqad kuntum tamannawna al-mawta min qabli an talqawhu faqad ra'aytumuhu wa-antum tanzurun﴾

This is a speech addressed to them in an extremely concise, summary form, so that it combines admonition (al-mau'iza), excuse (al-ma'dhira), and blame (al-malam). The waw is either conjunctive ('atifa) or circumstantial (haliyya).

The address is, without doubt, to the living, those who had not tasted death and had not attained martyrdom, and those whose portion on that day was defeat. His saying ﴿kuntum tamannawna al-mawt﴾ (you used to wish for death) refers to their wish to meet the enemy on the day of Uhud, and their unwillingness to remain fortified in Madina and take a defensive position, as the Messenger (ﷺ) had indicated. Yet they showed courage and love of encounter, even though it meant death, in view of the enemy's strength and numbers.

[p. 108]

So the wishing (al-tamanni) is the wish for encounter and for supporting the religion with their utmost effort. Since that requires each of them to be indifferent to the destruction of his own soul in the defence, in the hope that before his destruction he would have inflicted damage on the enemy and prepared victory for those who remained after him, [the text] makes their wish for encounter as if it were a wish for death from the outset, treating the end of the wish as if it were its beginning.

His saying ﴿min qabli an talqawhu﴾ (before you met it) is an allusion (ta'rid) that they wished for a matter while overlooking its severity for them; their wishing for it is like wishing for something whose calamities they did not know.

His saying ﴿faqad ra'aytumuhu﴾ means: you saw death. Seeing it means witnessing its certain causes, and seeing these is like witnessing death itself. So ﴿faqad ra'aytumuhu﴾ may be a figure of speech (tamthil). It may also be that "seeing" is used for intense anticipation, as "smelling" is used for this in the words of al-Harith ibn Hisham al-Makhzumi:

"I smelled the scent of death from their direction in a narrow pass, while the horses had not yet scattered."

And as it is used in the words of Ibn Ma'di Karib on the day of al-Qadisiyya: "He embraced me with an embrace from which I found the scent of death."

The fa' in ﴿faqad ra'aytumuhu﴾ is the fa' of elucidation (fa' al-fasiha) for his saying "you used to wish," and the implied meaning is: "and you were granted what you wished for, so you have seen it." The sense is: where then is the trial (bala') of one who wishes for death? This is like the saying of 'Abbas ibn al-Ahnaf:

"They said: Khurasan is the furthest that is aimed at us; then the return. Indeed we came to Khurasan."

From the same usage is His saying ﴿faqad kadhdhabukum bima taqulun﴾ [al-Furqan: 19], and His saying in Surat al-Rum ﴿fa-hadha yawm al-ba'th﴾ [al-Rum: 56].

The clause ﴿wa-antum tanzurun﴾ (while you were looking) is either an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida) for the meaning of ﴿ra'aytumuhu﴾, or it is a consequence (tafri'): you saw death, and your share of it was looking, without the striving that is needed at the time of danger; so you were stupefied.

The admonitory aspect of the verse is that a person should not seek a matter until he considers its consequences and tests how much he can bear its calamities. The excusing aspect is in His saying ﴿min qabli an talqawhu﴾ and His saying ﴿faqad ra'aytumuhu﴾, and the blaming aspect is in His saying ﴿wa-antum tanzurun﴾.

It is also possible that His saying ﴿tamannawna al-mawt﴾ means: you wish for the death of martyrdom in the way of God. Then ﴿faqad ra'aytum musharafat al-mawt iyyakum﴾ (you have seen death approaching you), ﴿wa-antum tanzurun man mata min ikhwanikum﴾ (while you were looking at those of your brothers who died), meaning: how did you find yourselves when you saw death? It is as if this is an allusion (ta'rid) that they are not at the station of one who wishes for martyrdom, since they became cowardly at the time of need and hastened toward the spoils. On this reading the speech is pure blame, and wishing for martyrdom is not blameworthy in itself; rather the blame is for wishing for what one cannot bear, as it is said:

"If you are unable to do something, leave it."

How could it be otherwise, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I would love to be killed in the way of God, then be brought to life, then be killed, then be brought to life, then be killed." And 'Umar said: "O God, I ask You for martyrdom in Your way." And Ibn Rawaha said:

"But I ask the Most Merciful for forgiveness, and a blow with a wide wound that throws out foam,

so that when they pass by my grave they will say: May God guide you, O one who went out to fight, for you have been guided."

On this possibility, the pronoun refers to death in the sense of its causes, treating the sight of its causes as the sight of death itself. This is like the figure of speech (al-istikhdam), but in my view it is closer than istikhdam, because it returns to the causes of death in consideration of treating them as death.

[Page 110]

The rebuke (inkar) is joined to the earlier reproach in His words, ﴿Or did you suppose that you would enter Paradise﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:214], and His words, ﴿And you used to wish for death before you encountered it﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:143]. All these sentences return to censure and reproach concerning many conditions that were the cause of the defeat at Uhud. Each of those present at the battle takes from this reproach the share suited to what He knows of his state, whether outward or inward.

The verse alludes to the disturbance that afflicted the Muslims when it was rumoured that the Messenger ﷺ had died. The hypocrites said: "If he were a prophet, he would not have been killed. Return to your old religion and to your brothers from the people of Makkah, and let us ask 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy to obtain safe-conduct for us from Abu Sufyan." They resolved to abandon fighting and to join the polytheists. A group of Muslims stood firm, among them Anas ibn al-Nadr al-Ansari, who said: "If Muhammad has been killed, the Lord of Muhammad is living and does not die. What good is life after him? Fight for the cause for which he fought."

Muhammad is the name of the Messenger of Allah, Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib ﷺ. His grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib named him with it. It was said to him: "Why did you name him Muhammad, when it is not among the names of your forefathers?" He said: "I hoped that people would praise him." It has also been said that no one among the Arabs was named Muhammad before the Messenger of Allah. Al-Suhayli mentioned in al-Rawd al-Unuf that before the birth of the Messenger of Allah only three Arabs bore this name: Muhammad ibn Sufyan ibn Mujashi', the great-grandfather of al-Farazdaq; Muhammad ibn Uhayha ibn al-Julah al-Awsi; and Muhammad ibn Himran from Rabi'ah.

This name is a passive participle from hammadahu tahmidan, meaning that he praised him excessively. Rasul is an intensive form (fa'ul) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), like their words halub (milked), rakub (ridden), and jazur (slaughtered).

The meaning of khalat is "passed away and came to an end," as in His words, ﴿Indeed, there have passed before you precedents﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:137], and in the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

". . . whoever was in the bygone age"

He restricted Muhammad to the attribute of messengerhood by a restriction of the described to the attribute (qasr mawsuf 'ala al-sifah), a relative restriction (qasr idafi), to refute what contradicts it, a refutation of denial, whether it is qasr qalb (restriction by reversal) or qasr ifrad (restriction by singling out).

It is apparent that the clause ﴿the messengers have passed away before him﴾ is a description of "messenger," so it is the locus of the restriction: that is, he is nothing but a messenger described as one before whom the messengers have passed away, meaning they have come to an end.

This statement is directed at refuting the belief of one who holds that the messengers did not pass away before him. Although this belief was not held by any of the addressees, when there proceeded from them what is characteristically an effect of this belief, namely their resolve to abandon supporting the religion and to submit to the enemy, they deserved to be placed in the position of one who believes that the messengers did not pass away before him. Their condition was that of one who imagines a necessary connection between the survival of a religion and the survival of its messenger, so he takes the continuance of the religion as proof of the continuance of its messenger. When the messenger of a religion dies, they assumed that its law had ended and that following it had been nullified.

On this reading the restriction is qasr qalb, namely the reversal of their belief in conclusions opposite to the attribute to which he is restricted, which is that the messengers passed away before him. Those conclusions are weakness and hesitation in continuing to spread the call of Islam. This is what the words of the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) suggest.

Al-Sakkaki (author of Miftah al-'Ulum) made the object of restriction the attribute of messengerhood, so the locus of the restriction is the word "messenger," not the words "the messengers have passed away before him." The restriction then becomes qasr ifrad, by placing the addressees in the position of one who believed that he was described as a messenger while being free from death, since they built upon the supposition of his death conjectures that only one who believes in his immunity from death would entertain. On this reading, the words ﴿the messengers have passed away before him﴾ are a resumptive sentence (istinaf), not a description. This is a distant reading, because the addressees had not done anything that would call for rejecting the report of his death; rather, they took it to be true.

On both readings the addressees have been placed in the position of one who ignores and denies the restriction of the described to this attribute. Therefore they were addressed by the method of negation and exception (al-nafy wa-l-istithna'), which is commonly used in addressing one who ignores and denies the ruling to which something is restricted, without any other method, as al-Sakkaki clarified in Miftah al-'Ulum.

His words ﴿Will you then, if he dies or is killed, turn back on your heels?﴾ are conjoined to His words ﴿Muhammad is only a messenger﴾, and so on. The fa' (then) indicates that the content of the conjoined clause follows from the content of the clause it is joined to. Since the content of the conjoined clause is the interrogative denial of the content of the earlier clause, which is the condition and its consequence, the sequential meaning conveyed by the conjunctive fa' has no sense except that the content of the conjoined clause follows from the content of the earlier clause, as an effect follows from its cause. The fa' is then causal, and the interrogative hamzah has been moved forward from its original position, as is its usual practice with conjunctions. The meaning is: the denial that they should turn back on their heels follows from the establishment of the content of the restrictive clause. For when the content of the restrictive clause is established, which is the reversal of belief or the singling out of one of the two beliefs, it follows that their turning back on their heels, supposing that he dies or is killed, would be an abominable matter that deserves not to occur. How then could it occur from them? This ruling reinforces what the restrictive clause requires of an implicit denial of their belief contrary to the content of the restrictive clause. Thus the denial directed at them was made twice: once by the implicit allusion drawn from the restrictive clause, and once by the explicit statement in this sentence.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: the hamzah is for denying that turning back is caused by the messenger's having passed away, and that is the causation indicated by the fa', meaning the denial of the whole of what the fa' signifies together with what it introduces, like the denial of sequence and interval in His words, ﴿Is it [only] when it has occurred that you will believe in it?﴾ [Yunus 10:51] and in the verse of al-Nabigha:

"Then do you make excuses to me for them? I have heard and I have seen."

By this he denies that they made their having known the passing away of the messengers before him a cause of their apostasy upon learning of his death. On this reading the hamzah is not moved from its place, since it entered upon the causal fa'. This is objected to on the ground that their knowledge of the passing away of the messengers before him, while their followers remained holding to their creeds, was not a cause of the addressees turning back on their heels. It is answered that the meaning is that, when they knew that the messengers had passed away before him while their creeds remained, they did not act according to what their knowledge required; so it was as if they made their knowledge a cause of producing the opposite of its effect, in the manner in which corruption of premise arises in dialectical reasoning. But this reading involves much strain and excessive subtlety.

A group went to the view that the fa' is merely for sequence in mention, or for resumption, and that this is the conjoining of an explicit denial to an implicit denial. Although this reading is easy, it makes the conjunction specifically by fa' and not by any other particle, and the fa' which indicates pure sequence in mention normally conjoins attributes, as in ﴿By those lined up in rows﴾ [al-Saffat 37:1], ﴿and those who drive [the clouds] with reproof﴾ [al-Saffat 37:2], or names of places, as in the verse:

"Between al-Dakhul and Hawmal, then Tudih, then al-Miqra. . ."

The verb inqalaba means to return to a place, as one says inqalaba ila manzilihi (he returned to his home). Here it is a metaphor for returning to the condition they had been in, namely the condition of disbelief. 'Ala (on) here is the metaphorical use of "on," since returning originally happens by way of a path. Al-a'qab is the plural of 'aqib, which is the back of a man's heel. In the hadith: "Woe to the heels from the Fire." The intended meaning is the direction of the heels, that is, the rear.

His words ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels, he will not harm Allah at all﴾ mean: not at all, not even a little, since apostasy from the religion is the nullification of what contains the welfare of people. The apostate harms himself and people, but does not harm Allah in any way. But the grateful one who remains firm in faith will be rewarded with thanks, because he strives for the welfare of people, and Allah loves welfare and does not love corruption.

The purpose of the verse is reproach for the disturbance that occurred, praise for those who stood firm and admonished the people, and warning against falling into apostasy at the death of the Messenger, peace be upon him. What Allah warned them of did occur after the death of the Messenger ﷺ, when many Muslims apostatized and assumed that following the Messenger had been confined to his lifetime. Then Allah guided them afterwards. Thus the verse contains a report about the future.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 145:

﴿And it is not for a soul to die except by the permission of Allah, at a decreed time.﴾

This is a parenthetical sentence (jumla mu'tarida), and the waw is a waw of parenthesis (waw i'tiradiyya).

If it is a continuation of the rebuke against their panic upon the supposed death of the Messenger, then the intended meaning is the generality of souls, not specifically the soul of the Messenger, peace be upon him. The verse would then be a reproach to the Muslims for their heedlessness of Allah's protection of His Messenger from being overpowered by his enemies, and from his lifespan being cut short before he conveyed the Message.

Also in His words ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 67], following His words ﴿Convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 67], which indicates that his protection from the people is for the sake of conveying the Shari'a. Allah has thus guaranteed him life until he conveys His law and fulfils His purpose. How, then, could they suppose he would be killed at the hands of his enemies? Moreover, this was before the announcement of the completion of the Shari'a. Do you not see that when Allah revealed His words ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3], up to the end of the verse, Abu Bakr wept and knew that the term of the Prophet ﷺ had drawn near, and said: "Nothing is completed except that it diminishes." Accordingly, the sentence in this case is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the waw is the waw of circumstance.

If, however, this is a fresh rebuke directed at those who panicked at the defeat and feared death, then the generality in "soul" is intended as: it was not fitting for you to fear, since you know that every soul has a term.

In this ruling the form of negation has been used for emphasis, to stress the impossibility of a death occurring before its term. On this view the sentence is parenthetical, and the waw is a waw of parenthesis. Truths of this kind are delivered in contexts where the aim is to cure souls of blameworthy defects. Otherwise, the end of the term is bound to the knowledge of Allah, and no one knows its time: ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾ [Luqman: 34]. The believer is commanded to preserve his life, except in the way of Allah; therefore, at the time of jihad it is incumbent upon him to return to the reality, which is that death comes at its appointed term. By "the permission of Allah" is meant His decree of the time of death and His placing of the signs indicating the arrival of that determined time, which He has expressed sometimes as (Be!), sometimes as a predestined decree, sometimes as the pen, and sometimes as the Book.

The word "Book" in His words ﴿a decreed term﴾ may be a noun meaning "that which is written," in which case it is a circumstantial clause (hal) of "permission" or of "death," as in His words ﴿For every term there is a Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 38]; and "decreed" (mu'ajjalan) is a second circumstantial clause. It may also be that "kitaban" is a verbal noun of kataba, used in the sense of kutub for emphasis, with "mu'ajjalan" as its attribute; it is then in place of its omitted verb, and the implied sense is: He decreed a decree, a decreed term, that is, a fixed one. Al-Kashshaf took it as an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the clause "And it is not for a soul..." and the verse; he means that together with its attribute, "decreed," it emphasises the meaning of "except by the permission of Allah," because His words "by the permission of Allah" indicate that it has a time which may be near or may be far. This is like His words ﴿The Book of Allah against you﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], after His words ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa': 23] and the verse.

* * *

﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him from it; and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him from it. And We will reward the grateful.﴾

This is a conjunction (atf) upon the parenthetical sentence.

That is: whoever desires this world without the Hereafter, like one who prefers life over death in the way of Allah, or like those who hastened for booty and thus caused the defeat. The intention is not that whoever desires the reward and pleasures of this world is deprived of the reward and pleasures of the Hereafter, for the legal evidences show that desiring the good of this world is a sound legal aim. Was the Shari'a not sent only to reform this world and to prepare for the perfect, eternal life of the Hereafter? Allah the Exalted said ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 148], and He the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Do you await for us except one of the two best things?﴾ [al-Tawba: 52], meaning victory (booty) or martyrdom; and other verses and hadiths on this are numerous. The sentence ﴿And We will reward the grateful﴾ is a concluding generalisation (tadhyil) covering the grateful, whether they desire the reward of this world or the reward of the Hereafter, and the reward is general, each according to its measure: that is, He rewards the grateful with the reward of this world and the Hereafter, or with the reward of this world alone.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 146–148 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And how many a prophet fought, and with him many devoted followers (ribbiyyun). They did not falter for what befell them in the way of Allah, nor did they weaken, nor did they submit. And Allah loves the steadfast.﴾ ﴿And their only utterance was that they said: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs, make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾ ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the excellent reward of the Hereafter. And Allah loves the good-doers.﴾

Page 116

It is an act of conjunction (ʿatf) upon His saying ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 144], and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD). It is the conjunction of an exemplary lesson (ʿibrah) upon an admonition (mawʿizah). His saying ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels﴾ is an admonition for whoever intends to turn back, and His saying ﴿And how many a prophet fought﴾ is a lesson drawn from the steadfastness of the followers of the messengers and prophets in the past, when their prophets were struck by calamity or killed in war or otherwise, because the two situations are alike. Thus the speech is an allusion, comparing the condition of the companions of Uhud with the condition of the companions of the earlier prophets, for the locus of the parable is not specifically the defeat in battle; rather, that is the thing being likened (al-mumaththal). As for the comparison (al-tashbih), it is with the steadfastness of the followers when calamities descend or when the one they follow dies.

(Wa-ka'ayyin) is a word meaning multiplicity (al-takthir). It has been said that it is simple, established for multiplicity; and it has been said that it is compound, from the particle of comparison "ka" and the interrogative "ayy", which is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. This "ayy" is not a genuine interrogative; rather the purpose of it is to remind the questioner of multiplicity, so its interrogative function is figurative. Its final nun was originally a tanwin, and when it was compounded and became one word, its tanwin was turned into a nun and it was made indeclinable (mabni). The more apparent view is that it is simple, and it has four dialectal forms, the most famous of which in prose is ka'ayyin, on the pattern of ka‘ayyin (scholars of lexicography and grammar have the custom, when measuring hamzated words, of substituting the letter ʿayn for the letter hamza, so that the hamza is not confused with the alif or the yaʾ written in the form of either of them). The most famous of them in poetry iska'in, with a nun, the active participle of kana, though it is not an active participle, contrary to al-Mubarrad; rather it is a lightened form of ka'ayyin.

Regarding how it was lightened, there are various explanations, the root of which is al-Khalil's statement: when its usage became frequent, the Arabs manipulated it by metathesis and elision in some cases. I say: its detailed treatment would be lengthy. My own view is that when they intended to lighten it, they made the hamza an alif; then two sakin letters met contrary to their rule, so they elided the sakin yaʾ, and the kasra yaʾ remained, which resembled the active participle of (kana), so they made it a hamza like the yaʾ that occurs after an extra alif. The most common occurrence in the speech of the Arabs is ka'ayyin, because it is lighter in verse and better suited to most meters at the beginnings and middles of lines, unlike ka'in. Al-Zajjaj said: the two good dialects are ka'ayyin and ka'in. Shaykh Ibn 'Arafa related in his tafsir, from his shaykh Ibn al-Hubab, who said: our shaykh

Page 117

Ahmad ibn Yusuf al-Sulami al-Kinani informed us, saying: I said to our shaykh Ibn 'Usfur: why did you give so many examples of ka'in in your commentary on al-Idah? He said: because I entered upon the sultan, the Amir al-Mustansir, meaning Muhammad al-Mustansir ibn Abi Zakariyya al-Hafsi, and the apparent view is that at that time he was the crown prince. I found Ibn Hisham, meaning Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hisham al-Khadrawi, resident and buried in Tunis, who died in the year 646, and he told me that he had asked him what he remembered of the examples on the reading of ka'ayyin, and he could recall only the verse from al-Idah:

"And many a friend in the valleys who would see me, if I were struck, would himself be struck."

Ibn 'Usfur said: when he asked me, I said: I have fifty verses memorized on it. When I recited to him about ten, he said: that is enough for you, and gave me fifty dinars. I went out and found Ibn Hisham sitting at the door, and I gave him half of them.

The Jumhur read (wa-ka'ayyin) with an open hamza after the kaf and a shadda-ed yaʾ after the hamza, on the pattern of the word (kasayyib). Ibn Kathir read (ka'in), with an alif after the kaf and a kasra-ed hamza after the alif, on the pattern of kahin.

The multiplicity derived from (ka'ayyin) falls upon its specification, which is the word nabiyy. It may be multiplicity in the sense of general number, in which case it does not exceed the plural of paucity; and it may be multiplicity in the sense of the plural of abundance, in which case some of them we know and some of them we do not know, as He, exalted, said: ﴿And among them are those We have not related to you﴾ [Ghafir: 78]. There come to my mind the names of six prophets who were killed: Irmiya, whom the Children of Israel killed; Hizqiyal, whom they also killed because he rebuked them for their evil deeds; Ash‘ya, whom Manasa ibn Hizqil, king of Israel, killed, because he rebuked and admonished him for his evil conduct, so he sawed him in two with a saw; Zakariyya and Yahya, whom the Children of Israel killed for their belief in the Messiah; and the people of al-Rass among the Arabs killed their prophet Handhala ibn Safwan in the period of 'Adnan; and the Apostles believed that the Messiah had been killed, yet they did not weaken in establishing his religion after him. This is not intended here; rather the lesson is the steadfastness of his followers upon his religion despite his separation from them, since the lesson lies in the messenger's absence and the continuation of his followers, whether by killing or otherwise. Among these there was no messenger except Handhala ibn Safwan, and among them there was also no one killed in jihad. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: we have not heard of a prophet killed in fighting.

Page 118

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (qutila) in the passive voice; Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and Abu Ja'far read (qatala) in the form of mufa'ala. According to the reading (qutila), in the passive, the subject of the verb is the pronoun referring to nabiyy. In both readings, it is permissible that the subject of both verbs be the pronoun referring to nabiyy, so the phrase ﴿ma'ahu ribbiyyun﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) from nabiyy; and it is permissible that the subject of both verbs be the word (ribbiyyun), so that the phrase ma'ahu is a circumstantial element (hal) from ribbiyyun placed in front.

This verse came in this wonderful arrangement, suitable for carrying the speech toward strengthening the Muslims in a state of defeat and in a state of rumour of the killing of the Prophet ﷺ; and in both possibilities regarding the position of the clause ﴿ma'ahu ribbiyyun﴾, the goodness of pausing differs, whether on the word (qutila) or on the word (kathir).

Al-ribbiyyun is the plural of ribbiyy, meaning one who follows the law of the Lord, like rabbaniyy. What is meant by them here is the followers of the messengers and the disciples of the prophets. Its ra may be vowelled with a fatha, by analogy, or with a kasra, as a change of the relative form; and it is the latter that was read in the mutawatir reading.

The locus of the lesson is the steadfastness of the rabbaniyyun upon the religion together with the death of their prophets and their callers.

His saying (kathir) is an attribute of (ribbiyyun), and it was brought in the singular form although the qualified noun is plural, because the words kathir and qalil are treated, with respect to what they qualify, as the word shay' or 'adad (number). Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And He spread from them many men and women﴾ [al-Nisa': 1]; and He said ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109]; and He said ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ [al-Anfal: 26]; and He said ﴿When Allah showed them to you in your dream as few; and had He shown them to you as many﴾ [al-Anfal: 43].

His saying "fa-ma wahanu" means the ribbiyyun, since it is known that the prophets do not weaken; so the example intended here is the imitation of the followers of the prophets, meaning that the followers of those who passed before the prophets should not be more resolute than the followers of Muhammad ﷺ.

He combined weakness (wahn) and frailty (du'f), and they are close to one another, nearly synonymous: wahn is lack of power to act and to rise to a matter, its verb being like wa'ada, wariha, and karuma. Du'f, with a dammah or fathah on the dad, is the opposite of strength in the body; and both are used here metaphorically. The first is closer to the slackening of resolve and the creeping of despair in souls and minds; the second is closer to surrender and failure in resistance. As for istikana, it is submission and abasement before the enemy. Among the subtle points is that they are ordered in mention according to the order of their occurrence: when resolve collapses, the limbs grow weak, and surrender comes, followed by abasement and submission to the enemy.

Know that if this was the condition of the followers of the prophets, and prophethood was guidance and instruction, then it is no wonder that this should be the condition of the people of knowledge and the followers of truth: that the resistance of an opponent, or the harm of an envious or ignorant person, should not weaken them, nor make them frail, nor subject them. In the authentic hadith in al-Bukhari: "Khabbab said to the Prophet ﷺ: We have suffered severe hardship from the polytheists; will you not supplicate Allah? He sat up, his face reddened, and said: Those before you were combed with iron combs, below the flesh and sinew, and that did not turn them from their religion; and a saw was placed upon the middle of a man's head and he was split in two, and that did not turn him from his religion." The hadith to its end.

His saying, exalted: ﴿And their only utterance was that they said: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins..."﴾ up to the end of the verse, is a conjunction upon (fa-ma wahanu), because when He described them with firmness of heart and steadiness of the soul, He described them afterwards with what indicates steadfastness in the utterances of the tongue, which flow from it at times of agitation and anguish. That is, what befell them did not stir in them any doubt about the truth of Allah's promise, nor did any complaint escape them; rather they knew that this was for a wisdom which He, glorified be He, knows, or perhaps it was a recompense for a shortcoming on their part in the performance of the duty of supporting His religion, or in fulfilling the trust of obligation. Therefore they besought Him at the descent of the calamity with their saying ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs﴾, fearing that what had befallen them was a recompense for what they had neglected. Then they asked Him for victory and its causes a second time, saying ﴿make firm our feet and help us against the disbelieving people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 250]. So the defeat that reached them did not turn them from hope in victory. In the Muwatta', from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "One of you is answered so long as he does not hurry, saying: I supplicated and I was not answered." So He restricted their saying, in that state in which such a saying rarely escapes, to their saying ﴿Our Lord, forgive us﴾ to the end.

Page 120

So the form of restriction in His saying ﴿And their only utterance was that they said﴾ is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), to refute the belief of one who might suppose that they uttered sayings revealing anguish, or panic, or doubt about victory, or submission to the disbelievers. In this restriction there is an allusion against those among the weaker Muslims or the hypocrites who grew impatient, one of whom said: "If only we spoke to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy so that he might get us a safe-conduct from Abu Sufyan."

The predicate of kana was placed before its subject in His saying ﴿wa-ma kana qawlahum illa an qalu﴾, because it is a predicate about a restricted subject (mahsur), since the intended meaning is to confine their utterances at that time to the saying ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾. So the restriction is real (haqiqi), since it is for their utterance issuing from them at the time when what befell them in the way of Allah occurred; that condition is understood from the context, similar to the restriction in His saying, exalted: ﴿The only saying of the believers when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, is that they say: "We hear and we obey"﴾ [al-Nur: 51]. That is a real restriction limited to a specific time, a limitation explicitly stated. This is better than the explanation for placing the predicate first in the verse, that the verbal noun in its underlying form (al-masdar al-muntasbik al-mu'awwal) is more definite than the explicit verbal noun, because the derived form indicates the relation and the time of the event, unlike an explicit verbal noun in construction; and that is permissible in the case of kana outside the forms of restriction. But in restriction (hasr), placing the restricted element first is obligatory.

And the intended meaning of "sins" is all of them. Then he conjoined some sins to them, namely what is expressed here by "excess in our affair." Al-israf (excess) is al-ifrat (going to extremes) and transgressing the limit. It may be that by it is meant the major sins (al-kaba'ir), as has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas and a group of scholars. On this view, by His words "(amrina)," meaning "our affair," is meant our religion and our obligations. Then this is a specific conjunction ('atf khass, a conjunction of the particular onto the general) for the sake of emphasis in seeking His forgiveness for it. The conjoined term (al-ma'tuf 'alayhi) is then restricted to the remaining sins, which are the minor sins (al-saghair).

In my view it is also permissible that the intended meaning of "excess in the affair" is negligence in their situation and organization regarding what pertains to the preparation for battle and readiness for it, or precaution against the enemy. This is the apparent sense of the word "amr" (affair), namely that they suspected that the defeat they suffered in the war with their enemy arose from two causes: an inner one and an outer one. In this restriction there is an allusion against those among the weaker Muslims or the hypocrites who grew impatient, one of whom said: "If only we spoke to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy so that he might get us a safe-conduct from Abu Sufyan."

The predicate of kana was placed before its subject in His saying ﴿wa-ma kana qawlahum illa an qalu﴾, because it is a predicate about a restricted subject (mahsur), since the intended meaning is to confine their utterances at that time to the saying ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾. So the restriction is real (haqiqi), since it is for their utterance issuing from them at the time when what befell them in the way of Allah occurred; that condition is understood from the context, similar to the restriction in His saying, exalted: ﴿The only saying of the believers when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, is that they say: "We hear and we obey"﴾ [al-Nur: 51]. That is a real restriction limited to a specific time, a limitation explicitly stated. This is better than the explanation for placing the predicate first in the verse, that the verbal noun in its underlying form (al-masdar al-muntasbik al-mu'awwal) is more definite than the explicit verbal noun, because the derived form indicates the relation and the time of the event, unlike an explicit verbal noun in construction; and that is permissible in the case of kana outside the forms of restriction. But in restriction (hasr), placing the restricted element first is obligatory.

And the intended meaning of "sins" is all of them. Then he conjoined some sins to them, namely what is expressed here by "excess in our affair." Al-israf (excess) is al-ifrat (going to extremes) and transgressing the limit. It may be that by it is meant the major sins (al-kaba'ir), as has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas and a group of scholars. On this view, by His words "(amrina)," meaning "our affair," is meant our religion and our obligations. Then this is a specific conjunction ('atf khass, a conjunction of the particular onto the general) for the sake of emphasis in seeking His forgiveness for it. The conjoined term (al-ma'tuf 'alayhi) is then restricted to the remaining sins, which are the minor sins (al-saghair).

In my view it is also permissible that the intended meaning of "excess in the affair" is negligence in their situation and organization regarding what pertains to the preparation for battle and readiness for it, or precaution against the enemy. This is the apparent sense of the word "amr" (affair), namely that they suspected that the defeat they suffered in the war with their enemy arose from two causes: an inner one and an outer one. The inner cause is Allah's anger against them because of their sins, and the outer cause is their negligence in readiness and precaution. This second view is preferable to the first.

Page 121

His words, ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾, inform us of the hastening of the answer to their supplication, since they attained the good of both this world and the Hereafter. The reward of this world is the conquest and the spoils, and the reward of the Hereafter is what was decreed for them of a good final outcome in the Hereafter. For this reason He described it with His words ﴿and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾, because it is better and more enduring. The discussion of reward (al-thawab) was already covered at His words, exalted is He, in Surat al-Baqara, ﴿a reward from Allah is better﴾ [al-Baqara: 103].

The clause ﴿And Allah loves the good-doers﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil), meaning that He loves every good-doer. The position of the concluding phrase indicates that those being spoken of are among those who did good. Thus the "al" is for the genus (al-lam li'l-jins), which conveys the meaning of comprehensiveness (istighraq). This is among the strongest pieces of evidence that the genus "al" (al-lam al-jinsiyya), when it enters upon a plural, cancels from it the meaning of plurality, and that the comprehensiveness conveyed by "al" is the same whether its complement is singular or a whole clause.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 149–150:

﴿O you who believe, if you obey those who disbelieve, they will turn you back on your heels, and you will become losers.﴾ ﴿Rather, Allah is your Protector, and He is the best of helpers.﴾

This is an independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) marking a transition from reproach, blame and rebuke to warning, through which it leads back to consolation for the defeat that had occurred. Within all of this are legal realities, ethical admonitions and historical lessons, in such number that one who seeks to enumerate them cannot do so.

Ta'ah (obedience) is applied to complying with the command of one who commands, which is well known, and to submitting to the authority of the dominant party; thus one says "the tribe of such-and-such submitted" (ta'at qabilatu kadha) and "the army brought the lands of such-and-such under its sway" (tawwa'a al-jaysh bilad kadha).

"Those who disbelieve" (alladhina kafaru) is commonly used in the terminology of the Qur'an to mean the polytheists, though the word, by its lexical form, applies to every disbeliever, whether a polytheist, a People of the Book, an open opponent or a hypocrite.

Radd 'ala al-a'qab (turning back on one's heels) means apostasy (irtidad), and inqilab (turning back) means returning. The discussion of these two terms has already preceded at His saying ﴿Is it so that if he dies or is killed you will turn back on your heels?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 144]. The apparent meaning is that

page 122
He intended by this speech to warn the believers against the thought that might occur to them of entering into a truce and safe-conduct with the polytheists, because that would show weakness before them and need for them. If they inclined toward them, they would lead them on gradually, by displaying lack of aversion to their religion, which opposes theirs, until they turned them away from their religion, for they would never be pleased with them until they returned to their creed. Thus the turning back on the heels, on this reading, occurs through gradual drift and eventual outcome. This lesson has in fact been realized in the obedience of the Muslims of al-Andalus to the tyrant of the Galicians (al-Jalaliqa). On this reading the verse alludes to the folly of the opinion of one who said: "If we spoke to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, so that he would obtain for us a safe-conduct from Abu Sufyan," as is indicated by His saying ﴿Rather, Allah is your Protector.﴾
It is also possible that by obedience is meant obedience in speech and gesture, that is, compliance, and this is the saying of the hypocrites to them: "If Muhammad were a prophet, he would not have been killed; so return to your brothers and your creed." The meaning of turning back on the heels on this reading is that it occurs immediately, at the very moment of their obeying them.

His saying ﴿Rather, Allah is your Protector﴾ is a turning away (idrab) to nullify what the preceding words contained. On the first reading the connection (munasabah) appears in the clearest way, because obedience on that reading is of the kind of alliance and pact (muwalah wa halif), so it fits to nullify it by reminding them that the Protector (mawla) of the believers is Allah, the Exalted. This reminder has a great effect: breaking an allegiance and a pact is a grave matter among the Arabs, for allegiance (wala') has among them a status like that of lineage (nasab). Islam established this meaning in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage or the conquest of Makkah: whoever claims descent from other than his father or attaches himself to other than his clients, upon him is the curse of Allah, the angels and all people. How much more so when the allegiance is to the lord of all clients.

On the second reading of the meaning of ﴿if you obey those who disbelieve﴾, the connection is in terms of what obeying the hypocrites contains of allegiance to them and abandonment of allegiance to Allah, the Exalted.

His saying ﴿and He is the best of helpers﴾ strengthens the connection of the first reading and increases its manifestness. ﴿The best of helpers﴾ means the most excellent of those described with this attribute in what is intended by it, in its place, and in its benefit. Victory (nasr) is aimed at repelling domination from the dominated; so whenever the repelling is more decisive against the dominator, the victory is more excellent. It is also aimed at repelling injustice; so whenever the victory is decisive against the oppressor's injustice, its position is more excellent and its benefit more complete. Victory is never free of praise, for in it appear courage, refusal of wrong, and valor. Dawwak ibn Thumayl al-Mazini said:

When they seek aid, they do not ask who called them, for what war, or in what place.

But when it is support for an oppressor or a highwayman, it carries blemish and blame; when it is manifesting the right of the one who is right and nullifying falsehood, it attains complete praiseworthiness. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) interpreted supporting an oppressor in a manner suited to the character of Islam, when he said: "Support your brother whether he is an oppressor or oppressed." Someone said: "O Messenger of Allah, I support him when he is oppressed; how do I support him when he is an oppressor?" He said: "That you restrain him from his oppression."
