﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, because they associated with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority. Their abode is the Fire, and wretched is the abode of the wrongdoers.﴾

A return to the consolation of the believers, the reassurance of their hearts, and the promise to them of victory over the enemy. The original sense of *al-ilqa'* (casting) is throwing something onto the ground, as in ﴿So they cast their ropes and their staves﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 44], or into water, as in ﴿Cast him into the sea﴾ [al-Qasas: 7]. It is also used for conveying speech, as in ﴿They lend an ear﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 223], and for the occurrence of something in the soul, as if a caster had cast it, that is, without prior preparation. ﴿And We cast enmity and hatred﴾ is here a *majaz* (figurative usage) meaning making and bringing into being, like His saying ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾ [al-Ahzab: 26].

*Al-ru'b* (terror) is fear arising from intense dread. It has two forms: *al-ru'b* with a sukun on the 'ayn, and *al-ru'ub* with a damma on the 'ayn. The majority of readers recited it with a sukun on the 'ayn, while Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i recited it with a damma on the 'ayn.

The *ba'* in His saying ﴿for that which they associated with Allah﴾ is for exchange, and is called *ba' al-muqabala* (the ba' of equivalence), as in the expression "this for that," and as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿as a recompense for what they earned﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38]. This is a worldly recompense that Allah, exalted is He, ordained for associating others with Him. Among His wisdom, exalted is He, is that He ordains corrupt effects for corrupt matters. Since *shirk* is the belief in the influence of one who has no influence, and since this belief is fixed in the souls of its adherents without any proof, it follows that its adherent is restless of soul and perplexed about the outcome, regarding which of the gods will prevail over the others. Thus every people has an idol to which they are especially attached, and in that state they believe that the other idols possess the same power and jealousy as theirs. So their gods are always in contest and enmity, just as their followers are always so. Those whose condition is as we have described never find a settled resolve in confidence of victory in their wars, for they do not know whether the gain lies with their gods or with their opposites. Accordingly, His saying ﴿for which He has sent down no authority﴾ is a relative clause attached to "that which they associated," and its purpose is not to define the partners, but to allude to the fact that it is among the causes of the casting of terror into their hearts, since they are without certainty regarding what they associated and believed. Their hearts are therefore trembling and unsteady, since everyone knows that it is impossible for authority to descend upon the partners.

If you say: what you have mentioned implies that *shirk* is the cause of casting terror into the hearts of its adherents, so terror must have been present in their hearts before this encounter, whereas Allah says "We shall cast" (*sanulqi*), meaning in the future. I reply: that is so, except that these qualities lie dormant in souls until a summoner calls them forth. Terror and courage are two qualities that appear only at the time of fighting, and they strengthen and weaken. The brave man's courage increases with repeated victory, and it may recede a little when he is defeated, but then his quality returns to him swiftly, as 'Amr ibn al-Itnaba described it in his saying:

*And say, whenever it [the heart] stirs and surges, "Stay where you are, you will be praised, or you will rest."*

And as al-Husayn ibn al-Humam said:

*I held back, seeking to preserve life, but I found no life for myself like advancing.*

Likewise, terror and cowardice may weaken at the appearance of a glimmer of victory. When the polytheists were routed at the outset of the Battle of Uhud, their resolve was broken, and then when Allah tested the believers with defeat, some courage and self-assurance returned to them, but after they withdrew

[p. 125]

their qualities returned to them,

*and natures refuse the transmitter [to be otherwise].*

So His saying "We shall cast" means the casting of the return of the quality into the souls. You may also take the *sin* in it to be merely for emphasis, meaning "We have cast and We cast," and the difficulty is dispelled.

Many exegetes mention that this terror had manifestations. Among them: when the polytheists gained the upper hand over the Muslims, they were in a position to press on to annihilate them, but terror prevented them from doing so. For when they turned away, intending to return to Makkah, regret arose in them along the way, and they said: "If we return and track down Muhammad and his companions, we will have killed them, and nothing will remain but the remnant and the fugitive. So let us return to them until we uproot them." This reached the Prophet ﷺ, who called upon the Muslims to meet them, and they answered the call, though they were in extreme weakness and burdened with wounds, to the point that it was said that one of them would carry another, and then the one carried would dismount and carry the one who had been carrying him. So Allah caused Ma'bad ibn Abi Ma'bad al-Khuza'i, who was then a disbeliever, to come to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and say: "Khuza'ah has been grieved by what has befallen you, and we would have wished that you had not been afflicted in your companions." Then Ma'bad joined Quraysh and found them at al-Rawha', having resolved to return to fight the Muslims. Abu Sufyan said to him: "What is behind you, O Ma'bad?" He said: "Muhammad and his companions have gone out seeking you with a host the like of which I have never seen. They burn with eagerness against you, and those who had stayed behind from him have joined him." He said: "Woe to you, what are you saying?" He replied: "I do not think you will depart until you see the forelocks of the horses. What I saw of them has moved me to say about them:

*My mount nearly broke under the clamour when the earth flowed with the swift, flocking horses.*

*They bear noble lions, not dwarf-reeds, at the encounter, nor weak, feeble ones.*

*So I continued running, thinking the earth was tilting, when they rallied behind a leader who was not forsaken.*"

Then terror fell into the hearts of the polytheists. Safwan ibn Umayya said: "Do not return, for I see that the people will have a fight other than the one that was."

[p. 126]

His saying ﴿for which He has sent down no authority﴾ means for which there is no authority. *Al-sultan* is proof and evidence, because it dominates the soul. The sending down of it is negated, and what is intended is the negation of its existence. For if it existed, it would have been sent down, that is, Allah would have revealed it to people, since Allah did not conceal from people the guidance to what is obligatory for them to believe, delivered through the tongues of the messengers. Thus *al-tanzil* (sending down) means either revelation, or the establishment of proofs for it, as people say: "Wisdom descended upon the tongues of the Arabs, the minds of the Persians, and the hands of the Chinese." Since truth cannot exceed these two states, for it is either known through revelation or through signs, the negation of the sending down of authority for associating others with Allah is a *kinayah* (allusion or metonymy) for the negation of authority itself, like the saying of the poet whose name is not known:

*Its terrors do not frighten the hare, nor do you see the lizard hiding in it.*

His saying ﴿and their abode is the Fire﴾ mentions their punishment in the Hereafter. *Al-ma'wa* is a noun of place from *awa ila kadha*, meaning to go to such a place, and *al-mathwa* is a noun of place from *thawa*, meaning to dwell. So the Fire is their destination and their resting place. The intended referents are the polytheists.

[Page 127]

﴿And God had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission, until when you lost heart, disputed about the matter, and disobeyed after He had shown you what you love. Among you were some who desired this world, and among you were some who desired the Hereafter. Then He turned you away from them in order to test you. Yet He has pardoned you, and God is full of bounty toward the believers.﴾

﴿And God had certainly fulfilled﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with His words ﴿We will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ [Al ʿImran: 151]. This is a return to consolation for what had befallen them, and a demonstration of the continuing care of God Most High for the believers. It also points to confidence in His promise of casting terror into the hearts of the polytheists, and it clarifies the cause of the Muslims' defeat. It is a reassurance to them by mentioning its like and its previous parallel, for this has a great effect in speech, in the sense of the saying "History repeats itself." It also serves to place the responsibility for the defeat upon them, and to show that God did not break His promise to them, but rather their poor conduct brought them into the calamity, as in His words ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ [al-Nisa: 79].

The truthfulness of a promise (ṣidq al-waʿd) means fulfilling it and carrying it out, since the meaning of truthfulness (ṣidq) is the correspondence of a statement to reality. Here ṣadaqa is construed with two objects, though its proper usage is to take only one object. Al-Zamakhshari said, regarding His words in Surat al-Ahzab ﴿Among the believers are men who were true to what they covenanted with God﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23], "One says ṣadaqanī akhūka and kadhdhabanī (your brother was truthful to me and lied to me) when he tells you the truth and falsehood. As for the proverb ṣadaqanī sinna bakrihi (he was truthful to me about the age of his young camel), its meaning is ṣadaqanī fī sinni bakrihi, with the preposition dropped and the verb made to reach its object directly." So here waʿdahu is in the accusative through omission and transitivity, and the original sentence is ṣadaqakum fī waʿdihi (He was truthful to you in His promise), or ṣadaqa is taken to include the meaning of "gave" (aʿṭā).

The promise here is the promise of victory, like His words ﴿O you who believe, if you help God, He will help you﴾ [Muhammad: 7], or it refers to a specific report concerning the Day of Uhud.

The permission of God (idhnu Allah) means decree and facilitation of the causes.

As for ʿidh in His words ﴿when you were killing them﴾, it is in the accusative of time (ẓarfiyya) governed by ṣadaqakum, meaning: God was truthful to you in the promise at the time when you were killing them by His permission, for that killing (ḥass) was the fulfilment of God's promise to them of victory. Here ʿidh refers to the past, and the present tense that follows it conveys renewal, that is, it narrates the continual recurrence of the killing in the past.

Al-ḥass (with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ) means killing. Most lexicographers gave it this general sense, but al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf restricted it to killing with a great slaughter, and this is more correct.

His words ﴿until when you lost heart﴾: ḥattā is a particle of termination and limit, indicating that the content of the sentence that follows is the limit of the content of the sentence before it. The meaning is: when you were killing them by God's facilitation, and your killing of them continued until failure befell you and dispute arose among you.

Here ḥattā is a preposition, and idhā is its object.

Idhā is a noun of time, and in most cases it refers to the future, though it may depart from this to time in general, as it does here. The likely purpose of this is to evoke the strange situation, following His words "you were killing them."

Idhā here is stripped of the meaning of a conditional, because when it refers to the past it loses its capacity to be conditional, since a condition cannot be past except by interpretation. Therefore it needs no apodosis, and there is no benefit in burdening the sentence with supposing an apodosis such as "you divided," nor in making the words that follow, ﴿Among you are some who desire this world﴾ to the end, a proof of it.

Failure (fashal) means weakness and exhaustion. Dispute (tanāzuʿ) means mutual opposition. Disobedience here refers to disobeying the command of the Messenger. The three acts in the verse are arranged according to the order of their occurrence: failure, which was the impatience of some archers with remaining at their position out of desire for booty, occurred first; from it arose dispute among them over remaining at the position and over joining the army for the booty; and from the dispute arose the determination of most of them to leave the position which the Messenger, peace be upon him, had commanded them to hold, and not to depart from it. This is the basic principle in the ordering of reports in the art of composition (ṣināʿat al-inshāʾ), unless the situation requires a deviation from it.

The definite article in His words ﴿in the matter﴾ replaces the genitive noun to which it refers, meaning "in your matter," that is, your affair.

The meaning of ﴿after He had shown you what you love﴾ refers to victory, for at the beginning of the Day of Uhud the wind was blowing in favour of the Muslims, so they defeated the polytheists and turned their backs in flight, until their women were seen lifting their garments up to their thighs on the high mountain, fleeing from capture, and among them was Hind bint ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa, the wife of Abu Sufyan. When the archers whom the Messenger had commanded to remain firm to protect the backs of the Muslims saw the booty, they joined the fighters. Khalid ibn al-Walid, who was then commander of the cavalry of the polytheists, saw an opportunity against the Muslims, so he came upon them from behind, and they were routed; they fell into confusion, pressed against one another, hurried to flee, and were defeated. This is what His words ﴿after He had shown you what you love﴾ refer to. In this case the prepositional phrase is connected to their failure. The discourse on this interpretation is a strong rebuke and censure.

The more evident view to me is that what you love means the booty, since wealth is beloved. In this case the prepositional phrase is governed by each of "you lost heart," "you disputed," and "you disobeyed." The reference to the booty by its name is replaced by the relative pronoun, to alert that they hastened to seek the beloved wealth. The discourse on this interpretation is a preparation for an extenuation, since their failure, dispute, and disobedience arose from one of the aims of warfare, which is expressed by ﴿one of the two best things﴾ [al-Tawba: 52], and it did not arise from cowardice, nor from weakness of faith, nor from the intention to abandon the Muslims. All of this is a preparation for His words that follow, ﴿He has certainly pardoned you﴾.

His words ﴿Among you are some who desire this world, and among you are some who desire the Hereafter﴾ are an elaboration of "you disputed," an explanation of "you disobeyed," and a specification of it, in that the disobedient were some of those addressed who disputed, since those who desired the Hereafter were not disobedient. For this reason this sentence is placed after the two verbs, whereas the apparent arrangement would have been to follow it with "you disputed about the matter." In this position the sentence covers the content of three sentences, and this is among the most excellent aspects of the inimitability of the Qur'an, and the indicator is clear.

What is meant by ﴿Among you are some who desire this world﴾ is the desire for the blessings and goods of this world, which is the booty, because one who desires booty does not strive for the reward of obeying the Messenger's command without some interpretation, and he is not entirely negligent of the Hereafter, nor does he regard securing worldly good in that action as causing him to forfeit the reward of the Hereafter in other actions. Therefore there is nothing in this discourse indicating that the group who desired the reward of this world had then apostatised from faith, for the eagerness to achieve a worldly benefit from an action, together with the lack of eagerness to achieve the reward of the Hereafter from that action, is not indicative of contempt for the Hereafter or denial of it, as is clear. There is no need to supply "Among you are some who desire this world only." The disobedience of those who opposed the Messenger's command was called disobedience even though that opposition arose from interpretation (ijtihād) and not from contempt, for they had said: "The Messenger of God commanded us to remain firm here to protect the backs of the Muslims, but now that God has granted victory to the Muslims, what have we to do with standing here, lest the spoils escape us?" So they were interpreting, but it is called disobedience here because the situation was not one for interpretation, since the nature of war is obedience to the commander without interpretation. Or because the interpretation was remote, so they were not excused by it. Or because it was an interpretation to satisfy love of wealth, and so it did not match the proof of the obligation to obey the Messenger.

[Page 130]

His words ﴿Then He turned you away from them in order to test you﴾ are phrased this way to show that this turning away was by God's permission and decree, just as the killing was by God's permission, and that its wisdom is trial, so that He might make manifest to the Messenger and to the people who among others stood firm in faith, and because trial contains great secrets in the reckoning between the servant and his Lord, glory be to Him. He has summarised this trial here and will explain it later.

He follows this censure with His words ﴿He has certainly pardoned you﴾ to calm their hearts, and in this there is gentleness towards them, in keeping with the Qur'an's manner of reproving the believers. Even more significant is the placing of the pardon before the censure in the Messenger's rebuke, peace be upon him, in His words ﴿God pardon you! Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawba: 43]. That is a more honourable rank than following the censure with mention of the pardon. It also indicates the sincerity of their faith, since He quickly informed them of the pardon, so that their souls would not fly away in dread and fear of the anger of God Most High.

Concluding with His words ﴿and God is full of bounty toward the believers﴾ reinforces what His words ﴿He has certainly pardoned you﴾ imply. The apparent meaning is that this pardon was on account of the interpretation. Therefore it does not require repentance. It is also possible that the pardon came after what appeared from them of regret and repentance. Because of this possibility, the verse is not suitable as evidence against the Khawarij and the Mu'tazila, who maintain that sin strips away faith.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 153:

﴿When you were climbing away, not turning aside for anyone, while the Messenger was calling you from behind; so He rewarded you with grief upon grief, so that you would not grieve over what escaped you nor over what befell you. And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾

Page 131

﴿Idh tus'idūna﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿He turned you away from them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152], meaning: He repelled you from the polytheists while you were ascending (muṣʿidūn).

Al-ʾisʿād (ascending) is going away into the land, because the land is called ṣaʿīd. Ja'far ibn 'Ulba said:

"My desire is with the Yemeni caravan, ascending."

Al-ʾisʿād also means travelling up the valley. Qatada and al-Rabi' said: "They ascended on the day of Uhud into the valley." The meaning is: you fled ascending, as if it were said: you went off into the land, that is, in flight. The phrase ʾidh is an adverb of time referring to the time that followed Allah turning them away and was among its consequences.

﴿And you did not turn aside for anyone﴾, that is, in this state. Al-layy is used figuratively in the sense of mercy and kindness, like ʿaṭf in its literal and figurative senses. So the meaning is: no one turned toward anyone else, and the expression is concise through ellipsis. What is meant by "for anyone" is "for anyone of you." That is: you fled, and no one showed mercy to another or was gentle with him. This is a depiction of the intensity of fleeing, to the point that one would trample another if he stood in his path.

The clause ﴿while the Messenger was calling you from behind﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Al-ukhrā is the rear of the army, that is, behind you. The Messenger's calling was his summoning them to stand firm and return from defeat, and this is the call of the Messenger, when he said: "Come to me, servants of Allah; whoever turns back will have Paradise." 

His saying ﴿so He rewarded you with grief﴾: if the pronoun in ʾathābakum refers to the Name of Majesty (Allah), which is the more apparent and agrees with His later saying ﴿then He sent down upon you, after the grief﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154], then it is coordinated with ṣaraqakum, meaning the turning away was followed by the reward. The original sense of ith-āba is giving a reward, which is something given as recompense for a gift or deed. Grief is not good, so ʾathābakum is either a mocking (tahakkumiyya) metaphor, like the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

"We hosted you and hastened your hospitality, before dawn, a crushing, grinding (meal)."

That is, Allah recompensed you for that ascending that accompanied the turning away with grief, meaning anxiety within your souls. The intent is that He punished you with grief, like His saying ﴿so give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21].

Page 132

This interpretation is distant, because the context is one of blame, not rebuke, and of excuse, not reproach. Or it is a conceptual correspondence (mushākala taqdīriyya), because when they went out to fight, they went out seeking reward, so they travelled paths by which they earned punishment. This is like the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"I fear that Ziyad's gift will be shackles, black or dark-brown fetters."

And the saying of another: "I said: cook for me a robe and a shirt." The point of this correspondence is to use it as a means to speak about the lesson that arose from this grief, and about Allah's care for them after it.

The bā' in His saying "with grief" (bi-ghammin) is for accompaniment, meaning grief together with grief, that is, the totality of griefs that came upon them from despair of victory after its signs had appeared, from the defeat, from the killing of those who were killed, and the wounding of those who were wounded. It is also permissible for the bā' to indicate exchange (ʿiwaḍ), meaning: Allah recompensed you with grief in your souls in exchange for the grief you caused the Messenger, even if the pronoun in His saying "so He rewarded you" refers to the Messenger in His saying "while the Messenger was calling you." This has a distance to it. Thus ith-āba is a metaphor in contrast to doing a good deed with its like, meaning: He recompensed you with grief. The bā' in "with grief" is the bā' of exchange. The first grief is the grief of the Messenger himself, and the second grief is the grief of the Muslims, and the meaning is that the Messenger grieved and was saddened by what befell you, just as you grieved over the report of his being killed; so his grief for your sake was a recompense for your grief for his sake.

His saying ﴿so that you would not grieve over what escaped you nor over what befell you﴾ is a first causal clause (taʿlīl) for "rewarded" (ʾathābakum), meaning: He distracted you with that grief so that you would not grieve over what escaped you of the spoils, and what befell you of killing and wounds. So He made you forget a great calamity by means of a small calamity. It has also been said: the lām is extra (zāʾida), and the meaning is "so that you would grieve," in which case it is an added intensification of rebuke and reproach if His saying "rewarded you" is mocking. Or the meaning is: the Messenger rewarded you with grief over what escaped you; that is, he remained silent about rebuking you, and showed you nothing but concern on your behalf, so that he would not remind you of the rebuke with grief over what escaped you, so he turned away from mentioning it to console your hearts. It has also been said: the meaning is that He afflicted you with the grief that arose from the defeat, so that you would become accustomed to the descent of calamities, and thus the panic and anguish at misfortunes would leave you.

In combining "what escaped you" and "what befell you" there is an antithesis (ṭibāq), which suggests another, implied antithesis, because what escaped was of the beneficial, and what befell was of the harmful.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 154 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then He sent down upon you, after distress, security in the form of drowsiness that overcame a group of you.﴾

The pronoun in His saying "Then He sent down" (thumma anzala) is the pronoun referring to the Name of Majesty (Allah), and this favours the pronoun in "He rewarded you" (athabakum) being of the same kind, so that this is not a return to the pronouns of the preceding context from His saying ﴿And Allah had already fulfilled His promise to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152]. The meaning is: then He covered you with drowsiness after the defeat. The covering is called "sending down" (inzal) because, since it was a drowsiness decreed by Allah for a specific wisdom, it was like something descending from the exalted realms, as one says: "the tranquillity (sakina) descended."

Al-amana (with a fatha on the mim) is security (al-amn), and al-nu'as is light sleep or the beginning of sleep. It removes fatigue and does not cause the one who has it to lose awareness, so it was a security, for had they slept deeply they would have been seized. Abu Talha al-Ansari, al-Zubayr and Anas ibn Malik said: "Drowsiness overtook us until the sword would fall from the hand of one of us." Through this they renewed their vigour and forgot their grief, because the lightness of grief begins after the first sleep that relieves it, as is observed in the sorrows of death and others. "Drowsiness" (nu'asan) is a precise apposition (badal mutabiq) to "security" (amana).

The apparent order would have been to place "drowsiness" first and "security" after, since "security" is in the position of a qualifier or an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), so its proper place is before the object, as in the verse of al-Anfal: ﴿when He covered you with drowsiness as a security from Him﴾ [al-Anfal: 11]. But here He placed the favour first, to honour its status, because it was made like something sent down from Allah for their victory; it is thus like the tranquillity (sakina), so it was fitting that it be made the object of "sent down," and that drowsiness be made an apposition to it.

Page 134

The majority (al-Jumhur) read yaghsha (with the yā' of the third person) on the basis that the pronoun refers to nu'as. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read taghsha (with the tā') by returning the pronoun to amana, and for this reason he described it with His saying "from you."

* * *

﴿And a group, who were concerned only for themselves, were thinking about Allah other than the truth, the thought of the Jahiliyya. They say: "Do we have any say in the matter?" Say: "Indeed the matter is entirely Allah's." They conceal within themselves what they do not reveal to you. They say: "If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here."﴾

When he mentioned the state of the group of believers, he moved on to mention the state of the group of hypocrites, as is known from the contrast, and from His saying ﴿thinking about Allah other than the truth, the thought of the Jahiliyya﴾, and from leaving out describing them with "from you" as he described the first group.

"A group" (ta'ifa) is the subject (mubtada'), described by the clause ﴿who were concerned only for themselves﴾. Its predicate (khabar) is the clause ﴿were thinking about Allah other than the truth﴾. The clause from His saying ﴿And a group, who were concerned only for themselves﴾ to His saying ﴿And Allah knows what is in the breasts﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) between the clause ﴿Then He sent down upon you﴾, the verse, and the clause ﴿Indeed those of you who turned away﴾ [Al 'Imran: 155], the verse.

The meaning of ﴿concerned only for themselves﴾ is that their selves recounted to them what brings them distress, namely their not being content with Allah's decree, their intense anguish over what had befallen them, and their regret over what had escaped them of what they thought would have saved them had they done it, i.e., remorse over what was lost. Since they were in this state, their souls were in turmoil that prevented them from tranquillity and from sleep, and this is like His later saying ﴿so that Allah may make that a regret in their hearts﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156]. It has also been said that the meaning of "concerned" (ahammathum) is that their selves brought them concern about disbelief and apostasy, and the head of this group was Mu'attib ibn Qushayr.

The clause ﴿were thinking about Allah other than the truth﴾ is either an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) arising from His saying ﴿who were concerned only for themselves﴾, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from "a group." The meaning of ﴿thinking about Allah other than the truth﴾ is that

Page 135

their vain imaginings led them to think about Allah false thoughts from the delusions of the Jahiliyya. In this there is an allusion that they had remained in their Jahiliyya and had not made their religion sincere to Allah. He has explained some of their thinking by His saying ﴿They say: "Do we have any say in the matter?"﴾. The "hal" here is the interrogative of denial, meaning negation, by the evidence of the addition of "min" before the indefinite noun, which is a characteristic of negation. It is a disavowal by themselves of being a cause in facing the enemy, to the point that what happened resulted from it; and it is an allusion that going out to fight at Uhud was an error and delusion. They also thought that Muhammad ﷺ was not a messenger, since had he been, he would have been supported with victory.

The discussion of ﴿Do we have any say in the matter?﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿You have no say in the matter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 128] mentioned earlier. "The matter" here means the affair of going out to fight. "The matter" in the sense of authority, from which comes "amir" (commander), and from it "ulu al-amr" (those in authority).

The clause ﴿They say: "Do we have any say in the matter?"﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the clause "they think," because the thought of the Jahiliyya includes the meaning of this statement. The meaning of ﴿If we had any say in the matter﴾ is: of the affair of going out to fight, or of the arrangement of people some say, i.e., an opinion, ﴿we would not have been killed here﴾, i.e., our people would not have been killed. The intended meaning is not the negation of killing along with going out to fight at Uhud; rather, the intended meaning is the negation of going out to Uhud, which was the cause of the killing of those who were killed, as the context of the indication in His saying "here" shows. So the statement is a kinayah (metonymy). This statement was made by 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul when they informed him of who among the Khazraj had been martyred that day. This is a disclaiming of the causes of war and an allusion against the Prophet and against those among the believers who advised going out, who had desired one of the two good outcomes.

This thought was not the truth because it is a confusion regarding knowledge of the attributes of Allah and the attributes of His Messenger, and of what is permissible and what is impossible. For Allah has command and guidance, and He has decree and facilitation; and likewise His Messenger has the call and legislation and the exertion of effort in supporting the religion, and he is infallible in that. But he is not infallible from the operation of worldly causes upon him, or from the war between him and his enemy being a back-and-forth (sijal). Abu Sufyan said to Heraclius when he asked him: "How was your fighting with him?"

Page 136

Abu Sufyan said to him: "He gains from us and we gain from him." Heraclius said: "Likewise is faith, until it is complete." Therefore their thinking that is not the truth.

Allah the Exalted has explained that it is the thought of the Jahiliyya, of those who did not know faith at all. These, who pretended to belief, had faith not entering their hearts, so their knowledge remained as it was since the age of the Jahiliyya.

"Jahiliyya" is an adjective applied to an omitted noun that is estimated as "group" (fi'a) or "community" (jama'a). It may sometimes be meant as the state of Jahiliyya, as in the phrase "the people of the Jahiliyya," and His saying the Exalted: "the display of the former Jahiliyya." The apparent meaning is that it is a relative noun from "jahil," i.e., one who does not know the religion and monotheism, for the Arabs used "jahl" for what is opposite to "hilm" (forbearance). Ibn al-Rumi said:

With ignorance like the ignorance of the sword while it is drawn, and with forbearance like the forbearance of the sword while it is sheathed.

And "jahl" was used for lack of knowledge. Al-Samaw'al said:

So the knowing and the ignorant are not equal.

And al-Nabigha said:

And none is ignorant of a thing like one who knows it.

I reckon that the term "Jahiliyya" is among the coinages of the Qur'an, applied to the people of polytheism to create aversion to ignorance and to encourage knowledge. For this reason the Qur'an mentions it in contexts of blame, as in His saying: ﴿Do they seek the judgment of the Jahiliyya?﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 50], ﴿and do not display yourselves as in the display of the former Jahiliyya﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33], and ﴿when those who disbelieved put into their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of the Jahiliyya﴾ [al-Fath: 26]. Ibn 'Abbas said: "I heard my father in the Jahiliyya saying: 'Give us a cup full to the brim.'" And in the hadith of Hakim ibn Hizam: that he asked the Prophet ﷺ about things he used to practise in the Jahiliyya, of charity, manumission, and maintaining family ties. And they said: "the poetry of the Jahiliyya" and "the days of the Jahiliyya." All of this was not heard except after the revelation of the Qur'an and in the speech of Muslims.

His saying "other than the truth" (ghayr al-haqq) is in the accusative as the object of "they think," as if it were said "the falsehood." The phrase "the thought of the Jahiliyya" is in the accusative as an absolute object (masdar) specifying the type, since everyone knows the beliefs of the Jahiliyya, whether one is engaged in them or has abandoned them.

Page 137

The clause "they conceal" (yukhfuna) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "they say," meaning they say that in a state where their intention is other than their outward speech. So "they conceal within themselves what they do not reveal to you" is an announcement of their hypocrisy, and that their saying "Do we have any say in the matter?" and their saying "If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here" is, although its outward form is the appearance of reproach for not being consulted, in its intent a criticism of the Prophet for his going out with the Muslims to Uhud, and that they had sounder judgment than he.

The clause "they say: If we had any say in the matter" is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the clause "they conceal within themselves," since they had said that among themselves and had not made it public; or it is an explanation of the clause "they say: Do we have any say in the matter?" when they expressed their statement to the Muslims, in which case the clause returns to the meaning of a substitution of inclusion from the clause "they think," because since it explains a clause that is a substitute, it too is like what it explains. This is more evident because of His saying after it: ﴿Say: Even if you had been in your houses﴾, for that implies that this saying spread and reached the Messenger. It is not fitting that the clause "they say: If we had any say" to its end be a fresh resumption, contrary to what is in the Kashshaf.

This statement came from Mu'attib ibn Qushayr. Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam said: "Drowsiness overcame me, and I heard Mu'attib ibn Qushayr saying: 'If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here.'" So the Qur'an related his statement as he said it, and it was attributed to all of them because they heard it and were content with it.

The clause ﴿Say: Indeed the matter is entirely Allah's﴾ is a reply rejecting this false excuse, meaning that Allah and His Messenger are not in need of your say. This clause is parenthetical. The majority read "kullahu" (entirely) with a fatha as an emphasis of the subject of "inna," and Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a damma on the basis of a new beginning (niyyat al-ibtida'), so the clause is the predicate of "inna."

* * *

﴿Say: Even if you had been in your houses, those for whom killing had been decreed would have gone out to their places of death.﴾

Page 138

Allah taught His Messenger the answer to their saying: "If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here." The answer is a refutation of their statement and an instruction to the believers to dispel what doubt might arise in their souls when they hear the words of the hypocrites; or it is an answer to the hypocrites, and knowledge is gained thereby by the believers. The clause is separated (fusilat) in following the narration of the exchange, as we have established more than once. This answer is in accordance with reality, which is that things proceed according to a decree from Allah, and submission to that after exhausting effort in seeking what is hoped for. So this answer and its like does not require abandoning causes, because the decree and judgment of Allah the Exalted are not known to us except after they occur. We are therefore commanded to strive in what may reveal Allah's agreement with our hope; if we exhaust our efforts and are deprived of what we hope for, we know that Allah's decree had earlier gone against our intent. As for abandoning causes, it is not our duty, it contradicts what Allah wills from us, and it is a turning away from what Allah has placed us in this world, and it is a distortion of the meaning of decree. The meaning is: even if you had not been here and had been in your houses, those whom Allah had written would die by being killed would have gone out and been killed in their beds in which they had lain, i.e., their places of fall, on the day of Uhud. So "was written" (kutiba) here means "was decreed," and "went out" (baraza) means went out into the open, al-baraz, which is the earth.

The majority read the ba' of "buyutikum" (your houses) with a kasra. Abu 'Amr, Warsh from Nafi', Hafs and Abu Ja'far read it with a damma.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 154 (part 2 of 2):**

*al-maḍāji'* is the plural of *maḍja'*, with a fatḥa on the *mīm* and on the *jīm*, and it is the place of *ḍujūʿ*. *Ḍujūʿ* means placing the side on the ground for rest and sleep. Its verb is of the *manaa* pattern (*bāb manaʿa*), and its regular verbal noun is *al-ḍajʿ*, whereas *al-ḍujūʿ* is not a regular verbal noun. Then the term *al-maḍja'* became dominant for the place of sleep. God the Exalted says: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾. In the hadith of Umm Zar': «His bed is like the sheath of a sword-blade» (*maḍjaʿuhu kamasalli shaṭbatin*). So the literal meaning of *ḍujūʿ* is placing the side down for sleep and rest, and here it is used figuratively (*ʿalā sabīl al-istiʿāra*) for the places where the slain fell. Its aptness lies in the fact that the martyrs are alive. Thus it is a metaphor (*istiʿāra*), or a *mushākala taqdīriyya* (an implied figurative correspondence), because their saying "we were not killed here" implies the meaning that the martyrs would have stayed in their houses, enjoying their bedding.

[Page 139]

﴿And that God may test what is in your breasts and purge what is in your hearts. And God is All-Knowing of what is in the breasts.﴾

*Wa-liyabtaliya Allāhu mā fī ṣudūrikum* is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with His saying *li-kaylā taḥzanū ʿalā mā fātakum* (so that you would not grieve over what escaped you). What lies between them consists of clauses, some of which are coordinated with the causal clause (*al-jumla al-muʿallila*) and some of which are parenthetical (*muʿtariḍa*). So this is undoubtedly addressed to the believers, and it is a second cause for His saying *fa-athābakum ghamman bi-ghamm*.

*Al-ṣudūr* (breasts) here means the inner faculties (*al-ḍamāʾir*). *Al-ibtilāʾ* means testing (*al-ikhtibār*), and here it is a metonymy (*kināya*) for its effect, which is making it manifest to people and establishing the proof against the owners of those inner faculties. This is indicated by the context of His saying *wa-llāhu ʿalīmun bi-dhāti al-ṣudūr*, as was mentioned previously in His saying, Exalted is He, *wa-liyaʿlama Allāhu alladhīna āmanū* (Āl ʿImrān 3:140).

*Al-tamḥīṣ* is the purification of a thing from what mixes with it that constitutes a defect in it, so it is like *al-tazkiya* (purification). *Al-qulūb* (hearts) here means beliefs (*al-ʿaqāʾid*). The meaning of purging what is in their hearts is cleansing them from the doubt that seeps into them upon hearing the insinuations of the hypocrites which they spread among themselves.

*Al-ṣudūr* is used for the inner faculties because *al-ṣadr* in the speech of the Arabs is used for inner feeling (*al-iḥsās al-bāṭinī*). In the hadith: «Sin is that which frets in your breast» (*al-ithmu mā ḥāka fī ṣadrika*). *Al-qalb* is used for belief because in the language of the Arabs the heart is that by which reflection and belief occur. The verb of testing is transitively linked to *al-ṣudūr* because it is the testing of dispositions and inner faculties, of what good and evil they contain, and so that what is in the self may be distinguished. The verb of purging is transitively linked to *al-qulūb* because opinions and beliefs need purging so that they may be the source of every good.

﴿Indeed, those of you who turned back on the day the two hosts met, it was only Satan who caused them to slip, because of some of what they had earned. And God has already pardoned them. Indeed God is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾

It is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence that is not grammatically tied to what precedes it) explaining the hidden cause of the defeat, which is that Satan made them slip. By "the day the two hosts met" he means the Day of Uhud. "Istazallahum" (he made them slip) means "azallahum," i.e., made them those who slip. Slipping (zalal) is a metaphor for committing a sin. The sin and the ta' in it are for emphasis, like in istafada (to benefit), istabshara (to receive good news) and istanshaqa (to inhale), and like the verse of al-Nabigha:

"They killed the Ta'i in the open plain by force, Abu Jabir, then they married Umm Jabir."

That is, nakahu (they married). From the same usage is the verse ﴿And God is free of need﴾ [al-Taghabun: 6], and his saying "He refused and became arrogant." It is not appropriate to read the sin and the ta' as meaning seeking (talab), because the intent is to rebuke them for falling into disobedience of the Messenger, so it is an actual slip that has occurred.

The intended meaning of slipping is fleeing in defeat. The use of "slipping" for this is well known and common, just as firmness of the foot is used for its opposite, which is victory. God says, ﴿And make firm our feet﴾.

The "ba'" in "bi-ba'di ma kasabu" (because of some of what they had earned) is causal (sababiyya). What is meant by "some of what they had earned" is leaving their position, disobeying the command of the Messenger, quarrelling, and hastening toward the spoils. The meaning is that what befell them was from the effects of Satan, and what they are in is due to some of their own conduct. The purpose of this is to place the responsibility for that defeat on their own shoulders, and to nullify what the hypocrites insinuated, namely attributing its responsibility to the Messenger's command to go out (to Uhud), and to God's urging the believers to fight. This is the habit of weak minds, that the concurrent act is confused with its cause. To free thought from this hidden error, the logicians set out the chapter on the implicative proposition (al-qadiyya al-luzumiyya, a conditional in which one thing necessarily follows from another) and the coincidental proposition (al-qadiyya al-ittifaqiyya, a proposition in which two things merely happen together).

The reason this verse is placed right after the preceding one is that God, after clarifying for them the rank of certainty (haqq al-yaqin) with His words ﴿Say: Even if you had been in your houses﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154], moved them to the level of apparent causes. He then explained to them that if causes have any effect, then the cause of their calamity was their own actions, which Satan inspired in them and led them astray with, so they did not perceive the cause, and it became confused for them with what merely coincided. The nature of this error is that it stands between the one who errs and correcting his mistake. The combination of these purposes in this passage, including correct knowledge, purification of souls, making God and His Messenger beloved to the believers, magnifying them in their hearts, turning them away from Satan, blameworthy deeds and disobedience of the Messenger, and exposing the foolishness of the polytheists and hypocrites, is clearly significant.

On this basis, the intended meaning of "those who turned back" is the very people addressed in His words ﴿Then He turned you away from them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152]. The pronoun in "minkum" (of you) refers to the whole army of Uhud, and so it includes those who stood firm and did not flee. According to al-Suddi, "those who turned back" were a group who fled to Medina.

As for the commentators' interpretations of His words "Satan made them slip because of some of what they had earned," al-Zamakhshari (author of al-Kashshaf) and al-Fakhr (al-Razi) mention several possibilities, but these are far from the intended purpose.

His words "And God has already pardoned them" repeat the announcement of pardon in order to console them, as in His words ﴿And God has already pardoned you﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 156:

﴿O you who have believed, do not be like those who disbelieved and said of their brothers when they traveled through the land or were raiders, "If they had remained with us, they would not have died or been killed," so that Allah may make that a regret in their hearts. And Allah gives life and causes death, and Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

A warning against returning to entertaining the beliefs of the polytheists, and an explanation of the bad outcome of those beliefs in this world as well. The speech is a fresh resumption (istnaf'). The address to the believers directly is a gentle kindness toward them all, after the reproach of a group among them, those who turned away on the day the two hosts met. The lam in His saying "to their brothers" (li-ikhwanihim) is not the lam that transitively introduces the verb of saying; rather it is the lam of causation, as in His exalted saying: "And they say to those who disbelieved, 'These are better guided than those who believed in the way'" (4:51), because the brothers are not the ones being addressed; rather they are the ones who died and were killed. The intended meaning of "brothers" is relatives by lineage, i.e., from the Khazraj who were believers, because the martyrs were among the believers.

The "idha" (when) here is a temporal adverb referring to the past, as evidenced by the verbs qalu and darabu, and a verb has been omitted, indicated by His saying "ma matu," its estimated form being: "so they died on their journey or were killed in the raid."

Ad-darb fi al-ard (striking through the land) is travel, the verb darb being used for walking, because the original sense of darb (striking) is the impact of one body upon another and its striking with it; so walking is a striking upon the earth with the feet. It is then applied to travel for trade, as in His exalted saying: "And others travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty" (73:20); and to travel in general, as here; and to travel for raiding, as in His exalted saying: "O you who have believed, when you go forth in the way of Allah, then verify" (4:94), and His saying: "And when you travel through the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer" (4:101). The apparent meaning here is travel in the interests of the Muslims, because that is what the disbelievers reproach them for; and it has been said that striking through the land was intended to mean trade. Accordingly, its being linked with killing in battle is because both are of that kind in the belief of the disbelievers.

Ghuzzan (raiders) is the plural of ghazin (one who raids). The pattern fu''al is rare as a plural of the defective active participle (fa'il), yet it is eloquent nonetheless. Its counterpart is 'ufan in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*lahā qulubun ufā al-ḥiyāḍi ujūnu*

His saying "so that Allah may make that a regret in their hearts" is a causal clause for "they said," in view of what it implies of believing that, together with declaring it, directing the prohibition against imitating them; i.e., "If you hold their belief, its effect will reach you as it reached them." So the reference of "that" (dhalika) is to the statement that indicates the belief, and on this reading the causal clause is separate from the imitation. It has been said that the lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), i.e., "Do not be like those who said," so that there followed from their saying that it became a regret in their hearts. Then His saying "so that He may make" on this reading is part of the relative clause of "those who," and among the states compared to it; thus it is understood that the prohibition against imitating them in it is because of the harm contained in it.

Al-hasrah is the intensity of grief, i.e., sorrow. This became a regret for them because they imagined that their calamity arose from their neglect of prudence, and that had they taken a course other than the one they took, they would have been saved; so they never cease to be distressed over what escaped them. The believer exerts his effort, and when he fails he submits to the decree of destiny.

His saying "And Allah is Seeing of what you do" is a warning to them against harboring a return to what they were forbidden.

﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah, or die, then forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they accumulate.﴾ ﴿And if you die or are killed, then to Allah you will be gathered.﴾

He mentioned both encouragement and warning. He made dying in the way of Allah and dying outside the way of Allah both, when forgiveness follows them, better than life and what people accumulate in it. He also made dying and being killed in the way of Allah a means to being gathered and reckoned, so let each person know with what he will meet his Lord. The waw is for conjunction, linking this to His saying ﴿Do not be like those who disbelieved﴾ and to His saying ﴿And Allah gives life and causes death﴾.

The lam in His saying ﴿And if you are killed﴾ is the preparatory lam (lam al-tawti'a), which signals that an oath is implied before it. A conditional clause follows it, so it occurs only with the conditional. The lam in His saying ﴿lamaghfiratun﴾ is the lam of the response of the oath (lam jawab al-qasam). The response is ﴿forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better﴾, because the intended sense is evidently: "forgiveness and mercy are yours."

Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read مِتُّمْ with a kasra on the mim, following the dialect of the Hijaz. They treated its past tense as like خافَ, considering its 'ayn to be kasra, and formed its present tense from the pattern of قامَ, saying يَمُوتُ and not يُماتُ. This is a mixing of the two dialects. As for the lower tribes of Mudar, they used it in both cases from the pattern of قامَ and read مُتُّمْ. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read it this way. The majority read ﴿what they accumulate﴾ with the ta' of address, while Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with the ya' of the third person, on the basis that the pronoun refers back to the polytheists. The meaning would then be: better for you than the spoils of the polytheists which they gathered and which you desired.

Killing was placed first in the first clause and dying first in the second, in consideration of the conjunction of what is thought to be more remote from the ruling. That being killed in the way of Allah is a cause of forgiveness is a near matter, whereas dying outside the way being like that is a hidden and far-fetched matter. Likewise, dying was placed first in the second clause, because killing in the way of Allah may be thought far from being followed by gathering. This also contains variety of expression, the returning of the last element to the first, and making killing the beginning and the return of the speech.

[p. 144]

﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah, or die, then forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they accumulate.﴾ ﴿And if you die or are killed, then to Allah you will be gathered.﴾

He mentioned both encouragement and warning. He made dying in the way of Allah and dying outside the way of Allah both, when forgiveness follows them, better than life and what people accumulate in it. He also made dying and being killed in the way of Allah a means to being gathered and reckoned, so let each person know with what he will meet his Lord. The waw is for conjunction, linking this to His saying ﴿Do not be like those who disbelieved﴾ and to His saying ﴿And Allah gives life and causes death﴾.

A conditional clause follows it, so it occurs only with the conditional. The lam in His saying ﴿lamaghfiratun﴾ is the lam of the response of the oath (lam jawab al-qasam). The response is ﴿forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better﴾, because the intended sense is evidently: "forgiveness and mercy are yours."

The meaning would then be: better for you than the spoils of the polytheists which they gathered and which you desired.
