That being killed in the way of Allah is a cause of forgiveness is a near matter, whereas dying outside the way being like that is a hidden and far-fetched matter. Likewise, dying was placed first in the second clause, because killing in the way of Allah may be thought far from being followed by gathering. This also contains variety of expression, the returning of the last element to the first, and making killing the beginning and the return of the speech.

[p. 144]

﴿It was by a mercy from God that you were gentle with them. Had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you. So pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter. And when you have resolved, then rely upon God. Indeed, God loves those who rely upon Him.﴾

The fa' (fa) here marks a consequence (tafri') drawn from the preceding discourse, which described the disobedience of groups among the believers and hypocrites toward the Messenger's command, and the pardon God granted them for what they did. Moreover, the event narrated in the preceding verses displays many instances of the Prophet's ﷺ gentleness toward the Muslims: he consulted them about going out, and he did not reproach them for abandoning their positions. Since God's pardon of them was known from the Messenger's treatment of them, God made the Messenger gentle toward them, in order to realize His mercy and pardon. The meaning is: God has pardoned them by His mercy, so the Messenger was gentle toward them by God's permission and by His creating him as one who shows mercy. God says: ﴿And We have sent you only as a mercy to the worlds﴾.

The bā' (ba') indicates accompaniment: "you were gentle together with the mercy of God," since his gentleness in all of this was a gentleness without any neglect of their interests, and without yielding to them in leniency regarding matters of religion. For this reason it deserved the name of mercy.

Placing the prepositional phrase first conveys restriction (qasr idafi, restriction relative to a particular context): "by a mercy from God, and not by anything else of their conditions." This restriction implies an allusion (ta'rid) that their conditions warranted severity toward them, but God softened the character of His Messenger out of mercy toward them, for a wisdom God knew in governing this community.

The particle "mā" was added after the preposition bā' to emphasize the sentence with the restriction it contains. Thus the fronting is determined to be for restriction, not merely for emphasis, and this was pointed out in al-Kashshaf (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari).

[p. 145]

Gentleness (al-lin) here is used figuratively (majaz) for broadness of character toward the community of the call and the Muslims, for overlooking the harshness of the polytheists, and for excusing slips. The past-tense verb in "lanta" (you were gentle) indicates that this quality was established and known from his character, and that his natural disposition was upon it by a mercy from God, since God created him thus. And [this is in harmony with] ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. Thus the Messenger's character is suited to realizing the outcome of God's purpose in sending him, because the Messenger comes with a law (shari'a) that he conveys from God. Thus conveying it is obligatory, with no compromise in it, and it is not affected by the character of the Messenger. He is also commanded to govern his community by that law and to implement it among them. This task is strongly connected to the suitability of the Messenger's character to the natures of his community, so that the means used to bring his community to the law fit his character, in order that the law succeed in bringing them to God's purpose for them.

Muhammad ﷺ was sent innately disposed to mercy, so he was a mercy from God toward the community in implementing His law without laxity, and with kindness and assistance in attaining it. Therefore his gentleness was made to accompany a mercy from God which God placed within him, since he was sent to mankind entirely. However, God chose that his call should first be among the Arabs, for a wisdom God intended, namely that the Arabs would be the ones who convey the law to the world.

The Arabs are a people known for their pride, their refusal of oppression, their soundness of disposition, and their quickness of understanding. They were the first to receive the religion. Harshness and severity did not suit them, but they needed to have their wildness coaxed down (istinzal ta'irihim, lit. bringing down their bird) in conveying the law to them, so that they would avoid obstinacy (mukabara), which is the sole barrier between them and submission to the truth. It is related that the Prophet's ﷺ forgiveness, pardon, and mercy were a cause for many to enter Islam, as 'Iyad mentioned some of this in his book al-Shifa'.

The pronoun in "lahum" (toward them) refers to the whole community, as the context of legislation and governance of the community requires. It does not refer to the Muslims who disobeyed the Messenger's command at Uhud, because that would not suit his following words "they would have scattered from around you," since it is not thought of the Muslims. Nor would it suit his following words "and consult them in the matter," if the purpose of consultation were seeking their opinions. Rather, the meaning is: "Had you been harsh, many of those who responded to you would have repelled you, and they would have perished." Or the pronoun refers to the hypocrites, who are referred to by his saying "and a group whose own selves had concerned them." Then the meaning is: "Had you been harsh, they would have openly declared disbelief and separated from you." It is not intended that you were gentle with them specifically at the battle of Uhud, because his later words "Had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you" etc. contradict that interpretation.

Fazza (harsh) means one of bad character, coarse in disposition. Ghaliz al-qalb (hard-hearted) means cruel, since "ghilza" (hardness) is used figuratively for cruelty and lack of tolerance, just as "lin" (gentleness) is used figuratively for the opposite. The slave girls of the Ansar said to 'Umar when he rebuked them: "You are harsher and more severe than the Messenger of God." They meant: "You are harsh and severe, unlike the Messenger of God."

Infidad (scattering) means dispersing. "Min hawlika" (from around you) means from your side and facing you. It is said: hawlahu, hawalayhi, hawlayhi, hawalihi, and bihiyalihi. The pronoun refers to those around the Messenger of God, that is, those who entered the religion, since they cannot bear harshness. The phrase is a figurative depiction (tamthil): the state of aversion from him and dislike of entering his religion is likened to scattering from around him, that is, fleeing from him in separate groups. It indicates that they were around him, that is, following him.

The tafri' (consequence) in his saying "so pardon them" follows his saying "you were gentle with them," because all the commanded actions suit gentleness. As for pardon and seeking forgiveness, their command is clear. As for the conjunction "and consult them," it is because the going out to Uhud was after consultation with them and their advice. This pronoun includes all those toward whom the Prophet ﷺ was gentle, namely his companions around him, whether or not some of them committed an act at the day of Uhud, and others.

Mushawara (consultation) is the verbal noun of shawara, and its name is shura and mashura (with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the shin). Its original form is maf'ula with a damma on the 'ayn, so the movement of the waw was transferred to the unvowelled letter before it.

It has been said: mushawara is derived from shara al-dabba, when one tests a beast's running at the time of presenting it to a buyer. The verb shara al-dabba is derived from mishwar, which is the place where animals gallop. Its origin is an arabicized form of the Persian (nashkhwar), which is what a beast leaves of its fodder. It has also been said: it is derived from shara al-'asal, meaning extracting honey from the hive, because through it truth and correctness are extracted. It occurs only in an important, difficult matter of a person's own affairs, or the affairs of a tribe, or the affairs of the community.

The alif-lam in "al-amr" (the matter) is for generality (li-l-jins), and the intended meaning of "the important matter" is the matter that is deliberated over. From this comes the saying: amrun amir (a serious matter). Abu Sufyan said to his companions, in the hadith of Heraclius: "The affair of the son of Abi Kabsha has become serious; he is feared by the king of the Banu al-Asfar." It has also been said: what is intended by "the matter" is the matter of war, so the alif-lam is for a known reference (li-l-'ahd).

The apparent meaning of "the matter" is that the intended consultation is the real one, aimed at seeking help from the opinions of those consulted, as is shown by his following words: "And when you have resolved, then rely upon God." So the plural pronoun in "and consult them" refers to the Muslims specifically. That is, consult those among the ones you were gentle toward who have embraced Islam. That is, do not let the poor judgment they showed at Uhud prevent you from seeking their opinions in other situations. What occurred was a momentary lapse on their part, and a slip from which you have rescued them.

It is also possible that what is intended is consulting 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions. Then the meaning is to take their outward conditions and their reconciliation into account, perhaps they would sincerely embrace Islam or at least not increase in hypocrisy, and to cut off their excuses in what is to come.

The verse indicates that the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to consult in what it expresses with "the matter," which is the important affairs of the community and its interests in war and other matters. That is in matters other than legislation, because if the matter contains revelation, there is no deviation from it. If there is no revelation in it, and we say that the Prophet ﷺ may exercise ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) in legislation, then consultation does not apply to it, because the nature of ijtihad is to rest upon evidences, not opinions. A mujtahid does not consult others except when he judges according to his ijtihad, as 'Umar and 'Uthman did.

Thus it is determined that the consultation commanded here is consultation in the affairs and interests of the community. God has commanded it here and praised it in the mention of the Ansar, where He says: ﴿and whose affair is by consultation among themselves﴾, and made it a condition in the matter of the family, where He says: ﴿But if they both desire weaning through mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them﴾. So with these verses He legislated consultation in all levels of interests: the interests of the family, the interests of the tribe or the city, and the interests of the community.

[p. 146]

The scholars differed regarding the implication of His saying "and consult them": whether it is for obligation (wujub) or recommendation (nadb), and whether it is specific to the Messenger, peace be upon him, or general to him and to all the rulers of the community.

The Malikis held that it is obligatory and general. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "Consultation is obligatory upon rulers. They consult the scholars regarding matters of religion that are unclear, they consult the commanders of the army regarding what concerns war, they consult the notables of the people regarding what concerns their interests, and they consult the secretaries, administrators, and ministers regarding what concerns the interests and development of the lands." Ibn al-'Arabi pointed to its obligation by saying that it is a cause of correctness, and he said: "Consultation is the measure of intellect and the cause of correctness." He indicates that we are commanded to seek correctness in the interests of the community, and whatever an obligation depends upon is itself obligatory. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Consultation is one of the foundations of the law and one of its firm rulings, and whoever does not consult the people of knowledge and religion, his removal is obligatory." And this is something on which there is no disagreement. Ibn 'Arafa objected to his statement "his removal is obligatory," but he did not object to its being obligatory. However, Ibn 'Atiyya stated that decisively, while Ibn 'Arafa objected to it by analogy with the view of the theologians that a commander is not removed if his corruption (fisq) becomes apparent. He meant: abandoning consultation does not add to its being abandoning an obligation, so it would be corruption. I say: whoever memorized has proof over whoever did not memorize. The analogy here has a valid distinction, because corruption's harm is limited to the self, whereas abandoning consultation exposes the interests of the Muslims to danger and loss. The implication of the command according to the Malikis is obligation, and the default principle for them is that there is no specificity in legislation unless there is evidence for it.

It is reported from al-Shafi'i that this is for recommendation (istihbab), so that the community may follow him, and it is general to the Messenger and others, in order to console his companions' hearts and raise their status. Something similar is reported from Qatada, al-Rabi', and Ibn Ishaq. Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn 'Ali al-Razi al-Hanafi, known as al-Jassas, rejected this, saying: "If it were known to them that when they had exhausted their effort in deriving the correct answer to what they were asked, it would not then be acted upon, there would be no consolation of their hearts nor elevation of their status in that. Rather, it would cause them distress. So consultation would have achieved nothing. Therefore this interpretation is invalid." Al-Nawawi said, at the beginning of the Book of Prayer in his commentary on Muslim: "The correct view among them is that it is obligatory, and this is the preferred opinion." Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: "The apparent meaning of the command is that it is for obligation." The scholars did not attribute to the Hanafis any view on this command, except that al-Jassas said in his book Ahkam al-Qur'an, at His saying "and whose affair is by consultation among themselves": "This indicates the great standing of consultation, since it is mentioned alongside faith and the establishment of prayer, and it indicates that we are commanded to it." The combined statement of al-Jassas indicates that the school of Abu Hanifa holds it to be obligatory.

Among the early generation (al-salaf) there were those who held that the obligation is specific to the Prophet ﷺ, as stated by al-Hasan and Sufyan. He was commanded to consult so that others would follow him and it would spread among his community, and that applies to matters in which there is no revelation. The Prophet ﷺ consulted his companions about going out to Badr, about going out to Uhud, about the matter of the captives on the day of Badr, and he consulted the whole army about returning the captives of Hawazin.

[p. 150]

The apparent meaning is that consultation does not apply to legal rulings (ahkam shar'iyyah). If a ruling comes by revelation, that is clear. If it is a matter of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), on the basis that the Prophet ﷺ was permitted to exercise ijtihad in legal matters, then ijtihad rests on evidence, not on opinions. If a mujtahid from his community does not seek consultation in his own ijtihad, how could consultation be obligatory for the Prophet ﷺ? Moreover, if he did exercise ijtihad, and we hold that error is possible for him, he would still not be left in error, by the agreement of the scholars.

It has never ceased to be the custom of the rightly-guided caliphs to consult people of opinion about the interests of the Muslims. Al-Bukhari said in the Book of I'tisam (Holding Fast) of his Sahih: "The imams after the Prophet ﷺ used to consult trustworthy people of knowledge, and the reciters (qurra') were the companions of Umar's counsel, whether elders or youths. He was reflective when it came to the Book of Allah." Al-Khatib narrated: "From Ali, who said: I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, a matter will arise after you about which the Qur'an has not been revealed and nothing has been heard from you.' He said: 'Gather for it the worshippers among my community, make it a matter of consultation among you, and do not decide it by the opinion of one person.'" Abu Bakr consulted on fighting the apostates (ahl al-riddah), and the Companions consulted on the matter of the caliphate after the death of the Prophet ﷺ. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, made the matter a shura after him among six whom he named, and made the oversight of the shura fifty men from the Ansar. Umar used to write to his governors, commanding them to consult, and he would quote to them in his letters the words of a poet, whose name I have not identified:

"My two companions, opinion does not reside in one breast;
so advise me with what you both see."

This, and shura, is something Allah has placed in human nature in its sound disposition (fitrah); that is, He created man with a love of what is good and a pursuit of success in his efforts. For this reason Allah linked the creation of the origin of mankind with consultation about his matter, when He said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to place a khalifah on the earth" (Qur'an 2:30). Allah is independent of the help of created beings in opinion, but He presented His intention to the angels so that consultation would be a practice among humans, since it is inseparably connected with their creation. The coexistence of one thing with another at the origin of creation makes them familiar and recognized to each other. Since shura is a meaning that has no independent existence, Allah made humans familiar with it through its being coexistent with their creation.

Shura has remained widespread among humans throughout the stages of history. Pharaoh consulted about the matter of Musa, peace be upon him, as Allah related about him, saying, "What do you advise?" (Qur'an 26:35). The Queen of Sheba consulted about the matter of Sulayman, peace be upon him, as Allah related of her, saying: "O chiefs, give me your opinion on my matter. I would not decide a matter until you witness me" (Qur'an 27:32). What distracts people from it is the love of despotism and the dislike of hearing what opposes one's desires. That comes from deviation of natures, not from the origin of fitrah. For this reason the despot rushes to shura in times of hardship.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said in Bahjat al-Majalis: "Shura is praised according to the common body of scholars. I do not know of anyone who was pleased with despotism except a seduced, deceptive man who seeks benefit from whoever he deals with, or a violent man who attacks when people are heedless; both of them are corrupt." The likeness of the first is the saying of Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah:

"He acted autocratically once,
but only the helpless is one who does not act autocratically."

The likeness of the second is the saying of Sa'd ibn Nashib:

"When he resolves, he casts his determination before his eyes,
and turns aside from considering the consequences.
He did not consult anyone about his affair except himself,
and was pleased with no companion but one who holds the sword."

Among the finest things said about shura is the saying of Bashshar ibn Burd:

"When opinion reaches the point of needing counsel, seek help
from the firm judgment of a sincere advisor, or the advice of a resolute one.
Do not consider shura a disgrace for you;
the outer feathers are the strength of the primary feathers."

There are many verses of this kind recorded in books of adab.

As for His saying, "So when you have resolved (fa-idha 'azamta), then rely upon Allah" (Qur'an 3:159): 'azm is the firm determination of opinion to act. The object of 'azamta is omitted because the following clause after "and consult them in the matter" indicates it. So the meaning is: "When you have resolved upon the matter." It is clear from this sequence that what is meant is: when you have resolved after consultation, that is, when the right course of action has become clear to you, and you have resolved to implement it, whether it accords with some of the opinions of those consulted, or is a different opinion whose soundness has become clear to the Messenger. An opinion may arise from the opinions of those consulted, and it is said in the proverb, "Between two opinions there is (sometimes) an opinion."

As for His saying, "then rely upon Allah" (fa-tawakkal 'ala Allah): tawakkul (reliance) in its real sense is dependence. Here it is used metaphorically for proceeding with the action while hoping from Allah for its soundness. This is the way of the people of faith. Tawakkul is an inner, rational state by which the doer turns to Allah, hoping for help and seeking refuge from failure and obstacles. It is often accompanied by a verbal expression, which is supplication for it. Thus it becomes clear that His saying "then rely upon Allah" is the indication of the response to idha and follows from it. The implied meaning is: "When you have resolved, then hasten and do not delay, and rely upon Allah," because delay has harms and hesitation wastes time. If tawakkul were the response to idha, consultation would have no benefit, because, as you know, the purpose of consultation is to seek out the most beneficial means for achieving the desired action in the best and nearest manner. Its purpose is to act on what becomes clear from it. If the intent were for tawakkul to arise from the first occurrence of the thought, there would be no benefit in the command to consult.

This verse is the clearest guidance to the meaning of tawakkul, which those who fall short, and those who follow their approach, have distorted in meaning, thereby corrupting this religion at its foundation.

As for His saying, "Indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him" (inna Allah yuhibb al-mutawakkilin): tawakkul is a sign of the truthfulness of faith. It involves contemplation of the greatness and power of Allah, the belief in one's need for Him, and not being independent of Him. This is a great courtesy toward the Creator, which indicates the servant's love for his Lord, and for this reason Allah loves him.

The verse: ﴿If Allah helps you, none can overcome you; and if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him? So let the believers rely upon Allah.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a sentence beginning a new thought), arising from His saying ﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah or die﴾ [Al 'Imran: 157], or from His saying ﴿Do not be like those who disbelieved and said of their brothers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156], and so on.

Were this report taken at its apparent sense, it would be an announcement of a matter already known to its addressees, since they are believers. No believer is ignorant that when Allah decrees the help of someone, none can repel His help, and that when He decrees that someone be forsaken, that person has no refuge from defeat. This meaning is established with respect to Allah, and no one who acknowledges His divinity and believes in His oneness is ignorant of it. And after believing that Allah has no partner in His dominion, is there any room to believe that there is an obstacle to His will? Therefore it is necessary that this report be intended in a sense other than its apparent sense. The best way to understand it is as an affirmation serving to console the believers for the defeat that befell them, so that they do not grieve over what has passed, because referring matters to Allah the Exalted when one is unable to remedy them is a solace for the soul and a consolation for the calamity.

Within this there is also an indication that Allah's granting victory to a people on some days, and forsaking them on others, happens only for wisdoms and causes. Therefore it is incumbent upon them to strive for the means of pleasing Allah, which necessitate victory, and to avoid the causes of His displeasure, which necessitate being forsaken, as indicated by His saying ﴿O you who believe, if you support Allah, He will support you﴾ [Muhammad: 7], and His saying ﴿So He rewarded you with grief upon grief﴾ [Al 'Imran: 153], and His later saying ﴿Why, when a calamity struck you, though you had inflicted twice as much, did you say, "From where is this?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 165].

Moreover, it is incumbent upon them to seek the causes by which victory was decreed for them, as on the day of Badr, and their opposites, by which they were forsaken on the day of Uhud. Reflection on this has a wide scope for uncovering the realities, the underlying causes, the causes, the wisdoms, the benefits and the harms, according to the breadth of the reflection that roams over it. Thus this great report releases thoughts from their tethers and sends them into the pastures of lessons and the race-courses of admonitions, and the foremost are the swift steeds. The report is therefore used in a lateral meaning of its sense, which is the exhortation to attain that. In this light the placement of this resumptive sentence after what preceded it becomes clear: after He had addressed them with various kinds of blame, excuse and consolation, from His saying "Indeed, precedents have passed before you" up to here, He gathered all of that for them in a comprehensive, beneficial statement, suitable for receiving the past and suitable for acting upon in the future.

It is also permissible that the report be framed as addressing one who knows as though he were one who does not know, since they displayed such greed for booty, such misinterpretation of the Messenger's command to them to stand firm, and such anguish over what befell them of defeat, killing and wounding, that their condition became like that of one who is ignorant that victory and forsaking are in the hand of Allah the Exalted. Thus the report is used in a sense contrary to what the apparent context requires.

*Al-nasr* (help): assistance in attaining deliverance from the overpowering of an enemy and of one who intends harm.

*Al-khidhlan* (forsaking), its opposite: withholding assistance while having the capacity to give it. It is derived from the wild animal's *khadhalat* when it lags behind the herd because its young one is unable to walk.

The meaning of ﴿if He helps you﴾ and ﴿if He forsakes you﴾ is: if He wills this for you. Otherwise the answer to the first condition, ﴿then none can overcome you﴾, would not be sound, since there would be no benefit in linking the non-overcoming to the actual occurrence of help, especially with the negation of the category in His saying ﴿none can overcome you﴾, because it would become an announcement of what is already known, as when you say: "If you stand, then you are not sitting." As for the verb of the second condition, ﴿and if He forsakes you﴾, it is understood similarly by analogy with its counterpart, although the meaning would stand without this interpretation. This is an instance of using the verb to mean the intention of the act, like His saying ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 6], and so on.

The answer is given in the phrase ﴿then none can overcome you﴾ rather than saying "you will not be overcome," in order to make explicit the generality of the answer, because the generality of the consequence of the condition is the general rule, though it may sometimes be particular, meaning "you will not be overcome by some of the overcomers." The intent in conveying generality is to remove the illusion of this.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿who is there that can help you after Him?﴾ is one of denial, meaning: no one helps you except Him.

The phrase *min ba'dihi* ("after Him") here is used in one of its implied meanings, which is difference and separation, meaning: who is it that helps you apart from Him, or other than Him, that is, apart from Allah? The pronoun therefore refers without doubt to the Name of Allah. The use of *ba'd* in this manner is common in the Qur'an, as He the Exalted said: ﴿Who then can guide him after Allah?﴾ [Al-Jathiyah: 23]. The origin of this usage is that it is like an implicit allegorical representation (*tamthiliyyah makniyyah*): the state resulting from the supposition of being broken is depicted as the state of one who was relied upon for help and then forsook and abandoned him, turning away from him, because a fighter beside you who turns his back on you has forsaken you. So the image that the state is likened to is omitted, and it is indicated by a concomitant, which is the phrase "after Him."

The clause ﴿and upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*), intended to command reliance upon Allah, a reliance that rests upon taking the means of Allah's help: both customary means, which is preparedness, and inner means, which are purifying the soul and following the good pleasure of Allah the Exalted.

[Page 153]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 161:

﴿It is not for a prophet to embezzle. Whoever embezzles will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection. Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾

The most apparent view is that it is joined to the whole preceding discourse by a conjunction of purpose to purpose (ʿaṭf al-gharaḍ ʿalā al-gharaḍ). Its place comes right after the statement ﴿If Allah helps you, none can overcome you﴾, etc., because it indicates that victory and abandonment are in the hand of Allah, which necessitates encouraging the seeking of His good pleasure, so that He may be gentle with those whose pleasure He seeks. Since these counsels and admonitions were addressed to them so that they would act upon them in their future military campaigns, they were alerted to something that the army takes lightly during campaigns, which is embezzlement (ghulūl), so that they would know that this does not please Allah the Exalted, and would beware of it, and be even more cautious about what most provokes the anger of Allah. This is the connection for the warning against embezzlement. What supports this is that the cause of their defeat on the Day of Uhud was their hastening to take the spoils. Ghulūl is hastening to take something from the spoils of war (ghanīma) that is being kept back.

You will not find anything other than this that is suitable as a connection for placing the verse of embezzlement after the verse of victory. The Battle of Uhud, whose story the surah recounts, saw no embezzlement, and there were no spoils for the Muslims in it. As for what some exegetes have mentioned of an incident of embezzlement that occurred at the Battle of Badr, concerning a red woollen cloak or a sword, it does not fit here, because of the distance between the Battle of Badr and the Battle of Uhud. Moreover, there is what some of them have mentioned about this verse being revealed concerning the greed of the Bedouins for the division of spoils on the Day of Ḥunayn, which occurred five years after the Battle of Uhud.

The majority of the ten readers recited ﴿yughalla﴾ with a ḍamma on the initial letter (yāʾ) and a fatḥa on the ghayn. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and ʿĀṣim recited it with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a ḍamma on the ghayn.

The verb is derived from ghulūl, which is taking something from the spoils without the permission of the commander of the army. Ghulūl is an irregular verbal noun (maṣdar ghayr qiyāsī), and the term ghulūl is also applied generally to betrayal in property.

The construction ﴿It is not for a prophet that he should embezzle﴾ is a construction of denial (ṣīghat juḥūd) that conveys emphasis in negation. Its discussion has already been given earlier, at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should give him the Book, judgement and prophethood﴾ in this surah. When it is used in a prohibitive sense, as here, it conveys emphasis in prohibition. The meaning, according to the recitation of the majority, is a prohibition to the army of the Prophet from embezzling, because embezzlement from the spoils of the Prophet ﷺ is embezzlement from the Prophet, since the division of the spoils belongs to him. As for the recitation of Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and ʿĀṣim, the meaning of the statement that the Prophet does not embezzle is that embezzlement does not occur within his army. So the attribution of embezzlement to the Prophet is metaphorical, due to the association of the army with its prophet. You may also take it as having an elided noun, so that the meaning is: It is not for the army of a prophet to embezzle.

Some of the early and later exegetes have interpretations of the meaning according to this recitation, and they contain awkwardness.

The meaning of ﴿Whoever embezzles will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is that he will come with it exposed and disgraced for theft.

Among the curious anecdotes is what al-Jāḥiẓ mentions in al-Bayān wa al-Tabyīn: that Mazīd, a man from among the Bedouins, stole a musk pouch. He was asked, "How do you steal it when Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Whoever embezzles will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection﴾?" He said, "In that case I will carry it, fragrant of scent and light of load." This is a witty remark, and the addressee receives a reply other than what he expected. Close to this is what is related from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, and the responsibility for the report lies with the one who related it. They said: When ʿUthmān sent to him to hand over his copy of the Qur'an so that he might burn it, after the Muslims had agreed upon the codex which had been written in the time of Abū Bakr, Ibn Masʿūd said: "Allah said: ﴿Whoever embezzles will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection﴾, and I am embezzling my codex, so whoever among you is able to embezzle his codex, let him do so." I do not trust the soundness of this report, because Ibn Masʿūd knows that this is not embezzlement.

His saying ﴿then every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾ is an alert to the punishment after the exposure, since it is already known that the preceding discourse is directed as a prohibition. The particle ﴿then (thumma)﴾ is used to indicate the long interval before the exposure. Among the souls who will be paid in full what they earned is the soul of the one who embezzles, so he has entered into the generality.

The clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) that emphasises the content of the clause before it, which is ﴿every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾.

The verse indicates the prohibition of embezzlement, which is taking something from the spoils (maghnam) without the permission of the commander of the army. It is among the major sins, because it is like theft. The most authentic hadith concerning embezzlement is the hadith in the Muwaṭṭaʾ: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned from Khaybar, heading for Wādī al-Qurā, he had a black slave called Midʿam. While he was unloading the saddle of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, a stray arrow came and killed him. The people said, 'Congratulations to him on paradise!' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, 'No! By the One in whose hand my soul is, the cloak which he took on the day of Khaybar from the spoils, before it was divided, will set fire to him.'"

Whoever embezzles from the spoils has taken from him what he embezzled, and he is disciplined according to independent judgement (ijtihād). There is no amputation for it, by consensus. This is the view of the majority. Al-Awzāʿī, Isḥāq, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and a group said: The goods of the embezzler are all burned, except his weapon and his saddle, and what he embezzled is returned to the public treasury (bayt al-māl). They cited a hadith narrated by Ṣāliḥ ibn Muḥammad ibn Zāʾida, Abū Wāqid al-Laythī, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb: "The Prophet ﷺ said: If you find a man has embezzled, burn his goods and beat him." It is a weak hadith. al-Tirmidhī said: "I asked Muḥammad" — meaning al-Bukhārī — "about it, and he said: It was only narrated by Ṣāliḥ ibn Muḥammad, and he is unreliable in hadith (munkar al-ḥadīth)." Moreover, even if it were sound, it would be necessary to interpret it, because the principles of the Sharia indicate that it must be interpreted. So acting upon it is an excessive clinging to the apparent meanings, and it is not part of understanding (tafaqquh) in anything.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 162–163:

Page 157
﴿Is one who pursues the good pleasure of Allah like one who has earned wrath from Allah, and whose refuge is Hell? And wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿They are of varying degrees with Allah, and Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾

This is a continuation of His saying ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 161], so it serves as an explanation of the full payment of every soul for what it earned.

The interrogative is a denial of the equivalence implied by the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih), so it carries the meaning of "they are not equal." The word ittiba' (following) here means pursuit (al-talab): it likens the state of one who seeks the pleasure of Allah through his deeds to the state of one who seeks a prey and follows it wherever it goes in order to catch it. In this comparison there is a fine admonition that attaining the pleasure of Allah the Exalted requires exceeding diligence. In the verb baa' (returned) in His saying ﴿as one who has earned wrath from Allah﴾ there is an image of the state of the person of sins, likened to one who went out seeking what would benefit him and returned with what would harm him, or who returned empty-handed, as was explained earlier regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿so their commerce did not profit﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. From this contrast the state of the people of obedience and the people of disobedience is known, or the state of the people of faith and the people of disbelief.

As for His saying ﴿They are of varying degrees with Allah﴾, the pronoun refers to (one who pursues the good pleasure of Allah), because they are the intended subject of the speech, and by the indication of His saying "varying degrees," since degrees are stations of elevation.

And His saying "with Allah" is an honouring of their stations.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 162–163:

Page 157
﴿Is one who pursues the good pleasure of Allah like one who has earned wrath from Allah, and whose refuge is Hell? And wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿They are of varying degrees with Allah, and Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾

This is a continuation of His saying ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 161], so it serves as an explanation of the full payment of every soul for what it earned.

The interrogative is a denial of the equivalence implied by the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih), so it carries the meaning of "they are not equal." The word ittiba' (following) here means pursuit (al-talab): it likens the state of one who seeks the pleasure of Allah through his deeds to the state of one who seeks a prey and follows it wherever it goes in order to catch it. In this comparison there is a fine admonition that attaining the pleasure of Allah the Exalted requires exceeding diligence. In the verb baa' (returned) in His saying ﴿as one who has earned wrath from Allah﴾ there is an image of the state of the person of sins, likened to one who went out seeking what would benefit him and returned with what would harm him, or who returned empty-handed, as was explained earlier regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿so their commerce did not profit﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. From this contrast the state of the people of obedience and the people of disobedience is known, or the state of the people of faith and the people of disbelief.

And His saying "with Allah" is an honouring of their stations.

[Page 158]

This is a resumptive statement (istinaf, a new clause that resumes the discourse) reminding the men of the Day of Uhud and the other believers of God's favour upon them. The reason for mentioning it here is that it contains a great measure of consolation for the calamity of the defeat, since it is well established that a grieving person is comforted and reassured by being reminded of the blessings he still has. It is also closely connected to His saying: ﴿It was by a mercy from Allah that you were gentle with them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. The verses on this theme in the account of Uhud came in this way, some arising from others, varied in their placement according to what the opportunities of transition from one theme to another allowed. Thus you will find that when the flow of speech gallops freely in the arena of digression (istitrad, the shifting from one topic to another), it always returns to its point of origin.

Here al-mann (the bestowal of favour) means conferring a favour, that is, a blessing, upon the one who receives it. It does not mean enumerating the blessing before the recipient, as in His saying: ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. Although this mention of the favour is itself a "mann" in the other sense, all of it is praiseworthy from God, Exalted is He, because mann was only blameworthy due to what it contains of displaying superiority over the one who receives the favour, and the bounty of Allah is not something to be denied.

By "the believers" (al-mu'minin) here is meant those who were believers at that time, namely those who were with the Prophet (ﷺ), as indicated by the context, namely His saying: ﴿when He sent among them a messenger from among themselves﴾, that is, from among their own Arab community.

The particle "idh" (when) is an adverbial complement (zarf) of "manna" (He bestowed), because the bestowal of this blessing took place at the time of the sending.

The meaning of "from among themselves" is similarity to them in the matters in which similarity is a cause of strong connection. Here these are lineage, language, and homeland. The Arabs say: "So-and-so is from the Banu so-and-so, from among themselves," meaning, from their pure stock; his affiliation to them is not by clientage (wala') or attachment. It seems that this is the reason the word "self" (nafs), which carries the sense of similarity, was applied to him. His being of their lineage, that is, being an Arab, requires their familiarity with him, their inclination toward him, and their not feeling estranged from him. His speaking their language makes them quick to understand what he brings. His being their neighbour and raised among them makes them hasten to affirm his message, since they would have known his affairs, recognized his excellence, and witnessed his uprightness and his miracles.

From al-Naqqash it is related: it was said that there is no tribe among the Arabs except that it had a kinship with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), except Taghlib. It was in this light that His saying was interpreted: ﴿Say, I do not ask you any reward for it except affection for kinship﴾ [al-Shura: 23].

[Page 159]

This favour is specific to the Arabs and is a distinction for them, in addition to the favour of the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) to all of mankind. The Arabs were the first of all people to receive the call, because Allah willed that the religion should appear among them, so that they might receive it in the complete manner suited to the purity of their minds and the speed of their understanding of the subtleties of the language. Then they would be its bearers to mankind, becoming helpers in the universality of the call. For whoever takes on the characteristics of the Arabs, masters their language, and is intimately acquainted with their customs and tastes, there is an approach to this distinction, and it is its greater part, since nothing of it is missed except lineage and homeland, and these two are only complements to a good reception. For this reason, during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the believers were exclusively Arabs, so that their reception of the call was equal in understanding, until the religion became firmly established. It has been reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever enters Islam is from the Arabs."

His saying "recites to them His verses" means he reads the Qur'an to them. The units of the Qur'an were called "verses" (ayat) because each one of them is a proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger, in terms of eloquence of expression and perfection of meaning, as was mentioned in the eighth introduction among the introductions to this commentary. Thus they were fit to understand what was recited to them without need of an interpreter (turjuman).

Al-tazkiyah (purification) means cleansing: He purifies the souls by the guidance of Islam.

Teaching the Book is clarifying the aims of the Qur'an and commanding them to memorize its wording, so that its meanings would be present with them.

By "wisdom" (al-hikmah) is meant what the Sharia contains of refining morals and regulating rulings, because all of that prevents souls from evil conditions and disorder of the system. That is part of the meaning of wisdom. What was said about this was already discussed under His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269].

The conjunction of "wisdom" with "the Book" is the conjunction of what is more specific in one respect to what is more general in one respect (*'atf al-akhass min wajh 'ala al-a'amm min wajh*). Some wisdom is in the Book, such as His saying: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾ [al-Hashr: 9]. Some wisdom is not in the Book, such as his saying, peace be upon him: "A believer is not stung twice from the same hole." And some things in the Book are knowledge but not wisdom, such as the obligation of prayer and pilgrimage.

[Page 160]

The clause ﴿and indeed they were before that in clear error﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). The particle *in* here is the light (mukhaffafah) and inactive (muhmalah) form of *inna*. The clause following it is a predicate of an omitted pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*). The clause is its predicate according to the opinion of the author of al-Kashshaf, and this is the correct view, since there is no reason for its governing power to cease while its meaning remains. Nor is there any reason to distinguish it from the open form (*an*) when it is lightened, for they have assumed for it a noun, which is the pronoun of the matter. Rather, we find that the kasra form (*in*) is more deserving of retaining its governing power when lightened, because it is the "mother of the category" (*umm al-bab*), so its governing power does not easily cease. The majority of grammarians (nuhat) said: its governing power is annulled, and a clause follows it. According to this, its being inactive means that it does not govern two nouns; rather, it governs a pronoun of the matter and a clause, either nominal or verbal, whose verb is usually one of the abrogating verbs (*nawasikh*).

The word "clear" (mubin) is applied to "error" because, owing to its severity, it is not confused by anyone with any admixture of guidance or doubt. So its state makes it evident that it is error, as in His saying: ﴿and they said, "This is clear magic"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 7].

What is meant by it is the error of polytheism, ignorance, mutual killing, and the rulings of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam).

It is permissible that His saying ﴿upon the believers﴾ includes the believers of all eras, and by His being "from among themselves" is meant that he is of the human species. The attribution to him of the teaching of the Book and wisdom combines both real and metaphorical attribution, because the teaching of these is received from him directly or through an intermediary.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 165:

﴿Why is it that when a disaster struck you, though you had inflicted twice as much (on the enemy), you said, "How is this?" Say, "It is from yourselves." Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾

The rhetorical interrogative of denial and wonder is joined to what preceded it, for their saying "How is this?" is something that is denied, and the listener is astonished that it came from them after they knew the causes of the disaster that they had brought about, since it should not be hidden from anyone of understanding. The placement of this interrogative comes after what has been repeated: recording upon them the responsibility for the defeat because of what they committed, namely disobedience to the command of the Messenger, and haste toward the spoils; and after He had commanded them to be content with what occurred, and reminded them of the victory that took place on the day of Badr, He joined to that here the denial of their wonder at the defeat that befell them.

Lamma (لَمّا) is a noun of time that carries the meaning of a conditional, so it indicates the existence of its answer due to the existence of its condition, and it is necessarily followed by a clause of its condition. The meaning is: "You said, when a disaster struck you: 'How is this?'"

The clause ﴿قَدْ أصَبْتُمْ مِثْلَيْها﴾ is a qualifier of (مُصِيبَةٌ). The meaning of أصَبْتُمْ is that you overcame the enemy and gained from them twice what they had inflicted on you with it; it is said أصاب when he overcame, as Qatari ibn al-Fuja'a said:

"Then I turned away, having overcome, and I was not overcome, a mature in insight, a seasoned in advance."

What is meant by مِثْلَيْها is two equivalents in kind or value, considering the aspect of similarity; that is: indeed you had gained twice what had struck you. The similarity here is similarity in measure and value, not in kind, for the calamities of war are of different kinds: killing, captivity, spoils, and booty. On the day of Uhud, the Muslims suffered killing, since seventy of them were killed, and they had killed seventy of the polytheists on the day of Badr; so this is one of the two equivalents. Then they had taken captives from the polytheists on the day of Badr, and that is another equivalent in quantity, since the captive is like the slain. Or it is meant that on the day of Uhud they inflicted killing, but their number was fewer, so it is an equivalent in kind, not in measure and value.

And (أنّى) is an interrogative meaning "from where", and they intended by it wonder and denial; the clause ﴿قُلْتُمْ أنّى هَذا﴾ is the answer of (لَمّا), and the interrogative with (أنّى) here is used for wonder.

Then the denial and wonder are concluded with His saying ﴿قُلْ هو مِن عِنْدِ أنْفُسِكم إنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾, meaning: indeed Allah is capable of your victory and of your abandonment; so when you disobeyed and drew anger upon yourselves, Allah decreed for you the abandonment.

[Page 162]

﴿Whatever befell you on the day the two hosts met was by the permission of God, and that He might know the believers﴾ ﴿and that He might know those who played the hypocrite. It was said to them, "Come, fight in the way of God, or repel [the enemy]." They said, "If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly follow you." They were nearer to disbelief that day than to faith, saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts, and God knows best what they conceal﴾ ﴿Those who said of their brothers, while they themselves sat back, "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed." Say, "Then avert death from yourselves, if you are truthful"﴾.

**[Page 165]**

His words, "*Wa-lā taḥsabanna*" (﴿And do not reckon﴾), are a continuation of His words "*Qul fa-dra'ū ʿan anfusikumu al-mawt*" (﴿Say: "Avert death from yourselves"﴾). When God commanded His Prophet to answer them in a way that rebuked them, He adopted the method of letting them have free rein in their assumption that their brethren who were killed had gone to waste. So it was said to them: death cannot be escaped in any case. After that, He turned away from addressing them, because of their lack of capacity, and addressed those who deserve to know. So He said, ﴿And do not reckon those who were killed in the way of God to be dead﴾. This is a refutation of what the hypocrites lamented over the loss of their slain.

The address may be directed to the Prophet (ﷺ) as an instruction to him, so that he may teach the Muslims. It may also follow the Arab practice of not intending a specific addressee.

*Al-ḥusbān* (reckoning, i.e., supposing) means *al-ẓann* (assumption). The prohibition is therefore against assuming that they are dead, and even more so against asserting outright that they are dead.

The majority (*al-Jumhūr*) read *alladhīna qutilū* with a light *tāʾ*. Ibn ʿĀmir read it with a doubled *tāʾ* (*quttilū*), meaning they were killed in great numbers.

His words, "*Bal aḥyāʾ*" (﴿Rather, they are alive﴾), are a *idrāb* (a turning away from a previous statement, here "do not reckon"). For this reason, what follows is a full clause (*jumla*) and not a single word, since it turns away from the judgment of the clause and not from a single element within it. The proper form of the following clause is nominal, consisting of an omitted subject and an expressed predicate, so the sense is "*Bal hum aḥyāʾ*" (Rather, they are alive). For this reason the Seven Readers read it with *raf*ʿ (nominative). It is also read with *naṣb* (accusative), on the basis that the clause is verbal, meaning "*Bal aḥasibtum aḥyāʾan*" (Do you suppose them alive?). Abu ʿAli al-Farisi rejected this reading.

The Qur'an has affirmed for the fighters in the cause of God an apparent death by His words "*qutilū*", and has denied them real death by His words "*bal aḥyāʾ ʿinda rabbihim yurzaqūn*" (﴿Rather, they are alive, with their Lord, provided for﴾). Thus we know that although they are dead in their bodies, they are alive in their spirits, with a life beyond the mere survival of spirits, one that does not perish. Rather, it is a life in the sense that the effects of life are realised for their spirits, through the attainment of pleasures and perceptions that gladden their souls and their delight in their brethren. For this reason His words "*ʿinda rabbihim*" (with their Lord) indicate that their life is specific to them. It is not the life commonly known in this world, I mean the life of bodies, the flowing of blood in the veins, and the beating of the heart. Nor is it the life of spirits that is common to the spirits of all people. Likewise, provision must be fitting to the life of the spirits, and this is the provision of bliss in Paradise.

If we attach "*ʿinda rabbihim*" to "*aḥyāʾ*", as is the apparent reading, the matter is clear. If we attach it to "*yurzaqūn*", the matter is likewise, since this life produces a provision that exists with God, so it is a life that is neither material nor worldly. In that case, placing the adverbial phrase first serves to emphasise the existence of this provision.

His words, "*farīḥīna*" (﴿rejoicing﴾), are a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of the pronoun in "*yurzaqūn*".

*Al-istibshār* is the attainment of good news. The *sīn* and *tāʾ* in it are as in His words, *wa-staghnā Allāh* (God is self-sufficient), and God has combined for them joy in themselves with joy in those of their brethren who remain behind. For in their remaining there is a rout of their enemies. And although they have attained the merit of martyrdom at the hands of the enemies, they wish for the destruction of their enemies, because in that destruction is the fulfilment of another hope for them, which is the hope of the victory of the religion.

So what is meant by "*alladhīna lam yalḥaqū bihim*" (those who have not yet joined them) is their companions who used to fight alongside them. The meaning of "*lam yalḥaqū bihim*" is that they have not been martyred, so as to arrive at the life of the Hereafter.

"*Min khalfihim*" (behind them) is a figure of speech meaning "after them". The sense is: they rejoice in those of their companions who have not yet gone to the Hereafter, that they are secure and free from what would grieve them. His words, "*allā khawfun ʿalayhim*" (﴿that there is no fear upon them﴾), are a *badal al-ishtimāl* (an inclusive substitution). The *lā* operates as *laysa* (like "not") and retains its meaning. The noun after *lā* is not built on *fatḥ* here, because it is evident that the intention is to negate the whole category, and there is no possibility of negating unity. Therefore there is no need to build the indefinite noun on *fatḥ*. This is like the saying of one of the women in the hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is like the night of Tihamah, neither hot nor cold, no fear and no weariness", with the three indefinite nouns in the nominative.

In this there is an indication that the spirits of these martyrs have been granted insight into those matters of those concerned with their affairs in this world that gladden them. This insight applies to all martyrs in the cause of God. It may be specific to the matters that gladden them, since those are a pleasure to them. It may also be general to all matters, since the pleasure of spirits is attained through knowledge. Moreover, the Imam al-Razi restricted true pleasure to knowledge, which is the pleasure of the wise in knowing the realities of things, even if those realities are bad.

In the verse there is also good news for the living companions of Uhud, that no calamity will befall them after that day.

**[Page 166]**

The pronoun in "*yastabshirūna bi-niʿmatin min Allāh*" (﴿they rejoice in a bounty from God﴾) may refer to "*alladhīna lam yalḥaqū bihim*", in which case the clause is a *ḥāl* of those who have not yet joined them. The sense is: there is no fear upon them and no grief, so they rejoice in a bounty from God. It is also possible that it is a repetition of His words "*yastabshirūna bi-alladhīna lam yalḥaqū bihim*", with the pronoun referring to "*alladhīna qutilū fī sabīl Allāh*". The purpose of the repetition is to confirm the meaning of good news, like His words, "*Our Lord, these are those whom we misled; we misled them as we ourselves were misled*", where He repeats "*aghwaynāhum*" (we misled them). Moreover, this rejoicing is from them, and it returns to their own selves, and it returns to their companions who responded to God and the Messenger after the wound. The first is in reference to their brethren.

*Al-niʿmah* is that by which there is goodness, and *al-faḍl* is an increase in the bounty.

His words, "*wa-anna Allāh lā yuḍīʿu ajr al-muʾminīn*" (﴿and that God does not waste the reward of the believers﴾), the majority read with *fatḥ* on the *hamzah* of *anna*, as a conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) on "*niʿmatin min Allāh wa-faḍl*". The purpose of this is to magnify what they attained of rejoicing and expansion of souls, by God combining for them both bodily particular pleasure and general rational pleasure. For the perception of universal realities is a great spiritual pleasure, because of the nobility of universal realities and the nobility of knowledge of them, and the soul's delight in their disclosure to it and its perception of them. That is, they rejoiced in having come to know a universal reality and a noble secret from the secrets of knowledge of God's attributes and perfections, whose effects encompass all people of perfection. Thus it includes both those who perceived it and others. Without this great meaning there would be no call for the addition "*wa-anna Allāh lā yuḍīʿu ajr al-muʾminīn*", since by its addition there is no increase in a bounty or favour of the same kind as the first bounty and favour for those who rejoice. Rather, there have come about two other bounties and favours.

Al-Kisa'i read the *hamzah* of "*inna*" with *kasra*, as an attachment to the clause "*yastabshirūna*" in the sense of a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*). It is then not included in what the martyrs rejoiced in. It is also possible, on this reading, that the clause is a new beginning of speech, and the *wāw* is then for resumption (*istiʾnāf*).

**[Page 165]**

When God commanded His Prophet to answer them in a way that rebuked them, He adopted the method of letting them have free rein in their assumption that their brethren who were killed had gone to waste. So it was said to them: death cannot be escaped in any case. After that, He turned away from addressing them, because of their lack of capacity, and addressed those who deserve to know. So He said, ﴿And do not reckon those who were killed in the way of God to be dead﴾. This is a refutation of what the hypocrites lamented over the loss of their slain.

The address may be directed to the Prophet (ﷺ) as an instruction to him, so that he may teach the Muslims. It may also follow the Arab practice of not intending a specific addressee.

*Al-ḥusbān* (reckoning, i.e., supposing) means *al-ẓann* (assumption). The prohibition is therefore against assuming that they are dead, and even more so against asserting outright that they are dead.

The majority (*al-Jumhūr*) read *alladhīna qutilū* with a light *tāʾ*. Ibn ʿĀmir read it with a doubled *tāʾ* (*quttilū*), meaning they were killed in great numbers.

His words, "*Bal aḥyāʾ*" (﴿Rather, they are alive﴾), are a *idrāb* (a turning away from a previous statement, here "do not reckon"). For this reason, what follows is a full clause (*jumla*) and not a single word, since it turns away from the judgment of the clause and not from a single element within it. The proper form of the following clause is nominal, consisting of an omitted subject and an expressed predicate, so the sense is "*Bal hum aḥyāʾ*" (Rather, they are alive). For this reason the Seven Readers read it with *raf*ʿ (nominative). It is also read with *naṣb* (accusative), on the basis that the clause is verbal, meaning "*Bal aḥasibtum aḥyāʾan*" (Do you suppose them alive?). Abu ʿAli al-Farisi rejected this reading.

The Qur'an has affirmed for the fighters in the cause of God an apparent death by His words "*qutilū*", and has denied them real death by His words "*bal aḥyāʾ ʿinda rabbihim yurzaqūn*" (﴿Rather, they are alive, with their Lord, provided for﴾). Thus we know that although they are dead in their bodies, they are alive in their spirits, with a life beyond the mere survival of spirits, one that does not perish. Rather, it is a life in the sense that the effects of life are realised for their spirits, through the attainment of pleasures and perceptions that gladden their souls and their delight in their brethren. For this reason His words "*ʿinda rabbihim*" (with their Lord) indicate that their life is specific to them. It is not the life commonly known in this world, I mean the life of bodies, the flowing of blood in the veins, and the beating of the heart. Nor is it the life of spirits that is common to the spirits of all people. Likewise, provision must be fitting to the life of the spirits, and this is the provision of bliss in Paradise.

If we attach "*ʿinda rabbihim*" to "*aḥyāʾ*", as is the apparent reading, the matter is clear. If we attach it to "*yurzaqūn*", the matter is likewise, since this life produces a provision that exists with God, so it is a life that is neither material nor worldly. In that case, placing the adverbial phrase first serves to emphasise the existence of this provision.

His words, "*farīḥīna*" (﴿rejoicing﴾), are a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) of the pronoun in "*yurzaqūn*".

*Al-istibshār* is the attainment of good news. The *sīn* and *tāʾ* in it are as in His words, *wa-staghnā Allāh* (God is self-sufficient), and God has combined for them joy in themselves with joy in those of their brethren who remain behind. For in their remaining there is a rout of their enemies. And although they have attained the merit of martyrdom at the hands of the enemies, they wish for the destruction of their enemies, because in that destruction is the fulfilment of another hope for them, which is the hope of the victory of the religion.

So what is meant by "*alladhīna lam yalḥaqū bihim*" (those who have not yet joined them) is their companions who used to fight alongside them. The meaning of "*lam yalḥaqū bihim*" is that they have not been martyred, so as to arrive at the life of the Hereafter.

"*Min khalfihim*" (behind them) is a figure of speech meaning "after them". The sense is: they rejoice in those of their companions who have not yet gone to the Hereafter, that they are secure and free from what would grieve them. His words, "*allā khawfun ʿalayhim*" (﴿that there is no fear upon them﴾), are a *badal al-ishtimāl* (an inclusive substitution). The *lā* operates as *laysa* (like "not") and retains its meaning. The noun after *lā* is not built on *fatḥ* here, because it is evident that the intention is to negate the whole category, and there is no possibility of negating unity. Therefore there is no need to build the indefinite noun on *fatḥ*. This is like the saying of one of the women in the hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is like the night of Tihamah, neither hot nor cold, no fear and no weariness", with the three indefinite nouns in the nominative.

In this there is an indication that the spirits of these martyrs have been granted insight into those matters of those concerned with their affairs in this world that gladden them. This insight applies to all martyrs in the cause of God. It may be specific to the matters that gladden them, since those are a pleasure to them. It may also be general to all matters, since the pleasure of spirits is attained through knowledge. Moreover, the Imam al-Razi restricted true pleasure to knowledge, which is the pleasure of the wise in knowing the realities of things, even if those realities are bad.

In the verse there is also good news for the living companions of Uhud, that no calamity will befall them after that day.
