Rather, there have come about two other bounties and favours.

Al-Kisa'i read the *hamzah* of "*inna*" with *kasra*, as an attachment to the clause "*yastabshirūna*" in the sense of a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*). It is then not included in what the martyrs rejoiced in. It is also possible, on this reading, that the clause is a new beginning of speech, and the *wāw* is then for resumption (*istiʾnāf*).

The clause "*alladhīna istajābū li-llāh wa-r-rasūl*" (﴿those who responded to God and the Messenger﴾) is either an attribute of "*al-muʾminīn*", or a subject whose predicate is "*lil-ladhīna aḥsanū minhum wa-ttaqaw ajrun ʿaẓīm*" (﴿for those among them who did good and were mindful of God, there is a great reward﴾). This response points to what occurred after Uhud, namely the rumour spread that the polytheists, after reaching al-Rawha', had considered that if they caught up with the Muslims they would destroy them utterly. This has already been mentioned, together with what happened to Ma'bad ibn Abi Ma'bad al-Khuza'i, at His words, ﴿O you who believe, if you obey those who disbelieve, they will turn you back on your heels﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:149). The matter of the wound was discussed earlier at His words, ﴿If a wound touches you﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:140). Apparently the wound here is figurative, and for this reason it is not made plural to say *qurūḥ* (wounds).

﴿Those to whom the people said: "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it increased them in faith, and they said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."﴾ ﴿So they returned with favour from Allah and bounty, no harm having touched them, and they followed the pleasure of Allah; and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ ﴿That is only the Satan who frightens his allies, so do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers.﴾

It is permissible that "those to whom the people said" through to the end [of the verse] is a substitution (badal) for "those who responded to Allah and the Messenger," or a qualifier (ṣifah) of it, or a second qualifier of "the believers" in His saying "and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers," following the method of omitting the conjunction in reports. The relative pronoun is repeated, rather than the relative clause being conjoined to the preceding relative clause, out of concern for this second relative clause, so that it does not appear as part of the previous clause. It is also permissible that this is the beginning of a new, resumed statement, in which case the subject is His saying "That is only the Satan who frightens his allies," meaning: that statement, as will come. This is a transition (takhallus) by mentioning an affair of the Muslims, with which Allah sufficed them against the might of their enemy one year after the Day of Uhud, in fulfilment of their promise with Abu Sufyan when he said: "Our appointment is Badr in the coming year." Abu Sufyan had disliked going out to meet the Muslims at that appointed time, and he schemed against the Muslims in order to show that they had broken the promise, so that he could make this a pretext for spreading rumours among the Arabs about the weakness of the Muslims. Thus he arranged for a caravan from ʿAbd al-Qays, passing through Marr al-Ẓahrān near Mecca and heading for Medina to trade for provisions, to inform the Muslims that the Quraysh had gathered a great army against them. With the caravan was Nuʿaym ibn Masʿūd al-Ashjaʿī. Nuʿaym and those with him informed the Muslims of this, and that increased the Muslims in readiness and in zeal for the religion, and they went out to the appointment,

[Page 169]

which was Badr. They did not find the polytheists, and they waited for them there. There was a market there, so they traded and returned safe and unharmed. That is His saying, may He be exalted: "Those to whom the people said," i.e. the ʿAbdī caravan: "Indeed the people have gathered against you," i.e. the Quraysh have gathered against you. He omitted the object of "gathered," i.e. they gathered themselves, their numbers and their allies, as they did on the first Day of Badr.

Some exegetes and grammarians (ahl al-ʿarabiyyah) said: the word "the people" (al-nās) here was applied to Nuʿaym ibn Masʿūd and Abu Sufyan, and they took this as evidence that "the people" is used to mean a single individual, and the verse allows it. The use of the word "the people" to mean one person, or something similar, is employed for the purpose of concealment (ibhām). From it is His saying: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ [Qur'an 4:54]. The exegetes said: by "the people" He means Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying "but it increased them in faith" means: the saying of the people increased them. The hidden pronoun of nominative case in "fa-zādahum" refers either to the statement derived from the verb "said to them the people," or to "the people." Since that statement was intended to frighten the Muslims and turn them back from their purpose, and what resulted from it was the opposite of what the polytheists intended, He made what resulted from it an increase in the faith of the Muslims. The apparent meaning is that "faith" (īmān) here is applied to action, that is, the resolve to help and to fight, and in this sense it increases and decreases. The question of the increase and decrease of faith is an old one, and the dispute about it is based on whether actions are called "faith," as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And Allah would not waste your faith﴾ [Qur'an 2:143], meaning your prayer. As for inner assent (taṣdīq qalbī), which is the heart's firm commitment to the affirmation of the existence of Allah and His attributes, His sending of messengers, and the truthfulness of the Messenger, it accepts neither decrease nor increase. For this reason there is no disagreement among Muslims regarding this meaning, and the disagreement is only about the wording. However, it has been established in the science of ethics (ʿilm al-akhlāq) that a firm conviction, when its proofs are repeated, or its time lengthens, or experiences accompany it, becomes clearer and more manifest, and this is what is expressed as a settled disposition (malakah). Perhaps this meaning is among what is intended by the increase, by the indication that the Qur'an did not apply the description of deficiency to faith but mentioned only increase. Abraham, peace be upon him, also said: ﴿Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest﴾ [Qur'an 2:260].

[Page 170]

Their saying: ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾ is a phrase which perhaps they were inspired with, or received from the Prophet (ﷺ). "Ḥasbu" means: sufficient. It is a fixed noun with the meaning of a qualifier, having no verb. They said: from it is His name, the Ḥasīb, which is a form of faʿīl with the meaning of mufʿil. It was said: "al-iḥsāb" is "al-ikfāʾ" (sufficing), and it was said: it is a verbal noun (ism fiʿl) meaning "kafā" (it suffices), and this is the apparent meaning of the Qāmūs (the lexicon). Ibn Hisham in his Tawḍīḥ refuted this, saying that the entry of governing particles upon it, as in "fa-inna ḥasbaka Allāh" and the saying "bi-ḥasbika dirham" (a dirham is enough for you), contradicts the claim that it is a verbal noun, because verbal nouns do not take governing particles. It was also said: it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and this is the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's speech. It is among the nouns that necessarily take an attached genitive (iḍāfah) in form but not in meaning, so it is built on ḍamm like "qabl" and "baʿd," as in their saying: "give him two dirhams and that is enough" (fa-ḥasb), and then a new meaning is renewed for it, so it means "and nothing else." Its being attached to a noun does not make it definite, because it has the force of a derived noun (mushtaqq), and for this reason an indefinite noun is described by it. It is invariable in singular and masculine form, so it is not dualised, pluralised, or feminised, because, being fixed, it resembles the verbal noun, or because it is a verbal noun, or because it is a verbal noun, which is the nature of verbal nouns. Its meaning is: they relied on Allah as helper, even though they were few and weak.

The clause "and He is the best Disposer of affairs" is conjoined to "Allah is sufficient for us" within the speech of the speakers, so the waw belongs to the reported speech, not to the reporting. This is conjunction of a performative (inshāʾ) statement to a declarative (khabar) statement in which only suitability is sought.

The one praised is omitted because its indicator has preceded.

"Al-Wakīl" is a form of faʿīl with the meaning of mafʿūl, i.e. one to whom affairs are entrusted (mawkūl). It is said: "wakala ḥājatahu ilā fulān" when he relied upon him to fulfil it and delegated to him its accomplishment. It is said of one who cannot manage his affairs by himself: "rajul wakal" (with two fatḥahs), i.e. one who relies heavily on others. So the wakīl is the one who takes care of the affairs of the one who appointed him, and this taking care varies according to the circumstances in which he is entrusted, and by this variation the meaning of "wakīl" varies. If the task is to repel hostility and oppression, the wakīl is the helper and defender, as in: ﴿Say: I am not a wakīl over you﴾, and from it: ﴿Who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be a wakīl over them?﴾. From it is the wakīl in litigation. If it concerns the affairs of life, the wakīl is the guarantor (kāfil) and the one who suffices. From it is

[Page 171]

His saying: ﴿that you do not take besides Me a wakīl﴾, as He said: ﴿And you have made Allah your guarantor (kafīl)﴾. For this reason, among His names, may He be exalted, is "al-Wakīl." His saying "and they said: Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs" is from it. From it is the wakīl over property, and for this reason the name kafīl was also applied to this meaning in His saying: ﴿And you have made Allah your guarantor﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī (in al-Kashshāf) understood al-wakīl to include this in his commentary on His saying: ﴿and He is Wakīl over all things﴾ in Sūrat al-Anʿām, saying: "He is the owner of all things, of sustenance and of terms, the watcher over deeds." That indicates that "al-wakīl" is a comprehensive name for the guardian and keeper in matters that people care to preserve, guard, and store, and for this reason it is restricted and generalised according to contexts.

His saying "so they returned with favour from Allah" is a consequence (taʿqīb) of the report of the firmness of their faith and their saying: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." It is a consequence of an omitted element indicated by the verb "fa-nqalabū," because "returning" (inqilāb) requires that they had gone out to meet the enemy, of whom it had reached them that they had gathered against them, and they did not heed the frightening of Satan. The estimate is: "so they went out, then returned with favour from Allah."

The bāʾ is for accompaniment (mulābasah), i.e. they were accompanied by favour and bounty from Allah. The favour is what they took of wealth, and the bounty is the bounty of jihād. The meaning of "no harm touched them" is that they did not encounter fighting with the polytheists.

The clause "That is only the Satan who frightens his allies" is either an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), if you make His saying "those to whom the people said" a substitution or qualifier, as has been mentioned; or it is a predicate of "those to whom the people said," if you make His saying "those to whom the people said" a subject, and the estimate is: "those to whom the people said, etc., indeed their saying is what Satan frightens with." The link (rābiṭ) of this clause to the subject, which is "those to whom the people said" on this estimate, is the demonstrative noun, and the demonstrative noun is the subject.

Then the demonstrative in His saying "that" either refers to the statement, so the word "Satan" on this is a second subject, and its word is used in its literal meaning, and the meaning is: that statement arose

[Page 172]

from the whispering of Satan in the souls of those who plotted the scheme of spreading rumours through that statement, to frighten the Muslims through the caravan of ʿAbd al-Qays.

Or the demonstrative refers to "the people" in His saying "the people said to them," because "the people" is interpreted as a single person, namely Nuʿaym ibn Masʿūd. Then "the Satan" is an apposition or explanation of the demonstrative, and the term "Satan" was applied to him by way of eloquent metaphor (tashbīh balīgh).

His saying "frightens his allies" is estimated as "frightens you with his allies," so the first object of "yukhawwif" is omitted, being indicated by His saying after it: "so do not fear them," because "kh-w-f" (causative) takes two objects, as it is the doubled form of the unaugmented "khāfa," which takes one object. By doubling it became transitive to two objects, after the pattern of "kasā," as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and Allah warns you of Himself﴾ [Qur'an 3:28].

The pronoun in "so do not fear them" on this reading refers to "his allies." The clause "but fear Me" is a parenthetical insertion between the clause "so do not fear them" and the clause "if you are believers."

His saying "if you are believers" is a conditional clause whose consequent (jawāb) is placed later, its indicator having preceded. It is an admonition and an urging of their faith. Otherwise it is known that they are truly believers.

His saying "but it increased them in faith" means: the saying of the people increased them. The hidden pronoun of nominative case in "fa-zādahum" refers either to the statement derived from the verb "said to them the people," or to "the people." Since that statement was intended to frighten the Muslims and turn them back from their purpose, and what resulted from it was the opposite of what the polytheists intended, He made what resulted from it an increase in the faith of the Muslims. The apparent meaning is that "faith" (īmān) here is applied to action, that is, the resolve to help and to fight, and in this sense it increases and decreases. The question of the increase and decrease of faith is an old one, and the dispute about it is based on whether actions are called "faith," as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And Allah would not waste your faith﴾ [Qur'an 2:143], meaning your prayer. As for inner assent (taṣdīq qalbī), which is the heart's firm commitment to the affirmation of the existence of Allah and His attributes, His sending of messengers, and the truthfulness of the Messenger, it accepts neither decrease nor increase. For this reason there is no disagreement among Muslims regarding this meaning, and the disagreement is only about the wording. However, it has been established in the science of ethics (ʿilm al-akhlāq) that a firm conviction, when its proofs are repeated, or its time lengthens, or experiences accompany it, becomes clearer and more manifest, and this is what is expressed as a settled disposition (malakah). Perhaps this meaning is among what is intended by the increase, by the indication that the Qur'an did not apply the description of deficiency to faith but mentioned only increase. Abraham, peace be upon him, also said: ﴿Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest﴾ [Qur'an 2:260].

[Page 170]

Their saying: ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾ is a phrase which perhaps they were inspired with, or received from the Prophet (ﷺ). "Ḥasbu" means: sufficient. It is a fixed noun with the meaning of a qualifier, having no verb. They said: from it is His name, the Ḥasīb, which is a form of faʿīl with the meaning of mufʿil. It was said: "al-iḥsāb" is "al-ikfāʾ" (sufficing), and it was said: it is a verbal noun (ism fiʿl) meaning "kafā" (it suffices), and this is the apparent meaning of the Qāmūs (the lexicon). Ibn Hisham in his Tawḍīḥ refuted this, saying that the entry of governing particles upon it, as in "fa-inna ḥasbaka Allāh" and the saying "bi-ḥasbika dirham" (a dirham is enough for you), contradicts the claim that it is a verbal noun, because verbal nouns do not take governing particles. It was also said: it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and this is the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's speech. It is among the nouns that necessarily take an attached genitive (iḍāfah) in form but not in meaning, so it is built on ḍamm like "qabl" and "baʿd," as in their saying: "give him two dirhams and that is enough" (fa-ḥasb), and then a new meaning is renewed for it, so it means "and nothing else." Its being attached to a noun does not make it definite, because it has the force of a derived noun (mushtaqq), and for this reason an indefinite noun is described by it. It is invariable in singular and masculine form, so it is not dualised, pluralised, or feminised, because, being fixed, it resembles the verbal noun, or because it is a verbal noun, or because it is a verbal noun, which is the nature of verbal nouns. Its meaning is: they relied on Allah as helper, even though they were few and weak.

The clause "and He is the best Disposer of affairs" is conjoined to "Allah is sufficient for us" within the speech of the speakers, so the waw belongs to the reported speech, not to the reporting. This is conjunction of a performative (inshāʾ) statement to a declarative (khabar) statement in which only suitability is sought.

The one praised is omitted because its indicator has preceded.

"Al-Wakīl" is a form of faʿīl with the meaning of mafʿūl, i.e. one to whom affairs are entrusted (mawkūl). It is said: "wakala ḥājatahu ilā fulān" when he relied upon him to fulfil it and delegated to him its accomplishment. It is said of one who cannot manage his affairs by himself: "rajul wakal" (with two fatḥahs), i.e. one who relies heavily on others. So the wakīl is the one who takes care of the affairs of the one who appointed him, and this taking care varies according to the circumstances in which he is entrusted, and by this variation the meaning of "wakīl" varies. If the task is to repel hostility and oppression, the wakīl is the helper and defender, as in: ﴿Say: I am not a wakīl over you﴾, and from it: ﴿Who will argue with Allah on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or who will be a wakīl over them?﴾. From it is the wakīl in litigation. If it concerns the affairs of life, the wakīl is the guarantor (kāfil) and the one who suffices. From it is

[Page 171]

His saying: ﴿that you do not take besides Me a wakīl﴾, as He said: ﴿And you have made Allah your guarantor (kafīl)﴾. For this reason, among His names, may He be exalted, is "al-Wakīl." His saying "and they said: Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs" is from it. From it is the wakīl over property, and for this reason the name kafīl was also applied to this meaning in His saying: ﴿And you have made Allah your guarantor﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī (in al-Kashshāf) understood al-wakīl to include this in his commentary on His saying: ﴿and He is Wakīl over all things﴾ in Sūrat al-Anʿām, saying: "He is the owner of all things, of sustenance and of terms, the watcher over deeds." That indicates that "al-wakīl" is a comprehensive name for the guardian and keeper in matters that people care to preserve, guard, and store, and for this reason it is restricted and generalised according to contexts.

His saying "so they returned with favour from Allah" is a consequence (taʿqīb) of the report of the firmness of their faith and their saying: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." It is a consequence of an omitted element indicated by the verb "fa-nqalabū," because "returning" (inqilāb) requires that they had gone out to meet the enemy, of whom it had reached them that they had gathered against them, and they did not heed the frightening of Satan. The estimate is: "so they went out, then returned with favour from Allah."

The bāʾ is for accompaniment (mulābasah), i.e. they were accompanied by favour and bounty from Allah. The favour is what they took of wealth, and the bounty is the bounty of jihād. The meaning of "no harm touched them" is that they did not encounter fighting with the polytheists.

The clause "That is only the Satan who frightens his allies" is either an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), if you make His saying "those to whom the people said" a substitution or qualifier, as has been mentioned; or it is a predicate of "those to whom the people said," if you make His saying "those to whom the people said" a subject, and the estimate is: "those to whom the people said, etc., indeed their saying is what Satan frightens with." The link (rābiṭ) of this clause to the subject, which is "those to whom the people said" on this estimate, is the demonstrative noun, and the demonstrative noun is the subject.

Then the demonstrative in His saying "that" either refers to the statement, so the word "Satan" on this is a second subject, and its word is used in its literal meaning, and the meaning is: that statement arose

[Page 172]

from the whispering of Satan in the souls of those who plotted the scheme of spreading rumours through that statement, to frighten the Muslims through the caravan of ʿAbd al-Qays.

Or the demonstrative refers to "the people" in His saying "the people said to them," because "the people" is interpreted as a single person, namely Nuʿaym ibn Masʿūd. Then "the Satan" is an apposition or explanation of the demonstrative, and the term "Satan" was applied to him by way of eloquent metaphor (tashbīh balīgh).

His saying "frightens his allies" is estimated as "frightens you with his allies," so the first object of "yukhawwif" is omitted, being indicated by His saying after it: "so do not fear them," because "kh-w-f" (causative) takes two objects, as it is the doubled form of the unaugmented "khāfa," which takes one object. By doubling it became transitive to two objects, after the pattern of "kasā," as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and Allah warns you of Himself﴾ [Qur'an 3:28].

The pronoun in "so do not fear them" on this reading refers to "his allies." The clause "but fear Me" is a parenthetical insertion between the clause "so do not fear them" and the clause "if you are believers."

His saying "if you are believers" is a conditional clause whose consequent (jawāb) is placed later, its indicator having preceded. It is an admonition and an urging of their faith. Otherwise it is known that they are truly believers.

﴿And do not let those who race to disbelief grieve you. Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all. Allah intends not to give them any share in the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment.﴾

This is a prohibition addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ) against grieving over the conduct of a people who eagerly pursue disbelief, meaning their deeds. The meaning of ﴿يُسارِعُونَ في الكُفْرِ﴾ (yusari'una fi al-kufr, "they race to disbelief") is that they plunge deeply into it, hasten to display and support it and to act upon it whenever opportunities arise, and are eager to instill it in people's souls. This meaning is expressed by the word yusari'un. It is said that this is an instance of *tadmin* (implicit meaning, a term denoting that a verb is used with the sense of another verb, so that it takes the preposition of that other verb). According to this view, yusari'un is taken to include the sense of yaq'una (fall into), and so it takes *fi*. This is the approach of al-Kashshaf and its commentaries. In my view, however, this is a *isti'arah tamthiliyyah* (an extended metaphorical image, a figurative comparison of a whole scene): the state of their eagerness and diligence in declaring people disbelievers, introducing doubt among the believers, waiting for misfortunes to befall them, and seizing opportunities is likened to the state of a seeker who hastens to obtain something he fears will escape him, while he is already deeply immersed in it and engaged with it. Therefore it takes *fi*, which indicates the speed of their haste as the haste of one seeking to be established (in it), not one seeking to attain it, since it is already present with them. Had it taken *ila* (to), it would have been understood that they did not disbelieve at the time of their hastening.

It has been said: these are the hypocrites. It has also been said: they are a people who embraced Islam and then, fearing the polytheists, apostatized.

The clause ﴿إنَّهم لَنْ يَضُرُّوا اللَّهَ شَيْئًا﴾ (innahum lan yadurru Allaha shay'an, "indeed they will not harm Allah in the least") is a reason for the prohibition against grieving him, on a ground that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is certain of. The position of *inna* in such a context is to give the sense of causation, and *inna* here serves the function of the causal *fa'* (so), as has been mentioned more than once before.

The negation in ﴿لَنْ يَضُرُّوا اللَّهَ﴾ is intended to deny that they can frustrate what He willed, since Allah had promised the Messenger that his religion would prevail over all religions, and the hypocrites' striving was to frustrate that. Allah forbade His Messenger to grieve over what appeared to him of the hypocrites' intensifying opposition to the call, and He showed him that they will not be able to nullify the will of Allah, reminding him that He had promised him that He would perfect His light.

The reason this prohibition is needed is that the soul of the Messenger, however high it rises in perfection, is not beyond the states of human souls that come over it in times of hardship: the influence of the apparent appearances of causes, and the expectation that ordinary effects will occur as their results, as happened to the Messenger (ﷺ) on the day of Badr while he was in the *'arish* (the shelter). When the harm they cause to Allah is negated, the harm they cause to the believers is negated as well, with respect to what Allah has promised them.

The majority of readers read ﴿يَحْزُنْكَ﴾ (yahzunka) with a fatha on the *ya'* and a damma on the *zay*, from *hazanahu* (he grieved him), when one causes grief to enter him. Nafi' read it with a damma on the *ya'* and a kasra on the *zay*, from *ahzanahu* (he made him grieve).

The clause ﴿يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ﴾ (yuridu Allah, "Allah intends") is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) explaining their recompense for their disbelief in the Hereafter, after He had explained their safety from their scheming in this world. The meaning is that Allah forsook them and deprived them of success, so they were racing in disbelief because He willed that they should have no share in the Hereafter. *Al-hazz* (share) means a portion of something beneficial.

[Page 173]

[Page 174]

﴿Indeed, those who have exchanged disbelief for faith will never harm Allah at all, and theirs will be a painful punishment.﴾

This is a repetition (tikrar) of the sentence ﴿Indeed, they will never harm Allah at all﴾ (Al 'Imran: 176). It is intended, together with emphasis (ta'kid), to convey this report as an independent statement, out of concern for it, after it had been mentioned as a reason (ta'lil) to console the Messenger. The variation between the two relative clauses (silah) suggests that the content of each clause is the cause of the report established for its relative pronoun. It is also an emphasis of his earlier statement ﴿Indeed, they will never harm Allah at all﴾ (Al 'Imran: 176), like the words of Labid:

*Like the smoke of a fire whose high humps rise up,*

after his saying:

*Like the smoke of a kindled flame whose blaze is ignited.*

This adds the explanation that they are well known for the content of the clause.

The word ishtira' (to purchase, to exchange) is used metaphorically (isti'arah) to mean istibdal (substitution), as was previously mentioned in His saying ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 16) in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 175]

﴿Let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our granting them respite is better for their souls. We grant them respite only that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment.﴾ This is coordinated (*'atf*, grammatical conjunction to a preceding clause) with His saying: ﴿Do not suppose that those who were killed in the way of Allah are dead﴾ [Āl 'Imrān: 169]. The purpose is to set the informing against the supposing in two situations. One of them appears to the observer as a state of harm, and the other appears as a state of good. Allah informs that both states are contrary to what appears to the observers.

It is also permissible that this clause is coordinated with His saying: ﴿Let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you﴾ [Āl 'Imrān: 176]. In that case, He forbade him (ﷺ) from letting that be a cause of his grief, because they cannot harm Allah in the least. Then He conveyed to him a report, intended to be communicated to the polytheists and their brothers, the hypocrites: that they should not suppose their survival is a benefit to them. Rather, it is a granting of respite to them, through which they increase in sins, so that their seizing (punishment) after that will be more severe.

[Page 176]

The majority of readers recited ﴿Let not those who disbelieve suppose﴾ with the *yā'* of the third person (*yā' al-ghaybah*), and the subject of the verb is ﴿those who disbelieve﴾. Ḥamzah alone recited it with the *tā'* of address (*tā' al-khiṭāb*).

So the address is either to the Messenger (peace be upon him), and it is a prohibition of a supposing that did not occur, so the prohibition serves as a warning against it; or it is a prohibition of a supposing that was a passing thought which crossed the mind of the Messenger (ﷺ), though it was a supposing of wonder, since the Messenger knows that the granting of respite is not good for them. Or the one addressed is the Messenger while the intended meaning is someone else, from among the believers who might assume that, in the manner of indirect allusion, like ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. Or the address is meant generally, to every addressee who is suitable for it.

On the reading with the *yā'* (third person), the prohibition is intended to make it reach them, so that they may know the evil of their outcome, and so that their life is embittered by this warning, because the Muslims did not suppose that before.

*Imlā'* (إملاء, granting of respite) means granting a delay in life. What is meant here is the postponement of their lives and the fact that they were not wiped out in war, since they rejoiced at the victory on the day of Uhud, and because the Muslims' dead on the day of Uhud were more than their dead.

It is also permissible that *imlā'* means leaving them free between themselves and their deeds in plotting against the Muslims and waging war against them, and not restraining their hands with defeat and killing, as happened on the day of Badr. It is said: *amlā li-farasihi* (he gave his horse free rein), when he loosened its tether in the pasture. It is derived from *al-malw* with a *wāw*, which is the fast pace of a camel. Then they said: *amlaytu lil-ba'īr wal-faras* (I gave the camel and the horse slack) when I widened its tether, because it can thereby gallop and run freely. So its action was likened to swift travel. They also said: *amlaytu li-Zaydin fī ghayyihi* (I left Zayd in his error), meaning I left him alone, as a metaphor. And *Allah amlā li-fulānin* means He postponed his punishment. He, exalted, said: ﴿And I grant them respite; indeed My plan is firm﴾ [al-A'rāf: 183]. The verb *tamallā* (to remain long) is used metaphorically for a long duration, likening the intelligible to the perceptible. So they said: *mallaaka Allāhu ḥabībaka tamlī'atan* (may Allah grant your beloved a long life), meaning He prolonged your life with him.

His saying ﴿that Our granting them respite is better for their souls﴾: *anna* (أنَّ) is the sister of *inna* with an open hamza, and *mā* (ما) here is a relative pronoun (*mawṣūlah*), not the redundant *mā*. It was written in the codex as a single word, just as *innamā* is written, which is composed of *inna* (the sister of *anna*) and the restrictive *mā* (*mā al-zā'idah al-kāffah*), which is a particle of restriction meaning "only" (*mā* and *illā*). Analogically it should have been written separately, but this is a convention that arose after the writing of the codices and was not consistent in the old orthography. On this basis, the words of the commentators, both earlier and later, have agreed. However, I am of the view that it is permissible that *annamā* in His saying ﴿that Our granting them respite is better for their souls﴾ is the sister of *innamā* with a broken hamza, and that it is composed of *an* (أنْ) and the redundant restrictive *mā* (*mā al-kāffah al-zā'idah*), and that it is one of the methods of restriction (*qaṣr*) according to the verifiers. The meaning is: "Let not those who disbelieve suppose that the confinement of Our granting them respite is only that it is better for them, because when they rejoiced at being safe from killing and at remaining alive, they concealed in their souls the belief that their survival is nothing but good for them, since they consider death to be an evil for them. For they do not believe in the reward of martyrdom in the Hereafter, because of their disbelief in resurrection." This is a true restriction in their assumption.

For this reason, their writing of the word *annamā* with an open hamza in the codex is in accordance with what the convention of orthography requires.

﴿That Our granting them respite is better for their souls﴾ is an inclusive apposition (*badal ishtimāl*, apposition in which the second term includes part of the first) for ﴿those who disbelieve﴾. It therefore takes the place of the two objects (of the verb of supposing), because the term replaced has become as if it were left out. This method of apposition was adopted because of what it contains of brevity followed by detail. The supposing's connection to the first object requires the hearer's eagerness toward the aspect to which the supposing is attached, which is the meaning of the second object. When he hears what takes the place of the two objects after that, it becomes firmly fixed in his soul, far more firmly, and the affirmation is increased.

His saying ﴿We grant them respite only that they may increase in sin﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'nāf*) which stands in the place of a causal explanation for the prohibition against supposing that the granting of respite is good. That is, it is not good, because during that period they increase in sin.

This *innamā* is a compound of *inna*, the particle of emphasis, and the redundant restrictive *mā*, which is a particle of restriction, meaning: "We grant them respite only so that they may increase in sin," so that their seizing (punishment) will be more severe. This is a restriction by reversal (*qaṣr qalb*, restriction that corrects a mistaken belief).

Its meaning is that He grants them respite and delays them while they are upon their disbelief, so they increase in sin during that period, and so their punishment is intensified for that. By this, the granting of respite is not good for them; rather, it is evil for them.

The *lām* in ﴿that they may increase in sin﴾ is the *lām* of consequence (*lām al-'āqibah*, expressing outcome rather than purpose), as in His saying: ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a cause of grief﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 8]. That is: "We grant them respite, and so they increase in sin." Since the increase in sin arises from the granting of respite, it is like its cause. Especially since the increase in sin is known to Allah, so when He granted them respite He knew that they would increase in sin through it. Thus the increase in sin bears a strong resemblance to a cause. As for the real cause of the granting of respite in reality and in fact, it is something else which Allah knows, and it is among the wisdom of creating the means of misguidance and its people, the devils, and harmful things. This is a matter settled in the science of theology (*'ilm al-kalām*), and it is among those things whose wisdom Allah has reserved for knowledge of Himself. The explanation for the prohibition against supposing that the granting of respite is good for them is achieved, because its basis is the mutual entailment between granting them respite and their increase in sin during the period of respite.

[Page 178]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah Al 'Imran, verse 179:

﴿It is not for Allah to leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good. Nor is it for Allah to inform you of the unseen, but Allah chooses from His messengers whomever He wills. So believe in Allah and His messengers. And if you believe and are mindful of Allah, you will have a great reward.﴾

This is an initial resumptive statement (istinaf ibtida'i), returning to explain the wise purposes, both worldly and otherworldly, behind the Muslims' calamity of defeat at Uhud. It is thus a return to the theme mentioned in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And what befell you on the day the two hosts met was by Allah's permission, and so that He might know the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 166]. Here He explains that Allah did not intend for the confusion of the believers and the hypocrites, and their intermingling, to continue indefinitely. He had decreed it for a period in which wisdom required its continuation, namely the days of the believers' weakness after their migration (hijra), when they badly needed to win the people over by outward goodness, so that division would not begin from the very first days of the migration. When faith became firmly established in souls, and the sincere believers settled in security, Allah wanted to end the mixing and to distinguish the wicked from the good. The hypocrites had been concealing their hypocrisy when they saw the believers' affairs prospering and saw their victory at Badr. So Allah willed to expose them and reveal their hypocrisy, by afflicting the believers with the wound of defeat until the hypocrites showed their joy at the victory of the polytheists. Allah thus recorded their hypocrisy, plainly visible to all, as the poet said:

"May Allah reward calamities with every good,
through them I came to know my enemy from my friend."

The phrase ﴿what you are in﴾ refers to the believers' indistinguishability from the hypocrites in outward appearance.

The two occurrences of ''ala'' (on) in ﴿on what you are in﴾ are for figurative elevation (al-isti'la' al-majazi), meaning being firmly settled in the thing that its object (majrur) denotes. The vague description in the relative clause is clarified by what follows ''hatta'' (until) in the words ﴿until He distinguishes the wicked from the good﴾, so it is known that what they are in is the failure to distinguish between the wicked and the good.

The meaning of ﴿It is not for Allah to leave the believers﴾ is the negation of this being something Allah wills, expressed with emphatic negation by the lam of denial (lam al-juhud). A parallel was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should give him the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 79], etc.

So His words ﴿on what you are in﴾ mean: on the mixing of the sincere believer with the hypocrite. The pronoun in ''antum 'alayhi'' is addressed to all Muslims, in view of the hypocrites among them.

By ''the believers'' is meant the believers who are pure of hypocrisy. This is why He referred to them as ''the believers'' and changed the style for that reason. He did not say ''to leave you in what you are in,'' to alert that the intended meaning of the addressed pronoun is broader than the intended meaning of the word ''the believers.'' For the same reason He did not say ''what they are in.''

His words ﴿until He distinguishes the wicked from the good﴾ are the limit (ghaya) of the denial derived from ﴿It is not for Allah to leave﴾. This implies that this leaving is not connected with Allah's will after the time of the statement, nor is it something that occurs from Him, until the wicked is distinguished from the good. When the wicked is distinguished from the good, this leaving becomes possible. Thus the will may be connected with its occurrence or non-occurrence. Its meaning returns to choice after the announcement of a state of impossibility.

''Hatta'' has a special usage after a negation of denial. Its meaning is the ending of the impossibility. The reason is that denial is more specific than mere negation, because the original function of this construction is to indicate that what follows the lam of denial is incompatible with the reality of the negated subject of kana. Its occurrence is therefore like something impossible. When the speaker sets a limit (ghaya) for it, that limit becomes a limit for the impossibility derived from the denial, and not a limit for the negation itself. Thus its implied meaning would not be that after the limit is reached, what had been negated becomes established. All of this is an allusion to the original function of the denial construction, which is to emphasize negation, not to its frequent use in the general sense of negation. The commentary of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) and those who followed him neglected to point out the problem of the limit here. Abu Hayyan noticed it and found it problematic, to the point that he was compelled to interpret the negation as an affirmation. He made the implied meaning: ''Indeed Allah sorts among you through testing until He distinguishes.'' He took this interpretation from the words of Ibn 'Atiyya, but there is no need for it. Moreover, it is possible to interpret it in a better way, namely by making the implied meaning of the limit inoperative, given the presence of an indication that the implied meaning is not intended. However, what I have mentioned is clearer and conforms to an elegant Arabic usage.

The ''min'' (from) in ﴿from the good﴾ means separation, that is, the separation of one of two opposites from the other. This is a meaning affirmed by Ibn Malik, and discussed by the author of Mughni al-Labib (Ibn Hisham). An example is His words ﴿Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ [al-Baqara: 220], which was discussed earlier at that verse in Surat al-Baqara.

It has also been said that the address in the pronoun of ''what you are'' is to the disbelievers, meaning: Allah will not leave the believers ignorant of your state of hypocrisy.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recite ''yamiza'' with a fatha on the initial yā' of the imperfect, a kasra on the mīm, and a sākin yā' after it, from ''maza yamizu.'' Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf recite it with a damma on the initial yā' of the imperfect, a fatha on the mīm, and a shadda kasra yā' after it, from ''mayyaza,'' the doubled form of ''maza.''

His words ﴿Nor is it for Allah to inform you﴾ are coordinated (atf) with His words ﴿It is not for Allah to leave﴾. That is, He willed to distinguish the wicked for you so that you would recognize your enemies. It was not part of Allah's way to inform you of the unseen, so He made causes of which it is the nature to provoke your enemies, so that they would show you enmity and you would thereby come to know them. He said ﴿Nor is it for Allah to inform you of the unseen﴾ because He, the Exalted, established the order of this world on deriving effects from their causes and results from their premises.

His words ﴿but Allah chooses from His messengers whomever He wills﴾ may be a corrective qualification (istidrak) on what His words ﴿Nor is it for Allah to inform you of the unseen﴾ convey, lest the hypocrites make it an argument against the believers regarding the denial of revelation and prophethood. The meaning would then be: ''Allah would not inform you of the unseen except what He informs His messenger of.'' It is part of the messenger's nature not to disclose what Allah has confided to him, as in His words ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone﴾ [al-Jinn: 26] ﴿except to a messenger He approves﴾ [al-Jinn: 27], etc. In that case it is like an exception from the generality of ''li yuti'akum'' (to inform you). It may also be a corrective qualification on what His words ﴿Nor is it for Allah to inform you of the unseen﴾ imply, namely that no one can know Allah's knowledge. In that case it is like an exception from the sense of ''the unseen,'' meaning: except the unseen that pertains to conveying the Sharia. As for anything else, Allah did not guarantee to His messengers that He would inform them of it; He may inform them, and He may not. He said ﴿And others besides them whom you do not know, Allah knows them﴾ [al-Anfal: 60].

His words ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers﴾: if it is an address to the believers, then what is intended is a specific faith, namely affirming that they (the messengers) do not speak from desire, and that Allah's promise is not broken. Accordingly, obedience to them in war and other matters is obligatory for them. Or what is intended is perseverance in faith, because the situation being spoken of may be expected to shake the faith of the weak and to give currency to the doubts of the hypocrites. The placement of ﴿And if you believe and are mindful of Allah﴾ is clear under both interpretations. Even if His words ''fa-aminu'' (so believe) are an address to the disbelievers among the hypocrites, based on the view that the address in ﴿on what you are in﴾ and ﴿to inform you of the unseen﴾ is to the disbelievers, the command to believe is evident. The connection of this result to what preceded is the seizing of opportunities for da'wa (calling to Islam) wherever they arise.

[p. 180]

This is connected (ʿaṭf) to "﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose﴾", because the apparent meaning is that this verse was revealed concerning the conditions of the hypocrites (munafiqun). They used to withhold (yabkhalun) and command people to withhold, as God related about them in Surat al-Nisa' with His words: ﴿Those who withhold and command people to withhold﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:37]. They used to say: ﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God until they disperse﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:7], and other such things. It is not permissible in any way that it was revealed concerning some of the Muslims, because the Muslims on that day were free of this act and of this supposition. For this reason, most of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: the verse was revealed concerning the withholding of zakat, meaning concerning those who withheld zakat. And who would withhold it on that day except a hypocrite? Perhaps the occasion for mentioning the revelation of this verse here is that some of them withheld spending in the cause of God at the Battle of Uhud. The meaning of their supposing it to be good (husbanuhu khayran) is that they thought they had preserved their wealth and escaped from giving it by excuses that were accepted from them.

As for its inclusion of withholding zakat, if it is not by the generality of the relative clause (ṣilat al-mawṣul), should the relative pronoun be for a specific referent (ʿahd) and not for a class (jins), then it is by the indication of the implicit meaning of the discourse (dalalat fahwa al-khitab).

Al-Jumhur read ﴿wa-la yahsabanna alladhina yabkhalun﴾ with the ya' of the third person, and Hamzah read it with the ta' of the second person, as was mentioned previously regarding its counterpart. Al-Jumhur read "tahsibanna" with a kasra on the sin, and Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah and ʿAsim read it with a fatha on the sin.

As for His words ﴿huwa khayran lahum﴾, al-Zamakhshari said: "huwa" is a pronoun of separation (ḍamir fasl). His statement may be based on the view that the pronoun of separation is not restricted to occurring with verbs that require a subject and a predicate. Al-Tibi reported from al-Zajjaj that he said: Sibawayh claimed that it is only a separating pronoun with the subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar), meaning that it is not valid here for it to be a pronoun of separation. For this reason Abu al-Baqa' gave two possibilities for it. One of them is that "huwa" is a pronoun standing in the position of the first object (mafʿul awwal), on the basis that it is the substitution of a nominative pronoun for an accusative pronoun. Perhaps what made it acceptable is that the referent is not mentioned, so it cannot be identified by an accusative pronoun, unlike a nominative pronoun, because it is like the essential element (ʿumdah) in the sentence. In any case, the pronoun refers back to the withholding (bukhl) which is implied by "yabkhalun", like ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:8], and like the saying of the poet:

"When the foolish one is forbidden, he rushes toward it and opposes, and the foolish one is toward opposition."

Then, if it is a pronoun of separation, one of the two objects of "hasiba" (to suppose) is omitted for brevity, because the pronoun of separation indicates it. So, according to the reading with the ta' (second person), the omitted element is a construct phrase (muḍāf), and the muḍāf ilayhi (the genitive that follows) has taken its place, meaning: "Let not those who withhold suppose withholding to be good." And according to the reading with the ya' (third person): "Let not those who withhold suppose their withholding to be good."

Al-bukhl, with a damma on the bāʾ and a sukun on the khāʾ, may also be said as bakhal with a fatha on both. Its verb in the dialect of the people of the Hijaz has a damma on the ʿayn in the past and present. The rest of the Arabs make it with a kasra on the ʿayn in the past and a fatha on it in the present. The Qur'an came in the dialect other than that of the people of the Hijaz because of the lightness of the kasra and the fatha, and therefore it is not recited except with them. It is the opposite of generosity (judd), meaning the restraint upon giving wealth without compensation. This is its true meaning. It is not applied to preventing the owner of something other than wealth from allowing another to benefit from his thing without harm to him, except metaphorically. It has been reported in a narration from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The miser is the one in whose presence I am mentioned but who does not send blessings upon me." People also say: "The eye withheld its tears (bakhilat al-ʿayn bi'l-dumuʿ)." Shuhh (avarice) is synonymous with bukhl, just as sakha' and samah (generosity) are synonymous with judd.

As for His words ﴿bal huwa sharrun lahum﴾, it is an emphasis of the negation of its being good, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"And she stretches out with a cheap, unblemished ..."

This is frequent in the speech of the Arabs. Moreover, in this position it conveys the negation of the supposition of an intermediate state between good and evil.

The clause ﴿sayutawwaqun﴾ ("they will be hung around the neck") is positioned as the cause (ʿillah) for His words ﴿bal huwa sharrun lahum﴾. "Yutawwaqun" may be derived from ṭāqah (capacity), which is bearing beyond one's capacity, meaning: they will bear what they withheld, that is, it will be a burden upon them on the Day of Resurrection. The more apparent view is that it is derived from ṭawq (a collar), which is what is worn under the neck above the chest, meaning: their wealth will be made into collars on the Day of Resurrection, and they will be punished by carrying it. This is like His (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever usurps a span of land will have it hung around his neck from seven earths on the Day of Resurrection." The Arabs say in their proverbs: "He wore it (i.e., the blameworthy deed) as the necklace of the dove." On both possibilities, the meaning is that they will be publicly disgraced with this blame among the people of the gathering, and they will be bound to the punishment for that.

His words ﴿wa-lillahi mirathu al-samawati wa'l-ard﴾ ("And to God belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth") are a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the admonition of the misers and others: that wealth is God's wealth, and no miser will fail to depart and leave his wealth behind. The one who disposes of all of that is God, so He inherits the heavens and the earth, meaning that His dominion over them continues after all of mankind, who benefited from some of that, has passed away. He possesses what is within them as a consequence of them. He is knowing of what people do of withholding and giving in charity. Thus the verse is an admonition, a warning and a promise, because the purpose is the implication of His words "Aware (khabir)".

[p. 181]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 181–182:

﴿God has certainly heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed, God is poor, and we are rich." We will record what they have said, and their killing of the prophets without right, and We will say, "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ ﴿That is for what your hands have put forward, and because God is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾

This is a resumptive clause (istі'naf) ﴿God has certainly heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed, God is poor, and we are rich"﴾, linked to the subject of stinginess, because they said this while rejecting the encouragement to give charity. Those who said this were the Jews, as is clear at the end of the verse in His words, "and their killing of the prophets without right." As for the one who said it, it has been said that he was Huyayy ibn Akhtab the Jew, the rabbi of the Jews, when he heard the words of the Exalted, ﴿Who is it that will loan God a good loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245], and Huyayy said, "Only the poor borrows from the rich." It has also been said that Finhas ibn 'Azura said it to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, on the occasion when "the Messenger of God ﷺ sent Abu Bakr to the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa' to call them. He came to the house of study and found a group of them gathered around Finhas, their rabbi. Abu Bakr invited them, and Finhas said, 'We have no need of God, but He is in need of us. If He were rich, He would not have borrowed our wealth as your companion claims.' Abu Bakr became angry, slapped Finhas, and intended to kill him, so the verse was revealed." Their statement spread among the Jews.

His words ﴿God has certainly heard﴾ are a threat, and they indicate that this statement is a great audacity, even if its aim was to slight the words of the Qur'an, since they uttered this expression without any reservation. Also, belittling the Messenger and his Qur'an is a grave sin and disbelief upon disbelief. For this reason the Exalted said ﴿has certainly heard﴾, using it in its implied meaning, which is a threat concerning a foul utterance, since the people of the religions know that God knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal. So the intended meaning is not to inform them that God knew this, but rather what this entails, which is what is required by His words ﴿We will record what they have said﴾. The meaning of "recording" is either that it is written down in the records of their sins, since no one would think it is written in the records of good deeds, and this is far-fetched, because the presence of the sign of the future indicates that the recording is something that will happen later. Thus the apparent meaning is that by recording is meant not pardoning or forgiving them, but rather that it will be established for them and they will be requited for it, so the recording is a metaphor for reckoning. According to the first interpretation it is a warning, and according to the second it is a threat.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿We will record what they have said and their killing﴾ with the first-person plural "nun" of majesty in "sa-naktub," and with the accusative "lam" in "qatlahum," as the object of "naktub," and "naqul" with "nun." Hamza read "sa-yuktab" with a third-person masculine "ya" that is damma-ed and a taa with fatha, in the passive voice, because the subject of the recording is known, namely God the Exalted, and with the nominative "lam" in "qatluhum" as the deputy subject. "Wa-yaqul" with a third-person "ya," and the pronoun refers back to the divine name in His words "inna Allah."

The conjunction of His words ﴿and their killing of the prophets without right﴾ adds to their blame by mentioning the evil deeds of their forebears, because those who killed the prophets are not the same as those who said ﴿Indeed, God is poor, and we are rich﴾, but rather they are among their forebears. So it is mentioned here to show that this is an old disposition among them, namely audacity against God and His messengers. The unity of the pronouns despite the difference in their referents is an Arabic manner of speaking about praises and blames attributed to tribes. Al-Hajjaj said in his sermon after the Day of Dayr al-Jamajim, addressing the people of Iraq: "Were you not my companions in al-Ahwaz when you concealed evil and hid disbelief..." until he said, "Then the Day of al-Zawiyah, and what is the Day of al-Zawiyah..." etc., although among them were those who had died and those who came later.

His words ﴿and We will say, "Taste the punishment of the burning"﴾ are conjoined: the effect of the recording is conjoined to the recording, meaning they will be requited for that without pardon, ﴿and We will say, "Taste"﴾, which is God's command that they enter the Fire.

The "dhawq" (tasting) is literally the perception of flavours, and here it is used figuratively as a metonymy (majaz mursal) for the sensation of punishment, its relation being generality. Its nuance is that "tasting," in common usage, entails repetition of that sensation, since tasting is followed by eating. With this consideration, "dhuqu" may be a metaphor (isti'ara).

The use of "dhawq" for the sensation of good or evil is widespread in the speech of the Arabs and occurs frequently in the Qur'an.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿That is for what your hands have put forward﴾ refers to the punishment witnessed on that day, and in it is an emphasis on the magnitude of the punishment. The "ba" is causal, to alert that this punishment, because of its great horror, is one whose cause is to be asked about. He conjoined His words ﴿and that God is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ to the object of the "ba," so that this punishment has two causes: what their hands have put forward, and the justice of God the Exalted. What their hands put forward made the punishment necessary, and God's justice made this punishment, in its witnessed measure of severity, something that they would not think to be excessive torment against them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 183–184:

﴿Those who said, "Indeed, Allah has taken a covenant with us that we should not believe in any messenger until he brings us an offering which fire devours." Say, "There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you speak of. So why did you kill them, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿And if they deny you, then messengers before you were denied, who came with clear proofs and the scriptures and the illuminating Book.﴾.

The phrase ﴿Those who said, "Indeed, Allah has taken a covenant with us"﴾ is a substitution (badal) from ﴿Those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181], to mention another atrocious statement of theirs, namely their lying against Allah in claiming that He made a covenant with them, through the tongues of their prophets, that they should not believe in a messenger until he brings them an offering (qurban), that is, until he slaughters an offering which fire descends from the heaven to consume, and that is the sign of acceptance. This had indeed occurred in the time of Musa (peace be upon him), when the first offering was slaughtered in the manner Allah had prescribed for the Children of Israel, and fire came out from before the Lord and consumed it, as in the Book of Leviticus. However, this was a miracle that is not generalized to all the prophets, as the Jews claimed, because the miracles of messengers come in accordance with what suits the confirmation of their community. In a hadith: "There is not a prophet among the prophets except that he was given signs such that people believed upon the like of them; and what I was given is revelation which Allah revealed to me, so I hope that I will have the most followers on the Day of Resurrection." So Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet: ﴿Say, "There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you speak of, so why did you kill them?"﴾.

This form of argument (jadal) is based on assumption (taslim), meaning: if we grant that, then your refusal to follow Islam is not due to waiting for this miracle, for you have already denied the messengers who brought it to you and killed them. It is not hidden that the assumption is according to the doctrine of the opponent, since there is no doubt that the Children of Israel killed prophets from among them after they had believed in them, such as Zechariah, John, Isaiah and Jeremiah. Thus belief in them at first implies that they brought the offering which fire consumes according to their claim, and their killing them later implies that the lack of steadfastness in belief in the prophets is an ancient trait of the Jews, and that they only follow their own desires; so it is no wonder that their successors come with the like of what their predecessors did.

His saying ﴿if you are truthful﴾ indicates clearly that what they claimed of a covenant made with them in this regard is a lie and baseless excuses.

He said ﴿and what you speak of﴾ by using the relative form for brevity, and to record upon them their attribution of this to Allah. A parallel is His saying, ﴿And he said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"﴾ [Maryam: 77] up to His saying ﴿And We will inherit from him what he says﴾ [Maryam: 80], meaning We will inherit his wealth and his children.

Then He consoled His Prophet ﷺ with His saying: ﴿And if they deny you, then messengers before you were denied﴾. What is mentioned after the fa' serves as the evidence of the response (jawab), because it is its cause, and the implied meaning is: "And if they deny you, then do not be surprised" or "do not grieve, for this is an ancient practice among the nations with messengers like you." That is not due to any deficiency in what you have brought. "Al-bayyinat" means the proofs of truthfulness. "Al-zubur" is the plural of zabur, which is fa'ul in the sense of maf'ul, like rasul, meaning maznur in the sense of written. It has been said that it is derived from zabara, meaning to repel or restrain, because a book is intended for judgment. By "al-zubur" is meant the books of the prophets and messengers, which contain admonitions and reminders, such as the Book of David and the Gospel.

As for "al-Kitab al-munir" (the illuminating Book): if the definite article is for the genus, it refers to the books of laws such as the Torah and the Gospel; if it is for a specific referent, it is the Torah. Describing it as "illuminating" is a metaphor meaning that which makes the truth clear, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44]. The conjunction is understood as distributive: some messengers came with the zubur, some with the illuminating Book, and all of them came with the clear proofs.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa'l-zubur" with the zubur conjoined without repeating the preposition bi (ba' al-jarr). Ibn 'Amir read "wa-bi'l-zubur" with the preposition bi repeated after the conjunction waw, and it is written thus in the Syrian codex (al-mushaf al-Shami).

The majority read "wa'l-kitab" without repeating the preposition bi. Hisham, on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, read "wa-bi'l-kitab" with the preposition repeated, and this reading is transmitted by Hisham alone. It has been said that it was written thus in some ancient Syrian codices, but it is not in the Imam codex (al-Mushaf al-Imam). It is quite likely that this transmission of Hisham from Ibn 'Amir is irregular (shadhdhah) in this verse, and that the codices in which the ba' was written in "wa-bi'l-kitab" were dictated from the memorizers of this irregular transmission.
