What is mentioned after the fa' serves as the evidence of the response (jawab), because it is its cause, and the implied meaning is: "And if they deny you, then do not be surprised" or "do not grieve, for this is an ancient practice among the nations with messengers like you." That is not due to any deficiency in what you have brought. "Al-bayyinat" means the proofs of truthfulness. "Al-zubur" is the plural of zabur, which is fa'ul in the sense of maf'ul, like rasul, meaning maznur in the sense of written. It has been said that it is derived from zabara, meaning to repel or restrain, because a book is intended for judgment. By "al-zubur" is meant the books of the prophets and messengers, which contain admonitions and reminders, such as the Book of David and the Gospel.

As for "al-Kitab al-munir" (the illuminating Book): if the definite article is for the genus, it refers to the books of laws such as the Torah and the Gospel; if it is for a specific referent, it is the Torah. Describing it as "illuminating" is a metaphor meaning that which makes the truth clear, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44]. The conjunction is understood as distributive: some messengers came with the zubur, some with the illuminating Book, and all of them came with the clear proofs.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa'l-zubur" with the zubur conjoined without repeating the preposition bi (ba' al-jarr). Ibn 'Amir read "wa-bi'l-zubur" with the preposition bi repeated after the conjunction waw, and it is written thus in the Syrian codex (al-mushaf al-Shami).

The majority read "wa'l-kitab" without repeating the preposition bi. Hisham, on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, read "wa-bi'l-kitab" with the preposition repeated, and this reading is transmitted by Hisham alone. It has been said that it was written thus in some ancient Syrian codices, but it is not in the Imam codex (al-Mushaf al-Imam). It is quite likely that this transmission of Hisham from Ibn 'Amir is irregular (shadhdhah) in this verse, and that the codices in which the ba' was written in "wa-bi'l-kitab" were dictated from the memorizers of this irregular transmission.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 185:

﴿Every soul shall taste death, and you will only be paid your rewards in full on the Day of Resurrection. Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into the Garden has indeed triumphed. And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion.﴾

This verse is connected to the principal purpose for which the discourse was directed, namely consoling the believers for what befell them on the day of Uhud, and refuting the claims of the hypocrites that, had the people consulted them about fighting, they would have advised what would secure their safety so that they would not perish. Having first explained to them what removes the suspicion that the defeat was a forsaking by God, and their astonishment at how it could befall a people who went out to support the religion, and that there was no cause for the defeat except that "Satan only caused them to slip" (Q. 3:155), He then explained to them that in that calamity there were benefits, by the saying of God Most High, "so that you may not grieve over what has escaped you" (Q. 3:153), and His saying, "and that He might know the believers" (Q. 3:166). Then He commanded them to submit to God in every state, saying, "And whatever afflicted you on the day the two hosts met was by the permission of God" (Q. 3:166), and He said, "O you who believe, do not be like those who disbelieved and said of their brothers" (Q. 3:156), and so on. He explained to them that the slain believers, over whom they grieved, are in fact alive, and that the believers who did not join them will not have their reward or the merit of their steadfastness lost by God. He explained to them that the safety of the disbelievers should not grieve the believers, nor should it gladden the disbelievers. In the course of this, He also nullified the speech of the hypocrites by His saying, "Say: Even if you had been in your houses, those destined to be killed would have come out to their places of death" (Q. 3:154), and by His saying, "Those who said of their brothers while they sat [at home]..." (Q. 3:168), up to His saying, "Say: Then avert death from yourselves, if you are truthful" (Q. 3:168). He concluded all of that with what encompasses both purposes, in His saying, "Every soul shall taste death, and you will only be paid your rewards in full on the Day of Resurrection," because the calamity and grief arose from the death of those among the best of the believers who were martyred. The meaning is that since death is the end of every living being, had they not died today they would have died after that. So do not grieve over the death of your slain in the way of God, and let the hypocrites not tempt you concerning that. His saying after it, "and you will only be paid your rewards in full on the Day of Resurrection," is a restrictive statement of reversal (qasr qalb), placing the believers, in their grief over their slain and over their defeat, in the position of one who expects from his deeds only the benefits of this world, namely victory and spoils, whereas the completion of reward is in the bliss of the Hereafter. For this reason He said, "you will be paid your rewards in full" (tuwaffawna ujurakum), meaning it will be completed for you. In it there is also an allusion that they had already obtained great rewards in this world for their support of the religion: among them the victory at Badr, and among them the restraint of the hands of the polytheists from them during their days of residence in Mecca until they were able to emigrate.

The word "taste" (dhawq) here is used for the experience of death, and its usage was previously explained at His saying, just before, "and We will say: Taste the punishment of the burning" (Q. 3:181). Its application to the occurrence of death became widespread, as God Most High said, "They will not taste death therein" (Q. 44:56), and it is said: "he tasted the taste of death."

Tawfiyah (tawfiyah) means giving a thing in full. The jurists use it for the general sense of giving and handing over. "Ujur" is the plural of "ajr" in the sense of reward, and the reason for its plural form is consideration of the varieties of deeds. "Yawm al-Qiyamah" is the Day of Gathering, named so because people rise on it from the stupor of death to the awakening of life.

The fa' in His saying "fa-man zuhziha" (so whoever is drawn away) is for consequence, following "you will be paid your rewards in full." The meaning of zuhziha is "was removed far away." The essential meaning of the verb zuhziha is a pull with speed; it is the doubled form of zahhahu, meaning he pulled him from the place when he pulled him hastily.

The reason that "drawn away from the Fire and admitted into the Garden" are combined, although admission to the Garden alone would suffice, is to indicate that entry into the Garden comprises two great blessings: deliverance from the Fire, and the bliss of the Garden.

The meaning of "then he has triumphed" (faqad faza) is that he attained his desired good. The consequence of triumph upon entry into the Garden and being drawn away from the Fire is known, so there is no benefit in mentioning the condition except for this purpose. The Arabs rely on context in this, so the answer may be identical to the condition, to clarify certainty, as in the saying of a speaker: "Whoever knows me, then he knows me." It may also be specified by adding a qualifier, as in His saying, "And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity" (Q. 25:72). It may also be intended to reach the furthest extent of the type of answer and condition, as in this verse, and in His saying, "Our Lord, indeed whomever You admit into the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him" (Q. 3:192) according to one of two interpretations, and in the Arab saying: "Whoever reaches the pasture of al-Samman has indeed reached it." All that has been established regarding the answer applies similarly to the attribute and the like, as in His saying, "Our Lord, these are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray just as we went astray" (Q. 28:63).

**Page 190**

The verse begins a new, resumed sentence (*isti'naf*, a sentence that starts anew rather than continuing the previous clause). Its purpose is to alert the believers to the trials that confront the people of truth and the helpers of the Messengers. It also warns them that if they are the sort whom defeat weakens, they are not worthy of supporting the truth. The verb is emphasised with the oath particle *lam* and with the heavy emphatic nun (*nun al-tawkid al-shadida*), to establish that the trial will certainly occur. The heavy emphatic nun is stronger in expressing emphasis than the light one.

The original form of *"latubla'unna"* is *latubla'uunanna*. When three nuns came together, the pronunciation became heavy, so the nun of the verbal ending (*nun al-raf'*) was dropped. Two consonants then met: the waw of the plural (*waw al-raf'*) and the heavy emphatic nun. The waw was dropped because it is not part of the root of the word, leaving *latubla'unna*. The same applies to the morphology and emphasis of His words, *"wa-latasma'unna"*.

Al-ibtila' means testing (*al-ikhtibar*). It is meant here in a sense that entails its consequence, which is affliction, because afflictions test the degree of steadfastness. The testing in wealth is the expenditure required for jihad and the loss of the wealth they left behind in Makkah. The testing in the self is killing and wounds. Added to this is hearing what is hateful from the People of the Book and from the polytheists, at the Battle of Uhud and after it.

*Al-adha* is harm by speech, as in His words, ﴿They will not harm you except with some abuse﴾ (Al 'Imran: 111), as has preceded just above. Therefore He described it here as *kathiran* (much), meaning beyond the limit that souls generally endure. All of this leads to weakness (*al-fashal*), so Allah commanded them to be patient in the face of it until victory is attained for them. He commanded them to have taqwa, meaning to persist in the matters of faith, to devote themselves to spreading it and supporting it. As for patience in the face of the testing in wealth and selves, it includes jihad. As for patience in the face of harm, it applies both in times of war and in times of peace. The verse therefore does not imply the prohibition of permission to fight, on the ground that it commanded them to be patient with the harm of the disbelievers, such that it would be abrogated (*mansukha*, subject to *naskh*, abrogation) by the verses of the sword. This is because it is apparent that the verse was revealed after the Battle of Uhud, and the command to fight came before it. This is what al-Qaffal said.

His words, *"fa-inna dhalika"* (indeed that), refer to what has preceded, namely patience and taqwa, with the interpretation: indeed what has been mentioned. ﴿'Azm al-umur﴾ is an idafa (construct phrase) of an attribute to the thing described, meaning *al-umur al-'azm* (the resolute matters). He described *al-umur*, which is plural, with *'azm*, which is singular, because the root *'azm* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) and so keeps one form. Here it is a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle, meaning among the matters upon which resolve is made. *Al-'azm* is the carrying out of an opinion and the absence of hesitation after the rightness of it has become clear. He said, ﴿And consult them in the matter; then when you have decided, rely upon Allah﴾ (Al 'Imran: 159). What is meant here is resolve in good things. He said, ﴿So be patient as the Messengers of firm resolve were patient﴾ (al-Ahqaf: 35), and He said, ﴿And We did not find in him resolve﴾ (Ta-Ha: 115).

The words ﴿indeed that is of the matters of resolve﴾ serve as the answer to the conditional clause, and the implied sense is: ﴿And if you are patient and fear Allah﴾ you will attain the reward of the people of resolve, ﴿indeed that is of the matters of resolve﴾.

(Page 191)

This is coordinated with His saying ﴿And you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 186], for lying against the Messenger is among the greatest harms done to the Muslims. Disparaging his speech and the rulings of his law is part of this, like their saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 181]. The discussion of the meaning of Allah's "taking" (akhdh) has already been given in His saying ﴿And when We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam﴾ [al-Baqarah: 34] and similar verses.

﴿Those who were given the Scripture﴾ are the Jews. This covenant was taken from their predecessors in the time of their Messenger and their prophets, and it contained what indicates that it applies generally to the scholars of their community across all their generations, until a Messenger comes.

The clause ﴿you will surely make it clear to the people﴾ explains the covenant. It is a report of the oath when it was imposed on them, and for this reason it comes in the form of addressing them directly with the object of the oath, as the majority recited it. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited it as "yubayyinunnahu" with the third-person yāʾ, following the manner of reporting in meaning, since those who were bound by this covenant were absent at the time of reporting about them. In Arabic, such reports have several forms. With regard to the speech of the reporter and the speech of the one reported, a report may have two forms, as with a report of a saying: "Zayd swore he will not do such-and-such" and "I swear I will not do such-and-such." It may also have three forms, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: Swear by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family﴾ [al-Naml: 49]. It was recited with nūn, with the upper tāʾ, and with the lower yāʾ: "lanubayyitannahu," "latubayyitannahu," "layubayyitannahu." If tuqāsamū is taken as a past verb, these readings stand; if it is taken as an imperative, two readings are allowed for "lanubayyitannahu," with nūn or with tāʾ. The discussion of the morphology and grammatical analysis of "latubayyinunnahu" is like the discussion of "latublawunna" mentioned shortly before.

The covenant was taken from them in two matters: the Book, meaning not leaving its meanings unexplained or distorting its interpretation (ta'wil, interpretation), and not concealing it, meaning hiding any part of it. Thus His saying ﴿and do not conceal it﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you will surely make it clear to the people﴾, and it is not joined with the emphatic nūn (nūn al-tawkīd, the emphatic nūn) because that nūn does not accompany a negated verb, as the implications of the two are contradictory.

His saying ﴿so they threw it﴾ is connected with the fāʾ, which indicates sequence, to point to their haste in doing so. Those who threw it behind their backs were the scholars of the Jews in their latest periods, close to the time of the Muhammadan message. The sequence between the taking of the covenant from them and their casting it away is considered in terms of their hastening to cast it aside immediately after the time when the taking of the covenant was realized, which is the time when each of their scholars became qualified to make the Book clear and proclaim it. So when one of them felt in himself the ability to understand the Book and to manipulate its meanings, he hastened to use that ability as a means to bad interpretation, distortion, and concealment. It is also permissible for the fāʾ to be used for its necessary implication, which is the intensity of haste in doing so when the situation calls for it and when it is a matter of concern and focus of thought. It is also permissible that the sequence is according to the events in which they misinterpreted the Book and took a small price for it, because when the covenant was general, each particular instance was covered by the covenant. So the particular instance in which they did not act according to the covenant involves the sequence of its covenant with casting away and trading.

Nabdh (casting away) means throwing and dropping. Here it is used figuratively (isti'ara, metaphor) for not acting upon the covenant, likening the covenant to a thrown-away thing that is of no benefit.

"Behind their backs" here is a figurative depiction (tamthil) of neglect and disregard, because a thing that is cared for and competed for is usually placed before the eye, guarded, and looked at, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, you are before Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48]. The custom with a thing that is rejected is to turn one's back on it and not look at it. In this depiction there is a supporting device (tarshih, a rhetorical reinforcement) for the metaphor of casting away, indicating the breaking of the covenant.

The two pronouns, the accusative and the genitive, may refer back to the covenant, meaning they treated Allah's covenant lightly and exchanged it for a small price, and this implies that they neglected what they had pledged regarding making the Book clear and not concealing it. They may also refer back to the Book, meaning they neglected the Book and did not care for it. What is intended is neglecting its rulings and exchanging their establishment for a small benefit. This indicates both types of neglect: neglecting its verses and neglecting its meanings.

"Trading" (ishtira') here is used figuratively (majaz) for exchange, and "small price" refers to what they took in bribes and gifts from people of desires and oppression, from rulers and common people, in order to support injustices and corruptions through false interpretations. Interpreting any ruling that strikes at the hands of tyrants and oppressors in a way that frees their hands to oppress the subjects, through various kinds of false interpretations, and warning those who openly call for changing what is wrong. Although this verse is about the People of the Book, its ruling includes whoever among the Muslims commits the same kind of act as theirs, because the ruling and its cause are one in kind.

**[Page 194]**

*Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Qur'an 3:188:*

﴿Do not let those who rejoice in what they have done, and love to be praised for what they did not do, think themselves safe from punishment; theirs is a painful torment.﴾

This is a continuation of the account of the People of the Book, describing the state of their character after the passage explained the corruption of their trustworthiness in conveying the religion. This is another type, brought by a different group among the People of the Book. For this reason the verse refers to them with the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "the relative pronoun"), in order to lead to mention of its strange connection with the condition of one who does evil and baseness and then does not stop at the limit of shame for what he did, or seek concealment of its ugliness, but rises higher, awaiting the praise of people for his bad deed and seeking commendation for it. It was said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and the address is to everyone who is fit to be addressed. The relative pronoun here carries the sense of the definite with the lam of previous reference (lam al-'ahd, "the lam of prior reference"), because it is intended for specific people among the Jews or the hypocrites. So the meaning of ﴿who rejoice in what they have done﴾ is that they rejoice in what they did of what has been mentioned before, namely abandoning the Book and trading it for a small price. They rejoiced only because of the benefit in this world that they gained through their action.

The meaning of ﴿and love to be praised for what they did not do﴾ is that they love to be praised for being guardians of the Law, its protectors, and those who know its interpretation, and that is contrary to reality. This is the apparent meaning of the verse, and it is the view of Mujahid. And from Ibn 'Abbas: they did the misguiding of their followers from belief in Muhammad (ﷺ), and they loved the praise of being scholars of the books of religion.

In al-Bukhari, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who used to stay behind from the military campaign with excuses, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would accept from them, ﴿and love to be praised﴾ for having the intention of the fighters. The relative pronoun here does not carry the sense of the lam of comprehensiveness (lam al-istighraq, "the lam of totality").

In al-Bukhari: Marwan ibn al-Hakam said to his doorkeeper, "Go, O Rafi', to Ibn 'Abbas and say: If every person who rejoices in what he has done and loves to be praised for what he did not do is punished, we will all be punished." Ibn 'Abbas said, "What is it to you with this? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) only summoned the Jews and asked them about something, and they informed him of other than it, and they showed him that they had sought praise from him for what they had told him, and they rejoiced in their concealment." Then Ibn 'Abbas recited ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187] up to His words ﴿Do not let those who rejoice in what they have done...﴾, the verse.

*[Page 195]*

Al-mafaza (the place of success) is the place of winning. It is the place where whoever dwells will be successful by being safe from the enemy. The wide wasteland was called mafaza because the one who is cut off in it saves himself from his enemies and from those seeking revenge against him, and they used to seek to dwell in it. Al-Nabigha said:

*Or I place the house in a deaf, dark desert, where the caravan is tied and the night traveler does not pass through it.*

*It repels people from us when we ride it, from injustices; it is called Umm Sabbar.*

Since the mafaza is general in relation to the success obtained in it, He clarified that by His words ﴿from punishment﴾. The particle (min, "from") here means substitution (al-badaliyya, "the sense of substitution"), like His words, exalted is He, ﴿It neither fattens nor satisfies from hunger﴾ [al-Ghashiya: 7]; or it means 'an' (from/away from), by implying in mafaza the meaning of deliverance (manjah).

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read ﴿Let not those who rejoice﴾ with the yā' of the third person (al-ghayba), and the rest read it with the tā' of address.

As for the sīn of ﴿taḥsabanna﴾, Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read it with a kasra. The rest read it with a fatha.

The structure of the verse has come in a wonderful arrangement, in that the second object of the first verb of supposing (af'al al-husban, "verbs of thinking") has been omitted, because of what is indicated by the object of ﴿So do not suppose them﴾. The estimate is: ﴿Let not those who rejoice...﴾ and so on, suppose themselves. The verb of supposing is repeated in His words ﴿So do not suppose them﴾, addressed to the second person, in the manner of a parenthetical insertion introduced by the fa' (isti'rad, "parenthetical insertion"), and after it comes the second object, which is ﴿in a place of safety from punishment﴾, so both verbs share it (tanazu'). On the reading of the majority, ﴿Do not let those who rejoice﴾ with the tā' of address, it is an address to an unspecified person so that it includes every addressee, and His words ﴿So do not suppose them﴾ is also a parenthetical insertion introduced by the fa', and the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), together with what there is in omitting the second object of the first verb of supposing, which is the place of benefit, from arousing the listener's eagerness to hear what he is forbidden to suppose. The majority read ﴿So do not suppose them﴾ with a fatha on the bā' (the letter ba'), on the basis that the verb is addressed to one person. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a ḍamma on the bā', on the basis that it is addressed to a plural. Since these two read the first with the yā' of the third person, the ḍamma on the bā' makes the subject and object of yaḥsabanna identical, meaning they do not suppose themselves. The identity of subject and object for one verb is one of the characteristics of verbs of supposing (af'al al-zann), as here, and a few other verbs were attached to them, namely: wajada (to find), 'adima (to lack), and faqada (to lose).

As for the sīn of ﴿taḥsabannahum﴾, the readings are parallel to what applies to the sīn of yaḥsabanna.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 189:

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾

A *tadhyil* (a concluding statement that reinforces the preceding meaning) containing a warning, indicating that nothing is hidden from Allah of what they conceal of their own dispositions.

[Page 196]

This topic is a new one (ghara[ḍ]) that is unrelated (unprecedented) compared with the topics that the surah has followed. The discussion moved from the introductions, the central aim, and the interjections occasioned by circumstances, to a new topic: taking lessons (i'tibar) from the creation of the worlds and their attributes, and praising those who draw lessons from the signs contained in them.

This kind of transition signals that the discussion of the surah's topics, with all their variety, is coming to an end. The surah had moved from one topic to a related one, and now it has shifted to a general topic: taking lessons from the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the condition of the believers in being admonished by that. This manner of transition occurs to the orator, and those like him, after giving a topic its due, moving to another topic as a sign that the speech is nearing its end. It is the way of the Qur'an to conclude with admonition, because it is the most important of the purposes of the message, as occurs at the close of Surat al-Baqarah.

The particle inna (indeed) is for emphasis on the information.

By "the creation of the heavens and the earth" here is meant either the effects of their creation, which is the order placed within them, or "creation" is taken to mean the created things, as in His saying, ﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾ [Luqman: 11]. "Ulu al-albab" [Ali 'Imran: 7] are the people of complete intellects, because the lubb (core) of a thing is its essence. We have already discussed in Surat al-Baqarah the signs contained in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day, at His saying, ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, and the ship...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], etc.

"Yadhkurun Allah" (they remember Allah) is either from the remembrance by the tongue or from the remembrance of the heart, which is reflection (tafakkur). By His saying, ﴿standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ He intends the generality of conditions, like the saying, "He struck him on the back and the belly," and the saying, "such-and-such is famous among the people of the East and the West." Moreover, these conditions are the customary conditions of human beings in ease, meaning the conditions of occupation, rest, and the intention to sleep. It has been said that He meant the conditions of those who pray: [one who is] able, [one who is] unable, and one who is severely unable. But the context of the verse is far from this meaning.

His saying, ﴿and they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a synonymous conjunction if by remembrance in what preceded is meant reflection; its repetition is for the difference in what is reflected upon. Or it is a different conjunction if by His saying "yadhkurun" is meant remembrance by the tongue. Reflection (tafakkur) is a great act of worship. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, in the Jami' al-'Utbiyyah, that he said: It was said to Umm al-Darda': "What was the matter of Abu al-Darda'?" She said: "Most of his matter was reflection." It was said to him: "Do you consider reflection to be one of the deeds?" He said: "Yes, it is certainty (yaqin)."

[Page 197]

"Khalq" (creation) here means the manner of the effect of creation, or the created things that are in the heavens and the earth, so the genitive construction is either in the sense of "li" (belonging to) or in the sense of "fi" (in).

His saying, ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ and what follows it is a clause standing in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), with an implied "saying": meaning, they reflect saying, "Our Lord, etc.," because this statement is intended as a quotation of their words, as evidenced by what follows it of supplication.

If you say: How did all of the people of intellect agree upon saying this glorification and supplication when reflecting, despite the difference in their reflections, their impressions, and their aims? I say: It is possible that they received it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so they would persist in it during reflection and after it. And it is possible that Allah inspired them with it, so it became their habitual utterance, like His saying, ﴿And they said: "We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285], and the verses. What supports this is the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas in the Sahih, who said: "I spent the night at the house of my maternal aunt Maymunah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) got up, wiped the sleep from his face, then recited the ten verses from Surat Al 'Imran," until the end of the hadith.

In my view it is also permissible that His saying, ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ be a report of their reflection within themselves. It is then the speech of the self, in which all reflecting people share, since they are equal in the validity of reflection, because it moves from one meaning to another branching out from it. The people of intellect spoken of here are equal in grasping these meanings. So the first of the reflection produced for them that created things were not created in vain; then from it branched the glorification of Allah and the request that He protect them from the punishment of the Fire, because they saw in created things the obedient and the disobedient, so they knew that behind this world there is reward and punishment, and so they sought refuge that they would not be among those upon whom the word of punishment is due. And they sought means to that by having exerted the utmost of their ability in seeking salvation, as they responded to the caller to faith, who was the Messenger, peace be upon him. They asked for forgiveness of sins and expiation of misdeeds, and dying in righteousness, and so on. Hardly any of the people of intellect is free from these reflections, and perhaps adds to them. When this verse was revealed and spread among them, those who had not previously noticed this reflection were guided to it, and it became widespread among the Muslims, in its meanings and its wording.

[Page 198]

The meaning of ﴿You did not create this in vain﴾ is: a vain creation; or: You did not create this while it is in the state of being vain. So it is a state (hal) that is necessarily mentioned in negation, though it is a supplementary element (fadlah) in affirmation, like His saying, ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38]. The aim is the negation of the beliefs of those whose belief leads to the conclusion that this creation is vain or was left devoid of wisdom. The Arabs often construct the negative form on the basis of the prior affirmation.

The particle of consequence (fa') is used in the quotation of their words, ﴿so protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, because it follows from knowledge that this creation is true, and it is part of the truth that the righteous and the wicked are not equal, nor the obedient and the disobedient. So they knew that each has a fitting abode, and they asked to be among the people of goodness who are kept away from the punishment of the Fire.

Their saying, ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him﴾ is brought as a justification (ta'lil) for the request for protection from the Fire, as the particle inna, used for the purpose of emphasis, indicates, since there is no context here for stressing. Khizy is the verbal noun of khazia, meaning to be humiliated and debased in the sight of people, and akhza-hu means to humiliate him before the eyes of the witnesses. The reason for the request for protection from the Fire being that entering it is a disgrace, after the allusion to what necessitates that request in their saying "the punishment of the Fire," is that the Fire, along with the painful torment in it, contains subjugation of the one tormented and public humiliation, and this is a meaning settled in the souls of people. From it is the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him, ﴿And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 87]. This is because the connection between the condition and the consequence is evident: whoever enters the Fire, You have disgraced him. Disgrace is something that souls cannot bear, so there is no need for an interpretation that they took, to the effect of "You have disgraced him with a great disgrace." The author of al-Kashshaf likened it to the saying of the Arab herdsmen, "Whoever reaches the pasture of al-Samman has reached [the pasture]," meaning he has reached pasture, lest the meaning of the consequence be necessarily obtained from the condition, and then there would be no benefit in conditioning by the condition, since it would render the speech devoid of benefit in that case. Some of this has preceded at His saying, ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has succeeded﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 185].

And for this reason they followed it with what is in human nature: seeking refuge from disgrace and humiliation by hastening to their allies and helpers. So they knew that there is no helper in the Hereafter for the wrongdoer, and thus they added

[Page 199]

emphasis to their eagerness to seek refuge from the punishment of the Fire, when they said, ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾, meaning: for the people of the Fire there are no helpers who could ward off disgrace from them.

His saying, ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling﴾: they meant by it the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). The munadi (caller) is one who raises his voice with speech. Al-nida' is raising the voice with speech strongly for the sake of making it heard, and it is derived from al-nida' (with a kasrah or damma on the nun), which is the high-pitched sound. It is said: "He is andá sawtan," meaning higher-voiced. So the origin of nida' is loudness of voice and crying out with it, and from this the calling of a person to a person to come to him is called nida', because it is his nature to raise the voice with it. Therefore they made for it extended letters, such as ya, a', ayā, and hayā. From it the adhan is called nida', and it is applied here to the exaggeration of making heard and inviting, even if there is no raising of voice in that. Nida' is also applied to requesting someone to come, in person or in understanding, with known letters, as in His saying, ﴿And We called him: "O Abraham"﴾ [al-Saffat: 104], ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ [al-Saffat: 105]. It is also permissible that this is what is meant here, since the Prophet calls people with expressions like "O people," "O sons of so-and-so," "O community of Muhammad," and similar. The explanation of the meanings of nida' will come at His saying, ﴿And they will be called: that is the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 43] in Surat al-A'raf. The lam is the lam of cause, meaning for the sake of faith in Allah.

The "an" in ﴿an amanu﴾ (that believe) is explanatory (tafsiriyyah) for what is in the verb yunadi of the meaning of saying, not its letters.

They used the particle of consequence (fa') in fa-amanna (so we believed), to indicate hastening and precedence to faith, and that is evidence of the soundness of their nature from error and obstinacy. They anticipated that their hastening to respond to the call of Islam would be appreciated by Allah, the Exalted. For this reason they built on it their saying, ﴿So forgive us our sins﴾, because when they expended all of their capacity in following the religion, they were worthy of hoping for forgiveness.

Ghafr (forgiveness) and takfir (expiation) are close in the root from which they are derived, except that ghafr and ghufran became common for pardon of sin, while takfir became common for compensating for a sin with a recompense; as if the recompense expiated the sin, meaning covered it. However, by "sins" they meant what was confined to their own selves, and for this they asked for its forgiveness; and they meant by "misdeeds" what involved the rights of people, so for these they asked for their expiation. It has been said that it is merely emphasis, which is fine. It has also been said that by "sins" they meant the major sins, and by "misdeeds" the minor ones, because avoiding major sins expiates minor ones, based on the view that dhanb (sin) is more indicative of wrongdoing than sayyi'ah (misdeed).

They asked for death along with the righteous, meaning that they should die in the state of righteousness, by having righteousness accompany them until death, and by not turning back on their heels. So if they die thus, they die among the righteous. The companionship here is a figurative companionship, which is participation in the complete state. Companionship with the righteous is more eloquent in the indication of attribute, because it is righteousness whose continuation and increase is hoped for, since its possessor is within a group that increase him in devotion to righteousness, by the tongue of speech and the tongue of condition.

When they asked for reward in this world and the Hereafter, they advanced in the request to seeking the realization of the reward, so they said, ﴿and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾.

The word ʿalā (upon/through) may be used to make the verb of promise transitive, and its meaning is causation, so the messengers would be those upon whom the promise is made; the meaning of "promise upon the messengers" is that it is a promise upon their affirmation, so it is necessary to posit an omitted noun (muḍāf). The complement of the preposition in such a case is a general "being" that is not general but a specific being, and there is no harm in that when the context indicates it. The meaning of ʿalā then is figurative elevation. [p. 201]

The promise conveyed through the messengers, or the reward given to those who believe in them, is most plausibly both the reward of the Hereafter and the reward of this world. This is based on His saying, ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 148], and His saying, ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 55], and His saying, ﴿And We had already written in the Zabur (Psalms) after the reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105]. The word "messengers" in His saying ﴿upon Your messengers﴾ refers specifically to Muhammad (ﷺ), and the plural term "messengers" is applied to him as a form of honour, based on His saying, ﴿So do not think that Allah will fail to fulfil His promise to His messengers﴾ [Ibrahim: 47]. Similarly is His saying, ﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾ [al-Furqan: 37].

[p. 201 continued]

If you ask: if they knew that Allah had promised them this, and that He does not break His promise, what is the purpose of their asking for it in their supplication? I answer: there are several aspects to this.

The first: they asked for it so that its fulfilment would be a sign of the acceptance of the deeds for which Allah had promised reward. They may think that they have performed what would bring them to that rank, yet fear that perhaps they have mixed their righteous deeds with things that nullify them. This may be the reason for the use of the conjunction "wa" (and) in their saying ﴿and grant us what You promised us﴾ rather than "fa" (so). They made it an independent supplication, so that it would be realised and its cause would be realised, and they did not make it the result of an action whose occurrence was certain. This interpretation is supported by His later saying, ﴿So their Lord responded to them: "I do not waste the work of any worker among you"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195], even though they did not here ask that their deeds not be wasted.

The second: al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: they wanted the success (tawfiq) to reach the means of what Allah had promised them through His messengers. So the statement is used metaphorically (kinayah) to mean the cause of that success, namely the ability to perform the deeds for which the reward was promised.

The third: he (al-Zamakhshari) also said, in substance: this may be a matter of courtesy (adab) towards Allah, so that they do not appear as one who deserves the promised reward by right, and so they humble themselves, like the messengers' request for forgiveness, peace be upon them, though they knew that Allah had forgiven them.

The fourth: al-Qarafi answered in al-Furuq (no. 273) that they asked for it because its fulfilment is conditional upon dying in faith. This may be supported by the fact that before it they had said, ﴿and let us die among the righteous﴾. However, this answer restricts the promised reward to the reward of the Hereafter, and they repeated the request for deliverance from the disgrace of the Day of Resurrection because of its severity upon them.

The fifth: the promise they asked for is victory over the enemy in particular. So their supplication, ﴿and grant us what You promised us upon Your messengers﴾, is intended to hasten that for them. That is, the promise was made to the whole community, so each individual who makes this supplication means that Allah should make him among those who witness the fulfilment of Allah's promise, out of fear that it might pass them by. This is like the saying of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt: "We emigrated with the Prophet seeking the face of Allah, and our reward fell upon Allah. Among us are those whose fruit ripened and who are now gathering it, and among us are those who died without consuming any of their reward. Among them was Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, who was killed on the day of Uhud, and we found nothing to shroud him in except a cloak..." etc.

[p. 202]

They began their supplication and interspersed it with the calling upon Him, may He be exalted, five times, to show their need for Allah's turning towards them. It is narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever is afflicted with a matter and says, 'O my Lord,' five times, Allah will deliver him from what he fears and give him what he desires." And recite: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides … up to His saying: "Indeed, You do not break the promise"﴾.

[Page 196]

This topic is a new one (ghara[ḍ]) that is unrelated (unprecedented) compared with the topics that the surah has followed. The discussion moved from the introductions, the central aim, and the interjections occasioned by circumstances, to a new topic: taking lessons (i'tibar) from the creation of the worlds and their attributes, and praising those who draw lessons from the signs contained in them.

This kind of transition signals that the discussion of the surah's topics, with all their variety, is coming to an end. The surah had moved from one topic to a related one, and now it has shifted to a general topic: taking lessons from the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the condition of the believers in being admonished by that. This manner of transition occurs to the orator, and those like him, after giving a topic its due, moving to another topic as a sign that the speech is nearing its end. It is the way of the Qur'an to conclude with admonition, because it is the most important of the purposes of the message, as occurs at the close of Surat al-Baqarah.

The particle inna (indeed) is for emphasis on the information.

By "the creation of the heavens and the earth" here is meant either the effects of their creation, which is the order placed within them, or "creation" is taken to mean the created things, as in His saying, ﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾ [Luqman: 11]. "Ulu al-albab" [Ali 'Imran: 7] are the people of complete intellects, because the lubb (core) of a thing is its essence. We have already discussed in Surat al-Baqarah the signs contained in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day, at His saying, ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, and the ship...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], etc.

"Yadhkurun Allah" (they remember Allah) is either from the remembrance by the tongue or from the remembrance of the heart, which is reflection (tafakkur). By His saying, ﴿standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ He intends the generality of conditions, like the saying, "He struck him on the back and the belly," and the saying, "such-and-such is famous among the people of the East and the West." Moreover, these conditions are the customary conditions of human beings in ease, meaning the conditions of occupation, rest, and the intention to sleep. It has been said that He meant the conditions of those who pray: [one who is] able, [one who is] unable, and one who is severely unable. But the context of the verse is far from this meaning.

His saying, ﴿and they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a synonymous conjunction if by remembrance in what preceded is meant reflection; its repetition is for the difference in what is reflected upon. Or it is a different conjunction if by His saying "yadhkurun" is meant remembrance by the tongue. Reflection (tafakkur) is a great act of worship. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, in the Jami' al-'Utbiyyah, that he said: It was said to Umm al-Darda': "What was the matter of Abu al-Darda'?" She said: "Most of his matter was reflection." It was said to him: "Do you consider reflection to be one of the deeds?" He said: "Yes, it is certainty (yaqin)."

[Page 197]

"Khalq" (creation) here means the manner of the effect of creation, or the created things that are in the heavens and the earth, so the genitive construction is either in the sense of "li" (belonging to) or in the sense of "fi" (in).

His saying, ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ and what follows it is a clause standing in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), with an implied "saying": meaning, they reflect saying, "Our Lord, etc.," because this statement is intended as a quotation of their words, as evidenced by what follows it of supplication.

If you say: How did all of the people of intellect agree upon saying this glorification and supplication when reflecting, despite the difference in their reflections, their impressions, and their aims? I say: It is possible that they received it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so they would persist in it during reflection and after it. And it is possible that Allah inspired them with it, so it became their habitual utterance, like His saying, ﴿And they said: "We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285], and the verses. What supports this is the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas in the Sahih, who said: "I spent the night at the house of my maternal aunt Maymunah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) got up, wiped the sleep from his face, then recited the ten verses from Surat Al 'Imran," until the end of the hadith.

In my view it is also permissible that His saying, ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ be a report of their reflection within themselves. It is then the speech of the self, in which all reflecting people share, since they are equal in the validity of reflection, because it moves from one meaning to another branching out from it. The people of intellect spoken of here are equal in grasping these meanings. I say: It is possible that they received it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so they would persist in it during reflection and after it. And it is possible that Allah inspired them with it, so it became their habitual utterance, like His saying, ﴿And they said: "We hear and we obey. It is then the speech of the self, in which all reflecting people share, since they are equal in the validity of reflection, because it moves from one meaning to another branching out from it. The people of intellect spoken of here are equal in grasping these meanings. And they sought means to that by having exerted the utmost of their ability in seeking salvation, as they responded to the caller to faith, who was the Messenger, peace be upon him. They asked for forgiveness of sins and expiation of misdeeds, and dying in righteousness, and so on. Hardly any of the people of intellect is free from these reflections, and perhaps adds to them. When this verse was revealed and spread among them, those who had not previously noticed this reflection were guided to it, and it became widespread among the Muslims, in its meanings and its wording.

[Page 198]

The meaning of ﴿You did not create this in vain﴾ is: a vain creation; or: You did not create this while it is in the state of being vain. So it is a state (hal) that is necessarily mentioned in negation, though it is a supplementary element (fadlah) in affirmation, like His saying, ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38]. The Arabs often construct the negative form on the basis of the prior affirmation.

The particle of consequence (fa') is used in the quotation of their words, ﴿so protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, because it follows from knowledge that this creation is true, and it is part of the truth that the righteous and the wicked are not equal, nor the obedient and the disobedient. So they knew that each has a fitting abode, and they asked to be among the people of goodness who are kept away from the punishment of the Fire.

Their saying, ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him﴾ is brought as a justification (ta'lil) for the request for protection from the Fire, as the particle inna, used for the purpose of emphasis, indicates, since there is no context here for stressing. Khizy is the verbal noun of khazia, meaning to be humiliated and debased in the sight of people, and akhza-hu means to humiliate him before the eyes of the witnesses. The reason for the request for protection from the Fire being that entering it is a disgrace, after the allusion to what necessitates that request in their saying "the punishment of the Fire," is that the Fire, along with the painful torment in it, contains subjugation of the one tormented and public humiliation, and this is a meaning settled in the souls of people. From it is the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him, ﴿And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 87]. This is because the connection between the condition and the consequence is evident: whoever enters the Fire, You have disgraced him. Disgrace is something that souls cannot bear, so there is no need for an interpretation that they took, to the effect of "You have disgraced him with a great disgrace." The author of al-Kashshaf likened it to the saying of the Arab herdsmen, "Whoever reaches the pasture of al-Samman has reached [the pasture]," meaning he has reached pasture, lest the meaning of the consequence be necessarily obtained from the condition, and then there would be no benefit in conditioning by the condition, since it would render the speech devoid of benefit in that case. Some of this has preceded at His saying, ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has succeeded﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 185].

And for this reason they followed it with what is in human nature: seeking refuge from disgrace and humiliation by hastening to their allies and helpers. So they knew that there is no helper in the Hereafter for the wrongdoer, and thus they added

[Page 199]

emphasis to their eagerness to seek refuge from the punishment of the Fire, when they said, ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾, meaning: for the people of the Fire there are no helpers who could ward off disgrace from them.

His saying, ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling﴾: they meant by it the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). The munadi (caller) is one who raises his voice with speech. Al-nida' is raising the voice with speech strongly for the sake of making it heard, and it is derived from al-nida' (with a kasrah or damma on the nun), which is the high-pitched sound. It is said: "He is andá sawtan," meaning higher-voiced. So the origin of nida' is loudness of voice and crying out with it, and from this the calling of a person to a person to come to him is called nida', because it is his nature to raise the voice with it. Therefore they made for it extended letters, such as ya, a', ayā, and hayā. From it the adhan is called nida', and it is applied here to the exaggeration of making heard and inviting, even if there is no raising of voice in that. Nida' is also applied to requesting someone to come, in person or in understanding, with known letters, as in His saying, ﴿And We called him: "O Abraham"﴾ [al-Saffat: 104], ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ [al-Saffat: 105]. It is also permissible that this is what is meant here, since the Prophet calls people with expressions like "O people," "O sons of so-and-so," "O community of Muhammad," and similar. The explanation of the meanings of nida' will come at His saying, ﴿And they will be called: that is the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 43] in Surat al-A'raf. The lam is the lam of cause, meaning for the sake of faith in Allah.

The "an" in ﴿an amanu﴾ (that believe) is explanatory (tafsiriyyah) for what is in the verb yunadi of the meaning of saying, not its letters.

They used the particle of consequence (fa') in fa-amanna (so we believed), to indicate hastening and precedence to faith, and that is evidence of the soundness of their nature from error and obstinacy. They anticipated that their hastening to respond to the call of Islam would be appreciated by Allah, the Exalted. For this reason they built on it their saying, ﴿So forgive us our sins﴾, because when they expended all of their capacity in following the religion, they were worthy of hoping for forgiveness.

Ghafr (forgiveness) and takfir (expiation) are close in the root from which they are derived, except that ghafr and ghufran became common for pardon of sin, while takfir became common for compensating for a sin with a recompense; as if the recompense expiated the sin, meaning covered it. From this comes the name of the expiation for breaking the fast in Ramadan, and the expiation for breaking an oath. However, by "sins" they meant what was confined to their own selves, and for this they asked for its forgiveness; and they meant by "misdeeds" what involved the rights of people, so for these they asked for their expiation. It has been said that it is merely emphasis, which is fine. It has also been said that by "sins" they meant the major sins, and by "misdeeds" the minor ones, because avoiding major sins expiates minor ones, based on the view that dhanb (sin) is more indicative of wrongdoing than sayyi'ah (misdeed).

They asked for death along with the righteous, meaning that they should die in the state of righteousness, by having righteousness accompany them until death, and by not turning back on their heels. So if they die thus, they die among the righteous. The companionship here is a figurative companionship, which is participation in the complete state. Companionship with the righteous is more eloquent in the indication of attribute, because it is righteousness whose continuation and increase is hoped for, since its possessor is within a group that increase him in devotion to righteousness, by the tongue of speech and the tongue of condition.

When they asked for reward in this world and the Hereafter, they advanced in the request to seeking the realization of the reward, so they said, ﴿and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾.

The word ʿalā (upon/through) may be used to make the verb of promise transitive, and its meaning is causation, so the messengers would be those upon whom the promise is made; the meaning of "promise upon the messengers" is that it is a promise upon their affirmation, so it is necessary to posit an omitted noun (muḍāf). It may also be that ʿalā is an established adverbial (ẓarf mustaqarr), meaning a promise established upon Your messengers, i.e., sent down upon them. The complement of the preposition in such a case is a general "being" that is not general but a specific being, and there is no harm in that when the context indicates it. The meaning of ʿalā then is figurative elevation. Or ʿalā may be made an established adverbial and a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from "what You promised us" also, by positing a general "being" but with an omitted noun added to "Your messengers," meaning: through the tongues of Your messengers.

[p. 201]

The promise conveyed through the messengers, or the reward given to those who believe in them, is most plausibly both the reward of the Hereafter and the reward of this world. This is based on His saying, ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 148], and His saying, ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 55], and His saying, ﴿And We had already written in the Zabur (Psalms) after the reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105]. The word "messengers" in His saying ﴿upon Your messengers﴾ refers specifically to Muhammad (ﷺ), and the plural term "messengers" is applied to him as a form of honour, based on His saying, ﴿So do not think that Allah will fail to fulfil His promise to His messengers﴾ [Ibrahim: 47]. Similarly is His saying, ﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾ [al-Furqan: 37].

[p. 201 continued]

If you ask: if they knew that Allah had promised them this, and that He does not break His promise, what is the purpose of their asking for it in their supplication? I answer: there are several aspects to this.

The first: they asked for it so that its fulfilment would be a sign of the acceptance of the deeds for which Allah had promised reward. They may think that they have performed what would bring them to that rank, yet fear that perhaps they have mixed their righteous deeds with things that nullify them. This may be the reason for the use of the conjunction "wa" (and) in their saying ﴿and grant us what You promised us﴾ rather than "fa" (so). They made it an independent supplication, so that it would be realised and its cause would be realised, and they did not make it the result of an action whose occurrence was certain. This interpretation is supported by His later saying, ﴿So their Lord responded to them: "I do not waste the work of any worker among you"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195], even though they did not here ask that their deeds not be wasted.

The second: al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: they wanted the success (tawfiq) to reach the means of what Allah had promised them through His messengers. So the statement is used metaphorically (kinayah) to mean the cause of that success, namely the ability to perform the deeds for which the reward was promised.

The third: he (al-Zamakhshari) also said, in substance: this may be a matter of courtesy (adab) towards Allah, so that they do not appear as one who deserves the promised reward by right, and so they humble themselves, like the messengers' request for forgiveness, peace be upon them, though they knew that Allah had forgiven them.

The fourth: al-Qarafi answered in al-Furuq (no. 273) that they asked for it because its fulfilment is conditional upon dying in faith. This may be supported by the fact that before it they had said, ﴿and let us die among the righteous﴾. However, this answer restricts the promised reward to the reward of the Hereafter, and they repeated the request for deliverance from the disgrace of the Day of Resurrection because of its severity upon them.

The fifth: the promise they asked for is victory over the enemy in particular. So their supplication, ﴿and grant us what You promised us upon Your messengers﴾, is intended to hasten that for them. That is, the promise was made to the whole community, so each individual who makes this supplication means that Allah should make him among those who witness the fulfilment of Allah's promise, out of fear that it might pass them by. This is like the saying of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt: "We emigrated with the Prophet seeking the face of Allah, and our reward fell upon Allah. Among us are those whose fruit ripened and who are now gathering it, and among us are those who died without consuming any of their reward. Among them was Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, who was killed on the day of Uhud, and we found nothing to shroud him in except a cloak..." etc.

[p. 202]

They began their supplication and interspersed it with the calling upon Him, may He be exalted, five times, to show their need for Allah's turning towards them. It is narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever is afflicted with a matter and says, 'O my Lord,' five times, Allah will deliver him from what he fears and give him what he desires." And recite: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides … up to His saying: "Indeed, You do not break the promise"﴾.
