When they asked for reward in this world and the Hereafter, they advanced in the request to seeking the realization of the reward, so they said, ﴿and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾.

The word ʿalā (upon/through) may be used to make the verb of promise transitive, and its meaning is causation, so the messengers would be those upon whom the promise is made; the meaning of "promise upon the messengers" is that it is a promise upon their affirmation, so it is necessary to posit an omitted noun (muḍāf). It may also be that ʿalā is an established adverbial (ẓarf mustaqarr), meaning a promise established upon Your messengers, i.e., sent down upon them. The complement of the preposition in such a case is a general "being" that is not general but a specific being, and there is no harm in that when the context indicates it. The meaning of ʿalā then is figurative elevation. Or ʿalā may be made an established adverbial and a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from "what You promised us" also, by positing a general "being" but with an omitted noun added to "Your messengers," meaning: through the tongues of Your messengers.

[p. 201]

The promise conveyed through the messengers, or the reward given to those who believe in them, is most plausibly both the reward of the Hereafter and the reward of this world. This is based on His saying, ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 148], and His saying, ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 55], and His saying, ﴿And We had already written in the Zabur (Psalms) after the reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105]. The word "messengers" in His saying ﴿upon Your messengers﴾ refers specifically to Muhammad (ﷺ), and the plural term "messengers" is applied to him as a form of honour, based on His saying, ﴿So do not think that Allah will fail to fulfil His promise to His messengers﴾ [Ibrahim: 47]. Similarly is His saying, ﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾ [al-Furqan: 37].

[p. 201 continued]

If you ask: if they knew that Allah had promised them this, and that He does not break His promise, what is the purpose of their asking for it in their supplication? I answer: there are several aspects to this.

The first: they asked for it so that its fulfilment would be a sign of the acceptance of the deeds for which Allah had promised reward. They may think that they have performed what would bring them to that rank, yet fear that perhaps they have mixed their righteous deeds with things that nullify them. This may be the reason for the use of the conjunction "wa" (and) in their saying ﴿and grant us what You promised us﴾ rather than "fa" (so). They made it an independent supplication, so that it would be realised and its cause would be realised, and they did not make it the result of an action whose occurrence was certain. This interpretation is supported by His later saying, ﴿So their Lord responded to them: "I do not waste the work of any worker among you"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195], even though they did not here ask that their deeds not be wasted.

The second: al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: they wanted the success (tawfiq) to reach the means of what Allah had promised them through His messengers. So the statement is used metaphorically (kinayah) to mean the cause of that success, namely the ability to perform the deeds for which the reward was promised.

The third: he (al-Zamakhshari) also said, in substance: this may be a matter of courtesy (adab) towards Allah, so that they do not appear as one who deserves the promised reward by right, and so they humble themselves, like the messengers' request for forgiveness, peace be upon them, though they knew that Allah had forgiven them.

The fourth: al-Qarafi answered in al-Furuq (no. 273) that they asked for it because its fulfilment is conditional upon dying in faith. This may be supported by the fact that before it they had said, ﴿and let us die among the righteous﴾. However, this answer restricts the promised reward to the reward of the Hereafter, and they repeated the request for deliverance from the disgrace of the Day of Resurrection because of its severity upon them.

The fifth: the promise they asked for is victory over the enemy in particular. So their supplication, ﴿and grant us what You promised us upon Your messengers﴾, is intended to hasten that for them. That is, the promise was made to the whole community, so each individual who makes this supplication means that Allah should make him among those who witness the fulfilment of Allah's promise, out of fear that it might pass them by. This is like the saying of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt: "We emigrated with the Prophet seeking the face of Allah, and our reward fell upon Allah. Among us are those whose fruit ripened and who are now gathering it, and among us are those who died without consuming any of their reward. Among them was Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, who was killed on the day of Uhud, and we found nothing to shroud him in except a cloak..." etc.

[p. 202]

They began their supplication and interspersed it with the calling upon Him, may He be exalted, five times, to show their need for Allah's turning towards them. It is narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever is afflicted with a matter and says, 'O my Lord,' five times, Allah will deliver him from what he fears and give him what he desires." And recite: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides … up to His saying: "Indeed, You do not break the promise"﴾.

[Page 196]

This topic is a new one (ghara[ḍ]) that is unrelated (unprecedented) compared with the topics that the surah has followed. The discussion moved from the introductions, the central aim, and the interjections occasioned by circumstances, to a new topic: taking lessons (i'tibar) from the creation of the worlds and their attributes, and praising those who draw lessons from the signs contained in them.

This kind of transition signals that the discussion of the surah's topics, with all their variety, is coming to an end. The surah had moved from one topic to a related one, and now it has shifted to a general topic: taking lessons from the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the condition of the believers in being admonished by that. This manner of transition occurs to the orator, and those like him, after giving a topic its due, moving to another topic as a sign that the speech is nearing its end. It is the way of the Qur'an to conclude with admonition, because it is the most important of the purposes of the message, as occurs at the close of Surat al-Baqarah.

The particle inna (indeed) is for emphasis on the information.

By "the creation of the heavens and the earth" here is meant either the effects of their creation, which is the order placed within them, or "creation" is taken to mean the created things, as in His saying, ﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾ [Luqman: 11]. "Ulu al-albab" [Ali 'Imran: 7] are the people of complete intellects, because the lubb (core) of a thing is its essence. We have already discussed in Surat al-Baqarah the signs contained in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day, at His saying, ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, and the ship...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], etc.

"Yadhkurun Allah" (they remember Allah) is either from the remembrance by the tongue or from the remembrance of the heart, which is reflection (tafakkur). By His saying, ﴿standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ He intends the generality of conditions, like the saying, "He struck him on the back and the belly," and the saying, "such-and-such is famous among the people of the East and the West." Moreover, these conditions are the customary conditions of human beings in ease, meaning the conditions of occupation, rest, and the intention to sleep. It has been said that He meant the conditions of those who pray: [one who is] able, [one who is] unable, and one who is severely unable. But the context of the verse is far from this meaning.

His saying, ﴿and they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a synonymous conjunction if by remembrance in what preceded is meant reflection; its repetition is for the difference in what is reflected upon. Or it is a different conjunction if by His saying "yadhkurun" is meant remembrance by the tongue. Reflection (tafakkur) is a great act of worship. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, in the Jami' al-'Utbiyyah, that he said: It was said to Umm al-Darda': "What was the matter of Abu al-Darda'?" She said: "Most of his matter was reflection." It was said to him: "Do you consider reflection to be one of the deeds?" He said: "Yes, it is certainty (yaqin)."

[Page 197]

"Khalq" (creation) here means the manner of the effect of creation, or the created things that are in the heavens and the earth, so the genitive construction is either in the sense of "li" (belonging to) or in the sense of "fi" (in).

His saying, ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ and what follows it is a clause standing in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), with an implied "saying": meaning, they reflect saying, "Our Lord, etc.," because this statement is intended as a quotation of their words, as evidenced by what follows it of supplication.

If you say: How did all of the people of intellect agree upon saying this glorification and supplication when reflecting, despite the difference in their reflections, their impressions, and their aims? I say: It is possible that they received it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so they would persist in it during reflection and after it. And it is possible that Allah inspired them with it, so it became their habitual utterance, like His saying, ﴿And they said: "We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285], and the verses. What supports this is the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas in the Sahih, who said: "I spent the night at the house of my maternal aunt Maymunah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) got up, wiped the sleep from his face, then recited the ten verses from Surat Al 'Imran," until the end of the hadith.

In my view it is also permissible that His saying, ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ be a report of their reflection within themselves. It is then the speech of the self, in which all reflecting people share, since they are equal in the validity of reflection, because it moves from one meaning to another branching out from it. The people of intellect spoken of here are equal in grasping these meanings. So the first of the reflection produced for them that created things were not created in vain; then from it branched the glorification of Allah and the request that He protect them from the punishment of the Fire, because they saw in created things the obedient and the disobedient, so they knew that behind this world there is reward and punishment, and so they sought refuge that they would not be among those upon whom the word of punishment is due. And they sought means to that by having exerted the utmost of their ability in seeking salvation, as they responded to the caller to faith, who was the Messenger, peace be upon him. They asked for forgiveness of sins and expiation of misdeeds, and dying in righteousness, and so on. Hardly any of the people of intellect is free from these reflections, and perhaps adds to them. When this verse was revealed and spread among them, those who had not previously noticed this reflection were guided to it, and it became widespread among the Muslims, in its meanings and its wording.

[Page 198]

The meaning of ﴿You did not create this in vain﴾ is: a vain creation; or: You did not create this while it is in the state of being vain. So it is a state (hal) that is necessarily mentioned in negation, though it is a supplementary element (fadlah) in affirmation, like His saying, ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38]. The aim is the negation of the beliefs of those whose belief leads to the conclusion that this creation is vain or was left devoid of wisdom. The Arabs often construct the negative form on the basis of the prior affirmation.

The particle of consequence (fa') is used in the quotation of their words, ﴿so protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, because it follows from knowledge that this creation is true, and it is part of the truth that the righteous and the wicked are not equal, nor the obedient and the disobedient. So they knew that each has a fitting abode, and they asked to be among the people of goodness who are kept away from the punishment of the Fire.

Their saying, ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him﴾ is brought as a justification (ta'lil) for the request for protection from the Fire, as the particle inna, used for the purpose of emphasis, indicates, since there is no context here for stressing. Khizy is the verbal noun of khazia, meaning to be humiliated and debased in the sight of people, and akhza-hu means to humiliate him before the eyes of the witnesses. The reason for the request for protection from the Fire being that entering it is a disgrace, after the allusion to what necessitates that request in their saying "the punishment of the Fire," is that the Fire, along with the painful torment in it, contains subjugation of the one tormented and public humiliation, and this is a meaning settled in the souls of people. From it is the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him, ﴿And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 87]. This is because the connection between the condition and the consequence is evident: whoever enters the Fire, You have disgraced him. Disgrace is something that souls cannot bear, so there is no need for an interpretation that they took, to the effect of "You have disgraced him with a great disgrace." The author of al-Kashshaf likened it to the saying of the Arab herdsmen, "Whoever reaches the pasture of al-Samman has reached [the pasture]," meaning he has reached pasture, lest the meaning of the consequence be necessarily obtained from the condition, and then there would be no benefit in conditioning by the condition, since it would render the speech devoid of benefit in that case. Some of this has preceded at His saying, ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has succeeded﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 185].

And for this reason they followed it with what is in human nature: seeking refuge from disgrace and humiliation by hastening to their allies and helpers. So they knew that there is no helper in the Hereafter for the wrongdoer, and thus they added

[Page 199]

emphasis to their eagerness to seek refuge from the punishment of the Fire, when they said, ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾, meaning: for the people of the Fire there are no helpers who could ward off disgrace from them.

His saying, ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling﴾: they meant by it the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). The munadi (caller) is one who raises his voice with speech. Al-nida' is raising the voice with speech strongly for the sake of making it heard, and it is derived from al-nida' (with a kasrah or damma on the nun), which is the high-pitched sound. It is said: "He is andá sawtan," meaning higher-voiced. So the origin of nida' is loudness of voice and crying out with it, and from this the calling of a person to a person to come to him is called nida', because it is his nature to raise the voice with it. Therefore they made for it extended letters, such as ya, a', ayā, and hayā. From it the adhan is called nida', and it is applied here to the exaggeration of making heard and inviting, even if there is no raising of voice in that. Nida' is also applied to requesting someone to come, in person or in understanding, with known letters, as in His saying, ﴿And We called him: "O Abraham"﴾ [al-Saffat: 104], ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ [al-Saffat: 105]. It is also permissible that this is what is meant here, since the Prophet calls people with expressions like "O people," "O sons of so-and-so," "O community of Muhammad," and similar. The explanation of the meanings of nida' will come at His saying, ﴿And they will be called: that is the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 43] in Surat al-A'raf. The lam is the lam of cause, meaning for the sake of faith in Allah.

The "an" in ﴿an amanu﴾ (that believe) is explanatory (tafsiriyyah) for what is in the verb yunadi of the meaning of saying, not its letters.

They used the particle of consequence (fa') in fa-amanna (so we believed), to indicate hastening and precedence to faith, and that is evidence of the soundness of their nature from error and obstinacy. They anticipated that their hastening to respond to the call of Islam would be appreciated by Allah, the Exalted. For this reason they built on it their saying, ﴿So forgive us our sins﴾, because when they expended all of their capacity in following the religion, they were worthy of hoping for forgiveness.

Ghafr (forgiveness) and takfir (expiation) are close in the root from which they are derived, except that ghafr and ghufran became common for pardon of sin, while takfir became common for compensating for a sin with a recompense; as if the recompense expiated the sin, meaning covered it. From this comes the name of the expiation for breaking the fast in Ramadan, and the expiation for breaking an oath. However, by "sins" they meant what was confined to their own selves, and for this they asked for its forgiveness; and they meant by "misdeeds" what involved the rights of people, so for these they asked for their expiation. It has been said that it is merely emphasis, which is fine. It has also been said that by "sins" they meant the major sins, and by "misdeeds" the minor ones, because avoiding major sins expiates minor ones, based on the view that dhanb (sin) is more indicative of wrongdoing than sayyi'ah (misdeed).

They asked for death along with the righteous, meaning that they should die in the state of righteousness, by having righteousness accompany them until death, and by not turning back on their heels. So if they die thus, they die among the righteous. The companionship here is a figurative companionship, which is participation in the complete state. Companionship with the righteous is more eloquent in the indication of attribute, because it is righteousness whose continuation and increase is hoped for, since its possessor is within a group that increase him in devotion to righteousness, by the tongue of speech and the tongue of condition.

When they asked for reward in this world and the Hereafter, they advanced in the request to seeking the realization of the reward, so they said, ﴿and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾.

The word ʿalā (upon/through) may be used to make the verb of promise transitive, and its meaning is causation, so the messengers would be those upon whom the promise is made; the meaning of "promise upon the messengers" is that it is a promise upon their affirmation, so it is necessary to posit an omitted noun (muḍāf). It may also be that ʿalā is an established adverbial (ẓarf mustaqarr), meaning a promise established upon Your messengers, i.e., sent down upon them. The complement of the preposition in such a case is a general "being" that is not general but a specific being, and there is no harm in that when the context indicates it. The meaning of ʿalā then is figurative elevation. [p. 201]

This is based on His saying, ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 148], and His saying, ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 55], and His saying, ﴿And We had already written in the Zabur (Psalms) after the reminder that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105]. Similarly is His saying, ﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them﴾ [al-Furqan: 37].

[p. 201 continued]

[p. 202]

They began their supplication and interspersed it with the calling upon Him, may He be exalted, five times, to show their need for Allah's turning towards them. It is narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever is afflicted with a matter and says, 'O my Lord,' five times, Allah will deliver him from what he fears and give him what he desires." And recite: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides … up to His saying: "Indeed, You do not break the promise"﴾.

﴿Then their Lord answered them: "I do not waste the work of any worker among you, whether male or female; you are of one another. So those who emigrated, were expelled from their homes, were harmed in My cause, fought, and were killed, I will surely remove their bad deeds from them and admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from Allah. And with Allah is the best of rewards."﴾

The fa' (ف) indicates the swiftness of the response, with the sought-after outcome immediately obtained. It also indicates that the servant's private intimate supplication to his Lord is a form of du'a' (supplication) that is capable of being answered.

Ist[i]jaba (استجاب) means ajaba (أجاب, "answered") according to the majority of the linguists. The sin and the ta' are for emphasis, as in istawqada ("kindled") and istakhlasa ("chose for himself"). However, al-Farra' and 'Ali ibn 'Isa al-Rabba'i held that istajaba is more specific than ajaba, because istajaba is said of one who accepts what he is called to, whereas ajaba is more general, being said of one who responds either with acceptance or with rejection. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: istijaba is the seeking of an answer and the preparation for it, but it is used to express answering because answering rarely separates from it. It is said istajaba lahu and istajabahu, and in the verse it is followed by the preposition lam (لـ), just as they say hamida lahu and shakara lahu, though it may also be followed directly by its object, like them.

Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi said, lamenting a relative of his:

"And a caller who called, 'O you who answers the call,' but then, at that moment, no answerer answered him."

Their expression in their supplication, describing "our Lord" rather than using the name of majesty (Allah), is because the attribute of lordship (rububiyya) conveys compassion toward the one who is nurtured, the love of good for him, and an acknowledgment that they are His servants; and it allows the possessive construction, which conveys honour and closeness. It also answers the goodness of their supplication with its like, by their saying "Our Lord, our Lord."

[Page 203]

The meaning of the negation of wasting their deed is the negation of nullifying its reward: making it like something lost that does not reach the hand of its owner.

Thus the negation of wasting the deed is a promise of counting their deed and reckoning it to their account. The response therefore includes the confirmation that the deed is not wasted, reassuring their hearts from the fear that it might not be accepted. In this is evidence that by their words, "And grant us what You promised us through Your messengers" (Q. 3:194), they meant the confirmation that their deeds are accepted and seeking refuge from habt (حبط, the nullification of deeds).

His saying ﴿from male or female﴾ is an explanation of "worker." The reason this explanation is needed here is that the deeds they performed were, chiefly, faith, then emigration, then jihad. Since jihad was more frequent, it could be feared that women have no share in fulfilling the promise God made through His messengers. So this clarifies that women do have their share: in faith and emigration they are equal to men, and they have their share in the reward of jihad, because they tend the sick, treat the wounded, and give drink to the army; that is a great work, by which the lives of the Muslims are preserved, and it is not less than fighting, by which the lives of the enemies of the believers are destroyed.

His saying ﴿you are of one another﴾: the min (مِن) here is ittisaliyya (اتصالية), meaning that some of those who are answered are connected to others. It is a phrase the Arabs use to mean that their affair is one and their matter is the same. God, Exalted, said: "The hypocrite men and hypocrite women are of one another; they enjoin the evil" (Q. 9:67), and so on. They also say, "He is from me and I am from him," and in its reverse they say, as al-Nabigha said:

"Indeed I am not from you, and you are not from me."

Most of the exegetes have understood it to mean that your women and your men share one origin. On this reading, the position of this clause is that of a reason for the generalization in His saying "from male or female," meaning: because your affair is one. Each of them is one who, if he did not do what he does, the interest of the other would be lost. Therefore they are equal in the fulfilment of God's promise to them, even though their deeds differ. This is like His saying, "For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned" (Q. 4:32).

[Page 204]

My own view is more apparent: this is not a reason for the content of His saying "from male or female," but rather an explanation of the equality in the predicates related to the pronouns of the addressees, meaning: you are equal in My care for your deeds. This is the fulfilment of the right of the righteous deeds they share equally, so that it becomes a preparation for the spread of the distinction of the emigrants by the merit of emigration, which comes in His saying "Then those who emigrated" and the verses that follow.

His saying ﴿Then those who emigrated﴾ is a branch from His saying "I do not waste the work of any worker." It is the mention of the particular after the general, for the sake of giving attention to that particular. It includes an explanation of what they excelled in among the deeds, namely emigration, by which the emigrants attained success.

Al-muhajara (المهاجرة, emigration) is leaving one's homeland with the intention of settling elsewhere. The mufa'ala (مفاعلة, verbal form denoting reciprocity or intensity) in it is for intensification, as if he abandoned his people and they abandoned him, because they did not care for his remaining. The origin of emigration is that it is due to a quarrel or the like. It applies both to those who emigrated to the land of Abyssinia and to those who emigrated to Medina.

His saying ﴿and were expelled from their homes﴾ is coordinated with "emigrated" to realize the meaning of the mufa'ala in hajara (هاجر), meaning: they emigrated an emigration that their people compelled them to, whether the expulsion was by explicit statement or by compulsion, through ill treatment. The Muslims made the first emigration to Abyssinia because of the ill treatment they suffered from the polytheists. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made his emigration to Medina, and all the Muslims joined him, because of the harm they suffered from the polytheists. There is nothing indicating that the polytheists expelled the Muslims; how could that be, when the concealment of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at the time of his departure to Medina shows the polytheists' eagerness to prevent him from leaving? This is also shown by the words of Ka'b:

"Among a band of Quraysh, whose speaker said, when they had embraced Islam in the valley of Mecca: 'Move on!'"

That is, a speaker from among the Muslims said, "Leave Mecca." Accordingly, whatever is reported saying that they were expelled from their homes without right should be interpreted as compulsion to leave. From this is the saying of Waraqa ibn Nawfal: "Would that I were with you when your people expel you." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Will they expel me?" He said: "No man has come with the like of what you have come with except that he was opposed."

[Page 205]

His saying ﴿and were harmed in My cause﴾ means they were afflicted with harm, which is a disliked thing, a little of speech or of action. It is understood from this that whoever is afflicted with harm is more deserving of reward and more complete in it. This state applies to those who were harmed before the emigration and after it.

His saying ﴿and fought and were killed﴾ joins the two together to indicate that both categories have reward. The majority read ﴿and fought and were killed﴾ [qatalu wa-qutilu]. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﴿and were killed and fought﴾ [qutilu wa-qatalu], the reverse of the majority reading. The outcome of both readings is one. This state applies to the emigrants and the Helpers (al-Ansar) who struggled and were martyred or who remained alive.

His saying ﴿I will surely remove their bad deeds from them﴾ and so on is emphasized with the lam of oath. The expiation of bad deeds was discussed earlier.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verses 196–198:

﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve through the lands deceive you.﴾ ﴿A brief enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.﴾ ﴿But those who fear their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally — a provision from Allah. And what is with Allah is best for the righteous.﴾.

This is a parenthetical statement (i'tiraD) within the conclusion of this passage, arising from His saying ﴿So their Lord answered them: "Indeed, I will not allow to be lost the work of any worker among you"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 195], in terms of what the non-loss of work implies regarding a complete reward for it in this world and the Hereafter, and what that necessarily entails regarding the deprivation of those who did not respond to the caller to faith, namely the polytheists. They are the intended meaning of "those who disbelieve," as is the technical usage of the Qur'an reciters (qurra').

The address is to an unspecified person who might be imagined to be deceived by the good condition of the polytheists in this world.

Al-gharr and al-ghurur mean: enticing someone with a beloved matter while intending that it will not occur, or presenting a harmful matter in the form of a beneficial one. It is derived from al-ghirrah (with a kasra on the ghayn), meaning heedlessness; and a man is described as ghirr (with a kasra on the ghayn) when he is easily deceived by one who deceives him. In the hadith: "The believer is ghirr (guileless) and generous" — meaning he assumes good of the people of evil when they show him good.

Here it is used metaphorically for a thing appearing in a beloved guise, while in its outcome it is disliked.

The verb of deception is attributed to "movement" because movement is its cause; this is a rational metonymy (majaz 'aqli), and the meaning is: it should not be that it deceives you. Its parallel is ﴿Let not Satan tempt you﴾ [al-A'raf: 27]. The "la" is a prohibitive, because the energetic nun (nun al-tawkid) does not come with negation.

The majority read: la yaghurrannaka, with a doubled ra' and a doubled nun, which is the heavy energetic nun. Ruways from Ya'qub read it with a sukun nun, which is the light energetic nun.

Al-taqallub: the free disposal, according to one's will, in wars, trade, planting, and the like. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve, so let not their movement through the lands deceive you﴾ [Ghafir: 4].

Al-bilad: the lands. Al-mata': the thing purchased for enjoyment by it.

The sentence ﴿A brief enjoyment﴾ to its end is an explanation of the sentence "let not deceive you." Al-mata': immediate benefit. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And the life of this world is nothing but enjoyment in comparison to the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26].

The sentence ﴿But those who fear their Lord﴾ to its end is introduced with the particle of exception (harf al-istidrak), because its content is the opposite of the preceding statement, since the meaning of "let not deceive you" etc. is a description of their condition as a brief enjoyment, i.e., not lasting, while the believing, God-fearing people have lasting benefits.

The majority read: (wa-lakin) with the nun light and unvocalized (sakinah mukhaffafah), being from the heavy form, and it is inoperative (muhmalah). Abu Ja'far read it with a heavy nun, fatha-vocalized, and it is operative, acting as inna does.

Al-nuzul, with a damma on the nun and the zay, and also with a damma on the nun with a sukun on the zay: what is prepared for the guest and visitor of honor and hospitality. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿For you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you ask﴾ [Fussilat: 31] ﴿as a hospitable welcome from the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [Fussilat: 32].

Al-abrar is the plural of al-barr, the one characterized by goodness and righteousness (al-birr), which is excellence of deeds, the opposite of immorality (al-fujur).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 3, verse 199:

﴿And indeed, among the People of the Scripture are those who believe in Allah and what has been revealed to you and what was revealed to them, humbling themselves before Allah. They do not exchange the signs of Allah for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾

This is conjoined to the sentence ﴿But those who fear their Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran: 198], to complete the mention of the distinction in receiving Islam. These are the group of those among the People of the Scripture who believed but did not openly display their faith out of fear for their people, like the Negus, Ashama. Allah praised them for not distorting the religion. The verse indicates that they were not known for this, for if they had been known for faith, there would have been no benefit in describing them as People of the Scripture. This category is the opposite of the state of the hypocrites. He emphasized the statement with "inna" (indeed) and the lam of emphasis, in response to the hypocrites who said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he prayed over the Negus: "Look at him, praying over a Christian who is not of his religion and whom he never saw." This is according to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and some of his companions that this was the occasion of revelation of this verse. Perhaps the death of the Negus occurred before the Battle of Uhud.

It has been said: what is meant here are those who openly displayed their faith and affirmation from among the Jews, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and Mukhayriq, and likewise those from the Christians of Najran who believed, namely those who embraced Islam while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in Makkah, if the report of their conversion is sound.

The demonstrative noun was used in His saying ﴿Those will have their reward with their Lord﴾ to draw attention to the fact that those referred to by it are deserving of what will be stated about them afterward, because of what preceded the demonstrative.

By His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ He indicated that He hastens to give them their reward in this world and will give it to them on the Day of Resurrection.

[p. 208]

﴿O you who believe, be patient, outdo others in patience, stand guard, and fear God, that you may prosper.﴾

The surah concludes with a comprehensive exhortation to the believers, renewing their resolve and rousing their determination to remain constantly prepared against the enemy, so that the setback they suffered does not discourage them. He commanded them to *sabr* (patience), which gathers all virtues and the qualities of perfection. Then He commanded them to *musabarah* (outdoing one another in patience), which is being patient in the face of a patient opponent. This is the most demanding form of patience in terms of steadfastness of the soul and the most likely to cause it to waver. Patience in the face of another patient person is very hard on the soul, because one must withstand an adversary who matches or surpasses one in endurance. Moreover, if this person who competes in patience does not persist until his opponent tires, he gains nothing from his patience, because the outcome of patience belongs to the most enduring of the patient. As Zufar ibn al-Harith said in excusing his flight:

*We gave them a cup, and they gave us one like it, but they were more patient in the face of death.*

Thus *musabarah* is the cause of success in war, as the Arab poet whose name is unknown said:

*You are not accustomed in the battle to outlasting endurance, by which every enemy of yours is burned in fires.*

His words *wa-rabitu* ("and stand guard") are a command to them to undertake *murabatah*, which is a form of *mufa'alah* from *rabt* (binding). It means tethering horses for guarding, apart from fighting, out of fear that the enemy might surprise them. God commanded the Muslims to do this so that they would always be on guard against their enemy, alerting them to what the polytheists plotted of surprising them unawares after the Battle of Uhud, as we mentioned just above. This did indeed happen from them at the Battle of the Confederates. When God commanded them to fight (*jihad*), He then commanded them to remain alert against their enemy.

In the Book of Jihad in al-Bukhari there is a chapter: "The Virtue of Guarding (*ribat*) for a Day in the Way of God, and the Saying of God, Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, be patient, outdo others in patience, and stand guard﴾," and so on. *Murabatah* was known in the pre-Islamic period, namely tethering a horse for guard duty at the *thughur* (frontier passes), that is, the places through which the enemy could reach the tribe, such as the mountain ravines. No one has described this better than Labid in his Mu'allaqah when he said:

*I have protected the tribe, bearing my weapons, a horse with a long tail, when I set out, its bridle in my hand,*
*So I climbed, watching from a height covered with dust, a rising ground, to inform them of its dust-cloud,*
*Until it cast a hand upon an infidel, and the darkness of night concealed the frontier passes.*

[p. 209]

Thus he mentions that he guarded the tribe from a watchful height, by tethering his horse at the frontier. The Muslims used to stand guard at the frontiers of Persia, Syria, and al-Andalus on land. Then, when the sway of Islam expanded and they came to control the seas, *ribat* was practised at the sea frontiers, which are the shores from which the enemy's landing is feared, such as the *Ribat* of al-Mustir in Tunisia in Ifriqiya, the *Ribat* of Sala in the Maghrib, and the *ribats* and watchposts of Tunisia, such as the watchpost of 'Ali ibn Salim near Sfax. So God commanded *ribat* just as He commanded *jihad*, with this meaning.

Some exegetes have been unaware of this. One of them said: by His words "and stand guard" He meant preparing horses tethered for jihad, and said that there was no fighting at the frontiers in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). Another said: by His words "and stand guard" He meant waiting for the prayer after finishing the prayer before it, based on what Malik narrated in the *Muwatta'* from Abu Hurayrah: "The Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned waiting for prayer after prayer, and said: That is *ribat*, that is *ribat*." This is attributed to Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The truth is that the meaning of this hadith is figurative, like his saying: 'The strong man is not one who wrestles well,' and his saying: 'The needy one is not this wanderer whom a morsel or two morsels turn away,' that is, and like his saying (ﷺ): 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad.'"

He followed this command with the command to piety, because it gathers all goods, and through it success is hoped for.

Surat al-Nisa' (The Women)

This surah was called Surat al-Nisa' in the speech of the early generation (*salaf*). In Sahih al-Bukhari, 'A'ishah said: "Surat al-Baqarah and Surat al-Nisa' were not revealed except while I was with him." It is likewise named so in the codices of the Qur'an, in books of Sunnah, and in books of tafsir, and no other name for it is known. However, it may be inferred from what is related in Sahih al-Bukhari from Ibn Mas'ud, in his saying: "Surat al-Nisa' al-Qusra (the Shorter Women) was revealed," meaning Surat al-Talaq, that it shared this surah's name in the longer form. I have not found this stated explicitly. In the book *Basa'ir dhawi al-tamyiz* of al-Firuzabadi there occurs that this surah is called Surat al-Nisa' al-Kubra (the Greater Women), and the name of Surat al-Talaq is Surat al-Nisa' al-Sughra (the Lesser Women). I have not seen this in anyone else's work.

The reason it is named with reference to women is that it opens with rulings on maintaining kinship ties, then with rulings specific to women, and it contains many rulings concerning women: wives and daughters. It also closes with rulings specific to women.

Its revelation began in Medina, as is authentically reported from 'A'ishah, who said: "Surat al-Baqarah and Surat al-Nisa' were not revealed except while I was with him." It is known that the Prophet (ﷺ) consummated his marriage with 'A'ishah in Medina in Shawwal, eight months after the Hijrah. The scholars agreed that Surat al-Nisa' was revealed after al-Baqarah, so it is established that its revelation was considerably later than the Hijrah. The majority said it was revealed after Al 'Imran, and it is known that Al 'Imran was revealed during the year three, that is, after the Battle of Uhud, so Surat al-Nisa' must have been revealed after it. On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: the first surahs revealed in Medina were al-Baqarah, then al-Anfal, then Al 'Imran, then Surat al-Ahzab, then al-Mumtahanah, then al-Nisa'. If that is so, Surat al-Nisa' was revealed after the Battle of the Confederates, which took place at the end of year four or the beginning of year five after the Hijrah, and after the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, which was in year six, since Surat al-Mumtahanah contained the condition of returning those who came from the polytheists fleeing to the Muslims, except women. It is the verse: ﴿When believing women come to you as emigrants﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], and so on. It has been said that the verse ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [al-Nisa': 2] was revealed concerning a man from Ghatafan who had an orphaned nephew, and the Ghatafan embraced Islam after the Battle of the Confederates, since they were among the Confederates, that is, after year five. Some scholars said Surat al-Nisa' was revealed at the time of the Hijrah. This is far-fetched. Even more strange is the one who said it was revealed in Mecca, because it opens with ﴿O mankind﴾, and whatever contains "O mankind" is Meccan. Perhaps he means that it was revealed in Mecca during the Conquest, not before the Hijrah, since they use the term "Meccan" in two senses. Some said its beginning was revealed in Mecca and the rest in Medina. The truth is that the address "O mankind" indicates only the intention to include the people of Mecca in the address, and does not necessitate that it was in Mecca or before the Hijrah, for many verses containing "O mankind" are Medinan by consensus.

There is no doubt that it was revealed after Al 'Imran, because Surat al-Nisa' contains details of rulings of the kind that belong to after the Muslims had settled in Medina, their affairs had been organized, and they were secure from their enemies. It contains the verse of tayammum (dry ablution), and tayammum was legislated on the day of the expedition of al-Muraysi' in year five; it was also said in year six. What appears is that the revelation of Surat al-Nisa' occurred around year seven, and the period of its revelation was prolonged. This is supported by the fact that many of the rulings that come in it in detail were previously mentioned in summary in Surat al-Baqarah, such as rulings on orphans, women, and inheritance. Most of what is in Surat al-Nisa' is detailed legislation on most aspects of the social life of Muslims: systems of property, social relations, governance, and other matters. Moreover, it has been said that the last verse of it, the verse of *kalalah* (one dying without descendants or ascendants), is the last verse revealed of the Qur'an. Yet it is possible that between the revelation of the rest of Surat al-Nisa' and the revelation of the verse of *kalalah* at its end there was a long interval, and that when the final verse of *kalalah* was revealed they were commanded to attach it to Surat al-Nisa', in which the first verse of *kalalah* is. It is reported in the Sunnah that the first verse of *kalalah* is called the verse of winter, and the last verse of *kalalah* is called the verse of summer.

Its beginning of revelation must have been before the Conquest of Mecca, because of His saying: ﴿And why should you not fight in the way of God and for the oppressed men, women, and children, who say: Our Lord, bring us out of this town whose people are wrongdoers﴾ [al-Nisa': 75], meaning Mecca. It contains the verse: ﴿God commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [al-Nisa': 58], which was revealed on the day of the Conquest of Mecca concerning the case of 'Uthman ibn Talhah al-Shaybi, keeper of the key of the Ka'bah. It contains no dispute with the polytheists except for belittling their religion, such as His saying: ﴿Whoever associates partners with God has indeed fabricated a tremendous sin﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], ﴿he has strayed far astray﴾ [al-Nisa': 116], and so on.

[p. 213]

Besides this, it contains a threat of fighting, the cutting off of excuses of those who held back from emigration, and the weakening of the might of the polytheists against the Muslims, which indicates that the matter of the polytheists had come to weakness, and the Muslims had come to be in a position of strength over them. Most of the surah, after the legislation, is extensive argument with the Jews and exposure of the conditions of the hypocrites. There is some argument with the Christians, though not extensive, but it is broader than what is in Surat Al 'Imran, which indicates that the mixing of Muslims with Christians began to appear because of the spread of Islam in the northern borderlands of the Hijaz and the conquest of most of the Hijaz and Tihamah.

It is counted as the ninety-third of the surahs, revealed after Surat al-Mumtahanah and before Surat ﴿When the earth is shaken﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1].

The number of its verses is one hundred and seventy-five according to the count of the people of Medina, Mecca, and Basra; one hundred and seventy-six according to the count of the people of Kufa; and one hundred and seventy-seven according to the count of the people of Syria.

It contains many purposes and rulings, most of which concern the legislation of dealings with relatives and their rights. Accordingly, its opening is fitting for this, by reminding of the blessing of God's creation, and that they are obliged to thank their Lord for it, and to observe the rights of the kind from which they were created, by maintaining their ties of kinship, near and distant, and by kindness to the weak of the kind, the orphans. They are to observe the rights of the category of women of their kind by establishing justice in dealings with them, and by indicating marriage and dowry, and by legislating the rules of conduct toward women in cases of both righteousness and deviation on the part of either spouse, living with them kindly, reconciling with them, and explaining what is lawful for marriage among them, and the prohibited degrees by kinship or marriage, and rulings concerning slave-girls by right of ownership. Likewise, the rights concerning the passing of property to relatives and its distribution, and the rights of preserving the property of orphans, preserving it for them, and guardianship over them.

Then come the rulings on dealings among the community of Muslims concerning property and blood, rulings on intentional and unintentional killing, establishing the legal judgment among Muslims concerning rights and the defence of the one who has been wronged, the command to establish justice without flattery, the warning against following desire, the command to righteousness and generosity, the rendering of trusts, and the preparation for prohibiting wine.

[p. 214]

And a group of rulings on prayer, purity, and the prayer of fear. Then the conditions of the Jews, because of their numbers in Medina, the conditions of the hypocrites and their scandals, the rulings on jihad to repel the might of the polytheists, the rulings on dealing with the polytheists and their evils, the obligation of the believers to emigrate from Mecca, and the nullifying of the glories of the pre-Islamic period.

Interspersed among all this are exhortations and encouragement, a prohibition of envy and of wishing for the advantages that others have, from which whoever is deprived by the ruling of the Shariah or by the nature of creation is deprived, and encouragement to moderation in good and reform, and the spreading of love among Muslims.
